footer.text: How to read the layers. Jewish life and law covers the Judaism of Jesus' day: temple, purity, Sabbath, the groups and their expectations. Greek and Roman world covers the empire around it: rulers, taxes, meals, crucifixion, city life. The first churches covers practices the early believers made their own, such as house churches and the Lord's day. Older Near Eastern roots covers ideas much older than the first century that are still working in the text, such as the sea and the council of the gods; many other cards also give dated older background inside their own boxes.

entries.title: The wilderness
entries.summary: The dry, empty country beyond the Jordan where John preached, Jesus was tested and a crowd was fed. It was hard ground, and it was where Israel's story with God began.
aliases: today, if you hear his voice
saved a people out of Egypt
entries.plain: **We went back out to the desert where it all started.** The wilderness in the Gospels is rough, empty country with little water and wild animals. It was also the place Israel passed through after God brought them out of Egypt. When a prophet set up out there, people remembered that old story and wondered if it was starting again.
entries.then: The wilderness was a place of hardship, yet it was also the safest place to draw a crowd. Next to Isaiah 40:3, quoted in Mark 1:3, it evokes the promised new exodus (Keener). The green strip along the Jordan quickly gave way to wilderness beyond it. Jesus' forty days of testing in 1:13 echo Israel's forty years of testing in the desert. Every Passover, Jews retold how God brought them through the sea and across the wilderness. Wright says John was turning that story into a drama with his hearers as the cast. There is an older layer too. Heiser argues that the desert lay outside holy ground and was tied to chaos and forces hostile to God. Leviticus 17:7 speaks of goat demons that Israelites sacrificed to. The name Azazel on the Day of Atonement points to a realm somewhere out in the desert. The feeding in 6:35 recalls the manna: as God fed Israel in the desert, Jesus feeds the crowd in a deserted place. Many people expected a deliverer to lead a new exodus from the wilderness. Prophets like Elijah lived outside society in times of apostasy. Much Jewish tradition pictured demons living in the desert. Jewish teachers debated whether the generation that died in the wilderness would share in the world to come. Psalm 95, which warns against repeating its rebellion, was known to most Jews who recited the Psalms. Elijah, David's band and the Maccabees all took refuge in the wilderness and its caves.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a nation's leaders holding a rally on the beach where the founders first landed. Nobody has to explain the location. The place makes the speech.
entries.changes: The wilderness signals that a new exodus may be starting, so a prophet who preaches there, as in Mark 1:4, makes a claim by his choice of place. Forty days of testing in the desert, as in Matthew 4:1-2, retell Israel's forty years. A crowd fed in a deserted place recalls the manna.
entries.not: **Not a proud monument to a founding victory.** A landing beach is remembered with pride. The wilderness was also where Israel grumbled, rebelled and died out over forty years, and some pictured it as ground haunted by demons. Going back there meant testing as well as hope. People now go to the desert for rest and quiet, which was not its sense then.
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, ed. John H. Walton and Craig S. Keener (Zondervan, 2016), notes on Mark 1:4 and 1:13

usedIn.n: Matthew 3:1-12, John at the Jordan
usedIn.s: John preaches repentance in the Judean wilderness because the kingdom of heaven has come near. He calls Pharisees and Sadducees a brood of vipers and warns of the winnowing fork.

usedIn.n: Matthew 3:13-4:11, Baptism and the test in the desert
usedIn.s: Jesus is baptized and hears the voice from heaven, then is led into the wilderness for forty days, where the devil tests him three times.

usedIn.n: Matthew 14:13-36, Bread in a deserted place, a walk on the sea
usedIn.s: Jesus feeds five thousand men, besides women and children, in a deserted place, then comes to the disciples walking on the lake, and Peter tries to walk to him.

usedIn.n: Mark 1:1-13, John in the wilderness
usedIn.s: John preaches and baptizes at the Jordan, dressed like Elijah. Jesus is baptized, hears the voice from heaven and is driven into the wilderness for forty days.

usedIn.n: Mark 6:30-52, Bread in a deserted place, a walk on the sea
usedIn.s: Jesus feeds five thousand men from five loaves and two fish, then comes to his disciples walking on the lake at night.

usedIn.n: Mark 11:1-11, The ride into Jerusalem
usedIn.s: Jesus sends for a colt no one has ridden and rides into Jerusalem over cloaks and branches while the crowd shouts Hosanna.

usedIn.n: Luke 3:1-20, John's answers for toll men and soldiers
usedIn.s: In the fifteenth year of Tiberius, John preaches repentance around the Jordan. He tells the crowds to share, tax collectors to take no more than is set, and soldiers not to extort, and Herod Antipas shuts him in prison.

usedIn.n: Luke 4:1-13, The devil offers the kingdoms
usedIn.s: Full of the Spirit, Jesus is led through the wilderness for forty days, where the devil tests him with bread, with all the kingdoms of the world, and with a leap from the temple.

usedIn.n: John 1:19-34, Not the Messiah, not Elijah, not the Prophet
usedIn.s: Priests and Levites from Jerusalem ask John who he is. He denies being the Messiah, Elijah or the Prophet, calls himself the voice in the wilderness, and points to Jesus as the Lamb of God.

usedIn.n: John 3:1-21, Born from above
usedIn.s: Nicodemus, a Pharisee and ruler, comes to Jesus at night. Jesus tells him that no one sees God's kingdom without being born from above, of water and Spirit, and speaks of the Son of Man lifted up like the serpent in the wilderness.

usedIn.n: John 6:1-21, Bread in the wilderness and a walk on the sea
usedIn.s: Near Passover Jesus feeds five thousand men from five barley loaves and two fish. The crowd hails him as the Prophet and wants to make him king, and that night he comes to his disciples walking on the sea.

usedIn.n: John 6:22-71, The bread from heaven
usedIn.s: In the synagogue at Capernaum the crowd asks for a sign like the manna. Jesus answers that he is the bread of life come down from heaven, and his hard words about eating his flesh drive many disciples away.

usedIn.n: Romans 8:12-17, Not slaves but adopted heirs
usedIn.s: Those led by God's Spirit are God's children. They have received the Spirit of adoption, not of slavery, and cry Abba, Father, as heirs of God with Christ.

usedIn.n: Romans 8:18-30, Groaning and firstfruits
usedIn.s: Creation groans as in labor, waiting to be freed from decay, and believers who have the firstfruits of the Spirit groan too as they wait for their adoption and the redemption of their bodies.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 10:1-22, Israel in the desert and the table of demons
usedIn.s: Paul warns that Israel too had its baptism and its spiritual food in the wilderness, yet fell into idolatry and immorality and was struck down, and tells the Corinthians that they cannot share both the Lord's table and the table of demons.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 8:1-15, The Macedonians' giving and the manna
usedIn.s: Paul holds up the generosity of the poor Macedonian churches, appeals to Christ who became poor, and asks the Corinthians to finish their gift so that there may be equality, as there was with the manna in the wilderness.

usedIn.n: Philippians 2:12-18, Lights in a crooked generation, poured out like a drink offering
usedIn.s: Paul urges the Philippians to work out their salvation without grumbling, shining like stars in a crooked generation, and pictures himself poured out like a drink offering on their sacrifice.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 3:1-4:13, Moses the servant, and the rest still open
usedIn.s: Moses was faithful in God's house as a servant; Jesus is faithful over it as the Son. Psalm 95's warning not to harden hearts as in the wilderness still speaks today, because the rest God promised was never reached under Joshua and remains open for God's people.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 11:32-40, Sawn in two, dressed in skins
usedIn.s: Time fails to tell of the judges, David, Samuel and the prophets, who conquered kingdoms and escaped the sword. Others were tortured and refused release to gain a better resurrection; they were mocked, flogged, chained, stoned, sawn in two, and wandered in skins and caves, people the world was not worthy of.

usedIn.n: Jude 5-7, Israel in the desert, the angels who left their place, and Sodom
usedIn.s: Jude reminds his readers that the Lord who saved a people out of Egypt later destroyed those who did not believe; that the angels who did not keep their position are held in darkness, bound in everlasting chains, for the judgment of the great day; and that Sodom and Gomorrah serve as an example of the punishment of eternal fire.

usedIn.n: Revelation 12:1-6, the woman, the child and the dragon
usedIn.s: A radiant woman, crowned with twelve stars and standing on the moon, labors to give birth while a great red dragon waits to devour her child. The child, destined to rule the nations, is caught up to God's throne, and the woman escapes to the wilderness, where she is kept safe for 1,260 days.

entries.title: The sea
entries.summary: To ancient Israel the sea stood for chaos and danger that only God could command. The Gospel stories on the lake of Galilee lean on that old picture.
aliases: the sea gave up its dead
entries.plain: **The storm did not care who was in the boat.** We think of a lake as a place to fish or swim. The Israelites were not sailors. For them deep water was where things went wrong, and their Scriptures pictured God taming the raging sea, sometimes as a monster he beat. When the lake in the Gospels turns violent, that old picture is close by.
entries.then: The roots are older than Israel. In the stories from Ugarit, a city in ancient Syria, the god Baal fights Yamm, the Sea. Yamm is a deity pictured as a violent, dragon-like monster, and Baal wins kingship over the gods by beating him (Heiser). Psalm 74 uses the same language for the God of Israel: he split the sea and crushed the heads of Leviathan. Heiser writes, "In the ancient world the sea was a thing of dread." The Psalms carry this into Jewish faith: God rules the raging of the sea and stills its waves (Psalms 65:7; 89:9; 107:29). Jewish people understood that God controls wind and waves, and they did not expect it of a human being. Some Jewish traditions had demons bound in bodies of water. Fishermen aside, Jews did not take to the sea and left seafaring to the Phoenicians. Wright adds, "In books like Daniel, the sea is where the monsters come from." The lake itself was dangerous. The surrounding hills can funnel sudden storms onto the water. The lake lies 696 feet below sea level, which produces violent downdrafts. Only local people called this lake a sea, so the usage reflects the memories of Jesus' Galilean disciples (Keener). Greek stories of figures who ruled wind and wave were set in a distant past. In Jewish tradition absolute authority over the sea belonged to God alone. The only one the Old Testament says trod upon the waters was God himself. Revelation's beast rises from the sea, and its new creation has no sea at all, which Heiser reads as chaos gone for good.
entries.bridge: An analogy: the deep forest in old village tales, the place past the last field where the rules of home stop working. Everyone has heard a story about something that came out of it.
entries.changes: The sea stands for chaos that only God commands, so a man who stills a storm, as in Mark 4:39, or walks on the water, as in Matthew 14:25, raises the question of who he is. Spirits sent into the sea go back to the place of disorder. Revelation 21:1 ends the story with no more sea.
entries.not: **Not a spooky place in folk stories.** Village tales leave the forest wild and unexplained. Israel's Scriptures put the sea under God's rule: he fought it, split it and stilled it, so the picture was about who rules creation. The lake was also an everyday workplace for Galilee's fishermen, and no one there worshiped it.
entries.dissent: What the storm shows about Jesus. The ESV Study Bible reads the calming of the storm as evidence that this man is truly God, since in the Old Testament it is God who calms the waves. Wright reads it through Daniel 7: just as one like a son of man puts the sea monsters to flight, Jesus takes the role of God's agent defeating the forces of chaos. Keener notes only that Jewish people expected this power of God and not of a human being.
sources: Michael S. Heiser, The Unseen Realm, ch. 19, Who Is like Yahweh?, and ch. 42, Describing the Indescribable

A sea monster God crushes in one poem and plays with in another.
A chaos monster God cuts to pieces, and also a nickname for Egypt.
Sea monsters, which Genesis pointedly lists among the things God made and called good.

usedIn.n: Matthew 4:12-25, Capernaum, fishermen and crowds
usedIn.s: Jesus moves to Capernaum, Galilee of the Gentiles, announces the kingdom of heaven, calls four fishermen, and draws crowds from Galilee, the Ten Towns, Jerusalem and beyond the Jordan.

usedIn.n: Matthew 8:18-34, Let the dead bury their dead, the storm and Gadara
usedIn.s: Jesus answers two would-be followers, calms a storm on the lake, and frees two men possessed by demons in the region of the Gadarenes.

usedIn.n: Matthew 13:1-23, The sower
usedIn.s: From a boat Jesus tells the parable of the sower to the crowd on the shore, explains why he speaks in parables, and interprets the story for his disciples.

usedIn.n: Matthew 14:13-36, Bread in a deserted place, a walk on the sea
usedIn.s: Jesus feeds five thousand men, besides women and children, in a deserted place, then comes to the disciples walking on the lake, and Peter tries to walk to him.

usedIn.n: Mark 1:14-20, Fishermen called
usedIn.s: Jesus announces that God's kingdom is near, then calls two pairs of brothers from their nets on the Sea of Galilee.

usedIn.n: Mark 4:35-41, The storm on the lake
usedIn.s: A storm swamps the boat while Jesus sleeps. He rebukes the wind and the sea, and the disciples ask who he is.

usedIn.n: Mark 5:1-20, Legion among the tombs
usedIn.s: Across the lake, in Gentile country, Jesus frees a man possessed by many spirits. They enter a herd of pigs that rushes into the sea.

usedIn.n: Mark 6:30-52, Bread in a deserted place, a walk on the sea
usedIn.s: Jesus feeds five thousand men from five loaves and two fish, then comes to his disciples walking on the lake at night.

usedIn.n: Luke 5:1-11, A catch that breaks the nets
usedIn.s: Jesus teaches from Simon's boat, then tells the tired fishermen to let down their nets in deep water. The catch nearly sinks two boats, and Simon, James and John leave everything to follow him.

usedIn.n: John 6:1-21, Bread in the wilderness and a walk on the sea
usedIn.s: Near Passover Jesus feeds five thousand men from five barley loaves and two fish. The crowd hails him as the Prophet and wants to make him king, and that night he comes to his disciples walking on the sea.

usedIn.n: John 21:1-14, Breakfast on the beach
usedIn.s: Back in Galilee, seven disciples fish all night and catch nothing. At dawn a man on the shore tells them to cast to the right side, the net fills with 153 large fish, and Jesus gives them bread and fish by a charcoal fire.

usedIn.n: Acts 27:1-26, Sailing late in the season
usedIn.s: Paul sails for Rome in the custody of a centurion named Julius, changing to an Alexandrian grain ship at Myra. With the Fast already past, the owner presses on against Paul's warning, and a northeaster drives the ship helpless for days until an angel promises Paul that all aboard will live.

usedIn.n: Revelation 12:1-6, the woman, the child and the dragon
usedIn.s: A radiant woman, crowned with twelve stars and standing on the moon, labors to give birth while a great red dragon waits to devour her child. The child, destined to rule the nations, is caught up to God's throne, and the woman escapes to the wilderness, where she is kept safe for 1,260 days.

usedIn.n: Revelation 13:1-10, the beast from the sea
usedIn.s: A beast with ten horns and seven heads rises from the sea, built from Daniel's leopard, bear and lion, and the dragon gives it his power. One head seems to have had a fatal wound that healed, the whole earth follows it in awe, and it is allowed to blaspheme and to make war on God's people for forty-two months.

usedIn.n: Revelation 20:7-15, Gog and Magog and the great white throne
usedIn.s: Released at the end of the thousand years, Satan gathers Gog and Magog, the nations from the four corners of the earth, around the camp of God's people, but fire from heaven consumes them and the devil is thrown into the lake of fire. Before a great white throne the dead, given up by the sea, death and Hades, are judged from the books, and anyone not found in the book of life is thrown into the lake of fire, the second death.

usedIn.n: Revelation 21:1-8, new heaven, new earth, no more sea
usedIn.s: John sees a new heaven and a new earth, with no more sea, and the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down from God like a bride dressed for her husband. A voice announces that God's dwelling is now with people, that he will wipe away every tear, and that he makes all things new; the thirsty will drink freely, while the cowardly, the faithless, murderers, sorcerers, idolaters and liars have their place in the lake of fire.

entries.title: Gentile territory
entries.summary: Across the lake and to the north lay Greek-run cities with pagan temples and pig herds. Jesus crossed into them more than once.
entries.plain: **Just over the border the signs changed language and the butcher sold pork.** Galilee was Jewish, but its neighbors were not. The Ten Towns across the lake, Tyre and Sidon on the coast, and Caesarea Philippi up north were Greek and Roman cities with other gods. A Jew who went there knew he was in someone else's country.
entries.then: The Decapolis was a group of Hellenistic cities near Galilee whose people were mostly Gentile, which explains the pigs in 5:11, since Jews would not have kept them. That side of the lake had never really been Jewish territory (Wright). Since Alexander, Greeks had been a ruling class, and Tyre and Sidon now considered themselves Greek. Some scholars suggest those cities lived off the countryside and imports from Judea. Caesarea Philippi was a Gentile city about 25 miles north of the lake. Its older name, Paneas, honored the god Pan, and Herod the Great built a temple there for worshiping Caesar. The ESV Study Bible traces its worship there from Baal to Pan and then to Caesar. Heiser places it in the Old Testament region of Bashan, at the foot of Mount Hermon. He says it was famous for Pan and for a temple to Zeus, who in Jesus' day was considered incarnate in Augustus. The Hebrew word for non-Jews carries overtones of both ancestry and idol worship, and there were taboos against contact (Wright). Some Jews shook the dust from their feet when leaving pagan territory. Josephus describes Panium, where Herod built a white marble temple near the springs of the Jordan, under a high mountain. Above it, Josephus writes, "a dark cave opens itself; within which there is a horrible precipice, that descends abruptly to a vast depth." The gates of Hades was a familiar phrase in the Old Testament, Greek literature and Jewish tradition. It meant the realm and power of death (Job 38:17).
entries.bridge: An analogy: driving across a border into a country with a different religion, a different language on the signs and different food. Nothing happens at the line, but everything around you says you are a foreigner now.
entries.changes: Crossing into Gentile territory puts Jesus among pigs, pagan temples and people outside Israel's law, as in Mark 5:11. Galilee itself was ringed by Greek cities, which is why Matthew 4:15 can call it Galilee of the Gentiles. Shaking off the dust on leaving a town treated it as pagan ground.
entries.not: **Not a trip abroad across a guarded national border.** These Gentile cities sat right beside Galilee, ringed it, and had Jews living in them. What marked the line was worship and purity. Some Jews shook the dust of pagan ground off their feet when they left, which no modern border asks of a traveler.
entries.dissent: First, the dogs saying in 7:27. Bailey argues that Jesus voices his disciples' prejudice against women and Gentiles in order to expose it. He also sets the woman a hard test, which she passes with honor. The ESV Study Bible reads it as a test of her faith, with the word first holding out hope for Gentiles. Keener puts the weight on the priority of Israel, which she has to acknowledge. He also notes the suggestion that her class had been taking bread the countryside needed. Second, the gates of Hades in Matthew 16:18. Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes read the realm and power of death: not even martyrdom will stop the church. Heiser places the saying at the foot of Hermon, where 1 Enoch says the Watchers came down. He argues the church is on the attack, since "Gates are defensive structures, not offensive weapons." Wright suggests that some Jewish traditions placed the gates of the underworld at the Jerusalem temple, which Jesus' new building replaces.
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Mark 3:8, 5:1, 5:17, 6:11, 7:26, 7:27, 7:31 and 8:27, and note on Matthew 16:18

usedIn.n: Matthew 9:35-10:15, The Twelve sent with nothing
usedIn.s: Seeing the crowds as sheep without a shepherd, Jesus sends twelve apostles to the lost sheep of Israel, with no money, bag or staff, to stay with whoever will have them.

usedIn.n: Matthew 15:21-28, A Canaanite mother and the dogs
usedIn.s: In the region of Tyre and Sidon a Canaanite woman begs the Son of David to free her daughter. Jesus is silent, then speaks of bread and dogs, and her answer wins him over.

usedIn.n: Matthew 16:13-28, The rock, the keys and the cross
usedIn.s: At Caesarea Philippi Peter confesses Jesus as the Messiah, the Son of the living God, and is called the rock and given the keys. When Jesus speaks of his death, Peter rebukes him and is called Satan.

usedIn.n: Matthew 28:16-20, Make disciples of all nations
usedIn.s: On a mountain in Galilee the risen Jesus claims all authority in heaven and on earth and sends the eleven to make disciples of all nations, baptizing and teaching them.

usedIn.n: Mark 5:1-20, Legion among the tombs
usedIn.s: Across the lake, in Gentile country, Jesus frees a man possessed by many spirits. They enter a herd of pigs that rushes into the sea.

usedIn.n: Mark 7:24-37, A Greek woman and a deaf man
usedIn.s: In the region of Tyre a Gentile mother asks Jesus to free her daughter, and answers his saying about dogs. In the Decapolis he heals a deaf man.

usedIn.n: Mark 8:27-9:1, Peter's answer at Caesarea Philippi
usedIn.s: Asked who he is, Peter says the Messiah. Jesus says the Son of Man must suffer, rebukes Peter, and calls followers to take up the cross.

usedIn.n: Luke 4:16-30, The year of the Lord's favor in Nazareth
usedIn.s: In the Nazareth synagogue Jesus reads Isaiah's promise of good news for the poor and release for captives and says it is fulfilled today. When he points to Elijah and Elisha helping foreigners, the town tries to throw him off a cliff.

usedIn.n: Luke 15:11-32, A father and two lost sons
usedIn.s: A younger son takes his share of the estate early, wastes it in a far country, and comes home to a father who runs to meet him. The older brother refuses to join the feast.

usedIn.n: Acts 10:24-11:18, Peter in Cornelius's house
usedIn.s: Peter enters a Gentile home, preaches Jesus, and sees the Spirit fall on the uncircumcised listeners. In Jerusalem he is criticized for eating with Gentiles, and his account silences the critics.

usedIn.n: Acts 13:13-52, The synagogue at Pisidian Antioch
usedIn.s: Invited to speak after the synagogue readings in a Roman colony, Paul tells Israel's story from the exodus to Jesus. Gentiles welcome the message, and the city's leading men and women drive the apostles out.

entries.title: Galilee and the Galileans
entries.summary: Small farming and fishing villages, ringed by Greek cities, with two new royal towns that the Gospels never say Jesus entered. Most of Jesus' story happens in places of a few hundred to a few thousand people.
entries.plain: **Everybody in the village knew whose son he was, which is why nobody would listen to him.** Galilee in Jesus' day was a country of villages: farmers, fishermen and craftsmen who knew each other's families. Nazareth was small. Capernaum was a bigger fishing town on the lake and on a trade road. A few miles from Nazareth stood Sepphoris, a city burned in a revolt and rebuilt by Herod Antipas.
entries.then: In the second century BC many Gentiles in Galilee were made Jews by force, and many Judeans then moved in. By Jesus' day most Galileans were Jewish by descent and by faith (Keener). The territories of Greek cities surrounded Galilee on every side except the Samaritan south. Capernaum was a fishing town of perhaps 1,000 to 2,000 people. It lay on the caravan route from Damascus to Caesarea, later called the way of the sea. Estimates for Nazareth run from about 200 to 2,000. Archaeology suggests settlers from Judea there, and it sat on a road a few miles from Sepphoris. After Herod the Great's death, says Josephus, the Roman general Varus "took Sepphoris, and made its inhabitants slaves, and burnt the city". Antipas later walled it and made it the chief city of Galilee. Most larger farming towns had fewer than three thousand people. The Gospels never place Jesus in Sepphoris or Tiberias. Galilee under Antipas and Judea under a Roman prefect were separate jurisdictions. Jerusalemites often looked down on Galileans as backward country people.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a string of farm towns around a lake, where the county seat burned in a riot when you were a boy and has been rebuilt by the governor's men. Everyone shops and works near it. Nobody from the villages feels at home there.
entries.changes: Village scale explains why one family's reputation could close a town's ears, and why a crowd of thousands in a deserted place, as at Mark 6:44, was larger than the towns it came from. Galilee's position, Jewish but ringed by Gentile cities on trade roads, is why Matthew 4:15 can call it Galilee of the Gentiles. The new royal cities are absent from the Gospels, so Jesus' work reads as village work. Jerusalem's leaders dismiss the idea of a prophet from Galilee in John 7:52.
entries.not: **Not a local riot and a county rebuilding.** Sepphoris was burned by a Roman army that enslaved its people, and Antipas rebuilt it as his capital under Rome, so the power behind it was foreign. The Gospels never place Jesus there. Nor was Galilee a backwater: Nazareth sat near a major road, and trade routes brought Gentiles through.
entries.dissent: Two points. First, how big were the villages? Josephus claims that Galilee's towns were so full that "the very least of them contain above fifteen thousand inhabitants." Keener puts most larger farming towns under three thousand people. The study Bibles estimate Nazareth at about 200 to 2,000. Second, who are the Jews in John's Gospel? Bailey notes that the Greek word means both Jews and Judeans, and says Jesus' quarrel was with the Judeans. Wright translates it Judaeans throughout. Keener reads it as usually the Jerusalem authorities, whom John matches with the opponents of his own day. The ESV Study Bible reads it as the leaders opposed to Jesus and the ordinary people who followed them. The cultural backgrounds article says most negative uses mean the Judean leaders. It suggests John may be turning the tables on synagogue leaders who treated his readers as outsiders. Carson, Moo and Morris say the hostility turns on accepting or rejecting revelation, not on race. They call anti-Semitic the wrong category for a book they think was written by a Jew, largely for Jews and proselytes.

usedIn.n: Matthew 2:13-23, Refugees in Egypt, home to Nazareth
usedIn.s: Joseph takes the family to Egypt by night. Herod kills the boys of Bethlehem, and after his death the family settles in Nazareth to stay clear of his son Archelaus.

usedIn.n: Matthew 4:12-25, Capernaum, fishermen and crowds
usedIn.s: Jesus moves to Capernaum, Galilee of the Gentiles, announces the kingdom of heaven, calls four fishermen, and draws crowds from Galilee, the Ten Towns, Jerusalem and beyond the Jordan.

usedIn.n: Matthew 11:2-30, John's question, children in the square, an easy yoke
usedIn.s: John asks from prison whether Jesus is the one to come. Jesus praises John, compares his generation to sulking children, pronounces woes on the lake towns, and offers rest under his yoke.

usedIn.n: Matthew 13:53-58, No honor in Nazareth
usedIn.s: Teaching in his hometown synagogue, Jesus is dismissed as the carpenter's son whose family everyone knows, and he says a prophet is not without honor except at home.

usedIn.n: Luke 1:26-56, A village girl, a greeting and a song of reversal
usedIn.s: Gabriel greets Mary, a betrothed girl in Nazareth, with news that she will bear the son of David. She goes to Elizabeth in the hill country and sings of God bringing down rulers and lifting up the humble.

usedIn.n: John 1:35-51, Come and see
usedIn.s: Two of John's disciples follow Jesus and spend the day with him. Andrew brings his brother Simon, Philip brings Nathanael, and Jesus promises they will see heaven opened and angels going up and down on the Son of Man.

usedIn.n: John 7:1-36, Up to the Festival of Tabernacles
usedIn.s: Jesus stays in Galilee while the Judeans look for a chance to kill him, then goes up to Tabernacles privately and teaches in the temple. The crowds argue over whether he is a deceiver or the Messiah, and the chief priests send guards to arrest him.

usedIn.n: John 7:37-52, Rivers of living water on the last day
usedIn.s: On the great last day of the feast Jesus cries out that the thirsty should come to him and drink. The crowd divides over whether he is the Prophet or the Messiah, and the Pharisees scorn a prophet from Galilee.

usedIn.n: John 11:1-44, Lazarus four days in the tomb
usedIn.s: Jesus waits two days after hearing that his friend Lazarus is ill, reaches Bethany to find him four days buried, weeps with the mourners, and calls him out of the tomb still bound in his grave clothes.

entries.title: Sowing, harvest and threshing
entries.summary: The farming year every hearer lived by: seed scattered on thin and thorny ground, weeds that look like wheat, the harvest rush, and grain winnowed in the wind while the chaff burned.
entries.plain: **Every farmer knows some of the seed will be wasted, and a good year still pays for it.** Most of Jesus' hearers grew their own food. They sowed by hand, often before plowing, so seed fell on paths, rocks and thorns. At harvest the grain was cut, carried to the village threshing floor and tossed in the wind so the light chaff blew away to be burned.
entries.then: Most people in the empire, and in Galilee, lived on the land. Jesus' stories stay with farmers, where later rabbinic parables favor royal courts (Keener). Seed was often, though not always, sown before plowing, so it met all the fates in the parable of the sower. Blomberg, citing Philip Payne, says both orders were used and some waste came either way. A tenfold yield was average for much of the land; thirty, sixty and a hundredfold were very good harvests. Darnel, a poisonous weed, looks like wheat until it heads, and its roots tangle with the wheat's. Dried, it could be burned as fuel. Grain was winnowed by tossing it into the wind, and the chaff was burned. Ripe grain had to come in quickly, so landowners hired extra hands. Jewish writers already used harvest as a picture of the end (4 Ezra 4:30-32). God as sower and people as soil were standard Jewish images (Blomberg). In Judea the first rains came in autumn, in October and November. The winter rains, about three quarters of the year's total, came from December. The late rains of March and April readied the grain. The wheat harvest ran from mid-April and was over by late May, sooner than in Greece or Italy. Grapes were picked around August or September and tipped into long troughs of wood or stone. There they were trodden, often to a flute, and wine was called the blood of grapes (Genesis 49:11). Harvest and vintage were the high points of joy in the farming year (Wright).
entries.bridge: An analogy: a farm family watching the weather in the last week before harvest. Everyone knows what a good yield looks like, what a weed costs, and that when the grain is ready, the work cannot wait.
entries.changes: Farm images were the common stock of village speech, so a sower, a weed or a harvest worker needed no explanation. Harvest and winnowing were already pictures of God's judgment, which is how John uses them at Matthew 3:12. The yields in Mark 4:8 are very good harvests, not impossible ones, and the urgent harvest of Matthew 9:37-38 is a call for hired hands.
entries.not: **Not a farm with machines, forecasts and crop insurance.** An ancient family sowed by hand, waited on the autumn and spring rains, and had nothing to fall back on if the crop failed. A bad harvest meant hunger. The images are also not gardening tips; they come from work that fed the family.
entries.dissent: Two farming questions. On sowing before plowing, Keener says seed was often sown first, and Blomberg, citing Payne, says both orders were in use. On an enemy sowing weeds in a field, Keener's cultural backgrounds notes say ancient legal sources show feuding farmers did it. Blomberg says Roman laws against it show it happened somewhere, but not that it happened in Palestine in Jesus' day.

usedIn.s: John preaches repentance in the Judean wilderness because the kingdom of heaven has come near. He calls Pharisees and Sadducees a brood of vipers and warns of the winnowing fork.

usedIn.n: Matthew 9:35-10:15, The Twelve sent with nothing
usedIn.s: Seeing the crowds as sheep without a shepherd, Jesus sends twelve apostles to the lost sheep of Israel, with no money, bag or staff, to stay with whoever will have them.

usedIn.n: Matthew 13:1-23, The sower
usedIn.s: From a boat Jesus tells the parable of the sower to the crowd on the shore, explains why he speaks in parables, and interprets the story for his disciples.

usedIn.n: Matthew 13:24-52, Darnel, mustard, yeast, treasure and a net
usedIn.s: More parables of the kingdom: weeds sown among wheat, a mustard seed, yeast in flour, treasure in a field, a pearl, and a dragnet, with the weeds and the net explained as the judgment at the end of the age.

usedIn.n: Matthew 20:1-16, A day's wage for an hour's work
usedIn.s: A landowner hires laborers for his vineyard at dawn and again through the day, then pays everyone a full denarius, starting with the last. Those hired first complain.

usedIn.n: Luke 13:10-21, A bent woman freed on the Sabbath; mustard and leaven
usedIn.s: Teaching in a synagogue on the Sabbath, Jesus frees a woman bent double for eighteen years. The synagogue ruler objects, and Jesus answers with an ox untied for water, then compares God's kingdom to a mustard seed and to leaven.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 15:35-58, Seeds, stars and the last trumpet
usedIn.s: Asked what kind of body the dead will have, Paul answers with the seed that dies and rises as a plant and with the differing glories of sun, moon and stars, sets the first Adam beside the last, and ends with the trumpet and death swallowed up.

usedIn.n: Galatians 5:13-6:10, Flesh and Spirit, burdens and teachers
usedIn.s: Called to freedom, the Galatians are to serve one another in love, which fulfills the law; Paul sets the works of the flesh against the fruit of the Spirit and urges them to restore the fallen gently, carry each other's burdens, share with their teachers and keep doing good.

usedIn.n: James 5:7-12, Early and late rains, Job, and no oaths
usedIn.s: James tells the oppressed to be patient until the Lord comes, as a farmer waits for the autumn and spring rains, to stop grumbling, to remember the prophets and Job, and above all not to swear.

usedIn.n: Revelation 14:6-20, Babylon fallen, the harvest and the winepress
usedIn.s: Three angels announce an eternal gospel, the fall of Babylon and the undiluted cup of God's wrath for those who worship the beast, and a voice blesses those who die in the Lord. Then one like a son of man reaps the earth's grain with a sickle, and an angel gathers its grapes into the great winepress, from which blood flows as high as the horses' bridles.

entries.title: Estates, tenants and day laborers
entries.summary: Wealthy owners, often living in town, let their land to tenant farmers for a share of the crop or hired day laborers in the marketplace and paid them a denarius at sundown.
aliases: the rich in this present world
entries.plain: **The men stood on the corner at dawn, hoping a truck would stop and someone would point at them.** Much farmland belonged to rich owners who lived somewhere else. Some let it to tenant farmers, who paid part of each harvest as rent. Others hired day laborers, who waited in the marketplace to be picked, worked from sunrise, and were paid that evening, because one day's pay fed a family for one day.
entries.then: Much of the rural empire belonged to wealthy landowners who lived in leisure, usually far off in cities. Tenant farmers worked their estates. Most were free peasants, as in Egypt, but some were slaves, as in Italy (Keener). Most Galileans worked the land. Many owned plots, but many landless peasants worked on larger estates. Tenants paid at harvest, either a share or a set amount. A share was usually at least a quarter and sometimes half. A new vineyard took about four years to turn a profit. Landowners held the legal and social power, and a few reportedly kept squads of hired killers for troublesome tenants. Such disputes were not uncommon. Blomberg, citing the papyri, writes that in them "possession was more than nine-tenths of the law of ownership". Sharecropping was old. A census of Harran under the Assyrian king Sargon II (722 to 705 BC) lists almost all tenant farmers (Podany). One, Se'-idri, tended 5,000 vines for a landowner and paid him a share of the crop, so a bad year meant a lower rent. Day laborers included tenants with small plots, sons who had inherited no land and men who had lost theirs. They waited in the marketplace, and work began around sunrise. A denarius was the usual day's wage. The law required paying them the same day, since the wage barely covered a day's needs (Deuteronomy 24:14-15). Bailey has watched jobless men wait each morning by the Damascus Gate in Jerusalem, hoping to be hired. Beyond the land, a rich class of merchants and shipowners grew in harbor cities such as Ephesus.
entries.bridge: An analogy: an owner who lives in the capital and rents out the family farm, and a hiring hall where workers wait each morning to be picked. Everyone in farm country knows both arrangements, and who holds the power in each.
entries.changes: Landowners, tenants and day laborers were familiar figures, so a story about a vineyard owner, as in Matthew 20:1-16 or Mark 12:1-9, could set God in the owner's place and the hearers among the workers. James 5:4 hears the withheld wages of field workers crying out against the rich.
entries.not: **Not a modern employer and employee.** There was no contract, no union and no safety net. A laborer still unhired at noon would have nothing to take home that night.
entries.dissent: Two points. First, why does the owner in Matthew 20 keep hiring through the day? Keener reads harvest urgency, with the crop to be brought in before dark. Bailey reads compassion for men who would otherwise go home with nothing. Blomberg allows the harvest setting but calls the owner's repeated failure to calculate his needs extraordinary. He calls deliberate overhiring just as unusual. Second, how should the owners and tenants be read? Some recent readings, following William Herzog, make the owners oppressive landlords and the tenants their victims. Blomberg rejects this, and reports Craig Evans's evidence that some tenants were comparatively well off.

usedIn.s: James rebukes traders who plan a year of business without God, then turns on rich landowners whose hoarded wealth is rotting, whose withheld wages cry out to the Lord of hosts, and who have fattened themselves for a day of slaughter and condemned the righteous one.

entries.title: Debts, talents and lending
entries.summary: A denarius was a day's pay and a talent about six thousand of them. Creditors could jail a debtor until someone paid, and people with spare money buried it or lent it at steep interest.
entries.plain: **He owed more than the whole town would earn in a lifetime, and everyone listening laughed at the number.** The Gospels count money in denarii and talents. A denarius was about a day's wage for a laborer; a talent was worth about six thousand of them. A debtor could be thrown in prison until someone paid for him, and anyone with spare money either buried it or lent it out at high interest.
entries.then: A talent was a unit of account, not a coin. It was worth about six thousand denarii, and a denarius was an average day's wage (Keener). Others put it differently: about twenty years' wages (ESV Study Bible), six thousand days' wages (CSB Study Bible), or fifteen years' earnings (Wright). Josephus puts the yearly tribute from Galilee and Perea under Herod at two hundred talents. I will repay was a standard promise in promissory notes. Creditors are reported choking debtors. A jailed man could not pay unless friends raised the money. Keener calls selling a debtor's wife and children a Gentile practice that Jews of this period found abhorrent. Jewish law forbade the torture that Gentile kings and Herod used. Few had capital, so those who did lent it at high rates. Temples doubled as banks, and Keener reports a patron who lent to a city at about fifty percent. The law forbade interest from fellow Israelites (Deuteronomy 23:19-20). Many wealthy Jewish aristocrats followed Greek custom anyway. Burying money was among the safest ways to protect it, and Blomberg cites a rabbinic saying commending it. The law cancelled debts in the seventh year and the Jubilee (Deuteronomy 15; Leviticus 25). So lenders grew wary as the release neared, and teachers found a way around it. The Dead Sea Scrolls read Isaiah 61 as a Jubilee promise, though some scholars doubt the Jubilee was still kept. Kings proclaimed releases long before. Around 2450 BC Enmetena of Lagash cancelled grain loans and reunited mothers and children held as debt slaves. In the Old Babylonian period, about 2004 to 1595 BC, kings every decade or so cancelled private debts. They also freed debt slaves and returned land sold under stress (Podany). The likeness to the sabbatical release is drawn here, not by Podany.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a gambling debt in the billions run up by a middle manager. The number alone tells listeners the story has left the real world, and that no payment plan could ever cover it.
entries.changes: Ancient Judaism often spoke of sins as debts before God, Keener notes, so a story about an unpayable debt, as in Matthew 18:24, measures what God forgives. Because the law already released debts in the seventh year, lending to the poor without hope of return, as in Luke 6:34-35, goes beyond what the law asked. Paul's promise in Philemon 19, I will repay, uses the wording of a promissory note.
entries.not: **Not a debt that only the debtor answers for.** A modern gambler faces a bankruptcy court, and his family keeps its freedom. In Matthew 18 the king orders the man, his wife and his children sold, and jail held a debtor until friends paid. The size of the sum works the same way; the stakes for the household do not.
entries.dissent: Three questions. First, was selling a debtor's family a Gentile practice or a common one? Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes say Jewish teachers forbade it and the king in Matthew 18 is a Gentile. The ESV Study Bible calls it common in the ancient world, pointing to 2 Kings 4:1 and Nehemiah 5. Second, was burying entrusted money prudent? Blomberg notes that a rabbinic maxim commended burial, so the servant may have looked careful. Keener says a deposit earning interest would have been just as safe, so the servant simply did not care. The cultural backgrounds notes say the money would have been safe with the bankers. The ESV Study Bible says there were no banks and burying valuables was common. Third, what was the document cancelled in Colossians 2:14? Keener and the ESV Study Bible read a handwritten note of debt before God. Keener writes, "Paul intends his readers to think of an IOU before God". The CSB Study Bible allows that it is the law of Moses. Wright reads the verse as the Torah set aside, the law of Moses that kept Gentiles out.

usedIn.s: Paul appeals to Philemon, on the basis of love, for Onesimus, the slave who became Paul's son in prison: he sends him back to be received as a beloved brother rather than as a slave, asks Philemon to welcome him as he would Paul, offers to repay anything he owes, and asks for a guest room.

entries.title: Fishing on the lake
entries.summary: Fishing was a real business on the lake of Galilee: boats, costly nets, partnerships between families, work through the night and fish sold in the morning. Fishermen did better than most peasants.
entries.plain: **They had been out all night, caught nothing, and still had to clean the nets before they could sleep.** Fishing on the lake of Galilee was hard work, but it paid better than most farming. Boats and nets cost a lot, so families went into business together. Much of the fishing was done at night, the catch went to market in the morning, and torn nets had to be mended before the next trip.
entries.then: Fishermen used a circular casting net about fifteen feet across, weighted with lead sinkers and thrown in shallow water. In deeper water they used a dragnet. Many found it easier to catch fish before sunrise, and the night's catch was sold in the morning (Keener). Washing the nets meant clearing out everything that was not edible. Equipment was costly, so fishermen often worked in cooperatives, and families joined together for profit. Other fishing cooperatives are known from ancient Palestine, so a partnership between Simon and Zebedee's family was nothing unusual. Torn nets had to be mended before the next trip. For those with less money that could mean taking a loan. A Galilean fishing boat that survives is about 27 feet long and 7.5 feet wide. It is built mostly of cedar planks, with a mast and four places for rowers. Garland measures it at 25.5 by 7.5 by 4.5 feet, with room for a crew of five and ten passengers. A trammel net could stretch five hundred feet and needed two boats (Garland). Fishermen were not elite, but they were usually better off than the peasant majority, and their work was less seasonal. Josephus says of the lake, "There are several kinds of fish in it, different both to the taste and the sight from those elsewhere." Bailey pictures the scene in Luke 5 as a crowd pressing onto a smelly landing. Tired men are cleaning empty nets after a fruitless night.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a family fishing business on a coast today, with a boat bought on credit, brothers and cousins sharing the crew, and the catch auctioned at dawn. Walking away from it means walking away from the family's living.
entries.changes: Leaving the boats and nets, as in Mark 1:18-20, gave up a better than average living and a family business. A catch large enough to break the nets and fill two boats, as in Luke 5:6-7, is a sign told in the trade's own terms. In John 21:3-6 the disciples go back to the boats, catch nothing in the night, and are told where to cast.
entries.not: **Not an independent business selling on an open market.** A modern family firm owns its boat once the loan is paid and sells to whoever bids. Galilean fishermen, Garland argues, leased their fishing rights and sold through a cooperative to wealthier middlemen, though how well off they were is disputed. Nor was it a hobby; the work fed the family.
entries.dissent: How well off were fishermen? Keener's notes say many believe they were not elite but usually better off than the peasant majority. Hired men in the boat point to a family business with ample income. Garland disagrees. Owning a boat no more made Zebedee's family well off than owning oxen made a farmer rich. Fishermen leased their fishing rights and probably belonged to a cooperative that sold to wealthier middlemen.

usedIn.n: John 21:1-14, Breakfast on the beach
usedIn.s: Back in Galilee, seven disciples fish all night and catch nothing. At dawn a man on the shore tells them to cast to the right side, the net fills with 153 large fish, and Jesus gives them bread and fish by a charcoal fire.

entries.title: The village house
entries.summary: Most village families lived in one main room, with a lower end by the door where the animals spent the night, a flat roof of beams, branches and mud, and sometimes a guest room on the roof or built on at the end.
entries.plain: **At night the donkey came in, the door was barred, and the whole family slept on mats in the one big room.** A village house in Jesus' world was simple. The family cooked, ate and slept in one main room. At the door end, a little lower, the animals were brought in each night, with feeding troughs cut into the floor. The roof was flat, reached by an outside stair, and made of beams covered with branches and packed mud. Some homes had a guest room on the roof or built on at the end.
entries.then: Bailey had seen such homes in Upper Galilee and in Bethlehem. He describes simple village houses with two rooms. One was a guest room, attached to the end of the house or built on the roof. The other was a family room where everyone cooked, ate and slept. The end of the family room by the door was lower or fenced off with timbers. The cow, the donkey and a few sheep were driven in there each night and tied in the courtyard by day. Mangers were cut into the floor. Bailey finds the same house behind 1 Samuel 28:24 and Judges 11, and behind the saying that one lamp gives light to everyone in the house. Wright likewise places the birth of Luke 2:7 on the ground floor of a house, where animals were often kept. Many homes had a single room. The children slept on mats on its floor, and the door was secured by a heavy bar run through rings. Roofs were beams laid over with branches or reeds and packed mud, reached by an outside staircase. They were strong enough to walk on and soft enough to dig through. Luke describes the tiled roofs his own readers knew. Flat roofs were used for work and rest, and a voice from them carried over the street. Walls of dried mud could be dug through, though better-off homes were built of stone.
entries.bridge: An analogy: an old farmhouse where the kitchen is the only warm room, the family sleeps by the stove in winter, and the animals are just through the door. Nobody thinks it strange; it is how a working family lives.
entries.changes: If the crowded space in Luke 2:7 was a guest room, the manger stood in an ordinary family room, not a stable. A roof of mud and branches can be opened to lower a sick man, as in Mark 2:4. Peter goes up on the flat roof to pray in Acts 10:9.
entries.not: **Not a farmhouse with the animals in a barn next door.** In the village house the animals came into the family room itself each night, at its lower end, with mangers cut into the floor. Bailey notes farmers wanted them inside for warmth and safety from thieves. It was ordinary and no sign of poverty or rejection.
entries.dissent: What was the crowded place in Luke 2:7? Bailey, following Plummer, reads it as the guest room of a private home. He points to Luke 22:11, where the same Greek word, katalyma, names a guest room. The baby is laid in a manger in the family room. Wright reads the ground floor of a house. Keener's background commentary takes the word as home or guest room, with the birth perhaps in a vacant cave outside used for livestock. The ESV Study Bible takes it as a public lodging place for travelers, full because of the census. The CSB Study Bible reads no room anywhere in Bethlehem, so the family used a stable or a cave. The cave tradition is early. Keener's notes say it was circulating in Bethlehem by the early second century, and Bailey traces it to Justin Martyr. Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary, takes it as a guest room or an informal public shelter. He notes that Luke uses another word for the inn of Luke 10:34, and leaves open an animal room in the house, a cave or an open feeding place.

entries.title: Israel the vine
entries.summary: The prophets and psalms pictured Israel as God's vine or vineyard, planted and tended by him and judged when it bore no fruit. A golden vine over the temple gate kept the picture in front of every worshiper.
entries.plain: **A grower who has dug, planted and pruned for years expects grapes, and he knows exactly what to do with a branch that gives none.** Vines grew all over the land, and everyone knew the work of the year: tie the vines up, prune them back, cut out the dead wood and burn it. Israel's Scriptures used that picture for the nation. God had planted Israel like a vine and came looking for fruit. Over the doorway of the temple hung a huge vine made of gold.
entries.then: The Old Testament and Jewish literature sometimes pictured Israel as a vineyard (Isaiah 5:7). Less often it was a vine (Psalm 80:8; Hosea 10:1), with God as the vinegrower. Isaiah has two songs of the vineyard (Isaiah 5:1-7; 27:2-6). Israel's failure to bear fruit brought judgment, and Ezekiel 15 says a barren vine is fit only for burning. Wright reads Psalm 80 as the background of the true vine: there God brings a vine out of Egypt and plants it in the land. Vines were grown across the Mediterranean and needed more attention than most crops. They were tied to posts and pruned through the year. At the severest annual pruning, the completely fruitless branches were cut out. They were useless for building, so they were burned. Keener writes, "A golden vine in the temple symbolized Israel's power." Josephus describes the gate of the temple: "it had also golden vines above it, from which clusters of grapes hung as tall as a man's height." In the Antiquities he says that under the crown-work of Herod's temple "was spread out a golden vine, with its branches hanging down from a great height."
entries.bridge: An analogy: a nation whose emblem is a tree, carved over the parliament door and stamped on every coin. Everyone knows the tree stands for the people, so a speech about the true tree is a speech about who the real nation is.
entries.changes: Because the vine stood for Israel, Jesus calling himself the true vine in John 15:1 claims to be what Israel was meant to be, with his followers as its branches. The vineyard of the tenants parable in Matthew 21:33 is Isaiah's vineyard, so hearers knew at once whose story was being told.
entries.not: **Not an emblem that only praises the nation.** Herod's temple did carry a golden vine, a sign of Israel's power. But in Scripture the vine came with a record of failure: the prophets sang of a vineyard with no good fruit, and Ezekiel called a barren vine fit only for burning. The image warned as well as comforted.

usedIn.s: Jesus calls himself the true vine and his Father the vinegrower, who cuts off fruitless branches and prunes the fruitful. He calls his disciples friends, not slaves, because he has told them everything.

entries.title: Travel by sea
entries.summary: Outside winter, ships were the quickest and cheapest way to travel, but they were built for cargo, not passengers, and from mid-September the sea grew dangerous. The great grain ships of Alexandria fed Rome.
entries.plain: **You did not book a cabin; you found a freighter going your way, brought your own food and slept on deck.** In Paul's world a ship could cover in a day what took a week on foot, and it cost less. But ships were built to carry goods. Passengers brought their own bedding and food and slept on deck. The sea was safe only part of the year: from mid-September it grew risky, and from about November to March almost no one sailed. The biggest ships of all were the grain carriers that took Egypt's wheat to Rome.
entries.then: Except in winter, travel by sea was quicker and cheaper than by land, perhaps a hundred miles a day. Ships were built for cargo, so passengers brought their own food and slept on deck. Sailing was risky from mid-September and shut down from about November 10 into March. In a good year, Keener says, it could reopen as early as February 8. Some scholars estimate that a fifth of long voyages met serious danger. The remains of over a thousand ancient wrecks are known. Rome took much of its grain from Egypt. The Alexandrian ships, some 180 feet long, made up what Keener calls the largest merchant fleet known to Europe before the 1700s. Because of the winds they sailed north to Asia Minor before turning west. Imperial policy rewarded owners who brought grain even in the dangerous season. Owners were usually wealthy though of low status, and most sailors were poor men or slaves. Without sun or stars a crew could not fix its position. Pagans believed the souls of the drowned "wandered aimlessly forever above the waters in which they perished" (Keener). Ships were named for a protecting god whose image stood at the bow. Castor and Pollux were the sailors' patrons. Josephus himself was wrecked in the Adriatic on a ship with some six hundred aboard. In Jewish tradition the sea stood for chaos and danger, and Paul planned his journeys so as not to sail in winter (Wright).
entries.bridge: An analogy: hitching a ride on a long-haul freight truck before the mountain passes close for winter. It is fast and cheap while the weather holds, the driver decides when to risk it, and nobody built the cab with you in mind.
entries.changes: The sailing season explains why a voyage after the Fast was already dangerous in Acts 27:9. Paul plans to stay the winter where he is in 1 Corinthians 16:6, and Keener reads his plan to winter in one place, in Titus 3:12, against the same calendar.
entries.not: **Not a ride where you can pull over and wait out the weather.** A truck can stop on the shoulder. A ship caught by a storm could not, and without sun or stars the crew could not even fix its position. Some scholars estimate a fifth of long voyages met serious danger. There were no passenger lines either; travelers rode cargo ships.
entries.dissent: Is the voyage of Acts 27 an eyewitness account? Keener follows the mariner James Smith in finding the nautical details exact. The cultural backgrounds notes say they fit the weather and geography too precisely to be invented. The CSB Study Bible calls an eyewitness author the most natural conclusion. Keener notes that some scholars regard the we passages as a literary device of sea stories.

usedIn.n: Acts 27:1-26, Sailing late in the season
usedIn.s: Paul sails for Rome in the custody of a centurion named Julius, changing to an Alexandrian grain ship at Myra. With the Fast already past, the owner presses on against Paul's warning, and a northeaster drives the ship helpless for days until an angel promises Paul that all aboard will live.

usedIn.n: Acts 28:1-10, Malta: the viper and the goddess Justice
usedIn.s: The islanders of Malta welcome the shipwrecked with a fire. When a viper fastens on Paul's hand they decide that Justice will not let a murderer live; when he takes no harm they call him a god. Publius, the island's chief man, takes them in, and Paul heals his father and many others.

usedIn.n: Acts 28:11-16, The Twin Brothers and the road to Rome
usedIn.s: After three months they sail in an Alexandrian ship with the Twin Brothers as its figurehead, land at Puteoli and walk the Appian Way toward Rome, where believers come out to meet Paul. In Rome he is allowed to live on his own with a soldier guarding him.

usedIn.s: Paul arranges a weekly setting aside of money for the believers in Jerusalem, plans his travels, commends Timothy, Apollos and the household of Stephanas, and closes with greetings, a line in his own hand and the Aramaic prayer Marana tha.

usedIn.s: Paul asks Timothy to come quickly and bring Mark, the cloak he left at Troas and his scrolls; Alexander the metalworker did him great harm, no one stood with him at his first defense, but the Lord rescued him from the lion's mouth, and Timothy must come before winter.

usedIn.n: Titus 3:9-15, A divisive person, winter at Nicopolis, and Zenas and Apollos
usedIn.s: Titus is to avoid foolish controversies, genealogies and quarrels about the law, and to warn a divisive person twice before having nothing more to do with him; Paul plans to winter at Nicopolis and asks Titus to send Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way with everything they need.

usedIn.n: Revelation 18:9-24, kings, merchants and the cargo list
usedIn.s: The kings, the merchants and the sea captains stand far off and mourn as Babylon burns, because no one buys their cargoes any more, a long list of luxuries that ends with human beings. An angel hurls a great millstone into the sea, and the sounds of music, craftsmen, the mill, the lamp and the wedding fall silent in the city where the blood of prophets and saints was found.

entries.title: Roads, robbers and the dangers of travel
entries.summary: Travel by land was slow and risky. Robbers worked the lonely roads, rivers had to be forded, and news moved no faster than the people who carried it.
entries.plain: **Before phones, you waved a friend off on a long drive and heard nothing until he wrote from the other end.** Rome built fine roads, but travel on them was still slow and dangerous. Robbers waited in lonely country, so people went in groups and stopped in towns for the night. Many rivers had no bridge and could flood after the rains. A letter or a piece of news traveled only as fast as the person carrying it, so a friend who was late might simply be delayed, or might be dead.
entries.then: Travel was among the more dangerous activities of antiquity (Keener). A later Jewish tradition had priests pray and fast twice each week for the safety of those on the road. Robbers were one of the worst fears on the road, and a reason many parties stayed off it after dark. Under the empire land robbers had decreased but remained a frequent danger. Pirates were much less common at sea than before. To avoid robbers in open country, people went in groups and spent the night in towns. Rivers could be dangerous to cross, especially during and after the rainy season. In Asia Minor robbers sometimes attacked boats coming upriver from the coast. Travelers often sought divine protection before setting out. In the hill country of Asia Minor they faced cold, and people avoided winter journeys whenever they could. Going overland was normally slower than sailing, and riskier too (Wright). News moved no faster than travelers. A writer could not know how his letter had been received until the carrier returned. A companion who failed to arrive at an agreed meeting place left his friends fearing for him. Carried money drew thieves. Wright notes that a well-known annual shipment of money would be an obvious target for highway robbery or embezzlement. That is why pilgrims to Jerusalem traveled in sizable groups and civic officials took some care for the money's safe delivery. Travel, especially at sea in late fall and early spring, lowered resistance to disease. Typhoid and malaria were common.
entries.bridge: An analogy: driving a remote highway with no phone signal, where the next town is the only safe place to stop for the night. You go in convoy if you can, and the people waiting at home cannot know you are safe until you walk in the door.
entries.changes: Because robbers worked the empty roads and news moved only with travelers, the man left half dead on the road down to Jericho in Luke 10:30 meets a familiar danger. Paul's dangers from rivers, robbers and the wilderness in 2 Corinthians 11:26 are the ordinary risks of travel, piled up to show how often he faced them.
entries.not: **Not a lonely road where the worst risk is a breakdown.** The chief fear was people: robbers on land and, less often by then, pirates at sea. Rivers, cold and disease added to it. And news did not arrive within hours; a letter writer waited until his carrier made the whole journey back.

entries.title: The olive tree and grafting
entries.summary: Olive trees lived for centuries, and growers grafted shoots from one tree into another. Scripture called God's people an olive tree, and Jewish writers pictured Israel as a tree whose roots were the patriarchs.
entries.plain: **The old tree in the yard was older than the house, and Grandpa kept it bearing by grafting new shoots onto it.** An olive tree could live for centuries. Growers also grafted, cutting a shoot from one tree and binding it into another so that it grew there and shared its sap. The prophets called Israel an olive tree, and Jewish writers pictured God's people as a tree whose roots were Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. So roots, branches and grafting made a ready picture of who belongs to God's people.
entries.then: Scripture portrays the people of God as an olive tree (Jeremiah 11:16-19; Hosea 14:6-7). The CSB Study Bible calls the olive tree a symbol of the nation of Israel. Jewish sources often pictured Israel as a plant or tree with the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac and Jacob as its roots, sometimes as an olive. A synagogue in Rome seems at some stage to have taken the name the Olive Tree. Olive trees live on century after century unless they are cut down and uprooted or burned right through (Wright). Grafting, adding a shoot of one tree to another, is reported in both Jewish and Greco-Roman literature. Keener says shoots from a wild olive were sometimes grafted onto a domestic olive that bore little fruit, to strengthen or save it. The barren original branches were cut away, and such a graft was thought to go against nature. Wright describes the usual practice the other way round. Wild olives were strong but bore poor fruit. So a gardener grafted shoots from a cultivated olive into the wild trunk, joining the wild tree's energy to the cultivated tree's fruit.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a family tree hanging in the hall, with the founders at the root. An adopted child's name is added to one of the branches; nobody pretends he was born there, and nobody may say he is not family.
entries.changes: Because Israel could be pictured as a tree rooted in the patriarchs, Paul's image in Romans 11:17-24 of wild shoots grafted in among the natural branches tells Gentile believers that they live from Israel's root and have no ground to boast. The prophets had already called Israel a green olive tree that God could set on fire.
entries.not: **Not a name written in once and for all.** On a family tree an added name stays put. Paul's branches draw their life from the root and can be cut off again, while the broken natural branches can be grafted back in. He also admits his graft runs against nature, so the picture is about belonging, not how olives are grown.
entries.dissent: Which way did grafting normally run? Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes describe wild shoots sometimes grafted into a weak cultivated tree to save it, which fits Paul's picture. Wright says gardeners grafted cultivated shoots into a wild trunk, so Paul's picture deliberately reverses normal practice.

entries.title: The Parthians beyond the Euphrates
entries.summary: The empire east of the Euphrates, Rome's most feared enemy, famous for mounted archers who could shoot backward as they rode. Its armies had destroyed a Roman army and once marched into Judea to put their own man on the throne.
aliases: Nero at the head of the Parthians
entries.plain: **Everyone in a border town knows which river the raiders would come across.** East of the Euphrates lay the Parthian empire, Rome's most feared enemy. Its horsemen shot arrows from the saddle, even while riding away, and had destroyed Roman armies. The Euphrates was the border everyone knew, and Romans dreaded what might cross it. Revelation's archer on a white horse, its long-haired riders and its armies from the Euphrates draw on that fear; how literally Parthia is meant is read in more than one way.
entries.then: The Euphrates was common knowledge as the traditional boundary between the Roman and Parthian empires (Keener). Wright adds that everyone from Jerusalem to Rome knew what a release beyond the Euphrates meant. The Parthians were the only mounted archers known in the Mediterranean world and Rome's most formidable enemy. "Romans admitted that they could not defeat the Parthians to the east", says the cultural backgrounds article on Parthia. The old Persian armies, whose heirs they were, kept sacred white horses. The Parthians could feign retreat up a hill and shoot backward at the legions that followed. They used flaming arrows and relied on cavalry, where Rome drew its horsemen from auxiliaries. Unlike most men of the empire, they wore their hair long. Rome had felt their power. Josephus writes of Crassus that "when he had passed over Euphrates, he perished himself, and his army with him" (War 1.8.8). He also tells how the Parthian prince Pacorus, promised a thousand talents, set out to restore Antigonus to the throne of Judea (War 1.13.1). The atlas dates the invasion to 40 BC, when the Parthians made Antigonus king and high priest. Many Jews lived in Parthian territory, and in the war of 66-70 many expected Parthia to step in. Josephus says that "the Jews hoped that all of their nation which were beyond Euphrates would have raised an insurrection together with them" (War, Preface 2). Jewish texts kept the fear alive. The Similitudes of Enoch imagined a Parthian invasion (Keener), stirred up by angels in 1 Enoch 56:5-8 (Beale). King of kings was the Parthian ruler's title. Rumor, echoed in the Sibylline Oracles, had Nero returning at the head of Parthian armies.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a frontier town in a Western that knows the raiders live across the river. One word about riders at the ford is enough to send everyone to bar the doors.
entries.changes: Because the Euphrates was the border with Rome's most feared enemy, an archer on a white horse in Revelation 6:2, and angels released at the great river three chapters later, would make a Roman province shudder before any further meaning was found. Acts 2:9 lists Parthians first among the Jews of the dispersion in Jerusalem at Pentecost, a reminder that many Jews lived under Parthian rule.
entries.not: **Not a band of raiders.** Parthia was an empire, the one power Rome admitted it could not defeat. It had destroyed Crassus's army and once put its own king on Judea's throne. Many Jews lived under Parthian rule, and in the war of 66-70 some hoped it would help them. Nor were the kings from the east modern nations.
entries.dissent: How literally Parthia is meant. The cultural backgrounds notes say the details of Revelation 9 evoke the Parthians whether or not literal Parthians are in view, and that few of the locusts' features are specifically Parthian. Beale grants that many see the first horseman of chapter 6 as at least partly an allusion to the Parthians, but reads the rider as an evil power. Wright treats the armies as symbols drawn from the readers' worst nightmares, and the CSB Study Bible takes the army of 9:16 as more likely demonic than human, perhaps both.

usedIn.n: Revelation 6:1-8, four horsemen
usedIn.s: As the Lamb opens the first four seals, four riders go out: a crowned archer on a white horse bent on conquest, a rider on a red horse who takes peace from the earth, a rider with scales on a black horse while wheat sells at famine prices, and Death on a pale horse with Hades following.

usedIn.n: Revelation 9:1-21, the Abyss opened and the armies from the Euphrates
usedIn.s: At the fifth trumpet a fallen star is given the key to the Abyss, and from its smoke come locusts like horses with human faces, women's hair and scorpions' stings, under a king called Abaddon and Apollyon. At the sixth, four angels bound at the Euphrates are released with a cavalry of two hundred million that kills a third of humanity, yet the survivors do not repent.

usedIn.n: Revelation 16:12-21, the Euphrates dried and Armageddon
usedIn.s: The sixth bowl dries up the Euphrates to make way for the kings from the east, and three frog-like spirits from the dragon, the beast and the false prophet gather the kings of the world to battle at the place called Armageddon. The seventh bowl brings a voice saying it is done, the greatest earthquake ever, the splitting of the great city and hundred-pound hailstones.

usedIn.n: Revelation 17:7-18, seven hills and seven kings
usedIn.s: The angel explains the woman and the beast: the beast once was, now is not and will come up from the Abyss; its seven heads are seven hills and also seven kings, five fallen, one living and one still to come, and the beast is an eighth who belongs to the seven. Its ten horns are ten kings who will make war on the Lamb, and in the end the beast and the horns turn on the woman, the great city that rules the kings of the earth, and burn her.

usedIn.n: Revelation 19:11-21, the rider on the white horse
usedIn.s: Heaven opens and a rider on a white horse, named Faithful and True and the Word of God, leads heaven's armies, his robe stained with blood and a sword coming from his mouth, his title King of kings. Birds are summoned to feast on the fallen, the beast and the false prophet are seized and cast into the fiery lake, and their armies fall to the rider's sword.

entries.title: Unclean by touch
entries.summary: Under the law, skin disease, bleeding, corpses, tombs and certain animals made a person ritually unclean, and touch could pass it on.
entries.plain: **Nobody wanted to shake the hand of the man who had just climbed out of the sewer.** Unclean in the Bible does not mean dirty, and it does not mean sinful. It meant not fit, for a time, to come near holy things. Some conditions passed that state to anyone who touched you. Washing, waiting and sometimes a priest's inspection made you clean again.
entries.then: Lepers were unclean under Leviticus 13:45-46, and anyone who touched them became ritually impure for a time. The word leprosy covered a range of severe skin conditions. Sufferers lived away from towns and called out unclean to warn people off. A healing had to be certified by a priest under Leviticus 14, and an offering in the temple should follow. Bleeding made a woman unclean (Leviticus 15), and even touching her clothes made the wearer impure. Contact with a bleeding person made you impure until evening. Touching a corpse made you impure for a week (Numbers 19). Jews regarded tombs and anything tied to the dead as impure, and pigs as unclean. The custom of washing hands arose after the Old Testament was finished, probably among Jews outside the land (Keener). People washed to remove impurity picked up in the markets, pouring water over the hands or dipping them to the wrist. Pharisees had detailed rules for purifying vessels. Wright says these rules were written down about two hundred years after Jesus but were already well known as oral tradition. Purity codes also marked a people's boundaries against the pagans around them. Dogs were treated as unclean and not kept as pets; Bailey says flatly, "Dogs are never pets." Spittle was usually thought unclean but was used in cures. Touching a leper was forbidden and revolting to most people. The bleeding woman should not even have been in a crowd, since anyone she touched became unclean. Vessels could carry impurity too. A pure vessel that touched an impure one sometimes had to be purified again, and cheap impure vessels were broken (Keener on 2 Timothy 2:20-21).
entries.bridge: An analogy: a hospital clean room. Touching the wrong thing does not make you a bad person, but you cannot go back in until you have scrubbed and waited.
entries.changes: Touching a leper, a bleeding woman or a corpse should have passed impurity to Jesus, as in Mark 1:41 and Matthew 9:20, so each touch is a scene in itself. Washing and food rules marked who was fit to come near holy things. Peter's vision in Acts 10:14 turns on the same categories.
entries.not: **Not about germs.** The hospital picture breaks here. Ritual impurity was not infection. It came from things no doctor fears, such as a dead body or a tomb, and it concerned access to holy things, not health.
entries.dissent: Do the vessels of 2 Timothy 2:20-21 carry purity at all? Keener reads them through Jewish purity rules, under which an impure vessel could defile a pure one. Wright hears honor and use instead, from fine ware kept for guests to the rag for the floor.
