usedIn.n: Matthew 8:1-17, A leper, a centurion and a mother-in-law
usedIn.s: Coming down the mountain, Jesus touches and heals a leper, heals a centurion's servant from a distance, and heals Peter's mother-in-law and many others.

usedIn.n: Matthew 9:18-34, A ruler's daughter, a bleeding woman, the blind and the mute
usedIn.s: A synagogue ruler asks Jesus to raise his daughter; on the way a woman touches the fringe of his cloak. Then two blind men call him Son of David, and a mute man speaks.

usedIn.n: Matthew 23:13-28, Oaths, mint, gnats and whitewashed tombs
usedIn.s: Jesus pronounces woes on the scribes and Pharisees: they shut the kingdom, play games with oaths, tithe herbs while neglecting justice, strain gnats and swallow camels, and look clean outside like whitewashed tombs.

usedIn.n: Mark 1:21-45, A Sabbath in Capernaum and a leper
usedIn.s: Jesus teaches in the synagogue, drives out a spirit, heals Simon's mother-in-law and, after sunset, the whole town. Then he touches and cleanses a leper.

usedIn.n: Mark 5:1-20, Legion among the tombs
usedIn.s: Across the lake, in Gentile country, Jesus frees a man possessed by many spirits. They enter a herd of pigs that rushes into the sea.

usedIn.n: Mark 5:21-43, A synagogue leader's daughter and a bleeding woman
usedIn.s: On the way to heal Jairus' dying daughter, Jesus is touched by a woman who has bled for twelve years. Then he raises the girl.

usedIn.n: Mark 7:1-23, Washed hands and the tradition of the elders
usedIn.s: Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem object that Jesus' disciples eat with unwashed hands. Jesus answers that what defiles comes from inside.

usedIn.n: Mark 7:24-37, A Greek woman and a deaf man
usedIn.s: In the region of Tyre a Gentile mother asks Jesus to free her daughter, and answers his saying about dogs. In the Decapolis he heals a deaf man.

usedIn.n: Luke 7:11-17, A widow's only son on the bier
usedIn.s: At the gate of Nain Jesus meets a funeral for a widow's only son. He touches the bier, raises the young man and gives him back to his mother, and the crowd says a great prophet has arisen.

usedIn.n: Luke 10:25-37, The Samaritan on the Jericho road
usedIn.s: A lawyer asks what he must do to inherit eternal life and then who his neighbor is. Jesus tells of a man left half dead on the road to Jericho, passed by a priest and a Levite and rescued by a Samaritan.

usedIn.n: Luke 11:37-54, Woes at a Pharisee's table
usedIn.s: At a Pharisee's meal Jesus does not wash before eating, and when his host is surprised he pronounces woes on Pharisees and lawyers: clean cups and greedy hearts, tithed herbs, the best seats, unmarked graves and the tombs of the prophets.

usedIn.n: Luke 16:19-31, The rich man and Lazarus
usedIn.s: A rich man feasts every day while a beggar named Lazarus lies at his gate. Both die; Lazarus is carried to Abraham's side, and the rich man finds himself in torment in Hades.

usedIn.n: Luke 17:11-19, Ten lepers and the Samaritan who came back
usedIn.s: On the border between Samaria and Galilee ten men with leprosy call to Jesus from a distance. He sends them to the priests, they are cleansed on the way, and only one, a Samaritan, comes back to thank him.

usedIn.n: John 2:1-12, Water into wine at a village wedding
usedIn.s: At a wedding in Cana the wine runs out. Jesus has the servants fill six stone purification jars with water, and the master of the feast tastes the best wine of the week.

usedIn.n: John 4:1-42, A Samaritan woman at Jacob's well
usedIn.s: Tired at noon, Jesus sits on Jacob's well and asks a Samaritan woman for a drink. They talk about living water, her husbands and the right mountain for worship, and her town comes out to meet him.

usedIn.n: John 11:45-57, Caiaphas: one man for the nation
usedIn.s: After the raising of Lazarus the chief priests and Pharisees call a council, afraid the Romans will take away their place and their nation. Caiaphas tells them it is better for one man to die for the people.

usedIn.n: John 18:28-40, Pilate's headquarters at dawn
usedIn.s: At daybreak the leaders bring Jesus to the governor's headquarters but will not go in, so as to stay clean for Passover. Pilate questions him about being king of the Jews, finds no case, and offers to release him, but the crowd asks for Barabbas.

usedIn.n: Acts 9:32-43, Lydda and Joppa
usedIn.s: Peter heals a paralyzed man at Lydda and, at Joppa, raises Tabitha, a disciple known for her charity, while the widows she clothed stand weeping. He stays on with a tanner.

usedIn.n: Acts 10:1-23, Cornelius and Peter's vision
usedIn.s: A God-fearing Roman centurion in Caesarea is told in a vision to send for Peter. At noon on a Joppa rooftop Peter sees a sheet full of unclean animals and hears a voice tell him to eat.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 6:14-7:1, Unequal yoke, Belial and the temple of God
usedIn.s: Paul tells the Corinthians not to be yoked with unbelievers, for light has no fellowship with darkness nor Christ with Belial, and calls them the temple of the living God, who must come out and be separate.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 2:14-26, Gangrene, a resurrection already past, and vessels in a great house
usedIn.s: Timothy is to warn the church against quarreling about words and to handle the word of truth correctly; the teaching of Hymenaeus and Philetus, who say the resurrection has already happened, spreads like gangrene, but God's foundation stands sealed, and in a great house some vessels are for honor and some for dishonor.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 9:11-22, Blood, ashes and a will
usedIn.s: Christ entered the greater tent once for all with his own blood, not the blood of goats and calves. If the ashes of a heifer could make the unclean outwardly clean, how much more will his blood cleanse the conscience; and as a will takes effect only at a death, the new covenant was put in force by his.

entries.title: Unclean spirits and exorcists
entries.summary: Spirits that defiled and harmed people. Exorcists of the day used names, oaths, spells and foul smells to drive them out. Jesus gave an order.
entries.plain: **The con man thought knowing your name gave him a hold over you.** People in Jesus' world believed evil spirits could take hold of a person. Exorcists tried to drive them out with spells, secret names and tricks, and the spirits were thought to try the same tricks back. Mark and Matthew call these spirits unclean.
entries.then: A few early Jewish sources linked evil spirits with impurity, and people linked spirits with tombs. People tried to expel demons with incantations or strong odors. Jewish exorcists sometimes used magic tied to Solomon or smelly roots. Gentile exorcists called on a higher spirit to drive out a lower one (Keener on Matthew 8:16). In magical texts, those trying to control a spirit announced its name and tried to bind it into service. The oath language of 5:7 appears in magical exorcisms. In Tobit the smoke of a fish's heart and liver drives off Asmodeus. The third-century Testament of Solomon gives Solomon a ring to control demons. The Old Testament prescribes no incantations or amulets against spirits. Exorcism by incantation is ancient. The physician of the Assyrian king Esarhaddon (681 to 669 BC) recited incantations against demons that might be causing an illness (Podany). Expelling a demon simply by command was extraordinary and drew amazement. Beelzebul is probably a corruption of Baalzebub, the god of Ekron in 2 Kings 1. Wright's glossary renders it lord of the flies, a name for the satan. Wright describes unclean spirits as non-physical powers that defile the person they inhabit. They make that person act against their calling as a human being. Some in antiquity linked madness with demons. Afflictions could happen without spirits, though spirits could also cause them. In ancient stories demons bargained for easy terms when forced out, and in Jewish tradition could die or be bound. Keener reads the seared consciences of 1 Timothy 4:2 against the branding iron used on livestock. On that reading the false teachers are marked as owned by evil spirits. His notes allow that it may mean a conscience that no longer works.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a hostage standoff where negotiators try every trick, names, bargains, threats. Then someone walks in whose plain order ends it, and everyone in the room wants to know who he is.
entries.changes: Driving out a spirit by plain command, where others used spells, names and roots, marked an exorcist as extraordinary, as in Mark 1:27. The charge that such power came from Beelzebul, as in Matthew 12:24, turned the question to whose side he was on. In Acts 19:13 Jewish exorcists try to use Jesus' name as a spell.
entries.not: **Not a human standoff with a hostage taker.** Here the captor was a spirit, thought to defile the very person it lived in and linked with tombs and impurity. Exorcists used names, oaths and smells to bind it. Nor do the sources reduce these spirits to mental illness or treat every sickness as a spirit.

usedIn.s: Jesus answers two would-be followers, calms a storm on the lake, and frees two men possessed by demons in the region of the Gadarenes.

usedIn.n: Matthew 12:22-50, Beelzebul, the strong man, Jonah and his true family
usedIn.s: When Jesus heals a blind and mute man, the crowds wonder if he is the Son of David and the Pharisees say he works by Beelzebul. Jesus answers with the strong man, refuses a sign except Jonah's, and names his true family.

usedIn.n: Matthew 15:21-28, A Canaanite mother and the dogs
usedIn.s: In the region of Tyre and Sidon a Canaanite woman begs the Son of David to free her daughter. Jesus is silent, then speaks of bread and dogs, and her answer wins him over.

usedIn.n: Mark 1:21-45, A Sabbath in Capernaum and a leper
usedIn.s: Jesus teaches in the synagogue, drives out a spirit, heals Simon's mother-in-law and, after sunset, the whole town. Then he touches and cleanses a leper.

usedIn.n: Mark 3:13-35, The Twelve, his family and Beelzebul
usedIn.s: Jesus appoints twelve. His family thinks he is out of his mind, and teachers from Jerusalem say he drives out demons by Beelzebul.

usedIn.n: Mark 5:1-20, Legion among the tombs
usedIn.s: Across the lake, in Gentile country, Jesus frees a man possessed by many spirits. They enter a herd of pigs that rushes into the sea.

usedIn.n: Luke 10:1-24, Seventy sent out, and Satan falling
usedIn.s: Jesus sends seventy others, or seventy-two, ahead of him in pairs, with no purse, bag or sandals, to towns that will welcome or refuse them. They come back rejoicing that even the demons obey, and Jesus says he saw Satan fall like lightning.

usedIn.n: Luke 11:14-26, By Beelzebul, or by the finger of God?
usedIn.s: When Jesus drives out a demon that kept a man from speaking, some say he does it by Beelzebul, the ruler of demons. He answers that a divided kingdom falls, and that if he drives out demons by the finger of God, God's kingdom has come.

usedIn.n: Acts 16:16-24, The slave girl with a Python spirit
usedIn.s: A slave girl who earns her owners money by fortune-telling follows Paul, crying out about the Most High God. Paul drives the spirit out, and her owners drag him and Silas before the magistrates, who have them beaten and jailed.

usedIn.n: Acts 19:8-20, The lecture hall and the burned books
usedIn.s: In Ephesus Paul teaches daily in the hall of Tyrannus for two years, and even cloths that touched him bring healing. When the sons of Sceva try to use Jesus' name as a spell, the spirit overpowers them, and believers burn their magic books in public.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 6:10-17, The armor of God
usedIn.s: Paul calls the believers to stand firm in God's armor, because their struggle is not against flesh and blood but against rulers, authorities and spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 4:1-5, Deceiving spirits, no marriage, no foods
usedIn.s: The Spirit warns that later on some will desert the faith for deceiving spirits and demonic teaching, banning marriage and certain foods, though God made food to be eaten with thanks.

usedIn.n: James 2:14-26, Faith that shudders, Abraham and Rahab
usedIn.s: Faith without deeds is dead, James argues. Wishing a hungry brother well helps no one, the demons believe that God is one and shudder, and Abraham and Rahab were counted righteous by what they did.

The seventh bowl brings a voice saying it is done, the greatest earthquake ever, the splitting of the great city and hundred-pound hailstones.

entries.title: Washing feet
entries.summary: A good host set out water so arriving guests could wash the dust of the road off their feet. Doing the washing yourself was a slave's work, and a disciple was not expected to touch even his teacher's feet.
aliases: wiped his feet with her hair
washing the feet of the Lord's people
entries.plain: **Handing a guest a towel at the door is good manners; kneeling down to wash his feet yourself is something else.** People walked dusty roads in sandals. A good host gave arriving guests water for their feet. The washing itself, untying the sandals and pouring the water over the feet, was the work of a slave or of someone in a very low place. That is why a teacher washing his students' feet, or a woman pouring perfume on a guest's feet, stopped the room.
entries.then: After travelers had come a long way, the host provided water for their feet, following Abraham's example (Genesis 18:4). But loosing sandals and washing another person's feet was servile work. Most often a servant did it, or very submissive wives or children (1 Samuel 25:41). Dirt roads made feet dusty, and the water was poured over the feet into a basin. The ESV and CSB Study Bibles call it a task for non-Jewish slaves, normally done on arrival rather than during the meal. Hosts gave water for the feet but anointed only the head, and only servants normally handled a person's feet. Disciples served their teachers, as Elisha served Elijah and Joshua served Moses. But the one service not expected even of them was handling the master's feet (Keener). Bailey, writing from Middle Eastern village life, says only the lowest servants tied up their robes for such work: "Servants, indeed, only lower-class servants and slaves, belt their robes." The Mishnah told worshipers to wash the dust of the street from their feet before approaching the sacred precincts (Berakhot 9.5).
entries.bridge: An analogy: a company's chief executive who, at the staff dinner, ties on a waiter's apron and serves the interns at their tables. Nobody can stop him, and nobody knows where to look.
entries.changes: Because the washing itself was a slave's job, a teacher kneeling with a basin before his own disciples, as in John 13:14, turns the known order of rank upside down. A host who offers no water at all, as in Luke 7:44, has slighted his guest. When 1 Timothy 5:10 lists washing the feet of God's people among a widow's good works, it names humble service, not a host's courtesy.
entries.not: **Not a gracious gesture from the top.** A modern boss who serves the staff can look generous. Here the act was so low that the disciple whose feet were being washed tried to refuse it, and the sources treat it as a slave's task, not a leader's kindness.

usedIn.n: John 12:1-11, Mary's nard and loosened hair
usedIn.s: Six days before Passover, at a dinner in Jesus' honor in Bethany, Mary pours a pound of costly nard on his feet and wipes them with her hair. Judas objects, and Jesus says she has kept it for the day of his burial.

usedIn.n: John 13:1-30, Washing the disciples' feet, and the morsel for Judas
usedIn.s: At supper before Passover Jesus takes off his outer clothes, ties a towel around himself and washes his disciples' feet. Then he hands Judas the dipped morsel, and Judas goes out into the night.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 5:1-16, Older men as fathers, and the widows' list
usedIn.s: Timothy is to treat older and younger believers as family; the church is to honor widows who are truly in need, families are to support their own, and only older widows of proven character are to be put on the list.

entries.title: Clean and unclean food
entries.summary: The law of Moses sorted animals into clean and unclean, and keeping kosher marked Jews off from their neighbors. Strict Jews also avoided Gentile food, Gentile wine and Gentile tables.
aliases: the sheet let down from heaven
to the pure all things are pure
entries.plain: **She would starve before she ate pork, and so would everyone she grew up with.** The law of Moses said which animals Israel could eat and which were unclean. Jews kept those rules even when they were lax about others, and some had died rather than break them. Strict Jews also kept away from food cooked by Gentiles and from their wine, so they did not eat at Gentile tables. That made Jews look standoffish to their neighbors, and it made a shared meal between a Jew and a Gentile a big step.
entries.then: Even Palestinian Jews who were lax in other matters kept kosher, and in the time of the Maccabees Jews had preferred death to unclean food. Clean and unclean food followed the Old Testament (Leviticus 11; Deuteronomy 14). Some elite Diaspora Jews took the rules as only symbolic. Philo allegorized them while insisting they still be kept, but most Jews kept them literally. For a strict pietist, unclean creatures touching clean ones would make the clean unclean too. Wright explains that the food laws marked Jews off from their neighbors. They were backed by a ban on sharing a table with Gentiles, since the people you eat with are your family. It was considered unclean to eat Gentiles' food or drink their wine. This did not forbid all contact, but it kept Jews from dining with Gentiles at banquets. It also made much of the Roman world think them antisocial. Jubilees 22:16 forbids eating with Gentiles as evil company, and lodging Gentiles overnight broke strict piety. Many Diaspora Jews were less strict than Judeans. Respectable Jews in Judea and Galilee kept away from Gentile tables. The CSB Study Bible notes that Peter's lifelong obedience to Leviticus 11 collided with the command in his vision. The Jerusalem council asked Gentile believers to keep away from food polluted by idols, from blood and from what was strangled. Jewish tradition applied these rules to foreigners living in Israel (Leviticus 17-18) and to righteous Gentiles, the descendants of Noah. The ESV Study Bible reads them as making shared meals with law-keeping Jewish believers possible.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a family that keeps a strict diet for their faith and will not eat in a restaurant that cannot promise how the food was cooked. Friends who invite them to dinner understand that the refusal is about the kitchen, and still feel it as a refusal of them.
entries.changes: Peter's horror at the sheet of unclean animals in Acts 10:14 is the reaction of a man who had never broken the food laws, and the complaint against him afterward is that he ate with Gentiles. The same line runs through Galatians 2:12, where Peter withdraws from the Gentiles' table, and through the clean and unclean foods of Romans 14:14.
entries.not: **Not a diet or a matter of taste.** Food laws were part of the covenant and marked who belonged to Israel, so eating across the line raised questions about belonging, not hygiene.
entries.dissent: What did Peter's vision overturn? The ESV Study Bible reads it as God setting aside the distinctions of clean and unclean food along with other ceremonial laws. It says the unlawfulness Peter mentions in Acts 10:28 belongs to later strict tradition rather than an Old Testament command. Keener says the lesson that God can make anything clean is aimed most of all at the Gentiles Peter is about to meet.

usedIn.n: Acts 10:1-23, Cornelius and Peter's vision
usedIn.s: A God-fearing Roman centurion in Caesarea is told in a vision to send for Peter. At noon on a Joppa rooftop Peter sees a sheet full of unclean animals and hears a voice tell him to eat.

usedIn.n: Acts 10:24-11:18, Peter in Cornelius's house
usedIn.s: Peter enters a Gentile home, preaches Jesus, and sees the Spirit fall on the uncircumcised listeners. In Jerusalem he is criticized for eating with Gentiles, and his account silences the critics.

usedIn.n: Acts 15:1-21, The council in Jerusalem
usedIn.s: Teachers from Judea insist that Gentile believers must be circumcised to be saved. The apostles and elders meet in Jerusalem; Peter and James argue that God has accepted Gentiles as they are, and James proposes a few rules for them to keep.

usedIn.n: Acts 15:22-35, The letter to the Gentile churches
usedIn.s: The council sends Judas and Silas with Paul and Barnabas to carry a letter to the Gentile believers of Antioch, Syria and Cilicia. It is read to the church at Antioch, who rejoice at its encouragement.

usedIn.n: Romans 14:1-23, Vegetables, holy days and wine
usedIn.s: Some believers eat only vegetables and keep certain days; others eat anything and treat every day alike. Paul tells both not to judge one another, since all will stand before God's judgment seat, and not to wreck another's faith over food.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 10:23-11:1, Dinner at an unbeliever's house
usedIn.s: Paul tells believers to eat whatever is sold in the meat market and whatever an unbelieving host serves without asking questions, unless someone points out that it was offered in sacrifice.

usedIn.n: Galatians 2:11-21, Peter leaves the table at Antioch
usedIn.s: At Antioch Peter, who had been eating with Gentile believers, draws back when people come from James, and Paul rebukes him in front of everyone, arguing that Jews and Gentiles alike are put right with God through Christ and faith, not by doing what the law requires.

usedIn.n: Colossians 2:16-23, Food, new moons, Sabbaths and the worship of angels
usedIn.s: Paul tells the believers not to let anyone judge them over food, drink, festivals, new moons or Sabbaths, or disqualify them with self-denial, the worship of angels and visions, and calls rules about what not to touch or taste human commands with no power over the flesh.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 4:1-5, Deceiving spirits, no marriage, no foods
usedIn.s: The Spirit warns that later on some will desert the faith for deceiving spirits and demonic teaching, banning marriage and certain foods, though God made food to be eaten with thanks.

usedIn.n: Titus 1:10-16, The circumcision group, and Cretans always liars
usedIn.s: Many rebellious talkers and deceivers, especially of the circumcision group, are upsetting whole households for dishonest gain; Paul quotes a Cretan prophet who called Cretans always liars, and warns against Jewish myths and human commands, for to the pure all things are pure.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 13:7-17, Foods, an altar and outside the camp
usedIn.s: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and for ever, so the readers must not be carried away by strange teachings about foods. Believers have an altar the tabernacle priests may not eat from; as the bodies of the sin offerings were burned outside the camp, Jesus suffered outside the gate, and they must go out to him, bearing his disgrace, seeking the city to come.

entries.title: Circumcision and becoming a Jew
entries.summary: Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham and the mark of a Jewish man. A Gentile man who joined Israel was circumcised; the first great quarrel in the church was over whether Gentile believers had to be.
entries.plain: **He had come to every service for years, but joining for real meant an operation no grown man looked forward to.** God gave circumcision to Abraham as the sign of his covenant, and Jewish boys were circumcised as babies. A Gentile man who wanted to become a Jew had to be circumcised as an adult. Many Jews believed that good Gentiles could be saved without it, but almost no one thought a Gentile could belong to God's people Israel without converting. When Gentiles began to believe in Jesus, the church had to decide whether they must be circumcised first.
entries.then: Circumcision was the badge of God's covenant with the Jews, required of anyone who belonged to God's people (Genesis 17:9-14). With the food laws and the purity rules, it made life in a Gentile community almost impossible for anyone who kept them (ESV Study Bible). Many Jews believed Gentiles were saved by keeping the laws God gave Noah, against idolatry, sexual immorality and the like. Others held that Gentiles had to convert. Men converted by circumcision, and for most of this group everyone was immersed. Even the lenient did not count an uncircumcised Gentile part of Israel. Only the strictest minority limited salvation to full converts (Keener). Josephus reported that some of his colleagues demanded circumcision of Gentiles who had fled to them, and that he forbade it. Hillel reportedly welcomed converts diplomatically. Shammai, whose stricter school probably dominated before AD 70, demanded the whole law from the start. Gentiles were thought continually impure, which is why converts were immersed. Timothy was the uncircumcised son of a Jewish mother and a Gentile father, so Jews would see him as a Gentile. A wife was expected to follow her husband's religion, so his father had probably refused it. Carson counts circumcision among the "features intrinsic to Judaism" that could not be required of all believers once Gentiles came in. Acts 15 and Galatians 2 record that tension. Attempts to restrict circumcision provoked revolts before and after Paul's time. Josephus says Antiochus "commanded them not to circumcise their sons". He adds that Jerusalem Hellenizers who wanted a gymnasium hid their circumcision, "that even when they were naked they might appear to be Greeks."
entries.bridge: An analogy: a club that welcomes guests at every event but lets only initiated members vote. The argument starts when guests are found running the meetings without ever having been initiated.
entries.changes: Circumcision marked who belonged to Israel, so the demand in Acts 15:1 that Gentile believers be circumcised was a demand that they become Jews first. Paul resists it in Galatians 5:2-6 and speaks in Romans 2:25-29 of a circumcision of the heart.
entries.not: **Not a club rule that members can vote to change.** Circumcision was a sign God gave in the covenant with Abraham, cut into the body and tied to belonging to Israel itself. Some Jews held that Gentiles had to take it to be saved. Nor was it a health practice: a rumor that Paul told Jews abroad to stop circumcising their sons alarmed Jerusalem.
entries.dissent: What does Paul mean by works of the law, the phrase he sets against faith in Galatians 2:16? The cultural backgrounds notes report that some take it to mean distinctively Jewish customs, such as circumcision and the food laws, that had become identity markers. The notes themselves lean to all the Bible's laws, while allowing that the markers were probably most prominent in people's minds. Wright reads the practices that marked Jews off from their pagan neighbors: Sabbath, food laws and circumcision. "The works of Torah are sociocultural identity markers," he writes, not flags of moral achievement. The ESV Study Bible takes the phrase to cover "not only circumcision, food laws, and Sabbath, but any human effort" to be justified by obeying a moral law. The CSB Study Bible sees the same issue as Acts 15:1-5: works of the law, circumcision above all, added to what was required for justification.

usedIn.n: Acts 15:1-21, The council in Jerusalem
usedIn.s: Teachers from Judea insist that Gentile believers must be circumcised to be saved. The apostles and elders meet in Jerusalem; Peter and James argue that God has accepted Gentiles as they are, and James proposes a few rules for them to keep.

usedIn.s: In Jerusalem James and the elders welcome Paul but warn him that thousands of believers zealous for the law have heard he teaches Jews abroad to abandon Moses. They ask him to pay for four men completing a vow and to purify himself with them in the temple.

usedIn.s: Paul turns on an imagined Jewish teacher who boasts in the law yet steals, commits adultery and robs temples, so that God's name is blasphemed among the nations, and says true circumcision is of the heart.

usedIn.n: Romans 4:1-25, Abraham, father of the uncircumcised too
usedIn.s: Paul argues from Genesis 15:6 that Abraham was counted righteous by trusting God before he was circumcised, so he is the father of all who believe, circumcised or not.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 7:17-24, Circumcised or not, slave or free
usedIn.s: Paul tells each believer to live the life the Lord assigned when he was called: the circumcised should not undo it, the uncircumcised should not seek it, and a slave should not be troubled, though he should take his freedom if he can.

usedIn.n: Galatians 2:1-10, Titus, the pillars and the right hand of fellowship
usedIn.s: Fourteen years later Paul goes up to Jerusalem with Barnabas and the uncircumcised Titus; Titus is not made to be circumcised, and the leaders reputed to be pillars give Paul the right hand of fellowship, asking only that he remember the poor.

usedIn.n: Galatians 2:11-21, Peter leaves the table at Antioch
usedIn.s: At Antioch Peter, who had been eating with Gentile believers, draws back when people come from James, and Paul rebukes him in front of everyone, arguing that Jews and Gentiles alike are put right with God through Christ and faith, not by doing what the law requires.

usedIn.n: Galatians 5:2-12, Circumcision, the whole law and the knife
usedIn.s: Paul warns that a man who accepts circumcision is bound to keep the whole law and is cut off from Christ, asks who cut in on their race, and wishes that the agitators would go further with the knife.

usedIn.n: Galatians 6:11-18, Large letters in his own hand, and the marks of Jesus
usedIn.s: Taking the pen himself, Paul writes in large letters that the rivals want the Galatians circumcised so they can boast in their flesh and avoid persecution, while he boasts only in the cross; he blesses those who follow this rule and the Israel of God, and says he bears the marks of Jesus.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 2:11-22, The dividing wall torn down, and a new temple
usedIn.s: Paul reminds Gentile believers that they were once far off, shut out of Israel's citizenship and covenants, and tells them Christ has broken down the dividing wall and built Jews and Gentiles into one household and one temple.

usedIn.n: Philippians 3:1-11, Dogs, mutilators, and a pedigree counted as loss
usedIn.s: Paul warns against teachers who press circumcision, calling them dogs and mutilators, lists his own credentials as a born Jew, a Pharisee and a zealous persecutor, and counts them all loss for the sake of knowing Christ.

usedIn.n: Colossians 2:8-15, The philosophy, a cancelled IOU and a triumph
usedIn.s: Paul warns against a philosophy built on human tradition and the elements of the world, tells Gentile believers they have already been circumcised in Christ, and pictures God cancelling their debt at the cross and leading the powers captive.

entries.title: Meat offered to idols
entries.summary: Most meat in a Greek city had passed through a sacrifice at a temple. Eating it at the temple's table, buying it in the market or meeting it at a friend's dinner raised the question of whether a believer was sharing in the worship of the god.
entries.plain: **The barbecue at the festival was free, but everyone knew whose festival it was.** In a city like Corinth animals were sacrificed to the gods at their temples. Part of the meat was eaten at feasts in the temple's own dining rooms, the priests took their share, and what was left was sold in the market. So a believer could meet meat from a sacrifice at a temple banquet, at the butcher's or on a friend's table. Jews in big cities avoided it, often with markets of their own. Gentile believers had to decide what eating it meant.
entries.then: Meat was offered to idols before it was served in temple dining halls, often as part of worship, or used for communal meals. Some of the meat in the market had been offered too. At a temple one knew the source; at a friend's home one could never be sure. Even ordinary banquets opened with a libation to some god, so most Gentile meals were somehow consecrated. Wright says most meat in a city like Corinth had passed through a sacrifice. He writes that "temples functioned effectively as a combination of butcher's shop and restaurant." Corinthians commonly dined in temples, which were centers of civic life. Bailey draws on the second-century traveler Pausanias. He describes Corinth's central market ringed by temples, with the meat market across a narrow street. The priests sold what they could not eat, and "During the numerous feasts there was an inevitable glut in the meat market." Most people could not afford meat and met it mainly when it was handed out at pagan festivals. So the poor tied meat to idols (Keener). Jews in large cities usually had their own markets. There they avoided both sacrificial meat and meat not drained of its blood. Palestinian Jewish teachers would never risk food that might have been offered to an idol. Invitations survive to dine at the table of the lord Serapis. Eating sacrificial meat was thought to join the eater to the god it was offered to. Heiser argues that Paul treats the gods behind the idols as real. So the danger lay in sharing the sacrifice rather than in the meat itself.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a company picnic held on a rival firm's grounds, with the rival's logo on every plate. The food is ordinary food, but sitting down at that table says whose guest you are.
entries.changes: Because sacrificial meat reached the temple tables, the market and private dinners, the questions in 1 Corinthians 8:1-13 turn on where the meat is eaten and who is watching. The Jerusalem letter of Acts 15:29 asks Gentile believers to abstain from it, and Revelation 2:14 counts eating it among a church's faults.
entries.not: **Not a question about clean and unclean animals.** The picnic picture breaks here: a rival firm is only a business, but a god's table was worship. Jewish food laws asked which animals could be eaten. This question was about worship: the same cut of meat could be ordinary food from the market or a share in a god's sacrifice at his table.
entries.dissent: What does Paul allow? The ESV Study Bible reads him as forbidding temple dinners as idolatry while allowing meat bought in the market. Arnold, following Fee, draws the same line, leaving meat eaten at home to the weaker believer's conscience. Keener sees chapters 8 to 10 as a careful compromise between two factions. One was the well-to-do who ate meat often, the other the poor who met it only at festivals. Heiser places the danger in taking part in the sacrifice. Who the weak were is also disputed. Keener takes them as the socially powerless. The cultural backgrounds notes allow either that or simply weaker consciences. Wright's biography, Carson, Moo and Morris, and Arnold take them as former idol-worshipers whose consciences drag them back.

entries.title: Sex, wine and Greek city ways
entries.summary: Greek and Roman men were expected to have sex outside marriage, with slaves or prostitutes, and the law allowed it. Jews and Christians called all of it porneia, sexual immorality; drunkenness at banquets and in taverns went with it, and the port of Corinth had an old name for it.
entries.plain: **In the port town everyone knew which streets to avoid, and nobody pretended the sailors stayed away.** In Greek and Roman cities most men took it for granted that they could have sex before and outside marriage, with slaves or with prostitutes. Prostitution was legal, a business like any other, and some thinkers said that what you did with your body did not matter. Many expected only the wife to be faithful. Jews thought this the clearest mark of Gentile life, and Corinth, a busy port, had a name for it going back centuries. Even so, some lines, such as sex with a stepmother, shocked pagans too.
entries.then: For most Greek men under thirty, sex was most available with slaves or prostitutes (Keener). Roman law permitted prostitution and forbade fornication only when both parties were of aristocratic birth. Prostitution was counted a business like any other. It was found in inns and taverns and stocked with slave girls raised from abandoned babies. Some pagans thought it a useful deterrent to adultery. Before marriage, most free Roman men and still more Greek men slept with slaves or others. Many Gentiles expected only the wife to be faithful, and Jewish tradition stressed Gentile sexual immorality. Corinth had a particular and long-standing reputation for prostitution. Dio Chrysostom, as Bailey reports, put the crowds at Corinth down to its harbors and its prostitutes. Wright's biography of Paul notes the large temple of Aphrodite on the Acrocorinth. His commentary says prostitution was often linked to temples "but was much wider as well, especially in a port city like Corinth." Some lines still held. Parent-child incest was abhorred everywhere in the Roman world, and relations with a stepmother counted as incest. Roman law punished it with banishment to an island. Wright notes that even lax Greco-Roman morals had taboos no self-respecting pagan would cross. Drink went with it. Drunkenness was common at the late-night banquets of the rich, often with sexual immorality, and in the taverns of the poor. The barmaids of travelers' inns were typically slaves who served as prostitutes at night. People linked drunkenness with loss of self-control and sometimes with possession by Dionysus, god of wine. His most active worshipers performed sexual acts, to the distaste of conservative Romans. Jewish wisdom despised drunkenness (Proverbs 23:20-35).
entries.bridge: An analogy: a garrison town where the bars and brothels by the gate are part of the local economy and nobody in authority objects. A congregation there that says no to all of it is swimming against the whole town.
entries.changes: Because sex outside marriage was ordinary for Greek and Roman men, the command to flee sexual immorality in 1 Corinthians 6:18 asked converts to break with what their city took for granted. The Jerusalem letter in Acts 15:29 names sexual immorality among the few things Gentile believers must avoid, and 1 Thessalonians 4:3-5 sets self-control against the passion of Gentiles who do not know God.
entries.not: **Not a vice tolerated at the edge of town.** In a garrison town the brothels sit by the gate. In Greek cities prostitution was legal, respectable men used it openly, and the women were often slaves raised from abandoned babies. It was often linked to temples too, so the Jewish and Christian line ran against the law, the custom and the worship of the city.
entries.dissent: Did Roman Corinth still have sacred prostitution at the temple of Aphrodite? Bailey holds that pagan worship in the city included sacred prostitution with Aphrodite's priestesses. The CSB Study Bible thinks cult prostitution at her temple was likely a major threat to the believers. The cultural backgrounds notes place the prostitutes dedicated to Aphrodite in old Corinth. Keener speaks of the religious prostitution common in pre-Roman Corinth. Wright says only that prostitution was often linked to temples. Carson, Moo and Morris think Strabo's thousand temple prostitutes belonged to the old city and were probably exaggerated. They warn against reading the old city's character into the new, though a great port was unlikely to be known for virtue. The Zondervan atlas and dictionary apply Strabo's figure to Paul's Corinth. A smaller difference concerns incest. Keener says Roman law punished it with banishment to an island. The CSB Study Bible says that for a son and his stepmother it was a capital crime in a Roman colony, punished by death or banishment.

usedIn.s: A church member is living with his stepmother and the church is proud of itself. Paul tells them to hand the man over to Satan, clear out the old leaven as a household does before Passover, and not eat with a so-called brother who lives that way.

usedIn.s: Answering slogans such as everything is permissible and food is for the stomach, Paul argues that the body belongs to the Lord, will be raised, and must not be joined to a prostitute, for believers were bought at a price.

usedIn.s: Paul tells Gentile believers to stop living as the Gentiles do, to put off the old self and put on the new, to give the devil no foothold, to work with their hands and share, and not to grieve the Spirit who sealed them.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 5:1-20, Children of light, and wine or the Spirit
usedIn.s: Paul calls believers to imitate God, to have nothing to do with sexual immorality, coarse joking or deeds done in the dark, and, instead of getting drunk on wine, to be filled with the Spirit, singing and giving thanks for everything.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 4:1-8, Holiness in the body
usedIn.s: Paul reminds the church of the instructions he passed on from the Lord Jesus: God's will is that they be holy, avoid sexual immorality, control their own bodies in holiness and honor, and not wrong a brother in this matter.

usedIn.n: Titus 1:1-9, Elders in every town, and God's steward
usedIn.s: Paul greets Titus, whom he left in Crete to put in order what was unfinished and to appoint elders in every town, and lists what an elder must be: blameless, faithful to his wife, with believing children, a steward of God's household, hospitable and able to hold to sound teaching.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 13:1-6, Strangers, angels, prisoners
usedIn.s: The writer turns to everyday duties: brotherly love, hospitality to strangers, since some have entertained angels without knowing it, care for prisoners as if in prison with them, honor for marriage, and freedom from the love of money.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 4:1-11, The neighbors' parties and their abuse
usedIn.s: Armed with Christ's attitude, the readers have done with the life of the Gentiles, its debauchery, drinking parties and idolatry, and their old companions are surprised and heap abuse on them; they will give account to God. The end of all things is near, so they must be sober, love one another, be hospitable without grumbling, and use their gifts as stewards of God's grace.

entries.title: Eating together
entries.summary: Sharing a table made a bond of friendship, so who you ate with told everyone whose side you were on.
aliases: I will come in and eat with them
entries.plain: **If you sit down to dinner with him, people will say you are one of his.** A shared meal was more than food. It made a bond, close to a promise. That is why it mattered who sat at Jesus' table, and why betrayal by someone who ate from the same dish was so ugly.
entries.then: People saw table fellowship as making a covenant of friendship (Keener). In one ancient story two warriors stopped fighting when they learned their fathers had once shared a meal. Eating with sinners therefore looked like endorsing them, and Scripture warned against keeping company with the ungodly (Psalm 1:1). Pharisees were careful about meals, for example that all food be tithed. Because a shared meal bound people together, betraying someone you had eaten with was thought especially low. By this period it was Jewish custom to thank God before a meal and then divide and share the food. A later blessing, perhaps already in use, ran: "Blessed are you . . . who bring forth bread from the earth." Polite hosts with means served enough for leftovers, and a host was expected to feed even unannounced guests. Wright reads Jesus' meals with outsiders against the prophets' picture of the kingdom as a great feast to which everyone was invited. Table fellowship meant intimacy, and the Pharisees did not like to eat with less scrupulous people. Respectable Jews in Judea and Galilee kept away from Gentile tables (Acts 10:28; 11:3). Growing nationalism in Judea pressed moderates to avoid offense. Wright traces the ban to the conviction that Gentiles were idolaters. He writes that "Eating with people is one of the most powerful symbols of association." Keener judges that at Antioch "withdrawing from table fellowship with culturally different Christians made them second-class citizens." The church's Lord's Supper was a full meal, also called a love feast. Shared meals "created a bond of friendship obligation" (Keener on Jude 12).
entries.bridge: An analogy: a wedding seating chart. Where people are placed tells the room who belongs with whom, and everyone reads it.
entries.changes: Sharing a table shows whose side a person is on, so eating with tax collectors, as in Mark 2:15-16, reads as endorsing them. A host who blesses, breaks and shares turns a meal into a sign, as at Matthew 14:19. In Galatians 2:12 the question is who will eat with Gentiles.
entries.not: **Not a seating plan where everyone is already a guest.** A wedding chart only arranges people who were all invited. Sharing food then made a bond like a covenant, and Jewish law and custom kept some people away from the table altogether. So eating with sinners or Gentiles looked like endorsing them. Today we eat with people we disagree with, and it means little.

usedIn.n: Luke 5:17-39, Through the roof, then a feast with toll men
usedIn.s: Friends lower a paralyzed man through the roof and Jesus forgives his sins. Then Levi leaves his tax booth and gives a banquet for Jesus with other tax collectors, and Jesus is asked why his disciples do not fast.

usedIn.n: Luke 13:22-35, The narrow door, the feast, the fox and the hen
usedIn.s: On the way to Jerusalem Jesus warns that many will find the door shut while people from east and west recline at the feast in God's kingdom. Warned that Herod wants to kill him, he calls Herod a fox and grieves over Jerusalem.

usedIn.n: Luke 15:1-10, A lost sheep and a lost coin
usedIn.s: Pharisees and teachers grumble that Jesus welcomes sinners and eats with them. He answers with a shepherd who searches for one lost sheep and a woman who sweeps the house for one lost coin.

usedIn.n: Luke 15:11-32, A father and two lost sons
usedIn.s: A younger son takes his share of the estate early, wastes it in a far country, and comes home to a father who runs to meet him. The older brother refuses to join the feast.

usedIn.n: Luke 18:35-19:10, A blind beggar and Zacchaeus at Jericho
usedIn.s: Near Jericho a blind beggar calls Jesus Son of David and receives his sight. In the town Jesus invites himself to the house of Zacchaeus, a rich chief tax collector, who promises to give half his goods to the poor and repay fourfold.

usedIn.n: Luke 24:13-35, A stranger on the Emmaus road
usedIn.s: Two disciples walking home to Emmaus are joined by a stranger who explains the Scriptures to them. They press him to stay, and they recognize him when he breaks the bread.

usedIn.n: John 13:1-30, Washing the disciples' feet, and the morsel for Judas
usedIn.s: At supper before Passover Jesus takes off his outer clothes, ties a towel around himself and washes his disciples' feet. Then he hands Judas the dipped morsel, and Judas goes out into the night.

usedIn.n: John 21:1-14, Breakfast on the beach
usedIn.s: Back in Galilee, seven disciples fish all night and catch nothing. At dawn a man on the shore tells them to cast to the right side, the net fills with 153 large fish, and Jesus gives them bread and fish by a charcoal fire.

usedIn.n: Acts 2:42-47, The common life
usedIn.s: The first believers devote themselves to teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and the prayers, share their possessions, and meet daily in the temple courts and in their homes.

usedIn.n: Acts 10:24-11:18, Peter in Cornelius's house
usedIn.s: Peter enters a Gentile home, preaches Jesus, and sees the Spirit fall on the uncircumcised listeners. In Jerusalem he is criticized for eating with Gentiles, and his account silences the critics.

usedIn.n: Acts 20:1-12, The collection party and Eutychus at Troas
usedIn.s: Paul leaves Ephesus for Macedonia and Greece, then sets out for Jerusalem with delegates from the churches. At Troas the believers meet on the first day of the week, and a young man who falls from a window is taken up alive.

usedIn.n: Acts 27:27-44, Shipwreck off Malta
usedIn.s: On the fourteenth night the sailors sense land, drop anchors from the stern and try to slip away in the ship's boat. Paul urges everyone to eat and gives thanks over bread, and when the ship breaks up the centurion stops the soldiers from killing the prisoners; all 276 reach the shore.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 5:1-13, A man and his father's wife
usedIn.s: A church member is living with his stepmother and the church is proud of itself. Paul tells them to hand the man over to Satan, clear out the old leaven as a household does before Passover, and not eat with a so-called brother who lives that way.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 10:1-22, Israel in the desert and the table of demons
usedIn.s: Paul warns that Israel too had its baptism and its spiritual food in the wilderness, yet fell into idolatry and immorality and was struck down, and tells the Corinthians that they cannot share both the Lord's table and the table of demons.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 11:17-34, The Lord's Supper in a rich man's house
usedIn.s: Paul rebukes the church because at the Lord's Supper some go hungry while others eat their fill and get drunk, retells the tradition of the Last Supper, and tells them to wait for one another.

usedIn.n: Galatians 2:11-21, Peter leaves the table at Antioch
usedIn.s: At Antioch Peter, who had been eating with Gentile believers, draws back when people come from James, and Paul rebukes him in front of everyone, arguing that Jews and Gentiles alike are put right with God through Christ and faith, not by doing what the law requires.

usedIn.n: 2 Thessalonians 3:6-18, The idle, the busybodies, and a greeting in Paul's own hand
usedIn.s: Paul tells the church to keep away from believers who are idle and will not work, recalls how he worked night and day to set an example, lays down that anyone unwilling to work should not eat, and signs the letter in his own hand.

usedIn.n: Jude 8-13, Michael and the body of Moses, and hidden reefs at the love feasts
usedIn.s: The intruders claim dream visions, defile the body, despise authority and slander the glorious ones, though the archangel Michael, disputing with the devil over the body of Moses, did not dare to slander him but left the rebuke to the Lord. They have taken the way of Cain, Balaam and Korah; they are hidden reefs at the love feasts, waterless clouds, wild waves and wandering stars.

usedIn.n: Revelation 3:14-22, Laodicea, lukewarm and rich
usedIn.s: To Laodicea the faithful and true witness says the church is neither cold nor hot but lukewarm, and he will spit it out. It thinks itself rich but is poor, blind and naked; he counsels it to buy gold, white clothes and eye salve, and stands at the door and knocks.

entries.title: Reclining at table
entries.summary: At banquets men lay on couches, propped on the left elbow, and where you lay showed your rank.
entries.plain: **At the formal dinner, the place cards told you exactly where you stood.** At a feast, Jesus and his guests did not sit upright on chairs. They lay on couches around low tables. Where you lay, close to the host or near the door, showed how important you were.
entries.then: Jewish people could sit for other meals, but at banquets men reclined, as Greeks did (Keener). They propped themselves on the left elbow and kept the right hand free to reach the food. The ESV Study Bible describes the formal layout. Couches stood around three sides of the room, with the host in the center and the most honored guests on either side of him. Each guest's feet pointed to the wall and his head to the tables. Reclining with someone signaled acceptance. Across the Mediterranean world guests at banquets were usually placed by social rank. At Herod's fortress of Machaerus archaeologists found two banquet halls, and as at Greek banquets men and women dined apart. At Passover, Wright says, people reclined because "free people didn’t just sit, they reclined." Dinners at patrons' homes and probably at social clubs ran far into the night with heavy drinking. Hosts poured libations to the gods at the start. The cultural backgrounds article on the triclinium describes the Roman dining room. Couches stood on three sides of a low table, three to a couch at a dinner party of nine. Each diner lay on his left side with his head near the table, so the head of one lay near the chest of the next. Pliny speaks of lying in another's bosom, and Livy says the lesser guest's head lay near the greater's torso. Many Jews had adopted the style by New Testament times.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a head table at a formal banquet, with seats assigned by rank. Everyone knows who is at the center, who is beside him, and who got the seat by the kitchen.
entries.changes: Reclining marks a meal as a feast, so where people lie and who lies beside whom says something about rank and acceptance, as in Mark 2:15. The same posture pictures the coming banquet, where many recline with Abraham in Matthew 8:11. In Luke 14:7-11 guests reach for the places of honor.
entries.not: **Not chairs in a row facing the room.** Guests lay on couches on their left sides, so one diner's head rested near the next one's chest, and closeness at table was literal. Lying down was not lazy, as it sounds to us; it was the formal posture of a feast, and ordinary meals could be eaten sitting.

usedIn.n: Matthew 14:1-12, John beheaded at a birthday feast
usedIn.s: Herod the tetrarch hears about Jesus and thinks John has risen. Matthew tells how Herod, bound by an oath at his birthday, had John beheaded.

usedIn.n: Matthew 26:17-30, The Passover and the cup
usedIn.s: Jesus eats the Passover with the Twelve in the city, names the one who dips with him as his betrayer, gives the bread and the cup new meaning, and vows not to drink wine again until the kingdom.

usedIn.n: Mark 2:13-22, Levi and the party
usedIn.s: Jesus calls a tax collector from his booth and eats with tax collectors and sinners. He is questioned about eating with them and about not fasting.

usedIn.n: Mark 6:14-29, Herod's banquet and John's death
usedIn.s: Herod hears of Jesus and thinks John has risen. Mark then tells how Herod, at his birthday banquet, had John beheaded.

usedIn.n: Mark 14:1-11, Perfume at Bethany
usedIn.s: Two days before Passover, at dinner in Bethany, a woman pours costly perfume on Jesus' head. He says she has anointed him for burial, and Judas goes to the chief priests.

usedIn.n: Mark 14:12-31, The Passover meal
usedIn.s: Jesus eats the Passover with the Twelve, names a betrayer at the table, gives the bread and the cup new meaning, and warns that all will scatter.

usedIn.n: Luke 7:36-50, A sinful woman at Simon's table
usedIn.s: At a Pharisee's banquet a woman known as a sinner weeps over Jesus' feet, wipes them with her hair and anoints them. Jesus answers his host's silent objection with a story of two debtors.

usedIn.n: Luke 14:1-14, Dropsy at a Pharisee's table, and guests who cannot repay
usedIn.s: On a Sabbath at the house of a leading Pharisee, Jesus heals a man with dropsy, tells the guests not to grab the best places, and tells the host to invite people who cannot invite him back.

usedIn.n: Luke 16:19-31, The rich man and Lazarus
usedIn.s: A rich man feasts every day while a beggar named Lazarus lies at his gate. Both die; Lazarus is carried to Abraham's side, and the rich man finds himself in torment in Hades.

usedIn.n: John 12:1-11, Mary's nard and loosened hair
usedIn.s: Six days before Passover, at a dinner in Jesus' honor in Bethany, Mary pours a pound of costly nard on his feet and wipes them with her hair. Judas objects, and Jesus says she has kept it for the day of his burial.

usedIn.n: John 13:1-30, Washing the disciples' feet, and the morsel for Judas
usedIn.s: At supper before Passover Jesus takes off his outer clothes, ties a towel around himself and washes his disciples' feet. Then he hands Judas the dipped morsel, and Judas goes out into the night.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 8:1-13, Knowledge, idols and the weak
usedIn.s: Answering those who know that an idol is nothing, Paul agrees there is one God and one Lord but warns that their freedom to eat sacrificial food, even in an idol's temple, can destroy a weaker believer.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 11:17-34, The Lord's Supper in a rich man's house
usedIn.s: Paul rebukes the church because at the Lord's Supper some go hungry while others eat their fill and get drunk, retells the tradition of the Last Supper, and tells them to wait for one another.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 4:1-11, The neighbors' parties and their abuse
usedIn.s: Armed with Christ's attitude, the readers have done with the life of the Gentiles, its debauchery, drinking parties and idolatry, and their old companions are surprised and heap abuse on them; they will give account to God. The end of all things is near, so they must be sober, love one another, be hospitable without grumbling, and use their gifts as stewards of God's grace.

entries.title: Hospitality to travelers
entries.summary: Taking in travelers was one of the great virtues of the ancient Mediterranean, above all among Jews. Messengers could travel light because they expected to be housed.
aliases: do not take them into your house
in a manner worthy of God
stand at the door and knock
entries.plain: **They knocked on a stranger's door at dusk, and the family set out bread and a bed without being asked.** There were few inns, and good ones were rare. Travelers relied on being taken in, and taking them in was a matter of honor and of faith. How a town treated a messenger was how it treated the one who sent him.
entries.then: Showing hospitality to travelers was one of the most important virtues of Mediterranean antiquity, especially in Judaism. Jewish travelers could count on it even far from home. Old Testament prophets had lodged with the faithful (2 Kings 4:8-11). Josephus says the Essenes "carry nothing at all with them when they travel into remote parts," except weapons against robbers. In every city a member of the group was appointed to look after strangers of their sect. A guest's greeting of peace, shalom, was a blessing on the house. A cup of cold water was what even the poorest could offer. Shaking dust off the feet on leaving a town treated it as pagan ground. The ESV Study Bible calls it "A sign used by Jews after leaving a Gentile region." At the door a good host supplied water for the guest's feet, which servants usually washed. He also gave a kiss of greeting and oil for the head. Abraham's welcome of three visitors in Genesis 18, at least two of them angels, was the model everyone cited (Josephus, Antiquities 1.11.2). In a village, Bailey writes, "the guest is guest of the community, not just of the individual". So the whole village's honor rode on feeding a late traveler, and a guest had to be served a fresh, unbroken loaf. Wright calls the laws of hospitality in the ancient Middle East strict. In Acts, Lydia counted it an honor to lodge Paul's company. Guests rarely stayed beyond three weeks. Jewish travelers avoided inns, which Keener says usually doubled as brothels. The shipwrecked had a special claim on kindness.
entries.bridge: An analogy: an old network of church families who take in traveling ministers. The visitor brings no money and no reservation, and the hosts treat him as they would treat the church that sent him.
entries.changes: Hospitality explains why Jesus can send messengers out with almost nothing, as in Matthew 10:9-11, and why refusing them was serious. Receiving the messenger meant receiving the sender. A host who skips the water, the kiss and the oil, as in Luke 7:44-46, insults his guest in front of the room. Paul's travels in Acts 16:15 depend on a household that takes the visitors in.
entries.not: **Not a favor kept within one circle.** A church network hosts its own people. In the ancient world hospitality was owed to strangers on the road as a public duty, and in a village the whole community's honor rode on how a late traveler was fed. Refusing it was a public failure. Nor was it entertaining friends.
entries.dissent: How much bread did a neighbor have for the midnight guest in Luke 11:5-8? Blomberg, following Stern and others, says three hand-sized loaves were the standard evening meal and bread was baked daily. So neighbors knew who had some left. Bailey says village bread is baked in batches and the loaves are large. He rejects both the small-loaf picture and daily baking. Keener's background commentary says many homes had used up the day's bread by nightfall, and a guest needed an unbroken loaf.

usedIn.n: Matthew 9:35-10:15, The Twelve sent with nothing
usedIn.s: Seeing the crowds as sheep without a shepherd, Jesus sends twelve apostles to the lost sheep of Israel, with no money, bag or staff, to stay with whoever will have them.

usedIn.n: Matthew 10:16-42, Wolves, floggings, a sword and a cup of water
usedIn.s: Jesus warns the Twelve of councils, floggings in synagogues and trials before governors and kings, of family turned against family, and promises that whoever receives them receives him.

usedIn.n: Matthew 25:31-46, Sheep, goats and the least of these
usedIn.s: The Son of Man comes in glory with his angels, gathers the nations, and separates them as a shepherd separates sheep from goats, judging them by how they treated the least of his brothers and sisters.

usedIn.n: Luke 7:36-50, A sinful woman at Simon's table
usedIn.s: At a Pharisee's banquet a woman known as a sinner weeps over Jesus' feet, wipes them with her hair and anoints them. Jesus answers his host's silent objection with a story of two debtors.

usedIn.n: Luke 10:1-24, Seventy sent out, and Satan falling
usedIn.s: Jesus sends seventy others, or seventy-two, ahead of him in pairs, with no purse, bag or sandals, to towns that will welcome or refuse them. They come back rejoicing that even the demons obey, and Jesus says he saw Satan fall like lightning.

usedIn.n: Luke 10:25-37, The Samaritan on the Jericho road
usedIn.s: A lawyer asks what he must do to inherit eternal life and then who his neighbor is. Jesus tells of a man left half dead on the road to Jericho, passed by a priest and a Levite and rescued by a Samaritan.

usedIn.n: Luke 10:38-42, Mary at the teacher's feet
usedIn.s: In Martha's house Mary sits at Jesus' feet listening while Martha works at serving. When Martha complains, Jesus says Mary has chosen the better part.

usedIn.n: Luke 11:1-13, Father, daily bread and a friend at midnight
usedIn.s: Asked to teach his disciples to pray, Jesus gives a short prayer to the Father, then tells of a man who wakes a neighbor at midnight to borrow bread for a guest.

usedIn.n: Luke 14:15-24, The great banquet and the excuses
usedIn.s: A guest blesses whoever will eat bread in God's kingdom. Jesus tells of a man whose invited guests all excuse themselves when the feast is ready, so he fills his house with the poor and with people from the roads.

usedIn.n: Luke 18:35-19:10, A blind beggar and Zacchaeus at Jericho
usedIn.s: Near Jericho a blind beggar calls Jesus Son of David and receives his sight. In the town Jesus invites himself to the house of Zacchaeus, a rich chief tax collector, who promises to give half his goods to the poor and repay fourfold.

usedIn.n: Luke 24:13-35, A stranger on the Emmaus road
usedIn.s: Two disciples walking home to Emmaus are joined by a stranger who explains the Scriptures to them. They press him to stay, and they recognize him when he breaks the bread.

usedIn.n: John 1:35-51, Come and see
usedIn.s: Two of John's disciples follow Jesus and spend the day with him. Andrew brings his brother Simon, Philip brings Nathanael, and Jesus promises they will see heaven opened and angels going up and down on the Son of Man.

usedIn.n: Acts 15:22-35, The letter to the Gentile churches
usedIn.s: The council sends Judas and Silas with Paul and Barnabas to carry a letter to the Gentile believers of Antioch, Syria and Cilicia. It is read to the church at Antioch, who rejoice at its encouragement.

usedIn.n: Acts 16:11-15, Lydia at the place of prayer
usedIn.s: In Philippi, a Roman colony, Paul finds women gathered by the river on the Sabbath. Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth from Thyatira, believes, is baptized with her household and insists that the missionaries stay at her house.

usedIn.n: Acts 17:1-9, Another king in Thessalonica
usedIn.s: Paul argues from the Scriptures in the synagogue at Thessalonica that the Messiah had to suffer and rise. Some believe; opponents raise a mob, drag Jason before the city officials and accuse the believers of defying Caesar by proclaiming another king.

usedIn.n: Acts 28:1-10, Malta: the viper and the goddess Justice
usedIn.s: The islanders of Malta welcome the shipwrecked with a fire. When a viper fastens on Paul's hand they decide that Justice will not let a murderer live; when he takes no harm they call him a god. Publius, the island's chief man, takes them in, and Paul heals his father and many others.

usedIn.n: Romans 12:1-21, A living sacrifice
usedIn.s: Paul urges believers to offer their bodies as a living sacrifice, to see themselves as members of one body, and to love without pretense: honoring one another, welcoming strangers, weeping with those who weep and repaying evil with good.

usedIn.n: Romans 15:14-24, To Spain by way of Rome
usedIn.s: Paul describes his priestly work of offering the Gentiles to God, from Jerusalem round to Illyricum, and his plan to visit Rome on his way to Spain and be helped on his journey there.

usedIn.n: Romans 16:17-27, Tertius, Gaius and Erastus
usedIn.s: Paul warns against those who cause divisions, promises that God will soon crush Satan under the believers' feet, and passes on greetings from Corinth, including his scribe Tertius, his host Gaius and Erastus the city treasurer.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 1:12-2:4, Changed plans, the seal and the down payment
usedIn.s: Accused of fickleness for changing his travel plans, Paul answers that his word is reliable because all God's promises are Yes in Christ, who has anointed and sealed them and given the Spirit as a down payment, and explains that he stayed away to spare them.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 7:2-16, Titus arrives and the letter that hurt
usedIn.s: In Macedonia Paul is comforted by Titus's arrival and his news that the Corinthians grieved over Paul's harsh letter in a way that led to repentance, and that they received Titus with fear and trembling.

usedIn.n: Galatians 1:11-24, Saul the zealot, Arabia, and fifteen days with Cephas
usedIn.s: Paul insists that his gospel came by revelation and not from human teachers, and tells of his zeal as a persecutor, his call, his time in Arabia and Damascus, and a short first visit to Jerusalem to get to know Cephas.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 3:1-13, Overseers, deacons and the women
usedIn.s: Paul lists what is required of an overseer, above reproach, faithful in marriage, hospitable, able to teach, managing his household well, and then of deacons and of the women, who must also be worthy of respect.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 1:8-18, Not ashamed of my chains, the deposit, and Onesiphorus
usedIn.s: Paul tells Timothy not to be ashamed of the Lord's testimony or of him as a prisoner, but to share his suffering and guard the good deposit; everyone in Asia has deserted him except Onesiphorus, who searched Rome until he found him.

usedIn.n: Titus 1:1-9, Elders in every town, and God's steward
usedIn.s: Paul greets Titus, whom he left in Crete to put in order what was unfinished and to appoint elders in every town, and lists what an elder must be: blameless, faithful to his wife, with believing children, a steward of God's household, hospitable and able to hold to sound teaching.

usedIn.n: Titus 3:9-15, A divisive person, winter at Nicopolis, and Zenas and Apollos
usedIn.s: Titus is to avoid foolish controversies, genealogies and quarrels about the law, and to warn a divisive person twice before having nothing more to do with him; Paul plans to winter at Nicopolis and asks Titus to send Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way with everything they need.

usedIn.n: Philemon 1-7, The church in Philemon's house
usedIn.s: Paul, a prisoner, and Timothy write to Philemon, to Apphia and Archippus, and to the church that meets in Philemon's house, and Paul thanks God for Philemon's love and faith, his partnership, and the way he has refreshed the hearts of God's people.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 13:1-6, Strangers, angels, prisoners
usedIn.s: The writer turns to everyday duties: brotherly love, hospitality to strangers, since some have entertained angels without knowing it, care for prisoners as if in prison with them, honor for marriage, and freedom from the love of money.

usedIn.n: James 2:14-26, Faith that shudders, Abraham and Rahab
usedIn.s: Faith without deeds is dead, James argues. Wishing a hungry brother well helps no one, the demons believe that God is one and shudder, and Abraham and Rahab were counted righteous by what they did.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 4:1-11, The neighbors' parties and their abuse
usedIn.s: Armed with Christ's attitude, the readers have done with the life of the Gentiles, its debauchery, drinking parties and idolatry, and their old companions are surprised and heap abuse on them; they will give account to God. The end of all things is near, so they must be sober, love one another, be hospitable without grumbling, and use their gifts as stewards of God's grace.

usedIn.n: 2 John 7-13, Deceivers at the door, paper and ink
usedIn.s: Many deceivers who refuse to confess that Jesus Christ came in the flesh are abroad in the world; such a one is the deceiver and the antichrist. Whoever runs ahead and does not keep to Christ's teaching does not have God, and the readers are not to take such a person into the house or greet him. The elder would rather not use paper and ink, and hopes to talk face to face.

usedIn.n: 3 John 1-8, Gaius and the traveling brothers
usedIn.s: The elder writes to his dear friend Gaius, praying that he is in good health and glad to hear that he walks in the truth. Gaius has been faithful in what he does for the brothers, strangers though they are; he should supply them for the next stage of their journey in a way that honors God, since they went out for the sake of the Name and took nothing from the pagans.

usedIn.n: Revelation 3:14-22, Laodicea, lukewarm and rich
usedIn.s: To Laodicea the faithful and true witness says the church is neither cold nor hot but lukewarm, and he will spit it out. It thinks itself rich but is poor, blind and naked; he counsels it to buy gold, white clothes and eye salve, and stands at the door and knocks.

entries.title: The banquet of the age to come
entries.summary: The feast Jews expected God to spread for the righteous when his kingdom came, with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob at the table.
aliases: many will come from east and west
I will come in and eat
stand at the door and knock
entries.plain: **Everyone who had waited through the hard years would finally sit down to the celebration dinner.** Isaiah promised that God would one day spread a rich feast for all peoples. By Jesus' day many Jews pictured the end as a great banquet, where the faithful of Israel would recline at table with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
entries.then: The future banquet in God's kingdom was a standard Jewish image. The Bible said it was for all peoples (Isaiah 25:6). Jewish literature of this period stressed that it was prepared for Israel, exalted over its enemies (Keener). People sat at ordinary meals but reclined at feasts, and were placed by rank. Sharing a table meant intimacy. So fellowship with the patriarchs was a hope for Israel, not for Gentiles, with whom Jews did not eat. Other Jewish texts used outer darkness for the place of the damned (1 Enoch 10:4-6). The ESV Study Bible reads Matthew 8:11-12 as Gentiles joining the patriarchs. It suggests the feeding of the five thousand may foreshadow the banquet. Wright says that when Israel's God acted, the nations were expected to share in it, for judgment or for blessing. Jesus, he says, turns the expectation: those who think themselves heirs may find themselves outside. The feast was expected to bring the unending wine the Bible had promised (Amos 9:13-14). Rabbis often told parables of a king's wedding feast for his son. Present fellowship at Jesus' table in Revelation 3:20 could foreshadow the expected banquet (Revelation 19:9). Keener calls it an invitation to a lavish banquet. Isaiah 25:6-8 also swallows up death. Some later Jewish teachers, as in 2 Baruch, said Leviathan would be served at the feast. Beale notes that a shared supper sealed close fellowship in the Semitic world.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a victory banquet promised at the end of a long war. Everyone who served expects a seat, and the guest list is the first thing people want to see.
entries.changes: The banquet stands behind sayings about who will eat in the kingdom, as at Matthew 8:11-12, where Gentiles recline with the patriarchs and expected heirs are left outside. Meals in the Gospels can preview it, so a crowd fed in a deserted place, as at Mark 6:42, may point ahead to the feast. The wedding supper of Revelation 19:9 uses the same picture.
entries.not: **Not a feast earned by service.** A victory dinner seats those who fought. The prophets said God would lay this feast for all peoples, though many Jewish writers of the period pictured Israel exalted over its enemies. In Wright's reading, Jesus warns that those who assumed a seat might find themselves outside. Nor is it a picture of heaven as an endless meal.

usedIn.n: Matthew 8:1-17, A leper, a centurion and a mother-in-law
usedIn.s: Coming down the mountain, Jesus touches and heals a leper, heals a centurion's servant from a distance, and heals Peter's mother-in-law and many others.

usedIn.n: Matthew 14:13-36, Bread in a deserted place, a walk on the sea
usedIn.s: Jesus feeds five thousand men, besides women and children, in a deserted place, then comes to the disciples walking on the lake, and Peter tries to walk to him.

usedIn.n: Matthew 22:1-14, The king's wedding feast
usedIn.s: A king's invited guests refuse to come to his son's wedding and kill his messengers. He burns their city, fills the hall with people from the roads, and throws out a guest without wedding clothes.

usedIn.n: Matthew 26:17-30, The Passover and the cup
usedIn.s: Jesus eats the Passover with the Twelve in the city, names the one who dips with him as his betrayer, gives the bread and the cup new meaning, and vows not to drink wine again until the kingdom.

usedIn.n: Luke 13:22-35, The narrow door, the feast, the fox and the hen
usedIn.s: On the way to Jerusalem Jesus warns that many will find the door shut while people from east and west recline at the feast in God's kingdom. Warned that Herod wants to kill him, he calls Herod a fox and grieves over Jerusalem.

usedIn.n: Luke 14:15-24, The great banquet and the excuses
usedIn.s: A guest blesses whoever will eat bread in God's kingdom. Jesus tells of a man whose invited guests all excuse themselves when the feast is ready, so he fills his house with the poor and with people from the roads.

usedIn.n: Revelation 3:14-22, Laodicea, lukewarm and rich
usedIn.s: To Laodicea the faithful and true witness says the church is neither cold nor hot but lukewarm, and he will spit it out. It thinks itself rich but is poor, blind and naked; he counsels it to buy gold, white clothes and eye salve, and stands at the door and knocks.

usedIn.n: Revelation 19:1-10, the marriage supper of the Lamb
usedIn.s: A vast heavenly crowd shouts hallelujah because God has judged the great prostitute, and again because the Lamb's wedding day has arrived and his bride stands ready in fine linen. The angel declares those invited to the wedding feast blessed, and when John bows to him, tells him to worship God alone.

entries.title: The synagogue
entries.summary: The local gathering place where Jews met on the Sabbath to pray and study Scripture. It was also a community center, run by people of standing.
aliases: reading of the Law and the Prophets
entries.plain: **Everyone in town was at the meeting hall on Saturday, so that is where the news broke.** The synagogue was not the temple. There was one temple, in Jerusalem, but a town could have its own synagogue: a place to pray, hear Scripture read and explained, and run the business of the community.
entries.then: On the Sabbath, Jews met in synagogues for prayer and the study of Scripture. The Greek title for a synagogue leader covered different roles in different places, sometimes even donors. But it nearly always meant a person of status and usually wealth. Synagogues doubled as community centers, and discipline could be carried out there. Keener describes, from somewhat later and idealized tradition, a flogging of 39 lashes, kept under the biblical limit of 40 (Deuteronomy 25:2-3). A synagogue court ordered it after a warning, and the attendant carried it out. An offender could escape it only by renouncing his Jewish community. Seating showed rank. The best seats were on the raised platform, and in some synagogues many people sat on the floor. Synagogues were led by priests or prominent laymen. As community courts, they could impose several levels of exclusion. The gravest left the offender treated as a pagan. Even outside the land Rome let Jewish communities discipline their own members. Services included readings from the Law and the Prophets. After them the rulers of the synagogue could invite a visiting teacher to speak, and popular visiting teachers normally were invited. Jerusalem had synagogues for Jews from abroad, among them one built by freedmen. A regular synagogue needed ten Jewish men. Where a town lacked them, Jews might meet at a place of prayer near water, since washing the hands before prayer was standard in the Diaspora.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a town hall that is also the chapel and the courtroom. The same room hosts Saturday prayers, the reading of Scripture, the leading families in the front seats, and the hearing where someone is punished.
entries.changes: The synagogue was where a town gathered, so teaching, healing or conflict there happened in front of everyone, as in Mark 1:21-28. It was also a place of local discipline, which is why followers are warned of floggings in synagogues in Matthew 10:17. Paul starts in the synagogue in town after town, as in Acts 17:1-2.
entries.not: **Not a hall for everyone in town.** The synagogue served the Jewish community, often a minority in a Gentile city. Its discipline reached only members, and an offender could escape it by leaving that community. Nor was it a church with a pastor; its leader was a person of local standing, sometimes a donor.
