usedIn.n: Matthew 6:1-18, Alms, prayer and fasting in secret
usedIn.s: Jesus warns against doing acts of piety to be seen, and teaches his disciples the Lord's Prayer.

usedIn.n: Matthew 9:18-34, A ruler's daughter, a bleeding woman, the blind and the mute
usedIn.s: A synagogue ruler asks Jesus to raise his daughter; on the way a woman touches the fringe of his cloak. Then two blind men call him Son of David, and a mute man speaks.

usedIn.n: Matthew 10:16-42, Wolves, floggings, a sword and a cup of water
usedIn.s: Jesus warns the Twelve of councils, floggings in synagogues and trials before governors and kings, of family turned against family, and promises that whoever receives them receives him.

usedIn.n: Matthew 12:1-14, Grain on the Sabbath, a withered hand
usedIn.s: Pharisees object when the disciples pick grain on the Sabbath. Jesus answers with David, the priests in the temple and mercy, then heals a withered hand in the synagogue.

usedIn.n: Matthew 13:53-58, No honor in Nazareth
usedIn.s: Teaching in his hometown synagogue, Jesus is dismissed as the carpenter's son whose family everyone knows, and he says a prophet is not without honor except at home.

usedIn.n: Matthew 18:15-20, Two or three witnesses and the assembly
usedIn.s: Jesus sets out how to deal with a brother who sins: privately, then with witnesses, then before the church. What they bind on earth is bound in heaven, and he is present where two or three gather in his name.

usedIn.n: Matthew 23:1-12, Moses' seat, wide phylacteries, the best seats
usedIn.s: Jesus tells the crowds to do what the scribes and Pharisees teach but not what they do, and mocks their wide phylacteries, long tassels, best seats and love of the title rabbi.

usedIn.n: Mark 1:21-45, A Sabbath in Capernaum and a leper
usedIn.s: Jesus teaches in the synagogue, drives out a spirit, heals Simon's mother-in-law and, after sunset, the whole town. Then he touches and cleanses a leper.

usedIn.n: Mark 5:21-43, A synagogue leader's daughter and a bleeding woman
usedIn.s: On the way to heal Jairus' dying daughter, Jesus is touched by a woman who has bled for twelve years. Then he raises the girl.

usedIn.n: Mark 13:1-37, The temple's fall and the Son of Man
usedIn.s: Leaving the temple, Jesus says not one stone will be left on another. On the Mount of Olives he warns of what is coming and of the Son of Man on the clouds.

usedIn.n: Luke 4:16-30, The year of the Lord's favor in Nazareth
usedIn.s: In the Nazareth synagogue Jesus reads Isaiah's promise of good news for the poor and release for captives and says it is fulfilled today. When he points to Elijah and Elisha helping foreigners, the town tries to throw him off a cliff.

usedIn.n: Luke 7:1-10, A centurion who built the synagogue
usedIn.s: Jewish elders in Capernaum plead for a centurion whose valued slave is dying, because he loves their nation and built their synagogue. The centurion sends word that Jesus need not come under his roof, only give the order.

usedIn.n: Luke 13:10-21, A bent woman freed on the Sabbath; mustard and leaven
usedIn.s: Teaching in a synagogue on the Sabbath, Jesus frees a woman bent double for eighteen years. The synagogue ruler objects, and Jesus answers with an ox untied for water, then compares God's kingdom to a mustard seed and to leaven.

usedIn.n: Luke 21:5-38, The temple's stones and Jerusalem surrounded
usedIn.s: When people admire the temple's stones, Jesus says not one will be left on another. He warns of false claimants, arrests in synagogues, Jerusalem surrounded by armies, and signs in the sky before the Son of Man comes.

usedIn.n: John 6:22-71, The bread from heaven
usedIn.s: In the synagogue at Capernaum the crowd asks for a sign like the manna. Jesus answers that he is the bread of life come down from heaven, and his hard words about eating his flesh drive many disciples away.

usedIn.n: Acts 6:8-7:53, Stephen's charge and speech
usedIn.s: Men from the Diaspora synagogues accuse Stephen of speaking against the temple and the law. He answers with Israel's story, from Abraham to the temple, and turns the charge back on his judges.

usedIn.n: Acts 9:1-31, Saul on the Damascus road
usedIn.s: Carrying the high priest's letters to the synagogues of Damascus, Saul is stopped by a light and a voice. Blinded, healed and baptized, the persecutor begins to proclaim Jesus and has to escape over the city wall.

usedIn.n: Acts 13:13-52, The synagogue at Pisidian Antioch
usedIn.s: Invited to speak after the synagogue readings in a Roman colony, Paul tells Israel's story from the exodus to Jesus. Gentiles welcome the message, and the city's leading men and women drive the apostles out.

usedIn.n: Acts 15:1-21, The council in Jerusalem
usedIn.s: Teachers from Judea insist that Gentile believers must be circumcised to be saved. The apostles and elders meet in Jerusalem; Peter and James argue that God has accepted Gentiles as they are, and James proposes a few rules for them to keep.

usedIn.n: Acts 17:1-9, Another king in Thessalonica
usedIn.s: Paul argues from the Scriptures in the synagogue at Thessalonica that the Messiah had to suffer and rise. Some believe; opponents raise a mob, drag Jason before the city officials and accuse the believers of defying Caesar by proclaiming another king.

usedIn.n: Acts 18:1-11, Tentmakers in Corinth
usedIn.s: In Corinth Paul lodges and works with Aquila and Priscilla, Jews lately expelled from Rome who share his trade. When the synagogue turns against him he moves next door to the house of Titius Justus, and the synagogue leader Crispus believes with his household.

usedIn.n: Acts 28:17-31, Two years in rented quarters
usedIn.s: Paul calls the Jewish leaders of Rome, explains why he is in chains, and spends a day arguing from Moses and the Prophets. Some are persuaded and some are not; for two whole years he lives at his own expense, welcoming everyone and preaching the kingdom without hindrance.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 5:1-13, A man and his father's wife
usedIn.s: A church member is living with his stepmother and the church is proud of itself. Paul tells them to hand the man over to Satan, clear out the old leaven as a household does before Passover, and not eat with a so-called brother who lives that way.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 6:1-11, Lawsuits before unbelievers
usedIn.s: Paul is appalled that believers take one another to court before pagan judges, reminds them that God's people will judge the world and even angels, and asks why they would not rather be wronged.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 14:26-40, Order when the church meets
usedIn.s: Paul regulates a meeting where everyone brings a hymn, a teaching, a revelation or a tongue: speakers take turns, prophets weigh one another's words, women are to be silent and ask at home, and everything is to be done decently and in order.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 2:5-13, Forgive the offender; no rest at Troas
usedIn.s: The man who caused the grief has been punished enough by the majority, so Paul urges the church to forgive him lest Satan outwit them, then tells how he left an open door at Troas because Titus had not come.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 3:1-18, Letters of recommendation and Moses' veil
usedIn.s: Paul needs no letters of recommendation, since the Corinthians are his letter, written by the Spirit on hearts; he sets the fading glory on Moses' veiled face against the greater glory of the new covenant.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 11:16-33, The fool's boast and the basket over the wall
usedIn.s: Forced to boast like a fool, Paul matches his rivals' Jewish credentials and then lists sufferings instead of achievements: lashes, rods, stoning, shipwreck, the dangers of the road, hunger and cold, and a night escape down the wall of Damascus.

usedIn.n: 2 Thessalonians 3:6-18, The idle, the busybodies, and a greeting in Paul's own hand
usedIn.s: Paul tells the church to keep away from believers who are idle and will not work, recalls how he worked night and day to set an example, lays down that anyone unwilling to work should not eat, and signs the letter in his own hand.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 4:6-16, Training for godliness, and a young leader
usedIn.s: Timothy is to train himself for godliness as an athlete trains his body, set an example despite his youth, devote himself to the public reading of Scripture and teaching, and not neglect the gift given when the elders laid hands on him.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 10:19-25, Through the curtain, bodies washed, meeting together
usedIn.s: Because Jesus' blood has opened a new and living way through the curtain, believers may enter the most holy place with confidence. With hearts sprinkled and bodies washed with pure water, they are to hold fast, spur one another on, and not give up meeting together.

usedIn.n: James 2:1-13, The gold ring and the good seat
usedIn.s: James forbids favoritism in the assembly. A rich man with a gold ring is given a good seat and a poor man in dirty clothes is told to stand, though it is the rich who drag believers into court and slander the noble name; the royal law of love rules out partiality, and mercy triumphs over judgment.

usedIn.n: Revelation 3:1-6, Sardis, alive in name only
usedIn.s: To Sardis the one who holds the seven spirits and seven stars says the church has a reputation for being alive but is dead, and warns that he will come like a thief if it does not wake up. A few have not soiled their clothes; the one who conquers will walk with him in white and will not be blotted out of the book of life.

entries.title: The Sabbath
entries.summary: The seventh day, a commanded rest from sundown to sundown, a badge of Jewish identity, and a law the experts argued over in detail.
aliases: shadow of what was to come
entries.plain: **The whole town plans its week around the day the stores are shut.** The Sabbath was the seventh day, when God's law said to stop work. You did not carry loads or harvest. Because it mattered so much, teachers argued about exactly what counted as work.
entries.then: The Sabbath was a regular reminder of creation and of the Exodus. In a pagan world it marked Jews out, alongside circumcision and the food laws (Wright). It was a sign that Israel belonged to the creator God, not a rule kept to earn favor. Jewish days ran from sundown to sundown, and one should not carry loads on the Sabbath. The law let hungry travelers pick heads of grain (Deuteronomy 23:25). The problem was doing it on the Sabbath, which the Mishnah later classed as reaping. Even Pharisees did not agree among themselves about which acts broke the Sabbath. The school of Hillel allowed prayer for the sick on the Sabbath, and the school of Shammai did not. Jewish tradition allowed washing and anointing a corpse on the Sabbath. But spices could not be bought until it was over, at sundown on Saturday. The day of Preparation means the day before a Sabbath. Keener warns against picturing the Pharisees as legalists. Jews across the ancient world honored the day and kept it with joy. Teachers agreed that some things came before it, such as temple service, saving a life and defensive war. Judaism also had its calendar of holy days, new moons and sabbatical years. Roman decrees let Jews keep the day without fines. Josephus quotes a decree of Ephesus that "no one of them should be hindered from keeping the sabbath day." Some Jewish writers expected the world to come to be the final Sabbath rest.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a union rule about breaks and overtime. Everyone agrees on the rule. The fights are over the edge cases, and a newcomer who seems careless about them gets watched.
entries.changes: Sabbath disputes turn on what counted as work, as in Mark 2:23-24, and the experts themselves disagreed. Healing on the Sabbath, as in Matthew 12:10, drew the sharpest debate. The day also sets the timetable of the burial and the empty tomb. Colossians 2:16 names Sabbaths with festivals and new moons among the things believers are not to be judged by.
entries.not: **Not a work rule negotiated between bosses and workers.** The Sabbath was God's command, a sign that Israel belonged to the creator, recalling creation and the Exodus. Jews kept it with joy as a badge of who they were. Nor was it a weekend to fill as you liked; the law said what you could do and carry.
sources: N. T. Wright, Mark for Everyone, comment on Mark 2:23-28, and Glossary, entry sabbath

usedIn.n: Matthew 24:15-28, The desolating sacrilege and the flight
usedIn.s: When the desolating sacrilege spoken of by Daniel stands in the holy place, those in Judea must flee to the mountains at once. False messiahs will say he is in the wilderness, but his coming will be like lightning.

usedIn.n: Matthew 27:57-66, Joseph's tomb and the sealed stone
usedIn.s: Joseph of Arimathea, a rich disciple, asks Pilate for the body and lays it in his own new tomb. The next day the chief priests get a guard and a seal on the stone.

usedIn.n: Mark 1:21-45, A Sabbath in Capernaum and a leper
usedIn.s: Jesus teaches in the synagogue, drives out a spirit, heals Simon's mother-in-law and, after sunset, the whole town. Then he touches and cleanses a leper.

usedIn.n: Mark 2:23-3:6, Grain and a withered hand on the Sabbath
usedIn.s: Jesus defends his disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath, heals a man's hand in the synagogue, and the Pharisees start plotting with the Herodians.

usedIn.n: Mark 15:42-16:8, The tomb
usedIn.s: Joseph of Arimathea buries Jesus before the Sabbath. When it is over, the women come with spices, find the stone rolled away, and hear that he has been raised.

usedIn.n: Luke 13:10-21, A bent woman freed on the Sabbath; mustard and leaven
usedIn.s: Teaching in a synagogue on the Sabbath, Jesus frees a woman bent double for eighteen years. The synagogue ruler objects, and Jesus answers with an ox untied for water, then compares God's kingdom to a mustard seed and to leaven.

usedIn.n: Luke 14:1-14, Dropsy at a Pharisee's table, and guests who cannot repay
usedIn.s: On a Sabbath at the house of a leading Pharisee, Jesus heals a man with dropsy, tells the guests not to grab the best places, and tells the host to invite people who cannot invite him back.

usedIn.n: John 5:1-18, The pool of Bethesda on the Sabbath
usedIn.s: At a pool with five porches, Jesus heals a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years and tells him to pick up his mat. It is the Sabbath, and the dispute that follows turns on Jesus calling God his own Father.

usedIn.n: John 7:1-36, Up to the Festival of Tabernacles
usedIn.s: Jesus stays in Galilee while the Judeans look for a chance to kill him, then goes up to Tabernacles privately and teaches in the temple. The crowds argue over whether he is a deceiver or the Messiah, and the chief priests send guards to arrest him.

usedIn.n: John 9:1-41, A man born blind is put out
usedIn.s: Jesus puts mud on a blind beggar's eyes and sends him to wash in Siloam. Because it is the Sabbath the man is questioned, his parents are afraid, and when he defends Jesus he is thrown out.

usedIn.n: John 19:31-42, Legs unbroken and a hundred pounds of spices
usedIn.s: Because the coming Sabbath is a high day, the leaders ask for the bodies to be taken down. The soldiers find Jesus already dead and pierce his side; Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus bury him with a lavish weight of spices in a new tomb in a garden.

usedIn.n: Acts 1:12-26, The Twelve made whole by lot
usedIn.s: Back in Jerusalem the apostles pray in an upstairs room with the women and Jesus' family. Peter says Judas's place must be filled, and the lot falls on Matthias.

usedIn.n: Romans 14:1-23, Vegetables, holy days and wine
usedIn.s: Some believers eat only vegetables and keep certain days; others eat anything and treat every day alike. Paul tells both not to judge one another, since all will stand before God's judgment seat, and not to wreck another's faith over food.

usedIn.n: Galatians 4:1-11, Heirs, slaves and the elements of the world
usedIn.s: An heir who is still a child is no better off than a slave, Paul says; so we were enslaved under the elements of the world until God sent his Son to redeem us and his Spirit to cry Abba, and he asks why the Galatians want to go back to observing special days, months, seasons and years.

usedIn.n: Colossians 2:16-23, Food, new moons, Sabbaths and the worship of angels
usedIn.s: Paul tells the believers not to let anyone judge them over food, drink, festivals, new moons or Sabbaths, or disqualify them with self-denial, the worship of angels and visions, and calls rules about what not to touch or taste human commands with no power over the flesh.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 3:1-4:13, Moses the servant, and the rest still open
usedIn.s: Moses was faithful in God's house as a servant; Jesus is faithful over it as the Son. Psalm 95's warning not to harden hearts as in the wilderness still speaks today, because the rest God promised was never reached under Joshua and remains open for God's people.

entries.title: The temple and its courts
entries.summary: Herod's huge rebuilt temple in Jerusalem, believed to be God's dwelling, laid out in courts that kept Gentiles, women and Jewish men at set distances.
aliases: sets himself up in God's temple
entries.plain: **You could tour the capitol, but signs told you which halls you were not allowed into.** There was one temple, in Jerusalem, and Jews believed God dwelt there. It was the place of sacrifice, a market for the animals, a bank, and the base of the priests' power.
entries.then: Herod the Great began rebuilding the temple in 19 BC. The work was finished in AD 63, and the Romans destroyed it in AD 70. It was believed to be the unique dwelling of God on earth, where heaven and earth met (Wright). It was the largest temple in the ancient world, larger than the temple of Artemis at Ephesus. The temple mount took up more than a quarter of Jerusalem and could hold an estimated 75,000 people. Pilgrims bought sacrificial animals on site, and money changers turned local coins into the standard currency. For purity reasons Herod's temple divided its space into courts. The court of Israel was for Jewish men, the court of the women lay below it, and an outer court was open to Gentiles. Josephus describes the stone barrier with pillars declaring, in Greek and Roman letters, "that no foreigner should go within that sanctuary". One such Greek warning, found in 1871, survives (Price and House). In Josephus's account of the siege, Titus reminds the Jews that Rome let them kill anyone who crossed it. Temples served as banks, and the treasury sat beside the court of the women. The temple had become the central symbol of Jewish faith. So a claim that someone was greater than it would sound presumptuous (Keener). Josephus dates the start of Herod's rebuilding to the eighteenth year of his reign. He calls the eastern cloister the work of King Solomon, a memory the ESV Study Bible connects with Solomon's Porch. Josephus also describes one gate of Corinthian brass, reached by fifteen steps from the court of the women. It outshone the gates plated with silver and gold. Keener identifies it with the Beautiful Gate of Acts 3:2, though the cultural backgrounds notes say that name is not attested elsewhere.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a national cathedral, the central bank and the supreme court in one walled compound, with security zones. The building is the nation's heart, and whoever runs it holds a great deal of power.
entries.changes: The temple was the center of Israel's worship and of priestly power, so an act or word against it, as in Mark 11:15-17, struck at both. Gifts at its altar assumed a right relationship with others, as in Matthew 5:23-24. In Acts 21:28 a charge of defiling it starts a riot.
entries.not: **Not one great church among many.** A national cathedral is a symbol, and worship goes on in every parish. The temple was the one place of sacrifice, believed to be God's own dwelling where heaven and earth met. Its security zones were purity lines, and a Gentile who crossed the barrier could be killed.
entries.dissent: Two points. First, what did Jesus do in 11:15-17? Keener suggests he may have objected to a misplaced emphasis, in the only court where Gentiles could worship. The ESV Study Bible reads it as purifying the temple and restoring it to its purpose. Wright rejects the commerce reading as too modern. He calls it "a dramatic acted parable of judgment", announcing God's condemnation of the temple, with brigands meaning violent revolutionaries, not thieves. The cultural backgrounds article on Herod's temple sides with Keener: the money changers' occupation of the court of the Gentiles limited access to it. Garland and Wilkins put the market in the Royal Stoa, not across the court. Garland finds no evidence that the outer court was thought of as a place for Gentiles to pray, since it marked how far they could go. Second, the torn curtain in 15:38. Keener, on Matthew 27:51, says it probably implies the departure of God's presence and the coming destruction, while some see new access to God. The ESV Study Bible reads it as access now opened through Jesus' sacrifice.

usedIn.n: Matthew 17:24-27, The coin in the fish's mouth
usedIn.s: Collectors of the two-drachma temple tax ask Peter whether his teacher pays. Jesus says the king's sons are free, then sends Peter to find a coin in a fish to pay for them both.

usedIn.n: Matthew 21:12-22, Tables, the blind and the lame, and a fig tree
usedIn.s: Jesus drives out the sellers and overturns the money changers' tables, heals the blind and the lame in the temple courts, and the next morning curses a leafy fig tree that withers at once.

usedIn.n: Matthew 24:1-14, Stones, birth pangs and false messiahs
usedIn.s: As the disciples admire the temple, Jesus says not one stone will be left on another. On the Mount of Olives he warns of false messiahs, wars and persecution, the beginning of the birth pangs.

usedIn.n: Matthew 27:27-56, Mock king, the cross and the torn curtain
usedIn.s: Soldiers dress Jesus as a mock king. He is crucified as king of the Jews between two rebels, cries out in the words of Psalm 22 and dies; the curtain tears, the earth shakes, and women watch from a distance.

usedIn.n: Mark 11:1-11, The ride into Jerusalem
usedIn.s: Jesus sends for a colt no one has ridden and rides into Jerusalem over cloaks and branches while the crowd shouts Hosanna.

usedIn.n: Mark 11:12-25, The fig tree and the temple
usedIn.s: Jesus curses a leafy fig tree with no fruit, overturns the tables in the temple, and the next morning the tree has withered.

usedIn.n: Mark 13:1-37, The temple's fall and the Son of Man
usedIn.s: Leaving the temple, Jesus says not one stone will be left on another. On the Mount of Olives he warns of what is coming and of the Son of Man on the clouds.

usedIn.n: Mark 14:53-72, At the high priest's house
usedIn.s: The council tries Jesus at night. He says he is the Messiah and quotes the Son of Man coming with the clouds, and is condemned for blasphemy while Peter denies him in the courtyard.

usedIn.n: Mark 15:21-41, The cross
usedIn.s: Jesus is crucified as king of the Jews between two bandits, mocked by passers-by, and dies with a loud cry. The temple curtain tears, and women watch from a distance.

usedIn.n: Luke 1:5-25, A priest's turn at the incense altar
usedIn.s: An elderly village priest, picked by lot to offer incense in the sanctuary, learns from the angel Gabriel that his childless wife will have a son who will prepare Israel for God with an Elijah-like power.

usedIn.n: Luke 2:21-40, Two birds, Simeon and Anna
usedIn.s: Jesus is circumcised and named on the eighth day. At the temple his parents make the offering the law allowed the poor, and two old people waiting for God's comfort, Simeon and the widow Anna, speak about the child.

usedIn.n: Luke 2:41-52, A twelve-year-old among the teachers
usedIn.s: On the family's yearly Passover pilgrimage the twelve-year-old Jesus stays behind in Jerusalem, and after three days his parents find him in the temple courts among the teachers.

usedIn.n: Luke 18:9-14, Two men go up to the temple to pray
usedIn.s: Jesus tells of a Pharisee who thanks God that he is not like other people and a tax collector who stands far off, beats his breast and asks for mercy. The tax collector goes home justified.

usedIn.n: Luke 19:28-48, The king rides down to the city and weeps over it
usedIn.s: Jesus rides a borrowed colt down the Mount of Olives while his disciples spread their cloaks and praise the king who comes. Seeing the city, he weeps over the siege to come, then drives the sellers out of the temple.

usedIn.n: Luke 20:45-21:4, Long robes and a widow's two coins
usedIn.s: Jesus warns against teachers of the law who love long robes and the best seats and devour widows' houses. Then he watches a poor widow put two small coins into the temple treasury.

usedIn.n: Luke 21:5-38, The temple's stones and Jerusalem surrounded
usedIn.s: When people admire the temple's stones, Jesus says not one will be left on another. He warns of false claimants, arrests in synagogues, Jerusalem surrounded by armies, and signs in the sky before the Son of Man comes.

usedIn.n: Luke 24:36-53, Not a ghost; hands lifted in blessing
usedIn.s: Jesus stands among the disciples, who think they are seeing a ghost. He shows his hands and feet and eats fish, opens the Scriptures to them, and leads them out to Bethany, where he lifts his hands and blesses them.

usedIn.n: John 1:1-18, The Word made flesh
usedIn.s: John begins before creation with the Word who was with God and was God, through whom everything was made, and who became flesh and lived among us.

usedIn.n: John 2:13-25, Tables overturned at Passover
usedIn.s: At Passover Jesus drives the animal sellers and money changers out of the temple courts. Asked for a sign, he tells them to destroy this temple and he will raise it in three days, and John explains that he meant his body.

usedIn.n: John 4:1-42, A Samaritan woman at Jacob's well
usedIn.s: Tired at noon, Jesus sits on Jacob's well and asks a Samaritan woman for a drink. They talk about living water, her husbands and the right mountain for worship, and her town comes out to meet him.

usedIn.n: John 8:12-30, The light of the world by the treasury
usedIn.s: Jesus calls himself the light of the world. Told that testimony about himself does not count, he answers with the law's rule of two witnesses: himself and the Father who sent him.

usedIn.n: John 10:22-42, In Solomon's Porch at the Festival of Dedication
usedIn.s: In winter, at the Festival of Dedication, the Judeans press Jesus to say plainly whether he is the Messiah. He says he and the Father are one, they pick up stones, and he answers from Psalm 82.

usedIn.n: John 11:45-57, Caiaphas: one man for the nation
usedIn.s: After the raising of Lazarus the chief priests and Pharisees call a council, afraid the Romans will take away their place and their nation. Caiaphas tells them it is better for one man to die for the people.

usedIn.n: John 14:1-31, Rooms in the Father's house, and another Advocate
usedIn.s: Jesus tells his troubled disciples that he is going to prepare a place for them in his Father's house, that he is the way, and that the Father will send another Advocate, the Spirit of truth. He leaves them his peace.

usedIn.n: Acts 2:42-47, The common life
usedIn.s: The first believers devote themselves to teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and the prayers, share their possessions, and meet daily in the temple courts and in their homes.

usedIn.n: Acts 3:1-26, The lame man at the Beautiful Gate
usedIn.s: At the afternoon hour of prayer Peter heals a man lame from birth who begged at the temple gate, then tells the gathering crowd that Jesus is the prophet Moses promised.

usedIn.n: Acts 6:8-7:53, Stephen's charge and speech
usedIn.s: Men from the Diaspora synagogues accuse Stephen of speaking against the temple and the law. He answers with Israel's story, from Abraham to the temple, and turns the charge back on his judges.

usedIn.n: Acts 8:26-40, The Ethiopian official
usedIn.s: On the desert road to Gaza, Philip meets a eunuch who serves the queen of the Ethiopians, reading Isaiah in his chariot on the way home from worship in Jerusalem, and baptizes him.

usedIn.n: Acts 21:17-26, James, the rumors and the vow
usedIn.s: In Jerusalem James and the elders welcome Paul but warn him that thousands of believers zealous for the law have heard he teaches Jews abroad to abandon Moses. They ask him to pay for four men completing a vow and to purify himself with them in the temple.

usedIn.n: Acts 21:27-40, Riot in the temple, rescue by the tribune
usedIn.s: Jews from Asia see Paul in the temple and cry that he has brought Greeks into the holy place. The city riots, and the Roman tribune's soldiers pull him from the crowd, chain him, and nearly mistake him for the Egyptian rebel.

usedIn.n: Romans 9:1-5, Israel's privileges
usedIn.s: Paul grieves for his own people and lists what belongs to Israel: the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the law, the worship, the promises, the patriarchs and the Messiah.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 3:1-23, Milk, builders and God's temple
usedIn.s: Paul calls the Corinthians infants still on milk, says he and Apollos are only servants, warns builders that fire will test their work, and reminds the church that it is God's temple and that all things are theirs.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 6:12-20, The body and the prostitute
usedIn.s: Answering slogans such as everything is permissible and food is for the stomach, Paul argues that the body belongs to the Lord, will be raised, and must not be joined to a prostitute, for believers were bought at a price.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 6:14-7:1, Unequal yoke, Belial and the temple of God
usedIn.s: Paul tells the Corinthians not to be yoked with unbelievers, for light has no fellowship with darkness nor Christ with Belial, and calls them the temple of the living God, who must come out and be separate.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 2:11-22, The dividing wall torn down, and a new temple
usedIn.s: Paul reminds Gentile believers that they were once far off, shut out of Israel's citizenship and covenants, and tells them Christ has broken down the dividing wall and built Jews and Gentiles into one household and one temple.

usedIn.n: 2 Thessalonians 2:1-12, The man of lawlessness and the restrainer
usedIn.s: Paul tells a church unsettled by claims that the day of the Lord has already come that the rebellion must come first and the man of lawlessness be revealed, who sets himself up in God's temple claiming to be God; something holds him back for now, and the Lord Jesus will destroy him by the breath of his mouth.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 9:1-10, The two rooms and their furniture
usedIn.s: The first covenant had a sanctuary on earth: an outer room with the lampstand, the table and the bread, and behind the second curtain the most holy place with the golden altar of incense, the ark and the cherubim. Priests entered the first room daily and the high priest the second once a year with blood, a sign that access to the holy place had not yet been opened.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 2:1-10, Living stones and a royal priesthood
usedIn.s: Like newborn babies the readers should crave pure milk. Coming to Christ, the living stone rejected by people but chosen by God, they are being built into a spiritual house and a holy priesthood; Peter strings together Scripture's stone texts and calls them a chosen people, a royal priesthood and a holy nation.

usedIn.n: Revelation 11:1-14, the measured temple and the two witnesses
usedIn.s: John is told to measure God's temple and its worshipers but to leave out the outer court, given to the nations to trample for forty-two months. Two witnesses in sackcloth prophesy with the powers of Elijah and Moses, are killed by the beast from the Abyss and left unburied in the great city, then raised and taken up to heaven.

usedIn.n: Revelation 21:9-27, the city of gold and twelve stones
usedIn.s: An angel carries John to a high mountain to show him the bride, the holy city Jerusalem, shining with God's glory, with twelve gates named for Israel's tribes and twelve foundations named for the Lamb's apostles. The city is a cube of pure gold, its foundations set with twelve precious stones and its gates each a single pearl; it has no temple, since God and the Lamb are its temple, and its gates never shut as the nations bring their glory into it.

entries.title: Passover and the pilgrim crowds
entries.summary: The spring festival that retold God's rescue of Israel from Egypt. Jerusalem filled with pilgrims, and hopes of freedom ran high.
aliases: day of Preparation of the Passover
out of darkness into his marvelous light
entries.plain: **The whole country came to the capital for the independence holiday, and the police were nervous.** Passover remembered the night God freed Israel from slavery in Egypt. Pilgrims poured into Jerusalem, lambs were sacrificed at the temple, and families ate the meal and told the story.
entries.then: Jerusalem's population grew fivefold at Passover, and the crowds sometimes led to riots with many deaths (Keener). By this time the Festival of Unleavened Bread and Passover were often treated as one festival, as in Josephus. Priests slaughtered the lambs brought by the people during the day. The city was packed, so those who knew people nearby lodged outside the walls, as Jesus did at Bethany. Passover custom had people stay up late retelling God's acts of rescue. The Sadducean chief priests, who were responsible for the temple, could not afford unrest at the festival. Wright calls Passover freedom time. The meal said that, despite appearances, Israel was God's free people, and the head of the family told the story. The ESV Study Bible says the pilgrims at the entry were looking for messianic liberation from Rome. The Passover lamb had to be eaten inside the walls of Jerusalem. Keener puts the Passover crowd at perhaps as many as 500,000. The Roman governor came up from Caesarea at the feasts, with more troops, to forestall trouble. The Hallel (Psalms 113 to 118) was sung through the season and would be fresh on everyone's mind. Josephus, counting the lambs at one later Passover, gives 256,500, at no fewer than ten people to a lamb. He also tells how in a riot at the feast under the governor Cumanus the crowd crushed itself "till ten thousand of them were killed." Paul applies the feast to the church. Passover bread was unleavened, and leaven as a picture almost always meant a corrupting influence. Jews expected a new redemption like the exodus.
entries.bridge: An analogy: an independence day held under foreign occupation, with huge crowds in the capital. Everyone celebrates freedom, and the occupiers double the guard.
entries.changes: Passover filled Jerusalem with pilgrims and with hopes of freedom, so a royal welcome at the gates, as in Mark 11:9-10, and a plot to arrest a popular teacher away from the crowds, as in Matthew 26:4-5, both take their shape from the feast. The meal retold the rescue from Egypt, which frames the Last Supper. In John 2:13 Jesus goes up to Jerusalem as the Passover draws near.
entries.not: **Not a civic holiday for a nation's own heroes.** Passover retold how God rescued Israel from Egypt, and it centered on worship: lambs slaughtered at the temple by priests and eaten inside the city walls. The hope it stirred was for God to act again. It had family meals, but the sources also describe riots and a doubled guard.
entries.dissent: Two points. First, when did the Passover meal fall in John? Matthew, Mark and Luke have Jesus eat the Passover with his disciples before his arrest. In John the priests have not yet eaten it the next morning, and Jesus dies on the day of Preparation, as the lambs were being slaughtered. Keener sees either a calendar difference among Jewish groups or a symbolic point by John. He calls reading eat the Passover as keeping the rest of the festival a very odd way to put it. The ESV and CSB Study Bibles take Preparation as the day before the Sabbath of Passover week, and the phrase as observing the festival. On that view all four Gospels put the meal on Thursday evening. The cultural backgrounds article allows a meal held a night early, or John telling the death as the Passover lamb's. Second, how far does later evidence describe Jesus' day? Keener puts the Passover crowd at perhaps as many as 500,000. Garland estimates 85,000 to 300,000 pilgrims in a city of 25,000 to 30,000. He cautions that the Passover rites known from the Mishnah developed after the temple fell and may not match Jesus' time.

usedIn.n: Matthew 21:1-11, A donkey, a colt and the Hallel
usedIn.s: Jesus sends for a donkey and her colt, rides into Jerusalem as Zechariah foretold, and the pilgrim crowds spread cloaks and branches, crying Hosanna to the Son of David.

usedIn.n: Matthew 21:12-22, Tables, the blind and the lame, and a fig tree
usedIn.s: Jesus drives out the sellers and overturns the money changers' tables, heals the blind and the lame in the temple courts, and the next morning curses a leafy fig tree that withers at once.

usedIn.n: Matthew 26:1-16, Perfume at Bethany and thirty pieces of silver
usedIn.s: The chief priests meet at Caiaphas's house to plot Jesus' arrest away from the festival crowds. At Bethany a woman pours costly perfume on his head, and Judas sells him for thirty pieces of silver.

usedIn.n: Matthew 26:17-30, The Passover and the cup
usedIn.s: Jesus eats the Passover with the Twelve in the city, names the one who dips with him as his betrayer, gives the bread and the cup new meaning, and vows not to drink wine again until the kingdom.

usedIn.n: Matthew 27:1-26, Blood money, Pilate and Barabbas
usedIn.s: At dawn the council hands Jesus to Pilate. Judas returns the silver and hangs himself, the priests buy a potter's field, and Pilate, warned by his wife's dream, releases Barabbas and washes his hands.

usedIn.n: Mark 11:1-11, The ride into Jerusalem
usedIn.s: Jesus sends for a colt no one has ridden and rides into Jerusalem over cloaks and branches while the crowd shouts Hosanna.

usedIn.n: Mark 11:12-25, The fig tree and the temple
usedIn.s: Jesus curses a leafy fig tree with no fruit, overturns the tables in the temple, and the next morning the tree has withered.

usedIn.n: Mark 14:1-11, Perfume at Bethany
usedIn.s: Two days before Passover, at dinner in Bethany, a woman pours costly perfume on Jesus' head. He says she has anointed him for burial, and Judas goes to the chief priests.

usedIn.n: Mark 14:12-31, The Passover meal
usedIn.s: Jesus eats the Passover with the Twelve, names a betrayer at the table, gives the bread and the cup new meaning, and warns that all will scatter.

usedIn.n: Mark 14:32-52, Gethsemane and the arrest
usedIn.s: At a place called Gethsemane Jesus prays in anguish while three disciples sleep. Judas arrives with an armed crowd from the chief priests, greets him with a kiss, and the disciples run.

usedIn.n: Mark 15:1-20, Before Pilate
usedIn.s: The chief priests hand Jesus to Pilate as king of the Jews. Pilate releases Barabbas to the crowd, has Jesus flogged, and the soldiers mock him as a king.

usedIn.n: Luke 2:41-52, A twelve-year-old among the teachers
usedIn.s: On the family's yearly Passover pilgrimage the twelve-year-old Jesus stays behind in Jerusalem, and after three days his parents find him in the temple courts among the teachers.

usedIn.n: Luke 13:1-9, Pilate's victims, the tower and the fig tree
usedIn.s: People tell Jesus about Galileans whose blood Pilate mixed with their sacrifices. He answers with a tower that fell in Siloam, a call to repent, and a fig tree given one more year.

usedIn.n: Luke 19:28-48, The king rides down to the city and weeps over it
usedIn.s: Jesus rides a borrowed colt down the Mount of Olives while his disciples spread their cloaks and praise the king who comes. Seeing the city, he weeps over the siege to come, then drives the sellers out of the temple.

usedIn.n: Luke 24:13-35, A stranger on the Emmaus road
usedIn.s: Two disciples walking home to Emmaus are joined by a stranger who explains the Scriptures to them. They press him to stay, and they recognize him when he breaks the bread.

usedIn.n: John 2:13-25, Tables overturned at Passover
usedIn.s: At Passover Jesus drives the animal sellers and money changers out of the temple courts. Asked for a sign, he tells them to destroy this temple and he will raise it in three days, and John explains that he meant his body.

usedIn.n: John 6:1-21, Bread in the wilderness and a walk on the sea
usedIn.s: Near Passover Jesus feeds five thousand men from five barley loaves and two fish. The crowd hails him as the Prophet and wants to make him king, and that night he comes to his disciples walking on the sea.

usedIn.n: John 6:22-71, The bread from heaven
usedIn.s: In the synagogue at Capernaum the crowd asks for a sign like the manna. Jesus answers that he is the bread of life come down from heaven, and his hard words about eating his flesh drive many disciples away.

usedIn.n: John 11:45-57, Caiaphas: one man for the nation
usedIn.s: After the raising of Lazarus the chief priests and Pharisees call a council, afraid the Romans will take away their place and their nation. Caiaphas tells them it is better for one man to die for the people.

usedIn.n: John 12:12-19, Palm branches and a donkey's colt
usedIn.s: The festival crowd goes out with palm branches, shouting Hosanna and hailing Jesus as King of Israel, and he rides in on a young donkey, as Zechariah had said Zion's king would come.

usedIn.n: John 18:28-40, Pilate's headquarters at dawn
usedIn.s: At daybreak the leaders bring Jesus to the governor's headquarters but will not go in, so as to stay clean for Passover. Pilate questions him about being king of the Jews, finds no case, and offers to release him, but the crowd asks for Barabbas.

usedIn.n: John 19:31-42, Legs unbroken and a hundred pounds of spices
usedIn.s: Because the coming Sabbath is a high day, the leaders ask for the bodies to be taken down. The soldiers find Jesus already dead and pierce his side; Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus bury him with a lavish weight of spices in a new tomb in a garden.

usedIn.n: Acts 12:1-25, Herod Agrippa, the prison and the king struck down
usedIn.s: King Herod Agrippa kills James and jails Peter at Passover, but an angel leads Peter out. Later, in Caesarea, the king accepts the crowd's cry that he speaks with a god's voice and is struck down.

usedIn.n: Romans 3:21-31, Redemption and the mercy seat
usedIn.s: Paul announces that God's righteousness has been revealed through faith in Jesus for all who believe, Jew and Gentile alike, through a redemption and an atoning death he links to the mercy seat.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 5:1-13, A man and his father's wife
usedIn.s: A church member is living with his stepmother and the church is proud of itself. Paul tells them to hand the man over to Satan, clear out the old leaven as a household does before Passover, and not eat with a so-called brother who lives that way.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 10:1-22, Israel in the desert and the table of demons
usedIn.s: Paul warns that Israel too had its baptism and its spiritual food in the wilderness, yet fell into idolatry and immorality and was struck down, and tells the Corinthians that they cannot share both the Lord's table and the table of demons.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 11:17-34, The Lord's Supper in a rich man's house
usedIn.s: Paul rebukes the church because at the Lord's Supper some go hungry while others eat their fill and get drunk, retells the tradition of the Last Supper, and tells them to wait for one another.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 1:13-25, Minds girded, foreigners, and the lamb
usedIn.s: Peter calls his readers to be ready and sober, holy as God is holy, and to live as foreigners in reverent fear, since they were ransomed not with silver or gold but with the blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish. Born again of imperishable seed, the living word, they must love one another deeply.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 2:1-10, Living stones and a royal priesthood
usedIn.s: Like newborn babies the readers should crave pure milk. Coming to Christ, the living stone rejected by people but chosen by God, they are being built into a spiritual house and a holy priesthood; Peter strings together Scripture's stone texts and calls them a chosen people, a royal priesthood and a holy nation.

usedIn.n: Revelation 5:1-14, the sealed scroll and the Lamb
usedIn.s: In God's right hand is a scroll written on both sides and sealed with seven seals, and no one is worthy to open it until the Lion of Judah, the Root of David, appears as a Lamb that looks slain. The living creatures, the elders, countless angels and all creation worship him.

usedIn.n: Revelation 15:1-16:11, the song of Moses and the first bowls
usedIn.s: Those who have overcome the beast stand beside a sea of glass mixed with fire and sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb. Seven angels dressed like priests come out of the heavenly temple with seven golden bowls of God's wrath, and the first five bring sores, seas and rivers turned to blood, scorching sun and darkness on the beast's throne.

entries.title: Blasphemy
entries.summary: Speech that dishonored God, including claiming what belonged to God alone. Under the law the penalty was death.
entries.plain: **Signing the owner's name on a check is not a small mistake.** Blasphemy meant speaking against God, or taking for yourself something that belonged only to God. The law of Moses punished it with death, so the word was a weapon.
entries.then: Priests might pronounce God's forgiveness, but only God could forgive sins (Micah 7:18). Later rabbis defined blasphemy narrowly, as cursing with the divine name (Leviticus 24:11). But the word in 2:7 can mean any demeaning speech, including speech that dishonors God. One could blaspheme the Spirit because most Jews saw the Spirit as divine. To credit the Spirit's work to an impure spirit was close to calling God Satan. Biblical law gave atonement for most sins but not for deliberate ones. Some thought false teachers spoke by demons, and the penalty for leading God's people astray was death (Deuteronomy 13:5). At the trial, Wright argues, the base charge was being a false prophet who led Israel astray. He notes that thinking oneself the Messiah was not a capital offense under Jewish law. Most Jews allowed some of God's representatives to speak for him. Keener judges that the scribes were mistaken to call Jesus' words blasphemy by any definition.
entries.bridge: An analogy: an employee who signs off on decisions only the owner can make. Even if every decision is good, the signature itself is the offense.
entries.changes: Blasphemy was the charge for claiming what belonged to God, as when Jesus forgives sins in Mark 2:7, and for insulting God's work, as in the Beelzebul dispute of Matthew 12:31-32. Because it carried death, it was the charge used when leaders wanted a case to end in execution. In Acts 6:11 it is brought against Stephen.
entries.not: **Not a breach of office policy.** An employee who oversteps gets fired. Speech that dishonored God could carry a death penalty, and leading God's people astray was a capital charge. The line was also less clear than a job description, since most Jews allowed some of God's agents to speak for him. Nor did the word mean only swearing with God's name.
entries.dissent: What counted as blasphemy at the trial? The ESV Study Bible says it was Jesus' claim to divine Sonship and an exalted place at God's right hand. Wright says there was "nothing wrong, let alone blasphemous, with thinking oneself to be Messiah". For him the explosive part was Jesus joining Psalm 110 and Daniel 7:13 to claim vindication and a share in God's throne. Wright adds that whether this was a crime under any official law code we will never know.

usedIn.n: Matthew 9:1-17, A paralyzed man, Matthew's table and the wedding guests
usedIn.s: Jesus forgives and heals a paralyzed man, calls Matthew from the tax booth and eats with tax collectors and sinners, and is asked why his disciples do not fast.

usedIn.n: Matthew 12:22-50, Beelzebul, the strong man, Jonah and his true family
usedIn.s: When Jesus heals a blind and mute man, the crowds wonder if he is the Son of David and the Pharisees say he works by Beelzebul. Jesus answers with the strong man, refuses a sign except Jonah's, and names his true family.

usedIn.n: Matthew 26:47-75, Arrest, twelve legions, the council and the rooster
usedIn.s: Judas comes with an armed crowd and a kiss. Jesus refuses the sword and the twelve legions of angels, is tried at night before Caiaphas, and is condemned for blasphemy while Peter swears he never knew him.

usedIn.n: Mark 3:13-35, The Twelve, his family and Beelzebul
usedIn.s: Jesus appoints twelve. His family thinks he is out of his mind, and teachers from Jerusalem say he drives out demons by Beelzebul.

usedIn.n: Mark 14:53-72, At the high priest's house
usedIn.s: The council tries Jesus at night. He says he is the Messiah and quotes the Son of Man coming with the clouds, and is condemned for blasphemy while Peter denies him in the courtyard.

usedIn.n: Luke 5:17-39, Through the roof, then a feast with toll men
usedIn.s: Friends lower a paralyzed man through the roof and Jesus forgives his sins. Then Levi leaves his tax booth and gives a banquet for Jesus with other tax collectors, and Jesus is asked why his disciples do not fast.

usedIn.n: John 5:1-18, The pool of Bethesda on the Sabbath
usedIn.s: At a pool with five porches, Jesus heals a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years and tells him to pick up his mat. It is the Sabbath, and the dispute that follows turns on Jesus calling God his own Father.

usedIn.n: John 8:31-59, Abraham's children, and before Abraham, I am
usedIn.s: Jesus tells Judeans who had believed him that the truth will make them free. They answer that they are Abraham's children and were never slaves, and the argument ends with Jesus saying before Abraham was, I am, and stones in their hands.

usedIn.n: John 10:22-42, In Solomon's Porch at the Festival of Dedication
usedIn.s: In winter, at the Festival of Dedication, the Judeans press Jesus to say plainly whether he is the Messiah. He says he and the Father are one, they pick up stones, and he answers from Psalm 82.

usedIn.n: Acts 6:8-7:53, Stephen's charge and speech
usedIn.s: Men from the Diaspora synagogues accuse Stephen of speaking against the temple and the law. He answers with Israel's story, from Abraham to the temple, and turns the charge back on his judges.

usedIn.n: Acts 14:1-20, Iconium and Lystra: taken for Zeus and Hermes
usedIn.s: After a plot in Iconium, Paul heals a lame man at Lystra and the crowd hails him and Barnabas as Hermes and Zeus. When they refuse the sacrifice, the crowd is turned against them and Paul is stoned.

usedIn.n: Romans 2:17-29, You who boast in the law
usedIn.s: Paul turns on an imagined Jewish teacher who boasts in the law yet steals, commits adultery and robs temples, so that God's name is blasphemed among the nations, and says true circumcision is of the heart.

entries.title: Anointing with oil
entries.summary: Oil poured on the head was a courtesy to a guest, the sign of a new king, a medicine, and care for the dead. The setting decided which.
entries.plain: **Opening the expensive bottle for one guest tells the whole room what you think of him.** Olive oil and perfume went on skin, on wounds, on honored guests, on kings when they were made king, and on bodies before burial. The same act could mean welcome, healing, crowning or farewell.
entries.then: Keener, citing Josephus, notes that many people believed olive oil had healing properties. Jews used it to cleanse sores and wounds, and against headaches and some diseases. Oil on a guest's head was a courtesy, expected above all for important guests. Yet a king too was anointed on the head (2 Kings 9:6). Expensive ointments were kept in sealed alabaster flasks that might have to be broken. Such long-necked containers have been found in tombs of this period near Jerusalem, and people lavished ointment on dead loved ones. The ESV Study Bible says the nard in 14:3 would have sold for more than 300 days' wages. Keener puts the perfume at Bethany at about a year's wages, probably kept in the family as an heirloom. Once its flask was broken, the perfume could be used fresh only once. Jewish tradition allowed washing and anointing a corpse even on the Sabbath, though spices had to be bought after it. Wright explains the women's purpose at the tomb as completing the first burial, out of reverence and to lessen the smell. The bones would later be gathered into an ossuary. Oil also consecrated priests and kings for their tasks (Exodus 30:30; 1 Samuel 10:1), and Messiah means anointed one. At times the anointing was tied to the Spirit (1 Samuel 16:13; Isaiah 61:1). Every believer receives such an anointing in 1 John 2:20.
entries.bridge: An analogy: the good bottle saved for a wedding or a funeral. When someone opens it for you at an ordinary dinner, the room goes quiet, and people start guessing which occasion this is.
entries.changes: Oil on the head could honor a guest, mark a king or prepare a body, so one anointing, as in Matthew 26:7-12, can carry several meanings at once. Oil was also medicine, which is why the Twelve anoint the sick in Mark 6:13 and James 5:14 tells the elders to do the same.
entries.not: **Not a luxury opened only to celebrate.** A good bottle marks an occasion and is drunk. Oil did more work: it treated wounds, honored guests, prepared the dead and consecrated kings and priests, and Messiah means anointed one. So one act with oil could point to more than one kind of occasion.
entries.dissent: What was the oil of James 5:14 for? Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes think believers joined a medicinal use with a sign of God's Spirit, as in Mark 6:13. The ESV Study Bible reports that some take it as medicinal or sacramental. It says the oil is "best seen as a symbol representing the healing power of the Holy Spirit". The CSB Study Bible writes that "Olive oil was considered a cure-all ointment in the ancient world", and places the healing power in the prayer. The Zondervan dictionary takes the purely medicinal side. It says the verb commonly meant rubbing oil on the skin as a household remedy, given with prayer. It adds, "This directive has perhaps wrongfully been assumed to refer to a church ritual." At the other end, Wright treats the anointing as a simple, lasting "sign of God's longing to heal people". For him it is meaningful in the way prayer and the sacraments are.

usedIn.n: Matthew 26:1-16, Perfume at Bethany and thirty pieces of silver
usedIn.s: The chief priests meet at Caiaphas's house to plot Jesus' arrest away from the festival crowds. At Bethany a woman pours costly perfume on his head, and Judas sells him for thirty pieces of silver.

usedIn.n: Mark 14:1-11, Perfume at Bethany
usedIn.s: Two days before Passover, at dinner in Bethany, a woman pours costly perfume on Jesus' head. He says she has anointed him for burial, and Judas goes to the chief priests.

usedIn.n: Mark 15:42-16:8, The tomb
usedIn.s: Joseph of Arimathea buries Jesus before the Sabbath. When it is over, the women come with spices, find the stone rolled away, and hear that he has been raised.

usedIn.n: Luke 7:36-50, A sinful woman at Simon's table
usedIn.s: At a Pharisee's banquet a woman known as a sinner weeps over Jesus' feet, wipes them with her hair and anoints them. Jesus answers his host's silent objection with a story of two debtors.

usedIn.n: John 12:1-11, Mary's nard and loosened hair
usedIn.s: Six days before Passover, at a dinner in Jesus' honor in Bethany, Mary pours a pound of costly nard on his feet and wipes them with her hair. Judas objects, and Jesus says she has kept it for the day of his burial.

usedIn.n: John 19:31-42, Legs unbroken and a hundred pounds of spices
usedIn.s: Because the coming Sabbath is a high day, the leaders ask for the bodies to be taken down. The soldiers find Jesus already dead and pierce his side; Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus bury him with a lavish weight of spices in a new tomb in a garden.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 1:12-2:4, Changed plans, the seal and the down payment
usedIn.s: Accused of fickleness for changing his travel plans, Paul answers that his word is reliable because all God's promises are Yes in Christ, who has anointed and sealed them and given the Spirit as a down payment, and explains that he stayed away to spare them.

usedIn.n: James 5:13-20, Elders, oil and Elijah's prayer
usedIn.s: The suffering should pray and the cheerful sing; the sick should call the church's elders to pray over them and anoint them with oil. The prayer of a righteous person is powerful, as Elijah's was, and whoever turns a sinner back covers a multitude of sins.

usedIn.n: 1 John 2:18-27, The last hour and many antichrists
usedIn.s: It is the last hour: the readers heard that antichrist is coming, and many antichrists have already come. They went out from the community, which shows they never belonged; whoever denies that Jesus is the Christ is the liar and the antichrist. The readers have an anointing from the Holy One and need no one else to teach them.

entries.title: Gifts to the poor
entries.summary: Giving to the needy was one of the three pillars of Jewish piety, with prayer and fasting. Greeks and Romans had nothing quite like it.
aliases: a brother or sister in need
entries.plain: **She left the envelope in the mailbox and never said who it was from.** Alms were gifts to the poor. For Jews of Jesus' day, giving to people in need was a basic duty of faith, alongside prayer and fasting. It was also a way to be seen and praised, which is what Jesus warns about.
entries.then: Prayer, fasting and gifts to the poor were the basic parts of Jewish piety (Tobit 12:8). Wright calls the three the key marks of Jewish observance. He says some Pharisees regarded them as equal to sacrifice for those far from Jerusalem. Greeks and Romans did not practice personal charity in this sense. Wealthy gifts to public projects or to poorer clients bought the giver popularity. For Jews charity was central, and some writers even said it saved a person. Later law limited giving to 20 percent beyond the tithe. The phrase they have their reward is the language of a receipt marked paid in full. Laying up treasure with God by giving was already a Jewish idea (Tobit 4:7-10). Begging at public places such as the temple gates was common. Only those who could not work begged, and piety was tied to generosity. In Judaism charity distributors made sure that widows and orphans with no relatives to help them were cared for. Greek society looked after freeborn orphans only.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a donor wall in a hospital lobby, with the biggest names in the largest letters. The money helps someone either way, but the wall shows what the giver was buying.
entries.changes: Because giving to the poor was expected of the devout, the question in the Gospels is usually how and why it is done, as in Matthew 6:2-4. Giving could be a bid for public honor, so secrecy marks a gift made to God. In Acts 10:2 a Gentile's alms mark him as devout.
entries.not: **Not a voluntary gift that earns its name in big letters.** A donor wall rewards giving with public credit, which is close to how Greek and Roman giving worked. For Jews, charity was a religious duty owed to God and the poor, and it laid up treasure with God. Public credit was the very reward that, in Jesus' words, closes the account.
entries.dissent: The trumpet in Matthew 6:2. The CSB Study Bible reads it as coins tossed noisily into the trumpet-shaped offering chests of the temple. Keener calls it hyperbole, since people did not blow trumpets when giving alms, perhaps playing on trumpet-shaped charity boxes.

usedIn.s: Jesus warns against doing acts of piety to be seen, and teaches his disciples the Lord's Prayer.

usedIn.n: Luke 18:18-30, A rich ruler and the needle's eye
usedIn.s: A ruler asks what he must do to inherit eternal life; told to sell everything and follow, he goes away sad, and Jesus says it is easier for a camel to go through a needle's eye than for a rich man to enter God's kingdom.

usedIn.n: Acts 3:1-26, The lame man at the Beautiful Gate
usedIn.s: At the afternoon hour of prayer Peter heals a man lame from birth who begged at the temple gate, then tells the gathering crowd that Jesus is the prophet Moses promised.

usedIn.n: Acts 11:19-30, Antioch, and the name Christian
usedIn.s: Scattered believers bring the message to Gentiles in Antioch, where the disciples are first called Christians. When a prophet foretells famine, the church sends relief to the elders in Judea.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 8:1-15, The Macedonians' giving and the manna
usedIn.s: Paul holds up the generosity of the poor Macedonian churches, appeals to Christ who became poor, and asks the Corinthians to finish their gift so that there may be equality, as there was with the manna in the wilderness.

usedIn.n: James 1:19-27, Slow to anger, and the widows and orphans
usedIn.s: James tells his readers to be quick to listen and slow to speak and to anger, to do the word and not merely hear it, and names the religion God accepts: care for orphans and widows in their distress and a life kept unstained by the world.

usedIn.n: 1 John 2:28-3:24, Children of God, Cain, and love in deed
usedIn.s: Those who do right are born of God, whose love makes them his children, and when he appears they will be like him. Whoever keeps on sinning belongs to the devil, who has sinned from the beginning, and the Son came to undo his work. The readers are not to be like Cain, who murdered his brother, but to love in deed and in truth, as Christ laid down his life.

entries.title: Prayer in Jesus' day
entries.summary: Set prayers, set hours, standing to pray, God addressed as Father, and prayers for his name and his kingdom. Jesus taught his own disciples a prayer inside that world.
aliases: God is good and does good
to the only God our Savior
entries.plain: **Grandpa said grace the same way every night, and the words still meant something to him.** Jews in Jesus' day prayed at set times, often with set words, usually standing. Their prayers called God Father and asked for his name to be honored and his kingdom to come. When Jesus taught his disciples to pray, he used words they already knew in a new way.
entries.then: Jews took regular prayer far more seriously than Greek and Roman religion did (Keener). The pious set aside two hours a day for it, and standing was a common posture. Most homes had no private room. The inner room of Matthew 6:6 may be a storeroom, the only room with a door. Our heavenly Father was a common address in Jewish prayer. Wright traces the title back to the Exodus, when God called Israel his son. Many Jewish benedictions opened with praise: Blessed be God who. A frequent synagogue prayer called God the merciful Father, and the daily prayers praised him as the one who raises the dead. A standard prayer of the day, the Kaddish, asked that God's great name be hallowed and his kingdom come soon. Bailey notes that the Tefillah, the Eighteen Benedictions, asks God to forgive. Greek prayers piled up divine titles to get a god's attention. They reminded gods of sacrifices owed, as if by contract. Jewish prayers in worship ended in praise, which is why later copies of Matthew add for yours is the kingdom. Jews often blessed one another with peace be with you. They regularly prayed for peace on Israel in the final benediction of the Amidah. Jews also knelt, especially in extremity. Greeks and Jews alike prayed with arms outstretched, and hearers answered a closing praise with Amen. Every day Jews recited the Shema, Deuteronomy 6:4 and its associated texts. Its confession that the Lord is one was the cornerstone of Jewish faith.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a family's table grace, said in the same words for generations. A newcomer can say it on the first night, and the familiar words carry meaning because everyone knows them.
entries.changes: Set prayers and set hours explain why Jesus can teach a prayer of his own, as in Matthew 6:9-13, and why the apostles go up to the temple at the hour of prayer in Acts 3:1. The Lord's Prayer echoes requests Jews already made, so its differences stand out. Praying to be seen was possible because prayer was public, which Jesus warns against at Matthew 6:5.
entries.not: **Not one family's custom.** A table grace belongs to a household and lasts a few seconds. Jewish prayer was shared by a whole people, with set times, set words such as the Shema and the benedictions, and postures such as standing and kneeling. The pious gave it two hours a day. Nor was it only private self-expression.
entries.dissent: Two points. First, was tying God's forgiveness to ours new? Bailey argues that the Tefillah's prayer for forgiveness is not tied to forgiving others, so Jesus departs from the tradition. Keener's cultural backgrounds notes point to earlier sages who made the link, citing Sirach 28:1-8. Second, what did Abba carry? Keener's background commentary renders it Papa, a word of great intimacy that Jews did not use of God except in an occasional parable. Garland agrees that no individual is known to have addressed God so before Jesus. But he says it does not mean Daddy, since Mark renders it with the ordinary word for father and disciples used it of an esteemed teacher.

usedIn.n: Mark 14:32-52, Gethsemane and the arrest
usedIn.s: At a place called Gethsemane Jesus prays in anguish while three disciples sleep. Judas arrives with an armed crowd from the chief priests, greets him with a kiss, and the disciples run.

usedIn.n: Luke 11:1-13, Father, daily bread and a friend at midnight
usedIn.s: Asked to teach his disciples to pray, Jesus gives a short prayer to the Father, then tells of a man who wakes a neighbor at midnight to borrow bread for a guest.

usedIn.n: Acts 2:42-47, The common life
usedIn.s: The first believers devote themselves to teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and the prayers, share their possessions, and meet daily in the temple courts and in their homes.

usedIn.n: Acts 3:1-26, The lame man at the Beautiful Gate
usedIn.s: At the afternoon hour of prayer Peter heals a man lame from birth who begged at the temple gate, then tells the gathering crowd that Jesus is the prophet Moses promised.

usedIn.n: Acts 10:1-23, Cornelius and Peter's vision
usedIn.s: A God-fearing Roman centurion in Caesarea is told in a vision to send for Peter. At noon on a Joppa rooftop Peter sees a sheet full of unclean animals and hears a voice tell him to eat.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 1:1-11, The God of all comfort and the sentence of death
usedIn.s: Paul opens by blessing the God of all comfort and tells the Corinthians that in Asia he was so crushed that he felt he had received the sentence of death, so that he learned to rely on the God who raises the dead.

usedIn.n: Galatians 6:11-18, Large letters in his own hand, and the marks of Jesus
usedIn.s: Taking the pen himself, Paul writes in large letters that the rivals want the Galatians circumcised so they can boast in their flesh and avoid persecution, while he boasts only in the cross; he blesses those who follow this rule and the Israel of God, and says he bears the marks of Jesus.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 3:14-21, Kneeling before the Father of every family
usedIn.s: Paul kneels in prayer before the Father of every family, heavenly and earthly, and asks that they be strengthened by the Spirit and grasp the vast dimensions of Christ's love, closing with praise.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 2:1-7, Prayers for kings and all in authority
usedIn.s: Paul asks for prayers for everyone, kings and all in authority included, so that believers may live peaceful and quiet lives, because God our Savior wants all to be saved and there is one God and one mediator.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 2:8-15, Lifted hands, braided hair, women learning, Eve and childbearing
usedIn.s: Paul wants men to pray without anger or arguing and women to dress modestly; women are to learn quietly, and he does not permit a woman to teach or have authority over a man, arguing from Adam and Eve, before a hard saying about being saved through childbearing.

usedIn.n: James 2:14-26, Faith that shudders, Abraham and Rahab
usedIn.s: Faith without deeds is dead, James argues. Wishing a hungry brother well helps no one, the demons believe that God is one and shudder, and Abraham and Rahab were counted righteous by what they did.

usedIn.n: James 5:13-20, Elders, oil and Elijah's prayer
usedIn.s: The suffering should pray and the cheerful sing; the sick should call the church's elders to pray over them and anoint them with oil. The prayer of a righteous person is powerful, as Elijah's was, and whoever turns a sinner back covers a multitude of sins.

usedIn.n: Jude 14-25, Enoch's prophecy, scoffers, and a closing doxology
usedIn.s: Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied about such people that the Lord comes with his countless holy ones to judge all and convict the ungodly. The apostles foretold scoffers in the last times; the readers are to build themselves up, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep themselves in God's love and show mercy, snatching some from the fire. Jude closes with praise to the one able to keep them from stumbling.

usedIn.n: Revelation 8:1-13, silence, incense and the first four trumpets
usedIn.s: The seventh seal brings half an hour of silence in heaven. Seven angels receive trumpets, an angel offers incense with the prayers of God's people at the golden altar and hurls fire to the earth, and the first four trumpets bring hail and fire, a burning mountain into the sea, the star Wormwood and a darkening of sun, moon and stars.

entries.title: Fasting
entries.summary: Going without food, and often washing and oil, as a sign of mourning, penitence and longing. The law required one fast a year; the devout kept many more.
entries.plain: **The family stopped eating normally after the funeral, and the whole street could tell.** To fast was to go without food for a time, usually with no washing or oil either, and often with ashes on the head. It was how people mourned, repented and pleaded with God. Because it showed on the face, it could also be a way to look holy.
entries.then: The law commanded a fast only on the Day of Atonement. Religious Jews added many more, the Pharisees above all, and many Pharisees may have fasted two days a week. Some went without water too, especially in the dry season. A fast also meant no washing, no oil on the skin and no intercourse, and the study Bibles add ashes and a grim face. Fasting belonged with mourning, and a wedding was the peak of joy, so no one fasted at a wedding feast. A teacher answered for how his disciples behaved, so disciples who never fasted would have looked odd. Wright puts the practice in a wider frame: "Fasting in this period was not, for Jews, simply an ascetic discipline." He argues that it marked Israel's ongoing exile and the fall of the temple, and that Zechariah had promised those fasts would turn into feasts.
entries.bridge: An analogy: wearing black for a season of mourning. Everyone who sees you knows something is wrong, and showing up in black at a wedding would be an insult to the couple.
entries.changes: Fasting was expected of the devout, so a teacher whose disciples did not fast drew questions, as at Mark 2:18. Because it went with grief, Jesus answers with a wedding. Since a fast showed on the face, it could become a performance, which is the warning at Matthew 6:16-18.
entries.not: **Not a message aimed at the neighbors.** Black clothes speak to the people who see them. A fast was first an act before God, joined to prayer, penitence and mourning, and the law commanded one every year. That it showed on the face was a risk, since it could turn into a show.
entries.dissent: What fasting meant then. Keener's notes treat it as joined to prayer, penitence and mourning. Wright argues that in this period it also carried a national meaning, grief for Israel's exile and the fallen temple, and reads Jesus' refusal to fast as a claim that the exile was ending; that wider reading is his.

entries.title: Oaths and vows
entries.summary: Calling God, or something holy, to witness that you speak the truth or will keep your word. People swore by lesser things to keep God's name safe if they broke it.
aliases: raised his right hand to heaven
swore by him who lives for ever
entries.plain: **I swear on my mother's grave I will pay you back.** An oath called on God, or on something sacred, as witness and judge of what you said. Break it and you were inviting punishment. Some people swore by heaven, by Jerusalem or by their own head instead of by God, thinking that a broken oath would then do less damage.
entries.then: An oath called on a god to witness that a statement was true, or to punish a lie. The custom is ancient. In the twenty-fifth century BC Eannatum of Lagash made the beaten king of Umma swear by six gods never to move the border. Podany explains why: "Only the gods could be trusted to hold a king" to his word. In Jesus' day people swore by heaven, earth, Jerusalem or their own heads, so that a broken oath would not profane God's name. Some swore by the temple, its gold or the altar for the same reason, and later rabbis had to rule on which oaths bound. Some radical sages and sects refused oaths altogether. Josephus says of the Essenes that "swearing is avoided by them, and they esteem it worse than perjury," yet every new member swore tremendous oaths on joining. To break an oath sworn before guests was shameful, even where Jewish teachers would have released it. People could vow property to God, which put it beyond the reach of others, even aged parents. Teachers who disliked the abuse still would not cancel such vows. Vows of abstinence were common, and a high priest could force testimony by putting a witness under oath in God's name. A Nazirite vow (Numbers 6) meant no wine, no contact with the dead and no haircut. It lasted at least thirty days and ended with a shaved head and a sacrifice at the temple, and paying a Nazirite's costs counted as piety. A charge given with God as witness bound as firmly as an oath.
entries.bridge: An analogy: signing a sworn statement in front of a notary. You may speak the truth without it, but once you sign, any lie becomes perjury, and some people learn exactly which forms count.
entries.changes: Oaths show up wherever a word had to be made binding in public. In Matthew 5:33-37 Jesus cuts through the rules about which oaths counted, and in Mark 6:26 a ruler kills a prophet rather than break an oath before his guests. A curse and an oath in a denial, as in Mark 14:71, called on God as witness.
entries.not: **Not a form with the state behind it.** A notary's stamp brings in the law of the land. An oath called on God, or on something holy, as witness and judge, so a broken oath invited his punishment. That is why some people swore by lesser things.
entries.dissent: The Essenes and oaths. Josephus says they avoided swearing and counted it worse than perjury, yet required entry oaths. Keener suggests they avoided oaths after the oath of entry. The CSB Study Bible adds a reading that an oath implied the power to destroy what one swore by; the other sources here do not make that point.
