usedIn.n: Matthew 5:33-48, No oaths, the other cheek, the second mile
usedIn.s: Jesus tells his hearers not to swear at all, not to resist an evildoer, to go a second mile with a soldier who forces one, and to love their enemies.

usedIn.n: Matthew 14:1-12, John beheaded at a birthday feast
usedIn.s: Herod the tetrarch hears about Jesus and thinks John has risen. Matthew tells how Herod, bound by an oath at his birthday, had John beheaded.

usedIn.n: Matthew 23:13-28, Oaths, mint, gnats and whitewashed tombs
usedIn.s: Jesus pronounces woes on the scribes and Pharisees: they shut the kingdom, play games with oaths, tithe herbs while neglecting justice, strain gnats and swallow camels, and look clean outside like whitewashed tombs.

usedIn.n: Matthew 26:17-30, The Passover and the cup
usedIn.s: Jesus eats the Passover with the Twelve in the city, names the one who dips with him as his betrayer, gives the bread and the cup new meaning, and vows not to drink wine again until the kingdom.

usedIn.n: Matthew 26:47-75, Arrest, twelve legions, the council and the rooster
usedIn.s: Judas comes with an armed crowd and a kiss. Jesus refuses the sword and the twelve legions of angels, is tried at night before Caiaphas, and is condemned for blasphemy while Peter swears he never knew him.

usedIn.n: Acts 18:18-28, A vow at Cenchreae and Apollos of Alexandria
usedIn.s: Paul has his hair cut at Cenchreae because of a vow and sails for Syria by way of Ephesus. In Ephesus Priscilla and Aquila teach the eloquent Alexandrian Apollos more accurately, and the believers write ahead to Achaia to welcome him.

usedIn.n: Acts 21:17-26, James, the rumors and the vow
usedIn.s: In Jerusalem James and the elders welcome Paul but warn him that thousands of believers zealous for the law have heard he teaches Jews abroad to abandon Moses. They ask him to pay for four men completing a vow and to purify himself with them in the temple.

usedIn.n: Acts 23:12-35, The oath, the nephew and the night march
usedIn.s: More than forty men bind themselves by an oath not to eat until they have killed Paul. His nephew learns of the ambush, and the tribune sends Paul under heavy escort by night to the governor Felix at Caesarea, with a letter explaining the case.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 1:12-2:4, Changed plans, the seal and the down payment
usedIn.s: Accused of fickleness for changing his travel plans, Paul answers that his word is reliable because all God's promises are Yes in Christ, who has anointed and sealed them and given the Spirit as a down payment, and explains that he stayed away to spare them.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 5:1-16, Older men as fathers, and the widows' list
usedIn.s: Timothy is to treat older and younger believers as family; the church is to honor widows who are truly in need, families are to support their own, and only older widows of proven character are to be put on the list.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 6:11-21, Fight the good fight, the King of kings, the rich, and the deposit
usedIn.s: Timothy, as a man of God, is to flee greed and fight the good fight of the faith, keeping his charge until the appearing of the Lord, the King of kings; the rich are to be generous, and Timothy is to guard what has been entrusted to him.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 4:1-8, Itching ears, a drink offering, and the crown
usedIn.s: Paul charges Timothy before God and Christ Jesus to preach the word in season and out of season, because people will gather teachers to suit their itching ears; he himself is already being poured out like a drink offering, has fought the good fight and finished the race, and awaits the crown.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 6:13-20, God's oath and the anchor behind the curtain
usedIn.s: When God promised Abraham, he swore by himself, since there was no one greater. Promise and oath, two things in which God cannot lie, give a hope that holds like an anchor and reaches behind the curtain, where Jesus has gone ahead as high priest for ever.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 7:11-28, A priest from Judah, by oath, for ever
usedIn.s: If the Levitical priesthood had brought perfection, no other priest would have been promised. Jesus comes from Judah, a priest by the power of an indestructible life and by God's oath, the guarantee of a better covenant; Levitical priests died and offered daily for their own sins, but he lives for ever and offered himself once for all.

usedIn.n: James 5:7-12, Early and late rains, Job, and no oaths
usedIn.s: James tells the oppressed to be patient until the Lord comes, as a farmer waits for the autumn and spring rains, to stop grumbling, to remember the prophets and Job, and above all not to swear.

usedIn.n: Revelation 10:1-11, the mighty angel and the little scroll
usedIn.s: A mighty angel robed in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, plants one foot on the sea and one on the land, swears by the one who lives for ever that there will be no more delay, and gives John a little scroll to eat, sweet in his mouth and bitter in his stomach.

entries.title: The temple tax
entries.summary: Every year free adult Jewish men across the empire paid two drachmas toward the temple in Jerusalem. After AD 70 Rome went on collecting the same sum for a pagan temple.
entries.plain: **Families in three countries still send money home every year to keep the old church roof on.** The law of Moses asked every grown man for half a shekel toward God's house. By Jesus' day that meant two drachmas a year, about two days' pay, collected from Jewish men wherever they lived and carried to Jerusalem. Paying it was a way of saying that you belonged to the temple and the land.
entries.then: The tax rested on the half-shekel of Exodus 30:13-16. Free adult Jewish men all over the ancient world paid it, as a sign of solidarity with the temple and the Holy Land. In New Testament times it came to two drachmas, about two days' wages. Josephus describes the Jews of Babylonia storing the half-shekel in fortified cities until it could go up to Jerusalem, with many thousands escorting it. The income was huge. The cultural backgrounds notes say the temple authorities added gold every year to a great golden vine on the temple. The same notes read the tax as a sign that Jews abroad stayed loyal to the temple. Some Jewish sects refused to pay. Priests exempted themselves (Mishnah Sheqalim 1:3-4), which annoyed some Pharisees. Kings did not tax their own households, and tax lists often named those who were exempt. After the war, Josephus writes, Rome laid a tribute on Jews wherever they lived. It "enjoined every one of them to bring two drachmae every year into the Capitol, as they used to pay the same to the temple at Jerusalem." So in Matthew's day, Keener notes, the money kept a pagan temple in repair, and some Jews may have refused to pay on principle.
entries.bridge: An analogy: yearly dues that members of a scattered people send to the headquarters of their faith. Paying says you belong. Then the headquarters is seized, and the occupiers keep collecting the dues for themselves.
entries.changes: The tax was paid by Jews everywhere as a mark of loyalty to the temple, so whether a teacher pays it, as in Matthew 17:24, says something about where he stands toward the temple. Exemption belonged to a king's own household, which is the turn Jesus gives the question. After AD 70 the same coins went to Rome.
entries.not: **Not voluntary dues.** Members can stop paying a club. The half-shekel was commanded in the law of Moses as an offering to God's house, and after AD 70 Rome did not simply keep it but sent it to a pagan temple in the Capitol.
entries.dissent: Why Jesus pays. Keener reads it as solidarity: any Jew loyal to Judaism paid, and Jesus is free of it because he is the hope of Judaism, yet pays. Wright writes, "Jesus didn't believe the Temple tax was proper," and reads the payment as avoiding a fight that belonged to another time and place. The ESV Study Bible says the sons are free because believers are no longer under the Old Testament law, and the CSB Study Bible says Jesus' disciples were exempt from supporting the temple.

entries.title: Ritual washing and convert immersion
entries.summary: Jews washed often for purity, but one immersion happened only once: the bath a Gentile took on becoming a Jew. John's baptism and the church's took that shape.
entries.plain: **You take the citizenship oath once, and from that day you belong to a new country.** Jews in Jesus' day washed and bathed often to be ritually clean. One immersion happened only once: when a Gentile turned to Israel's God, he was immersed in water as part of becoming a Jew. So when John called Jews to be baptized, and when Jesus' followers baptized new disciples, people understood it as a turning to God and a new start.
entries.then: Like many ancient peoples, Jews practiced ritual washings. Their only once-for-all washing was the immersion a non-Jew underwent on converting, probably watched by a religious expert, and John's baptizing fits that model (Keener). The immersion washed converts clean of the defilement of idol worship, which some Gentile writers of the first and second centuries attest. Sects such as the Essenes immersed new members too, but as the first of many washings. John's single baptism marked a turn to a new life. For Keener, the ultimate example of repentance was a non-Jew choosing to obey Israel's God, so John treated his Jewish hearers on the same terms as pagans. Josephus, describing John's baptism, says the washing would please God if used "for the purification of the body; supposing still that the soul was thoroughly purified beforehand by righteousness." Many Jews welcomed Gentile converts, and some outside the land sought them out, but there was no organized mission. When Jesus sends his followers to baptize the nations, baptism gave them a way of showing conversion that anyone would understand. The CSB Study Bible calls it the mark of entry into the faith community. Jewish teachers spoke of converts at their immersion as starting life again like newborn children, much as a Roman adoptee left his old family behind. Keener hears that background in the talk of new birth in John 3. Teachers expected Gentile converts to be baptized, and "these converts were baptized naked" and then dressed again, as later rabbis required. Jewish authors sometimes pictured a person clothed in the Spirit or in virtues.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a naturalization ceremony. Citizens renew licenses and papers all the time, but the oath that makes a foreigner a citizen is taken once, and everyone knows what it means.
entries.changes: Because Jews immersed Gentile converts, a baptism offered to Jews, as in Mark 1:4-5, treated them like outsiders who needed to turn. Baptism in Jesus' name marks entry into his people, as in Matthew 28:19 and Acts 2:38.
entries.not: **Not a legal ceremony.** Naturalization changes a person's papers. The convert's immersion was a washing that cleansed from idolatry and marked a turn to Israel's God. John offered it to people who were already Jews, as if citizens were asked to take the oath again.
entries.dissent: Was convert immersion practiced as early as John? The cultural backgrounds article on baptism notes that some have doubted it. It answers that the rite appears in various sources, the Stoic Epictetus among them. The rabbis of a later age were unlikely to take a practice over from Christians, it argues, and conversion without purification is hard to imagine. Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary, takes the other side. The Talmudic evidence for convert immersion is late, so whether it reaches back to the first century is questionable, and he reads John's rite as an end-time use of Jewish washing.

usedIn.s: Priests and Levites from Jerusalem ask John who he is. He denies being the Messiah, Elijah or the Prophet, calls himself the voice in the wilderness, and points to Jesus as the Lamb of God.

usedIn.s: Nicodemus, a Pharisee and ruler, comes to Jesus at night. Jesus tells him that no one sees God's kingdom without being born from above, of water and Spirit, and speaks of the Son of Man lifted up like the serpent in the wilderness.

usedIn.s: Peter explains the scene from Joel: God has poured out his Spirit, the crucified Jesus is raised and exalted as Lord and Messiah, and three thousand are baptized in his name.

usedIn.s: Baptized into Christ's death, believers are dead to sin. Once slaves of sin, they have been set free to become slaves of God, whose gift is eternal life.

usedIn.n: Galatians 3:23-29, The law as a guardian until faith came
usedIn.s: Before faith came, Paul says, we were held in custody under the law, which served as a guardian until Christ; now all who have been baptized into Christ are God's children, one in him, Abraham's seed and heirs.

usedIn.n: Titus 2:11-3:8, Grace has appeared, be subject to rulers, and the washing of rebirth
usedIn.s: God's grace has appeared, training believers to live with self-control now while they wait for Christ's glorious appearing; they are to respect rulers and be gentle to all, because God saved them by his mercy, giving them new birth and new life by the Holy Spirit.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 5:11-6:12, Milk, solid food and no way back
usedIn.s: The readers should be teachers by now but still need milk, so the writer urges them past the elementary teachings. Those who have been enlightened and shared in the Holy Spirit and then fall away cannot be brought back to repentance, though he is confident of better things for his readers.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 10:19-25, Through the curtain, bodies washed, meeting together
usedIn.s: Because Jesus' blood has opened a new and living way through the curtain, believers may enter the most holy place with confidence. With hearts sprinkled and bodies washed with pure water, they are to hold fast, spur one another on, and not give up meeting together.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 3:8-22, A defense, and the spirits in prison
usedIn.s: Peter calls for harmony and for blessing in return for insult, and tells his readers to be ready to make a defense of their hope. Christ suffered once for sins, was put to death in the body and made alive in the Spirit, and went and made proclamation to the spirits in prison who disobeyed in Noah's day; the flood that saved eight people prefigures baptism, and Christ has gone into heaven, where every angelic authority and power is subject to him.

entries.title: Priests on duty: the twenty-four courses
entries.summary: Israel's ordinary priests were divided into twenty-four courses that took turns at the temple, a week at a time. Most lived in the country and came up to Jerusalem when their turn came round.
entries.plain: **His shift came round twice a year, and the rest of the time he was home in the hills.** There were far more priests than the temple needed on any one day. They were organized into twenty-four divisions that took turns, and inside each division the jobs were handed out by lot. Most priests were not rich or powerful. They lived in towns and villages, came up to Jerusalem for their turn, and went home again.
entries.then: The twenty-four divisions go back to 1 Chronicles 24, where Abijah's is the eighth (24:10). Keener says each division served two separate weeks a year, besides the three great festivals. The ESV Study Bible says a week twice a year, with every division on duty at Passover, Pentecost and Tabernacles. Some estimate eighteen thousand priests and Levites, far more than were needed. So special duties were assigned by lot, and Jews believed God directed the lot. The incense was offered before the morning sacrifice and after the evening one. With so many priests a man might burn it once in his life, and he was expected to come straight back out. Priests often married the daughters of priests. Wright describes the ordinary priest's year. Apart from the chief priests, who lived in Jerusalem, priests lived away from the city. They lodged in the temple precincts while their division served, then went home to work as teachers and leaders in their own communities. They were meant to live on tithes, but high taxes and the ways of the priestly aristocracy pushed poorer priests to farm. Many priests lived at Jericho. Bailey reports a stone fragment from Caesarea recording that after Jerusalem fell, one of the twenty-four courses settled in Nazareth. Josephus writes that David "found of these priests twenty-four courses" and ordained that "one course should minister to God eight days, from sabbath to sabbath", a division that "hath remained to this day" (Antiquities 7.14.7). Keener thinks the twenty-four elders of Revelation 4 almost certainly allude to these orders, which later rabbis and inscriptions still discussed.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a rota of country doctors who each take a week at the big city hospital, sleep in the staff quarters, and then drive home to their own practice. The hospital is run by a few powerful families; most of the doctors are not among them.
entries.changes: The courses explain how an ordinary country priest could stand alone at the incense altar, as in Luke 1:8-9, while the people waited outside for him to come out. In Acts 6:7 a large number of priests become believers; Acts does not say which priests, but most priests were men of modest means, not the Jerusalem aristocracy.
entries.not: **Not a job anyone could apply for.** A doctor trains and is hired. A priest was born into his course, his duties fell to him by a lot that Jews believed God directed, and he was meant to live on tithes, not fees.
entries.dissent: Whether the twenty-four elders of Revelation 4 allude to these orders. Keener thinks so almost certainly. The Zondervan dictionary sees in them the heavenly priesthood of the church. Wright, Beale and the ESV and CSB Study Bibles prefer the twelve tribes with the twelve apostles. Heiser reads divine council members in his book, and in his podcast council members, glorified believers and star imagery at once.

entries.title: Caesar worshiped as savior and lord
entries.summary: Augustus and the emperors after him were hailed as savior, lord and son of a god, and in the eastern provinces they were worshiped. The titles the Gospels give Jesus were already being used for Caesar.
aliases: King of kings and Lord of lords
entries.plain: **The banners called him the father of the nation and the savior of the people, and nobody laughed out loud.** Augustus ended Rome's civil wars and made himself sole ruler. He declared his dead adoptive father a god, which made him the son of a god. Across the empire, inscriptions called the emperor savior and lord, his birthday was celebrated as good news, and in the eastern provinces people built temples and worshiped him. The first Christians used the same words for Jesus.
entries.then: Wright sums up Augustus. Adopted son of Julius Caesar, he became sole ruler after a bloody civil war and turned the Roman republic into an empire. He claimed to have brought justice and peace to the world, and after declaring his adoptive father divine he "styled himself as 'son of god'". People called him savior and lord, and in the east they more and more worshiped him as a god. Keener's notes say that "Inscriptions hailed Caesar as the empire's savior and lord," while Scripture called God the true savior (Isaiah 43:11). Pagans used the language of good news for the emperor's cult, above all on his birthday. Cities of the Greek east competed for the largest imperial cult. Its presidents in Asia, the Asiarchs, were the province's leading men, and to proclaim another king sounded like treason. Jews were unofficially excused from worshiping the emperor. In the east others had to show loyalty to the cult or face serious consequences, and believers put out of the synagogue could lose the Jewish exemption. Wright notes that "Domitian at least had himself called 'lord and god'," and hears Thomas's my Lord and my God as a challenge to the rising cult. Flattering rulers as gods had a long history in the Greek East, but under Rome even Caesar expected others to refuse it. Wright adds that Alexander had hinted at his own divinity, and that at Philippi Caesar's worship as savior and Lord was the colony's latest innovation. The roots go deeper. In the twenty-third century BC Naram-Sin of Akkad became the first Mesopotamian king to write the sign for a god before his own name. Yet Podany notes that Mesopotamian kings rarely claimed to be gods.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a regime that puts the leader's face on every coin and banner and calls him the nation's savior. Using that title for someone else in public is a political act, whether or not it is meant as one.
entries.changes: When an angel announces a savior who is Christ the Lord in Luke 2:11, the words are the ones on Caesar's inscriptions, so the birth story sets two rulers side by side. Confessing Jesus as Lord, as in Philippians 2:11, used a title the emperor claimed. Keener reads the enforced worship of the beast's image in Revelation 13:15 against the imperial cult.
entries.not: **Not politics without religion.** A modern personality cult flatters a living leader. In the eastern provinces the emperor had temples and priests and was worshiped as a god. Jews were unofficially exempt, and the pressure varied from city to city.
entries.dissent: Three questions. First, how loudly Philippians sets Jesus against Caesar. Wright and Bird read Philippians 2:6-11 as an implicit contrast with every human empire and call the church to live as "a counter-imperial colony of heavenly citizens". Keener, his notes and the ESV Study Bible root the titles Savior and Lord in Israel's language for God and treat the contrast as something the Philippians would hear. Second, who says peace and security in 1 Thessalonians 5:3. Keener hears an attack on "claims of earlier Roman emperors to have established peace and security", and Wright and Bird call it an imperial slogan. The ESV Study Bible allows imperial propaganda but thinks an echo of the false prophets of Jeremiah 6:14 and 8:11 more likely. Third, how hard the cult pressed on Christians in Revelation's Asia. The CSB Study Bible says Domitian made emperor worship mandatory. Carson, Moo and Morris think he made the confession lord and god a test of loyalty, yet find the evidence for persecution under him exaggerated. The cultural backgrounds article on the cult says no one hunted down absentees unless accused. Beale sees no widespread official demand, and Wright and Bird see pressure from local elites.

ddd.n: The beast from the earth / the false prophet
ddd.s: The second beast of Revelation, which looks like a lamb and talks like a dragon.

usedIn.n: Luke 2:8-20, Shepherds hear of a savior
usedIn.s: Angels announce to shepherds in the fields near Bethlehem the birth of a savior who is Christ the Lord, and the shepherds find the child lying in a manger as they were told.

usedIn.n: John 15:18-16:15, Hated by the world and put out of the synagogue
usedIn.s: Jesus warns that the world will hate his followers as it hated him, that they will be put out of the synagogues and even killed by people who think they are serving God, and that the Advocate will prove the world wrong.

usedIn.n: John 20:19-31, Locked doors, and my Lord and my God
usedIn.s: On the evening of the first day Jesus stands among the disciples behind locked doors, shows his hands and side, sends them as the Father sent him and breathes the Spirit on them. A week later Thomas sees the wounds and confesses him as Lord and God.

usedIn.n: Acts 12:1-25, Herod Agrippa, the prison and the king struck down
usedIn.s: King Herod Agrippa kills James and jails Peter at Passover, but an angel leads Peter out. Later, in Caesarea, the king accepts the crowd's cry that he speaks with a god's voice and is struck down.

usedIn.n: Acts 17:1-9, Another king in Thessalonica
usedIn.s: Paul argues from the Scriptures in the synagogue at Thessalonica that the Messiah had to suffer and rise. Some believe; opponents raise a mob, drag Jason before the city officials and accuse the believers of defying Caesar by proclaiming another king.

usedIn.n: Acts 19:23-41, Great is Artemis of the Ephesians
usedIn.s: Demetrius the silversmith rouses the craftsmen who make shrines of Artemis, warning that Paul's teaching threatens their trade and the goddess's honor. The city rushes into the theater chanting for two hours, until the city clerk calms them with a warning about Rome.

usedIn.n: Romans 1:1-7, A slave of the Messiah writes to Rome
usedIn.s: Paul opens with his name and titles, a short summary of the good news about God's Son, and a greeting of grace and peace to believers in Rome he has never met.

usedIn.n: Romans 1:8-17, Longing to see Rome
usedIn.s: Paul thanks God that the Roman believers' faith is spoken of everywhere, explains why he has not yet come, and states his theme: the good news is God's power to save everyone who believes, Jew and Greek.

usedIn.n: Romans 5:1-21, Peace with God, and Adam
usedIn.s: Justified by faith, believers have peace with God and are reconciled to him by the death of his Son. As sin and death came through Adam, grace and life come through Christ.

usedIn.n: Romans 13:1-7, The sword and the tax
usedIn.s: Paul tells believers to be subject to the governing authorities, whom God has put in place. The ruler bears the sword, and they should pay taxes and give honor where it is owed.

usedIn.n: Romans 15:14-24, To Spain by way of Rome
usedIn.s: Paul describes his priestly work of offering the Gentiles to God, from Jerusalem round to Illyricum, and his plan to visit Rome on his way to Spain and be helped on his journey there.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 2:6-16, The rulers of this age
usedIn.s: Paul speaks of a hidden wisdom of God, planned before time began, which the rulers of this age failed to grasp, or they would never have put Jesus to death.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 8:1-13, Knowledge, idols and the weak
usedIn.s: Answering those who know that an idol is nothing, Paul agrees there is one God and one Lord but warns that their freedom to eat sacrificial food, even in an idol's temple, can destroy a weaker believer.

usedIn.n: Galatians 6:11-18, Large letters in his own hand, and the marks of Jesus
usedIn.s: Taking the pen himself, Paul writes in large letters that the rivals want the Galatians circumcised so they can boast in their flesh and avoid persecution, while he boasts only in the cross; he blesses those who follow this rule and the Israel of God, and says he bears the marks of Jesus.

usedIn.n: Philippians 2:1-11, The form of a slave, a cross, and every knee
usedIn.s: Paul urges humility and concern for others, then sets out Christ, who did not exploit his equality with God but took the form of a slave and died on a cross, and whom God exalted so that every knee will bow.

usedIn.n: Philippians 3:12-4:1, The race, citizens of heaven, and a Savior from there
usedIn.s: Paul pictures himself as a runner straining toward the prize, warns against those whose god is their stomach, and reminds a Roman colony that its citizenship is in heaven, from where it awaits a Savior who will transform its lowly bodies.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 1:1-10, Turned to God from idols
usedIn.s: Paul, Silas and Timothy thank God for a young church that received the message in the middle of suffering, whose story is now told everywhere: they turned to God from idols to serve him and to wait for his Son from heaven.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 5:1-11, A thief in the night, and peace and security
usedIn.s: Paul reminds the church that the day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night: while people say peace and security, sudden destruction comes like labor pains, but they are children of the day who keep awake and sober, armed with faith, love and hope.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 2:1-7, Prayers for kings and all in authority
usedIn.s: Paul asks for prayers for everyone, kings and all in authority included, so that believers may live peaceful and quiet lives, because God our Savior wants all to be saved and there is one God and one mediator.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 6:11-21, Fight the good fight, the King of kings, the rich, and the deposit
usedIn.s: Timothy, as a man of God, is to flee greed and fight the good fight of the faith, keeping his charge until the appearing of the Lord, the King of kings; the rich are to be generous, and Timothy is to guard what has been entrusted to him.

usedIn.n: Titus 2:11-3:8, Grace has appeared, be subject to rulers, and the washing of rebirth
usedIn.s: God's grace has appeared, training believers to live with self-control now while they wait for Christ's glorious appearing; they are to respect rulers and be gentle to all, because God saved them by his mercy, giving them new birth and new life by the Holy Spirit.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 2:11-17, Foreigners among the nations; honor the emperor
usedIn.s: As foreigners and exiles the readers must keep their conduct good among the Gentiles, who slander them as wrongdoers. They are to submit to every human authority, the emperor and his governors, and so silence ignorant talk; they are free people, but slaves of God. Honor everyone, love the believers, fear God, honor the emperor.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 4:12-19, The fiery ordeal and the name Christian
usedIn.s: The readers should not be surprised at the fiery ordeal, but rejoice to share Christ's sufferings. No one should suffer as a murderer, a thief or a meddler, but anyone who suffers as a Christian should not be ashamed; judgment begins with God's household, so those who suffer should commit themselves to their faithful Creator.

usedIn.n: 2 Peter 1:1-21, A reminder before the tent is folded
usedIn.s: Simeon Peter writes to those who share a faith as precious as his, through whom they may share in the divine nature, and urges them to add virtue to virtue. Knowing his death is near, he means to remind them, for he was an eyewitness of Christ's majesty on the holy mountain, and the prophetic word is a lamp in a dark place until the morning star rises.

usedIn.n: 1 John 5:13-21, The sin that leads to death, the evil one and idols
usedIn.s: John writes so that believers may know they have eternal life, and that God hears them. They are to pray for a brother or sister whose sin does not lead to death, though there is a sin that does. Those born of God are kept from the evil one, while the whole world lies under his power; the letter ends with a warning to keep away from idols.

usedIn.n: Revelation 2:1-7, Ephesus and the Nicolaitans
usedIn.s: To Ephesus the one who holds the seven stars praises a church that tested false apostles and hates the works of the Nicolaitans, but warns that it has abandoned its first love and may lose its lampstand. The one who conquers will eat from the tree of life in God's paradise.

usedIn.n: Revelation 2:8-11, Smyrna, poor and slandered
usedIn.s: To Smyrna the risen Jesus says he sees their hardship and poverty and the abuse they suffer from local opponents claiming to be the true Jews, whom he condemns in harsh terms. Some will be jailed for a short time; if they stay loyal even to death he will reward them with life.

usedIn.n: Revelation 2:12-17, Pergamum, where Satan's throne is
usedIn.s: To Pergamum Jesus, who wields the sword of judgment, says they have stayed loyal in a city he calls Satan's seat, even after the martyrdom of Antipas. But some follow teaching like Balaam's that leads to idol meals and immorality. The faithful are promised hidden heavenly food and a white stone carrying a new name.

usedIn.n: Revelation 2:18-29, Thyatira, the guilds and Jezebel
usedIn.s: To Thyatira the Son of God, with eyes like fire and feet like bronze, praises a growing church but rebukes it for tolerating Jezebel, a self-styled prophetess who leads his servants into immorality and idol food. Those who hold fast are promised authority over the nations and the morning star.

usedIn.n: Revelation 4:1-11, the throne room and the twenty-four elders
usedIn.s: Through an open door John is called up to heaven and sees God on a throne, ringed by a rainbow, with twenty-four elders on thrones, four living creatures and a sea of glass. The creatures cry holy, holy, holy, and the elders lay down their crowns, saying the Lord and God is worthy because he created all things.

usedIn.n: Revelation 13:1-10, the beast from the sea
usedIn.s: A beast with ten horns and seven heads rises from the sea, built from Daniel's leopard, bear and lion, and the dragon gives it his power. One head seems to have had a fatal wound that healed, the whole earth follows it in awe, and it is allowed to blaspheme and to make war on God's people for forty-two months.

usedIn.n: Revelation 13:11-18, the beast from the earth, the mark and 666
usedIn.s: A second beast, harmless-looking like a lamb but speaking like the dragon, rises from the earth and drives everyone to worship the first beast, working wonders and making its statue speak. Trade is barred to anyone without its mark on hand or forehead, a mark tied to the beast's name and number, 666.

usedIn.n: Revelation 14:6-20, Babylon fallen, the harvest and the winepress
usedIn.s: Three angels announce an eternal gospel, the fall of Babylon and the undiluted cup of God's wrath for those who worship the beast, and a voice blesses those who die in the Lord. Then one like a son of man reaps the earth's grain with a sickle, and an angel gathers its grapes into the great winepress, from which blood flows as high as the horses' bridles.

usedIn.n: Revelation 18:1-8, come out of her, my people
usedIn.s: A shining angel announces that Babylon the great has fallen and become a haunt of demons and unclean birds, because the nations drank her wine and the merchants grew rich on her luxury. A voice calls God's people to come out of her, and to pay her back double, since she boasts that she sits as a queen and will never be a widow.

entries.title: Sacrifice and the daily offering
entries.summary: Animals were offered at the temple for sin, for thanks and for cleansing, and blood sealed covenants. Every day a lamb was offered at dawn and again in the afternoon, and Jews everywhere prayed at those hours.
aliases: poured out like a drink offering
entries.plain: **When the church bell rang at noon, farmers stopped in the fields and prayed where they stood.** At the temple in Jerusalem priests offered animals to God, for sin, for thanksgiving, and to mark a person clean again after an illness. Covenants were sealed with the blood of a sacrifice. Twice every day, at dawn and in the middle of the afternoon, a lamb was offered for the whole nation, with trumpets, singing and incense, while the people prayed. Jews far from the temple prayed at the same hours.
entries.then: Bailey writes that the only daily service in the temple was the atonement offering, at dawn and again at three in the afternoon. It began at the great altar, where a lamb was sacrificed for Israel's sins and its blood sprinkled on the altar. Then came silver trumpets, cymbals and a psalm, and a priest went into the sanctuary to offer incense while the people prayed outside. Many devout Jews away from the temple prayed at the hour of incense, and the hours of the morning and evening sacrifices were set aside for prayer. The Mishnah gives the afternoon times. The daily whole-offering was slaughtered at half past the eighth hour and offered at half past the ninth, an hour earlier on the eve of Passover (Pesahim 5.1). It describes the blessing from the porch steps, the cymbal, the Levites' song and the people bowing, and closes, "This was the rite of the Daily Whole-offering" in the temple (Tamid 7.2-3). Other sacrifices marked particular events. The law set offerings for a healed leper (Leviticus 14), and at Passover each family had the priests kill its lamb in the temple. Covenants were sealed with sacrificial blood, though Jewish law and custom recoiled from the thought of drinking blood. Psalmists, prophets and teachers all held that prayer and a clean heart mattered more than sacrifice, without rejecting sacrifice itself. Firstfruits were the real start of the harvest (Leviticus 23:10), and the first of the dough offered to God made the whole batch holy (Numbers 15:20-21). Drink offerings, usually wine but sometimes water, were poured in Israel's worship (Leviticus 23:18, 37). Gentiles poured them too, at the start of banquets and in memory of the dead.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a village church whose bell rings for morning and evening prayer, so that people at work miles away stop at the sound. The service happens in one place; the hour belongs to everyone.
entries.changes: Bailey sets the two men who go up to pray in Luke 18:10 at the daily offering, with its lamb for the sins of Israel in full view. Acts 3:1 calls the ninth hour the hour of prayer, close to the time the Mishnah gives for the afternoon offering. The blood of the covenant in Mark 14:24 draws on the way covenants were sealed by sacrifice.
entries.not: **Not a church service.** The daily offering was a sacrifice, a lamb killed and its blood put on the altar by priests for the nation. The people's part was to pray and bow while it happened.
entries.dissent: What sacrifice achieved. Keener writes that under the law sin could be expiated only by bloodshed, "God's anger appeased by substitution". Merrill, in an article in the CSB Study Bible, explains the Hebrew word for atonement as to cover. Atonement, he writes, involves "an innocent party taking the punishment that was due to a guilty party." Wright and Bird answer that the system was never about animals killed as a vicarious punishment, "not to punish people's sins so that they could enter God's presence". Its aim was to cleanse sin and death from people and sanctuary so that God could live among them: "The sacrificial blood acted as the cleansing, purifying agent". The cultural backgrounds notes on Leviticus 16:14 describe the high priest purging the sanctuary with blood on the Day of Atonement, where Israel's neighbors cleansed their temples with other substances.

usedIn.n: Luke 17:11-19, Ten lepers and the Samaritan who came back
usedIn.s: On the border between Samaria and Galilee ten men with leprosy call to Jesus from a distance. He sends them to the priests, they are cleansed on the way, and only one, a Samaritan, comes back to thank him.

usedIn.n: Luke 18:9-14, Two men go up to the temple to pray
usedIn.s: Jesus tells of a Pharisee who thanks God that he is not like other people and a tax collector who stands far off, beats his breast and asks for mercy. The tax collector goes home justified.

usedIn.n: Luke 23:26-49, The road to the cross, paradise, and the ninth hour
usedIn.s: Simon of Cyrene carries the cross, the women of Jerusalem mourn, and Jesus warns them of days to come. Crucified between two criminals, he promises one of them paradise and dies at the ninth hour.

usedIn.n: Luke 24:36-53, Not a ghost; hands lifted in blessing
usedIn.s: Jesus stands among the disciples, who think they are seeing a ghost. He shows his hands and feet and eats fish, opens the Scriptures to them, and leads them out to Bethany, where he lifts his hands and blesses them.

usedIn.n: John 1:19-34, Not the Messiah, not Elijah, not the Prophet
usedIn.s: Priests and Levites from Jerusalem ask John who he is. He denies being the Messiah, Elijah or the Prophet, calls himself the voice in the wilderness, and points to Jesus as the Lamb of God.

usedIn.n: Acts 3:1-26, The lame man at the Beautiful Gate
usedIn.s: At the afternoon hour of prayer Peter heals a man lame from birth who begged at the temple gate, then tells the gathering crowd that Jesus is the prophet Moses promised.

usedIn.n: Acts 21:17-26, James, the rumors and the vow
usedIn.s: In Jerusalem James and the elders welcome Paul but warn him that thousands of believers zealous for the law have heard he teaches Jews abroad to abandon Moses. They ask him to pay for four men completing a vow and to purify himself with them in the temple.

usedIn.n: Romans 3:21-31, Redemption and the mercy seat
usedIn.s: Paul announces that God's righteousness has been revealed through faith in Jesus for all who believe, Jew and Gentile alike, through a redemption and an atoning death he links to the mercy seat.

usedIn.n: Romans 8:18-30, Groaning and firstfruits
usedIn.s: Creation groans as in labor, waiting to be freed from decay, and believers who have the firstfruits of the Spirit groan too as they wait for their adoption and the redemption of their bodies.

usedIn.n: Romans 11:11-24, The olive tree
usedIn.s: Israel's stumbling has brought salvation to the Gentiles. Paul pictures Gentile believers as wild olive shoots grafted into Israel's tree and warns them not to boast over the natural branches.

usedIn.n: Romans 12:1-21, A living sacrifice
usedIn.s: Paul urges believers to offer their bodies as a living sacrifice, to see themselves as members of one body, and to love without pretense: honoring one another, welcoming strangers, weeping with those who weep and repaying evil with good.

usedIn.n: Philippians 2:12-18, Lights in a crooked generation, poured out like a drink offering
usedIn.s: Paul urges the Philippians to work out their salvation without grumbling, shining like stars in a crooked generation, and pictures himself poured out like a drink offering on their sacrifice.

usedIn.n: Philippians 4:10-23, A thank-you without a thank you, and Caesar's household
usedIn.s: Paul acknowledges the Philippians' gift in the language of contentment and of business receipts and sacrifice, without a direct thank you, and closes with greetings from the saints of Caesar's household.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 4:1-8, Itching ears, a drink offering, and the crown
usedIn.s: Paul charges Timothy before God and Christ Jesus to preach the word in season and out of season, because people will gather teachers to suit their itching ears; he himself is already being poured out like a drink offering, has fought the good fight and finished the race, and awaits the crown.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 9:11-22, Blood, ashes and a will
usedIn.s: Christ entered the greater tent once for all with his own blood, not the blood of goats and calves. If the ashes of a heifer could make the unclean outwardly clean, how much more will his blood cleanse the conscience; and as a will takes effect only at a death, the new covenant was put in force by his.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 9:23-10:18, Once for all, and a seated priest
usedIn.s: Christ entered heaven itself, not a copy, and offered himself once at the climax of the ages; as people die once and then face judgment, he will appear a second time to save. The yearly sacrifices only reminded people of sin, but his body offered once has made his people holy, and he has sat down, his offering finished.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 1:13-25, Minds girded, foreigners, and the lamb
usedIn.s: Peter calls his readers to be ready and sober, holy as God is holy, and to live as foreigners in reverent fear, since they were ransomed not with silver or gold but with the blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish. Born again of imperishable seed, the living word, they must love one another deeply.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 2:1-10, Living stones and a royal priesthood
usedIn.s: Like newborn babies the readers should crave pure milk. Coming to Christ, the living stone rejected by people but chosen by God, they are being built into a spiritual house and a holy priesthood; Peter strings together Scripture's stone texts and calls them a chosen people, a royal priesthood and a holy nation.

usedIn.n: Revelation 6:9-17, souls under the altar and the great day of wrath
usedIn.s: At the fifth seal the souls of those killed for God's word cry out from under the altar, how long, and are given white robes and told to wait. At the sixth a great earthquake shakes the world, the sky rolls up like a scroll, and kings and slaves alike hide in the caves from the wrath of the Lamb.

usedIn.n: Revelation 14:1-5, the Lamb and the 144,000 on Mount Zion
usedIn.s: The Lamb stands on Mount Zion with 144,000 who bear his name and his Father's on their foreheads, singing a new song only they can learn. They have kept themselves pure, follow the Lamb wherever he goes, and are offered as firstfruits to God and the Lamb.

entries.title: The Festival of Tabernacles
entries.summary: The autumn pilgrim feast, eight days long, when men lived in leafy shelters, priests poured water at the altar and torches lit the temple courts. It carried hopes of rain, of resurrection and of a coming king.
entries.plain: **The whole town camps out in the yard for a week, and the night the lights go up everyone is in the square.** Tabernacles was one of the three feasts when pilgrims went up to Jerusalem. For eight days the men lived in shelters made of branches, remembering Israel's years in the desert, and worshipers carried palm branches and fruit. Each morning priests carried water up from the pool of Siloam and poured it out at the altar, and at night torches lit the temple courts. It was a harvest feast and a feast of hope.
entries.then: Tabernacles ranked among the year's three great festivals and ran eight days in Jerusalem. Men lived in booths on rooftops or elsewhere, recalling God's care when Israel lived in booths in the wilderness, and the feast was known for its joy. Josephus explains that "when the season of the year is changing for winter, the law enjoins us to pitch tabernacles in every one of our houses." Worshipers carried "a branch of myrtle, and willow, and a bough of the palm-tree, with the addition of the pome citron." He tells how a crowd at this feast once pelted King Alexander Jannaeus at the altar with the citrons in their hands. For at least the first seven days priests carried water in procession from the pool of Siloam and poured it at the foot of the altar. The rite was first meant to bring rain, and pilgrims took home souvenir jars that pictured it. Zechariah 14, read at the feast with Ezekiel 47, promised living water flowing from the temple. Torches lit the city, and there was dancing in the Court of Women. Wright adds that wine was poured with the water and that the feast's prayers were for rain and for the resurrection of the dead. Like Passover, he writes, it was "a key symbol of the great national hope," the coming of the Messiah and freedom from Rome. A later source says the priests recited God's words in Isaiah 43:10 and 13, I am he, at this festival. Palm branches belonged especially to this feast, which Zechariah 14:16 says the remnant of all nations would one day keep.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a harvest festival and a national day rolled into one, with every family sleeping in a shelter in the yard. People give thanks for the crops and remember the hard years, and the lights at night make them dream of what the nation could become.
entries.changes: The water and the lights of Tabernacles are the setting when Jesus offers living water, as in John 7:37-38, and calls himself the light of the world. Peter's offer to build three shelters at the transfiguration in Matthew 17:4 uses the feast's word for booths. Revelation 22:1-2 pictures a river of life flowing from God's throne, the hope that Zechariah 14 and Ezekiel 47 gave the feast.
entries.not: **Not a civic holiday.** A national day is kept by the state. Tabernacles was commanded in the law and kept at the temple in Jerusalem, and its water and torch rites were acts of worship, prayers for rain and for the nation's hope.
entries.dissent: Whether the I am recital is early enough to matter. Keener reports the later tradition that priests spoke God's words from Isaiah 43 at this feast. He is not sure it is early enough to stand behind John 8:58, while the cultural backgrounds notes cite the same later source for that verse without the caution. Second, where the living water of John 7:38 flows from. Keener's punctuation makes it flow from Jesus, as from the temple's foundation stone. The ESV and CSB Study Bibles and Wright read it as flowing from believers. The cultural backgrounds article on Tabernacles and living water hears the Jewish picture of Jerusalem as the navel of the earth behind from his belly. It reads Jesus as the Spirit's source, while allowing the other reading.

usedIn.n: John 7:1-36, Up to the Festival of Tabernacles
usedIn.s: Jesus stays in Galilee while the Judeans look for a chance to kill him, then goes up to Tabernacles privately and teaches in the temple. The crowds argue over whether he is a deceiver or the Messiah, and the chief priests send guards to arrest him.

usedIn.n: John 7:37-52, Rivers of living water on the last day
usedIn.s: On the great last day of the feast Jesus cries out that the thirsty should come to him and drink. The crowd divides over whether he is the Prophet or the Messiah, and the Pharisees scorn a prophet from Galilee.

usedIn.n: John 8:12-30, The light of the world by the treasury
usedIn.s: Jesus calls himself the light of the world. Told that testimony about himself does not count, he answers with the law's rule of two witnesses: himself and the Father who sent him.

usedIn.n: John 9:1-41, A man born blind is put out
usedIn.s: Jesus puts mud on a blind beggar's eyes and sends him to wash in Siloam. Because it is the Sabbath the man is questioned, his parents are afraid, and when he defends Jesus he is thrown out.

usedIn.n: Revelation 7:1-17, the sealing of the 144,000 and the crowd in white
usedIn.s: Four angels hold back the winds until God's servants are sealed on their foreheads, 144,000 from the tribes of Israel. Then John sees a crowd no one can count, from every nation, in white robes with palm branches, who have come out of the great tribulation and whom the Lamb will shepherd.

entries.title: The Festival of Dedication
entries.summary: The eight-day winter feast of lights that remembered how Judas Maccabeus cleansed and rededicated the temple after Antiochus IV defiled it. It recalled liberation, and it called kings to mind.
entries.plain: **Every year the town lights candles on the night the tyrant's statue came down.** In the 160s BC a Greek king, Antiochus IV, set up pagan worship in the temple and sacrificed pigs on its altar. Jewish fighters led by Judas Maccabeus took the temple back, cleansed it and dedicated a new altar. The yearly feast that remembered it lasted eight days in winter, with lamps lit in the temple. Nobody was required to travel for it, but it was a feast of freedom.
entries.then: Josephus tells how Antiochus Epiphanes plundered the temple and forced pagan worship on the Jews, and that "when the king had built an idol altar upon God's altar, he slew swine upon it." Three years later, on the twenty-fifth of the month Casleu, Judas Maccabeus cleansed the temple, built a new altar and lit the lamps. The people made it a law to keep the restoration for eight days. Josephus adds, "And from that time to this we celebrate this festival, and call it Lights." The ESV and CSB Study Bibles date the desecration to 167 BC and the rededication to December 164 BC. It was not a required pilgrimage, but Keener writes that "the eight-day celebration of lights in the temple was beautiful." His notes say it drew pilgrims from Galilee and even from the Diaspora, though fewer than Tabernacles. Antiochus claimed to be divine, and a letter Josephus records from the people of Shechem addresses him as the god Epiphanes. Wright stresses kingship. By freeing and reconsecrating the temple, Judas and his family became kings and founded a dynasty that lasted about a hundred years. Herod the Great married one of its princesses to claim its line. So every Hanukkah, Wright says, people thought about kings and how they became kings.
entries.bridge: An analogy: an independence day that remembers the night an occupying army was driven out of the capital's great hall. The lights are beautiful, and the speeches always turn to who will lead the nation now.
entries.changes: Dedication remembered a temple set apart again and a ruler who claimed to be a god, so words about who is set apart by God and who may be called God's Son, as in John 10:36, land at a pointed moment. The feast is named only in John 10:22.
entries.not: **Not a secular holiday.** An independence day honors a state. Dedication remembered the temple cleansed and a new altar built after pagan sacrifice had defiled it, so its lamps were lit in God's house.

usedIn.s: In winter, at the Festival of Dedication, the Judeans press Jesus to say plainly whether he is the Messiah. He says he and the Father are one, they pick up stones, and he answers from Psalm 82.

usedIn.n: John 12:12-19, Palm branches and a donkey's colt
usedIn.s: The festival crowd goes out with palm branches, shouting Hosanna and hailing Jesus as King of Israel, and he rides in on a young donkey, as Zechariah had said Zion's king would come.

entries.title: Put out of the synagogue
entries.summary: A Jewish community could punish a member by shutting him out of its life for a time or for good. Since the synagogue was the center of town life, expulsion cut a person off from neighbors and worship, and often from a living.
aliases: have nothing more to do with them
those who say they are Jews and are not
entries.plain: **Being cut off from the only church in a small town means losing your friends, your customers and your place at every wedding and funeral.** A synagogue was where a Jewish town prayed, studied Scripture, settled disputes and met. It could also discipline its members, and its heaviest punishment was to shut someone out of the community, for a short time, a longer one or for good. John's Gospel says that people who confessed Jesus as the Messiah faced exactly that.
entries.then: Jewish communities had several kinds of discipline, beatings among them. They could also ban a member from community life for a short time, a longer one or for good. The cultural backgrounds notes find such bans in later rabbinic sources, before them in the Scrolls, at 1QS 6.24 to 7.25, and earlier still in Ezra 10:8. Keener calls excommunication one of the harshest forms of synagogue discipline, apparently rare and so very severe in Jesus' time. He describes it as the spiritual equal of a death sentence, used in place of the Old Testament death penalty, though a banned person who repented could be restored. It also shut people out of the community's meals. Under later rabbinic rules full excommunication treated a person as an outsider and put him under a curse, while lesser bans kept him inside the community. The Essenes also had levels of discipline. Wright stresses what was lost: "The synagogue was the focus of the whole community," and someone put out would probably do better to leave the area. The churches took over the synagogue's forms of discipline, apart from beatings. For John's first readers expulsion could be dangerous as well as lonely. Without recognized Jewish status, believers could lose the Jews' exemption from the imperial cult and face charges of disloyalty. Keener writes that synagogue leaders in Asia left Jewish Christians exposed by handing them to the Roman authorities as non-Jews. Rome let the Jewish communities of the Diaspora discipline their own members, and correction was to be private first and public only when that failed.
entries.bridge: An analogy: being shunned by a close-knit religious community where the same families run the farms, the shops and the school. The door of the meeting house closes, and every other door in town closes with it.
entries.changes: Expulsion from the synagogue was the threat that kept people who believed from saying so, as in John 9:22, and the fear of it shows in more than one scene. Paul tells a church to remove an offender from its fellowship in 1 Corinthians 5:13, and 2 Thessalonians 3:14-15 describes a milder ban that still treats the offender as a brother.
entries.not: **Not informal shunning.** Shunning is social pressure with no law behind it. A synagogue ban was formal discipline, graded from a short exclusion to a permanent one, and Rome let the communities impose it. In Asia it could strip believers of Jewish status and expose them to Roman charges.
entries.dissent: How formal the expulsion in John was, and when such expulsions began. Keener reads John 9 as the language of John's own day, the 90s, when his readers faced expulsion. He says excommunication was apparently rare in Jesus' time and its formality then unclear. The cultural backgrounds notes point out that forms of banishment already appear in the Dead Sea Scrolls, before Jesus. Wright treats the decision as already taken in Jesus' day by the Judaean leaders. Carson, Moo and Morris note that the theory of a ban on Christians agreed at Jamnia after AD 85 has been challenged at every point. The ESV and CSB Study Bibles say the way the man is thrown out in John 9:34 suggests an impulsive act rather than formal excommunication. Second, who was expected to do the killing in John 16:2. The CSB Study Bible thinks Jewish persecution most likely and says some rabbis believed killing heretics was an act of worship. The cultural backgrounds notes say deadly violence from fellow Jews happened but was not the norm, and that fatal persecution came especially from Gentiles. Keener says hostile synagogue leaders in Asia handed believers over to Rome rather than killing them directly.

usedIn.n: John 9:1-41, A man born blind is put out
usedIn.s: Jesus puts mud on a blind beggar's eyes and sends him to wash in Siloam. Because it is the Sabbath the man is questioned, his parents are afraid, and when he defends Jesus he is thrown out.

usedIn.n: John 12:20-50, Greeks at the feast, and the ruler of this world cast out
usedIn.s: Some Greeks who came up to worship ask to see Jesus. He says his hour has come, that the ruler of this world will be driven out, and that when he is lifted up he will draw everyone to himself; many leaders believe but stay silent.

usedIn.n: John 15:18-16:15, Hated by the world and put out of the synagogue
usedIn.s: Jesus warns that the world will hate his followers as it hated him, that they will be put out of the synagogues and even killed by people who think they are serving God, and that the Advocate will prove the world wrong.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 1:12-20, A blasphemer shown mercy, and two men handed over to Satan
usedIn.s: Paul thanks Christ for taking a former blasphemer and persecutor into his service as an example of mercy, then charges Timothy to fight the battle well, as the prophecies about him foretold, unlike Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom Paul has handed over to Satan.

usedIn.n: Titus 3:9-15, A divisive person, winter at Nicopolis, and Zenas and Apollos
usedIn.s: Titus is to avoid foolish controversies, genealogies and quarrels about the law, and to warn a divisive person twice before having nothing more to do with him; Paul plans to winter at Nicopolis and asks Titus to send Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way with everything they need.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 13:7-17, Foods, an altar and outside the camp
usedIn.s: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and for ever, so the readers must not be carried away by strange teachings about foods. Believers have an altar the tabernacle priests may not eat from; as the bodies of the sin offerings were burned outside the camp, Jesus suffered outside the gate, and they must go out to him, bearing his disgrace, seeking the city to come.

usedIn.n: Revelation 2:8-11, Smyrna, poor and slandered
usedIn.s: To Smyrna the risen Jesus says he sees their hardship and poverty and the abuse they suffer from local opponents claiming to be the true Jews, whom he condemns in harsh terms. Some will be jailed for a short time; if they stay loyal even to death he will reward them with life.

usedIn.n: Revelation 3:7-13, Philadelphia and the key of David
usedIn.s: To Philadelphia the one who holds the key of David sets before a weak but faithful church an open door no one can shut. Those of the synagogue of Satan will bow at their feet, and the one who conquers will be a pillar in God's temple, bearing the name of the new Jerusalem.

entries.title: Pentecost, the Festival of Weeks
entries.summary: The harvest feast fifty days after Passover, one of the three festivals that brought Jewish pilgrims to Jerusalem from across the world. Some Jews also tied it to the covenant at Sinai.
entries.plain: **Every harvest weekend the town fills up, because everyone who moved away comes home for the thanksgiving service.** Pentecost means fiftieth. The feast fell fifty days, seven weeks, after Passover, and thanked God for the first of the wheat harvest. It was one of the three feasts when Jews traveled to Jerusalem, so the city was crowded with visitors from far countries. Some Jews also connected the day with God's covenant at Sinai, though scholars disagree about how early that link was made.
entries.then: The feast came seven weeks after Passover (Leviticus 23:15-16) and celebrated the first of the wheat harvest. As one of the three pilgrim feasts it filled Jerusalem. The ESV Study Bible calls it the second of the year's harvest festivals. Wright writes, "For a first-century Jew, Pentecost was the fiftieth day after Passover." It was the day, he says, when farmers brought the first sheaf of wheat to God, partly in thanks and partly as a prayer that the rest of the crop would come in safely. Keener thinks it was probably the least popular of the three pilgrim feasts. Josephus attests the crowds: "Now when that festival which we call Pentecost was at hand, all the places about the temple, and the whole city, was full of a multitude of people." Jews came to the three main feasts from all over the Roman and Parthian worlds. Because Pentecost fell only fifty days after Passover, some who had spent heavily on a rare pilgrimage stayed for both. The Dead Sea Scrolls kept it as a feast of covenant renewal, and some later Jewish texts celebrate it as the day the law was given at Sinai.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a harvest homecoming when everyone who left the town comes back. The church is full, the square is full, and you hear the accents of every place they settled.
entries.changes: Because Pentecost filled Jerusalem with Jewish pilgrims from many lands, the crowd in Acts 2:5-11 is international before a word is preached. Paul plans his travels around the feast in 1 Corinthians 16:8, and the cultural backgrounds notes take that as a sign his Gentile readers knew the biblical festivals.
entries.not: **Not a family reunion.** People at a homecoming return to the town they left. Pentecost pilgrims came from across the Roman and Parthian worlds to the temple, to thank God for the first of the wheat harvest. In Acts 2 it is still a Jewish feast.
entries.dissent: Pentecost and Sinai. Wright reads the feast as remembering Israel's arrival at Sinai fifty days after the exodus. So Luke, in his reading, shows Jesus sending the Spirit as Moses brought down the law, and the CSB Study Bible says Pentecost commemorated the giving of the law. Keener grants that the Scrolls kept it as covenant renewal. He says the link with the law may be later than Luke and that little in Acts 2 suggests Luke draws it.

usedIn.s: On the day of Pentecost wind and fire come on the gathered believers, and Jewish pilgrims from every nation hear them speaking in their own languages.

entries.title: Jews of the dispersion
entries.summary: Most Jews of the first century lived outside the land, in cities from Parthia to Rome. They kept the law and their own synagogues, spoke Greek or Aramaic, and came up to Jerusalem for the feasts when they could.
entries.plain: **Her grandparents left the old country, she grew up speaking another language, and she still flies back for the big family weddings.** After the exiles of the Old Testament, many Jews never went back. By the first century large Jewish communities lived in Egypt, Syria, Asia Minor, Rome and the Parthian east. They kept the law, gathered in their own synagogues and mostly spoke Greek. Some came to Jerusalem for the feasts, and some moved there to spend their last years in the land. In Jerusalem they could be called Hellenists, Greek-speakers, to tell them apart from Jews raised in Judea and Galilee.
entries.then: Jews came to Jerusalem for the main feasts from all over the Roman and Parthian worlds. Those from Parthia would know Aramaic, those from the empire Greek, and many knew local languages as well. Most Israelites who never came back from exile lived in Parthia and the east. There were large communities in Alexandria, Cyrene, Syria, Asia Minor and Rome. The ESV Study Bible calls the list in Acts 2:9-11 one of the fullest ancient catalogs of the Diaspora, confirmed by Philo. The Hellenists of Acts 6:1 were probably Diaspora Jews or their descendants whose mother tongue was Greek. The Hebrews were traditional Judeans and Galileans, many of whom knew both Greek and Aramaic. Both groups were fully Jewish. Many foreign Jews moved to the land in old age, which left an unusually large number of widows; Wright reports the suggestion. Jerusalem had synagogues for such groups. Archaeologists found the dedication of a synagogue of the freedmen, descendants of former Roman slaves, and later sources name synagogues of the Alexandrians and the Cilicians. Wright and Bird call Diaspora synagogues a stepping-stone for the gospel, since many of the first Gentile believers had been involved in one. In Greek cities most Jews were resident aliens, a minority held local citizenship, and their communities ran their own internal affairs. Claudius expelled the Jews of Rome, probably in AD 49. Rome's own community, perhaps fifty thousand strong, was mostly poor and Greek-speaking, with many synagogues and no central organization. Tiberius had expelled it once before, Josephus says, after four Jewish swindlers cheated a noble convert.
entries.bridge: An analogy: an emigrant community in a great foreign city, with its own congregations, newspapers and accent. They are loyal to the old country and visit when they can, and when they do, the people back home notice how they talk.
entries.changes: A Pentecost crowd from every nation, as in Acts 2:5-11, is a crowd of Jews from the dispersion, and the quarrel over widows soon afterward runs along the line between Greek-speaking and local believers. James 1:1 and 1 Peter 1:1 address their readers as the scattered people of God.
entries.not: **Not recent emigrants.** An emigrant community remembers a move a generation or two back. Most Jews of the period lived outside the land, many descended from exiles who never returned, and what drew them to Jerusalem was the law and its feasts.
entries.dissent: How deep the line between Hellenists and Hebrews ran. Keener takes the Hellenists as Diaspora Jews settled in Jerusalem, not simply Greek-speaking locals; the CSB Study Bible says the distinction is probably one of language; Wright thinks it was probably a mix of elements. The ESV Study Bible rejects the view that Acts 6:1 hides a serious theological rift, while allowing that the Hellenists may have been less attached to the temple.

usedIn.n: Acts 2:1-13, Pentecost and the nations
usedIn.s: On the day of Pentecost wind and fire come on the gathered believers, and Jewish pilgrims from every nation hear them speaking in their own languages.

usedIn.n: Acts 6:1-7, The Hellenists' widows and the Seven
usedIn.s: Greek-speaking believers complain that their widows are overlooked in the daily distribution of food. The Twelve have the community choose seven men, and lay hands on them.

usedIn.n: Acts 11:19-30, Antioch, and the name Christian
usedIn.s: Scattered believers bring the message to Gentiles in Antioch, where the disciples are first called Christians. When a prophet foretells famine, the church sends relief to the elders in Judea.

usedIn.n: Acts 18:1-11, Tentmakers in Corinth
usedIn.s: In Corinth Paul lodges and works with Aquila and Priscilla, Jews lately expelled from Rome who share his trade. When the synagogue turns against him he moves next door to the house of Titius Justus, and the synagogue leader Crispus believes with his household.

usedIn.n: Acts 18:12-17, Gallio's judgment seat
usedIn.s: Jewish leaders bring Paul before Gallio, proconsul of Achaia, accusing him of teaching a worship contrary to the law. Gallio refuses to judge a dispute about words, names and their own law and drives them from the judgment seat.

usedIn.n: Acts 18:18-28, A vow at Cenchreae and Apollos of Alexandria
usedIn.s: Paul has his hair cut at Cenchreae because of a vow and sails for Syria by way of Ephesus. In Ephesus Priscilla and Aquila teach the eloquent Alexandrian Apollos more accurately, and the believers write ahead to Achaia to welcome him.

usedIn.n: Acts 19:23-41, Great is Artemis of the Ephesians
usedIn.s: Demetrius the silversmith rouses the craftsmen who make shrines of Artemis, warning that Paul's teaching threatens their trade and the goddess's honor. The city rushes into the theater chanting for two hours, until the city clerk calms them with a warning about Rome.

usedIn.n: Acts 28:17-31, Two years in rented quarters
usedIn.s: Paul calls the Jewish leaders of Rome, explains why he is in chains, and spends a day arguing from Moses and the Prophets. Some are persuaded and some are not; for two whole years he lives at his own expense, welcoming everyone and preaching the kingdom without hindrance.

usedIn.n: Romans 1:8-17, Longing to see Rome
usedIn.s: Paul thanks God that the Roman believers' faith is spoken of everywhere, explains why he has not yet come, and states his theme: the good news is God's power to save everyone who believes, Jew and Greek.

usedIn.n: Romans 2:17-29, You who boast in the law
usedIn.s: Paul turns on an imagined Jewish teacher who boasts in the law yet steals, commits adultery and robs temples, so that God's name is blasphemed among the nations, and says true circumcision is of the heart.

usedIn.n: Romans 11:11-24, The olive tree
usedIn.s: Israel's stumbling has brought salvation to the Gentiles. Paul pictures Gentile believers as wild olive shoots grafted into Israel's tree and warns them not to boast over the natural branches.

usedIn.n: Romans 13:1-7, The sword and the tax
usedIn.s: Paul tells believers to be subject to the governing authorities, whom God has put in place. The ruler bears the sword, and they should pay taxes and give honor where it is owed.

usedIn.n: Romans 16:3-16, Greet the church in their house
usedIn.s: Paul greets more than two dozen believers in Rome by name, from Prisca and Aquila and the church in their house to the households of Aristobulus and Narcissus, and tells them to greet one another with a holy kiss.

usedIn.n: Colossians 1:1-14, Epaphras's report and a change of kingdoms
usedIn.s: Paul and Timothy greet the believers at Colossae, a church Paul has never visited, thank God for what Epaphras has told them, and pray that they grow in knowledge, having been rescued out of darkness into the kingdom of God's Son.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 11:8-16, Strangers looking for a city
usedIn.s: By faith Abraham left home without knowing where he was going and lived in tents in the promised land as a foreigner, waiting for a city with lasting foundations that God himself designed and built. He and Sarah and their family died still waiting, admitting they were strangers on earth and longing for a better, heavenly country.

usedIn.n: James 1:1-18, To the twelve tribes scattered
usedIn.s: James greets the twelve tribes scattered among the nations, tells them to count their trials as joy and to ask God for wisdom, warns that the rich will wither like a wildflower, and insists that God tempts no one but gives every good gift from above, as the Father of lights.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 1:1-12, To the exiles of the dispersion
usedIn.s: Peter writes to God's chosen exiles scattered through five provinces of Asia Minor, blesses God for a new birth into a living hope and an inheritance kept in heaven, and tells them their trials test their faith as fire tests gold. The prophets searched for this salvation, and angels long to look into it.

entries.title: Laying on of hands
entries.summary: Hands laid on a person to bless, to heal, or to set someone apart for a task, the way Moses laid hands on Joshua. In the early church it went with prayer, the gift of the Spirit and sending people out.
aliases: do not be hasty in the laying on of hands
the laying on of my hands
entries.plain: **Before the young pastor left for his first church, the elders gathered round, put their hands on his shoulders and prayed.** In the Old Testament people laid hands on someone to bless them, and Moses laid his hands on Joshua to hand on his task. Jewish teachers later used the gesture to recognize a new teacher. In Acts the apostles and church leaders lay hands on people while they pray: to heal, when the Spirit is given, and when someone is sent out to a new work.
entries.then: Laying on hands could pass on a blessing (Genesis 48:14). The closer model for Acts 6:6 is Moses laying his hands on Joshua (Numbers 27:18, 23), who was then filled with the spirit of wisdom (Deuteronomy 34:9). Later rabbis ordained their successors in this way. Keener calls the act in Acts 6 something like ordination, comparable to the later semikah. The rabbis, he notes, laid hands only on sacrifices and on scholars they ordained, and laying on hands in prayer is rare in ancient Jewish sources, with one example in the Dead Sea Scrolls. The ESV Study Bible sorts its uses in Acts into three: commissioning for ministry (6:6; 13:3), healing (9:17) and the giving of the Spirit (8:18; 19:6). The CSB Study Bible reads the laying on of hands on the Seven as recognition that God had called them. By early Christian times seasoned Jewish teachers often recognized new teachers by this act. Wright says modern confirmation broadly matches what Peter and John do in Samaria, but warns that the earliest documents show no single pattern of Christian initiation. Oracles had long been used to confirm the right of kings and officials, and Keener reads the prophecies at Timothy's commissioning that way. Whoever laid hands on an untested elder, he adds, shared the blame if that man fell. The ESV Study Bible names the council of elders as those who laid hands on Timothy.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a retiring captain handing the armband to the new one in front of the whole team. The gesture is small, and everyone watching knows who now carries the responsibility and who gave it to him.
entries.changes: Hands laid on the Seven in Acts 6:6, and later on Barnabas and Saul, mark people set apart for a task, as Moses set apart Joshua. In 1 Timothy 4:14 the elders laid hands on Timothy, and Hebrews 6:2 lists the laying on of hands among the church's first teachings.
entries.not: **Not a handover between two people.** The captain gives away what was his. In Acts hands are laid on with prayer, the healing or the Spirit comes from God, and a council of elders could commission together. Simon is rebuked for thinking the power could be bought.
entries.dissent: Two points. Were the Seven the first deacons? The ESV Study Bible sets out both sides. The noun deacon does not occur in Acts 6, but the verb for serving does. The same verb is used of deacons in 1 Timothy 3:10 and 13, though it is a common word for service. Second, whether Timothy's laying on of hands (1 Timothy 4:14; 2 Timothy 1:6) was an ordination. The ESV Study Bible names the council of elders, and the Zondervan dictionary places it at Lystra. Carson, Moo and Morris note that 1 Timothy never calls it ordination and that 2 Timothy 1:6 may be nearer the later confirmation.
