usedIn.n: Acts 6:1-7, The Hellenists' widows and the Seven
usedIn.s: Greek-speaking believers complain that their widows are overlooked in the daily distribution of food. The Twelve have the community choose seven men, and lay hands on them.

usedIn.n: Acts 8:4-25, Samaria and Simon the magician
usedIn.s: Philip preaches the Messiah in Samaria, and even the famous magician Simon is baptized. When Peter and John lay hands on the Samaritans and they receive the Spirit, Simon offers money for the power.

usedIn.n: Acts 13:1-12, Sent from Antioch: the proconsul and the magician
usedIn.s: The church at Antioch fasts, prays and sends out Barnabas and Saul. On Cyprus the Roman proconsul believes after Paul confronts the Jewish magician in his entourage.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 4:6-16, Training for godliness, and a young leader
usedIn.s: Timothy is to train himself for godliness as an athlete trains his body, set an example despite his youth, devote himself to the public reading of Scripture and teaching, and not neglect the gift given when the elders laid hands on him.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 5:17-25, Double honor, two witnesses, the elect angels and a little wine
usedIn.s: Elders who lead well deserve double honor and pay; charges against them need two or three witnesses; Paul charges Timothy before God, Christ and the elect angels to act without favoritism, to lay hands on no one hastily, and to take a little wine.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 1:1-7, Lois, Eunice and the laying on of hands
usedIn.s: Writing from custody, Paul greets Timothy as his dear son, thanks God as he remembers him in prayer night and day, recalls the faith of Timothy's grandmother Lois and mother Eunice, and urges him to fan into flame the gift given when Paul laid hands on him.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 5:11-6:12, Milk, solid food and no way back
usedIn.s: The readers should be teachers by now but still need milk, so the writer urges them past the elementary teachings. Those who have been enlightened and shared in the Holy Spirit and then fall away cannot be brought back to repentance, though he is confident of better things for his readers.

entries.title: House churches
entries.summary: For their first three centuries Christians met in homes, the way some Jewish groups and private clubs did. A host with a large house gave the church its room, its table and often its protection.
aliases: church that meets at their house
the church that meets in your home
entries.plain: **The Bible study meets in the Johnsons' living room because they have the biggest house and the longest table.** The first Christians had no church buildings. They met in the homes of members who had room, often the better-off ones, for meals, prayer and teaching. Poorer Jewish groups and private associations did the same. In a big city there were several house churches at once, each gathered round a different household.
entries.then: In the first three centuries churches met mainly in homes, as some other associations did, which was cheap and at times safer. Poorer Jews who could not afford a synagogue building did the same. The house of Mary in Acts 12:12-13 had an outer gate, a servant girl to keep it and room for a crowd further in. That marks a fairly wealthy family, probably in Jerusalem's Upper City near the temple. Large upper rooms were also found in the wealthy Upper City. The ESV Study Bible observes that believers went on owning homes and meeting in them after the sharing of Acts 2, pointing to Romans 16:5, 1 Corinthians 16:19, Colossians 4:15 and Philemon 2. The CSB Study Bible says the first evangelism seems to have happened through gatherings in the temple and in houses. In Rome most people lived in apartments, so a church might meet in a hallway or on a roomier lower floor. The money saved on buildings could go to the poor. Wright and Bird describe Paul planting several house churches in Corinth, based around households such as those of Titius Justus, Crispus, Chloe and Stephanas. They describe the church in Rome as several house churches with quite different viewpoints. In Corinth, Keener writes, a patron's dining room normally seated nine, with as many as forty more in the atrium. The cultural backgrounds notes estimate that many large Corinthian homes held forty to fifty people. Well-to-do owners of homes where a religious group met were normally honored as its patrons.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a club that meets in members' living rooms because it cannot afford a hall. The host's furniture, food and neighbors shape every meeting, and in a big town there are several such rooms, each with its own feel.
entries.changes: Meetings in homes, as in Acts 12:12, put the church under a host's roof and at a host's table, which is why letters greet the church in someone's house, as in Romans 16:5 and 1 Corinthians 16:19. A city's believers could be spread across several households, so unity between them took work.
entries.not: **Not a gathering of equals in a borrowed room.** A club can rotate its hosts. A house church usually met with a well-off householder who was honored as its patron, and his dining room seated only a handful, with the rest further out in the house.

usedIn.n: Acts 1:12-26, The Twelve made whole by lot
usedIn.s: Back in Jerusalem the apostles pray in an upstairs room with the women and Jesus' family. Peter says Judas's place must be filled, and the lot falls on Matthias.

usedIn.n: Acts 2:42-47, The common life
usedIn.s: The first believers devote themselves to teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and the prayers, share their possessions, and meet daily in the temple courts and in their homes.

usedIn.n: Acts 12:1-25, Herod Agrippa, the prison and the king struck down
usedIn.s: King Herod Agrippa kills James and jails Peter at Passover, but an angel leads Peter out. Later, in Caesarea, the king accepts the crowd's cry that he speaks with a god's voice and is struck down.

usedIn.n: Acts 18:1-11, Tentmakers in Corinth
usedIn.s: In Corinth Paul lodges and works with Aquila and Priscilla, Jews lately expelled from Rome who share his trade. When the synagogue turns against him he moves next door to the house of Titius Justus, and the synagogue leader Crispus believes with his household.

usedIn.n: Acts 20:1-12, The collection party and Eutychus at Troas
usedIn.s: Paul leaves Ephesus for Macedonia and Greece, then sets out for Jerusalem with delegates from the churches. At Troas the believers meet on the first day of the week, and a young man who falls from a window is taken up alive.

usedIn.n: Romans 1:8-17, Longing to see Rome
usedIn.s: Paul thanks God that the Roman believers' faith is spoken of everywhere, explains why he has not yet come, and states his theme: the good news is God's power to save everyone who believes, Jew and Greek.

usedIn.n: Romans 14:1-23, Vegetables, holy days and wine
usedIn.s: Some believers eat only vegetables and keep certain days; others eat anything and treat every day alike. Paul tells both not to judge one another, since all will stand before God's judgment seat, and not to wreck another's faith over food.

usedIn.n: Romans 16:3-16, Greet the church in their house
usedIn.s: Paul greets more than two dozen believers in Rome by name, from Prisca and Aquila and the church in their house to the households of Aristobulus and Narcissus, and tells them to greet one another with a holy kiss.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 1:10-17, I belong to Paul, I belong to Apollos
usedIn.s: Told by Chloe's people that the church is splitting into camps behind Paul, Apollos, Cephas and Christ, Paul appeals for unity and asks whether Christ has been divided.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 11:17-34, The Lord's Supper in a rich man's house
usedIn.s: Paul rebukes the church because at the Lord's Supper some go hungry while others eat their fill and get drunk, retells the tradition of the Last Supper, and tells them to wait for one another.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 14:26-40, Order when the church meets
usedIn.s: Paul regulates a meeting where everyone brings a hymn, a teaching, a revelation or a tongue: speakers take turns, prophets weigh one another's words, women are to be silent and ask at home, and everything is to be done decently and in order.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 16:1-24, The collection and final greetings
usedIn.s: Paul arranges a weekly setting aside of money for the believers in Jerusalem, plans his travels, commends Timothy, Apollos and the household of Stephanas, and closes with greetings, a line in his own hand and the Aramaic prayer Marana tha.

usedIn.n: Colossians 4:7-18, Tychicus, Onesimus, Nympha's house and the letter from Laodicea
usedIn.s: Paul sends the letter with Tychicus and Onesimus, passes on greetings from Jewish and Gentile co-workers, greets Nympha and the church in her house, asks for this letter to be read at Laodicea and the Laodicean letter at Colossae, and signs off in his own hand.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 5:12-28, Leaders, prophets, a holy kiss and a letter read to all
usedIn.s: Paul asks the church to honor those who work hard over them, to warn the idle and help the weak, to rejoice, pray and give thanks, not to quench the Spirit or despise prophecy but test everything, and to have the letter read to all.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 3:14-16, God's household and the hymn
usedIn.s: Paul writes so that, if he is delayed, Timothy will know how people ought to behave in God's household, the church of the living God, and quotes what seems to be a hymn about Christ.

usedIn.n: Philemon 1-7, The church in Philemon's house
usedIn.s: Paul, a prisoner, and Timothy write to Philemon, to Apphia and Archippus, and to the church that meets in Philemon's house, and Paul thanks God for Philemon's love and faith, his partnership, and the way he has refreshed the hearts of God's people.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 10:19-25, Through the curtain, bodies washed, meeting together
usedIn.s: Because Jesus' blood has opened a new and living way through the curtain, believers may enter the most holy place with confidence. With hearts sprinkled and bodies washed with pure water, they are to hold fast, spur one another on, and not give up meeting together.

usedIn.n: 2 John 1-6, The elder to the chosen lady
usedIn.s: The elder writes to the chosen lady and her children, whom he loves in the truth. He is glad that some of her children walk in the truth, and he asks for no new command but the old one, that they love one another, which means walking in God's commands.

usedIn.n: 3 John 9-15, Diotrephes and Demetrius
usedIn.s: The elder wrote to the church, but Diotrephes, eager to be first, refuses to receive him; he spreads malicious talk, refuses to welcome the brothers and puts out of the church those who do. Gaius is not to imitate evil. Demetrius is well spoken of by everyone, and the elder adds his own testimony; he hopes to come soon and talk face to face.

entries.title: Many gods and their images
entries.summary: The Greek and Roman world was full of gods, each with temples, statues, priests and local stories. Jews and Christians called the images things made with hands, while holding that there were real powers behind them.
aliases: gods made with hands are no gods
idols of gold, silver, bronze, stone and wood
entries.plain: **Every town in the region had its own saint's statue and its own festival, and the stories about the saint were local pride.** Greeks and Romans worshiped many gods. Each city had temples, statues, priests and sacrifices, and stories of its own about gods who had visited it. Jews refused all of it. To them an idol was something made by human hands, and worshiping it was the first and worst sin. Many Jews also believed real spiritual powers stood behind the gods of the nations.
entries.then: Wright writes, "The primal sin, in all major Jewish writing, is idolatry." To call something made by hand, he explains, "meant that God had not made it or commanded it," and Stephen turns the phrase on the temple. Jewish writers stressed that idols were the work of human hands, a phrase that fit a man-made shrine just as well. The rabbis counted the golden calf Israel's worst sin. The idea is very old. At Uruk around 3200 BC, Podany explains, the goddess Inana's shrine was her home and her statue was the goddess present on earth. Every god's statue needed housing, food, drink and clothing, and no god was thought false. In the cities of Asia Minor each place had its gods: Apollo near Syrian Antioch, Aphrodite at old Paphos, the emperor and Men at Pisidian Antioch, and Cybele at Iconium. Near Lystra a legend told how Zeus and Hermes visited in disguise and only an old couple, Baucis and Philemon, took them in. Inscriptions show the two gods worshiped together there. Beside the violent and lustful Olympians, people served newer cults such as Sarapis and Isis, household gods, nymphs, Hekate and heroes such as Heracles. Heiser argues that Deuteronomy 32:17 calls the gods of the nations shedim, real spiritual beings, which Paul renders demons in 1 Corinthians 10:20: "they are not pieces of wood or stone." Athens was crowded with statues, the Hermae among them, and with altars to unknown gods, raised by tradition during a plague. Justice, Dike, was honored as a goddess who carried out the will of Fate, and survivors of deadly danger could be taken for gods.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a city where every guild and neighborhood has its patron saint, with a shrine, a feast day and a parade. Refusing to march is taken as an insult to the whole town.
entries.changes: Calling something made with hands, as Stephen does of the temple in Acts 7:48, borrows the standard Jewish verdict on idols. At Lystra in Acts 14:11-15 the crowd fits two visitors into a local story about Zeus and Hermes, and 1 Corinthians 10:20 says the sacrifices of the nations are offered to demons.
entries.not: **Not a single religion.** Paganism had no creed or central authority; it was a crowd of local cults, festivals and stories, and a person could honor many gods at once.
entries.dissent: What the gods were. Heiser holds that the beings behind the idols were real and dangerous. The cultural backgrounds notes on 1 Corinthians 10:20 say most early Jewish and Christian sources regarded them as demons. Arnold takes a middle line on 1 Corinthians 8:5. The gods have no existence in their own right, yet demons stand behind the images (10:20), and the gods are real to those who worship them. He notes that the Greek version of Psalm 96:5 calls the gods of the nations demons. Keener stresses the Jewish mockery of idols as vain and notes that Luke is not above making fun of pagan religion. On Stephen and the temple, Wright says the temple had become ambiguous at best and an idol at worst. Keener says Stephen does not deny God blessed it, but denies it was meant to be the idol his hearers made of it. The ESV Study Bible says Stephen is not calling the building of the temple wrong.

Israel must not worship the host of heaven, which Yahweh allotted to all the other peoples.
Paul tells the Areopagus that God fixed the times and the boundaries of the nations.

ddd.s: The chief Greek god, whom a crowd mistakes Barnabas for.
The Greek messenger god, whom the same crowd mistakes Paul for because he did the talking.

Two things at once: God's heavenly army, and the sun, moon and stars Israel was told not to worship.
The god associated with child sacrifice in a valley outside Jerusalem that gave us the word Gehenna.
Star gods carried in procession, where the Greek Bible and the Hebrew give different names.
An Athenian altar hedging against offending a god nobody could name, which Paul preached from.

usedIn.n: Acts 6:8-7:53, Stephen's charge and speech
usedIn.s: Men from the Diaspora synagogues accuse Stephen of speaking against the temple and the law. He answers with Israel's story, from Abraham to the temple, and turns the charge back on his judges.

usedIn.n: Acts 14:1-20, Iconium and Lystra: taken for Zeus and Hermes
usedIn.s: After a plot in Iconium, Paul heals a lame man at Lystra and the crowd hails him and Barnabas as Hermes and Zeus. When they refuse the sacrifice, the crowd is turned against them and Paul is stoned.

usedIn.n: Acts 17:16-21, Athens: idols, the marketplace and the philosophers
usedIn.s: Waiting in Athens, Paul is distressed at a city full of idols. He argues in the synagogue and the marketplace, and Epicurean and Stoic philosophers take him for a preacher of foreign gods and bring him to the Areopagus.

usedIn.n: Acts 17:22-34, Paul before the Areopagus
usedIn.s: Before the Areopagus, Paul starts from an altar to an unknown god and from the Athenians' own poets, speaks of the one Creator who made every nation from one man, and ends with a coming judgment and a man raised from the dead. Some mock; a few believe.

usedIn.n: Acts 28:1-10, Malta: the viper and the goddess Justice
usedIn.s: The islanders of Malta welcome the shipwrecked with a fire. When a viper fastens on Paul's hand they decide that Justice will not let a murderer live; when he takes no harm they call him a god. Publius, the island's chief man, takes them in, and Paul heals his father and many others.

usedIn.n: Acts 28:11-16, The Twin Brothers and the road to Rome
usedIn.s: After three months they sail in an Alexandrian ship with the Twin Brothers as its figurehead, land at Puteoli and walk the Appian Way toward Rome, where believers come out to meet Paul. In Rome he is allowed to live on his own with a soldier guarding him.

usedIn.n: Romans 1:18-32, Images of the immortal God
usedIn.s: Paul describes God's anger against people who knew him from creation yet traded his glory for images of humans and animals, and the disorder that followed.

usedIn.n: Romans 2:17-29, You who boast in the law
usedIn.s: Paul turns on an imagined Jewish teacher who boasts in the law yet steals, commits adultery and robs temples, so that God's name is blasphemed among the nations, and says true circumcision is of the heart.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 8:1-13, Knowledge, idols and the weak
usedIn.s: Answering those who know that an idol is nothing, Paul agrees there is one God and one Lord but warns that their freedom to eat sacrificial food, even in an idol's temple, can destroy a weaker believer.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 10:1-22, Israel in the desert and the table of demons
usedIn.s: Paul warns that Israel too had its baptism and its spiritual food in the wilderness, yet fell into idolatry and immorality and was struck down, and tells the Corinthians that they cannot share both the Lord's table and the table of demons.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 12:1-31, Mute idols and one body
usedIn.s: Paul reminds the Corinthians that as pagans they were led astray to mute idols, describes the many gifts of the one Spirit, and pictures the church as one body whose weaker and less honored members are indispensable.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 6:14-7:1, Unequal yoke, Belial and the temple of God
usedIn.s: Paul tells the Corinthians not to be yoked with unbelievers, for light has no fellowship with darkness nor Christ with Belial, and calls them the temple of the living God, who must come out and be separate.

usedIn.n: Galatians 4:1-11, Heirs, slaves and the elements of the world
usedIn.s: An heir who is still a child is no better off than a slave, Paul says; so we were enslaved under the elements of the world until God sent his Son to redeem us and his Spirit to cry Abba, and he asks why the Galatians want to go back to observing special days, months, seasons and years.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 1:1-10, Turned to God from idols
usedIn.s: Paul, Silas and Timothy thank God for a young church that received the message in the middle of suffering, whose story is now told everywhere: they turned to God from idols to serve him and to wait for his Son from heaven.

usedIn.n: 1 John 5:13-21, The sin that leads to death, the evil one and idols
usedIn.s: John writes so that believers may know they have eternal life, and that God hears them. They are to pray for a brother or sister whose sin does not lead to death, though there is a sin that does. Those born of God are kept from the evil one, while the whole world lies under his power; the letter ends with a warning to keep away from idols.

usedIn.n: Revelation 9:1-21, the Abyss opened and the armies from the Euphrates
usedIn.s: At the fifth trumpet a fallen star is given the key to the Abyss, and from its smoke come locusts like horses with human faces, women's hair and scorpions' stings, under a king called Abaddon and Apollyon. At the sixth, four angels bound at the Euphrates are released with a cavalry of two hundred million that kills a third of humanity, yet the survivors do not repent.

entries.title: Magic and sorcery
entries.summary: Spells, charms and incantations were sold and used across the ancient world, by Jews as well as pagans, and many feared the evil eye. People told a sorcerer, who worked in secret and for pay, from a holy man who acted openly.
entries.plain: **The man in the back of the market sold charms for love, luck and revenge, and he never did his work in daylight.** Magic was everywhere in the ancient world. People paid magicians for spells to heal, to bless, to curse or to keep demons away, and magicians bought and sold the formulas. Some of the most respected magicians were Jews, though Jewish teachers condemned magic. People drew a line between a sorcerer, who worked secretly and for money, and a holy man or prophet who acted in public and lived simply.
entries.then: Observers told sorcerers, who used their power for gain and worked in secret, from public wonderworkers who lived simply. Pagans and Jews alike turned to magic for healing, blessing and cursing, and to fend off curses and demons. They used incantations that called on the names of gods and demons, along with potions, amulets and incantation bowls. Magicians drew large followings. Jewish magicians were among the most respected, and Jewish elements often turn up in magical texts beside pagan ones, though mainstream Judaism opposed magic. Magic served private ends rather than the common good, and "Sorcerers could buy magical formulas" (Keener). Arnold cautions that the magical papyri survive mostly from Egypt and mostly from the second century AD. Spells on stone and metal, though, run back through the Hellenistic period with the same vocabulary. Romans generally distrusted magic, yet Roman officials kept diviners. Josephus says the governor Felix had a Cypriot Jewish friend who "pretended to be a magician." Ephesus was famous for magic. Practitioners believed that calling on a spirit's name let them control it, and that spells worked only while kept secret. Formulas rolled into amulets were known as Ephesian writings. One story told of an Ephesian wrestler at Olympia who lost three bouts in a row once the referee found the Ephesian letters on his ankle (Arnold). The word Paul uses for bewitched in Galatians 3:1 refers to spells or the evil eye, "a jealous look with magical efficacy" (Keener), sometimes a way of cursing someone. Wright adds that people who met a disfigured stranger feared the evil eye, which might be "warded off by apotropaic actions such as spitting."
entries.bridge: An analogy: a back-street dealer in good-luck charms and curses, set beside a doctor with a public clinic. Both may draw a crowd, but people know which one works for whoever pays.
entries.changes: Because magic was bought and sold for private ends, Simon's offer of money in Acts 8:18-19 shows he took the Spirit for one more power to purchase, and new believers at Ephesus burn their books of magic in public in Acts 19:19. Paul's question in Galatians 3:1, who has bewitched you, borrows the language of the evil eye.
entries.not: **Not medicine against superstition.** A doctor's clinic rests on medicine. In Acts both the sorcerer and the holy man claimed power from the spirit world, and people told them apart by secrecy, payment and private gain.
entries.dissent: Whether magic had real power behind it. The ESV and CSB Study Bibles see demonic influence in it. Arnold defines it as the manipulation of good and evil spirits, which Luke ties to Satan in three of his four episodes of magic. Keener notes that Judaism credited sorcerers' wonders to Belial and that, as in Exodus 7-8, they were limited in scale. The cultural backgrounds notes say magic could imitate signs but not match their scale. Their article adds that some Jewish teachers thought some magic fake and other cases real and dangerous, and that people tended to call magic any power that served a rival belief.

The New Testament word for demon, borrowed from a Greek word that was morally neutral.

usedIn.n: Acts 5:12-42, Peter's shadow, the prison and Gamaliel
usedIn.s: Crowds bring the sick for Peter's shadow to fall on them. The apostles are jailed, freed by an angel, and brought before the council, where Gamaliel compares the movement to the failed causes of Theudas and Judas the Galilean.

usedIn.n: Acts 8:4-25, Samaria and Simon the magician
usedIn.s: Philip preaches the Messiah in Samaria, and even the famous magician Simon is baptized. When Peter and John lay hands on the Samaritans and they receive the Spirit, Simon offers money for the power.

usedIn.n: Acts 13:1-12, Sent from Antioch: the proconsul and the magician
usedIn.s: The church at Antioch fasts, prays and sends out Barnabas and Saul. On Cyprus the Roman proconsul believes after Paul confronts the Jewish magician in his entourage.

usedIn.n: Acts 14:1-20, Iconium and Lystra: taken for Zeus and Hermes
usedIn.s: After a plot in Iconium, Paul heals a lame man at Lystra and the crowd hails him and Barnabas as Hermes and Zeus. When they refuse the sacrifice, the crowd is turned against them and Paul is stoned.

usedIn.n: Acts 19:8-20, The lecture hall and the burned books
usedIn.s: In Ephesus Paul teaches daily in the hall of Tyrannus for two years, and even cloths that touched him bring healing. When the sons of Sceva try to use Jesus' name as a spell, the spirit overpowers them, and believers burn their magic books in public.

usedIn.n: Galatians 3:1-14, Who bewitched you? Abraham's blessing and the law's curse
usedIn.s: Paul asks the Galatians who has bewitched them, since they received the Spirit by believing, then argues from Abraham that those who believe share his blessing, while Christ took the law's curse by being hung on a tree.

usedIn.n: Galatians 4:12-20, Welcomed as an angel of God
usedIn.s: Paul appeals to the Galatians as friends, reminding them that when he first preached to them in bodily weakness they did not scorn him but welcomed him as an angel of God, and asks whether he has now become their enemy by telling them the truth.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 1:15-23, Far above every name that is invoked
usedIn.s: Paul prays that the believers will know the hope, the inheritance and the power God showed when he raised Christ and seated him above every ruler, authority, power and name, in this age and the next.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 3:1-9, Terrible times, homes entered, and Jannes and Jambres
usedIn.s: Paul warns that the last days will bring terrible times and people who love themselves, money and pleasure, having a form of godliness but denying its power; some worm their way into homes and win over gullible women, opposing the truth as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 3:10-17, Antioch, Iconium and Lystra, and the sacred writings
usedIn.s: Timothy has followed Paul's teaching, life and sufferings, as in Antioch, Iconium and Lystra; he is to continue in what he learned, knowing from whom he learned it and how from infancy he has known the sacred writings, for all Scripture is God-breathed.

usedIn.n: Revelation 13:11-18, the beast from the earth, the mark and 666
usedIn.s: A second beast, harmless-looking like a lamb but speaking like the dragon, rises from the earth and drives everyone to worship the first beast, working wonders and making its statue speak. Trade is barred to anyone without its mark on hand or forehead, a mark tied to the beast's name and number, 666.

usedIn.n: Revelation 21:1-8, new heaven, new earth, no more sea
usedIn.s: John sees a new heaven and a new earth, with no more sea, and the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down from God like a bride dressed for her husband. A voice announces that God's dwelling is now with people, that he will wipe away every tear, and that he makes all things new; the thirsty will drink freely, while the cowardly, the faithless, murderers, sorcerers, idolaters and liars have their place in the lake of fire.

usedIn.n: Revelation 22:6-21, I am coming soon
usedIn.s: The angel confirms that the words are trustworthy, and Jesus says he is coming soon. John is told not to seal up the prophecy, since the time is near; those who wash their robes may enter the city while dogs, sorcerers and liars stay outside. The book closes with the Spirit and the bride saying come, a warning against adding to or taking from it, and the prayer, come, Lord Jesus.

entries.title: Oracles and fortune-telling
entries.summary: Greeks and Romans sought the future from oracles, omens and seers, above all from Apollo's priestess at Delphi. A girl with a Python spirit was linked to that famous oracle.
entries.plain: **People paid good money to the woman at the fair who could tell them what next year held.** Greeks and Romans wanted to know the future before they acted. They asked oracles at famous shrines, watched the flight of birds, cut open animals to read their insides, and took dreams and omens seriously before a journey or a battle. The most famous oracle of all was Apollo's priestess at Delphi, called the Pythoness. The Old Testament forbade all of it.
entries.then: Python was a title of Apollo, who had killed the dragon Python. His most famous temple, at Delphi, had a priestess called the Pythoness, who gave obscure messages in a trance for the priests to interpret. Her oracles were the most famous in antiquity. So the girl in Acts 16:16 has literally "the spirit of a Python," and the cultural backgrounds notes conclude, "This spirit is thus associated with the highest-level pagan prophetic powers." Keener calls it a powerful demon, and the ESV Study Bible a demonic spirit. Interest in oracles is how such a girl earned money for her owners. The Old Testament forbids fortune-telling (Deuteronomy 18:10; 1 Samuel 28:8), and the Greek Old Testament uses the same verb for it as Acts 16:16. Wright and Bird list "omens and oracles, even inspecting entrails" among the ordinary practices of ancient religion. Pagans setting out by sea sacrificed to the gods, and bad omens, astrology or dreams could keep a ship in port. Romans checked entrails and the flight of birds before war, and they respected divination more than inspired prophecy. Greeks treated a predictive oracle as a warning that might be avoided, and prophecies were sometimes conditional warnings. Divination is far older than Delphi. Podany describes the Assyrian king Esarhaddon (681 to 669 BC) consulting astronomers who read omens in the sky and diviners who read the gods' answers in the livers of sacrificed rams. When an enslaved girl in Harran spoke as the mouthpiece of the god Nusku, an official proposed testing her prophecy by such a reading. The likeness to the slave girl of Acts 16 is drawn here, not by Podany.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a celebrity psychic with a hotline and a long waiting list. People who would never call her still know her name, and a girl said to have her gift is worth money to whoever manages her.
entries.changes: A spirit linked to Apollo's oracle, as in Acts 16:16-18, sets the most famous prophetic power of the Greek world against the name of Jesus. On a voyage, where pagans looked for omens before sailing, Paul's warning in Acts 27:10 would sound to them like a seer's.
entries.not: **Not a private business.** A psychic sells her own gift. The Pythoness spoke for Apollo at his temple and priests interpreted her, and both the law of Moses and Acts treat the spirit behind such speech as real and hostile.

entries.title: Artemis of the Ephesians
entries.summary: The great goddess of Ephesus, whose temple was one of the seven wonders of the world and a bank as well. Her cult was the city's pride and the living of its craftsmen.
entries.plain: **Insult the town's patron saint and you have insulted its pride, its tourist trade and its bank all at once.** Ephesus belonged to Artemis. Her temple outside the city was one of the seven wonders of the world, about four times the size of the Parthenon in Athens. It also held people's money like a bank and owned great stretches of farmland. Craftsmen made souvenir shrines and statues of her, a month of the year was named for her, and crowds chanted her greatness. The Artemis of Ephesus was a local goddess with her own cult, not simply the Greek huntress of the stories.
entries.then: The temple ranked among the seven wonders of the ancient world and stood about a mile and a half northeast of the city. Its size is given differently. The cultural backgrounds notes give 425 by 230 feet and Price and House 450 by 225, each about four times the Parthenon, while Keener gives some 350 by 150. Temples served as banks, and this one, among the most famous, owned some 70,000 acres of farmland. About AD 44 a scandal broke when temple deposits passed into private hands. Keener stresses that the Ephesian Artemis was distinct from other forms of the goddess, with cult centers in at least thirty-three places. Arnold notes that she was called on in magical formulas and worshiped as a goddess of the underworld with power over the spirits of nature. Her image bore the zodiac, marking her as mistress of the astral powers of fate, and at least forty-four other gods had cults in the city. Civic pride and her worship went together. When men of Sardis abused her worshipers, forty-five were executed, and crying Great is Artemis was a standard acclamation. Craftsmen made souvenir shrines, mostly of terra cotta, and gold and silver statuettes of three to seven pounds to dedicate in the temple. The ESV Study Bible says the silver shrines were models of the temple for home altars or offerings. Wright pictures families keeping a silver Artemis in a little household shrine to bless family, fields, business and livestock. Wright and Bird write that she "was worshipped for her fertility blessings." Ephesus called itself guardian of her temple, a technical term found on inscriptions. Wright describes the goddess's cult as all female and powerful in the city and beyond.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a cathedral town whose shrine draws pilgrims from every country, whose souvenir trade feeds half the streets and whose treasury holds the townspeople's savings. A preacher who says the relics are worthless threatens all three at once.
entries.changes: Worship of Artemis tied religion, trade and civic pride together, so a message that gods made with hands are no gods, as in Acts 19:26-27, struck at the craftsmen's income and the city's honor in one blow. That is why a riot in Acts 19:34 turns into two hours of chanting her greatness.
entries.not: **Not a shrine to the one God.** A cathedral's relics point past themselves to the God it serves. At Ephesus the goddess herself was worshiped, at least forty-four other gods had cults in the city, and Artemis was called on in magic as mistress of the powers of fate.
entries.dissent: Three points. First, what kind of goddess she was. Wright calls her "a fertility goddess whose many-breasted silver statues were themselves famous." Arnold thinks the first Greek settlers gave the name Artemis to a local fertility goddess, whose rigid image looks nothing like the Greek huntress. Keener lists breasts, castrated parts, fruits or eggs as readings of the objects on her statue, and Price and House add bee hives and bulls' testicles. The cultural backgrounds notes say scholars disagree, but "ancient writers, however, regarded the Ephesian Artemis as a virgin." Second, the image that fell from heaven in Acts 19:35. The ESV Study Bible takes it as probably a meteorite, and Wright and the Zondervan dictionary as a meteorite revered as her image. The cultural backgrounds notes say no surviving source makes the claim for the Ephesian statue, which was carved. Third, whether Artemis stands behind 1 Timothy 2:12. Wright and Bird write that women should not usurp male leadership, "perhaps reflecting the all-female cult of Artemis in Ephesus". The ESV Study Bible holds that Paul's appeal to creation rules out explanations tied to the local setting. Neither of Keener's works brings Artemis into the passage.

entries.title: Fate and the stars
entries.summary: Most people in Paul's world believed their lives were ruled by Fate, worked out through the stars, which many took to be heavenly beings. Few thought there was any escape, and cults that promised one drew followers.
entries.plain: **Plenty of people still glance at a horoscope before a big day, half joking; in Paul's world hardly anyone was joking.** Most people then believed that Fate ruled the world and that the stars carried out its decrees. Many thought the stars were living beings, and most saw no way out from under them. Some religions became popular by promising to set their members free from Fate. Jews, and the first Christians after them, believed instead in a God who rules events himself.
entries.then: Keener writes that "Most people in Paul's day believed that the world was run by Fate." Fate usually worked through the stars, which were seen as heavenly beings, and most people "did not believe one had any hope of escape from Fate." Some mystery cults, Isis's among them, won followers by promising to release initiates from it. The powers ruling the nations were often thought to rule through the stars, and most Greeks of the first century feared Fate working through them. Many feared spirits as well. Keener counts astrology and attempts to escape Fate, with magic, in the occult background of believers around Ephesus. The ESV Study Bible sets God's purposeful plan against pagan gods thought fickle or bound by an unknowable fate. Some philosophers, Stoics above all, urged thanks for everything because they submitted to Fate. Jewish writers urged it because they trusted a personal God who guided events. Heiser notes that one sense of stoicheia, Paul's word for the elements, was astral deities, rooted in Greco-Roman thinking about the cosmos. Fate was pictured as a tyrant working through spirits of the stars, and Judaism had turned the elements pagans revered as gods into angels who ruled over nature. Reading the sky for the will of the gods is far older. From the eighth century BC, Podany notes, Mesopotamian astronomers kept daily records of the night sky for 700 years, with political events and epidemics beside them. They were looking for patterns, because every detail in the sky was a message from the gods. Josephus explains of the temple lampstand that "as to the seven lamps upon the candlesticks, they referred to the course of the planets" (Antiquities 3.7.7).
entries.bridge: An analogy: a weather forecast no one can change or argue with, read every morning to learn what the day will allow. Some people shrug, some carry a charm, and some join anyone who claims to control the weather.
entries.changes: Because most people believed Fate ruled through the stars, the claim in Ephesians 1:21 that Christ sits far above every power and name answered a daily fear, and believers seated with him share that place. Galatians 4:9 warns converts not to turn back to the weak elements they once served, and Romans 8:38-39 promises that no power above or below can separate believers from God's love.
entries.not: **Not a forecast that only describes.** Nobody thinks the weather report makes the rain. Fate was believed to rule events, working through stars that many took for living beings, and for most people it brought fear.
entries.dissent: Whether Paul has the stars in view. Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes read Ephesians 1:21 and 2:6 against the fear of Fate. Arnold reads God's choosing and working out everything in Ephesians 1 as comfort for converts who feared the stars. Keener reports that some scholars take height and depth in Romans 8:39 as astrological terms, while others take them simply as heaven and Hades. Heiser thinks Paul's use of stoicheia may favor a Greco-Roman reading of the air in Ephesians 2:2, but leaves the question open.

entries.title: The mystery cults
entries.summary: Cults that a person entered by a secret initiation, often held at night. Some promised freedom from Fate, some had a name for drunken or immoral rites, and Rome distrusted them as foreign.
entries.plain: **Some clubs still swear new members to secrecy and hold the ceremony late at night.** In the Greek and Roman world many people joined a cult through a private initiation whose details they swore never to tell. The cults differed widely, and because they kept their secrets, little is known about them for certain. Some promised to free their members from Fate. Some held their rites at night, and a few had a reputation for drink and sex. When Paul speaks of a mystery, he uses a word these cults also used.
entries.then: The mystery cults were various Greek cults entered by initiation, whose details members had to keep secret. They differed widely, so what is known of them is limited. Some, such as Mithraism, spread in the Roman world only after Christianity had, and borrowed Christian features in later centuries. Some, Isis's cult among them, drew followers by promising to release initiates from Fate. Initiations normally took place at night, some cults had immoral reputations, and Roman critics lumped Christians in with them. Romans suspected eastern cults of undermining family values. Rome banned the rites of Bacchus, or Dionysus, for a time, as much for their novelty as for their alleged immorality. The word mystery was used in the cults, but Keener finds the main background for Paul's use in Daniel 2 and the Dead Sea Scrolls. There it means God's plan for history, once hidden and now revealed, and the cultural backgrounds notes agree. Their article on the cults describes initiation as a ritual death and rebirth, one Mithraic initiate being "piously reborn". It ties a god's return from death to the yearly return of spring, unlike the Jewish and Christian hope of one bodily resurrection. It adds that converts to Christianity were never sworn to secrecy. Arnold, following Ramsay, reads Colossians 2:18 as a teacher boasting of what he saw at the climax of initiation, using a word found in inscriptions from Apollo's oracle at Claros. The CSB Study Bible draws the contrast sharply. The mystery religions held that the divine will was hidden from all but an enlightened few, while for Paul a mystery is revealed so that all can understand it.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a secret society with passwords, robes and a ceremony after dark, which outsiders suspect of the worst because they can never see inside. Members feel chosen, and the neighbors feel uneasy.
entries.changes: Because initiation into the cults was secret and often at night, the call in Ephesians 5:11-12 to expose what is done in darkness sets the church apart from the reputation such cults had. Paul's mystery in Romans 16:25-26 is a plan kept secret for long ages and now made known to the nations, the opposite of a secret kept for initiates.
entries.not: **Not a social club with rituals.** A secret society's ceremony binds members to one another. A mystery initiation was religious, pictured as a death and rebirth, and some cults promised freedom from Fate. The cults also differed so widely that little holds for all of them.
entries.dissent: How far Paul's language answers the cults. The CSB Study Bible says Paul implicitly addressed matters raised by the mystery religions of the region and sets his mystery against theirs. The Zondervan dictionary goes further, calling Paul's use of mystery "a clear allusion" to the cults. Keener grants that the cults used the word but places Paul's background in Daniel and the Dead Sea Scrolls, and the cultural backgrounds notes and their article do the same.

entries.title: The Day of Atonement and the mercy seat
entries.summary: Once a year the high priest went into the holy of holies with sacrificial blood, for his own sins and then the nation's. It was the one fast the law commanded, and the mercy seat on the ark was the place the blood was brought.
aliases: sin offering burned outside the camp
atoning sacrifice for the whole world
entries.plain: **Once a year the whole town fasted, owned up, and waited to hear that the slate had been wiped clean.** The Day of Atonement fell in early autumn. It was the one day the law of Moses told every Israelite to fast. On that day alone the high priest went into the innermost room of the sanctuary with the blood of a sacrifice, first for his own sins and then for the people's. The law describes the mercy seat as the gold cover of the ark, between two carved cherubim, where God said he would meet with Moses. One goat was sacrificed and another sent away alive into the desert.
entries.then: It was the one day the law commanded a fast, though religious Jews added many others. The Fast of Acts 27:9 is this day, which fell in September or October, and Wright dates it to October 5 in AD 59. On it alone the high priest entered the holy of holies, perhaps several times in the day (Leviticus 16:13-16). Special precautions kept him from defilement beforehand. Then he offered first for his own sins and then for the nation's. The people waited for him to come out again, the sign that the offering had been accepted. The cultural backgrounds notes call the mercy seat the place of propitiation, consecrated to God each year by sacrificial blood. They say that ancient Israel and its neighbors knew both the appeasing of a god's wrath and the cleansing of impurity. Palestinian Judaism held that the day, joined with repentance, was needed to forgive most breaches of the law. Keener reports the rabbinic view that repentance held off judgment until the day atoned, and the belief that records of sins were blotted out on it. Some Jewish texts expected God to vindicate Israel at the end, as he did each year on that day. In Jewish tradition prayer, alms and good deeds could also turn away wrath (Sirach 3:3, 20), but the law required blood. Some Jews already held that a martyr's death could turn God's wrath from his people (4 Maccabees 17:22). Heiser notes that in the ritual one goat was sacrificed as a sin offering and the other sent alive into the desert for Azazel. Later Jewish books made Azazel a demon, whose realm lay outside holy ground.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a nation's one solemn day of reckoning each year, when everyone stops work and fasts while a single official goes into the inner chamber on their behalf. What happens behind that door is the whole point of the day.
entries.changes: Paul's word for Jesus in Romans 3:25 points to the mercy seat, so the cross is pictured as the place where atonement is now made, once. The Fast in Acts 27:9 is this day, and its date told sailors the safe season was over. Hebrews 7:27 sets the high priest's offerings, first for his own sins and then for the people's, against an offering made once for all.
entries.not: **Not an official acting by right of office.** A state official stands for the people because he holds the post. The high priest had to offer first for his own sins, and he went into God's presence with sacrificial blood. The people waited for him to come out, the sign the offering had been accepted.
entries.dissent: What Paul's word in Romans 3:25 stresses. The ESV Study Bible says it means propitiation, the satisfying of God's wrath, and cannot be limited to the wiping away of sin. Keener also stresses the turning away of wrath. The cultural backgrounds notes say Israel's world knew both appeasing wrath and cleansing impurity. Wright reads the word chiefly as the meeting place, where and by which God meets his people and forgives them. Keener adds that nothing in Romans 3 suggests Paul has the yearly day itself in mind. The Zondervan dictionary sets out the same question for 1 John 2:2. Propitiation is done with reference to a person, expiation with reference to sins. Scholars who take God's wrath as his real attitude to sin hold that propitiation was needed; those who take it as a way of describing sin's results prefer expiation.

Jesus comes from Judah, a priest by the power of an indestructible life and by God's oath, the guarantee of a better covenant; Levitical priests died and offered daily for their own sins, but he lives for ever and offered himself once for all.

Priests entered the first room daily and the high priest the second once a year with blood, a sign that access to the holy place had not yet been opened.

Believers have an altar the tabernacle priests may not eat from; as the bodies of the sin offerings were burned outside the camp, Jesus suffered outside the gate, and they must go out to him, bearing his disgrace, seeking the city to come.

usedIn.n: 1 John 1:5-2:17, God is light, an advocate, and a world passing away
usedIn.s: God is light with no darkness in him, so to claim fellowship with him while walking in darkness is a lie; the blood of Jesus cleanses, and those who confess are forgiven. Anyone who sins has an advocate with the Father, the atoning sacrifice for the whole world. The old command of love is new, the darkness is passing, and the world is passing away.

entries.title: How Jews read Scripture
entries.summary: By the first century Jews held a known body of sacred writings, roughly the Old Testament, to be God's true word. They taught it to children from infancy, read it aloud in the synagogue and explained it, and Greek-speaking Jews called it the sacred writings.
aliases: linking texts by a key word
entries.plain: **In some homes children learn whole chapters of the Bible by heart before they can read a newspaper.** By the time of Jesus and Paul, Jews had a set of sacred books, the law of Moses, the prophets and the other writings, close to what Christians call the Old Testament. They held these books to come from God and to be true. Parents taught them to children from a young age, mostly by memory and recitation, and every Sabbath the synagogue read them aloud and explained them. Greek-speaking Jews called them the sacred writings. Some Jews outside Judea also read other books in Greek, which Judeans did not count as Scripture.
entries.then: Sacred writings was also a name for pagan religious texts, those of the cult of Isis among them. Greek-speaking Jewish sources used it for the Bible they had, what we call the Old Testament. Josephus says the Jews have only twenty-two books, "which contain the records of all the past times; which are justly believed to be divine." He counts five of Moses, thirteen written by the prophets after him, and four of hymns to God and rules for life (Against Apion 1.8). Most Judeans accepted those books. Some sects may have added others such as Jubilees and 1 Enoch, and many Diaspora Jews also read Greek books now in the Apocrypha, which Judeans did not count as canonical. Belief that gods inspired prophecy and even poetry was widespread. Jews held that God's Spirit inspired their Scriptures and that their message was true. The ESV Study Bible notes that the word Paul uses, God-breathed, appears in no Greek text before 2 Timothy. In devout Palestinian homes boys learned the sacred writings from about five, and other peoples marveled at how well Jewish children knew their traditions. Josephus says the law commands parents "to bring those children up in learning, and to exercise them in the laws" from infancy (Against Apion 2.26). In the synagogue the Law, probably with a reading from the Prophets, was read aloud and then explained. Interpreters had set ways of arguing from the text. They linked passages that shared a key word (gezerah shavah), reasoned from lesser to greater (qal vahomer, how much more), and argued from what a text leaves unsaid. Keener finds all three in Hebrews, with parallels in the Scrolls, the rabbis and Philo.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a family Bible handed down for generations, with the same books bound inside every copy. The arguments around the kitchen table are about what the verses mean, not about which pages belong between the covers.
entries.changes: Because Jews held a known body of Scripture to be God's word and taught it from childhood, Timothy's knowledge of the sacred writings from infancy in 2 Timothy 3:15 is the fruit of a Jewish upbringing. Reading Scripture aloud and then explaining it, as in the synagogue of Acts 13:15, carried over into the churches, where 1 Timothy 4:13 tells Timothy to devote himself to the public reading.
entries.not: **Not a single bound book with a table of contents.** The Scriptures were separate scrolls, counted in different ways, and some Greek-speaking Jews read books that Judeans did not count; what Jews held in common was the core of law, prophets and writings and the conviction that God spoke in them.
entries.dissent: Two points. First, whether all Scripture in 2 Timothy 3:16 already reaches beyond the Old Testament. The ESV Study Bible says it refers first to the Old Testament, but by implication to at least some New Testament writings already counted as Scripture, pointing to 1 Timothy 5:18. Keener writes that Timothy's Scriptures were, in his day, the Old Testament. Second, which books counted. The cultural backgrounds notes say some sects may have added books such as Jubilees and 1 Enoch, though others did not treat them as Scripture. They add that many Diaspora Jews read the books now in the Apocrypha, and Keener that the most common forms of the Greek Old Testament seem to have included them.

usedIn.s: Timothy has followed Paul's teaching, life and sufferings, as in Antioch, Iconium and Lystra; he is to continue in what he learned, knowing from whom he learned it and how from infancy he has known the sacred writings, for all Scripture is God-breathed.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 1:1-14, The Son above the angels
usedIn.s: God, who spoke in many ways through the prophets, has now spoken through a Son, heir of all things, who made purification for sins and sat down at the right hand of the Majesty. A chain of Scripture quotations sets the Son above the angels, who worship him and are sent to serve those who will inherit salvation.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 2:1-4, The message spoken through angels
usedIn.s: The readers must hold to what they have heard, or drift away. If the message spoken through angels was binding and every breach was punished, there is no escape for those who neglect the greater salvation announced by the Lord and confirmed by God with signs.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 7:1-10, Melchizedek, priest-king of Salem
usedIn.s: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, met Abraham, blessed him and received a tenth of the spoil. With no father, mother or genealogy recorded, he resembles the Son of God, and because Levi was still in Abraham's body when Abraham paid him, his priesthood ranks above Levi's.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 2:1-10, Living stones and a royal priesthood
usedIn.s: Like newborn babies the readers should crave pure milk. Coming to Christ, the living stone rejected by people but chosen by God, they are being built into a spiritual house and a holy priesthood; Peter strings together Scripture's stone texts and calls them a chosen people, a royal priesthood and a holy nation.

usedIn.n: 2 Peter 3:1-18, Scoffers, the flood and the day of fire
usedIn.s: Scoffers will ask where the promised coming is, since everything goes on as it has since creation. Peter answers that the world once made by God's word was destroyed by water and is now kept for fire on the day of judgment; the Lord does not count time as people do, and he delays out of patience. The day will come like a thief, and the readers wait for new heavens and a new earth, as Paul too wrote in letters some twist like the other Scriptures.

entries.title: The high priest
entries.summary: The head of Israel's priests, from Aaron's line, who offered for his own sins and then the people's and alone went into the holy of holies, once a year. By the first century Herod and Rome named and removed him at will.
aliases: fine linen of the high priest
entries.plain: **Only one person in the country could open that door, and only on one day of the year.** Israel's law set one man over all the priests: the high priest, a descendant of Aaron. He offered gifts and sacrifices for the people, and first for his own sins, because he was a man like them. On the Day of Atonement he alone went behind the last curtain into the holy of holies. By the time of Jesus the office was held by a few powerful families, and Herod and then the Romans named and removed high priests as they pleased.
entries.then: Josephus writes that it was the custom of his country "that no one should take the high priesthood of God but he who is of the blood of Aaron." No one of another stock could ever hold it, "though he were a king" (Antiquities 20.10). He counts eighty-three high priests from Aaron to the war with Rome, and says that at first they held office for life. The ESV Study Bible draws three marks of the office from Hebrews 5:1-4. A high priest was human and could deal gently with the weak. He offered sacrifices for sins, his own first (Leviticus 9:7; 16:6). And he was appointed by God, as Aaron was. Josephus says he wore the full robes only when he went into the holy of holies, "which he did but once in a year," on the day all kept a fast (War 5.5.7). Before that day he was guarded from defilement. Later rabbis say he was kept apart for a week, with precautions against a night emission. Josephus records that when the high priest Matthias was defiled by a dream the night before, a kinsman served in his place for that one day (Antiquities 17.6.4). High priests did not offer the daily sacrifices themselves but answered for the priests who did. In the Gospels and Acts the high priest presided over the Sanhedrin, and the chief priests were the aristocracy he came from. Philo made the divine Word God's high priest and played down the human high priest's full humanity. Rome had a powerful high priest of its own, the pontifex maximus, but Keener holds that Hebrews takes its model from the Old Testament and Jewish tradition.
entries.bridge: An analogy: the keeper of a nation's most sacred archive, the only person allowed into the vault, and only on one day a year. Before he goes in on everyone's behalf, he has to clear his own record.
entries.changes: Because one man stood between the people and the holy of holies, a high priest who shares human weakness and enters once for all, as in Hebrews 4:15, is the center of that letter's argument. The same office, filled by Rome's appointees, questions Jesus in Mark 14:61, and in Acts 23:2 the high priest Ananias has Paul struck on the mouth.
entries.not: **Not a custodian.** An archivist guards what is stored. The high priest went into the holy of holies to offer blood for the nation's sins, and in Jesus' day Herod and then Rome named and removed him at will.

usedIn.s: God did not put the world to come under angels. Psalm 8 promised rule to human beings; it is not yet seen, but Jesus, made a little lower than the angels for a while, is crowned with glory, and he shared flesh and blood to break the devil's power and become a merciful and faithful high priest.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 4:14-5:10, A high priest who can sympathize
usedIn.s: Jesus is a great high priest who has passed through the heavens and was tested in every way, yet without sin, so his people can approach the throne of grace with confidence. Like every high priest he was appointed by God, not self-chosen, and God named him a priest for ever in the order of Melchizedek.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 6:13-20, God's oath and the anchor behind the curtain
usedIn.s: When God promised Abraham, he swore by himself, since there was no one greater. Promise and oath, two things in which God cannot lie, give a hope that holds like an anchor and reaches behind the curtain, where Jesus has gone ahead as high priest for ever.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 7:1-10, Melchizedek, priest-king of Salem
usedIn.s: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, met Abraham, blessed him and received a tenth of the spoil. With no father, mother or genealogy recorded, he resembles the Son of God, and because Levi was still in Abraham's body when Abraham paid him, his priesthood ranks above Levi's.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 7:11-28, A priest from Judah, by oath, for ever
usedIn.s: If the Levitical priesthood had brought perfection, no other priest would have been promised. Jesus comes from Judah, a priest by the power of an indestructible life and by God's oath, the guarantee of a better covenant; Levitical priests died and offered daily for their own sins, but he lives for ever and offered himself once for all.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 8:1-13, Copy and shadow, and a new covenant
usedIn.s: The high priest believers have is seated in heaven and serves in the true tabernacle set up by the Lord. The earthly sanctuary was a copy and shadow built to the pattern shown to Moses, and Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant shows that the first was growing old and ready to disappear.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 9:1-10, The two rooms and their furniture
usedIn.s: The first covenant had a sanctuary on earth: an outer room with the lampstand, the table and the bread, and behind the second curtain the most holy place with the golden altar of incense, the ark and the cherubim. Priests entered the first room daily and the high priest the second once a year with blood, a sign that access to the holy place had not yet been opened.

usedIn.n: Revelation 21:9-27, the city of gold and twelve stones
usedIn.s: An angel carries John to a high mountain to show him the bride, the holy city Jerusalem, shining with God's glory, with twelve gates named for Israel's tribes and twelve foundations named for the Lamb's apostles. The city is a cube of pure gold, its foundations set with twelve precious stones and its gates each a single pearl; it has no temple, since God and the Lamb are its temple, and its gates never shut as the nations bring their glory into it.

entries.title: Melchizedek, priest-king of Salem
entries.summary: The king of Salem and priest of God Most High who blessed Abram and received a tenth of the spoil (Genesis 14). Psalm 110 promised a priest for ever in his order, and some Jews of the period made him a heavenly figure.
entries.plain: **A stranger walks into the family story for one scene, blesses the founder, and is never heard of again.** In Genesis 14, after a battle, Abram is met by Melchizedek, who ruled Salem and served as priest of God Most High. He brings bread and wine and blesses Abram, and Abram gives him a tenth of everything. The Old Testament names him only once more, in Psalm 110. There God swears that David's lord will be a priest for ever in the order of Melchizedek. Jewish readers in the first century already wondered about him, and they did not agree who he was.
entries.then: Salem was taken to be Jerusalem. Keener finds the reading supported by Psalm 76:2 and Egyptian execration texts, and Josephus, the Dead Sea Scrolls and the rabbis assume it. Josephus explains the name, "That name signifies, the righteous king," and says that for this he was made priest of God. He has him supply Abram's army and accept the tenth (Antiquities 1.10.2). Elsewhere he makes this Canaanite the city's founder, its "first priest of God, and first built a temple" there (War 6.10.1). Philo read the name the same way. Tithing was a Near Eastern custom before the law made it the Levites' due. A priest who was also a king was a live question. Israel had priest-kings only under the Hasmoneans, and some Jews opposed the combination. The Dead Sea Scrolls looked for an anointed priest from Levi and an anointed king from Judah. Wright and Bird call it a puzzle of the period: "could a coming Messiah be both a priest and a king?" Some Jewish circles, the Scrolls among them, made Melchizedek a heavenly figure, perhaps Michael or another angel. A Qumran scroll (11Q13), quoted by Wright and Bird, has him atone for the Sons of Light on a Day of Atonement at the end of the tenth jubilee. He also judges, with Psalm 82:1 applied to him, and the ESV Study Bible calls such writing speculation. Later rabbis claimed that God took the priesthood from Melchizedek, for blessing Abram before God, and gave it to Abraham. That may have been an answer to the Christian reading.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a charter older than the family firm, signed by a founder nobody can trace, which a later heir appeals to when he has no claim by descent. The older document outranks the newer line.
entries.changes: Psalm 110 makes the coming king a priest for ever in Melchizedek's order, which is why Hebrews 7:1-3 can argue for a priesthood that does not rest on descent from Levi. The same psalm's opening line, the king seated at God's right hand, lies behind Mark 12:36 and Acts 2:34.
entries.not: **Not a document or a dynasty.** Melchizedek is one man in one scene, with no successors in Genesis. The order of Melchizedek in Psalm 110 is a promise about a coming king, not a line of priests anyone could join.
entries.dissent: Two points. First, what Hebrews 7:3 means by without father, mother or genealogy. Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes see a Jewish technique, used especially by Philo, of arguing that what Scripture does not mention did not happen. They add that Greeks "viewed as divine whatever lacked beginning and ending." The ESV Study Bible says the details are simply not recorded in Scripture and that "Hebrews seems to view Melchizedek as an ordinary man". The CSB Study Bible's word note on apator says he had no traceable genealogy. Wright calls the deducing reading "unnecessary and unlikely": in the story "he is just there", and the point is a priesthood not inherited. Second, who Melchizedek was to Jews of the time. Some circles made him an exalted heavenly figure (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes; Wright and Bird on 11Q13). The ESV Study Bible reads Genesis 14 as describing an ordinary human king. Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes add that Hebrews itself does not use the heavenly tradition.

entries.title: The tabernacle and its heavenly pattern
entries.summary: The tent sanctuary Israel carried through the wilderness, with an outer room for the priests and an inner room, the holy of holies, for the ark. Moses built it to a pattern shown on the mountain, and many Jews thought of the earthly sanctuary as a copy of a heavenly one.
aliases: table and bread of the presence
as in heaven, so on earth
entries.plain: **A church that folds into a wagon and travels with the people, its holiest corner screened off.** Before Israel had a temple it had the tabernacle, a tent sanctuary built at Sinai and carried through the wilderness. An altar stood in the court outside. In the first room of the tent the priests tended a lampstand, a table of bread and an altar of incense. Behind a heavy curtain lay the inner room, the holy of holies, with the ark of the covenant and two carved cherubim above it. God told Moses to build it all to the pattern he was shown on the mountain, and Jews came to read that as a sign that the earthly sanctuary copied a heavenly one.
entries.then: Keener and the cultural backgrounds article on the tabernacle, which calls it "a portable temple", set the plan in its world. A three-part sanctuary with the holiest room at the back was the standard Egyptian temple design of Moses' day. The costliest materials sat nearest the ark, acacia was the only wood in Sinai, and nomads knew tent shrines. Lamps were needed because sanctuaries were shut off from daylight, and an incense altar answered the stench of sacrifices in closed rooms. The contrasts mattered more. Pagan temples kept a bed and furnishings for an image that was dressed and fed each day, and side shrines for lesser gods. Israel's had neither, and "where one would expect an image, there was none" (Keener). Other Near Eastern priests entered their inner rooms daily to feed the god's image, while Israel's high priest went in once a year. The god's house is very old. At Uruk around 3200 BC, Podany explains, the goddess Inana's shrine was her home, commoners could not approach her, and her statue needed food, drink and clothing. Heiser notes that gods and their councils were pictured living in tents on cosmic mountains. He reads the pattern shown to Moses as "as in heaven, so on earth", the heavens being God's own tent (Isaiah 40:22). Heavenly and earthly counterparts were common in Judaism and the older Near East, Marduk's temple in Babylon among them. Wisdom of Solomon 9:8 calls the temple an imitation of the heavenly one. Josephus reads the tent as the universe. Its two outer parts stood for land and sea, open to all, and the third was set apart for God "because heaven is inaccessible to men" (Antiquities 3.7.7). Of Herod's temple Josephus says the inner room held "nothing at all" (War 5.5.5).
entries.bridge: An analogy: an architect's scale model in the town hall, built carefully to the plans for the real building. You can learn a great deal from it, and it is not the building.
entries.changes: Because the sanctuary on earth was built to a heavenly pattern, Hebrews 8:5 can call it a copy and shadow and speak of Jesus entering the true one. Stephen recalls the tent built to the pattern Moses saw, in Acts 7:44, before saying that God does not live in houses made by hands. The curtain torn in Mark 15:38 belongs to the same plan, the barrier before the holy of holies.
entries.not: **Not a picture of heaven drawn to scale.** The sources that call it a copy do not agree on what kind of copy, a Platonic shadow, a Near Eastern counterpart of a god's dwelling, or a pointer to the age to come, and Hebrews draws only modest lessons from its furniture.
entries.dissent: Two points. First, in what sense the earthly sanctuary copies a heavenly one. Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes say copy and shadow sound like Plato and Philo. Keener adds that, unlike Plato, Hebrews has Jesus really go there. Wright holds that heaven in the Bible is not Plato's realm of ideas but "God's space, God's realm, which interlocks with our realm", with the temple as the place where the two met. Heiser reads the pattern as a Near Eastern principle, and the cultural backgrounds notes point out that Babylonians, Canaanites and others modeled earthly temples on heavenly ones. Price and House note that the Hebrew word behind pattern, tabnit, can mean the original or the replica. Second, why Hebrews speaks of the tabernacle rather than Herod's temple. Wright and Bird suggest the Jerusalem temple may in the author's day have been regarded as corrupt beyond repair. Wright's commentary suggests the writer avoided naming the central institution of Judaism too directly. Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes say he simply follows the biblical description. Carson, Moo and Morris say the letter "is not so much antitemple" as showing the old worship obsolete in principle.

The yearly sacrifices only reminded people of sin, but his body offered once has made his people holy, and he has sat down, his offering finished.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 10:19-25, Through the curtain, bodies washed, meeting together
usedIn.s: Because Jesus' blood has opened a new and living way through the curtain, believers may enter the most holy place with confidence. With hearts sprinkled and bodies washed with pure water, they are to hold fast, spur one another on, and not give up meeting together.

usedIn.n: Revelation 4:1-11, the throne room and the twenty-four elders
usedIn.s: Through an open door John is called up to heaven and sees God on a throne, ringed by a rainbow, with twenty-four elders on thrones, four living creatures and a sea of glass. The creatures cry holy, holy, holy, and the elders lay down their crowns, saying the Lord and God is worthy because he created all things.

usedIn.n: Revelation 8:1-13, silence, incense and the first four trumpets
usedIn.s: The seventh seal brings half an hour of silence in heaven. Seven angels receive trumpets, an angel offers incense with the prayers of God's people at the golden altar and hurls fire to the earth, and the first four trumpets bring hail and fire, a burning mountain into the sea, the star Wormwood and a darkening of sun, moon and stars.

usedIn.n: Revelation 11:15-19, the seventh trumpet and the ark
usedIn.s: At the seventh trumpet heaven announces that rule over the world now belongs to God and his Messiah for ever. The elders worship, the angry nations meet God's judgment, and the heavenly temple opens to reveal the ark of the covenant.

usedIn.n: Revelation 15:1-16:11, the song of Moses and the first bowls
usedIn.s: Those who have overcome the beast stand beside a sea of glass mixed with fire and sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb. Seven angels dressed like priests come out of the heavenly temple with seven golden bowls of God's wrath, and the first five bring sores, seas and rivers turned to blood, scorching sun and darkness on the beast's throne.

usedIn.n: Revelation 21:1-8, new heaven, new earth, no more sea
usedIn.s: John sees a new heaven and a new earth, with no more sea, and the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down from God like a bride dressed for her husband. A voice announces that God's dwelling is now with people, that he will wipe away every tear, and that he makes all things new; the thirsty will drink freely, while the cowardly, the faithless, murderers, sorcerers, idolaters and liars have their place in the lake of fire.

entries.title: The Lord's day
entries.summary: The day early Christians kept for Jesus, most likely Sunday, the weekday of the resurrection. In the cities of Asia one day a month was already given to honoring the emperor.
aliases: in the Spirit on the Lord's day
entries.plain: **A family that keeps one night a week for dinner together knows that night says something about who they are.** John says his vision came on the Lord's day. Most scholars take this to be Sunday, the day of the week on which Jesus rose, which the first believers had made their day to meet. In the cities of Asia one day a month was already set aside to honor the emperor, so naming a day for the Lord said something too. Whether John means every Sunday, Easter, or the coming day of the Lord is read in more than one way.
entries.then: Most scholars take the Lord's day to mean Sunday, the weekday of Jesus' resurrection. Keener suggests the early Jewish Christians may have preferred that day so as not to clash with the Sabbath. The CSB Study Bible says it had become the Christians' day of worship. It points to Acts 20:7 and 1 Corinthians 16:2, where believers gather, or set money aside, on the first day of the week. The ESV Study Bible calls it Sunday, the day Christ rose. Beale notes that by the later second century the phrase is used plainly and consistently for Sunday, and he cites the Epistle of Barnabas 15:9. The setting in Asia sharpens the name. Keener writes that in Asia Minor one day a month honored the emperor, while the Christians gave a day, probably each week, to Christ. The cultural backgrounds notes report the same contrast as a suggestion some scholars make. Some Jewish schemes of history ended in a seventh age of sabbath rest. Some early Christian interpreters moved the picture to an eighth age and called the Lord's day the eighth day. Keener leaves open whether these ideas are early enough, or close enough, to bear on John. In Revelation the day frames the whole vision. John is in the Spirit, which Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes connect with prophetic inspiration, as in Ezekiel. He hears a voice like a trumpet, which Keener hears as an echo of Sinai.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a country that marks a monthly holiday for its ruler, while a small group in every town quietly keeps its own weekly day for someone else. Nothing is said aloud, but the calendar shows whose people they are.
entries.changes: Because the first day of the week had become the day believers met, John's vision on the Lord's day in Revelation 1:10 comes as the churches gathered, and the meeting on the first day of the week in Acts 20:7 and the weekly collection of 1 Corinthians 16:2 show the same habit. In a province where a day each month honored the emperor, keeping a day for Jesus marked whose people the churches were.
entries.not: **Not a protest day.** In the analogy the weekly day answers the ruler's monthly one. The Christians' day was the day of the resurrection, and the contrast with the emperor's monthly day is a suggestion some scholars make, not a stated aim.
entries.dissent: What day is meant. Beale reports the view that the phrase means the end-time day of the Lord, which would make the whole book a vision of that day. He answers that the adjective is never used that way in the Greek Old Testament, the New Testament or the early fathers, and he prefers every Sunday to Easter Sunday. The cultural backgrounds notes give the contrast with a monthly day for the emperor as a suggestion some scholars make. Keener allows that the name may also look toward the coming day of the Lord.
