usedIn.n: Acts 20:1-12, The collection party and Eutychus at Troas
usedIn.s: Paul leaves Ephesus for Macedonia and Greece, then sets out for Jerusalem with delegates from the churches. At Troas the believers meet on the first day of the week, and a young man who falls from a window is taken up alive.

usedIn.n: Revelation 1:9-20, Patmos, the Lord's day, lampstands and stars
usedIn.s: On the island of Patmos, in the Spirit on the Lord's day, John hears a voice like a trumpet telling him to write to seven churches. He turns and sees one like a son of man among seven golden lampstands, holding seven stars, who holds the keys of death and Hades and explains what the stars and lampstands mean.

entries.title: The family's name
entries.summary: Families lived, worked and stood together. Walking out of the family business or putting kin second was a public offense.
aliases: loves the parent loves the child
entries.plain: **The son walked out of the family store, and the whole street talked about it.** Your family was your job, your home, your safety and your name. What one member did, the whole family wore in front of the village.
entries.then: Leaving a family business, which sons normally expected to take over one day, had dramatic consequences for the whole family. A family firm with hired men had ample income. Many homes in Capernaum were built around courtyards shared with other homes, and extended families often lived together. Relatives usually tried to hide behavior that could shame the family. Kinship words were used loosely, so a respected older woman could be called mother. Yet refusing to put your physical family first would look offensive in the ancient Mediterranean world. Wright says Jesus' mother brought the family to take him home, to stop him bringing dishonor on the family name. Bailey adds a point from Middle Eastern speech. A man gesturing to a crowd of men can call them brother, uncle and cousin, but cannot call them brother and sister and mother. Bailey makes the point on Matthew's version. Mark 3:35 has the same three words, and Bailey draws from them that the disciples around Jesus included women. Jewish tradition ranked honoring father and mother among the greatest commandments. Wright, writing on Jesus' family sayings, calls the demand to leave the dead unburied outrageous and argues that loyalty to Jesus formed an alternative family. Grown children were expected to support aged parents in return for their upbringing. Judaism counted this part of honoring father and mother, it was law as well as custom, and even pagans did it. Close friends, and above all a son, were expected to visit a dying man, and sons normally buried their fathers.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a family farm handed down for generations. When the eldest son leaves to join something new, it is not a career change. It is a hole in the family, and the neighbors can see it.
entries.changes: Putting a teacher before family, as when James and John leave their father in Mark 1:20, was a public offense, not a private choice. The saying about letting the dead bury their dead in Matthew 8:22 cuts against the strongest duty a son had. Naming his followers as his family redefined kinship.
entries.not: **Not a loss the parents bear alone.** A son leaving the farm today is sad news for his parents. Then he owed them support in old age by law and by the commandment to honor them, and the shame fell on kin who shared courtyards and lived together.

usedIn.n: Matthew 10:16-42, Wolves, floggings, a sword and a cup of water
usedIn.s: Jesus warns the Twelve of councils, floggings in synagogues and trials before governors and kings, of family turned against family, and promises that whoever receives them receives him.

usedIn.n: Matthew 12:22-50, Beelzebul, the strong man, Jonah and his true family
usedIn.s: When Jesus heals a blind and mute man, the crowds wonder if he is the Son of David and the Pharisees say he works by Beelzebul. Jesus answers with the strong man, refuses a sign except Jonah's, and names his true family.

usedIn.n: Matthew 13:53-58, No honor in Nazareth
usedIn.s: Teaching in his hometown synagogue, Jesus is dismissed as the carpenter's son whose family everyone knows, and he says a prophet is not without honor except at home.

usedIn.n: Mark 1:14-20, Fishermen called
usedIn.s: Jesus announces that God's kingdom is near, then calls two pairs of brothers from their nets on the Sea of Galilee.

usedIn.n: Mark 3:13-35, The Twelve, his family and Beelzebul
usedIn.s: Jesus appoints twelve. His family thinks he is out of his mind, and teachers from Jerusalem say he drives out demons by Beelzebul.

usedIn.n: Luke 2:41-52, A twelve-year-old among the teachers
usedIn.s: On the family's yearly Passover pilgrimage the twelve-year-old Jesus stays behind in Jerusalem, and after three days his parents find him in the temple courts among the teachers.

usedIn.n: Luke 9:51-62, A Samaritan refusal and three would-be followers
usedIn.s: Setting out for Jerusalem, Jesus is turned away by a Samaritan village and rebukes James and John for wanting to call down fire. On the road he tells three would-be followers what following him will cost.

usedIn.n: Luke 15:11-32, A father and two lost sons
usedIn.s: A younger son takes his share of the estate early, wastes it in a far country, and comes home to a father who runs to meet him. The older brother refuses to join the feast.

usedIn.n: Luke 18:18-30, A rich ruler and the needle's eye
usedIn.s: A ruler asks what he must do to inherit eternal life; told to sell everything and follow, he goes away sad, and Jesus says it is easier for a camel to go through a needle's eye than for a rich man to enter God's kingdom.

usedIn.n: John 19:16-30, The cross, the notice in three languages, and his mother
usedIn.s: Jesus carries his own cross to Golgotha. Pilate's notice, King of the Jews, is written in Aramaic, Latin and Greek; soldiers cast lots for his seamless tunic; he gives his mother to the beloved disciple, takes the sour wine and says it is finished.

usedIn.n: Romans 16:3-16, Greet the church in their house
usedIn.s: Paul greets more than two dozen believers in Rome by name, from Prisca and Aquila and the church in their house to the households of Aristobulus and Narcissus, and tells them to greet one another with a holy kiss.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 4:14-21, Ten thousand guardians, one father
usedIn.s: Paul writes as the Corinthians' father in the gospel, sends Timothy to remind them of his ways, and asks whether they want him to come with a rod or with love.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 4:9-12, A quiet life and your own hands
usedIn.s: Paul praises the church's love for the whole family of believers in Macedonia and urges them to love more, to live quietly, mind their own business and work with their hands, so that outsiders respect them and they depend on no one.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 5:1-16, Older men as fathers, and the widows' list
usedIn.s: Timothy is to treat older and younger believers as family; the church is to honor widows who are truly in need, families are to support their own, and only older widows of proven character are to be put on the list.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 1:1-7, Lois, Eunice and the laying on of hands
usedIn.s: Writing from custody, Paul greets Timothy as his dear son, thanks God as he remembers him in prayer night and day, recalls the faith of Timothy's grandmother Lois and mother Eunice, and urges him to fan into flame the gift given when Paul laid hands on him.

usedIn.n: 1 John 1:5-2:17, God is light, an advocate, and a world passing away
usedIn.s: God is light with no darkness in him, so to claim fellowship with him while walking in darkness is a lie; the blood of Jesus cleanses, and those who confess are forgiven. Anyone who sins has an advocate with the Father, the atoning sacrifice for the whole world. The old command of love is new, the darkness is passing, and the world is passing away.

usedIn.n: 1 John 5:1-12, Water, blood and three witnesses
usedIn.s: Whoever believes Jesus is the Christ is God's child, and loving the parent means loving the child. Faith overcomes the world. Jesus Christ came by water and blood, not by water only, and three testify, the Spirit, the water and the blood; God's testimony is that he has given eternal life in his Son.

entries.title: Honor before a crowd
entries.summary: Public standing was the currency of the ancient Mediterranean. People competed for honor and dreaded being shamed in front of others.
aliases: I could be bold and order you
entries.plain: **He could not back down in front of everyone, so he did the stupid thing.** In Jesus' world your worth was what other people saw and said about you. Losing face in public could be worse than losing money, and a crowd was always watching.
entries.then: People in the ancient Mediterranean prized honor and dreaded shame. Men commonly competed for honor, from friendly contests to deadly feuds. Breaking a public word was shameful, even when a rabbi could have released the oath. At the same time, people respected those who did not chase their own honor, and teachers who turned praise aside. In public debate the best speakers could silence and shame their opponents. Social inferiors were expected to greet superiors first. Disciples would not want to draw attention to their failures, and people were slow to admit ignorance. Being abandoned by your disciples, or betrayed by a friend, brought dishonor. Nakedness was a special shame for Jews, and crucifixion was built to humiliate. Bailey reads the Syro-Phoenician woman's story as an exam in which she wins the honor that comes to one who passes a very hard test. A blow on the right cheek, short of real injury, was the worst insult possible, and both Jewish and Roman law allowed prosecution for it. Cities had honor to lose as well. Citizens' first loyalty was to their city, rivalries between cities were bitter, and speakers used them to spur generosity, as Paul sets Macedonia against Corinth. By boasting of a church's promised gift Paul laid his own honor on the line, since communities publicly held benefactors to their promises. Self-praise offended unless one was defending oneself or boasting on another's behalf. "Jewish piety demanded that reproof be given in private," so a public rebuke marked an offense as grave and urgent (Keener).
entries.bridge: An analogy: a high school cafeteria where everyone watches who sits where and who gets laughed at. Your standing is whatever the room thinks of you.
entries.changes: Public standing explains scenes where someone cannot back down or is insulted in front of others, as when Herod is bound by his oath before his guests in Mark 6:26. A slap on the right cheek in Matthew 5:39 was an insult, not an injury. Luke 14:10 tells guests to take the lowest seat.
entries.not: **Not a passing school ranking.** Cafeteria status fades after graduation. Honor ruled adult life: an insulting blow could be taken to court, cities competed for honor, and a broken public promise shamed a man before everyone.
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Mark 1:44, 6:26, 9:28, 9:32, 9:34, 10:18, 10:44, 12:34, 12:38, 14:18, 14:50 and 15:24, and notes on Matthew 8:4 and 14:7

usedIn.n: Matthew 1:18-25, Joseph and the betrothal
usedIn.s: Mary is found pregnant while betrothed to Joseph. He plans a quiet divorce until an angel in a dream tells him to take her as his wife and name the child Jesus.

usedIn.n: Matthew 5:33-48, No oaths, the other cheek, the second mile
usedIn.s: Jesus tells his hearers not to swear at all, not to resist an evildoer, to go a second mile with a soldier who forces one, and to love their enemies.

usedIn.n: Matthew 15:21-28, A Canaanite mother and the dogs
usedIn.s: In the region of Tyre and Sidon a Canaanite woman begs the Son of David to free her daughter. Jesus is silent, then speaks of bread and dogs, and her answer wins him over.

usedIn.n: Matthew 18:21-35, Ten thousand talents and a hundred denarii
usedIn.s: Peter asks whether forgiving seven times is enough. Jesus tells of a king who cancels an impossible debt, and of the forgiven servant who then chokes a colleague over a small one.

usedIn.n: Matthew 20:1-16, A day's wage for an hour's work
usedIn.s: A landowner hires laborers for his vineyard at dawn and again through the day, then pays everyone a full denarius, starting with the last. Those hired first complain.

usedIn.n: Matthew 22:1-14, The king's wedding feast
usedIn.s: A king's invited guests refuse to come to his son's wedding and kill his messengers. He burns their city, fills the hall with people from the roads, and throws out a guest without wedding clothes.

usedIn.n: Matthew 23:1-12, Moses' seat, wide phylacteries, the best seats
usedIn.s: Jesus tells the crowds to do what the scribes and Pharisees teach but not what they do, and mocks their wide phylacteries, long tassels, best seats and love of the title rabbi.

usedIn.n: Matthew 25:1-13, Ten young women and the bridegroom
usedIn.s: Ten young women wait with their lights for a bridegroom who comes late at night. Five brought extra oil and go in to the feast; five go to buy oil and find the door shut.

usedIn.n: Mark 6:14-29, Herod's banquet and John's death
usedIn.s: Herod hears of Jesus and thinks John has risen. Mark then tells how Herod, at his birthday banquet, had John beheaded.

usedIn.n: Mark 7:24-37, A Greek woman and a deaf man
usedIn.s: In the region of Tyre a Gentile mother asks Jesus to free her daughter, and answers his saying about dogs. In the Decapolis he heals a deaf man.

usedIn.n: Mark 10:32-45, James and John ask for the best seats
usedIn.s: On the road to Jerusalem Jesus predicts his death a third time. James and John ask to sit at his right and left, and he tells them the first must be slave of all.

usedIn.n: Mark 15:21-41, The cross
usedIn.s: Jesus is crucified as king of the Jews between two bandits, mocked by passers-by, and dies with a loud cry. The temple curtain tears, and women watch from a distance.

usedIn.n: Luke 1:26-56, A village girl, a greeting and a song of reversal
usedIn.s: Gabriel greets Mary, a betrothed girl in Nazareth, with news that she will bear the son of David. She goes to Elizabeth in the hill country and sings of God bringing down rulers and lifting up the humble.

usedIn.n: Luke 6:20-36, Blessings, woes and lending with nothing back
usedIn.s: Jesus blesses the poor, the hungry, the weeping and the hated, pronounces woes on the rich and the well fed, and tells his hearers to love enemies, turn the other cheek and lend without expecting anything back.

usedIn.n: Luke 10:38-42, Mary at the teacher's feet
usedIn.s: In Martha's house Mary sits at Jesus' feet listening while Martha works at serving. When Martha complains, Jesus says Mary has chosen the better part.

usedIn.n: Luke 11:1-13, Father, daily bread and a friend at midnight
usedIn.s: Asked to teach his disciples to pray, Jesus gives a short prayer to the Father, then tells of a man who wakes a neighbor at midnight to borrow bread for a guest.

usedIn.n: Luke 11:37-54, Woes at a Pharisee's table
usedIn.s: At a Pharisee's meal Jesus does not wash before eating, and when his host is surprised he pronounces woes on Pharisees and lawyers: clean cups and greedy hearts, tithed herbs, the best seats, unmarked graves and the tombs of the prophets.

usedIn.n: Luke 14:1-14, Dropsy at a Pharisee's table, and guests who cannot repay
usedIn.s: On a Sabbath at the house of a leading Pharisee, Jesus heals a man with dropsy, tells the guests not to grab the best places, and tells the host to invite people who cannot invite him back.

usedIn.n: Luke 14:15-24, The great banquet and the excuses
usedIn.s: A guest blesses whoever will eat bread in God's kingdom. Jesus tells of a man whose invited guests all excuse themselves when the feast is ready, so he fills his house with the poor and with people from the roads.

usedIn.n: Luke 15:11-32, A father and two lost sons
usedIn.s: A younger son takes his share of the estate early, wastes it in a far country, and comes home to a father who runs to meet him. The older brother refuses to join the feast.

usedIn.n: Luke 16:1-13, The dishonest manager
usedIn.s: A rich man's manager, about to be dismissed for wasting his master's property, calls in the master's debtors and cuts their bills. The master praises his shrewdness.

usedIn.n: Luke 18:1-8, The widow and the judge
usedIn.s: Jesus tells of a judge who neither feared God nor respected people and a widow who kept coming to him for justice until he gave in. How much more, he says, will God see justice done for his chosen ones.

usedIn.n: Luke 20:20-26, Caesar's coin
usedIn.s: Spies sent by the leaders ask Jesus whether it is right to pay tribute to Caesar, hoping to hand him over to the governor. He asks whose image is on a denarius.

usedIn.n: John 2:1-12, Water into wine at a village wedding
usedIn.s: At a wedding in Cana the wine runs out. Jesus has the servants fill six stone purification jars with water, and the master of the feast tastes the best wine of the week.

usedIn.n: John 12:20-50, Greeks at the feast, and the ruler of this world cast out
usedIn.s: Some Greeks who came up to worship ask to see Jesus. He says his hour has come, that the ruler of this world will be driven out, and that when he is lifted up he will draw everyone to himself; many leaders believe but stay silent.

usedIn.n: John 18:1-27, Arrest across the Kidron, and Annas
usedIn.s: Judas brings soldiers and temple police with torches to a garden across the Kidron. Jesus answers I am he, they fall back, and he is taken bound to Annas while Peter denies him three times by a charcoal fire.

usedIn.n: Acts 4:1-31, Before the temple rulers
usedIn.s: The temple authorities arrest Peter and John for proclaiming the resurrection in Jesus. Before the council the unschooled fishermen speak boldly, are warned and released, and pray with the believers in the words of Psalm 2.

usedIn.n: Acts 4:32-5:11, Barnabas, Ananias and Sapphira
usedIn.s: The believers share everything, and Barnabas sells a field for the common fund. Ananias and Sapphira sell land too but lie about the price, and both fall dead.

usedIn.n: Acts 16:25-40, The jailer and the Roman citizens
usedIn.s: At midnight an earthquake opens the prison. The jailer, about to kill himself, believes with his household; next day Paul reveals that he and Silas are Roman citizens beaten without trial, and the magistrates come to apologize.

usedIn.n: Romans 12:1-21, A living sacrifice
usedIn.s: Paul urges believers to offer their bodies as a living sacrifice, to see themselves as members of one body, and to love without pretense: honoring one another, welcoming strangers, weeping with those who weep and repaying evil with good.

usedIn.n: Romans 13:1-7, The sword and the tax
usedIn.s: Paul tells believers to be subject to the governing authorities, whom God has put in place. The ruler bears the sword, and they should pay taxes and give honor where it is owed.

usedIn.n: Romans 15:14-24, To Spain by way of Rome
usedIn.s: Paul describes his priestly work of offering the Gentiles to God, from Jerusalem round to Illyricum, and his plan to visit Rome on his way to Spain and be helped on his journey there.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 1:18-2:5, The foolishness of the cross
usedIn.s: Paul sets the message of a crucified Messiah, folly to Greeks and a stumbling block to Jews, against the wisdom and eloquence Corinth admired, and reminds the believers that few of them were wise, powerful or well born.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 4:6-13, Apostles on display
usedIn.s: With biting irony Paul sets the Corinthians, already full, rich and reigning, beside the apostles, put on show last of all like men condemned to die, hungry, ragged, homeless and treated as the world's scum.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 6:1-11, Lawsuits before unbelievers
usedIn.s: Paul is appalled that believers take one another to court before pagan judges, reminds them that God's people will judge the world and even angels, and asks why they would not rather be wronged.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 11:2-16, Heads covered and uncovered
usedIn.s: Paul tells men who pray or prophesy to keep their heads uncovered and women who do so to cover theirs, arguing from headship, creation, the angels, nature and the custom of the churches.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 12:1-31, Mute idols and one body
usedIn.s: Paul reminds the Corinthians that as pagans they were led astray to mute idols, describes the many gifts of the one Spirit, and pictures the church as one body whose weaker and less honored members are indispensable.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 1:12-2:4, Changed plans, the seal and the down payment
usedIn.s: Accused of fickleness for changing his travel plans, Paul answers that his word is reliable because all God's promises are Yes in Christ, who has anointed and sealed them and given the Spirit as a down payment, and explains that he stayed away to spare them.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 8:16-9:15, Envoys for the collection and the cheerful giver
usedIn.s: Paul commends Titus and two brothers appointed by the churches to carry the gift, takes care that no one can fault him in handling it, and urges the Corinthians to have their promised gift ready, since God loves a cheerful giver.

usedIn.n: Galatians 2:1-10, Titus, the pillars and the right hand of fellowship
usedIn.s: Fourteen years later Paul goes up to Jerusalem with Barnabas and the uncircumcised Titus; Titus is not made to be circumcised, and the leaders reputed to be pillars give Paul the right hand of fellowship, asking only that he remember the poor.

usedIn.n: Galatians 2:11-21, Peter leaves the table at Antioch
usedIn.s: At Antioch Peter, who had been eating with Gentile believers, draws back when people come from James, and Paul rebukes him in front of everyone, arguing that Jews and Gentiles alike are put right with God through Christ and faith, not by doing what the law requires.

usedIn.n: Galatians 4:12-20, Welcomed as an angel of God
usedIn.s: Paul appeals to the Galatians as friends, reminding them that when he first preached to them in bodily weakness they did not scorn him but welcomed him as an angel of God, and asks whether he has now become their enemy by telling them the truth.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 3:1-13, The prisoner, the steward and the mystery shown to the powers
usedIn.s: Paul, a prisoner for the sake of the Gentiles, breaks off to explain the stewardship of grace given him: the mystery, now revealed, that Gentiles are co-heirs, made known through the church even to the rulers in the heavenly realms.

usedIn.n: Philippians 1:12-26, Chains known to the whole palace guard
usedIn.s: Paul tells how his imprisonment has carried the gospel through the palace guard and made other preachers bolder, some from rivalry, then weighs living against dying and expects to stay on for their sake.

usedIn.n: Philippians 2:1-11, The form of a slave, a cross, and every knee
usedIn.s: Paul urges humility and concern for others, then sets out Christ, who did not exploit his equality with God but took the form of a slave and died on a cross, and whom God exalted so that every knee will bow.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 2:1-12, Gentle as a nurse, firm as a father
usedIn.s: Paul reminds the church how he and his companions came to them after being mistreated in Philippi: no deceit, flattery or greed, gentle among them like a nursing mother, working night and day so as not to burden anyone, and urging each of them like a father.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 4:1-8, Holiness in the body
usedIn.s: Paul reminds the church of the instructions he passed on from the Lord Jesus: God's will is that they be holy, avoid sexual immorality, control their own bodies in holiness and honor, and not wrong a brother in this matter.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 3:1-13, Overseers, deacons and the women
usedIn.s: Paul lists what is required of an overseer, above reproach, faithful in marriage, hospitable, able to teach, managing his household well, and then of deacons and of the women, who must also be worthy of respect.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 1:8-18, Not ashamed of my chains, the deposit, and Onesiphorus
usedIn.s: Paul tells Timothy not to be ashamed of the Lord's testimony or of him as a prisoner, but to share his suffering and guard the good deposit; everyone in Asia has deserted him except Onesiphorus, who searched Rome until he found him.

usedIn.n: Titus 2:1-10, Older men, older women, young wives and slaves
usedIn.s: Titus is to teach what fits sound doctrine to each group in the household of faith, older men, older women, younger women, younger men and slaves, so that outsiders have no cause to speak against God's message and the teaching about God is made attractive.

usedIn.n: Philemon 8-25, Onesimus sent home with a letter
usedIn.s: Paul appeals to Philemon, on the basis of love, for Onesimus, the slave who became Paul's son in prison: he sends him back to be received as a beloved brother rather than as a slave, asks Philemon to welcome him as he would Paul, offers to repay anything he owes, and asks for a guest room.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 10:26-39, No sacrifice left; prison and plunder
usedIn.s: For anyone who goes on sinning deliberately after knowing the truth, no sacrifice for sins remains. The readers once endured a hard contest: public insult, prison and the seizure of their property, which they accepted with joy. They must not throw away their confidence now.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 12:1-13, The race, the shame and the Father's discipline
usedIn.s: Surrounded by a great cloud of witnesses, believers are to throw off every weight and run with endurance, eyes fixed on Jesus, who endured the cross and scorned its shame. Their hardships are a father's discipline, which only legitimate children receive.

usedIn.n: James 2:1-13, The gold ring and the good seat
usedIn.s: James forbids favoritism in the assembly. A rich man with a gold ring is given a good seat and a poor man in dirty clothes is told to stand, though it is the rich who drag believers into court and slander the noble name; the royal law of love rules out partiality, and mercy triumphs over judgment.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 2:18-25, Household slaves and a harsh master
usedIn.s: Peter tells household slaves to submit to their masters, the harsh as well as the kind, because suffering unjustly while doing good is commendable before God. Christ suffered for them, leaving an example: insulted, he did not insult in return, and by his wounds they have been healed.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 4:12-19, The fiery ordeal and the name Christian
usedIn.s: The readers should not be surprised at the fiery ordeal, but rejoice to share Christ's sufferings. No one should suffer as a murderer, a thief or a meddler, but anyone who suffers as a Christian should not be ashamed; judgment begins with God's household, so those who suffer should commit themselves to their faithful Creator.

usedIn.n: 3 John 9-15, Diotrephes and Demetrius
usedIn.s: The elder wrote to the church, but Diotrephes, eager to be first, refuses to receive him; he spreads malicious talk, refuses to welcome the brothers and puts out of the church those who do. Gaius is not to imitate evil. Demetrius is well spoken of by everyone, and the elder adds his own testimony; he hopes to come soon and talk face to face.

entries.title: Burial and mourning
entries.summary: Mourners came at once, the dead were buried the same day, wrapped in linen in rock tombs, and family carried the duty of burial. Pagan mourning, with little hope beyond a shadowy underworld, could be bleak.
entries.plain: **When someone in the village died, the wailing started before the doctor had left the house.** The dead were buried fast, on the day they died if possible. Family did the burying. Tombs were caves cut in rock and closed with a heavy stone.
entries.then: As soon as a death was announced, professional mourners gathered. Sleep was a common picture for death, but the mourners knew death when they saw it. Next of kin normally buried a body, or failing them a teacher's disciples. Romans left those executed for treason to vultures or dogs, and a member of the elite who asked for such a body took a real risk. Wealthy tombs were closed with a grooved stone disk that took several men to move, and a year later the bones went into an ossuary. Keener describes "The first week of deep grief after a close relative's burial" spent at home, sitting on the floor and visited by friends. Three weeks without adornment followed, then a year without common pleasures. Josephus says Archelaus mourned Herod seven days, "for so many days are appointed for it by the law of our fathers." Paid mourners and set days of grief are ancient. At a queen's funeral in Lagash in the twenty-fourth century BC, lament priests and women mourners were paid in bread and beer. At the funeral of the mother of Babylon's last king, in the sixth century BC, guests mourned seven days before they were feasted (Podany). Jewish custom wrapped the body tightly in linen and neither burned nor embalmed it. Even for the crucified, Josephus says the Jews "took down those that were condemned and crucified, and buried them before the going down of the sun." Keener writes, "Most pagans believed in a shadowy afterlife in the underworld". The ESV Study Bible finds that "most first-century Greeks had a strongly pessimistic view of death". Wright cites an epitaph so common it was carved by its initials: I was not, I was, I am not, I do not care.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a family vault on an old estate, where each generation is laid beside the last. Being buried there means you belong. Being left out of it is a disgrace.
entries.changes: Burial on the day of death and the family's duty to bury explain the rush and the obligations in many scenes, as when John's disciples bury him in Mark 6:29, and a son's duty to bury his father makes the saying in Matthew 8:21-22 shocking. Because most pagans expected little beyond a shadowy underworld, Paul's call in 1 Thessalonians 4:13 not to grieve like those who have no hope sets two kinds of mourning side by side.
entries.not: **Not a final resting place.** In a family vault each body stays where it is laid. In a Jewish rock tomb the body lay for a year, and then the bones were gathered into an ossuary. Burial had to come the same day, and the duty fell on next of kin.

usedIn.n: Matthew 8:18-34, Let the dead bury their dead, the storm and Gadara
usedIn.s: Jesus answers two would-be followers, calms a storm on the lake, and frees two men possessed by demons in the region of the Gadarenes.

usedIn.n: Matthew 9:18-34, A ruler's daughter, a bleeding woman, the blind and the mute
usedIn.s: A synagogue ruler asks Jesus to raise his daughter; on the way a woman touches the fringe of his cloak. Then two blind men call him Son of David, and a mute man speaks.

usedIn.n: Matthew 14:1-12, John beheaded at a birthday feast
usedIn.s: Herod the tetrarch hears about Jesus and thinks John has risen. Matthew tells how Herod, bound by an oath at his birthday, had John beheaded.

usedIn.n: Matthew 23:13-28, Oaths, mint, gnats and whitewashed tombs
usedIn.s: Jesus pronounces woes on the scribes and Pharisees: they shut the kingdom, play games with oaths, tithe herbs while neglecting justice, strain gnats and swallow camels, and look clean outside like whitewashed tombs.

usedIn.n: Matthew 26:1-16, Perfume at Bethany and thirty pieces of silver
usedIn.s: The chief priests meet at Caiaphas's house to plot Jesus' arrest away from the festival crowds. At Bethany a woman pours costly perfume on his head, and Judas sells him for thirty pieces of silver.

usedIn.n: Matthew 27:57-66, Joseph's tomb and the sealed stone
usedIn.s: Joseph of Arimathea, a rich disciple, asks Pilate for the body and lays it in his own new tomb. The next day the chief priests get a guard and a seal on the stone.

usedIn.n: Mark 5:21-43, A synagogue leader's daughter and a bleeding woman
usedIn.s: On the way to heal Jairus' dying daughter, Jesus is touched by a woman who has bled for twelve years. Then he raises the girl.

usedIn.n: Mark 6:14-29, Herod's banquet and John's death
usedIn.s: Herod hears of Jesus and thinks John has risen. Mark then tells how Herod, at his birthday banquet, had John beheaded.

usedIn.n: Mark 14:1-11, Perfume at Bethany
usedIn.s: Two days before Passover, at dinner in Bethany, a woman pours costly perfume on Jesus' head. He says she has anointed him for burial, and Judas goes to the chief priests.

usedIn.n: Mark 15:42-16:8, The tomb
usedIn.s: Joseph of Arimathea buries Jesus before the Sabbath. When it is over, the women come with spices, find the stone rolled away, and hear that he has been raised.

usedIn.n: Luke 7:11-17, A widow's only son on the bier
usedIn.s: At the gate of Nain Jesus meets a funeral for a widow's only son. He touches the bier, raises the young man and gives him back to his mother, and the crowd says a great prophet has arisen.

usedIn.n: Luke 9:51-62, A Samaritan refusal and three would-be followers
usedIn.s: Setting out for Jerusalem, Jesus is turned away by a Samaritan village and rebukes James and John for wanting to call down fire. On the road he tells three would-be followers what following him will cost.

usedIn.n: Luke 16:19-31, The rich man and Lazarus
usedIn.s: A rich man feasts every day while a beggar named Lazarus lies at his gate. Both die; Lazarus is carried to Abraham's side, and the rich man finds himself in torment in Hades.

usedIn.n: Luke 23:26-49, The road to the cross, paradise, and the ninth hour
usedIn.s: Simon of Cyrene carries the cross, the women of Jerusalem mourn, and Jesus warns them of days to come. Crucified between two criminals, he promises one of them paradise and dies at the ninth hour.

usedIn.n: John 11:1-44, Lazarus four days in the tomb
usedIn.s: Jesus waits two days after hearing that his friend Lazarus is ill, reaches Bethany to find him four days buried, weeps with the mourners, and calls him out of the tomb still bound in his grave clothes.

usedIn.n: John 12:1-11, Mary's nard and loosened hair
usedIn.s: Six days before Passover, at a dinner in Jesus' honor in Bethany, Mary pours a pound of costly nard on his feet and wipes them with her hair. Judas objects, and Jesus says she has kept it for the day of his burial.

usedIn.n: John 19:31-42, Legs unbroken and a hundred pounds of spices
usedIn.s: Because the coming Sabbath is a high day, the leaders ask for the bodies to be taken down. The soldiers find Jesus already dead and pierce his side; Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus bury him with a lavish weight of spices in a new tomb in a garden.

usedIn.n: John 20:1-18, The empty tomb and the gardener
usedIn.s: Mary Magdalene finds the stone moved and runs to Peter and the beloved disciple, who see the linen cloths lying in the empty tomb. Weeping outside, she takes the risen Jesus for the gardener until he says her name, and he sends her to tell the others.

usedIn.n: Acts 4:32-5:11, Barnabas, Ananias and Sapphira
usedIn.s: The believers share everything, and Barnabas sells a field for the common fund. Ananias and Sapphira sell land too but lie about the price, and both fall dead.

usedIn.n: Acts 7:54-8:3, The stoning of Stephen
usedIn.s: Stephen sees the Son of Man standing at God's right hand, and his hearers drag him out and stone him while a young man named Saul looks after their coats. Persecution scatters the church.

usedIn.n: Acts 9:32-43, Lydda and Joppa
usedIn.s: Peter heals a paralyzed man at Lydda and, at Joppa, raises Tabitha, a disciple known for her charity, while the widows she clothed stand weeping. He stays on with a tanner.

usedIn.n: Romans 12:1-21, A living sacrifice
usedIn.s: Paul urges believers to offer their bodies as a living sacrifice, to see themselves as members of one body, and to love without pretense: honoring one another, welcoming strangers, weeping with those who weep and repaying evil with good.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 15:1-11, What I received
usedIn.s: Paul reminds the Corinthians of the good news he handed on to them as he had received it: that Christ died for sins, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to Cephas, the Twelve, more than five hundred, James, all the apostles and last of all to Paul.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 15:12-34, If the dead are not raised
usedIn.s: Against some who say there is no resurrection of the dead, Paul argues that then Christ was not raised either, calls Christ the firstfruits, and asks why anyone is baptized for the dead or why he fights wild beasts if the dead are not raised.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 4:7-18, Treasure in clay jars
usedIn.s: Paul carries God's treasure in a clay jar, hard pressed but not crushed, carrying Jesus' dying in his body so that Jesus' life may show, while the outer self wastes away and the inner self is renewed day by day.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18, Grief with hope, and the welcoming party
usedIn.s: Paul tells a grieving church that believers who have died are not lost: when the Lord comes down from heaven with a shout, the archangel's voice and God's trumpet, the dead in Christ will rise first, and the living will be caught up with them to meet the Lord in the air.

usedIn.n: Revelation 11:1-14, the measured temple and the two witnesses
usedIn.s: John is told to measure God's temple and its worshipers but to leave out the outer court, given to the nations to trample for forty-two months. Two witnesses in sackcloth prophesy with the powers of Elijah and Moses, are killed by the beast from the Abyss and left unburied in the great city, then raised and taken up to heaven.

usedIn.n: Revelation 14:6-20, Babylon fallen, the harvest and the winepress
usedIn.s: Three angels announce an eternal gospel, the fall of Babylon and the undiluted cup of God's wrath for those who worship the beast, and a voice blesses those who die in the Lord. Then one like a son of man reaps the earth's grain with a sickle, and an angel gathers its grapes into the great winepress, from which blood flows as high as the horses' bridles.

usedIn.n: Revelation 18:9-24, kings, merchants and the cargo list
usedIn.s: The kings, the merchants and the sea captains stand far off and mourn as Babylon burns, because no one buys their cargoes any more, a long list of luxuries that ends with human beings. An angel hurls a great millstone into the sea, and the sounds of music, craftsmen, the mill, the lamp and the wedding fall silent in the city where the blood of prophets and saints was found.

usedIn.n: Revelation 19:11-21, the rider on the white horse
usedIn.s: Heaven opens and a rider on a white horse, named Faithful and True and the Word of God, leads heaven's armies, his robe stained with blood and a sword coming from his mouth, his title King of kings. Birds are summoned to feast on the fallen, the beast and the false prophet are seized and cast into the fiery lake, and their armies fall to the rider's sword.

entries.title: Women who followed
entries.summary: Women traveled with Jesus, paid for his movement, and stayed at the cross and the tomb when the men had gone.
entries.plain: **The volunteers who kept the whole thing running were the ones still standing there at the end.** In Jesus' world men and women who were not family did not mix freely in public. Yet the Gospels name women who followed Jesus from Galilee, gave him their support, watched him die and went to his tomb.
entries.then: Women acting as financial patrons was not unusual, and they often served as patrons of religious groups, though much less often than men. A movement's critics could still attack it. Women following a teacher, though, may have looked scandalous to outsiders. Women were not usually seen as a threat of revolt the way men were, and men tended to treat brave women as exceptions. Bailey, drawing on Ben Sirach, argues that by Jesus' day women were clearly ranked below men, and that self-respecting rabbis did not talk with women in public. He holds that Jesus had women disciples who traveled with him and helped fund the movement. Comparing Mark's burial account (15:40-47) with the resurrection account (16:1-8), Bailey finds the women at the edges of the first and at the center of the second. On the woman with the perfume, Keener suggests it may have been her dowry, an inheritance, or her own means. Family and friends were usually present at an execution, and only the male disciples were in danger as suspected allies of a rebel. Women's testimony counted for little. Keener says the surrounding culture "considered their witness worthless," so choosing women as the first witnesses of the resurrection runs against what the culture valued. Paul's greetings in Romans 16 name about twenty-eight people, nearly 40 percent of them women, and he commends the work of more than half of those women.
entries.bridge: An analogy: the people who ran the supply lines of a movement whose public speakers were all men. The history books list the speakers. The suppliers are in the account books and at the graveside.
entries.changes: Women followed and supported Jesus' movement, which outsiders could find scandalous, so their presence at the cross and the tomb, as in Mark 15:40-41, stands out after the men have fled. Luke 8:2-3 names women who supported the group from their own means, and Paul's greetings in Romans 16:1-7 commend women as patrons and coworkers.
entries.not: **Not staff behind the lines.** Suppliers stay out of sight. These women traveled with Jesus, stood at the cross and were the first witnesses of the resurrection, in a culture that counted women's witness for little.

usedIn.n: Matthew 27:27-56, Mock king, the cross and the torn curtain
usedIn.s: Soldiers dress Jesus as a mock king. He is crucified as king of the Jews between two rebels, cries out in the words of Psalm 22 and dies; the curtain tears, the earth shakes, and women watch from a distance.

usedIn.n: Matthew 28:1-15, Women at dawn and a bribed guard
usedIn.s: At dawn after the Sabbath an angel rolls back the stone and tells two women that Jesus is risen. They meet him on the road, while the chief priests pay the guards to say the disciples stole the body.

usedIn.n: Mark 14:1-11, Perfume at Bethany
usedIn.s: Two days before Passover, at dinner in Bethany, a woman pours costly perfume on Jesus' head. He says she has anointed him for burial, and Judas goes to the chief priests.

usedIn.n: Mark 15:21-41, The cross
usedIn.s: Jesus is crucified as king of the Jews between two bandits, mocked by passers-by, and dies with a loud cry. The temple curtain tears, and women watch from a distance.

usedIn.n: Mark 15:42-16:8, The tomb
usedIn.s: Joseph of Arimathea buries Jesus before the Sabbath. When it is over, the women come with spices, find the stone rolled away, and hear that he has been raised.

usedIn.n: Luke 8:1-3, Women who paid the bills
usedIn.s: As Jesus travels from town to town with the Twelve, women he has healed travel with them, among them Joanna, wife of Herod's household manager, and they support the group from their own means.

usedIn.n: Luke 10:38-42, Mary at the teacher's feet
usedIn.s: In Martha's house Mary sits at Jesus' feet listening while Martha works at serving. When Martha complains, Jesus says Mary has chosen the better part.

usedIn.n: John 19:16-30, The cross, the notice in three languages, and his mother
usedIn.s: Jesus carries his own cross to Golgotha. Pilate's notice, King of the Jews, is written in Aramaic, Latin and Greek; soldiers cast lots for his seamless tunic; he gives his mother to the beloved disciple, takes the sour wine and says it is finished.

usedIn.n: John 20:1-18, The empty tomb and the gardener
usedIn.s: Mary Magdalene finds the stone moved and runs to Peter and the beloved disciple, who see the linen cloths lying in the empty tomb. Weeping outside, she takes the risen Jesus for the gardener until he says her name, and he sends her to tell the others.

usedIn.n: Acts 1:12-26, The Twelve made whole by lot
usedIn.s: Back in Jerusalem the apostles pray in an upstairs room with the women and Jesus' family. Peter says Judas's place must be filled, and the lot falls on Matthias.

usedIn.n: Romans 16:1-2, Phoebe of Cenchreae
usedIn.s: Paul commends Phoebe, a servant or deacon of the church at Cenchreae and a patron of many, Paul included, and asks the Romans to welcome her and help her in whatever she needs.

usedIn.n: Romans 16:3-16, Greet the church in their house
usedIn.s: Paul greets more than two dozen believers in Rome by name, from Prisca and Aquila and the church in their house to the households of Aristobulus and Narcissus, and tells them to greet one another with a holy kiss.

entries.title: Family trees, myths and genealogies
entries.summary: Lists of ancestors that proved who you were: a true Israelite, a priest, an heir of David. Matthew opens with one. Some teachers also spun stories and family trees out of the Bible's lists, which 1 Timothy calls myths and endless genealogies.
entries.plain: **Her grandmother could name the family back seven generations, and everyone at the table knew why it mattered.** A genealogy is a list of ancestors. In Jesus' world it was proof: of belonging to Israel, of the right to serve as a priest, or of a claim to David's throne. Lists could skip names and round off numbers to make a pattern, and they normally named men only.
entries.then: Ancient biographies usually began with their subject's noble ancestry, and Jewish genealogies documented a person's line as a pure Israelite, a priest or royalty. At least partial records of important families, especially priestly ones, were kept in the temple. A claim to David's line made before AD 70 could still be checked (Keener, citing Romans 1:3). Josephus closes his own priestly pedigree with the words "Thus have I set down the genealogy of my family" and says he took it from the public records. Jews kept genealogies to establish heritage, inheritance, legitimacy and rights. Genealogies could leave out generations, and dividing history into eras was common. Women did not need to appear. Bailey writes, "Middle Eastern genealogies are expected to be lists of men." Wright adds that tracing your line through David and the kings of Judah was a political statement under Herod, who had no royal blood. Lists could also be spun out. Some Jewish works of the period expanded the Bible's genealogies, and some claimed ancestry the Bible never gave. Philosophers from Plato on dismissed myths and genealogies together. Philo and Josephus denied that Scripture held any myths, but stories elaborating on the Bible were common, and Keener thinks these are the myths of 1 Timothy. The ESV Study Bible takes the genealogies there as speculation built on Old Testament accounts of biblical figures and their family trees. Jewish tradition also named Pharaoh's magicians Jannes and Jambres, the kind of elaboration that may lie behind the myths Paul opposes. Keener takes the Jewish myths of Titus 1:14 to mean especially haggadot, stories that amplified or explained the Bible's narratives.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a royal line of succession printed in an official program. It looks like a dry list of names, but every name is a claim, and anyone who wants the crown has to appear on it.
entries.changes: A family tree at the start of a story states a claim before the story begins, as Matthew 1:1 does with David and Abraham, while Luke 3:23-38 runs the other way, from Jesus back to Adam, as Greek genealogies did. A list could be shaped, cut and counted to make a point, so its gaps and surprise names are part of the message. Speculation spun out of the Bible's family trees is what 1 Timothy 1:4 calls endless genealogies.
entries.not: **Not an exact official record.** A line of succession lists every heir in order. Ancient genealogies could leave out generations and shape history into eras, and some writers spun stories and claims out of the Bible's lists.
entries.dissent: Two points. First, why Matthew names four women. Keener and the CSB Study Bible read them as Gentiles, or tied to a Gentile, hinting at the coming mission to all peoples. Bailey sees saints and sinners, men and women, all showing initiative. Wright reads them as reminders of the strange ways God worked inside the royal family, preparing for Mary's story. Heiser, following Amy Richter, argues that each woman's story echoes the Watchers' sin as told in 1 Enoch. Matthew names them, he writes, "to portend a messianic reversal of the sin of the Watchers." Second, what the myths and endless genealogies of 1 Timothy 1:4 were. Keener and his notes take them as Jewish elaborations of biblical stories and family lines, and the ESV Study Bible as speculation on Old Testament accounts. Wright and Bird find the false teaching rooted in Jewish soil. If the letter is late, they add, the attack on myths and genealogies is more likely aimed at the Valentinians, whose teaching traced a genealogy of heavenly beings.

usedIn.n: Matthew 1:1-17, The family tree
usedIn.s: Matthew opens with Jesus' ancestry from Abraham through David and the exile, in three sets of fourteen generations, and names four women along the way.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 1:1-11, Myths, endless genealogies and would-be teachers of the law
usedIn.s: Paul greets Timothy, whom he left in Ephesus, and tells him to stop certain people teaching strange doctrines and spending themselves on myths and endless genealogies; they want to be teachers of the law without understanding it, while the law is meant for the lawless.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 3:1-9, Terrible times, homes entered, and Jannes and Jambres
usedIn.s: Paul warns that the last days will bring terrible times and people who love themselves, money and pleasure, having a form of godliness but denying its power; some worm their way into homes and win over gullible women, opposing the truth as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses.

usedIn.n: Titus 1:10-16, The circumcision group, and Cretans always liars
usedIn.s: Many rebellious talkers and deceivers, especially of the circumcision group, are upsetting whole households for dishonest gain; Paul quotes a Cretan prophet who called Cretans always liars, and warns against Jewish myths and human commands, for to the pure all things are pure.

usedIn.n: Titus 3:9-15, A divisive person, winter at Nicopolis, and Zenas and Apollos
usedIn.s: Titus is to avoid foolish controversies, genealogies and quarrels about the law, and to warn a divisive person twice before having nothing more to do with him; Paul plans to winter at Nicopolis and asks Titus to send Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way with everything they need.

entries.title: Betrothal and the wedding feast
entries.summary: A betrothal was a binding marriage contract made months before the couple lived together. The wedding that completed it was a week-long feast.
aliases: present you as a pure virgin
entries.plain: **They had signed the papers and were married in the eyes of the law, but the party and the move were a year away.** A Jewish betrothal was much more than an engagement. The families agreed terms, money changed hands, and the couple were called husband and wife, though they did not yet live together. Only divorce or death could end it. The wedding that followed was the biggest celebration a village knew.
entries.then: Betrothal bound more tightly than an engagement does today. It rested on a money agreement between the families, commonly lasted about a year, and could be ended only by divorce or death. The pair were already called husband and wife. Two witnesses, mutual consent and the groom's declaration made a Jewish betrothal; in Roman betrothals consent alone was enough. Marriage had three steps: the covenant at betrothal, the ceremony, and consummation, normally on the first night of a seven-day wedding. Paying a bride price to the bride's father was the older custom. A gift of money from her father was newer but now widespread. Before the wedding the bride was washed, perfumed, anointed and dressed. Later Jewish teachers called betrothal the bride's sanctification, by which she was set apart for her husband. During a wedding feast no one could fast, mourn or do hard labor. The wedding night began toward evening. The groom and his party came to fetch the bride, often late because of last haggling over gifts. A procession with torches, music and dancing led her to his family's home, where the feast ran about seven days. A feast's size displayed the host's honor, so hosts invited as many as they could. A first invitation was followed by a summons when the food was ready, and refusing at the second call broke a promise and insulted the host. Blomberg calls the first notice a "save the date" invitation. Guests were expected to come in clean clothes at the least.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a signed contract to buy a house, with moving day a year off. The deal binds you now, backing out takes a legal process, and the housewarming when it comes is for the whole street.
entries.changes: Betrothal explains how a man could be called a woman's husband before they lived together, and why ending it took a divorce, as in Matthew 1:18-19. Wedding joy suspended fasting and mourning, so the bridegroom saying in Mark 2:19 makes fasting look out of place while Jesus is present. John 2:1-11 sets a sign at a village wedding.
entries.not: **Not a deal over property.** A house contract binds two parties to a sale. A betrothal joined two families, with witnesses and money, and made the couple husband and wife in name, commonly about a year before they lived together.
entries.dissent: The night procession in Matthew 25. Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes say the women carried torches, sticks wrapped in oil-soaked rags that burned only a short time, and waited with the bride at her parents' home. Bailey says village women always carry lamps, held before their faces for their reputation and safety, and places the young women in the street by the groom's home, waiting for the procession to return. On the wedding clothes of Matthew 22, the ESV Study Bible and Blomberg report the view that the king supplied festal garments, while Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes say only that coming in soiled clothes insulted the host.

entries.title: Divorce and the certificate
entries.summary: A Jewish husband ended a marriage, or a betrothal, by handing his wife a written certificate before witnesses that left her free to marry again, and the teachers argued over the grounds. In Greek and Roman law either partner could end a marriage by leaving.
entries.plain: **One signed sheet of paper, two witnesses, and the marriage was over.** Under Jewish law a husband could divorce his wife by writing her a certificate. The paper's main job was to free her to marry someone else. Teachers argued about what reasons were good enough, and money and public shame rode on how it was done.
entries.then: The certificate's key phrase was "You are now free to marry another man" (the ESV Study Bible cites the Mishnah, Gittin 9.3). Josephus has a man who divorces his wife for any cause give her writing that "he will never use her as his wife any more," so that she may remarry. A divorce needed only a document and two witnesses, unless the wife sought it, when a judge was required. A man who divorced a faithful wife gave back what she had brought into the marriage. He kept it from an unfaithful wife, whom law and custom required him to divorce. Hillel's school permitted divorce on any grounds, Shammai's only for sexual immorality. The CSB Study Bible says rabbinic commentaries multiplied grounds, such as fading beauty or burnt food. Since Jewish law in principle allowed a man more than one wife, only the wife's divorce was a legal question. The imbalance was ancient. In Old Babylonian law, about 2004 to 1595 BC, a husband could divorce his wife easily, though he had to pay her support. She had to prove to the city council that he had slandered her without cause, and an Assyrian husband of that era said "You are not my wife!" (Podany). In Greek and Roman marriage either partner could end it with little notice. Divorce was widespread in a city such as Corinth, and the children normally went to the father. Judean marriage contracts bound a husband to have intercourse with his wife, and teachers debated how long he could vow to abstain. Roman law made a husband who learned of his wife's adultery divorce her or face a charge of pimping. Jews punished adultery with divorce and shame.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a release form in a contract dispute. Once it is signed and witnessed the other party is free to deal with someone else, and everyone argues about what reasons justify signing it.
entries.changes: The certificate explains how Joseph could end a betrothal quietly in Matthew 1:19, and why Jesus speaks of it in Mark 10:4. Because the grounds were debated between the schools, a question about divorce was a test of which side a teacher took. Where Greek and Roman law let either partner walk out, the words not bound in 1 Corinthians 7:15 echo the certificate's freedom to remarry.
entries.not: **Not a release both sides sign.** A contract release is agreed by both parties. Under Jewish law the husband wrote the certificate, and a judge came in only when the wife sought the divorce. Greek and Roman law let either partner leave.
entries.dissent: How to read Matthew 5:32. Keener reads it partly as hyperbole, a vivid warning against breaking a marriage, since Jesus elsewhere treats divorce as real though wrong. The ESV Study Bible reads it as a rule with one stated exception. The CSB Study Bible says Jesus held to Deuteronomy's original sense against the multiplied grounds.

entries.title: Children without standing
entries.summary: Children in the ancient world were loved but powerless. Status came with age, and a child had no rights or voice apart from the adults who provided for them.
aliases: fathers, do not embitter your children
entries.plain: **At the grown-ups' table the kids sit at the far end and wait to be served.** In Jesus' world children had no standing. They could not earn, speak in court or claim honor; status came with age. Parents loved them, but a child counted for something only through the family that cared for them. Speakers held up great men as models, never children.
entries.then: Little children were the most powerless people in ancient society. In most of that world, status and authority grew with age. Jewish culture loved its children and did not look down on them. Still, a child had no standing of its own; whatever power or privilege it had came through its parents (Keener). Children were easily overlooked, and speakers and writers held up powerful leaders as the heroes to copy. Rank and status were everyday questions, and some Jewish texts spoke of ranks within the kingdom. When people brought children to be blessed, the laying on of hands recalled Jacob blessing his grandsons (Genesis 48:14). Disciples who kept people away from their master might remind hearers of Gehazi pushing the Shunammite woman back (2 Kings 4:27). The ESV Study Bible draws out the point of the comparison: a child cannot push his or her own cause forward without a parent. Jewish and Greco-Roman writers agreed that children must honor their parents and obey them while young. Many Jewish teachers counted honoring parents the greatest commandment. Beating was a normal part of raising and schooling children, and only a few writers objected to harsh discipline. A Greek or Roman newborn became a legal person only when the father acknowledged it. Unwanted babies could be abandoned, and deformed ones killed. Jews and Christians opposed both abortion and abandonment.
entries.bridge: An analogy: the youngest intern in a large firm, with no title, no vote and no voice in meetings. Telling the partners to become like him would sound like a joke.
entries.changes: Because children had no standing, holding one up as the model of greatness, as in Matthew 18:3-4, turns the ladder of rank upside down, and welcoming a child in Jesus' name treats the powerless as his representatives. When the disciples turn children away in Mark 10:13-14, they are shielding their teacher in the usual way, and he overrules them. Ephesians 6:4 tells fathers not to exasperate their children, where most writers took beating for granted.
entries.not: **Not a junior employee on the way up.** An intern has a contract, rights and the hope of promotion. An ancient child had no standing of its own, and a Greek or Roman newborn did not even count as a legal person until the father acknowledged it.

entries.title: Slavery and slave managers
entries.summary: Slaves were everywhere in the Roman world, from field hands to stewards who ran whole estates and handled their master's money. A master away and slaves left in charge was a familiar story.
aliases: those who benefit from their service
entries.plain: **The owner was abroad for a year, and the manager had the keys, the accounts and the staff.** Slavery was part of ordinary life in Jesus' world. Many slaves did hard labor, but a wealthy household might put a trusted slave over the other slaves, the stores and even the money. Such a slave could live better than a free peasant, and could still be beaten or sold when the master came home.
entries.then: A well-to-do estate owner usually put one steward over his other slaves (Blomberg). Absentee owners were common. While the master was away, such a manager controlled the rations and could abuse his power, and stories used the master's long journey as the test. Roman law let slaves run estates, hold money and earn bonuses. Some imperial freedmen had more power than many aristocrats, and upper-level slaves could live better than most free peasants. Some laws treated slaves as persons, others as property, and masters could beat them. Keener puts the price of an average slave at five hundred to two thousand days' wages. Turning the roles of master and slave upside down was radical anywhere in antiquity. Redemption meant freeing a slave, usually for a price. Slaves could receive wages, the peculium, and sometimes buy their freedom with them. Wright and Bird estimate that slaves made up as much as 30 per cent of some cities. Keener estimates that perhaps 80 percent of Rome's people descended from freed slaves from the East. Wright adds that a story about a master and his slaves would almost certainly be heard as a story about God and Israel. Roman law made anyone sheltering a runaway slave return him. The law of Moses forbade handing an escaped slave back (Deuteronomy 23:15-16). A recaptured runaway faced severe punishment. Slavery was ancient. Around 2100 BC in the kingdom of Ur, Podany shows, people became slaves through debt, sale by poor parents or capture in war. Debt slaves went free when the debt was paid, but bought slaves had no legal way out. Ur-Namma's laws set a reward for returning a runaway.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a hired estate manager with power of attorney while the owner travels. He signs for everything, and the owner can come home without warning and audit the books.
entries.changes: A master who goes away and leaves a slave in charge was a stock story, so a parable like Matthew 24:45-51 asks what the slave does when no one is watching. Because slaves stood at the bottom of the ladder of honor, a call for leaders to be the slave of all, as in Mark 10:44, overturned rank. Paul calls himself a slave of Christ Jesus in Romans 1:1.
entries.not: **Not a free employee who can resign.** A hired manager signs a contract and can walk away. The ancient steward was usually a slave himself, owned by his master, open to beating or sale, and free only if he was released or bought his way out.
entries.dissent: Two questions. First, what Paul's household rules imply about slavery itself. Keener says no one in Paul's day proposed abolition, which not even a revolt could have won, but that telling masters to treat slaves the same way (Ephesians 6:9) points toward it. Wright and Bird stress that slavery's existence was never debated in antiquity. The cultural backgrounds article adds that freed slaves often bought slaves of their own. The ESV Study Bible says Paul does not condone the system and that it slowly died out through Christian influence; the CSB Study Bible says his words later helped inspire the anti-slavery movement. Second, how far Philemon challenges slavery. Keener says it goes beyond other documents of its time in asking for a slave's release because he is now a Christian. The CSB Study Bible says Paul accepts slavery as a legal fact without endorsing it, and so undermines it. Wright writes, "As a policy statement about slavery, the letter falls short", though he calls it brilliant as a one-off pastoral strategy. Carson, Moo and Morris say calling Onesimus a brother "makes slavery meaningless", though Paul asks only for a kind welcome.

usedIn.n: Matthew 18:21-35, Ten thousand talents and a hundred denarii
usedIn.s: Peter asks whether forgiving seven times is enough. Jesus tells of a king who cancels an impossible debt, and of the forgiven servant who then chokes a colleague over a small one.

usedIn.n: Matthew 24:29-51, The Son of Man on the clouds and the slave in charge
usedIn.s: After the distress, sun, moon and stars fail and the Son of Man comes on the clouds to gather his chosen. No one knows the day, so the household must stay ready, like a slave left in charge.

usedIn.n: Matthew 25:14-30, Five, two and one talent
usedIn.s: A man going abroad entrusts his property to three slaves. Two double what they were given and are rewarded; the third buries his talent and is thrown out.

usedIn.n: Luke 7:1-10, A centurion who built the synagogue
usedIn.s: Jewish elders in Capernaum plead for a centurion whose valued slave is dying, because he loves their nation and built their synagogue. The centurion sends word that Jesus need not come under his roof, only give the order.

usedIn.n: Luke 12:35-48, Slaves waiting up for the master
usedIn.s: Jesus tells his followers to be dressed for action with lamps lit, like slaves waiting for their master to come home from a wedding, and asks what a slave left in charge will do if the master is delayed.

usedIn.n: Luke 19:11-27, The nobleman who went to receive a kingdom
usedIn.s: Because people think the kingdom is about to appear, Jesus tells of a nobleman who travels to a far country to be made king while citizens who hate him send a delegation after him, and of the servants who trade with his money.

usedIn.n: Luke 22:24-38, Benefactors, thrones, sifting and two swords
usedIn.s: At the last supper the disciples argue over who is greatest. Jesus contrasts kings who are called benefactors with himself as one who serves, promises them thrones, warns Peter that Satan has asked to sift them, and speaks of swords.

usedIn.n: Romans 1:1-7, A slave of the Messiah writes to Rome
usedIn.s: Paul opens with his name and titles, a short summary of the good news about God's Son, and a greeting of grace and peace to believers in Rome he has never met.

usedIn.n: Romans 3:21-31, Redemption and the mercy seat
usedIn.s: Paul announces that God's righteousness has been revealed through faith in Jesus for all who believe, Jew and Gentile alike, through a redemption and an atoning death he links to the mercy seat.

usedIn.n: Romans 6:1-23, Slaves of a new master
usedIn.s: Baptized into Christ's death, believers are dead to sin. Once slaves of sin, they have been set free to become slaves of God, whose gift is eternal life.

usedIn.n: Romans 8:12-17, Not slaves but adopted heirs
usedIn.s: Those led by God's Spirit are God's children. They have received the Spirit of adoption, not of slavery, and cry Abba, Father, as heirs of God with Christ.

usedIn.n: Romans 16:3-16, Greet the church in their house
usedIn.s: Paul greets more than two dozen believers in Rome by name, from Prisca and Aquila and the church in their house to the households of Aristobulus and Narcissus, and tells them to greet one another with a holy kiss.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 6:12-20, The body and the prostitute
usedIn.s: Answering slogans such as everything is permissible and food is for the stomach, Paul argues that the body belongs to the Lord, will be raised, and must not be joined to a prostitute, for believers were bought at a price.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 7:17-24, Circumcised or not, slave or free
usedIn.s: Paul tells each believer to live the life the Lord assigned when he was called: the circumcised should not undo it, the uncircumcised should not seek it, and a slave should not be troubled, though he should take his freedom if he can.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 9:1-27, Free, unpaid and in training
usedIn.s: Paul defends his right as an apostle to be supported and explains why he has never used it, makes himself a slave to all to win more, and pictures his discipline as an athlete's training for a wreath that will not wither.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 12:1-31, Mute idols and one body
usedIn.s: Paul reminds the Corinthians that as pagans they were led astray to mute idols, describes the many gifts of the one Spirit, and pictures the church as one body whose weaker and less honored members are indispensable.

usedIn.n: Galatians 3:23-29, The law as a guardian until faith came
usedIn.s: Before faith came, Paul says, we were held in custody under the law, which served as a guardian until Christ; now all who have been baptized into Christ are God's children, one in him, Abraham's seed and heirs.

usedIn.n: Galatians 4:1-11, Heirs, slaves and the elements of the world
usedIn.s: An heir who is still a child is no better off than a slave, Paul says; so we were enslaved under the elements of the world until God sent his Son to redeem us and his Spirit to cry Abba, and he asks why the Galatians want to go back to observing special days, months, seasons and years.

usedIn.n: Galatians 4:21-5:1, Hagar, Sarah and Sinai in Arabia
usedIn.s: Paul reads the story of Abraham's two sons as a figure of two covenants: Hagar the slave stands for Sinai and the present Jerusalem, Sarah the free woman for the Jerusalem above, and he calls the Galatians to stand firm in freedom.

usedIn.n: Galatians 5:13-6:10, Flesh and Spirit, burdens and teachers
usedIn.s: Called to freedom, the Galatians are to serve one another in love, which fulfills the law; Paul sets the works of the flesh against the fruit of the Spirit and urges them to restore the fallen gently, carry each other's burdens, share with their teachers and keep doing good.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 6:1-9, Children, fathers, slaves and masters
usedIn.s: The household code goes on to children and fathers, then to slaves and masters, asking something of each side and reminding masters that they and their slaves have the same Master in heaven.

usedIn.n: Philippians 2:1-11, The form of a slave, a cross, and every knee
usedIn.s: Paul urges humility and concern for others, then sets out Christ, who did not exploit his equality with God but took the form of a slave and died on a cross, and whom God exalted so that every knee will bow.

usedIn.n: Colossians 1:1-14, Epaphras's report and a change of kingdoms
usedIn.s: Paul and Timothy greet the believers at Colossae, a church Paul has never visited, thank God for what Epaphras has told them, and pray that they grow in knowledge, having been rescued out of darkness into the kingdom of God's Son.

usedIn.n: Colossians 1:24-2:5, Sufferings for the body, and a steward of the mystery
usedIn.s: Paul rejoices to suffer for the church, fills up what is lacking in Christ's afflictions, calls himself the servant entrusted with God's long hidden mystery, and tells churches he has never met how hard he struggles for them.

usedIn.n: Colossians 3:1-17, Things above, and no Greek, Jew, barbarian or Scythian
usedIn.s: Raised with Christ, the believers are to set their minds on things above, put to death the old ways, take off the old self and put on the new, in which there is no Greek or Jew, barbarian, Scythian, slave or free, and above all put on love.

usedIn.n: Colossians 3:18-4:1, The household code
usedIn.s: Paul addresses wives and husbands, children and fathers, slaves and masters in the form of an ancient household code, tells husbands to love and fathers not to embitter, and reminds masters that they too have a Master in heaven.

usedIn.n: Colossians 4:7-18, Tychicus, Onesimus, Nympha's house and the letter from Laodicea
usedIn.s: Paul sends the letter with Tychicus and Onesimus, passes on greetings from Jewish and Gentile co-workers, greets Nympha and the church in her house, asks for this letter to be read at Laodicea and the Laodicean letter at Colossae, and signs off in his own hand.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 1:1-11, Myths, endless genealogies and would-be teachers of the law
usedIn.s: Paul greets Timothy, whom he left in Ephesus, and tells him to stop certain people teaching strange doctrines and spending themselves on myths and endless genealogies; they want to be teachers of the law without understanding it, while the law is meant for the lawless.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 6:1-10, Slaves under the yoke, and godliness as gain
usedIn.s: Slaves are to respect their masters so that the faith is not slandered, and those with believing masters are to serve them all the more; then Paul turns on teachers who treat godliness as a way to get rich, and warns that the craving for money breeds every kind of harm.

usedIn.n: Titus 2:1-10, Older men, older women, young wives and slaves
usedIn.s: Titus is to teach what fits sound doctrine to each group in the household of faith, older men, older women, younger women, younger men and slaves, so that outsiders have no cause to speak against God's message and the teaching about God is made attractive.

usedIn.n: Philemon 8-25, Onesimus sent home with a letter
usedIn.s: Paul appeals to Philemon, on the basis of love, for Onesimus, the slave who became Paul's son in prison: he sends him back to be received as a beloved brother rather than as a slave, asks Philemon to welcome him as he would Paul, offers to repay anything he owes, and asks for a guest room.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 2:18-25, Household slaves and a harsh master
usedIn.s: Peter tells household slaves to submit to their masters, the harsh as well as the kind, because suffering unjustly while doing good is commendable before God. Christ suffered for them, leaving an example: insulted, he did not insult in return, and by his wounds they have been healed.

usedIn.n: 2 Peter 2:10-22, The glorious ones, the way of Balaam, a dog and a sow
usedIn.s: The false teachers slander the glorious ones, which even angels do not dare to do. Like unreasoning animals they carouse in daylight, with eyes full of adultery; they have followed Balaam, who loved profit gained by wrongdoing and was rebuked by a donkey. They promise freedom while slaves of corruption, and they are like a dog returning to its vomit and a washed sow to the mud.

usedIn.n: Revelation 18:9-24, kings, merchants and the cargo list
usedIn.s: The kings, the merchants and the sea captains stand far off and mourn as Babylon burns, because no one buys their cargoes any more, a long list of luxuries that ends with human beings. An angel hurls a great millstone into the sea, and the sounds of music, craftsmen, the mill, the lamp and the wedding fall silent in the city where the blood of prophets and saints was found.

entries.title: Birth, naming and the shame of childlessness
entries.summary: A child, above all a son, was a family's future and its support in old age. A childless couple met suspicion and shame; a birth brought the neighbors in, and a Jewish boy was circumcised on the eighth day.
entries.plain: **Every year without a baby, the questions at family gatherings got harder.** In the world of the Bible, children were a family's security and a sign of God's blessing. A couple who could not have children faced pity, gossip and sometimes the suspicion that God was punishing them, and the wife usually took the blame. When a child came, the neighbors came too. A Jewish boy was circumcised on the eighth day, and his family chose a name that tied him to the family line.
entries.then: Childlessness was an economic and social disaster (Keener). No one would support the parents in old age. The law sometimes treated barrenness as a judgment for sin, many people assumed the worst, and most blamed the wife. In many Judean circles custom expected a husband to divorce a wife who had borne no children for many years, and shame clung to childlessness. The Old Testament remembers Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Hannah and Samson's mother as women God enabled to bear. Rachel's cry that God had taken away her disgrace (Genesis 30:23) lies behind Elizabeth's words. The ESV Study Bible stresses that Zechariah and Elizabeth's childlessness was not caused by any sin of theirs. Neighbors joined in when a child was born. A son was circumcised on the eighth day in the family home, usually by the father in this period. Children were often named after a grandfather, and the father had the final say. Keener adds that Jewish children had customarily been named at birth, and that naming at circumcision is attested only late, apart from Luke. Roman babies were named eight or nine days after birth, so Luke may reflect Greek and Roman influence on Jewish custom (Keener). Midwives normally helped at a birth. Babies were wrapped in long strips of cloth to keep their limbs straight, sometimes for up to two months. Bailey adds that swaddling, mentioned in Ezekiel 16:4, was still practiced among village people in Syria and Palestine. Under Roman custom, unlike Jewish, a father could even decide not to raise a newborn.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a family farm with no heir. Everyone in the district knows what happens to the land and the old couple when there is no one to take over, and some of them whisper about why.
entries.changes: A long childless marriage, as with Zechariah and Elizabeth in Luke 1:7, carried shame and a question of blame, so calling them righteous answers what the neighbors assumed. Hebrews 11:11 remembers Sarah, long past the age, receiving power to conceive, the first in a line of such births. Paul's circumcision on the eighth day, in Philippians 3:5, marks him as born inside the covenant.
entries.not: **Not a matter of property alone.** A farm without an heir is an economic problem. Childlessness then also brought shame, fell mostly on the wife, could end a marriage, and was sometimes taken as a judgment from God, so a birth set the parents right in public.
