usedIn.n: Luke 1:5-25, A priest's turn at the incense altar
usedIn.s: An elderly village priest, picked by lot to offer incense in the sanctuary, learns from the angel Gabriel that his childless wife will have a son who will prepare Israel for God with an Elijah-like power.

usedIn.n: Luke 2:1-7, A census and a manger
usedIn.s: Augustus orders a registration, and Joseph takes the pregnant Mary from Nazareth to Bethlehem, the town of David. She gives birth there and lays the child in a manger, because there is no room for them in the lodging.

usedIn.n: Luke 2:21-40, Two birds, Simeon and Anna
usedIn.s: Jesus is circumcised and named on the eighth day. At the temple his parents make the offering the law allowed the poor, and two old people waiting for God's comfort, Simeon and the widow Anna, speak about the child.

entries.title: Widows
entries.summary: A woman whose husband died usually lost her income with him and depended on a son, relatives or charity. A widow who stayed faithful to her husband's memory and did not remarry was honored.
entries.plain: **When her husband died, his wages died with him, and her son became her only safety net.** In the ancient world, women could rarely earn enough to live on. A widow depended on her sons, on relatives with means, or on charity. Losing an only son could leave her with nothing. At the same time, a widow who did not remarry and gave her life to prayer was respected as faithful.
entries.then: A woman ordinarily could not earn enough to live on, so a widow depended on her son in old age. For a widow's only son to die before her was thought a deep tragedy. Unless she had relatives with means, it left her relying on public charity, and the ESV Study Bible calls her situation desperate. Jews and Greco-Romans often admired widows who never remarried as devout and loyal. Judith, the famous widow of Jewish tradition, was said to have stayed a widow until she died at 105. Keener counts widows, with lepers, among the socially weak in Jesus' sermon at Nazareth, where Elijah is sent to a widow in Sidon (1 Kings 17). By custom the widow or the dead man's mother led the funeral procession, so a widow burying her son walked at its head. In the law the widow was the standard example of the oppressed, and judges were told to defend her (Exodus 22:22-24). Men controlled the courts, so she was easily exploited, and the unscrupulous could take her property by legal means. Levirate marriage, in which a man married his dead brother's widow (Deuteronomy 25:5-6), was meant to protect her. In Jerusalem, Jews from abroad who had settled there in old age left many widows without local family. Synagogues supported the widows of their own circle and helped their destitute widows. Since Augustus, quick remarriage for younger widows had been a Roman ideal, and a Jewish one too.
entries.bridge: An analogy: an elderly mother whose only grown child pays her rent, and who then loses that child. The grief comes with a question nobody says aloud: who will pay now?
entries.changes: A widow following her only son's bier, as in Luke 7:12, is losing her future along with her child. The first church in Jerusalem took on the daily care of widows, as Acts 6:1 shows, and 1 Timothy 5:3-16 sets rules for which widows the church should support.
entries.not: **Not a loss a modern safety net would catch.** The modern mother has pensions, welfare and courts that hear her. An ancient widow usually could not earn a living, men ran the courts, and her only cover was family, levirate marriage or synagogue charity.
entries.dissent: Three questions. First, Anna's age in Luke 2:37. Keener notes that if the eighty-four years were her widowhood, after seven years of marriage begun at the common age of fourteen, she would be 105, like Judith. The CSB Study Bible reads it the same way and calls the other reading a poor fit. The cultural backgrounds notes take eighty-four as her age, already exceptionally old then. Second, how helpless the widow was. The cultural backgrounds notes, the CSB Study Bible and Bailey treat the widow of Luke 18:1-8 as nearly powerless, with no bribe to offer and no man to speak for her. Levine argues that biblical widows, from Tamar and Ruth to Abigail and Judith, show strength and cunning against the stereotype of the poor, dependent woman. Third, who the widows on the list in 1 Timothy 5:9 were. Keener thinks they were a recognized group of widows serving the church, as in the second century, and adds, "Commentators disagree on this point." The ESV Study Bible calls an office unlikely, "since the stated issue is provision for those in need." Wright reads enrollment as a commitment to make the church one's primary family.

usedIn.n: Luke 2:21-40, Two birds, Simeon and Anna
usedIn.s: Jesus is circumcised and named on the eighth day. At the temple his parents make the offering the law allowed the poor, and two old people waiting for God's comfort, Simeon and the widow Anna, speak about the child.

usedIn.n: Luke 7:11-17, A widow's only son on the bier
usedIn.s: At the gate of Nain Jesus meets a funeral for a widow's only son. He touches the bier, raises the young man and gives him back to his mother, and the crowd says a great prophet has arisen.

usedIn.n: Luke 18:1-8, The widow and the judge
usedIn.s: Jesus tells of a judge who neither feared God nor respected people and a widow who kept coming to him for justice until he gave in. How much more, he says, will God see justice done for his chosen ones.

usedIn.n: Luke 20:27-40, The Sadducees and the woman with seven husbands
usedIn.s: Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, ask whose wife a woman married to seven brothers will be. Jesus answers that the risen do not marry and are like the angels, and argues from the burning bush.

usedIn.n: Luke 20:45-21:4, Long robes and a widow's two coins
usedIn.s: Jesus warns against teachers of the law who love long robes and the best seats and devour widows' houses. Then he watches a poor widow put two small coins into the temple treasury.

usedIn.n: John 19:16-30, The cross, the notice in three languages, and his mother
usedIn.s: Jesus carries his own cross to Golgotha. Pilate's notice, King of the Jews, is written in Aramaic, Latin and Greek; soldiers cast lots for his seamless tunic; he gives his mother to the beloved disciple, takes the sour wine and says it is finished.

usedIn.n: Acts 6:1-7, The Hellenists' widows and the Seven
usedIn.s: Greek-speaking believers complain that their widows are overlooked in the daily distribution of food. The Twelve have the community choose seven men, and lay hands on them.

usedIn.n: Acts 9:32-43, Lydda and Joppa
usedIn.s: Peter heals a paralyzed man at Lydda and, at Joppa, raises Tabitha, a disciple known for her charity, while the widows she clothed stand weeping. He stays on with a tanner.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 7:25-40, The present distress
usedIn.s: Because of the present distress and the shortness of the time, Paul advises the unmarried to stay as they are, though marrying is no sin, and tells a widow she is free to remarry, only in the Lord.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 5:1-16, Older men as fathers, and the widows' list
usedIn.s: Timothy is to treat older and younger believers as family; the church is to honor widows who are truly in need, families are to support their own, and only older widows of proven character are to be put on the list.

usedIn.n: James 1:19-27, Slow to anger, and the widows and orphans
usedIn.s: James tells his readers to be quick to listen and slow to speak and to anger, to do the word and not merely hear it, and names the religion God accepts: care for orphans and widows in their distress and a life kept unstained by the world.

entries.title: Adoption, heirs and wills
entries.summary: A family's property passed to its heirs; in Jewish practice the land went to the sons, the eldest with a double share. Roman law also let a man adopt a son, often a grown one, who left his old debts and ties behind and became his heir. A will, sealed before witnesses, settled who inherited and who looked after an heir too young to inherit.
aliases: heir no different from a slave
entries.plain: **He was thirty when the old man adopted him, and on that day his debts were gone and the business was his to inherit.** In Jesus' world a family's land passed from a father to his sons. Often the brothers kept it together, and the law gave the eldest a double share. If one brother wanted his part split off, the quarrel could tear the family apart. Romans had another way to make an heir: a man could adopt a son, even a grown one, and the adopted son left his old family's debts and ties behind and became heir to his new father's estate. A will was sealed before witnesses, and it named who would look after an heir still too young to take what was his.
entries.then: Under the law the eldest son received a double portion (Deuteronomy 21:17), and the shares were fixed. Rabbis were sometimes asked to settle disputes. Bailey describes the usual pattern: a father left the inheritance to his sons together, and Psalm 133:1 praised brothers living in harmony. The rabbis held that a division should be granted if one heir wanted it, while Roman law required both parties to agree (Bailey, citing Daube). A father could hand over his property before death but keep its use and income, so an heir could not legally sell his share. For people in Rome, adoption "meant a cancellation of old legal relationships, establishing a new relationship as an heir" (the cultural backgrounds notes). It had to be confirmed by witnesses. Romans usually adopted a grown man to make him their heir. Israel had its own sonship, since God called Israel his son at the exodus (Exodus 4:22), and Paul lists adoption among Israel's privileges. Ancient sources often set a householder's children, his heirs, against his slaves. Greeks used diatheke, Paul's word for covenant, for a will opened at death. Wills were sealed against alteration. "In Greek law, wills were irrevocable," though Roman law allowed changes (Keener). A minor heir stayed under guardians named in the will until the set time or puberty. Adoption to secure an heir is far older. In Old Babylonian Sippar, about 2004 to 1595 BC, Podany describes women devoted to the god Shamash who could not marry. They adopted nieces to care for them in old age and left them their property, and these daughters sometimes fought the women's brothers in court. An adopted slave gained freedom but little inheritance.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a family farm left to three children with no plan. As long as they work it together, it holds. The day one of them wants to sell his third, the lawyers come in, and the family may never sit at one table again.
entries.changes: Asking a teacher to divide an inheritance, as in Luke 12:13, asked for the kind of ruling a rabbi was expected to give. An heir who is still a child is no better off than a slave until the time his father set, as Galatians 4:1-2 puts it. Adoption made an outsider a full heir with his old debts cancelled, which is the picture behind Romans 8:15-17.
entries.not: **Not equal shares each child can sell at will.** Modern heirs usually split evenly and own their part outright. Under Israel's law the eldest took a double portion, and a share handed over before the father's death could not legally be sold while he kept its use and income.
entries.dissent: Four questions. First, what the man in Luke 12:13 wanted. The CSB Study Bible thinks he was probably a younger brother upset at the elder's double share. Bailey argues he was ordering Jesus to enforce a division already decided, knowing the rabbis allowed one whenever an heir asked. Second, whether asking for one's share early meant wishing the father dead. Keener says so; Levine, citing the Jewish legal scholar Bernard Jackson, says Jewish sources do not support the idea. Third, the background of adoption in Paul. Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes read Romans 8:15-16 against Roman legal adoption, and the ESV Study Bible calls sons a term of Roman adoption law. Wright reads it from Israel's story, adoption as Israel's calling since the exodus. Fourth, how closely Paul's legal pictures fit real law. Keener and the study Bibles treat Galatians 3:15 as an illustration from human wills. Wright answers that "The covenant is central; the making of wills is the fleeting analogy." On Hebrews 9:16-17, Keener sees a play on the one Greek word for covenant and will; the ESV Study Bible allows either a will or a Near Eastern covenant sealed by a sacrificial animal's death.

usedIn.n: Luke 12:13-21, Bigger barns
usedIn.s: A man asks Jesus to make his brother divide the inheritance. Jesus refuses, warns against greed, and tells of a rich farmer who plans bigger barns for his surplus and dies that night.

usedIn.n: Luke 15:11-32, A father and two lost sons
usedIn.s: A younger son takes his share of the estate early, wastes it in a far country, and comes home to a father who runs to meet him. The older brother refuses to join the feast.

usedIn.n: Luke 20:9-19, The tenants who killed the heir
usedIn.s: Jesus tells of a vineyard owner whose tenants beat his servants and kill his beloved son to take the inheritance. The leaders realize he has told it against them.

usedIn.n: Romans 8:12-17, Not slaves but adopted heirs
usedIn.s: Those led by God's Spirit are God's children. They have received the Spirit of adoption, not of slavery, and cry Abba, Father, as heirs of God with Christ.

usedIn.n: Romans 8:18-30, Groaning and firstfruits
usedIn.s: Creation groans as in labor, waiting to be freed from decay, and believers who have the firstfruits of the Spirit groan too as they wait for their adoption and the redemption of their bodies.

usedIn.n: Romans 9:1-5, Israel's privileges
usedIn.s: Paul grieves for his own people and lists what belongs to Israel: the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the law, the worship, the promises, the patriarchs and the Messiah.

usedIn.n: Galatians 3:15-22, A will no one can change, and a law given through angels
usedIn.s: Paul argues from the way a ratified will cannot be altered that the law, coming 430 years after the promise to Abraham and his seed, cannot cancel it, and says the law was added because of transgressions, put in place through angels by a mediator.

usedIn.n: Galatians 4:1-11, Heirs, slaves and the elements of the world
usedIn.s: An heir who is still a child is no better off than a slave, Paul says; so we were enslaved under the elements of the world until God sent his Son to redeem us and his Spirit to cry Abba, and he asks why the Galatians want to go back to observing special days, months, seasons and years.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 1:1-14, A circular letter opens with praise, a seal and a down payment
usedIn.s: Paul greets God's holy people and launches one long blessing of God for choosing, adopting, redeeming and sealing a mixed people, with the Spirit as the down payment of their inheritance.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 1:1-14, The Son above the angels
usedIn.s: God, who spoke in many ways through the prophets, has now spoken through a Son, heir of all things, who made purification for sins and sat down at the right hand of the Majesty. A chain of Scripture quotations sets the Son above the angels, who worship him and are sent to serve those who will inherit salvation.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 9:11-22, Blood, ashes and a will
usedIn.s: Christ entered the greater tent once for all with his own blood, not the blood of goats and calves. If the ashes of a heifer could make the unclean outwardly clean, how much more will his blood cleanse the conscience; and as a will takes effect only at a death, the new covenant was put in force by his.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 12:1-13, The race, the shame and the Father's discipline
usedIn.s: Surrounded by a great cloud of witnesses, believers are to throw off every weight and run with endurance, eyes fixed on Jesus, who endured the cross and scorned its shame. Their hardships are a father's discipline, which only legitimate children receive.

usedIn.n: Revelation 5:1-14, the sealed scroll and the Lamb
usedIn.s: In God's right hand is a scroll written on both sides and sealed with seven seals, and no one is worthy to open it until the Lion of Judah, the Root of David, appears as a Lamb that looks slain. The living creatures, the elders, countless angels and all creation worship him.

entries.title: Women in public
entries.summary: Custom kept unrelated men and women apart in public. Teachers warned men against talking much with women, a stranger was not to speak with a woman alone, and a woman's word counted for little in court. Most women were also taught far less than men, so a call for women to learn stood out.
aliases: I do not permit a woman to teach
entries.plain: **In some places a man does not chat with a woman he does not know, and people notice if he does.** In the world of the Gospels, men and women who were not family kept their distance in public. Jewish teachers told men not to talk much with women. A man speaking at length with a woman alone could be suspected of flirting, and her name suffered along with his. Her testimony also carried less weight than a man's. Most women also had far less schooling than men, above all in Scripture.
entries.then: Jewish piety warned men against talking much with women, and some rabbis said this applied even to their own wives (Keener). Most of the Mediterranean world disapproved of a man speaking with a woman in private. Bailey quotes the Mishnah tractate Abot: "talk not much with womankind". Asking a woman for water could look like flirting, especially if she was alone. Keener writes of Jesus at the well, "Jesus breaks all the rules of Jewish piety here." Women drew water together in the cooler hours, so a woman alone at noon stood out. A woman's word counted for little in court. For most legal matters Jewish men did not trust women as witnesses, though Roman courts restricted them less. Keener writes, "The witness of women was worth little in Judaism." Wright says flatly that "women were simply not acceptable as legal witnesses." Critics such as Celsus later mocked the Easter story for leaning on them. The CSB Study Bible finds "it is remarkable that Jesus appeared first to a woman" and sent her to tell the others. Bailey notes that at the well and at the tomb Jesus gives women commands that make them witnesses to men. Women were less often literate than men. They were rarely trained in philosophy, almost never in rhetoric, and in Judaism seldom taught the law, and most rabbis would not take them as disciples. Informed listeners usually asked questions at lectures, but uninformed questions were thought rude. Women had far less training than men in Scripture and public reasoning.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a pastor who keeps his office door open whenever a woman comes in to talk. Nothing need be wrong, but the rule protects both of them from gossip, and everyone notices when it is broken.
entries.changes: Because custom kept unrelated men and women apart, a teacher speaking at length with a woman, as Jesus does in John 4:27, surprises his own followers. Because most women had little schooling, a command that women learn, as in 1 Timothy 2:11, stood out in its day, whatever else the passage restricts. Because a woman's word counted for little, the first news of the empty tomb entrusted to women, as in Mark 16:7, runs against the culture.
entries.not: **Not a private precaution one man chooses.** The pastor's open door is his own policy. The ancient custom bound everyone, and it sat alongside courts that gave a woman's testimony little weight and teachers who rarely trained women.
entries.dissent: How far women's lack of training explains the limits on their teaching in 1 Timothy 2:11-15. Keener and his notes build a reading tied to the situation in Ephesus on it; the ESV Study Bible replies that inscriptions and literature show a number of well-educated women in Asia Minor at the time, and that Paul grounds the limit in creation. Wright's commentary on the Pastoral Letters reads the passage as a command that women be allowed to study, with verse 12 refusing a takeover like the Artemis cult's; the cultural backgrounds article on women's education adds that women taught men even more rarely than they studied.

usedIn.n: John 4:1-42, A Samaritan woman at Jacob's well
usedIn.s: Tired at noon, Jesus sits on Jacob's well and asks a Samaritan woman for a drink. They talk about living water, her husbands and the right mountain for worship, and her town comes out to meet him.

usedIn.n: John 20:1-18, The empty tomb and the gardener
usedIn.s: Mary Magdalene finds the stone moved and runs to Peter and the beloved disciple, who see the linen cloths lying in the empty tomb. Weeping outside, she takes the risen Jesus for the gardener until he says her name, and he sends her to tell the others.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 14:26-40, Order when the church meets
usedIn.s: Paul regulates a meeting where everyone brings a hymn, a teaching, a revelation or a tongue: speakers take turns, prophets weigh one another's words, women are to be silent and ask at home, and everything is to be done decently and in order.

usedIn.n: Philippians 4:2-9, Two women at odds, names in the book of life, and whatever is true
usedIn.s: Paul pleads with two women who worked beside him to agree, asks a companion to help them, notes that their names are in the book of life, and urges joy, prayer instead of worry, and thoughts fixed on whatever is true and excellent.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 2:8-15, Lifted hands, braided hair, women learning, Eve and childbearing
usedIn.s: Paul wants men to pray without anger or arguing and women to dress modestly; women are to learn quietly, and he does not permit a woman to teach or have authority over a man, arguing from Adam and Eve, before a hard saying about being saved through childbearing.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 1:1-7, Lois, Eunice and the laying on of hands
usedIn.s: Writing from custody, Paul greets Timothy as his dear son, thanks God as he remembers him in prayer night and day, recalls the faith of Timothy's grandmother Lois and mother Eunice, and urges him to fan into flame the gift given when Paul laid hands on him.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 3:1-9, Terrible times, homes entered, and Jannes and Jambres
usedIn.s: Paul warns that the last days will bring terrible times and people who love themselves, money and pleasure, having a form of godliness but denying its power; some worm their way into homes and win over gullible women, opposing the truth as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses.

usedIn.n: Titus 2:1-10, Older men, older women, young wives and slaves

entries.title: Friendship, and the friend of Caesar
entries.summary: The ancient world prized friendship: loyalty to the death, goods held in common, secrets shared. The same word covered a patron and his dependents, and friend of Caesar was a title a governor could not afford to lose.
aliases: lay down his life for his friends
I have you in my heart
you owe me your very self
entries.plain: **A real friend keeps your secrets, stands by you when it costs him, and treats what he has as yours.** Greeks and Romans wrote whole books about friendship and praised dying for a friend as the noblest thing a person could do. Friends were meant to share everything, including what was on their minds, and that was what set a friend apart from a servant. But friend was also the polite word for political ties: a powerful man called his dependents his friends, and a governor who was a friend of Caesar owed the emperor his loyalty.
entries.then: Ancient literature held up several ideals of friendship (Keener). A friend was loyal, sometimes to the death. Friends were equals who shared all they owned. A friend could be trusted with every confidence, and that closeness set a friend apart from a servant. Greeks prized laying down one's life for one's friends as the greatest act of friendship. Later rabbis gave it no special value, and Rabbi Akiba argued that one's own life came first. That friends hold all things in common was a commonly cited ideal. Philo contrasted being God's friends with being his servants. Scripture calls Abraham God's friend (2 Chronicles 20:7; Isaiah 41:8) and has God speak with Moses face to face. Friendship could also be political. Kings and lesser patrons called the dependents they supported their friends, and these lesser friends owed honor in return for favors. Friend of the king had been an office at Greek and Near Eastern courts, including Israel's from David to Herod the Great. Friend of the emperor was an official title with political weight, given in this period to clients of Sejanus. Josephus tells how a young Seleucid king made the high priest Jonathan "his friend and confederate." In Pilate's case the ESV Study Bible takes friend as a technical term for a client of Caesar, and the CSB Study Bible calls it a semiformal status of imperial favor. In Greek culture friendship was proved by sacrifice. Offering one's eyes for someone was a known figure of speech for great sacrifice. Moralists warned that flatterers did not care for their hearers' good.
entries.bridge: An analogy: the word partner, which can mean the person you share your life with or the firm that keeps you on retainer. Ancient friendship stretched the same way, from the closest bond there is to a political debt.
entries.changes: Because friends shared their minds and slaves did not, Jesus calling his disciples friends rather than slaves in John 15:15 takes them into his confidence. James 2:23 recalls that Abraham was called God's friend. Friendship also meant favors owed, which is why a governor told he would be no friend of Caesar had reason to be afraid.
entries.not: **Not a contract for paid services.** A firm on retainer is paid and can be dropped by either side. An ancient patron's friend owed public honor and loyalty for favors received, the bond was known to everyone, and losing a powerful friend could end a career.

entries.title: The household and its head
entries.summary: A household gathered family, slaves, freed slaves and workers under one head, and it was expected to follow that head's religion. When the head turned to a new god, the house often came too.
aliases: pillar and foundation of the truth
entries.plain: **When the owner of the farm decided the family would join a different church, the farmhands and their children came along too.** An ancient household was bigger than a family. Under one head it could take in a wife, children, slaves, freed slaves and workers. The head was expected to lead them in religion, and most of the time they followed his choice of gods. Homes had shrines to household spirits. So when the head of a house came to faith, it was natural for the whole household to hear the message and be baptized.
entries.then: Ancient households usually followed the religion of their head. They did not always, but it was the norm, and a husband was often embarrassed when his wife or children did not. Romans expected the head to lead his household in worshiping Rome's gods, and wives were expected to take their husband's religion (Keener). A household could include servants, freed persons or workers. Lydia apparently headed her own, which could mean she was widowed, divorced or a prosperous freedwoman. Keener thinks her household was mainly servants, or that she had a husband who left her religion alone. The CSB Study Bible observes that household baptisms recur in Acts without saying who was included. Wright and Bird describe the lares, household spirits honored at a home shrine called a lararium. Wright pictures Ephesian families setting a silver Artemis in a little shrine of its own. Homes also hosted gatherings. Churches met in houses for their first three centuries, and synagogues sometimes began in homes. A host answered for his guests as if they were his own household, as Jason did at Thessalonica. House meant both household and building, and the word Paul uses for administration was used for running a household. Stewards, often slaves or freedmen, ran wealthy homes and carried great responsibility and prestige. Writers sometimes derived a father's authority from God's. The Roman father held authority over all his descendants as long as he lived. A newborn became a legal person only when the father recognized it. The ESV Study Bible notes that slaves were counted part of the family.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a family firm in a small town, where the owner's choice of bank, pew and holiday table is taken to bind relatives and staff alike. A worker who chooses differently stands out.
entries.changes: Because a household followed its head, Lydia's conversion in Acts 16:15 brings her house with her, and Paul recalls baptizing the household of Stephanas in 1 Corinthians 1:16. Ephesians 2:19 calls Gentile believers members of God's household, the same word that then turns into God's temple.
entries.not: **Not an employer the staff can leave.** A worker who disagrees with the boss can quit. In an ancient household slaves were property, and a Roman father held legal authority over his descendants for life, so the head's religion carried a weight no modern owner's has.
entries.dissent: Whether household baptisms included children. The ESV Study Bible says Christians disagree over whether infants were included; Keener notes that if the Philippian jailer was a retired soldier he might have had young children, but says this cannot prove infant baptism; the CSB Study Bible reasons from Lydia's case that those baptized were old enough to respond for themselves.

entries.title: Household codes
entries.summary: From Aristotle on, moral writers told the male head of a household how to rule his wife, his children and his slaves, in that order. Religions under suspicion used the same form to show Rome they were no threat to the family.
aliases: so that no one will malign the word of God
entries.plain: **A company handbook spells out who reports to whom, and the boss's own duties take up one line at the end.** Greek and Roman moral writers had a standard way to talk about the home. They addressed the man at the head of it and told him how to rule three kinds of people under him: his wife, his children and his slaves. Romans worried that new religions from the East would undermine the family, so groups under suspicion often showed that they kept these values. Paul's letters use the same form, in the same order, and speak to every member of the household by name.
entries.then: Household codes go back at least to Aristotle in the fourth century BC (the cultural backgrounds notes). Many thinkers used them to teach the male head of an elite home how to govern his wife, his young children and his slaves, the order Aristotle followed. Keener adds that Paul takes the form straight from standard Greco-Roman moral writing. The codes spoke to the head of the house. They did not normally address wives, children or slaves themselves. Many Romans distrusted religions from the East, such as the cult of Isis, Judaism and Christianity, fearing they would erode traditional family values. Members of these minority faiths often used the codes to show they supported those values; the cultural backgrounds notes add the earlier cult of Dionysus. Wright and Bird write that pagan critics were ready to accuse Christians of threatening the social order. Most ancient writers expected wives to obey, and some marriage contracts demanded absolute obedience. Keener writes that "ancient household codes never list love as a husband's duty". The CSB Study Bible says society recognized wives' duties to husbands but not necessarily the reverse. To call every member of a group, the head included, to submit to one another "was unheard-of" (Keener). Wright and Bird read the codes as the place where Jesus' lordship shows in the most obvious social unit. They call it revolutionary to give instructions to children and slaves, treating them as responsible people. Keener reads the leaders' rules of 1 Timothy 3 as doing a household code's work for churches that met in homes. His notes add that groups thought to unsettle the order of masters and slaves drew particular suspicion.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a new company adopting an old staff handbook and keeping its headings so the inspectors recognize them. What matters is what has been written under each heading.
entries.changes: Because the codes were written to the head of the house about ruling others, a list that speaks to wives, children and slaves directly and gives husbands and masters duties of their own, like the one that begins at Ephesians 5:21, departs from the usual address of the pattern while keeping its shape. Colossians 3:18 opens the same form, and 1 Peter 2:18 begins a version addressed to slaves and wives in a setting of suspicion.
entries.not: **Not an internal rulebook a company can rewrite at will.** A handbook governs staff by agreement. The ancient codes described legal power a male head really held over wife, children and slaves, so Paul was writing inside a structure his readers could not opt out of.
entries.dissent: Two points. What submitting to one another in Ephesians 5:21 means. Keener says calling all members to submit to one another was unheard-of and that every instruction that follows rests on it, and Wright and Bird write, "Mutual submission is the order of the day". The ESV Study Bible takes it as "submitting to others according to the authority and order established by God," explained by the examples that follow, and rejects absolute mutual submission; the CSB Study Bible calls 5:21 a hinge on which what follows depends. Second, whether Paul's codes uphold or unsettle their culture. Keener says Paul undermines the codes' basic premise, the absolute authority of the male head, even as he relates Christianity to his culture's standards; the cultural backgrounds notes call the instructions a lifestyle apologetic that upholds the best in traditional values while adapting the codes, and their article on marriage roles ranks Paul with the moderate minority, such as Xenophon and Musonius Rufus; the ESV Study Bible says the commands do not merely reflect the culture of the day but present God's ideal for every marriage.

entries.title: Veils, hair and head coverings
entries.summary: In much of the eastern Mediterranean a respectable woman covered her hair in public, while fashionable rich women showed theirs off. Romans covered their heads to worship and Greeks did not, so in Corinth a covered or bare head sent several signals at once.
entries.plain: **In some places a woman still covers her hair when she goes out, and people read something into it when she does not.** In Paul's world a woman's hair was thought alluring, and in much of the eastern Mediterranean respectable women covered it in public. Rich women in fashion showed off their hairstyles instead. A shaved head shamed a woman. Among men, Romans pulled a fold of the toga over the head to pray to their gods, while Greeks prayed bareheaded. So in a church where men and women both prayed and prophesied aloud, what each wore on the head said something about modesty, class, marriage and worship.
entries.then: Keener writes that women's hair was a common object of lust. Across much of the eastern Mediterranean, custom required women to cover it, and Jewish Palestine even used face veils. Upper-class women keen to show off fashionable hairstyles did not cover. Men often saw women's hair as sexually attractive. A shaved head humiliated a woman, the greatest physical shame, in Keener's words. Bailey reports that most female statues he examined in Greek museums have covered heads, and writes, "We can assume that prostitutes did not cover their heads". Wright suggests that in Corinth the only women seen in public uncovered were prostitutes, while noting that Paul does not say so. The ESV Study Bible says a married woman who uncovered her head in public shamed her husband. In worship, "Romans covered their heads for worship but Greeks uncovered them" (the cultural backgrounds notes). The CSB Study Bible links the man's covered head to the Roman habit of pulling the toga over the head in pagan worship. It also suggests that women sometimes led prayer uncovered at pagan clubs meeting in private homes. Shorter hair was in fashion for men, though Greek heroes and Nazirites wore it long, and arguments from nature were a Stoic habit. Jewish interpreters commonly read Genesis 6:1-4 as angels lusting after women, and Heiser argues that the angels of 1 Corinthians 11:10 are those Watchers. Jewish and Greek moralists alike mocked women who dressed to turn other men's heads. Jewish writers warned of temptation, Greek and Roman writers of showing off, and wealthy women sometimes braided gold into their hair.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a wedding ring. It tells everyone who sees it something about the wearer, and taking it off in public is read as a message whether or not one was meant.
entries.changes: A covered or bare head sent signals about modesty, class and worship, so the instructions of 1 Corinthians 11:2-16 concern what the congregation's dress said to one another and to outsiders. 1 Timothy 2:9 and 1 Peter 3:3 warn women against display in braided hair and gold.
entries.not: **Not a personal choice with one meaning.** A ring says married, and leaving it off is a private decision. A woman's covering was expected by custom, and a bare head could signal wealth and fashion, sexual availability or disrespect to a husband, depending on who was watching.
entries.dissent: What was at stake. Keener sees a clash of class, fashionable rich women against lower-class concern for propriety. Bailey and Wright point to what a bare head signaled to outsiders. The ESV Study Bible makes the covering a married woman's sign; the CSB Study Bible suggests copying pagan clubs. Head may mean authority, as the ESV and CSB Study Bibles take it, or source, as Bailey reads it; Keener calls the matter vigorously debated. On the angels of 11:10, Heiser and the first option in Keener's two works see the Watchers of Genesis 6. The ESV Study Bible and Keener's second option, which cites the Dead Sea Scrolls, see angels present at worship. Keener's third option sees the angels believers will judge (1 Corinthians 6:3); the CSB Study Bible thinks of the church's witness to the angels. Bailey reads the covering as the woman prophet's sign of her authority to speak; the ESV Study Bible reads it as marking her submission to her husband. Whether the covering is a garment or long hair (11:15) is also debated. The Zondervan dictionary favors an outer covering such as a shawl and says first-century worship practice is hard to reconstruct.

entries.title: Celibacy and self-denial
entries.summary: Nearly everyone in the ancient world thought people should marry and have children. A few, from Cynic philosophers to some Essenes, refused marriage for a higher calling, and some in Corinth thought holiness meant giving up sex even within marriage.
aliases: it is good for a man not to touch a woman
entries.plain: **His family kept asking when he would settle down, and they did not think of staying single as a calling.** In Paul's world nearly everyone expected to marry and raise children, and Jews counted it a command of God. A few groups thought otherwise. Some philosophers, the Cynics above all, avoided marriage as a distraction from the wise life, though not always sex, and many Essenes lived without wives. In Corinth some believers seem to have gone further and decided that married couples should stop sleeping together to be more spiritual.
entries.then: Keener says most ancient writers condemned celibacy. Many Jewish teachers thought it sinful, since filling the earth was a commandment and marriage the proper guard against sexual sin. He sorts the views roughly three ways. The majority held that all who were able should marry and have children. The Cynics saw marriage as a distraction the wise man should avoid unless he found a wife equally devoted to philosophy; their one recorded exception was Hipparchia, wife of Crates. An early second-century rabbi held marriage right for most, with exceptions for those absorbed in other spiritual pursuits. Paul, Keener judges, combines the second and third. Some philosophical groups and many Essenes advocated celibacy, as did the Therapeutae. A few sages, mostly Cynics, rejected marriage while allowing prostitutes, and Augustus offered tax incentives to marry. Cynics feared marriage would pull them from a life without possessions or duties. Wandering sages normally could not marry, though most apostles by Paul's time were married and traveled with their wives. Bailey reads 1 Corinthians 7:1 as the Corinthians' question about the ascetic life. Wright describes teachers in Corinth urging celibacy, or abstinence within marriage, as the road to holiness. Jewish people expected great suffering just before the end, when marriage would be of little value (Keener). Wright ties Paul's present distress to a grain shortage across the Greek world in the years after he left Corinth. Asceticism was growing in Greco-Roman paganism in Paul's day. Josephus says of the Essenes, "They neglect wedlock, but choose out other persons children," though they did not reject marriage outright. Drinking only water often marked an ascetic.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a missionary who stays single for the work. Most people around him think it admirable in a few and strange as a rule, and some think it unnatural.
entries.changes: Because nearly everyone expected to marry, praise of staying single, as in 1 Corinthians 7:7-8, was unusual, and the same chapter answers the opposite pressure by telling married couples not to deprive each other. Jesus speaks of some who make themselves eunuchs for the kingdom in Matthew 19:12, and 1 Timothy 4:3 condemns teachers who forbid marriage.
entries.not: **Not a practical career choice.** The missionary stays single to travel light. In Corinth some urged celibacy, even abstinence inside marriage, as the road to holiness, and Paul ties his advice to a present distress; most apostles of his day were married.
entries.dissent: Whose words open 1 Corinthians 7:1, with its saying against a man touching a woman. Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes take it as a line from the Corinthians' letter that Paul answers. Bailey reports that most of the Syriac, Arabic and Hebrew versions he assembled read it as a statement, and two ninth-century Arabic versions as a question; he takes it as the Corinthians' question. Why Paul counsels staying single also divides the sources. Keener and his notes point to the Jewish expectation of suffering before the end, Wright to a famine in the years after Paul left Corinth. A third question is whether the foods of 1 Timothy 4:3 were those of the Jewish food laws, as Keener thinks, or an ascetic diet in general, which his notes leave open.

entries.title: The child's guardian
entries.summary: A trusted household slave walked a boy to school and back, watched his manners and kept him out of trouble until he came of age. He was neither the teacher nor anything like the father.
entries.plain: **The nanny took the boy to school, sat at the back of the class and made sure he behaved, but she was not his mother.** Well-off Greek and Roman families gave a son a slave called a paidagogos. He walked the boy to school and home again, taught him manners and tried to keep him out of mischief. Children respected him, but he was a servant, not the teacher and certainly not the father, and his job ended when the boy grew up.
entries.then: The guardians were slaves who saw boys safely to and from school (the cultural backgrounds notes). Keener writes that the guardian was respected by the child and taught him manners, but was not himself a teacher. Wright and Bird list child guardians among the many jobs slaves did; the paidagogos kept a son out of mischief until he grew up. Wright calls him a baby-sitter, usually a resident slave who watched the children while the parents were out and tried, often in vain, to keep them out of trouble. Bailey describes him as a well-known figure in Greek culture with much responsibility for shaping a child's character, though the father naturally mattered more. Students could fondly call a teacher father, and fathers were responsible for their sons' education. So a teacher who claimed to be the father placed the other teachers among the slave attendants. Children sometimes resented their guardians but often grew fond of them and later freed them. Guardians were usually better educated than the free masses, so the image was not demeaning in itself. Jewish teachers, though, called the law Israel's teacher, and calling it a guardian would have shocked them (Keener). In most Mediterranean cultures a boy came of age at about thirteen or fourteen, and then no longer needed the guardian. A Roman boy came of age at about sixteen, when he traded the toga of childhood for the all-white toga of a man. Wright calls the paidagogos "neither parent nor teacher but the person in charge for certain purposes."
entries.bridge: An analogy: a boarding-school housemaster. He has real authority over a boy day to day, but everyone knows it lasts only until the boy is grown, and he does not stand in the parents' place.
entries.changes: The guardian was a slave with charge of a child for a time, so setting ten thousand guardians against one father, as in 1 Corinthians 4:15, ranks the other teachers well below the founder. In Galatians 3:24-25 the law is such a guardian until faith comes, a role that ends when the heir grows up.
entries.not: **Not a professional with standing of his own.** A housemaster is a free, paid member of staff. The paidagogos was a household slave who escorted and minded the boy, and the boy might one day free him; the lessons came from someone else.

entries.title: Herod Antipas and the Herodians
entries.summary: Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ran Galilee for Rome as a tetrarch, not a king. The Herodians were his backers.
entries.plain: **The local boss calls himself king, but everyone knows who gave him the job.** After Herod the Great died, his son Antipas got Galilee and Perea, under Rome. People called him king. The Herodians were the party that backed him.
entries.then: Keener identifies Mark's King Herod as Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great. Antipas was technically a tetrarch, governor of a territory, not a king, though Galileans probably felt him to be a king locally. The ESV Study Bible dates his rule from 4 BC to AD 39 and calls him an administrator under Rome. Antipas divorced the daughter of the Nabatean king Aretas IV to marry Herodias, his brother's wife. Aretas later defeated him in battle, and his own people took the defeat as judgment for executing John (Josephus, Antiquities 18.5.1-2). Josephus says John was killed at the fortress of Machaerus. As a tetrarch under Rome, Antipas had no power to give away half a kingdom. His hunt for the title king finally cost him his rule. Augustus had refused him the title, and when he asked Caligula for it in AD 39 he was banished (Garland). The cultural backgrounds article adds that he ruled first from Sepphoris and later from Tiberias. Wright's glossary says the Herodians backed Antipas's claim to be the true king of the Jews. Keener says the Herodian family worked for Rome, and that Pharisees, many of them nationalists, worked with Herodians only in urgent cases. His coins carried a reed as their emblem, and Matthew uses his correct title, tetrarch.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a regional governor installed by a foreign power who wants his people to treat him as their own king. His supporters call him king. His paperwork says governor.
entries.changes: Antipas' rule explains the political danger around John and Jesus in Galilee, as in Mark 6:17-18. He was a tetrarch, not a king, so royal language about him, as in Matthew 14:9, is popular usage. In Luke 13:31-32 Jesus calls him that fox.
entries.not: **Not an outsider sent in to govern.** A governor installed by a foreign power usually comes from that power. Antipas was a son of Herod the Great, ruling a share of his father's kingdom, and the royal title he wanted was Rome's to grant or refuse.
entries.dissent: Why John was killed. Mark says John told Herod the marriage was unlawful and Herodias wanted him dead. Josephus says Herod feared John's influence "might put it into his power and inclination to raise a rebellion" and killed him first. Keener holds that John's criticism was moral but politically sensitive. Wright argues that John's charge struck at Herod's ambition to be accepted as the true king of the Jews. Garland holds that Josephus's political reason and Mark's account of Herodias's grudge do not contradict each other.

entries.title: Tolls and tax collectors
entries.summary: Local men who collected tolls and taxes for rulers backed by Rome, distrusted as collaborators and cheats.
entries.plain: **Nobody loves the man at the toll booth, and everyone assumes he is skimming.** Taxes and tolls went to rulers who worked with Rome. The men who collected them were locals, so their neighbors saw them as traitors working for the other side.
entries.then: Most people in the empire disliked tax collectors, and Jews saw them as traitors (Keener). Collectors could search property and seize anything not declared, and people sometimes paid bribes to avoid worse. Each tariff was small, but they multiplied at every border. Customs income usually went to local governments run by elites who cooperated with Rome. Later rabbis set the Pharisees, the godliest people one would meet, against tax collectors, the most ungodly. The ESV Study Bible says Levi collaborated with Herod Antipas, who collaborated with Rome, and that the system was corrupt and most collectors skimmed. The Roman coin of 12:14 was required for poll taxes in all the provinces. Wright adds that Galileans paid local taxes, temple taxes and taxes to Herod on top of Rome's. Keener thinks a collector at Capernaum was more likely a customs agent, charging duties on goods along the trade routes, in a secure and well-paid post. Across the empire people paid a tax on property, often around 1 percent, and a tax on each person. Local taxes and customs duties came on top. The money paid for roads, armies and temples of the emperor's cult. The rabbis even allowed lying to a tax collector to protect one's property (Garland; Strauss, citing the Mishnah). A tax collector was thought to have given up his place as a son of Abraham (Strauss).
entries.bridge: An analogy: a local man hired by an occupying army to collect fees at a checkpoint. He may need the work, but his neighbors see whose uniform he wears.
entries.changes: Tax collectors stand for people seen as traitors and cheats, so Jesus' welcome of them, as in Mark 2:15-16, scandalized the observant. Calling one to be a disciple, as in Matthew 9:9, took such a man into the inner circle. In Luke 19:8 Zacchaeus promises fourfold repayment.
entries.not: **Not a wage earner in a foreign uniform.** A checkpoint hand draws a fixed wage from the army. Levi likely served Herod Antipas, a Jewish ruler who answered to Rome, and collectors could search goods, seize what went undeclared and skim for themselves.
entries.dissent: What Levi collected. Keener gives two views: some scholars see a customs officer charging tariffs on goods passing through Capernaum, others a collector of local taxes for agents of Antipas. Wright places the toll at Capernaum as the border town between the lands of Antipas and Philip. The ESV Study Bible reads the booth by the sea as taxing fishermen. Garland combines the views: a customs house near the border with Philip's territory, in Antipas's service, which may also have taxed the fishing trade.

entries.title: Rome in charge
entries.summary: Rome ruled through client princes, local elites and governors. It kept the power to execute, and its soldiers, coins and taxes were everywhere.
aliases: ruler of the kings of the earth
city that rules the kings of the earth
entries.plain: **The occupying army does not have to stand on every corner for everyone to know who is boss.** Rome had taken over the land. Herod's family and the priests ran things day to day, but Rome had the soldiers, the coins and the final word.
entries.then: Wright sketches the history. Israel had been ruled by others since Babylon and was partly independent under the Hasmoneans from about 163 to 63 BC. Then Rome took over, and where Rome ruled, Rome taxed. Only Rome could execute, so the Jerusalem leaders had to hand Jesus to the governor. The coin in 12:16 was most likely a silver denarius bearing Tiberius' image and the title son of the divine Augustus. Judean copper coins left the image off. The silver denarius, probably minted at Lyon, was required for taxes in Palestine as everywhere in the empire. Josephus tells how Pilate brought standards with Caesar's image into Jerusalem by night, and the people came in crowds to protest for days until he backed down. Pilate governed Judea from AD 26 to 36, and his time began with conflict, from the standards to the use of temple money. A Roman legion was 6,000 men on paper, closer to 5,000 in the field. Centurions, the army's backbone, commanded sixty to eighty men. A cohort of about six hundred was normally stationed at the Antonia fortress in Jerusalem and reinforced at the feasts. Five cohorts were stationed at Caesarea, the governor's seat. Soldiers served twenty years and were officially barred from marrying. They had the legal right to press local people's labor, animals or goods into service. Jesus' picture of Gentiles who lord it over others is an accurate sketch of power from the emperor down (Keener). A proconsul was the highest official of a senatorial province such as Cyprus.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a country under foreign occupation that leaves the local mayor in office. Day to day you deal with locals, but the face on the money and the guns at the gate belong to someone else.
entries.changes: Rome's power stands behind the governors, client rulers, soldiers and taxes of the Gospels, as when the chief priests must hand Jesus to Pilate in Mark 15:1. A soldier's right to press local people into carrying his gear is behind the second mile of Matthew 5:41. Paul's appeal to Caesar in Acts 25:11 uses the same system from the other side.
entries.not: **Not a temporary occupation awaiting liberation.** A modern occupation is expected to end. Rome ruled as a settled empire, kept the power of execution for itself and set its own governor over Judea, while local partners such as the chief priests ran daily affairs.
entries.dissent: Two points. On Legion in 5:9, Keener and the ESV Study Bible read the name as saying only that the spirits are many. Wright reads the scene against Rome: Rome was the monster from the sea, "Rome was a nation of pigs," and the man is possessed by Rome's unclean legions. On the coin in 12:17, the ESV Study Bible says Jesus implies it is right to pay taxes to Caesar. Wright says the words carry the flavor of sending the image-stamped coin back where it came from, contempt without sedition, and echo a Maccabean slogan.

usedIn.s: Spies sent by the leaders ask Jesus whether it is right to pay tribute to Caesar, hoping to hand him over to the governor. He asks whose image is on a denarius.

usedIn.n: Luke 23:1-25, Before Pilate, before Antipas, and Barabbas
usedIn.s: The council brings Jesus to Pilate charged with forbidding tribute and claiming to be a king. Pilate sends him to Herod Antipas, who mocks him, and in the end Pilate gives in to the crowd and releases Barabbas.

usedIn.n: John 11:45-57, Caiaphas: one man for the nation
usedIn.s: After the raising of Lazarus the chief priests and Pharisees call a council, afraid the Romans will take away their place and their nation. Caiaphas tells them it is better for one man to die for the people.

usedIn.n: John 14:1-31, Rooms in the Father's house, and another Advocate
usedIn.s: Jesus tells his troubled disciples that he is going to prepare a place for them in his Father's house, that he is the way, and that the Father will send another Advocate, the Spirit of truth. He leaves them his peace.

usedIn.n: John 18:1-27, Arrest across the Kidron, and Annas
usedIn.s: Judas brings soldiers and temple police with torches to a garden across the Kidron. Jesus answers I am he, they fall back, and he is taken bound to Annas while Peter denies him three times by a charcoal fire.

usedIn.n: John 18:28-40, Pilate's headquarters at dawn
usedIn.s: At daybreak the leaders bring Jesus to the governor's headquarters but will not go in, so as to stay clean for Passover. Pilate questions him about being king of the Jews, finds no case, and offers to release him, but the crowd asks for Barabbas.

usedIn.n: Acts 10:1-23, Cornelius and Peter's vision
usedIn.s: A God-fearing Roman centurion in Caesarea is told in a vision to send for Peter. At noon on a Joppa rooftop Peter sees a sheet full of unclean animals and hears a voice tell him to eat.

usedIn.n: Acts 13:1-12, Sent from Antioch: the proconsul and the magician
usedIn.s: The church at Antioch fasts, prays and sends out Barnabas and Saul. On Cyprus the Roman proconsul believes after Paul confronts the Jewish magician in his entourage.

usedIn.n: Acts 18:12-17, Gallio's judgment seat
usedIn.s: Jewish leaders bring Paul before Gallio, proconsul of Achaia, accusing him of teaching a worship contrary to the law. Gallio refuses to judge a dispute about words, names and their own law and drives them from the judgment seat.

usedIn.n: Acts 21:27-40, Riot in the temple, rescue by the tribune
usedIn.s: Jews from Asia see Paul in the temple and cry that he has brought Greeks into the holy place. The city riots, and the Roman tribune's soldiers pull him from the crowd, chain him, and nearly mistake him for the Egyptian rebel.

usedIn.n: Acts 23:12-35, The oath, the nephew and the night march
usedIn.s: More than forty men bind themselves by an oath not to eat until they have killed Paul. His nephew learns of the ambush, and the tribune sends Paul under heavy escort by night to the governor Felix at Caesarea, with a letter explaining the case.

usedIn.n: Acts 24:1-27, The hearing before Felix
usedIn.s: The high priest's orator Tertullus charges Paul before Felix with stirring up riots and trying to profane the temple. Paul answers point by point; Felix puts off a decision and keeps him in custody for two years, hoping for a bribe.

usedIn.n: Acts 25:1-12, Festus and the appeal to Caesar
usedIn.s: The new governor Festus hears the case again at Caesarea. When he asks whether Paul will be tried in Jerusalem, Paul appeals to Caesar, and after conferring with his council Festus grants it.

usedIn.n: Romans 5:1-21, Peace with God, and Adam
usedIn.s: Justified by faith, believers have peace with God and are reconciled to him by the death of his Son. As sin and death came through Adam, grace and life come through Christ.

usedIn.n: Romans 8:31-39, Angels, rulers and powers
usedIn.s: With God on the believers' side, Paul asks who could oppose them, then names hardships and powers, from the sword to angels, rulers, height and depth, and none of them can cut believers off from God's love in Christ.

usedIn.n: Romans 13:1-7, The sword and the tax
usedIn.s: Paul tells believers to be subject to the governing authorities, whom God has put in place. The ruler bears the sword, and they should pay taxes and give honor where it is owed.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 2:1-7, Prayers for kings and all in authority
usedIn.s: Paul asks for prayers for everyone, kings and all in authority included, so that believers may live peaceful and quiet lives, because God our Savior wants all to be saved and there is one God and one mediator.

usedIn.n: Titus 2:11-3:8, Grace has appeared, be subject to rulers, and the washing of rebirth
usedIn.s: God's grace has appeared, training believers to live with self-control now while they wait for Christ's glorious appearing; they are to respect rulers and be gentle to all, because God saved them by his mercy, giving them new birth and new life by the Holy Spirit.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 2:11-17, Foreigners among the nations; honor the emperor
usedIn.s: As foreigners and exiles the readers must keep their conduct good among the Gentiles, who slander them as wrongdoers. They are to submit to every human authority, the emperor and his governors, and so silence ignorant talk; they are free people, but slaves of God. Honor everyone, love the believers, fear God, honor the emperor.

usedIn.n: Revelation 1:1-8, a revelation sent as a letter
usedIn.s: The book opens as a revelation God gave Jesus, sent by his angel to his servant John, with a blessing on the one who reads it aloud and on those who hear. It then greets seven churches in Asia like a letter, from the one who is, was and is to come, and from Jesus, ruler of the kings of the earth, who is coming with the clouds.

usedIn.n: Revelation 2:12-17, Pergamum, where Satan's throne is
usedIn.s: To Pergamum Jesus, who wields the sword of judgment, says they have stayed loyal in a city he calls Satan's seat, even after the martyrdom of Antipas. But some follow teaching like Balaam's that leads to idol meals and immorality. The faithful are promised hidden heavenly food and a white stone carrying a new name.

usedIn.n: Revelation 6:1-8, four horsemen
usedIn.s: As the Lamb opens the first four seals, four riders go out: a crowned archer on a white horse bent on conquest, a rider on a red horse who takes peace from the earth, a rider with scales on a black horse while wheat sells at famine prices, and Death on a pale horse with Hades following.

usedIn.n: Revelation 17:1-6, the woman on the scarlet beast
usedIn.s: An angel carries John into a wilderness to see the great prostitute who sits on many waters, riding a scarlet beast full of blasphemous names. Dressed in purple and scarlet and glittering with gold and pearls, she holds a golden cup of filth, bears the name Babylon the great on her forehead and is drunk with the blood of God's people.

usedIn.n: Revelation 17:7-18, seven hills and seven kings
usedIn.s: The angel explains the woman and the beast: the beast once was, now is not and will come up from the Abyss; its seven heads are seven hills and also seven kings, five fallen, one living and one still to come, and the beast is an eighth who belongs to the seven. Its ten horns are ten kings who will make war on the Lamb, and in the end the beast and the horns turn on the woman, the great city that rules the kings of the earth, and burn her.

entries.title: Hailing a king
entries.summary: A colt nobody had ridden, cloaks on the road, waving branches, kneeling, the cry Hail, and the delegation that went out to meet a visiting ruler: the public gestures that greeted a king.
aliases: meet the Lord in the air
the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ
entries.plain: **When the crowd lines the road and spreads out the red carpet, everyone knows who they think is coming.** Kings were greeted with set gestures. Doing them on purpose made a claim. Doing them as a joke was mockery of the claim.
entries.then: Animals never ridden were preferred for things dedicated to God, and Roman soldiers and kings could commandeer animals (Keener). Jesus riding a colt into Jerusalem evokes the humble king of Zechariah 9:9. Officials rode donkeys in civil processions, not military ones (1 Kings 1:33), so this was the welcome of a meek king, not a Roman triumph. Festal pilgrims were often greeted this way, though not on this scale. Laying cloaks on the road before a ruler declared him king (2 Kings 9:13). People waved branches to celebrate victories (1 Maccabees 13:51; 2 Maccabees 10:7). The ESV Study Bible reads the cry Hosanna, from Psalm 118, as greeting Jesus as a Davidic messiah. Bailey describes a Middle Eastern custom: villagers honor an important guest by walking out of town to meet him and escorting him in, and the size of the crowd measures his standing. The Roman layer shows in the mockery. Hail, the Latin Ave, was a common address to rulers, and so was kneeling; the soldiers were mocking the Jewish people as well (Keener). Wright adds that purple was worn by kings, and the reed stands in for a scepter. Delegations from a city went out to meet an important visitor. The same welcome lies behind Paul's word for Christ's coming. Parousia was "a term that could apply to the visit of a king or royal dignitary" (Keener). With it, the word for meeting meant a city's envoys going out to escort the visitor in.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a red carpet and a royal salute. Roll it out for a pop star and you are making a claim about him. Roll it out as a joke for a prisoner and you are making a different one.
entries.changes: The gestures of a royal welcome, an animal no one had ridden, cloaks on the road, branches and acclamation, made a public claim, as in Matthew 21:8-9. Done as a joke they mocked the claim, as when soldiers kneel and cry Hail in Mark 15:18-19. When Paul pictures believers going out to meet the Lord in the air in 1 Thessalonians 4:17, he uses the word for a city's welcoming party.
entries.not: **Not honor without a political claim.** A red carpet flatters a guest and threatens no one. Cloaks on the road and the Hosanna cry named a king in a land Rome ruled, and the colt pointed hearers to the humble king Zechariah promised.
entries.dissent: Whether the meeting of 1 Thessalonians 4:17 means a return to earth. Keener, his notes, Wright and Wright and Bird read it as the welcoming party that turns back to escort the king to the city; Wright describes "a meeting outside the city, after which the civic leaders escort the dignitary" in. The ESV Study Bible says the word may point to a downward movement but warns against pressing apocalyptic detail. The CSB Study Bible reads the passage as the rapture of believers caught up while still alive, and the Zondervan dictionary has the living taken up to heaven.

usedIn.n: Matthew 21:1-11, A donkey, a colt and the Hallel
usedIn.s: Jesus sends for a donkey and her colt, rides into Jerusalem as Zechariah foretold, and the pilgrim crowds spread cloaks and branches, crying Hosanna to the Son of David.

usedIn.n: Matthew 27:27-56, Mock king, the cross and the torn curtain
usedIn.s: Soldiers dress Jesus as a mock king. He is crucified as king of the Jews between two rebels, cries out in the words of Psalm 22 and dies; the curtain tears, the earth shakes, and women watch from a distance.

usedIn.n: Mark 11:1-11, The ride into Jerusalem
usedIn.s: Jesus sends for a colt no one has ridden and rides into Jerusalem over cloaks and branches while the crowd shouts Hosanna.

usedIn.n: Mark 15:1-20, Before Pilate
usedIn.s: The chief priests hand Jesus to Pilate as king of the Jews. Pilate releases Barabbas to the crowd, has Jesus flogged, and the soldiers mock him as a king.

usedIn.n: Luke 19:28-48, The king rides down to the city and weeps over it
usedIn.s: Jesus rides a borrowed colt down the Mount of Olives while his disciples spread their cloaks and praise the king who comes. Seeing the city, he weeps over the siege to come, then drives the sellers out of the temple.

usedIn.n: John 12:12-19, Palm branches and a donkey's colt
usedIn.s: The festival crowd goes out with palm branches, shouting Hosanna and hailing Jesus as King of Israel, and he rides in on a young donkey, as Zechariah had said Zion's king would come.

usedIn.n: John 19:1-16, Flogged, mocked, and no friend of Caesar
usedIn.s: Pilate has Jesus flogged, the soldiers crown him with thorns and hail him as king, and Pilate shows him to the crowd. Warned that releasing him makes Pilate no friend of Caesar, he sits on the judgment seat at the Stone Pavement and hands him over.

usedIn.n: Acts 28:11-16, The Twin Brothers and the road to Rome
usedIn.s: After three months they sail in an Alexandrian ship with the Twin Brothers as its figurehead, land at Puteoli and walk the Appian Way toward Rome, where believers come out to meet Paul. In Rome he is allowed to live on his own with a soldier guarding him.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18, Grief with hope, and the welcoming party
usedIn.s: Paul tells a grieving church that believers who have died are not lost: when the Lord comes down from heaven with a shout, the archangel's voice and God's trumpet, the dead in Christ will rise first, and the living will be caught up with them to meet the Lord in the air.

usedIn.n: 2 Thessalonians 2:1-12, The man of lawlessness and the restrainer
usedIn.s: Paul tells a church unsettled by claims that the day of the Lord has already come that the rebellion must come first and the man of lawlessness be revealed, who sets himself up in God's temple claiming to be God; something holds him back for now, and the Lord Jesus will destroy him by the breath of his mouth.

entries.title: Crucifixion
entries.summary: Rome's public, shaming death for rebels, after flogging, with the charge posted for passers-by to read.
entries.plain: **The bodies along the highway were the message.** Crucifixion was how Rome killed people who resisted it. It was slow, public and humiliating on purpose.
entries.then: Wright writes, "The cross was a political symbol long before it became a religious symbol." It announced that Rome was in charge. Rome crucified thousands of Jewish rebels during Jesus' boyhood and thousands more in AD 70, and polite Romans avoided even the word. Outside Italy, treason was normally punished by crucifixion. Flogging came first, by Roman practice until the flogger tired, with a whip that could tear the flesh. Prisoners often carried the crossbeam, through jeering crowds. Men were usually executed naked and could not drive off birds or flies. Most died of shock or dehydration. Crosses were often low, and the execution squad, typically four men, could keep the prisoner's clothes (Keener). The only crucified man's bones yet found, those of Jehohanan from Giv'at ha-Mivtar, show a nail through the heel, and he was buried in his family tomb. Romans preferred public places such as major roads, so that passers-by would learn the danger of resisting Rome. A tablet could state the charge. Wright's glossary says crucifixion would have been seen as clear proof that a man was not the Messiah. The Jewish king Alexander Jannaeus crucified about 800 Pharisees, and Qumran texts applied Deuteronomy 21:23 to Roman crucifixion. It was the most shameful and painful death in the Roman world. It was kept for non-Roman criminals who were slaves or the lowest free persons, and no one wanted to be linked with the crucified. The ESV Study Bible calls it "a public statement by Rome that the crucified one was beyond contempt."
entries.bridge: An analogy: a hanging left on display at a crossroads in a frontier town. It punishes one man and warns everyone who rides past.
entries.changes: Crucifixion was Rome's death for rebels, so a call to take up the cross, as in Matthew 10:38, meant walking the road of the condemned. The forced carrying of the beam, the stripping and the posted charge in Mark 15:21-26 follow Roman practice. Paul calls the cross a stumbling block in 1 Corinthians 1:23.
entries.not: **Not a quick death.** A hanging kills fast. A crucified man was flogged first, hung naked where he could not drive off birds or flies, and died slowly of shock or dehydration, a death so shameful that it was kept for slaves and the lowest free persons.
