usedIn.n: Matthew 10:16-42, Wolves, floggings, a sword and a cup of water
usedIn.s: Jesus warns the Twelve of councils, floggings in synagogues and trials before governors and kings, of family turned against family, and promises that whoever receives them receives him.

usedIn.n: Matthew 16:13-28, The rock, the keys and the cross
usedIn.s: At Caesarea Philippi Peter confesses Jesus as the Messiah, the Son of the living God, and is called the rock and given the keys. When Jesus speaks of his death, Peter rebukes him and is called Satan.

usedIn.n: Matthew 27:1-26, Blood money, Pilate and Barabbas
usedIn.s: At dawn the council hands Jesus to Pilate. Judas returns the silver and hangs himself, the priests buy a potter's field, and Pilate, warned by his wife's dream, releases Barabbas and washes his hands.

usedIn.n: Matthew 27:27-56, Mock king, the cross and the torn curtain
usedIn.s: Soldiers dress Jesus as a mock king. He is crucified as king of the Jews between two rebels, cries out in the words of Psalm 22 and dies; the curtain tears, the earth shakes, and women watch from a distance.

usedIn.n: Mark 10:32-45, James and John ask for the best seats
usedIn.s: On the road to Jerusalem Jesus predicts his death a third time. James and John ask to sit at his right and left, and he tells them the first must be slave of all.

usedIn.n: Mark 15:1-20, Before Pilate
usedIn.s: The chief priests hand Jesus to Pilate as king of the Jews. Pilate releases Barabbas to the crowd, has Jesus flogged, and the soldiers mock him as a king.

usedIn.n: Mark 15:21-41, The cross
usedIn.s: Jesus is crucified as king of the Jews between two bandits, mocked by passers-by, and dies with a loud cry. The temple curtain tears, and women watch from a distance.

usedIn.n: Luke 23:26-49, The road to the cross, paradise, and the ninth hour
usedIn.s: Simon of Cyrene carries the cross, the women of Jerusalem mourn, and Jesus warns them of days to come. Crucified between two criminals, he promises one of them paradise and dies at the ninth hour.

usedIn.n: John 19:1-16, Flogged, mocked, and no friend of Caesar
usedIn.s: Pilate has Jesus flogged, the soldiers crown him with thorns and hail him as king, and Pilate shows him to the crowd. Warned that releasing him makes Pilate no friend of Caesar, he sits on the judgment seat at the Stone Pavement and hands him over.

usedIn.n: John 19:16-30, The cross, the notice in three languages, and his mother
usedIn.s: Jesus carries his own cross to Golgotha. Pilate's notice, King of the Jews, is written in Aramaic, Latin and Greek; soldiers cast lots for his seamless tunic; he gives his mother to the beloved disciple, takes the sour wine and says it is finished.

usedIn.n: John 19:31-42, Legs unbroken and a hundred pounds of spices
usedIn.s: Because the coming Sabbath is a high day, the leaders ask for the bodies to be taken down. The soldiers find Jesus already dead and pierce his side; Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus bury him with a lavish weight of spices in a new tomb in a garden.

usedIn.n: John 21:15-25, Feed my sheep, and stretch out your hands
usedIn.s: Three times Jesus asks Peter whether he loves him and three times tells him to tend his sheep. He foretells Peter's death and answers his question about the beloved disciple, whose testimony closes the book.

usedIn.n: Acts 22:22-29, A Roman citizen under the lash
usedIn.s: When Paul speaks of his mission to the Gentiles, the crowd erupts again. The tribune orders him examined by flogging, until Paul asks the centurion whether it is lawful to flog an uncondemned Roman citizen.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 1:18-2:5, The foolishness of the cross
usedIn.s: Paul sets the message of a crucified Messiah, folly to Greeks and a stumbling block to Jews, against the wisdom and eloquence Corinth admired, and reminds the believers that few of them were wise, powerful or well born.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 1:1-11, The God of all comfort and the sentence of death
usedIn.s: Paul opens by blessing the God of all comfort and tells the Corinthians that in Asia he was so crushed that he felt he had received the sentence of death, so that he learned to rely on the God who raises the dead.

usedIn.n: Galatians 2:11-21, Peter leaves the table at Antioch
usedIn.s: At Antioch Peter, who had been eating with Gentile believers, draws back when people come from James, and Paul rebukes him in front of everyone, arguing that Jews and Gentiles alike are put right with God through Christ and faith, not by doing what the law requires.

usedIn.n: Galatians 3:1-14, Who bewitched you? Abraham's blessing and the law's curse
usedIn.s: Paul asks the Galatians who has bewitched them, since they received the Spirit by believing, then argues from Abraham that those who believe share his blessing, while Christ took the law's curse by being hung on a tree.

usedIn.n: Galatians 6:11-18, Large letters in his own hand, and the marks of Jesus
usedIn.s: Taking the pen himself, Paul writes in large letters that the rivals want the Galatians circumcised so they can boast in their flesh and avoid persecution, while he boasts only in the cross; he blesses those who follow this rule and the Israel of God, and says he bears the marks of Jesus.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 2:11-22, The dividing wall torn down, and a new temple
usedIn.s: Paul reminds Gentile believers that they were once far off, shut out of Israel's citizenship and covenants, and tells them Christ has broken down the dividing wall and built Jews and Gentiles into one household and one temple.

usedIn.n: Philippians 2:1-11, The form of a slave, a cross, and every knee
usedIn.s: Paul urges humility and concern for others, then sets out Christ, who did not exploit his equality with God but took the form of a slave and died on a cross, and whom God exalted so that every knee will bow.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 5:11-6:12, Milk, solid food and no way back
usedIn.s: The readers should be teachers by now but still need milk, so the writer urges them past the elementary teachings. Those who have been enlightened and shared in the Holy Spirit and then fall away cannot be brought back to repentance, though he is confident of better things for his readers.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 12:1-13, The race, the shame and the Father's discipline
usedIn.s: Surrounded by a great cloud of witnesses, believers are to throw off every weight and run with endurance, eyes fixed on Jesus, who endured the cross and scorned its shame. Their hardships are a father's discipline, which only legitimate children receive.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 13:7-17, Foods, an altar and outside the camp
usedIn.s: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and for ever, so the readers must not be carried away by strange teachings about foods. Believers have an altar the tabernacle priests may not eat from; as the bodies of the sin offerings were burned outside the camp, Jesus suffered outside the gate, and they must go out to him, bearing his disgrace, seeking the city to come.

entries.title: Herod the Great
entries.summary: Rome's king of Judea from 37 to 4 BC: an Idumean, a great builder, and a ruler who killed anyone he saw as a threat, his own family included.
entries.plain: **The old dictator built beautiful palaces and had his own sons killed.** Herod the Great ruled the Jews as king by Rome's appointment. He rebuilt the temple on a grand scale and built fortresses and whole cities. He was also known for murdering rivals, a wife and several sons. When he died, his kingdom was split among his sons.
entries.then: Herod ruled from 37 to 4 BC as Rome's appointee. He built the temple, Caesarea, Masada, the fortress of Herodium and pagan temples abroad. He had been Mark Antony's friend. When Octavian won, Herod promised Caesar the same loyalty, then named cities and built temples in his honor. He was an Idumean. Josephus says the Hasmonean ruler Hyrcanus had forced the Idumeans to be circumcised and keep Jewish law, and reports that a rival called Herod "an Idumean, i.e. a half Jew." Bailey sums him up as an Arab by race, Jewish by religion, Greek by culture and Roman in politics. Josephus records the drowning of the young high priest Aristobulus in a pool at Jericho, which archaeology shows was very shallow. He also records the execution of Herod's wife Mariamne, two sons strangled at Sebaste, and his son Antipater killed five days before Herod's own death. Near death Herod shut the leading men of the nation in the hippodrome at Jericho with orders to kill them, so that he would have "the honor of a memorable mourning at his funeral." They were released instead. He had filled the council with his supporters (Keener). When young disciples of religious teachers pulled down the golden eagle he had set on the temple, he had them executed. After 4 BC the kingdom was divided among Archelaus, Antipas and Philip, and Rome banished Archelaus to Gaul in AD 6.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a strongman installed by a superpower who builds the nation's grandest monuments and keeps a list of enemies. His people admire the buildings and fear the knock on the door.
entries.changes: Herod's record makes the killing of Bethlehem's boys in Matthew 2:16 fit what was known of him, and explains why foreign visitors asking for a newborn king were a threat. His family ruled after him under the same name, so a reader must ask which Herod a passage means: his son Antipas in Mark 6:14, or his grandson Agrippa in Acts 12:1.
entries.not: **Not a native son of the nation he ruled.** A strongman is usually one of his own people. Herod was an Idumean from a people forced into Judaism, and a rival mocked him as a half Jew. The Gospels and Acts also give the family name to several rulers, so each passage must be read for which one it means.
entries.dissent: Three points. Was he Jewish? The CSB Study Bible says he was not a Jew; Wright says not even fully Jewish; Bailey calls him Jewish in religion; Josephus records both the forced conversion of the Idumeans and the insult half Jew. When did he die? Keener, the ESV Study Bible and the CSB Study Bible say 4 BC, and Carson, Moo and Morris call late March or early April of 4 BC almost certain; Heiser, following Ernest Martin and others, argues for 1 BC. Did the massacre happen? No source outside Matthew mentions it; the CSB Study Bible notes that sceptics deny it and answers that it fits Herod's documented conduct, as do Keener and Bailey.

usedIn.n: Matthew 2:1-12, Magi at Herod's court
usedIn.s: Magi from the east arrive in Jerusalem asking for the newborn king of the Jews. Herod consults his scholars, sends the visitors to Bethlehem, and they go home another way.

usedIn.n: Matthew 2:13-23, Refugees in Egypt, home to Nazareth
usedIn.s: Joseph takes the family to Egypt by night. Herod kills the boys of Bethlehem, and after his death the family settles in Nazareth to stay clear of his son Archelaus.

usedIn.n: Luke 19:11-27, The nobleman who went to receive a kingdom
usedIn.s: Because people think the kingdom is about to appear, Jesus tells of a nobleman who travels to a far country to be made king while citizens who hate him send a delegation after him, and of the servants who trade with his money.

entries.title: Keys, binding and loosing
entries.summary: In a king's house a senior official carried the keys and decided who came in. Teachers spoke of binding and loosing for forbidding and permitting, and a court bound or loosed when it condemned or released.
entries.plain: **Whoever holds the keys to the building decides who gets in after hours.** In a royal palace the keys were large, and a senior official carried them. Jewish teachers used two other words, bind and loose, for deciding what the law forbade and what it allowed, and the same words fit a court that condemned or released someone. Many believed that a faithful court on earth was carrying out decisions already made in heaven.
entries.then: The picture of the keys comes from Isaiah 22:20-22, where a high official in the king's house is given the key of David. Keener calls the keeper of the keys one of the most important posts a household servant could hold. He reads the keys of Matthew 16:19 as authority to admit people into the kingdom, the opposite of those who shut it in 23:13. The Qumran community also had officials who decided whether to admit new members. Binding and loosing were standard terms for the rabbis' authority to interpret Scripture, forbidding and permitting. The words normally meant tying up or freeing a prisoner, so they also served for a court's verdict. Many Jews believed their high court ruled with the authority of God's court in heaven. Keener notes that the verb tenses of 18:18 suggest the heavenly court decides first. The CSB Study Bible likewise says Peter would permit or forbid only what heaven had already permitted or forbidden. Later rabbis believed their rulings matched the decrees of the heavenly court.
entries.bridge: An analogy: the chief of staff who holds the keys and the guest list at a head of state's residence. Visitors deal with him, but he matters only because he speaks for the one who lives there.
entries.changes: Keys and the words bind and loose describe authority to admit people to God's kingdom and to settle cases among his people, as in Matthew 18:18. In John 20:23 the disciples are given authority to forgive or retain sins. Revelation 3:7 calls Jesus the holder of the key of David, who opens and no one shuts.
entries.not: **Not one man's discretion over a guest list.** A chief of staff decides who gets in and can be overruled later. Binding and loosing meant ruling on what Scripture permits or forbids, and by the verb tenses of 18:18 the heavenly court has already decided.
entries.dissent: Who holds the keys, and what binding covers. Keener reads Peter as the rock in his role as the one who confessed Jesus, with others building on the same confession, and the keys as admitting people on the basis of that truth. The ESV Study Bible says the authority to admit through preaching is later given to all who proclaim the gospel, and that 18:18 extends Peter's authority to the whole community. The CSB Study Bible stresses that Peter was an agent who could permit or forbid only what heaven had already decided. The cultural backgrounds notes say binding may include discipline and perhaps the vetting of those to be admitted.

usedIn.n: Matthew 16:13-28, The rock, the keys and the cross
usedIn.s: At Caesarea Philippi Peter confesses Jesus as the Messiah, the Son of the living God, and is called the rock and given the keys. When Jesus speaks of his death, Peter rebukes him and is called Satan.

usedIn.n: Matthew 18:15-20, Two or three witnesses and the assembly
usedIn.s: Jesus sets out how to deal with a brother who sins: privately, then with witnesses, then before the church. What they bind on earth is bound in heaven, and he is present where two or three gather in his name.

entries.title: Witnesses and advocates in court
entries.summary: Jewish law convicted no one on a single witness: it demanded two or three, examined them closely and gave little weight to the word of women. Courts also had accusers and advocates, and Jewish pictures of God's heavenly court gave those roles to Satan and to defenders of Israel.
aliases: the Spirit, the water and the blood
three that bear record in heaven
entries.plain: **One person's word against another's will not convict anyone in this courtroom.** The law of Moses required at least two witnesses before anyone could be condemned. Judges questioned them closely, and a witness caught lying could suffer the penalty he wanted for the accused. Whose word counted was limited too: the courts of the day gave little weight to women or slaves. A court also had people who spoke for each side, and Jews pictured God's own court the same way, with an accuser bringing charges and an advocate pleading for Israel.
entries.then: Deuteronomy 17:6 and 19:15 were the standard texts for requiring two witnesses, a rule the cultural backgrounds notes call foundational. Keener says the rabbis held that one eyewitness was not enough, even against a murderer caught with the bloody knife in hand. Josephus states the law: "let not a single witness be credited, but three, or two at the least, and those such whose testimony is confirmed by their good lives." Witnesses were cross-examined, and contradictory testimony should have ended a case. False witnesses in a capital case were to be put to death (Deuteronomy 19:16-21). Pharisaic tradition tightened the rule, and a witness who could not be questioned in court did not count. Gentile courts were laxer, and some Greek handbooks taught how to give false testimony persuasively. Women's testimony carried limited weight in both Jewish and Roman law. Josephus writes, "But let not the testimony of women be admitted, on account of the levity and boldness of their sex," and Keener says the culture "considered their witness worthless." Courts also had advocates. Keener says the word John uses for the Spirit probably comes from the courtroom, meaning advocate or defending attorney. In Jewish pictures of God's heavenly court, Satan is the chief prosecutor, while God, his mercy or the angel Michael defends Israel. Roman courts had no public prosecutor and relied on an interested party to bring charges. Wright describes the advocate as the one who explains to judge or jury how things look from the client's side. The ESV Study Bible traces through John's Gospel a trial in which, in the end, the world and not Jesus is in the dock.
entries.bridge: An analogy: the rule that a confession alone cannot convict without corroborating evidence. The bar is set high on purpose, and anyone caught lying under oath is punished.
entries.changes: The two-witness rule lies behind the steps for settling a case among believers in Matthew 18:16, and Paul cites it in 2 Corinthians 13:1. When John 14:16 calls the Spirit another Advocate, the word comes from the courtroom, where in John's telling the world, not Jesus, turns out to be on trial. Because women's word was discounted, women chosen as the first witnesses of the resurrection go against the culture.
entries.not: **Not a rule that any evidence can satisfy.** Modern corroboration can come from records or forensics. The ancient rule counted people, two or three qualified witnesses, and the law barred some, such as women, from counting at all. A false witness faced the penalty he had sought for the accused.
entries.dissent: What the word for the Spirit in John 14:16 means. Keener says its background is debated but probably the courtroom, an advocate or defending attorney. The cultural backgrounds notes say the term did not always carry a legal sense, though it sometimes did. The ESV Study Bible renders it Helper, a helping presence, without stressing the court.

usedIn.n: Matthew 18:15-20, Two or three witnesses and the assembly
usedIn.s: Jesus sets out how to deal with a brother who sins: privately, then with witnesses, then before the church. What they bind on earth is bound in heaven, and he is present where two or three gather in his name.

usedIn.n: Matthew 26:47-75, Arrest, twelve legions, the council and the rooster
usedIn.s: Judas comes with an armed crowd and a kiss. Jesus refuses the sword and the twelve legions of angels, is tried at night before Caiaphas, and is condemned for blasphemy while Peter swears he never knew him.

usedIn.n: Matthew 28:1-15, Women at dawn and a bribed guard
usedIn.s: At dawn after the Sabbath an angel rolls back the stone and tells two women that Jesus is risen. They meet him on the road, while the chief priests pay the guards to say the disciples stole the body.

usedIn.n: Luke 18:1-8, The widow and the judge
usedIn.s: Jesus tells of a judge who neither feared God nor respected people and a widow who kept coming to him for justice until he gave in. How much more, he says, will God see justice done for his chosen ones.

usedIn.n: John 5:19-47, The Son sent by the Father, and his witnesses
usedIn.s: Jesus answers the charge of making himself equal with God: the Son does what he sees the Father doing, gives life and judges, and has witnesses in John, in his works, in the Father and in the Scriptures.

usedIn.n: John 8:12-30, The light of the world by the treasury
usedIn.s: Jesus calls himself the light of the world. Told that testimony about himself does not count, he answers with the law's rule of two witnesses: himself and the Father who sent him.

usedIn.n: John 9:1-41, A man born blind is put out
usedIn.s: Jesus puts mud on a blind beggar's eyes and sends him to wash in Siloam. Because it is the Sabbath the man is questioned, his parents are afraid, and when he defends Jesus he is thrown out.

usedIn.n: John 14:1-31, Rooms in the Father's house, and another Advocate
usedIn.s: Jesus tells his troubled disciples that he is going to prepare a place for them in his Father's house, that he is the way, and that the Father will send another Advocate, the Spirit of truth. He leaves them his peace.

usedIn.n: John 15:18-16:15, Hated by the world and put out of the synagogue
usedIn.s: Jesus warns that the world will hate his followers as it hated him, that they will be put out of the synagogues and even killed by people who think they are serving God, and that the Advocate will prove the world wrong.

usedIn.n: John 20:1-18, The empty tomb and the gardener
usedIn.s: Mary Magdalene finds the stone moved and runs to Peter and the beloved disciple, who see the linen cloths lying in the empty tomb. Weeping outside, she takes the risen Jesus for the gardener until he says her name, and he sends her to tell the others.

usedIn.n: John 21:15-25, Feed my sheep, and stretch out your hands
usedIn.s: Three times Jesus asks Peter whether he loves him and three times tells him to tend his sheep. He foretells Peter's death and answers his question about the beloved disciple, whose testimony closes the book.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 12:19-13:14, Two or three witnesses
usedIn.s: Paul warns that on his third visit every charge will be established by two or three witnesses and that he will not spare the unrepentant, then closes with a call to restoration, the holy kiss and a threefold blessing.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 5:17-25, Double honor, two witnesses, the elect angels and a little wine
usedIn.s: Elders who lead well deserve double honor and pay; charges against them need two or three witnesses; Paul charges Timothy before God, Christ and the elect angels to act without favoritism, to lay hands on no one hastily, and to take a little wine.

usedIn.n: 1 John 1:5-2:17, God is light, an advocate, and a world passing away
usedIn.s: God is light with no darkness in him, so to claim fellowship with him while walking in darkness is a lie; the blood of Jesus cleanses, and those who confess are forgiven. Anyone who sins has an advocate with the Father, the atoning sacrifice for the whole world. The old command of love is new, the darkness is passing, and the world is passing away.

usedIn.n: 1 John 5:1-12, Water, blood and three witnesses
usedIn.s: Whoever believes Jesus is the Christ is God's child, and loving the parent means loving the child. Faith overcomes the world. Jesus Christ came by water and blood, not by water only, and three testify, the Spirit, the water and the blood; God's testimony is that he has given eternal life in his Son.

usedIn.n: Revelation 11:1-14, the measured temple and the two witnesses
usedIn.s: John is told to measure God's temple and its worshipers but to leave out the outer court, given to the nations to trample for forty-two months. Two witnesses in sackcloth prophesy with the powers of Elijah and Moses, are killed by the beast from the Abyss and left unburied in the great city, then raised and taken up to heaven.

entries.title: Rebels and would-be messiahs
entries.summary: In the decades around Jesus, men rose up claiming to deliver Israel: tax rebels, leaders of armed bands, and prophets who promised signs in the wilderness. Rome treated them all as rebels.
entries.plain: **Every few years another leader promised to free the country, gathered a crowd, and was gone by the next harvest.** Under Roman rule some Jews would not accept a foreign master. Some led tax revolts. Some gathered followers in the desert and promised miracles like those of Moses or Joshua. Rome cut them down, and their followers scattered once the leader was taken.
entries.then: When Judea came under a Roman governor in AD 6, Josephus says, a Galilean named Judas urged his countrymen to revolt. He "said they were cowards if they would endure to pay a tax to the Romans and would after God submit to mortal men as their lords." Two of Judas's sons, James and Simon, were later crucified on the orders of the governor Tiberius Alexander. Keener calls it a disastrous tax revolt that met terrible Roman retaliation. Wright says Rome left crosses around the countryside as a warning, and adds that anyone leading a kingdom-of-God movement was expected to oppose the tax. Many would-be messiahs drew large and devoted followings in the first century. Josephus, writing for Gentile readers, calls them false prophets, but their political aims usually show (Keener). Some promised to part the Jordan or make Jerusalem's walls fall, and most went out into the wilderness to imitate Moses. Josephus tells of impostors who led crowds into the desert promising signs of liberty, cut down by the governor Felix. He also tells of an Egyptian false prophet who gathered thirty thousand men and led them from the wilderness to the Mount of Olives to take Jerusalem. The word translated robbers was Josephus's standard term for revolutionaries. Keener suggests that the two men crucified with Jesus were colleagues of Barabbas. Wright notes that such claimants came and went, and their followers scattered quickly once the leader was caught. Under Felix, Josephus writes, the sicarii killed in daylight at the festivals. They "concealed daggers under their garments, with which they stabbed those that were their enemies," and their first victim was the high priest Jonathan. Their last stand came at Masada in AD 73.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a string of resistance leaders under a foreign occupation, each hailed as the one who will finally win. The occupiers keep a file on every one, and each new claimant is judged by how the last one ended.
entries.changes: Because claimants to Israel's deliverance came and went, any teacher with a following was watched as a possible rebel, which is the trap in the tax question of Mark 12:14. Warnings about false messiahs who appear in the wilderness, as in Matthew 24:26, describe a pattern hearers knew. Gamaliel names two such leaders, Theudas and Judas the Galilean, in Acts 5:36-37.
entries.not: **Not purely military commanders.** A resistance leader wins with weapons and planning. These claimants promised that God would act, parting the Jordan or bringing down Jerusalem's walls, and led crowds into the wilderness like a new Moses. Rome still treated them as rebels.
entries.dissent: Two points. First, how Rome answered Judas's revolt. Wright says Rome crushed it and left crosses around the countryside. Keener speaks of terrible retaliation without describing it. The passages of Josephus cited here report Judas's teaching and, decades later, the crucifixion of his sons, but not crosses after the revolt itself. Second, what the word robber or bandit meant, as at Mark 14:48 and 15:27. Keener calls it Josephus's standard term for revolutionaries, and Wright reads the men crucified with Jesus as revolutionaries; Garland, citing another scholar, says Josephus used it for social bandits who preyed on the rich and never for a revolutionary against Rome.

usedIn.n: Matthew 22:15-22, Caesar's coin
usedIn.s: Pharisees and Herodians ask Jesus whether it is lawful to pay the poll tax to Caesar. He asks for the coin, asks whose image is on it, and tells them to give Caesar and God what is theirs.

usedIn.n: Matthew 24:1-14, Stones, birth pangs and false messiahs
usedIn.s: As the disciples admire the temple, Jesus says not one stone will be left on another. On the Mount of Olives he warns of false messiahs, wars and persecution, the beginning of the birth pangs.

usedIn.n: Matthew 24:15-28, The desolating sacrilege and the flight
usedIn.s: When the desolating sacrilege spoken of by Daniel stands in the holy place, those in Judea must flee to the mountains at once. False messiahs will say he is in the wilderness, but his coming will be like lightning.

usedIn.n: Matthew 27:1-26, Blood money, Pilate and Barabbas
usedIn.s: At dawn the council hands Jesus to Pilate. Judas returns the silver and hangs himself, the priests buy a potter's field, and Pilate, warned by his wife's dream, releases Barabbas and washes his hands.

usedIn.n: Mark 14:32-52, Gethsemane and the arrest
usedIn.s: At a place called Gethsemane Jesus prays in anguish while three disciples sleep. Judas arrives with an armed crowd from the chief priests, greets him with a kiss, and the disciples run.

usedIn.n: Luke 20:20-26, Caesar's coin
usedIn.s: Spies sent by the leaders ask Jesus whether it is right to pay tribute to Caesar, hoping to hand him over to the governor. He asks whose image is on a denarius.

usedIn.n: Luke 21:5-38, The temple's stones and Jerusalem surrounded
usedIn.s: When people admire the temple's stones, Jesus says not one will be left on another. He warns of false claimants, arrests in synagogues, Jerusalem surrounded by armies, and signs in the sky before the Son of Man comes.

usedIn.n: Luke 22:24-38, Benefactors, thrones, sifting and two swords
usedIn.s: At the last supper the disciples argue over who is greatest. Jesus contrasts kings who are called benefactors with himself as one who serves, promises them thrones, warns Peter that Satan has asked to sift them, and speaks of swords.

usedIn.n: Luke 23:1-25, Before Pilate, before Antipas, and Barabbas
usedIn.s: The council brings Jesus to Pilate charged with forbidding tribute and claiming to be a king. Pilate sends him to Herod Antipas, who mocks him, and in the end Pilate gives in to the crowd and releases Barabbas.

usedIn.n: John 10:1-21, The good shepherd and the hired hand
usedIn.s: Jesus contrasts the shepherd who enters by the gate, calls his sheep by name and lays down his life for them with thieves who climb in another way and a hired hand who runs from the wolf.

usedIn.n: John 18:28-40, Pilate's headquarters at dawn
usedIn.s: At daybreak the leaders bring Jesus to the governor's headquarters but will not go in, so as to stay clean for Passover. Pilate questions him about being king of the Jews, finds no case, and offers to release him, but the crowd asks for Barabbas.

usedIn.n: Acts 5:12-42, Peter's shadow, the prison and Gamaliel
usedIn.s: Crowds bring the sick for Peter's shadow to fall on them. The apostles are jailed, freed by an angel, and brought before the council, where Gamaliel compares the movement to the failed causes of Theudas and Judas the Galilean.

usedIn.n: Acts 21:27-40, Riot in the temple, rescue by the tribune
usedIn.s: Jews from Asia see Paul in the temple and cry that he has brought Greeks into the holy place. The city riots, and the Roman tribune's soldiers pull him from the crowd, chain him, and nearly mistake him for the Egyptian rebel.

usedIn.n: Acts 23:12-35, The oath, the nephew and the night march
usedIn.s: More than forty men bind themselves by an oath not to eat until they have killed Paul. His nephew learns of the ambush, and the tribune sends Paul under heavy escort by night to the governor Felix at Caesarea, with a letter explaining the case.

usedIn.n: James 3:1-4:10, The tongue on fire, zeal and wars
usedIn.s: James warns would-be teachers that the tongue is a small fire set alight by hell, contrasts bitter envy and selfish ambition with the peaceable wisdom from above, traces fights and quarrels to desires at war within, calls friendship with the world enmity with God, and tells his readers to resist the devil.

entries.title: The war with Rome and the fall of Jerusalem
entries.summary: In AD 66 Judea rose against Rome. By AD 70 Roman armies had starved and burned Jerusalem, destroyed the temple and sacrificed to their standards where it had stood.
entries.plain: **The grandparents could still point to where the old cathedral stood before the bombing.** About forty years after Jesus, Judea rose against Rome. Rebel factions fought one another inside Jerusalem while the Roman legions closed in. The city starved, the temple burned, and Roman soldiers sacrificed to their own standards in its courts. The Gospels' first readers knew how it ended.
entries.then: Josephus, the main witness, began the war as a rebel leader and watched the siege from Titus's side. The outer wall fell around May of AD 70 and the temple at the end of August. Most Jews held the temple to be invincible, though a minority, including the Qumran community, expected it to be judged. Daniel's abomination that makes desolate (Daniel 9:27; 11:31; 12:11) had been seen fulfilled before. The ESV Study Bible recalls how Antiochus IV ordered an altar to Zeus set up in the temple in 167 BC. When Pilate brought standards bearing Caesar's image into Jerusalem, the crowds said they "would take their death very willingly, rather than the wisdom of their laws should be transgressed" (Josephus). Wright notes that in AD 40 the emperor Gaius Caligula tried to put a statue of himself in the temple. When the war came, Josephus saw the zealots' bloodshed in the temple as fulfilling an ancient oracle. The city would fall, it said, "when a sedition should invade the Jews, and their own hand should pollute the temple of God." He tells of a starving mother who killed and ate her son during the siege. He also tells of fugitives trapped by the flooded Jordan in 68 and slaughtered. After the burning, the soldiers brought their ensigns to the temple "and set them over against its eastern gate; and there did they offer sacrifices to them." The Burnt House in the upper city held revolt coins of 67 to 69 and none later (Garland). Many Jews saw God's judgment in the destruction. Early Christian historians say the Jerusalem Christians fled to Pella, as the ESV Study Bible reports from Eusebius.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a city that remembers the year its great cathedral burned in a war. Every sermon about judgment preached afterward is heard against that memory.
entries.changes: Warnings about the temple's fall and a time to flee, as in Matthew 24:15-16, point to the war of 66 to 70, and the cultural backgrounds notes set the burned city of a king's parable, as in Matthew 22:7, beside Rome's burning of Jerusalem a generation later. Luke 21:20 speaks of Jerusalem surrounded by armies.
entries.not: **Not the loss of one building among many.** A burned cathedral leaves the city and its other churches standing. In AD 70 the temple most Jews thought could never fall was burned, the city was starved by siege, and Roman soldiers sacrificed to their standards in its courts.
entries.dissent: Three questions. First, what the desolating sacrilege was. Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes follow Josephus: the zealots' bloodshed in the temple, then the Roman standards in its ruins. The ESV Study Bible sees Antiochus as an earlier pattern, with fulfillment in AD 70 and in a future image of the Antichrist. The CSB Study Bible says Jesus' word standing makes it an idolatrous object, not an event. Wright reads it as the pagan invasion ending with blasphemous objects in the temple. Second, the flight to the mountains. Keener says both the hills and the route to Pella could have offered refuge, and that the flight to Pella shows the saying was not invented later. Wright argues that no one would call a descent of three thousand feet to Pella fleeing to the hills. Third, whether the warnings were written after the event. Many scholars read the burned city of Matthew 22:7 and the detail of Mark 13 as hindsight, and Garland dates Mark to AD 68 to 70 on that basis. Carson, Moo and Morris answer that both use the stock language of sieges, not the events of 70, and say the same of Luke 19:43 and 21:20.

usedIn.n: Matthew 22:1-14, The king's wedding feast
usedIn.s: A king's invited guests refuse to come to his son's wedding and kill his messengers. He burns their city, fills the hall with people from the roads, and throws out a guest without wedding clothes.

usedIn.n: Matthew 24:15-28, The desolating sacrilege and the flight
usedIn.s: When the desolating sacrilege spoken of by Daniel stands in the holy place, those in Judea must flee to the mountains at once. False messiahs will say he is in the wilderness, but his coming will be like lightning.

usedIn.n: Luke 13:1-9, Pilate's victims, the tower and the fig tree
usedIn.s: People tell Jesus about Galileans whose blood Pilate mixed with their sacrifices. He answers with a tower that fell in Siloam, a call to repent, and a fig tree given one more year.

usedIn.n: Luke 13:22-35, The narrow door, the feast, the fox and the hen
usedIn.s: On the way to Jerusalem Jesus warns that many will find the door shut while people from east and west recline at the feast in God's kingdom. Warned that Herod wants to kill him, he calls Herod a fox and grieves over Jerusalem.

usedIn.n: Luke 19:28-48, The king rides down to the city and weeps over it
usedIn.s: Jesus rides a borrowed colt down the Mount of Olives while his disciples spread their cloaks and praise the king who comes. Seeing the city, he weeps over the siege to come, then drives the sellers out of the temple.

usedIn.n: Luke 21:5-38, The temple's stones and Jerusalem surrounded
usedIn.s: When people admire the temple's stones, Jesus says not one will be left on another. He warns of false claimants, arrests in synagogues, Jerusalem surrounded by armies, and signs in the sky before the Son of Man comes.

usedIn.n: Luke 23:26-49, The road to the cross, paradise, and the ninth hour
usedIn.s: Simon of Cyrene carries the cross, the women of Jerusalem mourn, and Jesus warns them of days to come. Crucified between two criminals, he promises one of them paradise and dies at the ninth hour.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 8:1-13, Copy and shadow, and a new covenant
usedIn.s: The high priest believers have is seated in heaven and serves in the true tabernacle set up by the Lord. The earthly sanctuary was a copy and shadow built to the pattern shown to Moses, and Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant shows that the first was growing old and ready to disappear.

usedIn.n: James 4:13-5:6, Merchants, landowners and the wages that cry out
usedIn.s: James rebukes traders who plan a year of business without God, then turns on rich landowners whose hoarded wealth is rotting, whose withheld wages cry out to the Lord of hosts, and who have fattened themselves for a day of slaughter and condemned the righteous one.

entries.title: Roman trials, the judgment seat and appeal
entries.summary: A Roman governor heard a case only when someone brought a formal charge, questioned the accused himself, and gave sentence from the judgment seat. In Judea only Rome could put a man to death, and a Roman citizen could ask for his case to go to Caesar.
aliases: not permitted to put anyone to death
entries.plain: **No case comes to court until somebody files a complaint and stands behind it.** Roman courts had no state prosecutor. An accuser had to bring a charge before the governor, and the governor then questioned the accused and decided the case himself. He could free, flog or execute, and in a province like Judea the power to put someone to death belonged to him, not to the local council. A death sentence was given formally, from a raised platform called the judgment seat. A Roman citizen could also ask for his case to be sent up to the emperor's own court.
entries.then: Roman law had no public prosecutor and depended on private accusers. A governor had to hear a case only once an official charge was laid. Governors first decided whether to take a case at all. They normally refused charges that were no offense under Roman law, such as breaches of local religious custom, as Gallio does in Acts 18:14-15. The governor looked into the facts himself, a procedure called cognitio, and his decree was binding in every capital case. Keener says that, though scholars debate it, Rome apparently let Jewish courts execute no one except a Gentile who entered the temple's inner courts. Wright writes that "officially the Romans had prohibited the Jews from carrying out the death penalty." Josephus says the first governor of Judea came "having the power of [life and] death put into his hands by Caesar." When the high priest Ananus had James stoned between governors, critics protested that "it was not lawful for Ananus to assemble a sanhedrim without his consent" (Josephus). A death sentence was pronounced from the judgment seat, a raised platform. Josephus shows Pilate at Caesarea, where "he came and sat upon his judgment-seat." The accuser spoke first, and if accusers failed to appear the case was supposed to be dropped. A Roman citizen could appeal to the emperor; Keener writes that "Roman citizens had the right to appeal to Caesar's tribunal". Appealing before a verdict, as Paul did, was less common, and the governor first conferred with his council. Wright stresses that "An appeal of this kind was not an appeal against sentence," but a request that the whole case go to the highest court.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a territory where the local police and courts handle everyday cases, but any death sentence must go to the federal governor, who alone can sign it. The local leaders can arrest and accuse; only he can order an execution.
entries.changes: Because only the governor could order an execution, the leaders in John 18:31 must bring Jesus to Pilate with a charge Rome would punish, and the death becomes a Roman crucifixion rather than a Jewish stoning. A citizen could take his case out of a governor's hands by appealing to Caesar, as Paul does in Acts 25:11. When Paul says everyone will stand before God's judgment seat in Romans 14:10, he borrows the governor's platform.
entries.not: **Not a review under fixed procedure.** A federal governor signing a sentence works within set rules and appeals. A Roman governor heard the case himself, needed a private accuser to bring it and could refuse it outright, and Keener notes that politics could weigh with him as much as guilt. Only a citizen could carry it to Caesar.
entries.dissent: Three questions. First, whether the Jewish council had lost the power to execute. Keener notes that later rabbinic sources date the loss to about AD 30 or AD 70. He answers that Josephus would have mentioned such a right if the council had it, and that later rabbis read their own authority back into the time before 70. The ESV Study Bible cites Talmud passages saying the Romans revoked the right before Jesus' death, and explains the exceptions as mob actions, such as Stephen's stoning, or acts when Roman oversight was weak. Josephus has Titus remind the Jews that Rome let them kill anyone who passed the temple barrier, "though he were a Roman." Second, where the judgment seat stood. Keener and his notes place the Stone Pavement by Herod's palace and date the Antonia pavement later. The CSB Study Bible says that kind of pavement has been excavated at the Antonia. The ESV Study Bible calls the location uncertain. Third, whether Festus had to grant Paul's appeal. The CSB Study Bible notes that scholars disagree. Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes say refusing it would have been politically awkward, and sending Paul on spared Festus a hard choice.

usedIn.n: John 18:28-40, Pilate's headquarters at dawn
usedIn.s: At daybreak the leaders bring Jesus to the governor's headquarters but will not go in, so as to stay clean for Passover. Pilate questions him about being king of the Jews, finds no case, and offers to release him, but the crowd asks for Barabbas.

usedIn.n: John 19:1-16, Flogged, mocked, and no friend of Caesar
usedIn.s: Pilate has Jesus flogged, the soldiers crown him with thorns and hail him as king, and Pilate shows him to the crowd. Warned that releasing him makes Pilate no friend of Caesar, he sits on the judgment seat at the Stone Pavement and hands him over.

usedIn.n: Acts 18:12-17, Gallio's judgment seat
usedIn.s: Jewish leaders bring Paul before Gallio, proconsul of Achaia, accusing him of teaching a worship contrary to the law. Gallio refuses to judge a dispute about words, names and their own law and drives them from the judgment seat.

usedIn.n: Acts 24:1-27, The hearing before Felix
usedIn.s: The high priest's orator Tertullus charges Paul before Felix with stirring up riots and trying to profane the temple. Paul answers point by point; Felix puts off a decision and keeps him in custody for two years, hoping for a bribe.

usedIn.n: Acts 25:1-12, Festus and the appeal to Caesar
usedIn.s: The new governor Festus hears the case again at Caesarea. When he asks whether Paul will be tried in Jerusalem, Paul appeals to Caesar, and after conferring with his council Festus grants it.

usedIn.n: Acts 25:13-26:32, Agrippa and Bernice hear Paul
usedIn.s: King Agrippa II and his sister Bernice visit Festus, who asks them to hear Paul so that he will have something to write to the emperor. Paul tells his story; Festus calls him mad, Agrippa turns the question aside, and all agree he could have been set free had he not appealed to Caesar.

usedIn.n: Acts 28:17-31, Two years in rented quarters
usedIn.s: Paul calls the Jewish leaders of Rome, explains why he is in chains, and spends a day arguing from Moses and the Prophets. Some are persuaded and some are not; for two whole years he lives at his own expense, welcoming everyone and preaching the kingdom without hindrance.

usedIn.n: Romans 14:1-23, Vegetables, holy days and wine
usedIn.s: Some believers eat only vegetables and keep certain days; others eat anything and treat every day alike. Paul tells both not to judge one another, since all will stand before God's judgment seat, and not to wreck another's faith over food.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 6:1-11, Lawsuits before unbelievers
usedIn.s: Paul is appalled that believers take one another to court before pagan judges, reminds them that God's people will judge the world and even angels, and asks why they would not rather be wronged.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 5:1-10, The tent and the judgment seat
usedIn.s: Paul sets the earthly tent of the body against a building from God, longs to be clothed rather than found naked, names the Spirit as a down payment, and says that all must appear before the judgment seat of Christ.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 4:9-22, The cloak, the scrolls, the first defense, and before winter
usedIn.s: Paul asks Timothy to come quickly and bring Mark, the cloak he left at Troas and his scrolls; Alexander the metalworker did him great harm, no one stood with him at his first defense, but the Lord rescued him from the lion's mouth, and Timothy must come before winter.

usedIn.n: James 2:1-13, The gold ring and the good seat
usedIn.s: James forbids favoritism in the assembly. A rich man with a gold ring is given a good seat and a poor man in dirty clothes is told to stand, though it is the rich who drag believers into court and slander the noble name; the royal law of love rules out partiality, and mercy triumphs over judgment.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 3:8-22, A defense, and the spirits in prison
usedIn.s: Peter calls for harmony and for blessing in return for insult, and tells his readers to be ready to make a defense of their hope. Christ suffered once for sins, was put to death in the body and made alive in the Spirit, and went and made proclamation to the spirits in prison who disobeyed in Noah's day; the flood that saved eight people prefigures baptism, and Christ has gone into heaven, where every angelic authority and power is subject to him.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 4:12-19, The fiery ordeal and the name Christian
usedIn.s: The readers should not be surprised at the fiery ordeal, but rejoice to share Christ's sufferings. No one should suffer as a murderer, a thief or a meddler, but anyone who suffers as a Christian should not be ashamed; judgment begins with God's household, so those who suffer should commit themselves to their faithful Creator.

entries.title: Agrippa I and the later Herods
entries.summary: Herod the Great's grandson Agrippa I was made king of all Judea by Claudius and ruled from AD 41 to 44, courting his Jewish subjects. His son Agrippa II later ruled smaller territories and heard Paul's defense.
entries.plain: **The playboy prince who partied with the emperor's nephew ended up a king, and he made sure his people saw him at prayer.** Agrippa I was Herod the Great's grandson. He spent years in Rome, became a friend of the future emperor Caligula, and was made king. Under Claudius he ruled all the lands his grandfather had held, from AD 41 until his sudden death in 44. Part Hasmonean on his grandmother's side, he was accepted as Jewish, and he worked hard to please his Jewish subjects. Acts calls him King Herod.
entries.then: Agrippa I was the grandson of Herod the Great and of the Hasmonean princess Mariamne. He was the brother of Herodias, who once had to lend him money. In Rome he became close to Gaius Caligula, and he became the first king of Judea since his grandfather. Wright and Bird say he helped Claudius become emperor after Caligula's murder and was rewarded with the territory his grandfather had ruled. The CSB Study Bible dates his rule in Palestine from AD 37 to 44. Because of his Hasmonean grandmother he was counted Jewish as well as Idumean. He was popular, favored the Pharisees and was often in the temple. Josephus says "he loved to live continually at Jerusalem, and was exactly careful in the observance of the laws of his country," offering sacrifice every day. He worked to prove his Jewish identity to his people, and his reign began a nationalist revival that ran on to the revolt of AD 66. As king he held the power of life and death that the Sanhedrin lacked. Wright calls him the Jews' own man and trusted by Rome. Josephus tells of his death at Caesarea. At shows in honor of Caesar, wearing "a garment made wholly of silver," he let flatterers call him a god. He was seized with pains in the belly and died five days later, aged fifty-four. His son Agrippa II was only seventeen, so Judea went back to direct Roman rule (Wright and Bird). Agrippa II later ruled small, mostly Gentile territories, appointed high priests and stayed loyal to Rome. His sister Drusilla left the king of Emesa to marry the governor Felix. His sister Bernice, who lived with him, later became the mistress of Titus.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a well-connected heir installed by a foreign power to govern his grandfather's old kingdom. He keeps both audiences happy, the capital that appointed him and the crowds at home, until the day a public show goes wrong.
entries.changes: The King Herod of Acts 12:1 is Agrippa I, who killed James to please his Jewish subjects and died after accepting divine honors, so the chapter sets a king who takes worship against apostles who refuse it. His son Agrippa II, with his sister Bernice, hears Paul in Acts 25:13.
entries.not: **Not a governor who only had to keep order.** An installed heir can rule on the foreign power's backing alone. Agrippa also had to prove himself a Jew to his people, sacrificing daily at the temple. Nor is he the Herod of the nativity or of John the Baptist; those were his grandfather and his uncle Antipas.
entries.dissent: When his rule began. The CSB Study Bible says he ruled in Palestine from AD 37 to 44; the cultural backgrounds notes count him king of Judea from AD 41 to 44. Wright and Bird reconcile the two: Caligula gave him the northern territories first, and Claudius added Judea in 41. On the occasion of his death, Josephus speaks of a festival for Caesar's safety, Keener suggests the emperor's birthday or a festival in March AD 44, and Wright and Bird place it at Passover in AD 44. Bernice is also judged differently: the CSB Study Bible speaks of her checkered sexual and marital history, while the cultural backgrounds notes say she appears favorably in Josephus and that the rumor of incest with her brother was almost certainly slander.

usedIn.s: King Herod Agrippa kills James and jails Peter at Passover, but an angel leads Peter out. Later, in Caesarea, the king accepts the crowd's cry that he speaks with a god's voice and is struck down.

entries.title: Stoning
entries.summary: The law of Moses named stoning as the penalty for blasphemy, but under Rome Jewish courts could not execute without the governor. In practice stoning was what angry crowds did, in Jewish and Gentile towns alike.
aliases: dragged him out of the city
entries.plain: **The crowd did not wait for a judge; they grabbed whatever was on the ground.** The law of Moses made stoning the punishment for blasphemy and a few other crimes. By the first century Rome kept the death penalty for itself, so a lawful stoning needed the governor's approval. But stones were always at hand, and in Jewish and Greek cities alike an angry crowd could turn into a mob and stone someone it hated. Executions and burials took place outside the city.
entries.then: Stoning was the biblical penalty for blasphemy (Leviticus 24:16) and several other crimes. Rome, though, forbade executions unless the governor allowed them. Jewish and Gentile texts alike show that mobs often stoned people to death. In the ideal procedure of second-century Jewish tradition, the condemned was thrown from a height at least twice a man's height. The witnesses threw the first large stones, aiming for the chest. The condemned was to be stripped and to confess his sins. Executions and burials took place outside cities, and even after a mob killing inside a city the body would be dragged out. In Gentile cities stoning was a frequent act of urban mobs, who threw tiles and whatever else came to hand. The ESV Study Bible weighs whether Stephen died by formal sentence or by mob violence, since under Rome the Sanhedrin had no right to execute. Wright, telling Paul's story, says Stephen was stoned illegally because only the Romans could carry out the death penalty. God's disobedient people had threatened to stone his servants before (Exodus 17:4; Numbers 14:10). Josephus reports that in AD 62, between governors, the high priest Ananus assembled the Sanhedrin and "brought before them the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ, whose name was James," with some others, and had them stoned. The most fair-minded citizens protested, and Ananus lost the high priesthood after three months (Antiquities 20.9.1).
entries.bridge: An analogy: a lynching in a frontier town, where everyone knows the law says to wait for the circuit judge. The crowd tells itself it is doing what the law would have done anyway.
entries.changes: When crowds pick up stones, as in John 8:59, they treat a claim as blasphemy and take the verdict into their own hands. Stephen's death in Acts 7:58 follows the shape of a legal stoning outside the city, though Rome reserved the death penalty, and Paul could later say, in 2 Corinthians 11:25, that he had once been stoned.
entries.not: **Not a crime against the people's own law.** A lynch mob defies the law it claims to anticipate. Stoning was the penalty the law of Moses itself set for blasphemy; what the crowd ignored was Rome's rule that only the governor could order a death.
entries.dissent: Lawful sentence or lynching in Stephen's case. The ESV Study Bible notes that Stephen stood before the council, which favors a formal sentence, but that the haste of the stoning suggests a mob. Keener says his hearers lynch him according to their own law, and the cultural backgrounds notes point out how often mobs stoned people.

usedIn.n: Acts 7:54-8:3, The stoning of Stephen
usedIn.s: Stephen sees the Son of Man standing at God's right hand, and his hearers drag him out and stone him while a young man named Saul looks after their coats. Persecution scatters the church.

usedIn.n: Acts 14:1-20, Iconium and Lystra: taken for Zeus and Hermes
usedIn.s: After a plot in Iconium, Paul heals a lame man at Lystra and the crowd hails him and Barnabas as Hermes and Zeus. When they refuse the sacrifice, the crowd is turned against them and Paul is stoned.

usedIn.n: James 4:13-5:6, Merchants, landowners and the wages that cry out
usedIn.s: James rebukes traders who plan a year of business without God, then turns on rich landowners whose hoarded wealth is rotting, whose withheld wages cry out to the Lord of hosts, and who have fattened themselves for a day of slaughter and condemned the righteous one.

entries.title: Roman citizenship
entries.summary: In the eastern provinces few people outside the colonies were citizens of Rome. A citizen could not be beaten or chained without trial, could appeal to Caesar, and outranked almost everyone around him.
entries.plain: **The officer was about to have him whipped, until he showed the passport that said he was one of them.** Being a citizen of Rome was a rare privilege in the eastern provinces. You could be born to it, be freed by a Roman master, live in a Roman colony, earn it in the army or by service, and under some emperors you could buy it. A citizen could not be beaten or chained without a trial and could ask for his case to go to Caesar. Lying about it could cost you your life.
entries.then: In this period Roman citizenship in the provinces marked high status, and the cultural backgrounds notes call it very rare in the East outside the colonies. Keener lists the ways in. A man could be born to a Roman father, belong to a colony, be discharged from the auxiliary army, or belong to a local aristocracy Rome had honored. Most commonly, after birth in Rome or a colony, he could be freed by a Roman owner. Some bought it with bribes, which was common under Claudius, and being born a citizen ranked higher. The Porcian and Julian laws forbade binding or beating a citizen without trial, and even chaining an untried citizen was illegal. The CSB Study Bible adds exemption from crucifixion. A claim had to be honored before it could be checked. It was checked against records in the citizen's home city, or against the small wooden tablets some carried like a passport. Keener writes, "Falsely claiming citizenship was a capital offense." Magistrates who abused a citizen could lose their office. Wright notes that officials remembered Cicero's prosecution of Verres, whose crowning fault was crucifying a Roman citizen. The protection was not always honored. Josephus tells how the governor Florus had Jerusalem men of equestrian rank whipped and crucified, "although they were by birth Jews, yet were they of Roman dignity notwithstanding." Citizenship of a Greek city such as Tarsus was a local honor and did not make a man Roman. In many cities settled foreigners stayed resident aliens for generations. They had no vote but ranked above newcomers, and most Jewish communities held that status. Wright and Bird note that Paul never mentions his Roman citizenship in his letters.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a traveler under arrest abroad who produces a diplomatic passport. The guards who were rough a minute ago start worrying about their careers, because they have mistreated someone the law protects.
entries.changes: Citizenship explains why magistrates who beat Paul without trial come to apologize in Acts 16:37-39 and why a tribune halts a flogging in Acts 22:25-29. Paul tells believers in a Roman colony, in Philippians 3:20, that their citizenship is in heaven.
entries.not: **Not immunity from arrest or trial.** A diplomatic passport puts its holder beyond local law. A Roman citizen could still be held and tried; what he gained was freedom from binding, beating or crucifixion without trial, and even that was not always honored.
entries.dissent: How Paul's family became citizens. The cultural backgrounds notes suggest ancestors freed from slavery in Rome; Keener, special service to Rome or freedom granted by a well-to-do Roman; the CSB Study Bible, an ancestor's service, perhaps making tents for the army. Wright and Bird say no one can tell, though a Judean captive later freed is one possibility. Why Paul waited to speak at Philippi is read two ways: Keener sees a strategy that left the magistrates in the wrong; the cultural backgrounds notes suggest Paul and Silas may not have expected the illegality to be taken seriously there. Third, what heavenly citizenship in Philippians 3:20 implies. Keener and his notes stress that the Philippians knew what it was to be citizens of a supreme city they had never seen; Wright and Bird stress that citizens of Rome were agents of Roman civilization where they lived, not people waiting to retire to the mother city.

usedIn.n: Acts 16:25-40, The jailer and the Roman citizens
usedIn.s: At midnight an earthquake opens the prison. The jailer, about to kill himself, believes with his household; next day Paul reveals that he and Silas are Roman citizens beaten without trial, and the magistrates come to apologize.

usedIn.n: Acts 22:22-29, A Roman citizen under the lash
usedIn.s: When Paul speaks of his mission to the Gentiles, the crowd erupts again. The tribune orders him examined by flogging, until Paul asks the centurion whether it is lawful to flog an uncondemned Roman citizen.

usedIn.n: Acts 25:1-12, Festus and the appeal to Caesar
usedIn.s: The new governor Festus hears the case again at Caesarea. When he asks whether Paul will be tried in Jerusalem, Paul appeals to Caesar, and after conferring with his council Festus grants it.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 11:16-33, The fool's boast and the basket over the wall
usedIn.s: Forced to boast like a fool, Paul matches his rivals' Jewish credentials and then lists sufferings instead of achievements: lashes, rods, stoning, shipwreck, the dangers of the road, hunger and cold, and a night escape down the wall of Damascus.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 2:11-22, The dividing wall torn down, and a new temple
usedIn.s: Paul reminds Gentile believers that they were once far off, shut out of Israel's citizenship and covenants, and tells them Christ has broken down the dividing wall and built Jews and Gentiles into one household and one temple.

usedIn.n: Philippians 1:12-26, Chains known to the whole palace guard
usedIn.s: Paul tells how his imprisonment has carried the gospel through the palace guard and made other preachers bolder, some from rivalry, then weighs living against dying and expects to stay on for their sake.

usedIn.n: Philippians 1:27-30, Live as citizens, contend like athletes
usedIn.s: Paul tells a church in a Roman colony to conduct itself as citizens worthy of the gospel, standing firm and striving together, unafraid of opponents, in the same struggle they once saw him face.

usedIn.n: Philippians 3:12-4:1, The race, citizens of heaven, and a Savior from there
usedIn.s: Paul pictures himself as a runner straining toward the prize, warns against those whose god is their stomach, and reminds a Roman colony that its citizenship is in heaven, from where it awaits a Savior who will transform its lowly bodies.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 1:1-12, To the exiles of the dispersion
usedIn.s: Peter writes to God's chosen exiles scattered through five provinces of Asia Minor, blesses God for a new birth into a living hope and an inheritance kept in heaven, and tells them their trials test their faith as fire tests gold. The prophets searched for this salvation, and angels long to look into it.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 1:13-25, Minds girded, foreigners, and the lamb
usedIn.s: Peter calls his readers to be ready and sober, holy as God is holy, and to live as foreigners in reverent fear, since they were ransomed not with silver or gold but with the blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish. Born again of imperishable seed, the living word, they must love one another deeply.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 2:11-17, Foreigners among the nations; honor the emperor
usedIn.s: As foreigners and exiles the readers must keep their conduct good among the Gentiles, who slander them as wrongdoers. They are to submit to every human authority, the emperor and his governors, and so silence ignorant talk; they are free people, but slaves of God. Honor everyone, love the believers, fear God, honor the emperor.

usedIn.n: Revelation 20:1-6, Satan bound and the thousand years
usedIn.s: An angel with the key to the Abyss and a great chain seizes the dragon, binds him for a thousand years and seals him in the Abyss so that he cannot deceive the nations. Those beheaded for their witness, who refused the beast and its mark, come to life and reign with Christ for the thousand years, the first resurrection, over which the second death has no power.

entries.title: Prison, chains and Roman custody
entries.summary: Roman prisons held people until trial or execution; they were not a punishment in themselves. How a prisoner was kept, in the stocks of an inner cell or lightly chained to one soldier, depended on his rank.
entries.plain: **The man in the cell was waiting for his day in court, and if his friends did not bring food he went hungry.** Roman prisons held people until their case was heard or their sentence carried out. They were dark, filthy and crowded, and prisoners relied on friends outside for food and clothes. Treatment depended on rank: a poor man might sit in the stocks in an inner cell, while a citizen of standing could be kept in a palace or in his own rented rooms with one soldier chained to him. The guard answered for his prisoner, sometimes with his own life.
entries.then: Keener notes that prison and chains held a person until trial; they were not a punishment. Prisons were filthy, and prisoners slept on cold floors. Clothing and anything beyond bare rations had to come from outside, often with a bribe to the guards. Wright says captors did not normally feed prisoners at all. Stocks in an inner cell added security and pain, and were thought fit only for people of low status. A prisoner could be chained by each hand to a soldier on either side. Custody followed rank. Felix kept Paul in Herod's palace at Caesarea, high-status prisoners were treated better, and friends could be allowed to supply their needs. At Rome Paul lived in his own lodging chained to one soldier. The cultural backgrounds notes take this as a sign he was treated as a man of rank who posed no danger. Keener says the soldier would be from the Praetorian Guard, under the prefect Burrus. No army was allowed in Italy, so the emperor's elite guard filled that role. Its men, the best paid in the army, counted as the emperor's clients and so as part of his household. That household took in all his slaves and freedmen and always carried prestige. Detention and chains were normally a mark of shame, and people often drew back from friends in custody. Chains were heavy and humiliating and chafed the skin, and "the prisoner's sweat sometimes rusted them on the arm" (the cultural backgrounds notes).
entries.bridge: An analogy: a holding center for people awaiting trial, where an important detainee gets a private room and visitors while a poor one sleeps on the floor of the common cell. Nobody there has been sentenced; the conditions say who they are.
entries.changes: Because prison was for holding, not punishing, a prisoner's conditions show how officials ranked him, from the stocks of Acts 16:24 to the rented quarters of Acts 28:30. Paul writes in Philippians 1:13 that his chains have become known to the whole palace guard.
entries.not: **Not a center that feeds and houses its detainees.** A modern holding center provides meals and a bed. Roman prisoners relied on friends outside for food and clothing, often bribing the guards, and wore chains that marked them with shame.
entries.dissent: Two questions. First, what happened to a guard who lost a prisoner. The CSB Study Bible says he suffered the prisoner's punishment. The cultural backgrounds notes say shipwreck would normally absolve soldiers, though they took no chances; Keener says guards were less liable if prisoners died at sea than if they escaped. Second, where Paul was held when he wrote the prison letters. Keener, his notes and the ESV and CSB Study Bibles favor Rome, around AD 60 to 62; the CSB Study Bible names Caesarea, around AD 57 to 59, as the other option. Wright, with several scholars, and Wright and Bird argue for an imprisonment at Ephesus in the mid fifties. The praetorium of Philippians 1:13 is read to match. Keener, his notes and the CSB Study Bible take it as the Praetorian Guard; the ESV Study Bible allows that or a governor's residence. Wright and Bird argue that Ephesus too had an imperial residence with officials and a small garrison. Carson, Moo and Morris set Caesarea aside and lean slightly to Rome for Colossians and Philemon but to Ephesus for Philippians, citing inscriptions placing part of the guard at Ephesus. They call the question insoluble.
