usedIn.n: Acts 16:16-24, The slave girl with a Python spirit
usedIn.s: A slave girl who earns her owners money by fortune-telling follows Paul, crying out about the Most High God. Paul drives the spirit out, and her owners drag him and Silas before the magistrates, who have them beaten and jailed.

usedIn.n: Acts 16:25-40, The jailer and the Roman citizens
usedIn.s: At midnight an earthquake opens the prison. The jailer, about to kill himself, believes with his household; next day Paul reveals that he and Silas are Roman citizens beaten without trial, and the magistrates come to apologize.

usedIn.n: Acts 21:27-40, Riot in the temple, rescue by the tribune
usedIn.s: Jews from Asia see Paul in the temple and cry that he has brought Greeks into the holy place. The city riots, and the Roman tribune's soldiers pull him from the crowd, chain him, and nearly mistake him for the Egyptian rebel.

usedIn.n: Acts 22:22-29, A Roman citizen under the lash
usedIn.s: When Paul speaks of his mission to the Gentiles, the crowd erupts again. The tribune orders him examined by flogging, until Paul asks the centurion whether it is lawful to flog an uncondemned Roman citizen.

usedIn.n: Acts 23:12-35, The oath, the nephew and the night march
usedIn.s: More than forty men bind themselves by an oath not to eat until they have killed Paul. His nephew learns of the ambush, and the tribune sends Paul under heavy escort by night to the governor Felix at Caesarea, with a letter explaining the case.

usedIn.n: Acts 24:1-27, The hearing before Felix
usedIn.s: The high priest's orator Tertullus charges Paul before Felix with stirring up riots and trying to profane the temple. Paul answers point by point; Felix puts off a decision and keeps him in custody for two years, hoping for a bribe.

usedIn.n: Acts 27:1-26, Sailing late in the season
usedIn.s: Paul sails for Rome in the custody of a centurion named Julius, changing to an Alexandrian grain ship at Myra. With the Fast already past, the owner presses on against Paul's warning, and a northeaster drives the ship helpless for days until an angel promises Paul that all aboard will live.

usedIn.n: Acts 27:27-44, Shipwreck off Malta
usedIn.s: On the fourteenth night the sailors sense land, drop anchors from the stern and try to slip away in the ship's boat. Paul urges everyone to eat and gives thanks over bread, and when the ship breaks up the centurion stops the soldiers from killing the prisoners; all 276 reach the shore.

usedIn.n: Acts 28:11-16, The Twin Brothers and the road to Rome
usedIn.s: After three months they sail in an Alexandrian ship with the Twin Brothers as its figurehead, land at Puteoli and walk the Appian Way toward Rome, where believers come out to meet Paul. In Rome he is allowed to live on his own with a soldier guarding him.

usedIn.n: Acts 28:17-31, Two years in rented quarters
usedIn.s: Paul calls the Jewish leaders of Rome, explains why he is in chains, and spends a day arguing from Moses and the Prophets. Some are persuaded and some are not; for two whole years he lives at his own expense, welcoming everyone and preaching the kingdom without hindrance.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 3:1-13, The prisoner, the steward and the mystery shown to the powers
usedIn.s: Paul, a prisoner for the sake of the Gentiles, breaks off to explain the stewardship of grace given him: the mystery, now revealed, that Gentiles are co-heirs, made known through the church even to the rulers in the heavenly realms.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 6:18-24, An ambassador in chains, and the man who carried the letter
usedIn.s: Paul asks for prayer that he may speak boldly, calling himself an ambassador in chains, and sends Tychicus to carry the letter and tell them his news.

usedIn.n: Philippians 1:1-11, A letter between friends, and a partnership in the gospel
usedIn.s: Paul and Timothy greet the believers at Philippi with their overseers and deacons, thank God for their partnership in the gospel from the first day, and pray that their love will grow until the day of Christ.

usedIn.n: Philippians 1:12-26, Chains known to the whole palace guard
usedIn.s: Paul tells how his imprisonment has carried the gospel through the palace guard and made other preachers bolder, some from rivalry, then weighs living against dying and expects to stay on for their sake.

usedIn.n: Philippians 4:10-23, A thank-you without a thank you, and Caesar's household
usedIn.s: Paul acknowledges the Philippians' gift in the language of contentment and of business receipts and sacrifice, without a direct thank you, and closes with greetings from the saints of Caesar's household.

usedIn.n: Colossians 4:7-18, Tychicus, Onesimus, Nympha's house and the letter from Laodicea
usedIn.s: Paul sends the letter with Tychicus and Onesimus, passes on greetings from Jewish and Gentile co-workers, greets Nympha and the church in her house, asks for this letter to be read at Laodicea and the Laodicean letter at Colossae, and signs off in his own hand.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 1:8-18, Not ashamed of my chains, the deposit, and Onesiphorus
usedIn.s: Paul tells Timothy not to be ashamed of the Lord's testimony or of him as a prisoner, but to share his suffering and guard the good deposit; everyone in Asia has deserted him except Onesiphorus, who searched Rome until he found him.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 2:1-13, Soldier, athlete and farmer, and a prisoner in chains
usedIn.s: Timothy is to pass on what he heard to reliable people who will teach others, and to endure hardship like a soldier, compete by the rules like an athlete and work like a farmer, remembering Jesus Christ, raised from the dead and descended from David, for whom Paul is chained like a criminal.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 4:9-22, The cloak, the scrolls, the first defense, and before winter
usedIn.s: Paul asks Timothy to come quickly and bring Mark, the cloak he left at Troas and his scrolls; Alexander the metalworker did him great harm, no one stood with him at his first defense, but the Lord rescued him from the lion's mouth, and Timothy must come before winter.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 10:26-39, No sacrifice left; prison and plunder
usedIn.s: For anyone who goes on sinning deliberately after knowing the truth, no sacrifice for sins remains. The readers once endured a hard contest: public insult, prison and the seizure of their property, which they accepted with joy. They must not throw away their confidence now.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 11:32-40, Sawn in two, dressed in skins
usedIn.s: Time fails to tell of the judges, David, Samuel and the prophets, who conquered kingdoms and escaped the sword. Others were tortured and refused release to gain a better resurrection; they were mocked, flogged, chained, stoned, sawn in two, and wandered in skins and caves, people the world was not worthy of.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 13:1-6, Strangers, angels, prisoners
usedIn.s: The writer turns to everyday duties: brotherly love, hospitality to strangers, since some have entertained angels without knowing it, care for prisoners as if in prison with them, honor for marriage, and freedom from the love of money.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 13:18-25, Timothy released, greetings from Italy
usedIn.s: The writer asks for prayer so that he may be restored to his readers soon, blesses them in the name of the God of peace who brought back from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep, calls the letter a brief word of exhortation, and reports that Timothy has been released. Those from Italy send greetings.

entries.title: The triumph and the arena
entries.summary: Rome celebrated a great victory with a triumph, a parade of the general, his army and the spoils, with chained captives at the end who were killed or sold. Cities also staged shows in which condemned criminals fought or were thrown to beasts.
entries.plain: **The parade ended in the city square, and the prisoners at the back of it did not leave alive.** When a Roman general won a great war he was given a triumph, a grand procession through Rome. He rode in a chariot, his army marched behind, wagons carried the loot, and last of all came the chained captives, who were killed or sold at the end. Cities across the empire also put on shows in their theaters, where criminals and prisoners were made to fight or were thrown to wild animals to entertain the crowd. Both were familiar ways of putting the beaten and the condemned on display.
entries.then: Bailey describes the triumph. The conqueror came near the head of the procession in his chariot. Behind him walked priests and leading men, then the army that had won and carts loaded with booty. At the very end came captives in chains, killed at the end of the route in a public sacrifice to the Roman gods. Wright describes the triumphal arches the procession passed through, the public show of glory and power, and the bedraggled prisoners at the back. He says the day usually ended with the prisoners killed or sold. In his commentary on Colossians he adds that the defeated king came last and was executed as the climax. So every crucifixion of a rebel king was a small Roman triumph. The senate decreed public thanksgivings before a triumph, and incense burned along the way as at sacrifices. These were "great celebrations for the victors and great humiliations for the defeated" (Keener; the cultural backgrounds notes). Josephus watched the triumph of Vespasian and Titus, with the spoils of the temple carried through Rome. He writes that at the temple of Jupiter "it was the Romans' ancient custom to stay till somebody brought the news that the general of the enemy was slain." The arena was the other great spectacle. The official in charge of the games showed off the gladiators who would fight wild beasts. The last show of the day was normally kept for the most wretched criminal condemned to die. Keener writes that "Corinth's theater seated eighteen thousand." Older than the triumph was the conqueror's custom, behind Psalm 68:18, of taking tribute and plunder from the defeated. He handed most of the spoils to his soldiers. Heiser notes that conquerors paraded captives and demanded tribute, then shared out the booty.
entries.bridge: An analogy: the victory parade at the end of a war, when the winning army marches through the capital past cheering crowds and the defeated enemy is put on show. Nobody watching mistakes which side the prisoners are on.
entries.changes: Because the triumph ended with its captives and the arena kept the condemned for last, the apostles displayed last of all like men sentenced to death, in 1 Corinthians 4:9, are pictured at the bottom of public shame. 2 Corinthians 2:14 pictures God leading his people in triumph, and Colossians 2:15 has the powers disarmed and put on display.
entries.not: **Not a civic celebration that ends when the march does.** A modern victory parade honors the troops and sends everyone home. The triumph was also a religious rite, with incense and thanksgivings to the gods, and for the captives at the back it ended in death or slavery.
entries.dissent: Which picture lies behind 1 Corinthians 4:9. Wright and Bailey read the triumph, with the apostles as the captives at the end of the procession; the ESV Study Bible thinks probably the triumph, or else gladiators condemned in the arena; Keener, his notes and the CSB Study Bible think the arena likelier, with the apostles as the last show of the day; the Zondervan dictionary joins the two, since the captives at the end of a triumph were condemned to fight beasts. On 1 Corinthians 15:32 the sources read agree that Paul's fight with beasts at Ephesus is figurative, since Roman citizens were exempt from that death and he survived.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 4:6-13, Apostles on display
usedIn.s: With biting irony Paul sets the Corinthians, already full, rich and reigning, beside the apostles, put on show last of all like men condemned to die, hungry, ragged, homeless and treated as the world's scum.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 15:12-34, If the dead are not raised
usedIn.s: Against some who say there is no resurrection of the dead, Paul argues that then Christ was not raised either, calls Christ the firstfruits, and asks why anyone is baptized for the dead or why he fights wild beasts if the dead are not raised.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 2:14-17, Led in God's triumph
usedIn.s: Paul thanks God, who leads him in triumphal procession and spreads the fragrance of Christ through him, a smell of death to some and of life to others, and denies that he peddles God's word for profit.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 4:1-16, The conqueror goes up and gives gifts
usedIn.s: Paul urges unity, one body and one Spirit, then reads Psalm 68 as Christ ascending in victory and handing out gifts: apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers, to equip the church to grow up into him.

usedIn.n: Colossians 2:8-15, The philosophy, a cancelled IOU and a triumph
usedIn.s: Paul warns against a philosophy built on human tradition and the elements of the world, tells Gentile believers they have already been circumcised in Christ, and pictures God cancelling their debt at the cross and leading the powers captive.

usedIn.n: Revelation 17:1-6, the woman on the scarlet beast
usedIn.s: An angel carries John into a wilderness to see the great prostitute who sits on many waters, riding a scarlet beast full of blasphemous names. Dressed in purple and scarlet and glittering with gold and pearls, she holds a golden cup of filth, bears the name Babylon the great on her forehead and is drunk with the blood of God's people.

usedIn.n: Revelation 19:11-21, the rider on the white horse
usedIn.s: Heaven opens and a rider on a white horse, named Faithful and True and the Word of God, leads heaven's armies, his robe stained with blood and a sword coming from his mouth, his title King of kings. Birds are summoned to feast on the fallen, the beast and the false prophet are seized and cast into the fiery lake, and their armies fall to the rider's sword.

entries.title: Roman soldiers and their gear
entries.summary: The legionary was the most familiar picture of armed strength in the provinces: helmet, breastplate, boots, a big shield and a short sword, fighting shoulder to shoulder. Legions that held their ranks were thought almost unbeatable.
aliases: helmet of the hope of salvation
entries.plain: **Anyone who has watched riot police lock their shields together knows what a line of trained men can do.** Most people in the Roman provinces had seen soldiers. A legionary wore a helmet and a breastplate of leather and metal, sturdy half boots and a belt or apron, and he carried a large shield and a short sword for close fighting. The armor covered only the front, because soldiers fought facing forward, side by side. As long as the ranks held, a legion was very hard to beat.
entries.then: Paul borrows the Old Testament picture of God as a warrior in armor (Isaiah 59:17; Wisdom of Solomon 5:17-20). Keener writes that most of his hearers had seen Roman soldiers, though, and would picture one ready for battle. The belt may be the leather apron under the armor or the metal belt over the lower belly. The breastplate was usually leather covered with metal. Like the bronze or iron helmet with its cheek pieces, it was worn only for battle. Soldiers wore the caliga, a half boot, so they could advance without worrying about what lay underfoot. The large rectangular wooden shield stood about four feet high. It was faced with leather that was soaked before a battle against flaming arrows. When the front rank held shields forward and those behind held theirs overhead, legionaries were nearly proof against such arrows. The gladius, 20 to 24 inches long, was for close combat once the lances had been thrown. Soldiers often carried two pila, driving the first into an enemy's shield to make it unwieldy. Generals urged their men to stand, counting retreat and wounds in the back as shameful. Legions that held ranks on open ground were considered almost invincible. Josephus writes that "The footmen are armed with breastplates and head-pieces, and have swords on each side". Generals addressed their troops before battle. Philosophers spoke of their fight against wicked ideas and for the truth as wrestling or war. Soldiers served about twenty years and could not marry while serving, though some kept concubines. About half lived to retire.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a firefighter's protective gear, each piece made for one danger, worn only when the alarm sounds and little use to a crew member who wanders off alone.
entries.changes: Because the legionary was the most familiar picture of armed strength, the armor of God in Ephesians 6:10-17 would bring a Roman soldier to mind alongside Isaiah's warrior God. 1 Thessalonians 5:8 gives a shorter version, the breastplate of faith and love and the helmet of the hope of salvation.
entries.not: **Not purely protective gear.** A firefighter's kit only shields its wearer. The Roman soldier also carried the gladius for close combat and stood in ranks against a living enemy; in Paul's picture that enemy is spiritual and the one weapon is God's word.
entries.dissent: Which picture comes first. Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes say that although the language comes from Isaiah, most hearers would first picture a Roman soldier. The ESV Study Bible says the description draws mainly on Old Testament allusions, though "the terms used also overlap well with Roman weaponry", especially the tall, door-like shield and the short sword for stabbing. Arnold and Wright also put Isaiah first (11:5; 52:7; 59:17), Arnold calling it unimportant which soldier Paul had in mind; the Zondervan dictionary thinks the picture drawn from Paul's contact with his Roman guards.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 6:10-17, The armor of God
usedIn.s: Paul calls the believers to stand firm in God's armor, because their struggle is not against flesh and blood but against rulers, authorities and spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms.

usedIn.n: Philippians 1:27-30, Live as citizens, contend like athletes
usedIn.s: Paul tells a church in a Roman colony to conduct itself as citizens worthy of the gospel, standing firm and striving together, unafraid of opponents, in the same struggle they once saw him face.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 5:1-11, A thief in the night, and peace and security
usedIn.s: Paul reminds the church that the day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night: while people say peace and security, sudden destruction comes like labor pains, but they are children of the day who keep awake and sober, armed with faith, love and hope.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 1:12-20, A blasphemer shown mercy, and two men handed over to Satan
usedIn.s: Paul thanks Christ for taking a former blasphemer and persecutor into his service as an example of mercy, then charges Timothy to fight the battle well, as the prophecies about him foretold, unlike Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom Paul has handed over to Satan.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 2:1-13, Soldier, athlete and farmer, and a prisoner in chains
usedIn.s: Timothy is to pass on what he heard to reliable people who will teach others, and to endure hardship like a soldier, compete by the rules like an athlete and work like a farmer, remembering Jesus Christ, raised from the dead and descended from David, for whom Paul is chained like a criminal.

entries.title: Envoys and ambassadors
entries.summary: An ambassador spoke for one state to another, in Paul's day usually as the emperor's legate in the East. The way an envoy was received honored or insulted the one who sent him, and communities chose respected envoys to carry their gifts.
entries.plain: **When the embassy car pulls up, everyone knows the visitor speaks for a whole government.** Kings and cities sent envoys to speak for them: to make peace, to carry gifts, or to deliver a demand. In Paul's day the best-known ambassadors were the emperor's own representatives in the eastern provinces. An envoy was supposed to be safe from harm, and the way he was treated counted as treatment of the one who sent him. Towns and communities also chose respected people, sometimes by a show of hands, to carry money or messages on their behalf.
entries.then: An ambassador represented one state to another. In this period the word was used mostly for the emperor's legates in the East. Heralds, ambassadors and other representatives were supposed to have diplomatic immunity, and how one treated them honored or shamed the sender. A representative was received with the honor due to the one he represented. Behind the picture stood the Old Testament prophets, God's messengers. They often spoke in the form of a covenant lawsuit, or in the words a great king's messengers used to vassal rulers. Keener adds that "emperors normally took action against unrepentant client states that had offended them"; the ESV Study Bible speaks of God's peace treaty. The word apostle means one who is sent and could be used of an ambassador or official delegate (Wright's glossary). The ESV Study Bible adds that the Greek Old Testament used the related verb for those commissioned to act in the sender's name. Communities sent envoys too. Those appointed by the churches may have been elected by a show of hands, as in Greek administration. Diaspora synagogues sent respected representatives with their temple tax to Jerusalem, and honorary inscriptions praised benefactors for sending honorable representatives. Chaining or insulting another country's envoy normally invited war. The office is far older than Rome. Podany describes the envoys of the kings of Egypt, Babylonia, Mittani and Hatti in the fourteenth century BC, known from the Amarna letters. These experienced diplomats visited an ally's court at least once a year with a letter and greeting gifts, and were to be welcomed with banquets and personal gifts. One king wrote that he had "exalted like gods" two Egyptian envoys.
entries.bridge: An analogy: an ambassador presenting her government's terms in a foreign capital. She is not speaking for herself, and how she is received is how her country is received.
entries.changes: Because an envoy carried his sender's word and honor, the ambassadors for Christ of 2 Corinthians 5:20 bring a king's terms of peace, and refusing them refuses him. Ephesians 6:20 has an ambassador in chains, and in Luke 14:32 a weaker king sends a delegation to ask for terms.
entries.not: **Not a career diplomat in a permanent embassy.** An envoy was usually sent on one mission, and in Paul's world the greatest envoys spoke for an emperor whose anger could fall on a whole people.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 5:11-6:13, New creation, Christ's ambassadors and a list of hardships
usedIn.s: Because one died for all, anyone in Christ is a new creation; Paul, God's ambassador, appeals to the Corinthians to be reconciled to God and commends his ministry with a long list of hardships and paradoxes.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 8:16-9:15, Envoys for the collection and the cheerful giver
usedIn.s: Paul commends Titus and two brothers appointed by the churches to carry the gift, takes care that no one can fault him in handling it, and urges the Corinthians to have their promised gift ready, since God loves a cheerful giver.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 6:18-24, An ambassador in chains, and the man who carried the letter
usedIn.s: Paul asks for prayer that he may speak boldly, calling himself an ambassador in chains, and sends Tychicus to carry the letter and tell them his news.

entries.title: Patrons, clients and benefactors
entries.summary: Favors in the Roman world came with strings. A patron gave help and protection, the client paid it back in loyalty and public honor, and rulers who gave gifts to the public were hailed as benefactors.
aliases: those over you in the Lord
entries.plain: **She brought us a casserole when we moved in, so now we owe her a dinner.** In the Roman world almost every favor worked like that, with far more at stake. A powerful person, the patron, did favors and gave protection. The person helped, the client, paid it back with loyalty and public praise. Rulers and rich citizens who paid for buildings or food for a city were honored as benefactors, and a dinner invitation was usually given with the return invitation in mind.
entries.then: Keener's glossary describes the Roman patron as the social superior who granted favors to his clients and acted as their political sponsor. The duties ran both ways, and clients were to honor their patrons as benefactors. Inscriptions across the empire honored rulers and other powerful people as benefactors for their gifts to the public, and eastern rulers even claimed to be divine. Benefaction was widely praised in Greek circles. Ancient culture stressed returning favors, and people kept careful track of what they owed. Hosts invited people of somewhat lower status, such as clients, in return for honor, but not beggars or the destitute. Peers expected to be invited back. Blomberg speaks of the "pervasive practice of patron-client relationships and reciprocity between benefactors and those helped by them" in the world of Luke's first readers. In Acts, Lydia acts as patron of the mission, as well-to-do women sponsored associations; perhaps a tenth of ancient benefactors were women. Between people of unequal rank, friends often meant benefactors, as with Paul's friends among the Asiarchs. The islanders of Malta repaid Paul's healings with honors and supplies. The word Paul uses of Phoebe was applied especially to patrons. The patron of a religious association, usually well-to-do, hosted it and held some authority (Keener). At Corinth an inscription records that Erastus laid a pavement at his own expense in return for his aedileship. Gratitude to benefactors was an essential virtue. Yet a plain thank you could cast the receiver as a dependent client, and asking for money put one in a lower place.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a mill town where the owner paid for the library, the ballpark and the new church roof. His name is on every building, people greet him with respect in the street, and everyone knows which candidate he wants them to vote for.
entries.changes: Because a favor created a debt of honor, giving to people who can never repay, as in Luke 14:12-14, deliberately steps outside the system. The title benefactor was a ruler's boast, which is why Luke 22:25 sets it against service. Ronald Hock, as Blomberg reports, reads the unforgiving servant of Matthew 18:23-35 against the expectation that someone helped by a superior would do the same for those below him.
entries.not: **Not one rich man's local generosity.** A mill owner's gifts sit on top of wages, laws and a secret ballot. Ancient patronage ran the whole society, from emperors hailed as divine benefactors down to hosts and guests, and both sides kept count of every favor in public.
entries.dissent: How Paul's gift relationship with Philippi worked. Keener and his notes read Philippians 4:10-20 as a thank-you that avoids casting Paul as a client; Wright and Bird call it a reciprocal financial partnership, set against his refusal of Corinth's money; the ESV Study Bible likens the letter to a missionary support letter.

usedIn.n: Luke 14:1-14, Dropsy at a Pharisee's table, and guests who cannot repay
usedIn.s: On a Sabbath at the house of a leading Pharisee, Jesus heals a man with dropsy, tells the guests not to grab the best places, and tells the host to invite people who cannot invite him back.

usedIn.n: Luke 16:1-13, The dishonest manager
usedIn.s: A rich man's manager, about to be dismissed for wasting his master's property, calls in the master's debtors and cuts their bills. The master praises his shrewdness.

usedIn.n: Luke 22:24-38, Benefactors, thrones, sifting and two swords
usedIn.s: At the last supper the disciples argue over who is greatest. Jesus contrasts kings who are called benefactors with himself as one who serves, promises them thrones, warns Peter that Satan has asked to sift them, and speaks of swords.

usedIn.n: Acts 16:11-15, Lydia at the place of prayer
usedIn.s: In Philippi, a Roman colony, Paul finds women gathered by the river on the Sabbath. Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth from Thyatira, believes, is baptized with her household and insists that the missionaries stay at her house.

usedIn.n: Acts 28:1-10, Malta: the viper and the goddess Justice
usedIn.s: The islanders of Malta welcome the shipwrecked with a fire. When a viper fastens on Paul's hand they decide that Justice will not let a murderer live; when he takes no harm they call him a god. Publius, the island's chief man, takes them in, and Paul heals his father and many others.

usedIn.n: Romans 15:25-33, The gift for Jerusalem
usedIn.s: Before coming west Paul must take a gift from the churches of Macedonia and Achaia to the poor among the believers in Jerusalem. He asks for prayer that he will be kept safe and the gift accepted.

usedIn.n: Romans 16:1-2, Phoebe of Cenchreae
usedIn.s: Paul commends Phoebe, a servant or deacon of the church at Cenchreae and a patron of many, Paul included, and asks the Romans to welcome her and help her in whatever she needs.

usedIn.n: Romans 16:17-27, Tertius, Gaius and Erastus
usedIn.s: Paul warns against those who cause divisions, promises that God will soon crush Satan under the believers' feet, and passes on greetings from Corinth, including his scribe Tertius, his host Gaius and Erastus the city treasurer.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 1:18-2:5, The foolishness of the cross
usedIn.s: Paul sets the message of a crucified Messiah, folly to Greeks and a stumbling block to Jews, against the wisdom and eloquence Corinth admired, and reminds the believers that few of them were wise, powerful or well born.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 7:17-24, Circumcised or not, slave or free
usedIn.s: Paul tells each believer to live the life the Lord assigned when he was called: the circumcised should not undo it, the uncircumcised should not seek it, and a slave should not be troubled, though he should take his freedom if he can.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 9:1-27, Free, unpaid and in training
usedIn.s: Paul defends his right as an apostle to be supported and explains why he has never used it, makes himself a slave to all to win more, and pictures his discipline as an athlete's training for a wreath that will not wither.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 10:23-11:1, Dinner at an unbeliever's house
usedIn.s: Paul tells believers to eat whatever is sold in the meat market and whatever an unbelieving host serves without asking questions, unless someone points out that it was offered in sacrifice.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 11:17-34, The Lord's Supper in a rich man's house
usedIn.s: Paul rebukes the church because at the Lord's Supper some go hungry while others eat their fill and get drunk, retells the tradition of the Last Supper, and tells them to wait for one another.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 1:1-11, The God of all comfort and the sentence of death
usedIn.s: Paul opens by blessing the God of all comfort and tells the Corinthians that in Asia he was so crushed that he felt he had received the sentence of death, so that he learned to rely on the God who raises the dead.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 8:1-15, The Macedonians' giving and the manna
usedIn.s: Paul holds up the generosity of the poor Macedonian churches, appeals to Christ who became poor, and asks the Corinthians to finish their gift so that there may be equality, as there was with the manna in the wilderness.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 11:1-15, The betrothed virgin, the free gospel and the angel of light
usedIn.s: Jealous as a father who has promised his daughter to one husband, Paul fears the Corinthians will be led astray as Eve was; he defends preaching to them free of charge and calls his rivals false apostles disguised as Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 12:11-18, Not a burden: parents save for their children
usedIn.s: Paul says the Corinthians forced him to play the fool; the signs of an apostle were done among them, and his only fault was not to burden them, since parents save up for their children, not children for their parents.

usedIn.n: Philippians 1:1-11, A letter between friends, and a partnership in the gospel
usedIn.s: Paul and Timothy greet the believers at Philippi with their overseers and deacons, thank God for their partnership in the gospel from the first day, and pray that their love will grow until the day of Christ.

usedIn.n: Philippians 2:19-30, Timothy and Epaphroditus, commended and sent
usedIn.s: Paul commends Timothy as a son who serves with him and plans to send him soon, and sends home Epaphroditus, the church's messenger, who nearly died on their errand.

usedIn.n: Philippians 4:10-23, A thank-you without a thank you, and Caesar's household
usedIn.s: Paul acknowledges the Philippians' gift in the language of contentment and of business receipts and sacrifice, without a direct thank you, and closes with greetings from the saints of Caesar's household.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 4:9-12, A quiet life and your own hands
usedIn.s: Paul praises the church's love for the whole family of believers in Macedonia and urges them to love more, to live quietly, mind their own business and work with their hands, so that outsiders respect them and they depend on no one.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 5:12-28, Leaders, prophets, a holy kiss and a letter read to all
usedIn.s: Paul asks the church to honor those who work hard over them, to warn the idle and help the weak, to rejoice, pray and give thanks, not to quench the Spirit or despise prophecy but test everything, and to have the letter read to all.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 5:1-16, Older men as fathers, and the widows' list
usedIn.s: Timothy is to treat older and younger believers as family; the church is to honor widows who are truly in need, families are to support their own, and only older widows of proven character are to be put on the list.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 6:1-10, Slaves under the yoke, and godliness as gain
usedIn.s: Slaves are to respect their masters so that the faith is not slandered, and those with believing masters are to serve them all the more; then Paul turns on teachers who treat godliness as a way to get rich, and warns that the craving for money breeds every kind of harm.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 1:8-18, Not ashamed of my chains, the deposit, and Onesiphorus
usedIn.s: Paul tells Timothy not to be ashamed of the Lord's testimony or of him as a prisoner, but to share his suffering and guard the good deposit; everyone in Asia has deserted him except Onesiphorus, who searched Rome until he found him.

usedIn.n: Philemon 1-7, The church in Philemon's house
usedIn.s: Paul, a prisoner, and Timothy write to Philemon, to Apphia and Archippus, and to the church that meets in Philemon's house, and Paul thanks God for Philemon's love and faith, his partnership, and the way he has refreshed the hearts of God's people.

usedIn.n: James 2:1-13, The gold ring and the good seat
usedIn.s: James forbids favoritism in the assembly. A rich man with a gold ring is given a good seat and a poor man in dirty clothes is told to stand, though it is the rich who drag believers into court and slander the noble name; the royal law of love rules out partiality, and mercy triumphs over judgment.

usedIn.n: 2 Peter 1:1-21, A reminder before the tent is folded
usedIn.s: Simeon Peter writes to those who share a faith as precious as his, through whom they may share in the divine nature, and urges them to add virtue to virtue. Knowing his death is near, he means to remind them, for he was an eyewitness of Christ's majesty on the holy mountain, and the prophetic word is a lamp in a dark place until the morning star rises.

entries.title: Roman colonies
entries.summary: Cities refounded by Rome for its veterans and settlers, run on Roman law with Latin on their monuments. A colony was a small copy of Rome in the provinces, and its citizens were citizens of Rome.
entries.plain: **The old garrison town still flies the flag of the country that settled it, and the street signs are in the settlers' language.** After its civil wars Rome settled thousands of retired soldiers in new or refounded cities across the empire. These colonies copied Rome in their buildings, government and holidays. Their leading citizens were Roman citizens, Latin was the language of the city's business, and the emperor had pride of place in its temples, while the farmers around them went on speaking their own languages.
entries.then: Wright explains that after the civil wars Augustus settled veterans in colonies far from Italy, and "Pisidian Antioch was the most important such colony in the region." Renamed Colonia Caesarea, it copied Rome in its buildings, government and holidays. An imperial cult complex dominated its center, with an arch celebrating Augustus's victory over the Pisidians. Iconium and Lystra were also settled with veterans in 26 BC (Wright). Antioch held about five thousand colonists, a minority of its people, and its most prominent temple honored the emperor. The ESV Study Bible speaks of the high status of a Roman colony. The local elite were Roman citizens, among them the families of the Caristanii and the Sergii Paulii. Lystra's citizens enjoyed Roman privileges. A third of its inscriptions are in Latin; the landowning citizens spoke Latin, and the crowds of Anatolian noncitizens spoke Lycaonian. As a colony, Philippi gave its citizens the legal standing of citizens of Rome, with every privilege that came with it. Philippi had been a colony since 42 BC, and Augustus renamed it Colonia Iulia Augusta Philippensis. It was so Roman that over 80 percent of its inscriptions are in Latin. Its citizens lived under Roman law, paid no tribute and shaped their constitution on Rome's. The city held the ius Italicum, rights legally equal to those of Italian cities. Its two chief magistrates, the duoviri, styled themselves praetors and were attended by lictors carrying rods. Corinth, destroyed in 146 BC, was refounded as a colony in 44 BC, with Latin as the language of civic business.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a military base town abroad, where the retired officers run the council, the main street is named for the home country's president, and the locals who work there speak another language at home.
entries.changes: In a colony such as Pisidian Antioch, Acts 13:50, the Roman citizen elite held power and the emperor's temple stood at the center, so stirring up the leading men meant stirring up Rome's own people. Philippians 3:20 speaks to a colony when it tells believers their citizenship is in heaven.
entries.not: **Not a temporary posting on foreign soil.** A base town's soldiers rotate home. Roman colonists settled for good on land they owned, and the city itself held Roman status, living under Roman law and free of tribute, while the noncitizens around them kept their own languages.
entries.dissent: Was Iconium a colony too? Wright says both Iconium and Lystra were settled with veterans by Augustus. The cultural backgrounds notes and the ESV Study Bible describe Iconium as culturally Phrygian and call Lystra, not Iconium, a colony. Second, who settled Philippi and how Roman it was. Wright, Wright and Bird and the ESV Study Bible speak of the victors' veterans after 42 BC, the CSB Study Bible of the defeated armies, and the Zondervan dictionary of Antony's partisans settled after Actium. Against the 80 percent of inscriptions in Latin, the Zondervan dictionary calls the city "still more Greek in culture than Roman", and Wright pictures a resented Latin-speaking elite ruling a Greek town.
sources: N. T. Wright, Paul: A Biography, ch. 5, Cyprus and Galatia

usedIn.n: Acts 13:13-52, The synagogue at Pisidian Antioch
usedIn.s: Invited to speak after the synagogue readings in a Roman colony, Paul tells Israel's story from the exodus to Jesus. Gentiles welcome the message, and the city's leading men and women drive the apostles out.

usedIn.n: Acts 14:1-20, Iconium and Lystra: taken for Zeus and Hermes
usedIn.s: After a plot in Iconium, Paul heals a lame man at Lystra and the crowd hails him and Barnabas as Hermes and Zeus. When they refuse the sacrifice, the crowd is turned against them and Paul is stoned.

usedIn.n: Acts 16:11-15, Lydia at the place of prayer
usedIn.s: In Philippi, a Roman colony, Paul finds women gathered by the river on the Sabbath. Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth from Thyatira, believes, is baptized with her household and insists that the missionaries stay at her house.

usedIn.n: Acts 16:16-24, The slave girl with a Python spirit
usedIn.s: A slave girl who earns her owners money by fortune-telling follows Paul, crying out about the Most High God. Paul drives the spirit out, and her owners drag him and Silas before the magistrates, who have them beaten and jailed.

usedIn.n: Acts 18:1-11, Tentmakers in Corinth
usedIn.s: In Corinth Paul lodges and works with Aquila and Priscilla, Jews lately expelled from Rome who share his trade. When the synagogue turns against him he moves next door to the house of Titius Justus, and the synagogue leader Crispus believes with his household.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 1:1-9, Grace to the church in Corinth
usedIn.s: Paul and Sosthenes greet the church of God in Corinth and thank God that its members have been made rich in every kind of speech and knowledge as they wait for the Lord to be revealed.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 1:10-17, I belong to Paul, I belong to Apollos
usedIn.s: Told by Chloe's people that the church is splitting into camps behind Paul, Apollos, Cephas and Christ, Paul appeals for unity and asks whether Christ has been divided.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 7:17-24, Circumcised or not, slave or free
usedIn.s: Paul tells each believer to live the life the Lord assigned when he was called: the circumcised should not undo it, the uncircumcised should not seek it, and a slave should not be troubled, though he should take his freedom if he can.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 10:1-18, Weighty letters, a weak presence and the siege of the mind
usedIn.s: Answering the charge that he is bold in letters but weak in person, Paul describes a war that takes every thought captive and refuses to compare himself with rivals who measure themselves by themselves.

usedIn.n: Philippians 1:27-30, Live as citizens, contend like athletes
usedIn.s: Paul tells a church in a Roman colony to conduct itself as citizens worthy of the gospel, standing firm and striving together, unafraid of opponents, in the same struggle they once saw him face.

entries.title: Philosophers and their schools
entries.summary: Stoics, Epicureans and other schools taught a whole way of life in lecture halls and marketplaces. A traveling teacher with a message about God would be heard, and judged, as one more philosopher.
aliases: godliness as a means to gain
entries.plain: **The new speaker in the park drew a crowd, and the regulars sized him up as one more man with a theory.** Philosophy in Paul's world meant a whole way of looking at life, close to what we call a worldview. The Stoics taught that the divine filled everything and that the wise man lived by reason. The Epicureans said the gods, if they existed, took no interest in us, and that a calm, painless life was the goal. Teachers lectured in rented halls and argued in the marketplace, and some were frauds who lived off their hearers. A traveling Jew talking about God and a man raised from the dead would be measured against all of them.
entries.then: Carson writes that in the ancient world philosophy meant something like a worldview, with teachers offering rival ones. The Epicureans had influence mainly among the educated upper classes. They held that the gods stayed out of human affairs and that life's goal was pleasure, meaning freedom from pain and disturbance. The Stoics were more popular, opposed pleasure and believed God filled all things and needed nothing. Philosophers dealt mainly with ethics, and pagan religion with ritual. Popular opinion counted many philosophers impious for questioning the old gods. The charge of bringing in strange gods recalled Socrates, who was brought before the Areopagus and executed. Sages and orators without schools of their own worked the marketplace, and philosophers lectured in rented halls. Early observers took Christians for a club or a philosophical school. Many sages were charlatans, so honest ones had to deny greed. Philosophers lived on fees, rich patrons or begging, and despised manual work. For three centuries Greek-speaking Jews had borrowed from Greek philosophy to make their faith respectable to Greeks. Stoics and Cynics claimed that only the wise man was truly rich and a king, and that all things were theirs as friends of the gods. Cynics wandered homeless, begged and abused their hearers, and sages listed their hardships to prove their integrity. Philosophers held that the wise needed no law. Stoic-influenced moralists praised contentment with little or much and said the wise man needed no one but himself. Stoics held imprisonment, death and anxiety beyond one's control to be of no account.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a university town where every café has its circle of argument and a newcomer with a big idea is invited to give a talk. Some come to learn, some to mock, and the faculty decide whether he gets a lecture hall.
entries.changes: In Athens, in Acts 17:18, Paul is heard as one more lecturer in the marketplace and his message is sorted against Stoic and Epicurean ideas. The Corinthians' claim to be already rich and reigning in 1 Corinthians 4:8 borrows the sage's boast, and Colossians 2:8 warns against hollow and deceptive philosophy.
entries.not: **Not salaried scholars debating ideas.** University faculty draw a salary and argue theory. Ancient philosophers lived on fees, patrons or begging, taught a whole way of life, and a charge of bringing in strange gods could put a speaker on trial, as it had Socrates.
entries.dissent: Whether the philosophy of Colossians 2:8 was a real group. The ESV Study Bible takes the Greek article to show that the teachers called their own teaching the philosophy, and Bird, writing with Wright, thinks a specific group or person is in view. Wright reads the chapter as a general warning in ironic philosophical terms, with no false teachers present, only neighbors to conform to.

usedIn.n: Acts 17:16-21, Athens: idols, the marketplace and the philosophers
usedIn.s: Waiting in Athens, Paul is distressed at a city full of idols. He argues in the synagogue and the marketplace, and Epicurean and Stoic philosophers take him for a preacher of foreign gods and bring him to the Areopagus.

usedIn.n: Acts 17:22-34, Paul before the Areopagus
usedIn.s: Before the Areopagus, Paul starts from an altar to an unknown god and from the Athenians' own poets, speaks of the one Creator who made every nation from one man, and ends with a coming judgment and a man raised from the dead. Some mock; a few believe.

usedIn.n: Acts 19:8-20, The lecture hall and the burned books
usedIn.s: In Ephesus Paul teaches daily in the hall of Tyrannus for two years, and even cloths that touched him bring healing. When the sons of Sceva try to use Jesus' name as a spell, the spirit overpowers them, and believers burn their magic books in public.

usedIn.n: Acts 20:17-38, Farewell to the Ephesian elders
usedIn.s: Hurrying to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost, Paul calls the elders of Ephesus to Miletus. He reminds them how he lived among them, warns of wolves who will attack the flock, charges them as overseers to shepherd God's church, and leaves them in tears.

usedIn.n: Acts 25:13-26:32, Agrippa and Bernice hear Paul
usedIn.s: King Agrippa II and his sister Bernice visit Festus, who asks them to hear Paul so that he will have something to write to the emperor. Paul tells his story; Festus calls him mad, Agrippa turns the question aside, and all agree he could have been set free had he not appealed to Caesar.

usedIn.n: Romans 1:18-32, Images of the immortal God
usedIn.s: Paul describes God's anger against people who knew him from creation yet traded his glory for images of humans and animals, and the disorder that followed.

usedIn.n: Romans 7:1-25, Bound while the husband lives
usedIn.s: A wife is bound to her husband only while he lives, and believers have died to the law to belong to Christ. Then Paul describes a divided self that knows the good and cannot do it.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 3:1-23, Milk, builders and God's temple
usedIn.s: Paul calls the Corinthians infants still on milk, says he and Apollos are only servants, warns builders that fire will test their work, and reminds the church that it is God's temple and that all things are theirs.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 4:6-13, Apostles on display
usedIn.s: With biting irony Paul sets the Corinthians, already full, rich and reigning, beside the apostles, put on show last of all like men condemned to die, hungry, ragged, homeless and treated as the world's scum.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 7:1-16, Married couples and unbelieving spouses
usedIn.s: Replying to the Corinthians' letter, Paul tells married couples not to deprive each other, advises the unmarried and widows, repeats the Lord's word against divorce, and says a believer deserted by an unbelieving spouse is not bound.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 9:1-27, Free, unpaid and in training
usedIn.s: Paul defends his right as an apostle to be supported and explains why he has never used it, makes himself a slave to all to win more, and pictures his discipline as an athlete's training for a wreath that will not wither.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 2:14-17, Led in God's triumph
usedIn.s: Paul thanks God, who leads him in triumphal procession and spreads the fragrance of Christ through him, a smell of death to some and of life to others, and denies that he peddles God's word for profit.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 4:7-18, Treasure in clay jars
usedIn.s: Paul carries God's treasure in a clay jar, hard pressed but not crushed, carrying Jesus' dying in his body so that Jesus' life may show, while the outer self wastes away and the inner self is renewed day by day.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 5:11-6:13, New creation, Christ's ambassadors and a list of hardships
usedIn.s: Because one died for all, anyone in Christ is a new creation; Paul, God's ambassador, appeals to the Corinthians to be reconciled to God and commends his ministry with a long list of hardships and paradoxes.

usedIn.n: Galatians 5:13-6:10, Flesh and Spirit, burdens and teachers
usedIn.s: Called to freedom, the Galatians are to serve one another in love, which fulfills the law; Paul sets the works of the flesh against the fruit of the Spirit and urges them to restore the fallen gently, carry each other's burdens, share with their teachers and keep doing good.

usedIn.n: Philippians 1:12-26, Chains known to the whole palace guard
usedIn.s: Paul tells how his imprisonment has carried the gospel through the palace guard and made other preachers bolder, some from rivalry, then weighs living against dying and expects to stay on for their sake.

usedIn.n: Philippians 3:12-4:1, The race, citizens of heaven, and a Savior from there
usedIn.s: Paul pictures himself as a runner straining toward the prize, warns against those whose god is their stomach, and reminds a Roman colony that its citizenship is in heaven, from where it awaits a Savior who will transform its lowly bodies.

usedIn.n: Philippians 4:2-9, Two women at odds, names in the book of life, and whatever is true
usedIn.s: Paul pleads with two women who worked beside him to agree, asks a companion to help them, notes that their names are in the book of life, and urges joy, prayer instead of worry, and thoughts fixed on whatever is true and excellent.

usedIn.n: Philippians 4:10-23, A thank-you without a thank you, and Caesar's household
usedIn.s: Paul acknowledges the Philippians' gift in the language of contentment and of business receipts and sacrifice, without a direct thank you, and closes with greetings from the saints of Caesar's household.

usedIn.n: Colossians 2:8-15, The philosophy, a cancelled IOU and a triumph
usedIn.s: Paul warns against a philosophy built on human tradition and the elements of the world, tells Gentile believers they have already been circumcised in Christ, and pictures God cancelling their debt at the cross and leading the powers captive.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 2:1-12, Gentle as a nurse, firm as a father
usedIn.s: Paul reminds the church how he and his companions came to them after being mistreated in Philippi: no deceit, flattery or greed, gentle among them like a nursing mother, working night and day so as not to burden anyone, and urging each of them like a father.

usedIn.n: 2 Thessalonians 3:6-18, The idle, the busybodies, and a greeting in Paul's own hand
usedIn.s: Paul tells the church to keep away from believers who are idle and will not work, recalls how he worked night and day to set an example, lays down that anyone unwilling to work should not eat, and signs the letter in his own hand.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 1:1-11, Myths, endless genealogies and would-be teachers of the law
usedIn.s: Paul greets Timothy, whom he left in Ephesus, and tells him to stop certain people teaching strange doctrines and spending themselves on myths and endless genealogies; they want to be teachers of the law without understanding it, while the law is meant for the lawless.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 6:1-10, Slaves under the yoke, and godliness as gain
usedIn.s: Slaves are to respect their masters so that the faith is not slandered, and those with believing masters are to serve them all the more; then Paul turns on teachers who treat godliness as a way to get rich, and warns that the craving for money breeds every kind of harm.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 3:1-9, Terrible times, homes entered, and Jannes and Jambres
usedIn.s: Paul warns that the last days will bring terrible times and people who love themselves, money and pleasure, having a form of godliness but denying its power; some worm their way into homes and win over gullible women, opposing the truth as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses.

usedIn.n: Titus 1:10-16, The circumcision group, and Cretans always liars
usedIn.s: Many rebellious talkers and deceivers, especially of the circumcision group, are upsetting whole households for dishonest gain; Paul quotes a Cretan prophet who called Cretans always liars, and warns against Jewish myths and human commands, for to the pure all things are pure.

usedIn.n: 2 Peter 1:1-21, A reminder before the tent is folded
usedIn.s: Simeon Peter writes to those who share a faith as precious as his, through whom they may share in the divine nature, and urges them to add virtue to virtue. Knowing his death is near, he means to remind them, for he was an eyewitness of Christ's majesty on the holy mountain, and the prophetic word is a lamp in a dark place until the morning star rises.

usedIn.n: 2 Peter 2:1-10, Angels in Tartarus, Noah, Sodom and Lot
usedIn.s: As there were false prophets in Israel, so false teachers will come, greedy and denying the Master who bought them. God punished the angels who sinned, keeping them bound in darkness in Tartarus for judgment; he swept away the ancient world but kept Noah; he burned Sodom and Gomorrah but rescued righteous Lot. So the Lord knows how to rescue the godly and keep the unrighteous for judgment.

usedIn.n: 2 Peter 2:10-22, The glorious ones, the way of Balaam, a dog and a sow
usedIn.s: The false teachers slander the glorious ones, which even angels do not dare to do. Like unreasoning animals they carouse in daylight, with eyes full of adultery; they have followed Balaam, who loved profit gained by wrongdoing and was rebuked by a donkey. They promise freedom while slaves of corruption, and they are like a dog returning to its vomit and a washed sow to the mud.

usedIn.n: 2 Peter 3:1-18, Scoffers, the flood and the day of fire
usedIn.s: Scoffers will ask where the promised coming is, since everything goes on as it has since creation. Peter answers that the world once made by God's word was destroyed by water and is now kept for fire on the day of judgment; the Lord does not count time as people do, and he delays out of patience. The day will come like a thief, and the readers wait for new heavens and a new earth, as Paul too wrote in letters some twist like the other Scriptures.

usedIn.n: 1 John 2:28-3:24, Children of God, Cain, and love in deed
usedIn.s: Those who do right are born of God, whose love makes them his children, and when he appears they will be like him. Whoever keeps on sinning belongs to the devil, who has sinned from the beginning, and the Son came to undo his work. The readers are not to be like Cain, who murdered his brother, but to love in deed and in truth, as Christ laid down his life.

entries.title: Trades and trade guilds
entries.summary: Craftsmen of one trade lived and worked in the same streets and banded together in guilds, which set standards, defended their interests and met for meals in honor of a patron god.
entries.plain: **All the jewelers on the street belonged to the same association, ate at the same annual dinner and stood together when business was threatened.** In ancient cities people of one trade usually lived and kept shops in the same neighborhood. They formed guilds that set standards for the work and protected members' interests. Each guild had a patron god, and its meetings included meals of food offered to that god, which made it hard for a Jew to belong. Craftsmen were proud of their skill, but the upper classes looked down on anyone who worked with his hands.
entries.then: In the ancient economy people of one trade did not compete as they do now. They lived together in one part of town and formed guilds, called collegia, which set standards and united to defend their economic interests. Each guild had a patron deity, and its banquets included sacrificial food. That kept practicing Jews out and made them glad to find other Jews in their trade. In Ephesus the silversmiths' shops apparently lined the street from the theater to the harbor, and commerce and religion were closely intertwined. Artisans like Demetrius made their living from cult objects. Thyatira was known for its dyers' guilds, and inscriptions show Thyatiran agents selling purple dye in Macedonia. Its records name more guilds than any other Asian city's, and Beale writes, "The city had a guild for almost every trade." The guilds' common meals, normally monthly, honored their patron gods. A believer who refused them was cut off socially and economically (Keener). The word for tentmaker was used of leatherworkers in general, perhaps working the goat-hair cloth of Cilicia. Leatherworking tools were easy to carry from city to city. Wright suggests tentmaking was the family business in which Saul was apprenticed. Artisans were proud of their work and ranked above peasants. The elite despised manual labor and most Gentile sages avoided it, while some Jewish teachers had a trade, often learned from their fathers. Wright traces the riot at Ephesus through the same links: "A theological proclamation had produced economic challenges, which were then interpreted as civic insults."
entries.bridge: An analogy: a trade union with its own chapel. Members share the work, the wage rates and the annual feast, and the feast opens with a toast to the patron saint that a member of another faith cannot drink.
entries.changes: Guild life explains why Paul lodges and works with fellow Jews of the same trade in Acts 18:3, and why craftsmen whose living depends on a cult band together against him in Acts 19:24-27. When Paul reminds a church that he worked night and day, as in 1 Thessalonians 2:9, he sets himself apart from teachers who lived off fees or patrons.
entries.not: **Not a union with a chapel on the side.** In a guild the god stood at the center, and its regular meals honored the patron deity with sacrificial food. A Jew or a believer who stayed away lost more than a toast; he was cut off from his trade's social and economic life.

usedIn.n: Acts 18:1-11, Tentmakers in Corinth
usedIn.s: In Corinth Paul lodges and works with Aquila and Priscilla, Jews lately expelled from Rome who share his trade. When the synagogue turns against him he moves next door to the house of Titius Justus, and the synagogue leader Crispus believes with his household.

usedIn.n: Acts 19:23-41, Great is Artemis of the Ephesians
usedIn.s: Demetrius the silversmith rouses the craftsmen who make shrines of Artemis, warning that Paul's teaching threatens their trade and the goddess's honor. The city rushes into the theater chanting for two hours, until the city clerk calms them with a warning about Rome.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 9:1-27, Free, unpaid and in training
usedIn.s: Paul defends his right as an apostle to be supported and explains why he has never used it, makes himself a slave to all to win more, and pictures his discipline as an athlete's training for a wreath that will not wither.

usedIn.n: Revelation 2:18-29, Thyatira, the guilds and Jezebel
usedIn.s: To Thyatira the Son of God, with eyes like fire and feet like bronze, praises a growing church but rebukes it for tolerating Jezebel, a self-styled prophetess who leads his servants into immorality and idol food. Those who hold fast are promised authority over the nations and the morning star.

usedIn.n: Revelation 13:11-18, the beast from the earth, the mark and 666
usedIn.s: A second beast, harmless-looking like a lamb but speaking like the dragon, rises from the earth and drives everyone to worship the first beast, working wonders and making its statue speak. Trade is barred to anyone without its mark on hand or forehead, a mark tied to the beast's name and number, 666.

usedIn.n: Revelation 18:9-24, kings, merchants and the cargo list
usedIn.s: The kings, the merchants and the sea captains stand far off and mourn as Babylon burns, because no one buys their cargoes any more, a long list of luxuries that ends with human beings. An angel hurls a great millstone into the sea, and the sounds of music, craftsmen, the mill, the lamp and the wedding fall silent in the city where the blood of prophets and saints was found.

entries.title: Manual work and the leisured class
entries.summary: The well-to-do despised people who worked with their hands. A respectable teacher was expected to live on a patron, on fees or even on begging, so an apostle who made tents for his keep looked low class.
aliases: let the thief no longer steal
anyone unwilling to work should not eat
entries.plain: **The new pastor insisted on paying his own way by fixing cars on weekends, and some of the board found it embarrassing.** In Paul's world people of standing did not work with their hands. Craftsmen were usually better off than peasants, but they were poor, worked long hours and had little status. Teachers and philosophers were expected to live on a rich patron's support, on fees from their students, or on begging. Paul supported himself with a trade, and in a city that cared about status, people noticed.
entries.then: Keener writes that "the well-to-do despised artisans". A teacher was expected to live on a patron, on fees from students or even on begging, but not on a working-class job. Artisans were usually better off than peasants. Still, they toiled, stayed poor and had little social status, especially those who moved from place to place, as Paul the leatherworker did. Some well-to-do Corinthians wanted Paul to take payment like a regular philosophical teacher. They were embarrassed that he kept himself as a low-status artisan. Taking a patron's money had a cost. "Sages on the payroll of patrons" had less freedom to challenge their patrons' values, while refusing a gift could be read as refusing friendship. Keener and his notes suggest two reasons Paul refused pay: so as not to look like a sophist teaching for gain, or so as not to become his hearers' dependent client. Wright suggests he did not want anyone in Achaea to think that paying him meant owning him and trimming his message. Paul still defended the right of apostles to be supported. Wright and Bird say the rival teachers in Corinth disparaged Paul "for his manual labour, his refusal to accept payment." Bailey states the expectation plainly: "Intellectuals were expected to be financially independent." Humility was a Jewish virtue, but Greeks heard it as humiliation, fitting only for people of very low status. Judaism valued labor with one's hands and sharing with the poor. Jewish sages, and probably artisans themselves, respected manual work, while people of status across the Mediterranean despised it.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a visiting lecturer who turns down the fee and pays his hotel bill by working shifts in a local warehouse. Some admire him; the sponsors who wanted their names on the program feel snubbed.
entries.changes: Because the elite looked down on manual work and expected teachers to be supported, Paul's reminder that his own hands met his needs, as in Acts 20:34, was a deliberate lowering of himself. In 1 Thessalonians 2:9 he labored day and night to avoid weighing on anyone, and in 2 Corinthians 11:7 his free preaching is turned against him.
entries.not: **Not a refusal of all support.** Paul defended the right of apostles to be paid and took gifts from other churches; what he refused was to become the paid client of the people he was teaching.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 5:11-6:13, New creation, Christ's ambassadors and a list of hardships
usedIn.s: Because one died for all, anyone in Christ is a new creation; Paul, God's ambassador, appeals to the Corinthians to be reconciled to God and commends his ministry with a long list of hardships and paradoxes.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 11:1-15, The betrothed virgin, the free gospel and the angel of light
usedIn.s: Jealous as a father who has promised his daughter to one husband, Paul fears the Corinthians will be led astray as Eve was; he defends preaching to them free of charge and calls his rivals false apostles disguised as Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 12:11-18, Not a burden: parents save for their children
usedIn.s: Paul says the Corinthians forced him to play the fool; the signs of an apostle were done among them, and his only fault was not to burden them, since parents save up for their children, not children for their parents.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 4:17-32, No longer as the Gentiles live
usedIn.s: Paul tells Gentile believers to stop living as the Gentiles do, to put off the old self and put on the new, to give the devil no foothold, to work with their hands and share, and not to grieve the Spirit who sealed them.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 2:1-12, Gentle as a nurse, firm as a father
usedIn.s: Paul reminds the church how he and his companions came to them after being mistreated in Philippi: no deceit, flattery or greed, gentle among them like a nursing mother, working night and day so as not to burden anyone, and urging each of them like a father.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 4:9-12, A quiet life and your own hands
usedIn.s: Paul praises the church's love for the whole family of believers in Macedonia and urges them to love more, to live quietly, mind their own business and work with their hands, so that outsiders respect them and they depend on no one.

usedIn.n: 2 Thessalonians 3:6-18, The idle, the busybodies, and a greeting in Paul's own hand
usedIn.s: Paul tells the church to keep away from believers who are idle and will not work, recalls how he worked night and day to set an example, lays down that anyone unwilling to work should not eat, and signs the letter in his own hand.

entries.title: Free cities, assemblies and riots
entries.summary: Some Greek cities, such as Thessalonica and Ephesus, kept a measure of self-rule under Rome, with their own officials and a citizen assembly. A riot could cost a city those privileges.
entries.plain: **The town council knew that one more riot in the square and the state would send in its own man to run things.** Under Rome, some old Greek cities were allowed to run their own affairs. They had their own magistrates and a citizen assembly that met in the theater to vote and even to judge. That freedom lasted only as long as Rome was pleased. Officials feared mobs, because a riot could bring Roman punishment and the loss of the city's privileges.
entries.then: Thessalonica was a free city with some autonomy. It was the seat of Macedonia's governor and perhaps as large as 200,000. Its officials were politarchs, a title used almost only in Macedonia. Rome let them run the city but held them answerable for their actions. The title was once dismissed as Luke's mistake, but it appears in many inscriptions from the second century BC on, and "five times it refers to Thessalonica itself" (the Zondervan dictionary). Thessalonica's freedom brought tax exemptions (Wright and Bird), and it was not a Roman colony in Paul's day (Wright). A ban imposed by its politarchs held only there and only while they were in office. In a free city the gathered citizen body could act as a court. At Ephesus the city clerk was the top official. He announced the assembly's rulings and represented the city to the Roman authorities. The assembly met regularly in the theater, which by the sources' estimates held some 20,000 to 25,000 people, and emergency assemblies were sometimes called. Keener notes that Luke uses the word for citizen assembly ironically of a mob. A lawful assembly enjoyed Rome's favor, while a mob could bring Roman discipline. Unemployed idlers in the marketplace were easily stirred to mob action, and those who stirred them were despised as demagogues. Rome had little tolerance for riots, and some cities lost their privileges after unrest. Rulings in one city had no force in the next, so opponents had to start again in each.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a self-governing territory that keeps its own parliament as long as the capital is satisfied. A street riot there is never only local news, because everyone knows who may be watching.
entries.changes: The fear of Roman discipline explains why city officials take a bond from Jason and let the matter drop in Acts 17:9, and why the clerk at Ephesus in Acts 19:40 warns the crowd that they could be charged with rioting. A mob in the theater was not the lawful assembly, even when it gathered in the same place.
entries.not: **Not a parliament of elected members.** The city's assembly was the gathered body of citizens itself, meeting in the theater, and it could even sit as a court. Its freedom was a privilege Rome could withdraw after unrest, and some cities lost it that way.

usedIn.n: Acts 17:1-9, Another king in Thessalonica
usedIn.s: Paul argues from the Scriptures in the synagogue at Thessalonica that the Messiah had to suffer and rise. Some believe; opponents raise a mob, drag Jason before the city officials and accuse the believers of defying Caesar by proclaiming another king.

usedIn.n: Acts 19:23-41, Great is Artemis of the Ephesians
usedIn.s: Demetrius the silversmith rouses the craftsmen who make shrines of Artemis, warning that Paul's teaching threatens their trade and the goddess's honor. The city rushes into the theater chanting for two hours, until the city clerk calms them with a warning about Rome.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 2:17-3:13, Orphaned, blocked by Satan, crowned
usedIn.s: Torn away from the church, Paul tells how he longed to come back but Satan blocked the way, how he sent Timothy from Athens, how Timothy's good news has revived him, and prays that the Lord will make them blameless at his coming with all his holy ones.

entries.title: Letters, scribes and carriers
entries.summary: Letters were usually dictated to scribes, carried by trusted travelers because there was no public post, and read aloud to the people they were sent to.
aliases: a letter as if from us
a letter in place of a visit
I hope to come to you soon
greetings from those with the writer
title on the outside of the scroll
do not add or take away
entries.plain: **The letter came in the bag of a friend who was traveling that way, and the whole church gathered to hear it read out.** There was no post office for ordinary people. Letters went with slaves, friends or anyone trusted who was heading in the right direction. Most were written by a trained scribe from the sender's dictation. Since many people could not read, a letter to a group was read aloud to everyone, and the person who carried it might be asked to explain it.
entries.then: The empire, except perhaps Egypt, had no postal service beyond official business. Most people sent letters by slaves, friends or travelers. Most letters were written by a paid scribe, either from shorthand dictation or with the scribe helping to shape the wording. The author's closing in his own hand worked like a signature. Paul chose couriers both he and the churches trusted, and Tertius penned Romans. Greek letters opened with a standard greeting and closed with Farewell. Officials sent respected representatives to carry decrees and circular letters. The formula translated it seemed good belonged to council resolutions and imperial decrees. Literacy may have been around ten percent, and reading was nearly always aloud, so churches heard letters read in their services. Wright and Bird note that "Romans is many times longer than the average first-century letter," and Wright has Phoebe carry it to Rome and read it aloud. Polite letters opened with a thanksgiving, and leaving it out marked a letter of blame. A direct rebuke at the opening is "found only among the harshest of ancient letters" (Keener and his notes on Galatians 1). Letters stood in for the writer's presence. News too risky to write traveled by the carrier's mouth, and a carrier known to both sides vouched for the copy. Letters are far older than Rome. Podany dates the first known ones to Sumerian kings writing to other kings before 2334 BC. Assyrian merchants of about 1950 to 1740 BC sent theirs in clay envelopes with caravans. Since a scribe wrote it and read it aloud, such a letter was not private.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a message sent by hand with a friend because the official mail does not reach your village. The friend reads it aloud at the meeting, answers questions about what the writer meant, and carries a reply back.
entries.changes: Because letters traveled with trusted people and were read aloud, the Jerusalem letter of Acts 15:22-31 goes with chosen messengers who can explain it, and Paul's letters were heard by whole churches. In Romans 16:22 the scribe, Tertius, adds a greeting of his own, and in Galatians 6:11 Paul takes the pen himself.
entries.not: **Not a note handed to whoever happened to be going.** A letter like Paul's was usually written by a trained scribe from dictation, closed in the sender's own hand, and carried by someone both sides trusted. It stood in for the writer's presence, and the carrier might add news too risky to put in writing.
