usedIn.n: Acts 15:22-35, The letter to the Gentile churches
usedIn.s: The council sends Judas and Silas with Paul and Barnabas to carry a letter to the Gentile believers of Antioch, Syria and Cilicia. It is read to the church at Antioch, who rejoice at its encouragement.

usedIn.n: Acts 23:12-35, The oath, the nephew and the night march
usedIn.s: More than forty men bind themselves by an oath not to eat until they have killed Paul. His nephew learns of the ambush, and the tribune sends Paul under heavy escort by night to the governor Felix at Caesarea, with a letter explaining the case.

usedIn.n: Acts 28:17-31, Two years in rented quarters
usedIn.s: Paul calls the Jewish leaders of Rome, explains why he is in chains, and spends a day arguing from Moses and the Prophets. Some are persuaded and some are not; for two whole years he lives at his own expense, welcoming everyone and preaching the kingdom without hindrance.

usedIn.n: Romans 1:1-7, A slave of the Messiah writes to Rome
usedIn.s: Paul opens with his name and titles, a short summary of the good news about God's Son, and a greeting of grace and peace to believers in Rome he has never met.

usedIn.n: Romans 16:1-2, Phoebe of Cenchreae
usedIn.s: Paul commends Phoebe, a servant or deacon of the church at Cenchreae and a patron of many, Paul included, and asks the Romans to welcome her and help her in whatever she needs.

usedIn.n: Romans 16:17-27, Tertius, Gaius and Erastus
usedIn.s: Paul warns against those who cause divisions, promises that God will soon crush Satan under the believers' feet, and passes on greetings from Corinth, including his scribe Tertius, his host Gaius and Erastus the city treasurer.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 1:1-9, Grace to the church in Corinth
usedIn.s: Paul and Sosthenes greet the church of God in Corinth and thank God that its members have been made rich in every kind of speech and knowledge as they wait for the Lord to be revealed.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 16:1-24, The collection and final greetings
usedIn.s: Paul arranges a weekly setting aside of money for the believers in Jerusalem, plans his travels, commends Timothy, Apollos and the household of Stephanas, and closes with greetings, a line in his own hand and the Aramaic prayer Marana tha.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 1:1-11, The God of all comfort and the sentence of death
usedIn.s: Paul opens by blessing the God of all comfort and tells the Corinthians that in Asia he was so crushed that he felt he had received the sentence of death, so that he learned to rely on the God who raises the dead.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 2:5-13, Forgive the offender; no rest at Troas
usedIn.s: The man who caused the grief has been punished enough by the majority, so Paul urges the church to forgive him lest Satan outwit them, then tells how he left an open door at Troas because Titus had not come.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 7:2-16, Titus arrives and the letter that hurt
usedIn.s: In Macedonia Paul is comforted by Titus's arrival and his news that the Corinthians grieved over Paul's harsh letter in a way that led to repentance, and that they received Titus with fear and trembling.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 10:1-18, Weighty letters, a weak presence and the siege of the mind
usedIn.s: Answering the charge that he is bold in letters but weak in person, Paul describes a war that takes every thought captive and refuses to compare himself with rivals who measure themselves by themselves.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 12:19-13:14, Two or three witnesses
usedIn.s: Paul warns that on his third visit every charge will be established by two or three witnesses and that he will not spare the unrepentant, then closes with a call to restoration, the holy kiss and a threefold blessing.

usedIn.n: Galatians 1:1-10, A letter with no thanksgiving, and a curse
usedIn.s: Paul opens by insisting that his commission came from God and not from people, skips the thanksgiving his letters usually give, and pronounces a curse on anyone, even an angel, who preaches a different gospel.

usedIn.n: Galatians 4:12-20, Welcomed as an angel of God
usedIn.s: Paul appeals to the Galatians as friends, reminding them that when he first preached to them in bodily weakness they did not scorn him but welcomed him as an angel of God, and asks whether he has now become their enemy by telling them the truth.

usedIn.n: Galatians 6:11-18, Large letters in his own hand, and the marks of Jesus
usedIn.s: Taking the pen himself, Paul writes in large letters that the rivals want the Galatians circumcised so they can boast in their flesh and avoid persecution, while he boasts only in the cross; he blesses those who follow this rule and the Israel of God, and says he bears the marks of Jesus.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 1:1-14, A circular letter opens with praise, a seal and a down payment
usedIn.s: Paul greets God's holy people and launches one long blessing of God for choosing, adopting, redeeming and sealing a mixed people, with the Spirit as the down payment of their inheritance.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 6:18-24, An ambassador in chains, and the man who carried the letter
usedIn.s: Paul asks for prayer that he may speak boldly, calling himself an ambassador in chains, and sends Tychicus to carry the letter and tell them his news.

usedIn.n: Philippians 1:1-11, A letter between friends, and a partnership in the gospel
usedIn.s: Paul and Timothy greet the believers at Philippi with their overseers and deacons, thank God for their partnership in the gospel from the first day, and pray that their love will grow until the day of Christ.

usedIn.n: Philippians 2:12-18, Lights in a crooked generation, poured out like a drink offering
usedIn.s: Paul urges the Philippians to work out their salvation without grumbling, shining like stars in a crooked generation, and pictures himself poured out like a drink offering on their sacrifice.

usedIn.n: Colossians 1:1-14, Epaphras's report and a change of kingdoms
usedIn.s: Paul and Timothy greet the believers at Colossae, a church Paul has never visited, thank God for what Epaphras has told them, and pray that they grow in knowledge, having been rescued out of darkness into the kingdom of God's Son.

usedIn.n: Colossians 1:24-2:5, Sufferings for the body, and a steward of the mystery
usedIn.s: Paul rejoices to suffer for the church, fills up what is lacking in Christ's afflictions, calls himself the servant entrusted with God's long hidden mystery, and tells churches he has never met how hard he struggles for them.

usedIn.n: Colossians 4:7-18, Tychicus, Onesimus, Nympha's house and the letter from Laodicea
usedIn.s: Paul sends the letter with Tychicus and Onesimus, passes on greetings from Jewish and Gentile co-workers, greets Nympha and the church in her house, asks for this letter to be read at Laodicea and the Laodicean letter at Colossae, and signs off in his own hand.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 2:17-3:13, Orphaned, blocked by Satan, crowned
usedIn.s: Torn away from the church, Paul tells how he longed to come back but Satan blocked the way, how he sent Timothy from Athens, how Timothy's good news has revived him, and prays that the Lord will make them blameless at his coming with all his holy ones.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 5:12-28, Leaders, prophets, a holy kiss and a letter read to all
usedIn.s: Paul asks the church to honor those who work hard over them, to warn the idle and help the weak, to rejoice, pray and give thanks, not to quench the Spirit or despise prophecy but test everything, and to have the letter read to all.

usedIn.n: 2 Thessalonians 2:13-3:5, Hold to the traditions, and let the word run
usedIn.s: Paul thanks God for choosing the Thessalonians, urges them to stand firm and hold to the traditions they were taught by word or by letter, prays for them, and asks them to pray that the Lord's message will run swiftly.

usedIn.n: 2 Thessalonians 3:6-18, The idle, the busybodies, and a greeting in Paul's own hand
usedIn.s: Paul tells the church to keep away from believers who are idle and will not work, recalls how he worked night and day to set an example, lays down that anyone unwilling to work should not eat, and signs the letter in his own hand.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 3:14-16, God's household and the hymn
usedIn.s: Paul writes so that, if he is delayed, Timothy will know how people ought to behave in God's household, the church of the living God, and quotes what seems to be a hymn about Christ.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 4:9-22, The cloak, the scrolls, the first defense, and before winter
usedIn.s: Paul asks Timothy to come quickly and bring Mark, the cloak he left at Troas and his scrolls; Alexander the metalworker did him great harm, no one stood with him at his first defense, but the Lord rescued him from the lion's mouth, and Timothy must come before winter.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 13:18-25, Timothy released, greetings from Italy
usedIn.s: The writer asks for prayer so that he may be restored to his readers soon, blesses them in the name of the God of peace who brought back from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep, calls the letter a brief word of exhortation, and reports that Timothy has been released. Those from Italy send greetings.

usedIn.n: James 1:1-18, To the twelve tribes scattered
usedIn.s: James greets the twelve tribes scattered among the nations, tells them to count their trials as joy and to ask God for wisdom, warns that the rich will wither like a wildflower, and insists that God tempts no one but gives every good gift from above, as the Father of lights.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 1:1-12, To the exiles of the dispersion
usedIn.s: Peter writes to God's chosen exiles scattered through five provinces of Asia Minor, blesses God for a new birth into a living hope and an inheritance kept in heaven, and tells them their trials test their faith as fire tests gold. The prophets searched for this salvation, and angels long to look into it.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 5:1-14, Elders, the roaring lion, and greetings from Babylon
usedIn.s: As a fellow elder Peter urges the elders to shepherd God's flock willingly, not for gain, until the Chief Shepherd gives them an unfading crown. All must be humble, for their adversary the devil prowls like a roaring lion. Peter writes through Silvanus and sends greetings from she who is in Babylon and from his son Mark.

usedIn.n: 2 John 1-6, The elder to the chosen lady
usedIn.s: The elder writes to the chosen lady and her children, whom he loves in the truth. He is glad that some of her children walk in the truth, and he asks for no new command but the old one, that they love one another, which means walking in God's commands.

usedIn.n: 2 John 7-13, Deceivers at the door, paper and ink
usedIn.s: Many deceivers who refuse to confess that Jesus Christ came in the flesh are abroad in the world; such a one is the deceiver and the antichrist. Whoever runs ahead and does not keep to Christ's teaching does not have God, and the readers are not to take such a person into the house or greet him. The elder would rather not use paper and ink, and hopes to talk face to face.

usedIn.n: 3 John 1-8, Gaius and the traveling brothers
usedIn.s: The elder writes to his dear friend Gaius, praying that he is in good health and glad to hear that he walks in the truth. Gaius has been faithful in what he does for the brothers, strangers though they are; he should supply them for the next stage of their journey in a way that honors God, since they went out for the sake of the Name and took nothing from the pagans.

usedIn.n: Revelation 1:1-8, a revelation sent as a letter
usedIn.s: The book opens as a revelation God gave Jesus, sent by his angel to his servant John, with a blessing on the one who reads it aloud and on those who hear. It then greets seven churches in Asia like a letter, from the one who is, was and is to come, and from Jesus, ruler of the kings of the earth, who is coming with the clouds.

usedIn.n: Revelation 22:6-21, I am coming soon
usedIn.s: The angel confirms that the words are trustworthy, and Jesus says he is coming soon. John is told not to seal up the prophecy, since the time is near; those who wash their robes may enter the city while dogs, sorcerers and liars stay outside. The book closes with the Spirit and the bride saying come, a warning against adding to or taking from it, and the prayer, come, Lord Jesus.

entries.title: Letters of recommendation
entries.summary: A traveler often carried a letter from someone his hosts trusted, vouching for him and asking them to receive him. Such letters opened homes, synagogues and churches.
aliases: receive him as you would me
welcome him as you would welcome me
we also speak well of him
entries.plain: **She arrived in the new city with a note from her old pastor, and by evening she had a bed and a church.** In the ancient world a stranger was trusted when someone his hosts trusted vouched for him. People of standing wrote letters for those below them, praising them and asking that they be welcomed and helped. Usually the person recommended carried the letter himself. Jewish travelers used such letters to find lodging with Jewish families along the way.
entries.then: Throughout the empire, social superiors wrote letters of introduction to their peers or inferiors for people they recommended. Such letters were standard in Greco-Roman society. Jewish travelers often carried them so that Jewish householders elsewhere would trust them with lodging. A recommendation carried more weight than a person's own claims. Anyone trusted could write one, and by such a letter a sender could also authorize a messenger. The person recommended usually carried the letter himself and might be called on to explain it, so the bearer's own qualifications mattered. Commending oneself was thought proper only for good reason, such as self-defense. Keener suggests that a letter from the proconsul Sergius Paulus could explain a quick welcome at Pisidian Antioch. Wright notes that in Corinth some later wanted Paul himself to bring letters of recommendation from someone they trusted. The strongest letters said, in effect, receive this person as you would me. Messengers were received with the honor due their sender (2 Samuel 19:37-38). Superlative praise for more than one person was rare and noteworthy. Bailey notes that the word Paul uses for welcoming such a person means welcoming him into fellowship, accepting him as a friend. Keener reads 1 Timothy itself as an open letter of recommendation, read in the house churches to back Timothy's authority.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a reference letter from a former employer that a job seeker hands over in person. The new boss trusts the old one, so the stranger at the door is no longer a stranger.
entries.changes: A letter vouching for a traveler opened doors, so Saul's letters to the synagogues of Damascus in Acts 9:2 gave him standing there, and the believers at Ephesus write ahead for Apollos in Acts 18:27. In 2 Corinthians 3:1 Paul asks whether he needs such letters for a church he founded.
entries.not: **Not a reference for a job.** The letter asked its readers to take the bearer into their homes and their fellowship, often to receive him as they would the writer himself. A traveler's lodging, and his welcome in a synagogue or a church, could hang on it.
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Acts 9:2 and 18:27, on 2 Corinthians 3:1 and on Romans 16:1-2

usedIn.n: Acts 9:1-31, Saul on the Damascus road
usedIn.s: Carrying the high priest's letters to the synagogues of Damascus, Saul is stopped by a light and a voice. Blinded, healed and baptized, the persecutor begins to proclaim Jesus and has to escape over the city wall.

usedIn.n: Acts 18:18-28, A vow at Cenchreae and Apollos of Alexandria
usedIn.s: Paul has his hair cut at Cenchreae because of a vow and sails for Syria by way of Ephesus. In Ephesus Priscilla and Aquila teach the eloquent Alexandrian Apollos more accurately, and the believers write ahead to Achaia to welcome him.

usedIn.n: Romans 16:1-2, Phoebe of Cenchreae
usedIn.s: Paul commends Phoebe, a servant or deacon of the church at Cenchreae and a patron of many, Paul included, and asks the Romans to welcome her and help her in whatever she needs.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 16:1-24, The collection and final greetings
usedIn.s: Paul arranges a weekly setting aside of money for the believers in Jerusalem, plans his travels, commends Timothy, Apollos and the household of Stephanas, and closes with greetings, a line in his own hand and the Aramaic prayer Marana tha.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 3:1-18, Letters of recommendation and Moses' veil
usedIn.s: Paul needs no letters of recommendation, since the Corinthians are his letter, written by the Spirit on hearts; he sets the fading glory on Moses' veiled face against the greater glory of the new covenant.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 8:16-9:15, Envoys for the collection and the cheerful giver
usedIn.s: Paul commends Titus and two brothers appointed by the churches to carry the gift, takes care that no one can fault him in handling it, and urges the Corinthians to have their promised gift ready, since God loves a cheerful giver.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 10:1-18, Weighty letters, a weak presence and the siege of the mind
usedIn.s: Answering the charge that he is bold in letters but weak in person, Paul describes a war that takes every thought captive and refuses to compare himself with rivals who measure themselves by themselves.

usedIn.n: Philippians 2:19-30, Timothy and Epaphroditus, commended and sent
usedIn.s: Paul commends Timothy as a son who serves with him and plans to send him soon, and sends home Epaphroditus, the church's messenger, who nearly died on their errand.

usedIn.n: Colossians 4:7-18, Tychicus, Onesimus, Nympha's house and the letter from Laodicea
usedIn.s: Paul sends the letter with Tychicus and Onesimus, passes on greetings from Jewish and Gentile co-workers, greets Nympha and the church in her house, asks for this letter to be read at Laodicea and the Laodicean letter at Colossae, and signs off in his own hand.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 1:1-11, Myths, endless genealogies and would-be teachers of the law
usedIn.s: Paul greets Timothy, whom he left in Ephesus, and tells him to stop certain people teaching strange doctrines and spending themselves on myths and endless genealogies; they want to be teachers of the law without understanding it, while the law is meant for the lawless.

usedIn.n: Titus 3:9-15, A divisive person, winter at Nicopolis, and Zenas and Apollos
usedIn.s: Titus is to avoid foolish controversies, genealogies and quarrels about the law, and to warn a divisive person twice before having nothing more to do with him; Paul plans to winter at Nicopolis and asks Titus to send Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way with everything they need.

usedIn.n: Philemon 8-25, Onesimus sent home with a letter
usedIn.s: Paul appeals to Philemon, on the basis of love, for Onesimus, the slave who became Paul's son in prison: he sends him back to be received as a beloved brother rather than as a slave, asks Philemon to welcome him as he would Paul, offers to repay anything he owes, and asks for a guest room.

usedIn.n: 3 John 9-15, Diotrephes and Demetrius
usedIn.s: The elder wrote to the church, but Diotrephes, eager to be first, refuses to receive him; he spreads malicious talk, refuses to welcome the brothers and puts out of the church those who do. Gaius is not to imitate evil. Demetrius is well spoken of by everyone, and the elder adds his own testimony; he hopes to come soon and talk face to face.

entries.title: Seals, down payments and deposits
entries.summary: A seal pressed into wax showed who owned or witnessed a document or a jar of goods and proved that no one had opened it. A down payment was the first part of the price, paid as a pledge that the rest would follow. A deposit left in someone's keeping had to be guarded and returned.
aliases: sealed for the day of redemption
entries.plain: **The first check on a new car is a promise in money that the rest is coming.** In Paul's world an important letter or contract was rolled up, tied with string and sealed with hot wax pressed with a stamp or signet ring. An unbroken seal showed who stood behind the document and that no one had tampered with it. Merchants sealed jars of goods the same way. In business, a down payment was the first part of the price, paid to show that the buyer would pay the whole.
entries.then: A seal showed that no one had tampered with what it closed, whether a document or a jar of goods. The witness's stamp was pressed into hot wax over the string around the rolled-up document. Documents carried the identity marks of witnesses, and containers those of owners. Important documents often had about six seals, and "a sealed document was one that had not been tampered with" (the cultural backgrounds notes). A seal was also a mark of ownership, often used by kings. Wright pictures a signet ring pressed into wax so the reader knew who sent the letter and that it arrived untouched. Sealing is far older than wax. By about 3500 BC at Uruk, officials rolled carved cylinder seals over clay on jars, doors and shipments. Podany explains that "Anyone could see if the seal was broken" and who had sealed it. Important people also rolled their seals on clay documents to attest a transaction. The word Paul uses for deposit, arrabon, was the business term for a down payment or first installment. It was a pledge to complete the purchase, and Wright compares it to a lump sum put down on a large purchase. The New Testament always uses the word of the Spirit (the CSB Study Bible). Judaism linked the Spirit with the end of the age, so Keener and his notes read the Spirit as deposit as the first taste of the age to come. Keener also reads Paul's sealing of the fruit in Romans 15:28 against the seal on commercial goods. A deposit could also be property left in someone's keeping, a sacred trust, and writers extended the picture to teaching handed on.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a tamper-evident seal on a bottle of medicine, together with the deposit that holds a house for a buyer. The first shows the contents are as the maker left them; the second shows the buyer means to pay in full.
entries.changes: Because a seal marked ownership and guarded what it closed, and a down payment promised the full price, the Spirit as seal and deposit in 2 Corinthians 1:22 speaks both of belonging now and of more to come, and Ephesians 1:13-14 uses the same pair. A deposit held in trust is the picture in 1 Timothy 6:20, where Timothy is to guard what has been entrusted to him.
entries.not: **Not a factory seal or a refundable deposit.** An ancient seal carried the mark of a particular owner or witness, so it said who stood behind the contents as well as that they were untouched. The arrabon was the first part of the price itself, a pledge that the rest would follow.
entries.dissent: Three questions. First, whether the verb translated stand firm or establish in 2 Corinthians 1:21 carries a business sense. Keener says it was often a business term for confirming a sale, tied to the down payment in the next verse. The cultural backgrounds notes say Paul usually uses it generically, and only that the business sense might be relevant. Second, what sealing stresses in Ephesians 1:13 and 4:30. The ESV Study Bible names two options, protection until the inheritance and certification as genuine, and prefers protection. Keener stresses attestation that no one had tampered with the contents. The cultural backgrounds notes stress divine certification for the day of judgment, and the CSB Study Bible speaks of ownership and a pledge of redemption to come. Third, how many witnesses sealed a legal document. The cultural backgrounds article Sealing Documents and Revelation 5 says "usually about six in number". Keener says often seven, and Beale says seven for a Roman will, which bears on the seven seals of Revelation 5:1.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on 2 Corinthians 1:21, 1:22 and 5:5, and on Romans 15:28

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 1:12-2:4, Changed plans, the seal and the down payment
usedIn.s: Accused of fickleness for changing his travel plans, Paul answers that his word is reliable because all God's promises are Yes in Christ, who has anointed and sealed them and given the Spirit as a down payment, and explains that he stayed away to spare them.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 5:1-10, The tent and the judgment seat
usedIn.s: Paul sets the earthly tent of the body against a building from God, longs to be clothed rather than found naked, names the Spirit as a down payment, and says that all must appear before the judgment seat of Christ.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 1:1-14, A circular letter opens with praise, a seal and a down payment
usedIn.s: Paul greets God's holy people and launches one long blessing of God for choosing, adopting, redeeming and sealing a mixed people, with the Spirit as the down payment of their inheritance.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 4:17-32, No longer as the Gentiles live
usedIn.s: Paul tells Gentile believers to stop living as the Gentiles do, to put off the old self and put on the new, to give the devil no foothold, to work with their hands and share, and not to grieve the Spirit who sealed them.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 6:11-21, Fight the good fight, the King of kings, the rich, and the deposit
usedIn.s: Timothy, as a man of God, is to flee greed and fight the good fight of the faith, keeping his charge until the appearing of the Lord, the King of kings; the rich are to be generous, and Timothy is to guard what has been entrusted to him.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 1:8-18, Not ashamed of my chains, the deposit, and Onesiphorus
usedIn.s: Paul tells Timothy not to be ashamed of the Lord's testimony or of him as a prisoner, but to share his suffering and guard the good deposit; everyone in Asia has deserted him except Onesiphorus, who searched Rome until he found him.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 2:14-26, Gangrene, a resurrection already past, and vessels in a great house
usedIn.s: Timothy is to warn the church against quarreling about words and to handle the word of truth correctly; the teaching of Hymenaeus and Philetus, who say the resurrection has already happened, spreads like gangrene, but God's foundation stands sealed, and in a great house some vessels are for honor and some for dishonor.

usedIn.n: Revelation 5:1-14, the sealed scroll and the Lamb
usedIn.s: In God's right hand is a scroll written on both sides and sealed with seven seals, and no one is worthy to open it until the Lion of Judah, the Root of David, appears as a Lamb that looks slain. The living creatures, the elders, countless angels and all creation worship him.

usedIn.n: Revelation 6:1-8, four horsemen
usedIn.s: As the Lamb opens the first four seals, four riders go out: a crowned archer on a white horse bent on conquest, a rider on a red horse who takes peace from the earth, a rider with scales on a black horse while wheat sells at famine prices, and Death on a pale horse with Hades following.

usedIn.n: Revelation 7:1-17, the sealing of the 144,000 and the crowd in white
usedIn.s: Four angels hold back the winds until God's servants are sealed on their foreheads, 144,000 from the tribes of Israel. Then John sees a crowd no one can count, from every nation, in white robes with palm branches, who have come out of the great tribulation and whom the Lamb will shepherd.

usedIn.n: Revelation 10:1-11, the mighty angel and the little scroll
usedIn.s: A mighty angel robed in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, plants one foot on the sea and one on the land, swears by the one who lives for ever that there will be no more delay, and gives John a little scroll to eat, sweet in his mouth and bitter in his stomach.

usedIn.n: Revelation 13:11-18, the beast from the earth, the mark and 666
usedIn.s: A second beast, harmless-looking like a lamb but speaking like the dragon, rises from the earth and drives everyone to worship the first beast, working wonders and making its statue speak. Trade is barred to anyone without its mark on hand or forehead, a mark tied to the beast's name and number, 666.

usedIn.n: Revelation 14:1-5, the Lamb and the 144,000 on Mount Zion
usedIn.s: The Lamb stands on Mount Zion with 144,000 who bear his name and his Father's on their foreheads, singing a new song only they can learn. They have kept themselves pure, follow the Lamb wherever he goes, and are offered as firstfruits to God and the Lamb.

entries.title: Greeks, barbarians and the nations
entries.summary: Greeks split humanity into Greeks and barbarians, people whose speech sounded like babble. Jews split it into Israel and the nations. Paul uses both maps.
entries.plain: **To the people of the capital, everyone from the provinces sounded as if they were mumbling.** Greeks divided the human race in two: Greeks, and everyone else, whom they called barbarians. They also tended to think of themselves as the wise ones. Jews had their own way of dividing the world: Israel, and the nations, or Gentiles. Jews often called the nations simply the Greeks, because so much of that world spoke Greek. When Paul says he owes the gospel to Greeks and barbarians, and to Jew and Greek, he is using both maps at once.
entries.then: Greeks counted everyone else in the world barbarians, and usually thought of themselves as wise and others as foolish. Wright explains that the word probably came from the way other languages sounded to Greek ears, meaningless mumbling beside the music of Greek. To a true Greek even Latin-speaking Romans were barbarians. Some educated Jews classed themselves as Greeks, but Greeks still counted them barbarians. Jews divided the world differently, into Jews and the rest. They called the rest the nations, the Gentiles or sometimes the Greeks, since in Jewish eyes the wider world was a Greek-speaking one (Wright). The word for nations could exclude Israel or could mean peoples in general, Israel included. Jewish people regarded idolatry and sexual immorality as the marks of Gentile life. Greeks were the most anti-Jewish of peoples, Keener adds, so a gospel for both Jew and Greek was a gospel for everyone in between. On Malta the common people spoke Punic. Keener notes that Greeks used barbarian for any non-Greek speaker and did not expect kindness from such people. Wright and Bird write that Paul's new people was called from among Jews, Greeks, barbarians and anyone else, and was no longer defined by ethnicity.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a capital city that calls everyone outside it provincials, and a minority faith that calls everyone outside it unbelievers. Someone who says he owes a debt to capital and provinces, insiders and outsiders alike, has refused both ways of sorting people.
entries.changes: Paul's debt to Greeks and barbarians in Romans 1:14 uses the Greek map of the world, and his Jew and Greek two verses later uses the Jewish one. The islanders of Acts 28:2 are barbarians only in the sense that they did not speak Greek. Colossians 3:11 names Greek and Jew, barbarian and Scythian among the distinctions that no longer rank people.
entries.not: **Not a matter of capital and provinces within one country.** Barbarian put a person outside Greek speech and culture altogether, even a Latin-speaking Roman. The Jewish line between Israel and the nations ran by descent and worship, not by belief alone, and neither map sorted people by color.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Romans 1:5-6, 1:14-15, 1:16 and 1:24-32, and on Acts 28:2
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Romans 1:14 and 1:23
N. T. Wright, Paul for Everyone: Romans, Part One, comment on Romans 1:14-17

usedIn.n: Acts 28:1-10, Malta: the viper and the goddess Justice
usedIn.s: The islanders of Malta welcome the shipwrecked with a fire. When a viper fastens on Paul's hand they decide that Justice will not let a murderer live; when he takes no harm they call him a god. Publius, the island's chief man, takes them in, and Paul heals his father and many others.

usedIn.n: Romans 1:8-17, Longing to see Rome
usedIn.s: Paul thanks God that the Roman believers' faith is spoken of everywhere, explains why he has not yet come, and states his theme: the good news is God's power to save everyone who believes, Jew and Greek.

usedIn.n: Romans 1:18-32, Images of the immortal God
usedIn.s: Paul describes God's anger against people who knew him from creation yet traded his glory for images of humans and animals, and the disorder that followed.

usedIn.n: Colossians 3:1-17, Things above, and no Greek, Jew, barbarian or Scythian
usedIn.s: Raised with Christ, the believers are to set their minds on things above, put to death the old ways, take off the old self and put on the new, in which there is no Greek or Jew, barbarian, Scythian, slave or free, and above all put on love.

entries.title: Orators, rhetoric and boasting
entries.summary: Public speaking was the great skill of the Greek city. Traveling orators performed for crowds and gathered paying students, audiences judged them on voice and gesture as well as argument, and the fans of rival speakers boasted of their own man against the rest.
aliases: receiving no help from the pagans
entries.plain: **The visiting preacher packed the hall, and afterward everyone argued over whether he was better than last year's.** In Paul's world fine public speaking was what educated people admired most. Orators traveled from city to city, gave a showcase speech, and if the crowd liked them settled down and took paying students. Audiences judged a speaker's voice, gestures and style as closely as his argument, and the fans of rival speakers sometimes came to blows. Speakers also had accepted ways of praising themselves, and lists of the hardships they had endured to show they were genuine.
entries.then: Corinthian culture prized speech and even competed in it, and the nearby Isthmian Games included speech contests. An orator arriving in a city gave a scheduled oration and, if it won him students, settled there. "Urban hearers in places such as Corinth regularly judged and ranked speakers" (the cultural backgrounds notes). Bailey quotes Dio Chrysostom on the scene at the games: "Crowds of wretched sophists around Poseidon's temple shouting and reviling one another." Greeks expected a forceful tone, the right accent and gestures, even the right clothes and grooming. Even famous orators played down their ability before speaking brilliantly. Philosophers had attacked rhetoric since Socrates for valuing skill over truth. Speakers and philosophers alike were accused of selling the truth for gain, like merchants watering their goods. Self-praise had rules. Rhetoricians such as Quintilian and moralists such as Plutarch allowed it only under necessity, in self-defense or for the hearers' good. Plutarch wrote a whole essay on praising oneself inoffensively. Boasting of one's friends was always acceptable, and comparison with rivals was a standard technique. Sages listed the hardships they had endured, sometimes in triads, to prove their integrity. They meant the list to show their strength, not their weakness. Roman officials displayed their careers, the cursus honorum. Wright notes that the first soldier over an enemy wall could claim the wall crown, the corona muralis, on oath. He reads 2 Corinthians 11 as "an upside-down boasting list, a cursus pudorum." Speeches of praise loved parallelism and repetition. The florid style valued in Asia Minor, piling up synonyms, was well known and controversial among Roman orators.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a celebrity speaker on tour. People come for the performance, rate the delivery, and attach themselves to the speaker they like best against his rivals.
entries.changes: Because audiences ranked speakers and attached themselves to favorites, slogans such as I belong to Apollos in 1 Corinthians 1:12 sound like the fans of rival orators. Apollos is introduced as an eloquent man in Acts 18:24, and Paul's critics in 2 Corinthians 10:10 say his letters are weighty but his speaking contemptible.
entries.not: **Not a speaker who comes and goes.** A successful orator settled in the city and lived on the fees of the students he won. Speech was also judged in formal contests, as at the Isthmian Games, and philosophers attacked the whole trade for valuing skill over truth.
entries.dissent: How far Greek rhetoric explains Corinth. Carson reports a dispute over reading 1 and 2 Corinthians against an early Sophist movement in the city, with Bruce Winter arguing for it and Jerome Murphy-O'Connor his most articulate critic. Bailey traces Paul's patterns of composition to the Hebrew prophets and says they are not directly related to classical Greek rhetoric. Keener and his notes find many rhetorical devices in Paul's writing and think his weakness lay in delivery, while Wright thinks Paul writes polished rhetoric in 1 Corinthians 1:18-25 on purpose, teasing his readers.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 1:1-9, Grace to the church in Corinth
usedIn.s: Paul and Sosthenes greet the church of God in Corinth and thank God that its members have been made rich in every kind of speech and knowledge as they wait for the Lord to be revealed.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 1:10-17, I belong to Paul, I belong to Apollos
usedIn.s: Told by Chloe's people that the church is splitting into camps behind Paul, Apollos, Cephas and Christ, Paul appeals for unity and asks whether Christ has been divided.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 1:18-2:5, The foolishness of the cross
usedIn.s: Paul sets the message of a crucified Messiah, folly to Greeks and a stumbling block to Jews, against the wisdom and eloquence Corinth admired, and reminds the believers that few of them were wise, powerful or well born.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 4:6-13, Apostles on display
usedIn.s: With biting irony Paul sets the Corinthians, already full, rich and reigning, beside the apostles, put on show last of all like men condemned to die, hungry, ragged, homeless and treated as the world's scum.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 13:1-13, Noisy bronze and a dim mirror
usedIn.s: Paul says that tongues, prophecy, knowledge, faith and even martyrdom are nothing without love, describes what love is, and sets today's partial knowledge, like a dim reflection in a mirror, against seeing face to face.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 2:14-17, Led in God's triumph
usedIn.s: Paul thanks God, who leads him in triumphal procession and spreads the fragrance of Christ through him, a smell of death to some and of life to others, and denies that he peddles God's word for profit.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 3:1-18, Letters of recommendation and Moses' veil
usedIn.s: Paul needs no letters of recommendation, since the Corinthians are his letter, written by the Spirit on hearts; he sets the fading glory on Moses' veiled face against the greater glory of the new covenant.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 4:1-6, The god of this age
usedIn.s: Paul renounces cunning and tampering with God's word; if his gospel is veiled, it is veiled to the perishing, whose minds the god of this age has blinded, while God has made his light shine in believers' hearts.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 4:7-18, Treasure in clay jars
usedIn.s: Paul carries God's treasure in a clay jar, hard pressed but not crushed, carrying Jesus' dying in his body so that Jesus' life may show, while the outer self wastes away and the inner self is renewed day by day.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 5:11-6:13, New creation, Christ's ambassadors and a list of hardships
usedIn.s: Because one died for all, anyone in Christ is a new creation; Paul, God's ambassador, appeals to the Corinthians to be reconciled to God and commends his ministry with a long list of hardships and paradoxes.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 10:1-18, Weighty letters, a weak presence and the siege of the mind
usedIn.s: Answering the charge that he is bold in letters but weak in person, Paul describes a war that takes every thought captive and refuses to compare himself with rivals who measure themselves by themselves.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 11:1-15, The betrothed virgin, the free gospel and the angel of light
usedIn.s: Jealous as a father who has promised his daughter to one husband, Paul fears the Corinthians will be led astray as Eve was; he defends preaching to them free of charge and calls his rivals false apostles disguised as Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 11:16-33, The fool's boast and the basket over the wall
usedIn.s: Forced to boast like a fool, Paul matches his rivals' Jewish credentials and then lists sufferings instead of achievements: lashes, rods, stoning, shipwreck, the dangers of the road, hunger and cold, and a night escape down the wall of Damascus.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 12:1-10, Caught up to the third heaven; the thorn
usedIn.s: Paul tells of a man caught up to the third heaven and into paradise who heard things no one may utter, then of the thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan, which God would not remove because his power is made perfect in weakness.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 12:19-13:14, Two or three witnesses
usedIn.s: Paul warns that on his third visit every charge will be established by two or three witnesses and that he will not spare the unrepentant, then closes with a call to restoration, the holy kiss and a threefold blessing.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 1:1-14, A circular letter opens with praise, a seal and a down payment
usedIn.s: Paul greets God's holy people and launches one long blessing of God for choosing, adopting, redeeming and sealing a mixed people, with the Spirit as the down payment of their inheritance.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 4:1-16, The conqueror goes up and gives gifts
usedIn.s: Paul urges unity, one body and one Spirit, then reads Psalm 68 as Christ ascending in victory and handing out gifts: apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers, to equip the church to grow up into him.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 6:18-24, An ambassador in chains, and the man who carried the letter
usedIn.s: Paul asks for prayer that he may speak boldly, calling himself an ambassador in chains, and sends Tychicus to carry the letter and tell them his news.

usedIn.n: Philippians 3:1-11, Dogs, mutilators, and a pedigree counted as loss
usedIn.s: Paul warns against teachers who press circumcision, calling them dogs and mutilators, lists his own credentials as a born Jew, a Pharisee and a zealous persecutor, and counts them all loss for the sake of knowing Christ.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 6:1-10, Slaves under the yoke, and godliness as gain
usedIn.s: Slaves are to respect their masters so that the faith is not slandered, and those with believing masters are to serve them all the more; then Paul turns on teachers who treat godliness as a way to get rich, and warns that the craving for money breeds every kind of harm.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 2:14-26, Gangrene, a resurrection already past, and vessels in a great house
usedIn.s: Timothy is to warn the church against quarreling about words and to handle the word of truth correctly; the teaching of Hymenaeus and Philetus, who say the resurrection has already happened, spreads like gangrene, but God's foundation stands sealed, and in a great house some vessels are for honor and some for dishonor.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 4:1-8, Itching ears, a drink offering, and the crown
usedIn.s: Paul charges Timothy before God and Christ Jesus to preach the word in season and out of season, because people will gather teachers to suit their itching ears; he himself is already being poured out like a drink offering, has fought the good fight and finished the race, and awaits the crown.

usedIn.n: 3 John 1-8, Gaius and the traveling brothers
usedIn.s: The elder writes to his dear friend Gaius, praying that he is in good health and glad to hear that he walks in the truth. Gaius has been faithful in what he does for the brothers, strangers though they are; he should supply them for the next stage of their journey in a way that honors God, since they went out for the sake of the Name and took nothing from the pagans.

entries.title: The games and the victor's wreath
entries.summary: Greek cities held great athletic festivals, and Corinth hosted the Isthmian Games every two years, second only to the Olympics. Athletes trained for months under oath for a wreath of leaves that soon withered.
aliases: crown in which we will glory
I have fought the good fight
entries.plain: **The whole town was in the stands, and the winner went home with a ribbon worth nothing and fame worth everything.** Greek cities loved athletic festivals. The biggest drew crowds from all over the Greek world for races, boxing and wrestling, with speech and music contests besides. Athletes trained hard for months and competed for their cities. The prize was a simple wreath of leaves that would soon wither, but the honor lasted. Corinth hosted one of the great festivals, the Isthmian Games, every other year.
entries.then: Every two years Corinth staged games on the isthmus for the whole Greek world. After the Olympics, held every four years, they were the best-attended Greek festivals. Keener notes that "The pine garland was awarded at these Isthmian games", as wild olive was at Olympia and parsley at Nemea. The ESV Study Bible suggests that Paul's stay in Corinth may have overlapped the games of AD 49 or 51. Bailey notes that spectators and athletes were housed in tents, good business for tentmakers such as Paul, Priscilla and Aquila. Athletes competed for their cities under strict rules of training. Entrants at Olympia swore by Zeus to ten months of strict training, and breaking the rules could bring whipping, fines or a ban. The footrace came before the other contests of the pentathlon. Boxers wore leather gloves covering most of the forearm, so shadowboxing was no preparation. The wreath would rot, which made the effort for it all the more striking. Philosophers often used athletic pictures, the race among them, for the striving after truth and wise living. Diaspora Jewish writers such as Philo and the author of 4 Maccabees followed them. Greek runners usually ran a straight course and back, so a runner who glanced behind could lose. At the end, heralds called the winner up for his prize, a palm branch at Olympia. Crowns were given to heroes too, but they meant above all the athlete's wreath. Greek men exercised naked in the gymnasium, "the center of civic life in Hellenized towns" (the cultural backgrounds notes). Moralists used physical training as a picture of moral discipline.
entries.bridge: An analogy: an Olympic athlete who trains for years for a medal worth little as metal. Everyone understands the discipline, and nobody thinks the metal is the point.
entries.changes: Corinth's own games stand behind the runners and boxers of 1 Corinthians 9:24-27, where a wreath that perishes sets off one that lasts. The race and the prize return in Philippians 3:12-14 and 2 Timothy 4:7-8.
entries.not: **Not a medal that lasts.** A metal medal can hang on the wall for life, but the wreath of leaves soon withered, and that is the contrast Paul draws. The games were also religious festivals, and entrants at Olympia swore by Zeus to their training.
entries.dissent: What the Isthmian victor's wreath was made of. Keener writes that the pine garland was awarded at the Isthmian games. The cultural backgrounds article Athletic Imagery in 1 Corinthians 9 says pine or withered celery. The Zondervan dictionary, describing the Isthmian games, names laurel, olive leaves or pine needles.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 9:1-27, Free, unpaid and in training
usedIn.s: Paul defends his right as an apostle to be supported and explains why he has never used it, makes himself a slave to all to win more, and pictures his discipline as an athlete's training for a wreath that will not wither.

usedIn.n: Galatians 5:2-12, Circumcision, the whole law and the knife
usedIn.s: Paul warns that a man who accepts circumcision is bound to keep the whole law and is cut off from Christ, asks who cut in on their race, and wishes that the agitators would go further with the knife.

usedIn.n: Philippians 1:27-30, Live as citizens, contend like athletes
usedIn.s: Paul tells a church in a Roman colony to conduct itself as citizens worthy of the gospel, standing firm and striving together, unafraid of opponents, in the same struggle they once saw him face.

usedIn.n: Philippians 3:12-4:1, The race, citizens of heaven, and a Savior from there
usedIn.s: Paul pictures himself as a runner straining toward the prize, warns against those whose god is their stomach, and reminds a Roman colony that its citizenship is in heaven, from where it awaits a Savior who will transform its lowly bodies.

usedIn.n: Colossians 1:24-2:5, Sufferings for the body, and a steward of the mystery
usedIn.s: Paul rejoices to suffer for the church, fills up what is lacking in Christ's afflictions, calls himself the servant entrusted with God's long hidden mystery, and tells churches he has never met how hard he struggles for them.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 2:17-3:13, Orphaned, blocked by Satan, crowned
usedIn.s: Torn away from the church, Paul tells how he longed to come back but Satan blocked the way, how he sent Timothy from Athens, how Timothy's good news has revived him, and prays that the Lord will make them blameless at his coming with all his holy ones.

usedIn.n: 2 Thessalonians 2:13-3:5, Hold to the traditions, and let the word run
usedIn.s: Paul thanks God for choosing the Thessalonians, urges them to stand firm and hold to the traditions they were taught by word or by letter, prays for them, and asks them to pray that the Lord's message will run swiftly.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 4:6-16, Training for godliness, and a young leader
usedIn.s: Timothy is to train himself for godliness as an athlete trains his body, set an example despite his youth, devote himself to the public reading of Scripture and teaching, and not neglect the gift given when the elders laid hands on him.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 6:11-21, Fight the good fight, the King of kings, the rich, and the deposit
usedIn.s: Timothy, as a man of God, is to flee greed and fight the good fight of the faith, keeping his charge until the appearing of the Lord, the King of kings; the rich are to be generous, and Timothy is to guard what has been entrusted to him.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 2:1-13, Soldier, athlete and farmer, and a prisoner in chains
usedIn.s: Timothy is to pass on what he heard to reliable people who will teach others, and to endure hardship like a soldier, compete by the rules like an athlete and work like a farmer, remembering Jesus Christ, raised from the dead and descended from David, for whom Paul is chained like a criminal.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 4:1-8, Itching ears, a drink offering, and the crown
usedIn.s: Paul charges Timothy before God and Christ Jesus to preach the word in season and out of season, because people will gather teachers to suit their itching ears; he himself is already being poured out like a drink offering, has fought the good fight and finished the race, and awaits the crown.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 10:26-39, No sacrifice left; prison and plunder
usedIn.s: For anyone who goes on sinning deliberately after knowing the truth, no sacrifice for sins remains. The readers once endured a hard contest: public insult, prison and the seizure of their property, which they accepted with joy. They must not throw away their confidence now.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 12:1-13, The race, the shame and the Father's discipline
usedIn.s: Surrounded by a great cloud of witnesses, believers are to throw off every weight and run with endurance, eyes fixed on Jesus, who endured the cross and scorned its shame. Their hardships are a father's discipline, which only legitimate children receive.

usedIn.n: Revelation 2:8-11, Smyrna, poor and slandered
usedIn.s: To Smyrna the risen Jesus says he sees their hardship and poverty and the abuse they suffer from local opponents claiming to be the true Jews, whom he condemns in harsh terms. Some will be jailed for a short time; if they stay loyal even to death he will reward them with life.

entries.title: The seven cities of Asia
entries.summary: Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia and Laodicea, proud cities of the Roman province of Asia, strung along a road a courier could walk. Each letter in Revelation 2 and 3 speaks into its own city's history, trades and temples.
entries.plain: **A letter to a town council lands harder when it mentions the bridge everyone knows is cracked.** Revelation is addressed to churches in seven real cities in Rome's province of Asia, today the western part of Turkey. They lay along a road a messenger could walk, one after another. Each church's letter speaks into the life of its own city: its proudest buildings, its trades, its earthquakes, its gods and its temples to the emperor. Seven was also a number of completeness, and many readers take the seven to stand for every church as well.
entries.then: A messenger from Patmos would reach Ephesus first, and the other cities follow in walking order, thirty to forty-five miles apart. The ESV Study Bible notes that "The order in which the churches are listed traces the route" a courier would take. There were other churches in Asia, so the choice of seven is deliberate. William Ramsay found local color in each letter; Keener judges some of his links strained and others apt. Wright and Bird stress how thoroughly the emperor's cult had filled the province. By the end of the century "all seven cities that John mentions had cultic sites for imperial devotion". Six had imperial temples, and five had imperial altars with a priesthood. Sardis and Philadelphia were wrecked in AD 17 and rebuilt with imperial help. Laodicea was damaged in AD 60 and refused Roman relief. Ephesus was the leading city of the province, and Keener calls Ephesus and Smyrna the oldest centers of the imperial cult. The atlas and the Zondervan dictionary put the first Asian temple to an emperor at Pergamum in 29 BC and the second at Smyrna in AD 26. The churches' troubles differed. Wright and Bird write that not all were persecuted, and that several faced affluence and the pull to compromise; the cultural backgrounds notes count Ephesus, Thyatira, Sardis and Laodicea among them. Each letter keeps a set pattern. The speaker describes himself, says I know, praises and blames, calls the church to hear, and promises a reward to the one who conquers. Keener likens the form to imperial edicts posted in Asian cities; the cultural backgrounds article Letters to the Seven Churches finds the prophets' oracles on the nations a closer model.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a touring speaker who gives the same talk in seven towns but opens each night with the local news, the mill that closed, the flood last spring. Each audience knows the talk is meant for them.
entries.changes: Because each letter speaks into its own city, the lukewarm water of Revelation 3:16 carried a local sting before it carried a general lesson. Colossians 4:13 ties the believers of Laodicea and Hierapolis together through one worker, and Acts 19:10 says the whole province heard the message while Paul was based in Ephesus.
entries.not: **Not one talk with a local opening.** Each letter keeps the same frame, but the praise and blame change from city to city, since not every church was persecuted and several faced wealth and compromise instead. Keener reads the real road and the local color as signs of actual churches, not stages of church history.

usedIn.n: Revelation 1:9-20, Patmos, the Lord's day, lampstands and stars
usedIn.s: On the island of Patmos, in the Spirit on the Lord's day, John hears a voice like a trumpet telling him to write to seven churches. He turns and sees one like a son of man among seven golden lampstands, holding seven stars, who holds the keys of death and Hades and explains what the stars and lampstands mean.

usedIn.n: Revelation 2:1-7, Ephesus and the Nicolaitans
usedIn.s: To Ephesus the one who holds the seven stars praises a church that tested false apostles and hates the works of the Nicolaitans, but warns that it has abandoned its first love and may lose its lampstand. The one who conquers will eat from the tree of life in God's paradise.

usedIn.n: Revelation 3:1-6, Sardis, alive in name only
usedIn.s: To Sardis the one who holds the seven spirits and seven stars says the church has a reputation for being alive but is dead, and warns that he will come like a thief if it does not wake up. A few have not soiled their clothes; the one who conquers will walk with him in white and will not be blotted out of the book of life.

usedIn.n: Revelation 3:7-13, Philadelphia and the key of David
usedIn.s: To Philadelphia the one who holds the key of David sets before a weak but faithful church an open door no one can shut. Those of the synagogue of Satan will bow at their feet, and the one who conquers will be a pillar in God's temple, bearing the name of the new Jerusalem.

usedIn.n: Revelation 3:14-22, Laodicea, lukewarm and rich
usedIn.s: To Laodicea the faithful and true witness says the church is neither cold nor hot but lukewarm, and he will spit it out. It thinks itself rich but is poor, blind and naked; he counsels it to buy gold, white clothes and eye salve, and stands at the door and knocks.

entries.title: Following a teacher
entries.summary: A disciple walked behind his teacher, lived with him, learned his ways and carried his reputation. Jesus chose his own, which only radical teachers did.
aliases: share all good things with the instructor
as a son with his father
what you have learned and seen in me
like a father with his children
imitators of us and of the Lord
your children walking in the truth
my children walking in the truth
entries.plain: **You can tell she was his apprentice by the way she holds the tools.** In Jesus' world you did not learn a teacher's way from a book. You lived with him, walked behind him and watched. And whatever his disciples did, people blamed or praised him for it.
entries.then: Only the most radical teachers called disciples instead of waiting for disciples to choose them (compare Elijah and Elisha, 1 Kings 19:19). Disciples usually sought out their own teachers. To come after a teacher was the posture of a disciple, and disciples were expected to walk behind their teachers. Some radical Greek philosophers tested recruits by repelling them with huge demands. Teachers rarely had the means to feed their disciples. Some sages kept certain teaching for their closest disciples, and teachers sometimes explained things privately. Public opinion judged a teacher by his disciples' behavior, and teachers were held responsible for it. Rabbi was a respectful Aramaic title meaning my master, and disciple means pupil or apprentice. Jewish teachers spoke of taking on the yoke of the law and the yoke of the kingdom, submitting to God's rule and keeping his commands. Keener's notes also point to Sirach's yoke of wisdom, and Wright notes that the Pharisees spoke of the yoke of the Torah. Keener writes that one of the first rules of discipleship was "Never criticize the teacher, especially publicly". Making disciples was what rabbis did, but they made them for themselves, where Jesus' followers were to make disciples for him. Received and handed on were the words for passing on a tradition. The Mishnah tractate Abot opens with Moses receiving the Torah at Sinai and handing it on to Joshua. Students memorized what they learned so they could pass it on in turn. Disciples could call a teacher father and imitate him, which Keener calls one of the most common ideas in Greek literature.
entries.bridge: An analogy: an apprentice electrician who rides in the master's van all day. He learns by watching, he does not correct the master in front of the customer, and if he botches a job, it is the master's name on the van.
entries.changes: A disciple's life with a teacher explains the calls and costs in the Gospels: Jesus does the choosing, as in Mark 1:17, where disciples usually chose their teacher. Would-be followers meet hard demands, as in Matthew 8:19-22. Paul hands on what he received in 1 Corinthians 15:3, the language of a pupil passing on his teachers' tradition.
entries.not: **Not a trade picked for a living.** An apprentice learns a skill to earn by, usually from a master he chose. Disciples usually chose their teachers too, but Jesus did the choosing, as only radical teachers did, and his followers left nets, boats and family to walk behind a person.

usedIn.s: Jesus moves to Capernaum, Galilee of the Gentiles, announces the kingdom of heaven, calls four fishermen, and draws crowds from Galilee, the Ten Towns, Jerusalem and beyond the Jordan.

usedIn.n: Matthew 5:1-12, The Beatitudes

usedIn.n: Matthew 11:2-30, John's question, children in the square, an easy yoke
usedIn.s: John asks from prison whether Jesus is the one to come. Jesus praises John, compares his generation to sulking children, pronounces woes on the lake towns, and offers rest under his yoke.

usedIn.n: Matthew 16:13-28, The rock, the keys and the cross
usedIn.s: At Caesarea Philippi Peter confesses Jesus as the Messiah, the Son of the living God, and is called the rock and given the keys. When Jesus speaks of his death, Peter rebukes him and is called Satan.

usedIn.n: Matthew 23:1-12, Moses' seat, wide phylacteries, the best seats
usedIn.s: Jesus tells the crowds to do what the scribes and Pharisees teach but not what they do, and mocks their wide phylacteries, long tassels, best seats and love of the title rabbi.

usedIn.n: Matthew 28:16-20, Make disciples of all nations
usedIn.s: On a mountain in Galilee the risen Jesus claims all authority in heaven and on earth and sends the eleven to make disciples of all nations, baptizing and teaching them.

usedIn.n: Mark 1:14-20, Fishermen called
usedIn.s: Jesus announces that God's kingdom is near, then calls two pairs of brothers from their nets on the Sea of Galilee.

usedIn.n: Mark 4:1-34, Parables by the lake
usedIn.s: From a boat Jesus tells the crowd the sower, the lamp, the growing seed and the mustard seed, and explains them in private.

usedIn.n: Mark 7:1-23, Washed hands and the tradition of the elders
usedIn.s: Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem object that Jesus' disciples eat with unwashed hands. Jesus answers that what defiles comes from inside.

usedIn.n: Mark 8:27-9:1, Peter's answer at Caesarea Philippi
usedIn.s: Asked who he is, Peter says the Messiah. Jesus says the Son of Man must suffer, rebukes Peter, and calls followers to take up the cross.

usedIn.n: Luke 2:41-52, A twelve-year-old among the teachers
usedIn.s: On the family's yearly Passover pilgrimage the twelve-year-old Jesus stays behind in Jerusalem, and after three days his parents find him in the temple courts among the teachers.

usedIn.n: Luke 5:1-11, A catch that breaks the nets
usedIn.s: Jesus teaches from Simon's boat, then tells the tired fishermen to let down their nets in deep water. The catch nearly sinks two boats, and Simon, James and John leave everything to follow him.

usedIn.n: Luke 8:1-3, Women who paid the bills
usedIn.s: As Jesus travels from town to town with the Twelve, women he has healed travel with them, among them Joanna, wife of Herod's household manager, and they support the group from their own means.

usedIn.n: Luke 9:51-62, A Samaritan refusal and three would-be followers
usedIn.s: Setting out for Jerusalem, Jesus is turned away by a Samaritan village and rebukes James and John for wanting to call down fire. On the road he tells three would-be followers what following him will cost.

usedIn.n: Luke 10:38-42, Mary at the teacher's feet
usedIn.s: In Martha's house Mary sits at Jesus' feet listening while Martha works at serving. When Martha complains, Jesus says Mary has chosen the better part.

usedIn.n: Luke 18:18-30, A rich ruler and the needle's eye
usedIn.s: A ruler asks what he must do to inherit eternal life; told to sell everything and follow, he goes away sad, and Jesus says it is easier for a camel to go through a needle's eye than for a rich man to enter God's kingdom.

usedIn.n: John 1:35-51, Come and see
usedIn.s: Two of John's disciples follow Jesus and spend the day with him. Andrew brings his brother Simon, Philip brings Nathanael, and Jesus promises they will see heaven opened and angels going up and down on the Son of Man.

usedIn.n: John 6:22-71, The bread from heaven
usedIn.s: In the synagogue at Capernaum the crowd asks for a sign like the manna. Jesus answers that he is the bread of life come down from heaven, and his hard words about eating his flesh drive many disciples away.

usedIn.n: John 13:1-30, Washing the disciples' feet, and the morsel for Judas
usedIn.s: At supper before Passover Jesus takes off his outer clothes, ties a towel around himself and washes his disciples' feet. Then he hands Judas the dipped morsel, and Judas goes out into the night.

usedIn.n: John 15:1-17, The true vine, and friends rather than slaves
usedIn.s: Jesus calls himself the true vine and his Father the vinegrower, who cuts off fruitless branches and prunes the fruitful. He calls his disciples friends, not slaves, because he has told them everything.

usedIn.n: John 17:1-26, The prayer: your name made known
usedIn.s: Before his arrest Jesus lifts his eyes to heaven and prays that the Father will glorify him, keep those given him in the Father's name and set them apart by the truth, and make all who believe one.

usedIn.n: John 18:1-27, Arrest across the Kidron, and Annas
usedIn.s: Judas brings soldiers and temple police with torches to a garden across the Kidron. Jesus answers I am he, they fall back, and he is taken bound to Annas while Peter denies him three times by a charcoal fire.

usedIn.n: John 21:15-25, Feed my sheep, and stretch out your hands
usedIn.s: Three times Jesus asks Peter whether he loves him and three times tells him to tend his sheep. He foretells Peter's death and answers his question about the beloved disciple, whose testimony closes the book.

usedIn.n: Acts 4:1-31, Before the temple rulers
usedIn.s: The temple authorities arrest Peter and John for proclaiming the resurrection in Jesus. Before the council the unschooled fishermen speak boldly, are warned and released, and pray with the believers in the words of Psalm 2.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 1:10-17, I belong to Paul, I belong to Apollos
usedIn.s: Told by Chloe's people that the church is splitting into camps behind Paul, Apollos, Cephas and Christ, Paul appeals for unity and asks whether Christ has been divided.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 3:1-23, Milk, builders and God's temple
usedIn.s: Paul calls the Corinthians infants still on milk, says he and Apollos are only servants, warns builders that fire will test their work, and reminds the church that it is God's temple and that all things are theirs.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 4:14-21, Ten thousand guardians, one father
usedIn.s: Paul writes as the Corinthians' father in the gospel, sends Timothy to remind them of his ways, and asks whether they want him to come with a rod or with love.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 10:23-11:1, Dinner at an unbeliever's house
usedIn.s: Paul tells believers to eat whatever is sold in the meat market and whatever an unbelieving host serves without asking questions, unless someone points out that it was offered in sacrifice.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 11:2-16, Heads covered and uncovered
usedIn.s: Paul tells men who pray or prophesy to keep their heads uncovered and women who do so to cover theirs, arguing from headship, creation, the angels, nature and the custom of the churches.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 15:1-11, What I received
usedIn.s: Paul reminds the Corinthians of the good news he handed on to them as he had received it: that Christ died for sins, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to Cephas, the Twelve, more than five hundred, James, all the apostles and last of all to Paul.

usedIn.n: Galatians 1:11-24, Saul the zealot, Arabia, and fifteen days with Cephas
usedIn.s: Paul insists that his gospel came by revelation and not from human teachers, and tells of his zeal as a persecutor, his call, his time in Arabia and Damascus, and a short first visit to Jerusalem to get to know Cephas.

usedIn.n: Galatians 5:13-6:10, Flesh and Spirit, burdens and teachers
usedIn.s: Called to freedom, the Galatians are to serve one another in love, which fulfills the law; Paul sets the works of the flesh against the fruit of the Spirit and urges them to restore the fallen gently, carry each other's burdens, share with their teachers and keep doing good.

usedIn.n: Philippians 2:19-30, Timothy and Epaphroditus, commended and sent
usedIn.s: Paul commends Timothy as a son who serves with him and plans to send him soon, and sends home Epaphroditus, the church's messenger, who nearly died on their errand.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 1:1-10, Turned to God from idols
usedIn.s: Paul, Silas and Timothy thank God for a young church that received the message in the middle of suffering, whose story is now told everywhere: they turned to God from idols to serve him and to wait for his Son from heaven.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 2:1-12, Gentle as a nurse, firm as a father
usedIn.s: Paul reminds the church how he and his companions came to them after being mistreated in Philippi: no deceit, flattery or greed, gentle among them like a nursing mother, working night and day so as not to burden anyone, and urging each of them like a father.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 4:1-8, Holiness in the body
usedIn.s: Paul reminds the church of the instructions he passed on from the Lord Jesus: God's will is that they be holy, avoid sexual immorality, control their own bodies in holiness and honor, and not wrong a brother in this matter.

usedIn.n: 2 Thessalonians 2:13-3:5, Hold to the traditions, and let the word run
usedIn.s: Paul thanks God for choosing the Thessalonians, urges them to stand firm and hold to the traditions they were taught by word or by letter, prays for them, and asks them to pray that the Lord's message will run swiftly.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 4:6-16, Training for godliness, and a young leader
usedIn.s: Timothy is to train himself for godliness as an athlete trains his body, set an example despite his youth, devote himself to the public reading of Scripture and teaching, and not neglect the gift given when the elders laid hands on him.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 1:1-7, Lois, Eunice and the laying on of hands
usedIn.s: Writing from custody, Paul greets Timothy as his dear son, thanks God as he remembers him in prayer night and day, recalls the faith of Timothy's grandmother Lois and mother Eunice, and urges him to fan into flame the gift given when Paul laid hands on him.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 2:1-13, Soldier, athlete and farmer, and a prisoner in chains
usedIn.s: Timothy is to pass on what he heard to reliable people who will teach others, and to endure hardship like a soldier, compete by the rules like an athlete and work like a farmer, remembering Jesus Christ, raised from the dead and descended from David, for whom Paul is chained like a criminal.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 3:10-17, Antioch, Iconium and Lystra, and the sacred writings
usedIn.s: Timothy has followed Paul's teaching, life and sufferings, as in Antioch, Iconium and Lystra; he is to continue in what he learned, knowing from whom he learned it and how from infancy he has known the sacred writings, for all Scripture is God-breathed.

usedIn.n: Philemon 8-25, Onesimus sent home with a letter
usedIn.s: Paul appeals to Philemon, on the basis of love, for Onesimus, the slave who became Paul's son in prison: he sends him back to be received as a beloved brother rather than as a slave, asks Philemon to welcome him as he would Paul, offers to repay anything he owes, and asks for a guest room.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 5:11-6:12, Milk, solid food and no way back
usedIn.s: The readers should be teachers by now but still need milk, so the writer urges them past the elementary teachings. Those who have been enlightened and shared in the Holy Spirit and then fall away cannot be brought back to repentance, though he is confident of better things for his readers.

usedIn.n: 1 John 1:5-2:17, God is light, an advocate, and a world passing away
usedIn.s: God is light with no darkness in him, so to claim fellowship with him while walking in darkness is a lie; the blood of Jesus cleanses, and those who confess are forgiven. Anyone who sins has an advocate with the Father, the atoning sacrifice for the whole world. The old command of love is new, the darkness is passing, and the world is passing away.

usedIn.n: 2 John 1-6, The elder to the chosen lady
usedIn.s: The elder writes to the chosen lady and her children, whom he loves in the truth. He is glad that some of her children walk in the truth, and he asks for no new command but the old one, that they love one another, which means walking in God's commands.

usedIn.n: 3 John 1-8, Gaius and the traveling brothers
usedIn.s: The elder writes to his dear friend Gaius, praying that he is in good health and glad to hear that he walks in the truth. Gaius has been faithful in what he does for the brothers, strangers though they are; he should supply them for the next stage of their journey in a way that honors God, since they went out for the sake of the Name and took nothing from the pagans.

entries.title: The Twelve
entries.summary: Jesus chose twelve men to be with him and to be sent out. The number matched Israel's twelve tribes.
entries.plain: **The new team had exactly as many seats as there were founding families.** Twelve was Israel's number: twelve tribes, from Jacob's twelve sons. By choosing twelve, Jesus made a statement before he said a word.
entries.then: Twelve was the sacred number of Israel's tribes. Groups who saw themselves as a remnant or renewal of Israel could signal it by choosing twelve leaders, as in the Dead Sea Scrolls (1QS 8.1-2). Wright says every Jew knew there had been twelve tribes. Ten had been lost when the Assyrians carried them off seven centuries before, and the prophets had promised a restoration. When Jesus set twelve apart, nobody could miss the point. Groups were sometimes named for their original number and kept the name, and Matthias replaced Judas to keep the symbol whole. The Twelve had a double task, to be with him and to be sent out, and probably stood for the tribes. Apostle means one who is sent: a commissioned agent who acted on the full authority of the sender within his commission. By the Jewish principle of agency, receiving the agent meant receiving the sender. Heiser reads the twelve as one for each tribe of the people God kept as his own portion. By the first century the tribes no longer existed as separate bodies. Only Judah, Benjamin and Levi were still recognized as ancestors, so the twelve tribes sealed in Revelation 7 draw on the Jewish hope that Israel would be restored.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a new government that names one minister for each of the nation's original provinces. The number is a claim about who the government thinks it is.
entries.changes: Twelve chosen followers signal a renewed Israel, as in Mark 3:14, and when they are sent out as agents they carry Jesus' own authority, as in Matthew 10:40. In Acts 1:26 Judas' place is filled to keep the number whole.
entries.not: **Not ministers over provinces that still existed.** Ten of the twelve tribes had been lost for seven centuries, so twelve men pointed to a promised restoration, not a present map. The Twelve were also chosen to be with Jesus and to be sent out, and a list with fishermen, a tax collector and a Zealot shows the number mattered more than skills.

usedIn.n: Mark 14:12-31, The Passover meal
usedIn.s: Jesus eats the Passover with the Twelve, names a betrayer at the table, gives the bread and the cup new meaning, and warns that all will scatter.
