usedIn.s: At the last supper the disciples argue over who is greatest. Jesus contrasts kings who are called benefactors with himself as one who serves, promises them thrones, warns Peter that Satan has asked to sift them, and speaks of swords.

usedIn.n: Acts 1:12-26, The Twelve made whole by lot
usedIn.s: Back in Jerusalem the apostles pray in an upstairs room with the women and Jesus' family. Peter says Judas's place must be filled, and the lot falls on Matthias.

usedIn.n: Acts 6:1-7, The Hellenists' widows and the Seven
usedIn.s: Greek-speaking believers complain that their widows are overlooked in the daily distribution of food. The Twelve have the community choose seven men, and lay hands on them.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 15:1-11, What I received
usedIn.s: Paul reminds the Corinthians of the good news he handed on to them as he had received it: that Christ died for sins, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to Cephas, the Twelve, more than five hundred, James, all the apostles and last of all to Paul.

usedIn.n: Revelation 7:1-17, the sealing of the 144,000 and the crowd in white
usedIn.s: Four angels hold back the winds until God's servants are sealed on their foreheads, 144,000 from the tribes of Israel. Then John sees a crowd no one can count, from every nation, in white robes with palm branches, who have come out of the great tribulation and whom the Lamb will shepherd.

usedIn.n: Revelation 21:9-27, the city of gold and twelve stones
usedIn.s: An angel carries John to a high mountain to show him the bride, the holy city Jerusalem, shining with God's glory, with twelve gates named for Israel's tribes and twelve foundations named for the Lamb's apostles. The city is a cube of pure gold, its foundations set with twelve precious stones and its gates each a single pearl; it has no temple, since God and the Lamb are its temple, and its gates never shut as the nations bring their glory into it.

entries.title: Teachers of the law
entries.summary: Trained experts in the law of Moses, also called scribes, some local and some from Jerusalem, who taught by citing earlier teachers.
entries.plain: **The lawyers from the capital came down to hear what the country preacher was saying.** Few people could write well. Scribes drew up documents, and the top ones were experts in God's law. They taught by quoting the rulings of experts before them.
entries.then: In a world where many could not write, scribes drew up contracts for business and marriage. Many were therefore legal experts and quite possibly Pharisees, though a scribe could hold various views (Wright's glossary). Many villages had scribes who wrote legal documents, and the scribes at the top were probably teachers of the law. Jerusalem was home to most Pharisees and many teachers. They often cited the opinions of earlier teachers. The ESV Study Bible suggests the scribes of Mark 1:22 may have been local, pious, literate men who taught in synagogues. The higher-ranking scribes of 3:22 came down from Jerusalem. Judging from later rabbis, teachers of the law were skilled in argument. The scribes Herod consulted were experts in the law, and most of them were also teachers. Parts of Palestinian Judaism had standards for accredited teachers, but Keener notes that nothing in law stopped anyone from claiming to teach the Bible.
entries.bridge: An analogy: legal scholars who settle a question by citing precedent. A ruling carries weight because of the earlier rulings stacked behind it.
entries.changes: Scribes were the experts in Scripture, so the chief priests and scribes can name Bethlehem from Micah, as in Matthew 2:4-6. A teacher who spoke on his own authority without citing earlier teachers, as in Mark 1:22, stood out at once. In Acts 23:9 scribes of the Pharisees' party take Paul's side.
entries.not: **Not secular lawyers.** The law they studied was the law of Moses, God's law, so a legal expert was also a religious teacher.

usedIn.n: Luke 2:41-52, A twelve-year-old among the teachers
usedIn.s: On the family's yearly Passover pilgrimage the twelve-year-old Jesus stays behind in Jerusalem, and after three days his parents find him in the temple courts among the teachers.

usedIn.s: A lawyer asks what he must do to inherit eternal life and then who his neighbor is. Jesus tells of a man left half dead on the road to Jericho, passed by a priest and a Levite and rescued by a Samaritan.

usedIn.s: Jesus warns against teachers of the law who love long robes and the best seats and devour widows' houses. Then he watches a poor widow put two small coins into the temple treasury.

usedIn.s: A wife is bound to her husband only while he lives, and believers have died to the law to belong to Christ. Then Paul describes a divided self that knows the good and cannot do it.

usedIn.s: Paul greets Timothy, whom he left in Ephesus, and tells him to stop certain people teaching strange doctrines and spending themselves on myths and endless genealogies; they want to be teachers of the law without understanding it, while the law is meant for the lawless.

entries.title: The Pharisees
entries.summary: A mostly lay movement devoted to careful keeping of the law and of oral tradition, respected by the people and watchful of new teachers.
aliases: a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees
as for the law, a Pharisee
entries.plain: **The strictest members of the club noticed who the new man was eating with.** Pharisees wanted Israel to live by God's law in daily life: food, tithes, washing, the Sabbath. They followed traditions passed down from earlier teachers, and they kept an eye on anyone who claimed to speak for God.
entries.then: The Pharisees were an unofficial but powerful pressure group, largely led by laymen. Their aim was to purify Israel through stricter keeping of the law, and they had their own traditions about how to apply Scripture. In public life they championed the ancestral customs and led the way in revolts (Wright). In Jesus' day there were two schools, the stricter Shammai and the more lenient Hillel. They were known for meticulous interpretation of the law, care at meals such as tithing all food, faithful keeping of oral tradition, and special care about washing hands. They were popular with the people, though Jesus was more so. They normally lacked the political power to act against Jesus, unlike the Sadducees of Jerusalem. Many were nationalists, which is why working with the Herodians was unusual. In Jesus' generation they were also debating the grounds for divorce. Keener calls them the most respected religious people of the day, who stressed the right intention of the heart. He says the modern picture of them as legalists trivializes their piety. Gamaliel I, the most prominent Pharisee of his day and Saul's teacher, belonged to the school of Hillel and was later honored as Rabban. Pharisees valued the traditions of their fathers, so Paul's traditions of my fathers probably means Pharisaic tradition. They seem to have lived only in the Holy Land, concentrated around Jerusalem. Josephus calls them those "esteemed most skillful in the exact explication of their laws".
entries.bridge: An analogy: a devout reform movement that asks ordinary members to keep the rules usually kept by monks. Many admire it, and it watches public figures closely to see if they measure up.
entries.changes: Pharisees watched public teachers closely on food, purity, the Sabbath and tithes, so their questions, as in Mark 2:16, come from shared concerns. Their standing for piety made Jesus' demand that his followers exceed them, in Matthew 5:20, a shock. Paul calls himself a Pharisee in Philippians 3:5.
entries.not: **Not a movement inside a church.** The Pharisees were a lay pressure group with no official office, and their piety had a political edge: many were nationalists, and some led revolts. Later rabbis still remembered them as the godliest people one could meet, so the Gospels' conflicts are not a portrait of the whole movement.
entries.dissent: What the quarrel was about. Wright argues that Jesus' debates with the Pharisees were at least as much about agenda and policy, his opposition to their separatist nationalism, as about details of piety. Keener's notes frame the disputes mainly as questions of law and tradition: Sabbath, tithing, washing, divorce.

usedIn.n: Matthew 12:1-14, Grain on the Sabbath, a withered hand
usedIn.s: Pharisees object when the disciples pick grain on the Sabbath. Jesus answers with David, the priests in the temple and mercy, then heals a withered hand in the synagogue.

usedIn.n: Matthew 19:1-15, Any and every reason, and the children
usedIn.s: Pharisees ask whether a man may divorce his wife for any and every reason. Jesus answers from creation, the disciples wonder whether it is better not to marry, and children are brought for his blessing.

usedIn.n: Matthew 22:15-22, Caesar's coin
usedIn.s: Pharisees and Herodians ask Jesus whether it is lawful to pay the poll tax to Caesar. He asks for the coin, asks whose image is on it, and tells them to give Caesar and God what is theirs.

usedIn.n: Matthew 23:1-12, Moses' seat, wide phylacteries, the best seats
usedIn.s: Jesus tells the crowds to do what the scribes and Pharisees teach but not what they do, and mocks their wide phylacteries, long tassels, best seats and love of the title rabbi.

usedIn.n: Matthew 23:13-28, Oaths, mint, gnats and whitewashed tombs
usedIn.s: Jesus pronounces woes on the scribes and Pharisees: they shut the kingdom, play games with oaths, tithe herbs while neglecting justice, strain gnats and swallow camels, and look clean outside like whitewashed tombs.

usedIn.n: Mark 2:13-22, Levi and the party
usedIn.s: Jesus calls a tax collector from his booth and eats with tax collectors and sinners. He is questioned about eating with them and about not fasting.

usedIn.n: Mark 2:23-3:6, Grain and a withered hand on the Sabbath
usedIn.s: Jesus defends his disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath, heals a man's hand in the synagogue, and the Pharisees start plotting with the Herodians.

usedIn.n: Mark 7:1-23, Washed hands and the tradition of the elders
usedIn.s: Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem object that Jesus' disciples eat with unwashed hands. Jesus answers that what defiles comes from inside.

usedIn.n: Mark 12:13-17, The coin with Caesar's face
usedIn.s: Pharisees and Herodians ask whether it is right to pay tax to Caesar. Jesus asks for a coin and asks whose image is on it.

usedIn.n: Luke 7:36-50, A sinful woman at Simon's table
usedIn.s: At a Pharisee's banquet a woman known as a sinner weeps over Jesus' feet, wipes them with her hair and anoints them. Jesus answers his host's silent objection with a story of two debtors.

usedIn.n: Luke 11:37-54, Woes at a Pharisee's table
usedIn.s: At a Pharisee's meal Jesus does not wash before eating, and when his host is surprised he pronounces woes on Pharisees and lawyers: clean cups and greedy hearts, tithed herbs, the best seats, unmarked graves and the tombs of the prophets.

usedIn.n: Luke 18:9-14, Two men go up to the temple to pray
usedIn.s: Jesus tells of a Pharisee who thanks God that he is not like other people and a tax collector who stands far off, beats his breast and asks for mercy. The tax collector goes home justified.

usedIn.n: John 3:1-21, Born from above
usedIn.s: Nicodemus, a Pharisee and ruler, comes to Jesus at night. Jesus tells him that no one sees God's kingdom without being born from above, of water and Spirit, and speaks of the Son of Man lifted up like the serpent in the wilderness.

usedIn.n: John 7:37-52, Rivers of living water on the last day
usedIn.s: On the great last day of the feast Jesus cries out that the thirsty should come to him and drink. The crowd divides over whether he is the Prophet or the Messiah, and the Pharisees scorn a prophet from Galilee.

usedIn.n: John 9:1-41, A man born blind is put out
usedIn.s: Jesus puts mud on a blind beggar's eyes and sends him to wash in Siloam. Because it is the Sabbath the man is questioned, his parents are afraid, and when he defends Jesus he is thrown out.

usedIn.n: John 10:1-21, The good shepherd and the hired hand
usedIn.s: Jesus contrasts the shepherd who enters by the gate, calls his sheep by name and lays down his life for them with thieves who climb in another way and a hired hand who runs from the wolf.

usedIn.n: Acts 5:12-42, Peter's shadow, the prison and Gamaliel
usedIn.s: Crowds bring the sick for Peter's shadow to fall on them. The apostles are jailed, freed by an angel, and brought before the council, where Gamaliel compares the movement to the failed causes of Theudas and Judas the Galilean.

usedIn.n: Acts 15:1-21, The council in Jerusalem
usedIn.s: Teachers from Judea insist that Gentile believers must be circumcised to be saved. The apostles and elders meet in Jerusalem; Peter and James argue that God has accepted Gentiles as they are, and James proposes a few rules for them to keep.

usedIn.n: Acts 22:30-23:11, Paul before the council
usedIn.s: The tribune brings Paul before the chief priests and the council. Struck on the high priest's order, Paul calls him a whitewashed wall, then declares himself a Pharisee on trial for the hope of the resurrection, and the council splits.

usedIn.n: Galatians 1:11-24, Saul the zealot, Arabia, and fifteen days with Cephas
usedIn.s: Paul insists that his gospel came by revelation and not from human teachers, and tells of his zeal as a persecutor, his call, his time in Arabia and Damascus, and a short first visit to Jerusalem to get to know Cephas.

usedIn.n: Philippians 3:1-11, Dogs, mutilators, and a pedigree counted as loss
usedIn.s: Paul warns against teachers who press circumcision, calling them dogs and mutilators, lists his own credentials as a born Jew, a Pharisee and a zealous persecutor, and counts them all loss for the sake of knowing Christ.

entries.title: Chief priests, elders and the council
entries.summary: The Jerusalem aristocracy of priestly families and elders who ran the temple and the Sanhedrin and dealt with Rome.
entries.plain: **The old families who run the capital do not like a stranger telling them how to run it.** The high priest and the leading priestly families controlled the temple. With the elders and the teachers of the law they made up the council in Jerusalem, the highest Jewish court.
entries.then: The elders, chief priests and teachers of the law together presumably made up the Sanhedrin, Jerusalem's municipal senate. Keener notes that these aristocrats stood closer in outlook to the Greek and Roman upper class than to Galilean peasants. Any challenge to legal temple practice was a challenge to the priests who ran it, and unlike the Pharisees they held real political power. By this period every member of the high-priestly families could be called a chief priest. A Roman governor appointed Caiaphas, who kept the office from AD 18 to 36. Josephus, the Pharisees and the Essenes all report abuse of power by the priestly aristocracy. Meeting for a legal decision in the high priest's home broke accepted legal ethics. Keener holds that only Rome could execute, so they had to hand Jesus to the governor. Wright's glossary identifies the Sadducees as Jerusalem's aristocracy, including most leading priestly families, who denied the resurrection. Where Pharisees opposed hasty executions, the Sadducees had a name for punishing harshly and often quickly. Josephus says Herod named high priests at will, and "Archelaus also, Herod's son, did like his father in the appointment of the high priests, as did the Romans also" (Antiquities 20.10). From Herod to the fall of the temple there were twenty-eight of them. Later Agrippa II also installed and deposed them. Herod the Great had purged the council and filled it with supporters, whose descendants dominated it through the New Testament period. The captain of the temple, the sagan, commanded the Levite temple police and ranked next to the high priest.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a few old-money families who hold the top offices of a city under a colonial governor. They keep order, they keep their seats, and they decide who gets handed over.
entries.changes: The priestly aristocracy held real power in Jerusalem and dealt with Rome, so their moves against Jesus, as in Mark 14:1, were politics as well as religion. Their scholars could answer Herod's question about the Messiah's birthplace in Matthew 2:4-5 and still not go. In Acts 4:5-6 the same families confront the apostles.
entries.not: **Not a secular city council.** Their power came from running the temple, so a challenge to its practice was a challenge to them. The office itself was in foreign hands, since Herod and then Rome appointed and deposed high priests at will. Nor were they the people as a whole; Keener notes they feared the crowds who favored Jesus.
entries.dissent: Could the council put anyone to death? Keener and his notes say only Rome could. Garland agrees, citing the Jerusalem Talmud's tradition that the right to try capital cases was withdrawn forty years before the temple fell. The cultural backgrounds article on Herod's successors says the Jewish leadership seems to have kept that power in purely religious cases, especially those touching the temple's sanctity. It adds that Rome kept the high priest's vestments in its own custody. Strauss, in the same commentary as Garland, cites Josephus: the high priest Ananus was deposed for having James, Jesus' brother, put to death between two Roman governors. Strauss takes this to confirm that the council lacked that power.

usedIn.n: Matthew 2:1-12, Magi at Herod's court
usedIn.s: Magi from the east arrive in Jerusalem asking for the newborn king of the Jews. Herod consults his scholars, sends the visitors to Bethlehem, and they go home another way.

usedIn.n: Matthew 21:12-22, Tables, the blind and the lame, and a fig tree
usedIn.s: Jesus drives out the sellers and overturns the money changers' tables, heals the blind and the lame in the temple courts, and the next morning curses a leafy fig tree that withers at once.

usedIn.n: Matthew 21:23-46, By what authority, two sons and the tenants
usedIn.s: The chief priests and elders demand to know Jesus' authority. He answers with a question about John, then with two parables: a son who says no and goes, and tenants who kill the owner's son.

usedIn.n: Matthew 22:23-33, Seven brothers and one bride
usedIn.s: Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, pose a riddle about a woman married in turn to seven brothers. Jesus answers that the raised do not marry, and that God is the God of the living.

usedIn.n: Matthew 26:1-16, Perfume at Bethany and thirty pieces of silver
usedIn.s: The chief priests meet at Caiaphas's house to plot Jesus' arrest away from the festival crowds. At Bethany a woman pours costly perfume on his head, and Judas sells him for thirty pieces of silver.

usedIn.n: Matthew 26:47-75, Arrest, twelve legions, the council and the rooster
usedIn.s: Judas comes with an armed crowd and a kiss. Jesus refuses the sword and the twelve legions of angels, is tried at night before Caiaphas, and is condemned for blasphemy while Peter swears he never knew him.

usedIn.n: Matthew 27:1-26, Blood money, Pilate and Barabbas
usedIn.s: At dawn the council hands Jesus to Pilate. Judas returns the silver and hangs himself, the priests buy a potter's field, and Pilate, warned by his wife's dream, releases Barabbas and washes his hands.

usedIn.n: Matthew 27:57-66, Joseph's tomb and the sealed stone
usedIn.s: Joseph of Arimathea, a rich disciple, asks Pilate for the body and lays it in his own new tomb. The next day the chief priests get a guard and a seal on the stone.

usedIn.n: Mark 10:32-45, James and John ask for the best seats
usedIn.s: On the road to Jerusalem Jesus predicts his death a third time. James and John ask to sit at his right and left, and he tells them the first must be slave of all.

usedIn.n: Mark 11:12-25, The fig tree and the temple
usedIn.s: Jesus curses a leafy fig tree with no fruit, overturns the tables in the temple, and the next morning the tree has withered.

usedIn.n: Mark 14:32-52, Gethsemane and the arrest
usedIn.s: At a place called Gethsemane Jesus prays in anguish while three disciples sleep. Judas arrives with an armed crowd from the chief priests, greets him with a kiss, and the disciples run.

usedIn.n: Mark 14:53-72, At the high priest's house
usedIn.s: The council tries Jesus at night. He says he is the Messiah and quotes the Son of Man coming with the clouds, and is condemned for blasphemy while Peter denies him in the courtyard.

usedIn.n: Luke 19:28-48, The king rides down to the city and weeps over it
usedIn.s: Jesus rides a borrowed colt down the Mount of Olives while his disciples spread their cloaks and praise the king who comes. Seeing the city, he weeps over the siege to come, then drives the sellers out of the temple.

usedIn.n: Luke 20:9-19, The tenants who killed the heir
usedIn.s: Jesus tells of a vineyard owner whose tenants beat his servants and kill his beloved son to take the inheritance. The leaders realize he has told it against them.

usedIn.n: Luke 20:20-26, Caesar's coin
usedIn.s: Spies sent by the leaders ask Jesus whether it is right to pay tribute to Caesar, hoping to hand him over to the governor. He asks whose image is on a denarius.

usedIn.n: Luke 20:27-40, The Sadducees and the woman with seven husbands
usedIn.s: Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, ask whose wife a woman married to seven brothers will be. Jesus answers that the risen do not marry and are like the angels, and argues from the burning bush.

usedIn.n: John 7:1-36, Up to the Festival of Tabernacles
usedIn.s: Jesus stays in Galilee while the Judeans look for a chance to kill him, then goes up to Tabernacles privately and teaches in the temple. The crowds argue over whether he is a deceiver or the Messiah, and the chief priests send guards to arrest him.

usedIn.n: John 10:1-21, The good shepherd and the hired hand
usedIn.s: Jesus contrasts the shepherd who enters by the gate, calls his sheep by name and lays down his life for them with thieves who climb in another way and a hired hand who runs from the wolf.

usedIn.n: John 11:45-57, Caiaphas: one man for the nation
usedIn.s: After the raising of Lazarus the chief priests and Pharisees call a council, afraid the Romans will take away their place and their nation. Caiaphas tells them it is better for one man to die for the people.

usedIn.n: John 18:1-27, Arrest across the Kidron, and Annas
usedIn.s: Judas brings soldiers and temple police with torches to a garden across the Kidron. Jesus answers I am he, they fall back, and he is taken bound to Annas while Peter denies him three times by a charcoal fire.

usedIn.n: John 19:1-16, Flogged, mocked, and no friend of Caesar
usedIn.s: Pilate has Jesus flogged, the soldiers crown him with thorns and hail him as king, and Pilate shows him to the crowd. Warned that releasing him makes Pilate no friend of Caesar, he sits on the judgment seat at the Stone Pavement and hands him over.

usedIn.n: Acts 4:1-31, Before the temple rulers
usedIn.s: The temple authorities arrest Peter and John for proclaiming the resurrection in Jesus. Before the council the unschooled fishermen speak boldly, are warned and released, and pray with the believers in the words of Psalm 2.

usedIn.n: Acts 5:12-42, Peter's shadow, the prison and Gamaliel
usedIn.s: Crowds bring the sick for Peter's shadow to fall on them. The apostles are jailed, freed by an angel, and brought before the council, where Gamaliel compares the movement to the failed causes of Theudas and Judas the Galilean.

usedIn.n: Acts 9:1-31, Saul on the Damascus road
usedIn.s: Carrying the high priest's letters to the synagogues of Damascus, Saul is stopped by a light and a voice. Blinded, healed and baptized, the persecutor begins to proclaim Jesus and has to escape over the city wall.

usedIn.n: Acts 22:30-23:11, Paul before the council
usedIn.s: The tribune brings Paul before the chief priests and the council. Struck on the high priest's order, Paul calls him a whitewashed wall, then declares himself a Pharisee on trial for the hope of the resurrection, and the council splits.

usedIn.n: Acts 25:1-12, Festus and the appeal to Caesar
usedIn.s: The new governor Festus hears the case again at Caesarea. When he asks whether Paul will be tried in Jerusalem, Paul appeals to Caesar, and after conferring with his council Festus grants it.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 4:14-5:10, A high priest who can sympathize
usedIn.s: Jesus is a great high priest who has passed through the heavens and was tested in every way, yet without sin, so his people can approach the throne of grace with confidence. Like every high priest he was appointed by God, not self-chosen, and God named him a priest for ever in the order of Melchizedek.

usedIn.n: James 4:13-5:6, Merchants, landowners and the wages that cry out
usedIn.s: James rebukes traders who plan a year of business without God, then turns on rich landowners whose hoarded wealth is rotting, whose withheld wages cry out to the Lord of hosts, and who have fattened themselves for a day of slaughter and condemned the righteous one.

entries.title: Magi and the star
entries.summary: Eastern astrologers and dream readers, respected across the empire for reading the sky. A star that meant a new king meant danger for the old one.
entries.plain: **The visitors from the east said the sky had announced a new king, and the old king did not sleep that night.** Magi were a priestly class from the east who read the stars and interpreted dreams. People across the Roman world took astrology seriously and believed the heavens could announce the birth or death of rulers. Israel's Scriptures forbade it.
entries.then: The Greek Old Testament uses the word magi only in Daniel, for the king's experts. By this period the term covered astrology, dream interpretation, the study of sacred writings and magic. Keener calls the magi pagan astrologers whose skills were widely respected, since everyone agreed the East produced the finest astrologers. The Old Testament forbade such prediction from signs (Deuteronomy 18). The ancients thought comets and falling stars foretold the fall of rulers. Nero reportedly killed nobles so that a comet's omen would fall on them and not on him. Greeks thought magi especially skilled at reading dreams. Astronomers and astrologers were then the same people, who expected events in the sky to mirror events on earth. Heiser points out that in 1 Enoch the Watchers taught the signs of the stars, and reads the magi as practitioners of those arts who now come to worship.
entries.bridge: An analogy: foreign intelligence analysts arriving at a palace to ask where the new heir has been born. They mean no harm, but the question itself is treason in that room.
entries.changes: Because rulers feared astrological signs of their end, the question of the magi in Matthew 2:2 alarms Herod and all Jerusalem with him. Gentiles skilled in forbidden arts come to honor Israel's king, while Herod's scholars know the text and stay home. The same word names the sorcerer Bar-Jesus in Acts 13:6, which shows how the word could also be heard.
entries.not: **Not analysts working from reports.** The magi read the sky, and nearly everyone then believed the stars could announce the rise or fall of a ruler, which is why their question frightened a king. Their arts were ones Israel's Scriptures forbade. Matthew gives them no number and no crowns.
entries.dissent: Two questions. First, where they came from. Keener's notes, the CSB Study Bible and the ESV Study Bible say Persia or Babylon. Bailey says Arabia, on the evidence of the gifts and early Christian writers. Second, what the star was. Wright mentions the conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn three times in 7 BC. Heiser, following others, argues for signs involving Jupiter and Regulus with a birth on 11 September 3 BC. Keener and the study Bibles leave it open among a comet, a nova and other suggestions. Wilkins sets out a conjunction of 7 BC, a nova of 5 BC, a supernatural light and an angel. Carson, Moo and Morris think no identification certain, and doubt that a star which went ahead and stopped was a natural phenomenon.

usedIn.n: Matthew 2:1-12, Magi at Herod's court
usedIn.s: Magi from the east arrive in Jerusalem asking for the newborn king of the Jews. Herod consults his scholars, sends the visitors to Bethlehem, and they go home another way.

entries.title: The Samaritans
entries.summary: The people of the hill country between Judea and Galilee worshiped Israel's God on Mount Gerizim, not in Jerusalem. Jews and Samaritans each claimed to be the true heirs of Israel, and centuries of hostility lay between them.
entries.plain: **Two neighboring towns, both sure they kept the old faith properly, both still telling stories about what the other side did.** The Samaritans lived between Galilee and Judea. They worshiped the same God and kept the law of Moses, but they held that Mount Gerizim, not Jerusalem, was the place to worship him. Jews thought them half-foreign and wrong. Samaritans resented Jerusalem. Galilean pilgrims passing through their country could meet insults and sometimes violence.
entries.then: The Samaritans worshiped Israel's one God. They rejected Israel's history after Joshua and wrote worship on Mount Gerizim into the Ten Commandments. Josephus tells how the Jewish ruler Hyrcanus took Shechem and Gerizim, with the Samaritans' temple, which "was now deserted two hundred years after it was built". Keener says John Hyrcanus destroyed it. While Coponius governed Judea, Josephus reports, some Samaritans "came privately into Jerusalem, and threw about dead men's bodies, in the cloisters" during Passover. They were shut out of the temple afterward. Galileans traveled through Samaria to the festivals, and under the governor Cumanus the villagers of Ginea killed Galilean pilgrims (Josephus). Each side circulated stories of the other's atrocities. Violence was the exception, Keener notes, but the writings of both are hostile. Jewish tradition held a Samaritan woman to be continually unclean, so a Jew who drank from her vessel would be defiled. Wright says each side held that it alone inherited what God promised Abraham and Moses, and so owned the land by right. Jews counted Samaritans half-breeds and false worshipers. Blomberg, citing Martina Böhm, notes that the two main differences were where to worship and how. Herod rebuilt the old capital as a Greek city named Sebaste for Augustus, while the Samaritans lived in the countryside around Shechem. They awaited a restorer like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15-18), and Josephus tells of a false prophet who drew them after him. Magen's excavations on Mount Gerizim found a sacred precinct with an altar and burned bones. It was first built in the Persian period on the pattern of Jerusalem's (Price and House).
entries.bridge: An analogy: two churches that split generations ago, each with its own building on its own hill, each sure it is the true one. They share a Bible and a history, and their members still cross the street to avoid each other.
entries.changes: A Samaritan village refusing pilgrims bound for Jerusalem, as in Luke 9:52-53, acts out an old quarrel over where God should be worshiped, and a Samaritan hero in a story told to Jews turns the expected ranking upside down. In John 4:9 a Samaritan woman is surprised that a Jew asks her for a drink. In Acts 8:5 the message goes to a city of Samaria.
entries.not: **Not two churches with the same Bible.** The Samaritans rejected Israel's history after Joshua and wrote worship on Mount Gerizim into their Ten Commandments. The quarrel had blood in it too: a Jewish ruler destroyed their temple, and pilgrims were killed on the road. Still, they were neither foreigners nor pagans; they worshiped Israel's God.
entries.dissent: Which road the Galilean pilgrims took. Josephus says it was the custom of the Galileans to travel through Samaria to the festivals. Keener's notes say pilgrims often took that short route, though some went around. Wright says most pilgrims preferred to go down the Jordan valley to Jericho and up to Jerusalem, as safer. Bailey goes further, writing that "Pious Jews usually traveled around Samaria to avoid defilement." Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary, and the Zondervan atlas side with Josephus. For them the road through Samaria was the usual one, three days at the least, since the way through Perea meant passing through Gentile territory, though some went around.

usedIn.n: Luke 9:51-62, A Samaritan refusal and three would-be followers
usedIn.s: Setting out for Jerusalem, Jesus is turned away by a Samaritan village and rebukes James and John for wanting to call down fire. On the road he tells three would-be followers what following him will cost.

usedIn.n: Luke 10:25-37, The Samaritan on the Jericho road
usedIn.s: A lawyer asks what he must do to inherit eternal life and then who his neighbor is. Jesus tells of a man left half dead on the road to Jericho, passed by a priest and a Levite and rescued by a Samaritan.

usedIn.n: Luke 17:11-19, Ten lepers and the Samaritan who came back
usedIn.s: On the border between Samaria and Galilee ten men with leprosy call to Jesus from a distance. He sends them to the priests, they are cleansed on the way, and only one, a Samaritan, comes back to thank him.

usedIn.n: John 4:1-42, A Samaritan woman at Jacob's well
usedIn.s: Tired at noon, Jesus sits on Jacob's well and asks a Samaritan woman for a drink. They talk about living water, her husbands and the right mountain for worship, and her town comes out to meet him.

usedIn.n: John 8:31-59, Abraham's children, and before Abraham, I am
usedIn.s: Jesus tells Judeans who had believed him that the truth will make them free. They answer that they are Abraham's children and were never slaves, and the argument ends with Jesus saying before Abraham was, I am, and stones in their hands.

usedIn.n: Acts 8:4-25, Samaria and Simon the magician
usedIn.s: Philip preaches the Messiah in Samaria, and even the famous magician Simon is baptized. When Peter and John lay hands on the Samaritans and they receive the Spirit, Simon offers money for the power.

entries.title: Converts and God-fearers
entries.summary: Gentiles drawn to Israel's God stood at two distances. Converts took on the whole law, circumcision included, and became Jews. God-fearers worshiped Israel's God, gave to the synagogue and kept some customs, but did not convert.
entries.plain: **He came to the services, paid for the new roof and knew the prayers, but he never formally joined.** Some Gentiles in the Roman world admired the Jewish faith. A few went all the way and became Jews, with circumcision for men. Many more stopped short: they worshiped Israel's God, came to the synagogue, gave generously and kept some of the customs, but did not convert. Jews respected them, but they were still Gentiles.
entries.then: Non-Jews who feared God and gave large sums to the Jewish community were well respected. Gentile benefactors of synagogues were much more common in the Diaspora than in the land. Such a man was not a full convert, so in Jewish eyes his home kept some of a Gentile's uncleanness, especially in its food. A Jewish teacher would not normally enter it. God-fearers were Gentiles who worshiped Israel's God and were attached in some way to a synagogue without submitting to conversion, above all circumcision. The ESV Study Bible warns that the phrase cannot be shown to carry this special sense as early as the Psalms. They respected Jewish ways, food laws and holy days among them. They stopped short of becoming proselytes because that meant circumcision and other rites (the CSB Study Bible). Josephus, explaining the temple's wealth, says that "all the Jews throughout the habitable earth, and those that worshipped God" sent contributions to it. Wright pictures the centurion of Luke 7 as an outsider peering in at Israel and its God, and liking the view. The Greeks who came to worship at the Passover in John 12:20 were probably God-fearers not yet converted, though Keener allows they could be Greek-speaking Jews. Prominent women were often drawn to Judaism, which did not require circumcision of them. A convert was bound to keep the whole law, 613 commandments by rabbinic count. Josephus shows Jews divided. King Izates of Adiabene was told by his teacher Ananias that he "might worship God without being circumcised". But a Galilean named Eleazar asked him, "How long wilt thou continue uncircumcised?" and the king was circumcised.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a longtime supporter of a club who comes to every match and pays for the new stand but never takes out membership. Everyone knows and values him; in the members' room he is still a guest.
entries.changes: A Gentile who built a synagogue, as in Luke 7:5, belonged to this circle, which is why Jewish elders plead for him and why Jesus coming under his roof was a question. Acts 10:2 calls Cornelius a devout man who feared God, and the Greeks who come up to worship at the feast in John 12:20 are read the same way.
entries.not: **Not a membership form left unsigned.** Joining meant circumcision for a man and keeping the whole law, and that cost kept many admirers outside. Short of it, a God-fearer's house still counted as Gentile, so a Jewish teacher would not normally go under his roof.

usedIn.s: A God-fearing Roman centurion in Caesarea is told in a vision to send for Peter. At noon on a Joppa rooftop Peter sees a sheet full of unclean animals and hears a voice tell him to eat.

usedIn.s: Peter enters a Gentile home, preaches Jesus, and sees the Spirit fall on the uncircumcised listeners. In Jerusalem he is criticized for eating with Gentiles, and his account silences the critics.

usedIn.s: Invited to speak after the synagogue readings in a Roman colony, Paul tells Israel's story from the exodus to Jesus. Gentiles welcome the message, and the city's leading men and women drive the apostles out.

usedIn.s: Teachers from Judea insist that Gentile believers must be circumcised to be saved. The apostles and elders meet in Jerusalem; Peter and James argue that God has accepted Gentiles as they are, and James proposes a few rules for them to keep.

usedIn.n: Acts 16:11-15, Lydia at the place of prayer
usedIn.s: In Philippi, a Roman colony, Paul finds women gathered by the river on the Sabbath. Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth from Thyatira, believes, is baptized with her household and insists that the missionaries stay at her house.

usedIn.n: Romans 4:1-25, Abraham, father of the uncircumcised too
usedIn.s: Paul argues from Genesis 15:6 that Abraham was counted righteous by trusting God before he was circumcised, so he is the father of all who believe, circumcised or not.

usedIn.n: Galatians 2:1-10, Titus, the pillars and the right hand of fellowship
usedIn.s: Fourteen years later Paul goes up to Jerusalem with Barnabas and the uncircumcised Titus; Titus is not made to be circumcised, and the leaders reputed to be pillars give Paul the right hand of fellowship, asking only that he remember the poor.

usedIn.n: Galatians 5:2-12, Circumcision, the whole law and the knife
usedIn.s: Paul warns that a man who accepts circumcision is bound to keep the whole law and is cut off from Christ, asks who cut in on their race, and wishes that the agitators would go further with the knife.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 2:11-22, The dividing wall torn down, and a new temple
usedIn.s: Paul reminds Gentile believers that they were once far off, shut out of Israel's citizenship and covenants, and tells them Christ has broken down the dividing wall and built Jews and Gentiles into one household and one temple.

entries.title: The one who is sent
entries.summary: Jewish law held that a man's agent was as the man himself, backed by his authority as long as he represented him faithfully. How people treated the agent showed how they treated the one who sent him.
aliases: as the Father has sent me
no messenger is greater than the one who sent him
to reject the messengers is to reject the sender
entries.plain: **Turn away the ambassador and you have insulted his country.** In Jesus' world a man could send someone to act for him: to buy, to sign, to speak. The agent carried the sender's full authority as long as he did what he was sent to do. Welcoming him was welcoming the sender, and refusing him was refusing the sender. In John's Gospel Jesus speaks of himself again and again as the one the Father sent.
entries.then: Jewish law taught that a man's agent stood in his place and carried his authority, as long as the agent represented him faithfully (Keener). The CSB Study Bible cites the Mishnah (Berakot 5.5) for the rule that "a man's agent is like the man himself". It compares Moses' words that the Lord had sent him and he did nothing of his own will (Numbers 16:28). Moses and the Old Testament prophets were sometimes viewed as God's agents. The principle held across the ancient Mediterranean. How someone welcomed an envoy, an authorized agent or a son revealed how he regarded the one who sent him. To be sent from the Father means to be his commissioned agent, an authorized representative. Wright, on the bread from heaven, puts it in one line: "Moses was only God's agent." Apostle means one who is sent, used of an ambassador or delegate. The same principle applies to the disciples Jesus sends out: whoever receives them receives him, and whoever receives him receives the one who sent him. An agent was always subordinate to his sender, and his authority reached only as far as his commission. Only subordinates served and were sent. In Jewish tradition prophets often appointed successors.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a lawyer holding power of attorney. When she signs, her client has signed, as long as she stays within what she was told to do.
entries.changes: The agent stands for the sender, so honoring or rejecting the Son is honoring or rejecting the Father, as in John 5:23. The same rule makes receiving Jesus' messengers the same as receiving him and the one who sent him, in Matthew 10:40.
entries.not: **Not a legal paper for business alone.** Power of attorney covers signatures. The Jewish agent principle reached further: Moses and the prophets could be seen as God's agents, and how people received an agent, or a son, showed how they treated the sender. The agent was always subordinate, and in John the argument turns on how far the Son's commission reaches.
entries.dissent: What the agency language does in John 5. Keener says the picture of the Son as the Father's agent answers the charge that Jesus made himself equal with God, though his hearers could easily take 5:23 as a claim to deity. The ESV and CSB Study Bibles read 5:23 as establishing Jesus' right to be worshiped, a claim to deity.

usedIn.s: On the evening of the first day Jesus stands among the disciples behind locked doors, shows his hands and side, sends them as the Father sent him and breathes the Spirit on them. A week later Thomas sees the wounds and confesses him as Lord and God.

usedIn.s: Carrying the high priest's letters to the synagogues of Damascus, Saul is stopped by a light and a voice. Blinded, healed and baptized, the persecutor begins to proclaim Jesus and has to escape over the city wall.

usedIn.s: In Macedonia Paul is comforted by Titus's arrival and his news that the Corinthians grieved over Paul's harsh letter in a way that led to repentance, and that they received Titus with fear and trembling.

usedIn.s: The elder wrote to the church, but Diotrephes, eager to be first, refuses to receive him; he spreads malicious talk, refuses to welcome the brothers and puts out of the church those who do. Gaius is not to imitate evil. Demetrius is well spoken of by everyone, and the elder adds his own testimony; he hopes to come soon and talk face to face.

entries.title: Holding goods in common
entries.summary: The first believers in Jerusalem shared their possessions and sold property to meet each other's needs. Ancient writers used the same words for ideal communities, and only a few groups, such as the Essenes, tried it.
aliases: laid it at the apostles' feet
entries.plain: **Three generations worked in the family shop and drew what they needed from the same till.** In Jerusalem the first believers treated each other as family. People who had extra land or houses sold them and brought the money to the apostles, who gave it out to anyone in need. Greek writers described ideal communities in these words, but almost no one lived that way. The Essenes did, and a member who joined gave up his property to the group.
entries.then: Luke describes the believers in the words other writers used for ideal, even utopian, communities. Such sharing was very rare. The Essenes, about four thousand of them, and the Pythagoreans rejected private property. Josephus says of the Essenes, "These men are despisers of riches," and that "there is, as it were, one patrimony among all the brethren." Groups that made members hand over their goods normally allowed a trial period, during which a newcomer could still take back his property and go (Keener). At Qumran a member who lied about his property was barred from the common meal for a year and had his rations cut by a quarter. The Christians, by contrast, sold property as needs arose, not all at once, and acted from love rather than a rule. In Judean circles designated leaders gave out the charity. Wright compares a family business where three generations share a common purse. He notes that the Twelve already had a common purse with Jesus. They sold extra land, which for Jews was part of their ancestral inheritance, while keeping the houses they met in.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a family firm where the takings go into one account and everyone draws what they need. It works because they see each other as family, and it falls apart the moment someone starts hiding money from the others.
entries.changes: Sharing everything, as in Acts 2:44-45, is the way a family handles money, stretched to a whole community, which is why lying about a gift in Acts 5:1-4 is so serious. Jesus and the Twelve had already lived from a common purse, supported by women such as those named in Luke 8:1-3.
entries.not: **Not a family that already owned the business together.** The believers were not kin, and they pooled by selling, often extra land that for Jews was ancestral inheritance, as needs arose. Peter tells Ananias the land and its price were his own, so the sharing was voluntary, and believers kept the homes where the church met.
entries.dissent: How radical it was. The ESV Study Bible stresses that the giving was voluntary, that private property was not abolished and that the passage is not early communism. Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes stress how unusual it was by ancient standards, and Keener warns against treating it as a mistake. No source says it was compulsory.

entries.title: Zeal for God and the law
entries.summary: Zeal meant burning loyalty to God and his law, and its heroes, Phinehas, Elijah and the Maccabees, had used force against those who betrayed it. Saul the persecutor saw himself in that line.
aliases: eager to do what is good
entries.plain: **Arguing with people who betrayed the cause was not enough for him; he would stop them, whatever it took.** In Jewish memory, zeal was the passion of heroes who defended God's honor by action. Phinehas speared an Israelite who brought idolatry into the camp. Elijah killed the prophets of Baal. The Maccabees took up arms against a pagan king. In Paul's day, to be zealous for the law could mean being ready to use force against Jews who seemed to betray it. Later, some Jewish rebels against Rome called themselves Zealots.
entries.then: Wright traces the tradition. Phinehas's spear in Numbers 25 was the defining moment of zeal, and Psalm 106 says it was reckoned to him as righteousness. In Wright's words, "Zeal was the outward badge of the unbreakable relationship." Elijah was the other great model, and 1 Maccabees 2 couples him with Phinehas. The feast of Hanukkah kept the zeal of Judas Maccabaeus fresh. The Palestinian picture of zeal was rooted in Phinehas and the Maccabees, who were willing to kill for God. In Josephus, Mattathias kills a Jew who sacrificed at the king's command. Then he cries out, "If," said he, "any one be zealous for the laws of his country, and for the worship of God, let him follow me." Some models of zeal for the law used violence. By AD 66 some nationalists called themselves zealous after Phinehas and the Maccabees, and one faction in the Judean revolt was known as the Zealots. Saul arrested women as well as men, which shows him more zealous than most of his contemporaries thought necessary. Wright describes Saul as prepared to go further than the high priest had envisaged. He calls the Pharisees a populist pressure group without official power. Paul later acknowledged his zeal, and others knew him by it. The men who stoned Stephen thought they were cleansing the city (Wright). By the late 50s Agrippa I's reign had fanned Judean nationalism, and many believers in Jerusalem were zealous for the law. Sicarii were then murdering aristocrats suspected of collaborating with Gentiles.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a vigilante who thinks the authorities are too soft on traitors and takes the matter into his own hands. He sees himself as the most loyal citizen of all.
entries.changes: Saul's raids on believers, as in Acts 8:3, are zeal in the old sense, loyalty to God shown by force. Paul looks back on it in Galatians 1:13-14 and lists his zeal in persecuting the church among his former credentials in Philippians 3:6.
entries.not: **Not an outlaw.** A vigilante defies the law, but zeal had Scripture on its side: Phinehas's spear was reckoned to him as righteousness, and Elijah and the Maccabees were national heroes. Zeal meant defending God's honor, often by force, against fellow Jews who seemed to compromise it.

usedIn.s: James tells his readers to be quick to listen and slow to speak and to anger, to do the word and not merely hear it, and names the religion God accepts: care for orphans and widows in their distress and a life kept unstained by the world.

usedIn.n: James 3:1-4:10, The tongue on fire, zeal and wars
usedIn.s: James warns would-be teachers that the tongue is a small fire set alight by hell, contrasts bitter envy and selfish ambition with the peaceable wisdom from above, traces fights and quarrels to desires at war within, calls friendship with the world enmity with God, and tells his readers to resist the devil.

entries.title: Elders
entries.summary: Older men respected for wisdom led Israel's villages in the Old Testament and still led Jewish communities and synagogues in the first century, usually as a group. The first churches took over the pattern, calling their elders overseers too, with deacons beside them.
entries.plain: **The village did not have a mayor; it had the old men who sat at the gate and settled things together.** In the Old Testament, towns were run by elders, older men known for wisdom. In Jesus' day Jewish communities and synagogues were still led by groups of elders, and Greek cities had councils of elders too. When Paul and Barnabas set up new churches, they appointed elders in each one, following the same pattern.
entries.then: Certain older men earned a name for wisdom and maturity. In the Old Testament chosen elders governed and judged the villages, and the role stayed a respected one, usually held as a group. Elders did the same in much of the Mediterranean world. Most ancient synagogues had several elders acting as councils, and the Greek East gave much influence to the Gerousia, clubs of elders. Elders were traditionally the leaders of Jewish communities. In the Diaspora, local leadership varied. The ESV Study Bible says Paul's churches copied the synagogue's rule by elders, placing several in every church. They appointed them from the start, even in young churches. The CSB Study Bible argues that formal offices existed from the church's earliest stage, and that being led by the Spirit and having appointed leaders do not conflict. At Miletus Paul calls the Ephesian elders overseers and charges them to shepherd the flock. Overseer was a Greek administrative title. It also appears in the Greek Old Testament and, in Hebrew form, in the Dead Sea Scrolls. The ESV Study Bible takes elders, overseers and pastors as names for one office. In 1 Timothy and Titus overseer and elder name one office, which had changed by Ignatius's time early in the second century (Keener). Carson, Moo and Morris find the two equated in Titus 1:5-7, and Wright finds them at least overlapping. Keener compares the deacon with the synagogue attendant, the chazan, who looked after the building and often owned the house where the congregation met. His notes find the first-century meaning elusive.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a village council of senior members who know every family and settle disputes together. No one of them is boss, and the town trusts them because they have lived there longest.
entries.changes: Elders appointed in every church, as in Acts 14:23, follow the leadership pattern of the synagogue and the village. James 5:14 tells the sick to call the elders, and 1 Timothy 5:17 speaks of elders who lead well.
entries.not: **Not simply the oldest members.** Elder was a recognized office with responsibility for the community, and in the churches elders were appointed.
entries.dissent: Two points. First, how early the churches had formal offices. The CSB Study Bible answers those who think the earliest church had none, and the ESV Study Bible says elders were appointed from the beginning. Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes describe the Jewish and Greek pattern without arguing the point. Second, whether the offices of 1 Timothy fit Paul's lifetime. Wright and Bird report the view that fixed offices of overseer and deacon, filled from the top down, mark a church of the late first or second century. They answer that Paul's churches already had household leaders, elders and deacons, still far from Ignatius's single bishop. These letters, they add, deal with leaders' character, not their institutional power. Carson, Moo and Morris find nothing that demands more than the overseers and deacons of Philippians 1:1, though this office soon became the single bishop. Wright leaves open whether the overseer of 1 Timothy 3 was one leader or one of a team.

usedIn.s: Scattered believers bring the message to Gentiles in Antioch, where the disciples are first called Christians. When a prophet foretells famine, the church sends relief to the elders in Judea.

usedIn.n: Acts 14:21-28, Elders appointed, and home to Antioch
usedIn.s: Paul and Barnabas retrace their route, warning that the kingdom comes through hardships and appointing elders in each church, then report to Antioch that God has opened a door of faith to the Gentiles.

usedIn.n: Acts 20:17-38, Farewell to the Ephesian elders
usedIn.s: Hurrying to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost, Paul calls the elders of Ephesus to Miletus. He reminds them how he lived among them, warns of wolves who will attack the flock, charges them as overseers to shepherd God's church, and leaves them in tears.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 3:1-13, Overseers, deacons and the women
usedIn.s: Paul lists what is required of an overseer, above reproach, faithful in marriage, hospitable, able to teach, managing his household well, and then of deacons and of the women, who must also be worthy of respect.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 4:6-16, Training for godliness, and a young leader
usedIn.s: Timothy is to train himself for godliness as an athlete trains his body, set an example despite his youth, devote himself to the public reading of Scripture and teaching, and not neglect the gift given when the elders laid hands on him.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 5:17-25, Double honor, two witnesses, the elect angels and a little wine
usedIn.s: Elders who lead well deserve double honor and pay; charges against them need two or three witnesses; Paul charges Timothy before God, Christ and the elect angels to act without favoritism, to lay hands on no one hastily, and to take a little wine.

usedIn.n: Titus 1:1-9, Elders in every town, and God's steward
usedIn.s: Paul greets Titus, whom he left in Crete to put in order what was unfinished and to appoint elders in every town, and lists what an elder must be: blameless, faithful to his wife, with believing children, a steward of God's household, hospitable and able to hold to sound teaching.

usedIn.n: James 5:13-20, Elders, oil and Elijah's prayer
usedIn.s: The suffering should pray and the cheerful sing; the sick should call the church's elders to pray over them and anoint them with oil. The prayer of a righteous person is powerful, as Elijah's was, and whoever turns a sinner back covers a multitude of sins.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 5:1-14, Elders, the roaring lion, and greetings from Babylon
usedIn.s: As a fellow elder Peter urges the elders to shepherd God's flock willingly, not for gain, until the Chief Shepherd gives them an unfading crown. All must be humble, for their adversary the devil prowls like a roaring lion. Peter writes through Silvanus and sends greetings from she who is in Babylon and from his son Mark.

usedIn.n: 2 John 1-6, The elder to the chosen lady
usedIn.s: The elder writes to the chosen lady and her children, whom he loves in the truth. He is glad that some of her children walk in the truth, and he asks for no new command but the old one, that they love one another, which means walking in God's commands.

entries.title: The collection for Jerusalem
entries.summary: Paul gathered money from his mostly Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem, much as Jews everywhere sent the temple tax to the holy city.
entries.plain: **Every church in the region took up an offering for the struggling mother church, and a few trusted people drove it there.** Jews all over the world sent money to Jerusalem every year for the temple, carried by trusted messengers. Paul organized something like it among the churches he had founded. Gentile believers in Macedonia and Achaia gave money for the poor among the believers in Jerusalem, and Paul planned to take it there himself. For him it showed that Jewish and Gentile believers belonged to one family.
entries.then: Sending money to Jerusalem was a common Jewish practice around the Mediterranean. Above all there was the annual temple tax, the half-shekel every Jewish man paid, carried to Jerusalem by trusted messengers. It expressed the solidarity of Jews everywhere with the holy city. Keener and his notes say the Gentile believers' offering expressed the same solidarity between Gentile and Jewish believers. Rome protected the Jewish practice. Josephus quotes a decree of Augustus that the Jews' "sacred money be not touched, but be sent to Jerusalem" and that anyone caught stealing it from a synagogue be treated as sacrilegious. In some Judean circles, Qumran especially, the poor had become a name for the devout. Jewish teachers treated the laws on caring for the poor as a test of whether a Gentile convert had truly accepted God's law. Wright thinks the Jerusalem church was poor because its members had pooled their property and then faced a famine and the hostility of their neighbors. Many Jews expected the nations to bring tribute to Jerusalem at the end (Isaiah 60:11-14). Some Jerusalem believers may have seen the gift that way, while Paul may have thought more broadly of unity. The risks were practical too. Before banknotes, Wright points out, Paul's party had to carry large sums by road and ship and stay at wayside inns. Refusing a gift declared enmity, so a refusal would be rare, though Wright thinks some Jewish believers may have found Gentile money tainted. Paul's sealing of the fruit recalls the seal on commercial goods that guaranteed their contents.
entries.bridge: An analogy: churches in a prosperous new suburb sending relief to the struggling old congregation downtown that first sent them missionaries. The money helps, but the real message is that the two congregations belong to each other.
entries.changes: Because Jews everywhere sent money to Jerusalem, Paul's gift from Gentile churches in Romans 15:25-27 spoke the language of solidarity in a new way, Gentiles giving to Jewish believers. He urges it on the Corinthians in 2 Corinthians 8-9 and mentions the alms he brought to his nation at his hearing in Acts 24:17.
entries.not: **Not relief between two branches of one people.** The gift crossed the line between Gentile and Jew, which is why Paul asked for prayer that it would be welcomed. It also carried echoes a suburban gift does not: the temple tax every Jewish man sent, and the hope that the nations would one day bring tribute to Jerusalem.
entries.dissent: How Jerusalem would see the gift. Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes suggest some may have seen it as the beginning of the nations' promised tribute to Zion, while Paul thought of unity. Wright thinks some Jewish believers may have found it hard to accept money from Gentile sources at all, which is why Paul asks for prayer that it be welcomed.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Romans 15:16, 15:25-26, 15:27 and 15:28
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Romans 15:16, 15:26, 15:27 and 15:31
Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews 16.6.2, trans. William Whiston
N. T. Wright, Paul for Everyone: Romans, Part Two, comment on Romans 15:25-33

usedIn.n: Acts 20:1-12, The collection party and Eutychus at Troas
usedIn.s: Paul leaves Ephesus for Macedonia and Greece, then sets out for Jerusalem with delegates from the churches. At Troas the believers meet on the first day of the week, and a young man who falls from a window is taken up alive.

usedIn.n: Romans 15:25-33, The gift for Jerusalem
usedIn.s: Before coming west Paul must take a gift from the churches of Macedonia and Achaia to the poor among the believers in Jerusalem. He asks for prayer that he will be kept safe and the gift accepted.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 16:1-24, The collection and final greetings
usedIn.s: Paul arranges a weekly setting aside of money for the believers in Jerusalem, plans his travels, commends Timothy, Apollos and the household of Stephanas, and closes with greetings, a line in his own hand and the Aramaic prayer Marana tha.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 8:1-15, The Macedonians' giving and the manna
usedIn.s: Paul holds up the generosity of the poor Macedonian churches, appeals to Christ who became poor, and asks the Corinthians to finish their gift so that there may be equality, as there was with the manna in the wilderness.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 8:16-9:15, Envoys for the collection and the cheerful giver
usedIn.s: Paul commends Titus and two brothers appointed by the churches to carry the gift, takes care that no one can fault him in handling it, and urges the Corinthians to have their promised gift ready, since God loves a cheerful giver.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 12:11-18, Not a burden: parents save for their children
usedIn.s: Paul says the Corinthians forced him to play the fool; the signs of an apostle were done among them, and his only fault was not to burden them, since parents save up for their children, not children for their parents.

usedIn.n: Galatians 2:1-10, Titus, the pillars and the right hand of fellowship
usedIn.s: Fourteen years later Paul goes up to Jerusalem with Barnabas and the uncircumcised Titus; Titus is not made to be circumcised, and the leaders reputed to be pillars give Paul the right hand of fellowship, asking only that he remember the poor.

entries.title: Martyrs
entries.summary: Jews remembered those who died rather than break God's law, above all the Maccabean martyrs tortured under Antiochus, and the prophets said to have been stoned or sawn in two. Their hope was the resurrection.
aliases: of whom the world was not worthy
lay down our lives for one another
faithful to the point of death
drunk with the blood of the saints
entries.plain: **Every nation tells the stories of those who would not bow, even when it cost them everything.** In 167 BC the Syrian king Antiochus Epiphanes tried to stamp out Jewish practice. Those who kept the law were whipped, tortured and killed, and their stories, told in the books of the Maccabees, were known to nearly every Jew. One family of brothers died with their mother, declaring that God would raise them. Jews also told of prophets killed for their message, Isaiah sawn in two under King Manasseh and Jeremiah stoned. By the first century the martyr was a hero whose reward waited at the resurrection.
entries.then: Nearly all Jews knew the stories of the Maccabean martyrs, tortured by scalding, flaying and the wheel. Regular Greek torture included fire, thumbscrews and stretching on a wheel to break the joints, and the martyrs were scourged as well. Josephus writes of Antiochus's victims: "they were whipped with rods, and their bodies were torn to pieces, and were crucified, while they were still alive, and breathed" (Antiquities 12.5.4). Their hope was the resurrection. All Jewish sources that addressed the question agreed that martyrs would be honored at the resurrection, and 2 Maccabees makes that the hope that let them endure. Wright recalls the brothers and their mother who declared, as they were tortured, that God would raise them bodily. The Greek-speaking Jewish work 4 Maccabees applied the image of athletes in a contest to the martyrs, and said they looked to God as they endured. The earlier martyrs held that breaking the commandments to save one's life profaned God's name in public. Some Jewish teachers allowed most laws to be broken to save a life. Jewish literature also gave martyrs a past. Abel was counted the first. Tradition told of prophets killed for their message: Isaiah, hiding in a tree, sawn in two under Manasseh, and Jeremiah stoned. Charles introduces the Jewish Martyrdom of Isaiah, which survives inside the later Ascension of Isaiah. He retells how Manasseh "caused Isaiah to be sawn asunder with a wood saw", and notes that Origen already tied the story to Hebrews 11:37.
entries.bridge: An analogy: the resistance fighters a country names its streets after, whose stories every schoolchild learns. Remembering them tells the next generation what loyalty may cost.
entries.changes: The roll of those tortured, stoned and sawn in two in Hebrews 11:35-37 draws on martyr stories every Jewish reader knew. Jesus counts the blood of the prophets from Abel onward against his generation in Matthew 23:35, and the souls under the altar in Revelation 6:9-10 ask how long until their blood is avenged.
entries.not: **Not fighters who fell in battle.** The martyrs were killed for refusing to break God's law or to stop speaking his word, and their honor came from faithfulness under torture. Their hope also lay beyond the nation's memory: every Jewish source that took up the question expected them to be honored at the resurrection.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Hebrews 11:4, 11:35-36 and 11:37, introduction to Hebrews 12:1-3, and on 12:2 and 12:4
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Hebrews 11:35 and 11:37

usedIn.n: Hebrews 11:32-40, Sawn in two, dressed in skins
usedIn.s: Time fails to tell of the judges, David, Samuel and the prophets, who conquered kingdoms and escaped the sword. Others were tortured and refused release to gain a better resurrection; they were mocked, flogged, chained, stoned, sawn in two, and wandered in skins and caves, people the world was not worthy of.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 12:1-13, The race, the shame and the Father's discipline
usedIn.s: Surrounded by a great cloud of witnesses, believers are to throw off every weight and run with endurance, eyes fixed on Jesus, who endured the cross and scorned its shame. Their hardships are a father's discipline, which only legitimate children receive.

usedIn.n: 1 John 2:28-3:24, Children of God, Cain, and love in deed
usedIn.s: Those who do right are born of God, whose love makes them his children, and when he appears they will be like him. Whoever keeps on sinning belongs to the devil, who has sinned from the beginning, and the Son came to undo his work. The readers are not to be like Cain, who murdered his brother, but to love in deed and in truth, as Christ laid down his life.

usedIn.n: Revelation 2:8-11, Smyrna, poor and slandered
usedIn.s: To Smyrna the risen Jesus says he sees their hardship and poverty and the abuse they suffer from local opponents claiming to be the true Jews, whom he condemns in harsh terms. Some will be jailed for a short time; if they stay loyal even to death he will reward them with life.

usedIn.n: Revelation 2:12-17, Pergamum, where Satan's throne is
usedIn.s: To Pergamum Jesus, who wields the sword of judgment, says they have stayed loyal in a city he calls Satan's seat, even after the martyrdom of Antipas. But some follow teaching like Balaam's that leads to idol meals and immorality. The faithful are promised hidden heavenly food and a white stone carrying a new name.

usedIn.n: Revelation 6:9-17, souls under the altar and the great day of wrath
usedIn.s: At the fifth seal the souls of those killed for God's word cry out from under the altar, how long, and are given white robes and told to wait. At the sixth a great earthquake shakes the world, the sky rolls up like a scroll, and kings and slaves alike hide in the caves from the wrath of the Lamb.

usedIn.n: Revelation 12:7-17, war in heaven and the accuser thrown down
usedIn.s: Michael and his angels fight the dragon and throw him out of heaven, and a voice celebrates the fall of the accuser of the brothers, defeated by the Lamb's blood and the witnesses' testimony. On earth the dragon chases the woman, who is given eagle's wings, and when the earth swallows the river he spews after her, he turns to make war on her other children.

usedIn.n: Revelation 17:1-6, the woman on the scarlet beast
usedIn.s: An angel carries John into a wilderness to see the great prostitute who sits on many waters, riding a scarlet beast full of blasphemous names. Dressed in purple and scarlet and glittering with gold and pearls, she holds a golden cup of filth, bears the name Babylon the great on her forehead and is drunk with the blood of God's people.

usedIn.n: Revelation 20:1-6, Satan bound and the thousand years
usedIn.s: An angel with the key to the Abyss and a great chain seizes the dragon, binds him for a thousand years and seals him in the Abyss so that he cannot deceive the nations. Those beheaded for their witness, who refused the beast and its mark, come to life and reign with Christ for the thousand years, the first resurrection, over which the second death has no power.

entries.title: Early false teachers and splits
entries.summary: Late in the first century a group left the churches John wrote to, taking a different view of Jesus with them. Some may have denied that he was the Messiah; others that he truly became human, as the Docetists and Cerinthus later taught.
aliases: Jesus Christ has come in the flesh
entries.plain: **A few members walk out of a church and start meeting across town, saying the old teaching was too simple.** Something like that happened in the churches John wrote to: people who had belonged left, and John calls them liars, deceivers and antichrists. What exactly they taught is harder to say. Some scholars think they stopped calling Jesus the Messiah so that they could stay in the synagogue. Others think they held that Jesus only seemed to be human, a view later called Docetism, from a Greek word meaning to seem, or that a divine Christ came on the man Jesus at his baptism and left him before the cross, as a teacher named Cerinthus taught. The sources leave both possibilities open.
entries.then: Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes call one point beyond dispute: "the primary troublemakers are clearly" secessionists. These were people who had belonged to the community and withdrawn. John tests them on two counts: whether they love their fellow believers, and whether they hold a true view of who Jesus is. Keener sets out three possible settings. Believers had been expelled from the synagogue, and some of their colleagues went back by denying that Jesus was the Messiah. Or false prophets urged compromise with idolatry, the imperial cult above all. Or movements were heading toward Gnosticism. Wright and Bird think denials of Jesus' messiahship and of his true humanity were both in play, and that the rival teachers left after failing to win support. Docetism takes its name from the Greek verb dokeo, to seem: Jesus only seemed to be human. It appealed to anyone who held that God could not be touched by change, suffering or shame. It had a pagan precedent in Ovid, whose Vesta snatched Julius Caesar away so that "what died by the steel was Caesar's shadow" (Wright and Bird). Cerinthus was an Egyptian who came to Ephesus and was remembered as John's gnostic opponent. He taught that the Christ came on Jesus at his baptism and left him before the cross (Wright and Bird, citing Irenaeus). Keener dates his teaching around AD 100. Greek gods had ichor, a watery fluid, in place of blood, so some may have taken the water and blood of John 19:34 for a demigod's. Gnostic systems proper are "not really attested until decades after 1 John" (the cultural backgrounds notes). Irenaeus reports, from hearers of Polycarp, that John at Ephesus "rushed out of the bath-house without bathing" on finding Cerinthus inside (Against Heresies 3.3.4).
entries.bridge: An analogy: a breakaway congregation that keeps the old name and the old hymns but changes what it says about the founder. Those who stay behind have to spell out what the founder really taught and why it matters.
entries.changes: Because former members had left with a different view of Jesus, 1 John 4:2 makes the confession that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh the test of a spirit, and 2 John 7 calls the same deceivers antichrists. John 19:34-35 stresses that blood and water came from the side of a man who had truly died, which Wright reads as an answer to those who would soon say otherwise.
entries.not: **Not a split whose teaching we can read.** A modern breakaway leaves its own statements behind, but John's opponents survive only in his replies, so what they taught has to be inferred. A denial that Jesus was the Messiah and a denial of his true humanity are both proposed, and the full Gnostic systems came decades later.
entries.dissent: What the secessionists denied. Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes keep several settings open. On 1 John 4:2-3 Keener thinks a Docetic denial more likely than a Jewish one. For 2 John he judges a relativizing of Jesus, to allow compromise with paganism, more likely than synagogue pressure. The ESV and CSB Study Bibles read 1 John 4:2 against a denial of Jesus' true humanity. Wright and Bird hold that denials of his messiahship and of his humanity were both in play. On Gnosticism, the ESV Study Bible says that John had it in mind "can neither be proven nor ruled out", and the cultural backgrounds notes and Carson place the developed systems later. Carson, Moo and Morris conclude that John faces "an embryonic Docetism or Cerinthianism". Raymond Brown, as they report, held that the secessionists denied the significance of Jesus' humanity for salvation, not the humanity itself. Wright, in his commentary, reads the antichrists of 1 John 2:18-27 as rival messianic movements, as political as religious, that drew believers away. He finds that 4:1-6 looks like an early branch of what became Gnosticism, while warning that the group may be one we know nothing of.
sources: Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, introduction to 1 John (Situation), on 1 John 1:1-4, 2:22-23, 4:2-3 and 5:6-13, and introduction to 2 John (Situation)
