usedIn.n: 1 John 1:1-4, What our hands have touched
usedIn.s: The letter opens with the Word of life, which was from the beginning and which the writer and those with him heard, saw and touched. They announce the eternal life that was with the Father and appeared to them, so that the readers may share their fellowship with the Father and the Son.

usedIn.n: 1 John 2:18-27, The last hour and many antichrists
usedIn.s: It is the last hour: the readers heard that antichrist is coming, and many antichrists have already come. They went out from the community, which shows they never belonged; whoever denies that Jesus is the Christ is the liar and the antichrist. The readers have an anointing from the Holy One and need no one else to teach them.

usedIn.n: 1 John 4:1-6, Test the spirits
usedIn.s: The readers must test every spirit instead of trusting each one, since many false prophets are now abroad. A spirit that confesses Jesus Christ as truly come in the flesh is from God, and one that refuses is the spirit of the antichrist. God in them is greater than the power in the world, and this is how the Spirit of truth is told from the spirit of error.

usedIn.n: 1 John 5:1-12, Water, blood and three witnesses
usedIn.s: Whoever believes Jesus is the Christ is God's child, and loving the parent means loving the child. Faith overcomes the world. Jesus Christ came by water and blood, not by water only, and three testify, the Spirit, the water and the blood; God's testimony is that he has given eternal life in his Son.

usedIn.n: 2 John 7-13, Deceivers at the door, paper and ink
usedIn.s: Many deceivers who refuse to confess that Jesus Christ came in the flesh are abroad in the world; such a one is the deceiver and the antichrist. Whoever runs ahead and does not keep to Christ's teaching does not have God, and the readers are not to take such a person into the house or greet him. The elder would rather not use paper and ink, and hopes to talk face to face.

entries.title: God's kingdom
entries.summary: Kingdom meant God's reign, God becoming king in fact. It was the good news Isaiah promised, and in Jesus' day it was also a slogan.
aliases: a kingdom that cannot be shaken
kingdom of our Lord and of his Messiah
entries.plain: **The rightful owner is back, and things are about to change around here.** The kingdom of God is not a place on a map, and it is not heaven after death. It means God ruling. Jews in Jesus' day longed for the time when God would finally rule, put the world right and free his people.
entries.then: Kingdom means reign. Isaiah's good news (40:9; 52:7) was the news that God reigns and would restore his people, and Isaiah 52:7 joins good news and God's reign in one verse. Wright's glossary defines the kingdom as the kingship, the sovereign and saving rule, of Israel's God. Around Jesus' time kingdom of God and slogans like no king but God had become revolutionary slogans. Good news had a second, Roman meaning: the announcement of an emperor's accession or birthday. The secret of the kingdom in Mark 4:11 is a revelation now given, as in Daniel 2. The birds in the branches borrow Daniel's picture of a great kingdom (Daniel 4:12) to say God's kingdom was already at work in a hidden way. Entering the kingdom did not mean going to heaven after death. Kingdom of heaven, Matthew's usual phrase, was an accepted Jewish way of saying the same thing (Daniel 2:44). Jews prayed daily for the time when God's rule would be set over all the earth. The cultural backgrounds article on the kingdom gives the ancient opening of one such prayer, the Kaddish: "Exalted and hallowed be his great name." Many then took Daniel's fourth and final kingdom to be Rome, the power God's everlasting kingdom would overthrow (Daniel 2:44). Hebrews 12:28 speaks of a kingdom that cannot be shaken, perhaps echoing the Greek of Psalm 96:10 (Keener).
entries.bridge: An analogy: a radio bulletin that the rightful government has come back from exile and is retaking the capital. It is news, not advice, and it splits listeners at once.
entries.changes: The kingdom announced in Mark 1:15 is God's reign arriving, not a place after death. Matthew usually says kingdom of heaven, an accepted Jewish phrase for the same thing (Matthew 4:17). Parables describe it starting hidden and small.
entries.not: **Not a government retaking its capital.** The king in this news was God himself, and his reign came first in hidden, small ways, like the seed that grows into a tree with birds in its branches. Nor is it a place you go when you die; the word names who rules.
sources: NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, notes on Mark 1:1, 1:15, 4:11, 4:31-32 and 15:26

Craig S. Keener, The IVP Bible Background Commentary: New Testament, on Hebrews 12:28
NIV Cultural Backgrounds Study Bible, article Kingdom

usedIn.n: Matthew 3:1-12, John at the Jordan
usedIn.s: John preaches repentance in the Judean wilderness because the kingdom of heaven has come near. He calls Pharisees and Sadducees a brood of vipers and warns of the winnowing fork.

usedIn.n: Matthew 4:12-25, Capernaum, fishermen and crowds
usedIn.s: Jesus moves to Capernaum, Galilee of the Gentiles, announces the kingdom of heaven, calls four fishermen, and draws crowds from Galilee, the Ten Towns, Jerusalem and beyond the Jordan.

usedIn.n: Matthew 5:1-12, The Beatitudes
usedIn.s: Jesus sits on a mountain to teach and pronounces God's blessing on the poor in spirit, the mourners, the meek, the merciful, the peacemakers and the persecuted.

usedIn.n: Matthew 13:1-23, The sower
usedIn.s: From a boat Jesus tells the parable of the sower to the crowd on the shore, explains why he speaks in parables, and interprets the story for his disciples.

usedIn.n: Matthew 13:24-52, Darnel, mustard, yeast, treasure and a net
usedIn.s: More parables of the kingdom: weeds sown among wheat, a mustard seed, yeast in flour, treasure in a field, a pearl, and a dragnet, with the weeds and the net explained as the judgment at the end of the age.

usedIn.n: Mark 1:1-13, John in the wilderness
usedIn.s: John preaches and baptizes at the Jordan, dressed like Elijah. Jesus is baptized, hears the voice from heaven and is driven into the wilderness for forty days.

usedIn.n: Mark 1:14-20, Fishermen called
usedIn.s: Jesus announces that God's kingdom is near, then calls two pairs of brothers from their nets on the Sea of Galilee.

usedIn.n: Mark 4:1-34, Parables by the lake
usedIn.s: From a boat Jesus tells the crowd the sower, the lamp, the growing seed and the mustard seed, and explains them in private.

usedIn.n: Mark 4:35-41, The storm on the lake
usedIn.s: A storm swamps the boat while Jesus sleeps. He rebukes the wind and the sea, and the disciples ask who he is.

usedIn.n: Luke 4:1-13, The devil offers the kingdoms
usedIn.s: Full of the Spirit, Jesus is led through the wilderness for forty days, where the devil tests him with bread, with all the kingdoms of the world, and with a leap from the temple.

usedIn.n: Luke 6:20-36, Blessings, woes and lending with nothing back
usedIn.s: Jesus blesses the poor, the hungry, the weeping and the hated, pronounces woes on the rich and the well fed, and tells his hearers to love enemies, turn the other cheek and lend without expecting anything back.

usedIn.n: Luke 10:1-24, Seventy sent out, and Satan falling
usedIn.s: Jesus sends seventy others, or seventy-two, ahead of him in pairs, with no purse, bag or sandals, to towns that will welcome or refuse them. They come back rejoicing that even the demons obey, and Jesus says he saw Satan fall like lightning.

usedIn.n: Luke 11:1-13, Father, daily bread and a friend at midnight
usedIn.s: Asked to teach his disciples to pray, Jesus gives a short prayer to the Father, then tells of a man who wakes a neighbor at midnight to borrow bread for a guest.

usedIn.n: Luke 11:14-26, By Beelzebul, or by the finger of God?
usedIn.s: When Jesus drives out a demon that kept a man from speaking, some say he does it by Beelzebul, the ruler of demons. He answers that a divided kingdom falls, and that if he drives out demons by the finger of God, God's kingdom has come.

usedIn.n: Luke 13:10-21, A bent woman freed on the Sabbath; mustard and leaven
usedIn.s: Teaching in a synagogue on the Sabbath, Jesus frees a woman bent double for eighteen years. The synagogue ruler objects, and Jesus answers with an ox untied for water, then compares God's kingdom to a mustard seed and to leaven.

usedIn.n: Luke 18:18-30, A rich ruler and the needle's eye
usedIn.s: A ruler asks what he must do to inherit eternal life; told to sell everything and follow, he goes away sad, and Jesus says it is easier for a camel to go through a needle's eye than for a rich man to enter God's kingdom.

usedIn.n: John 3:1-21, Born from above
usedIn.s: Nicodemus, a Pharisee and ruler, comes to Jesus at night. Jesus tells him that no one sees God's kingdom without being born from above, of water and Spirit, and speaks of the Son of Man lifted up like the serpent in the wilderness.

usedIn.n: Acts 1:1-11, The kingdom question and the cloud
usedIn.s: Luke's second volume opens with the risen Jesus speaking about God's kingdom for forty days. Asked whether he will now restore the kingdom to Israel, he promises the Spirit, sends the apostles as witnesses to the end of the earth, and is taken up in a cloud.

usedIn.n: Acts 14:21-28, Elders appointed, and home to Antioch
usedIn.s: Paul and Barnabas retrace their route, warning that the kingdom comes through hardships and appointing elders in each church, then report to Antioch that God has opened a door of faith to the Gentiles.

usedIn.n: Romans 10:1-21, How beautiful are the feet
usedIn.s: Paul prays for Israel, whose zeal for God lacks knowledge, and argues from Scripture that the word of faith is near, that whoever calls on the Lord will be saved, and that heralds must be sent.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 6:1-11, Lawsuits before unbelievers
usedIn.s: Paul is appalled that believers take one another to court before pagan judges, reminds them that God's people will judge the world and even angels, and asks why they would not rather be wronged.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 5:1-20, Children of light, and wine or the Spirit
usedIn.s: Paul calls believers to imitate God, to have nothing to do with sexual immorality, coarse joking or deeds done in the dark, and, instead of getting drunk on wine, to be filled with the Spirit, singing and giving thanks for everything.

usedIn.n: Colossians 1:1-14, Epaphras's report and a change of kingdoms
usedIn.s: Paul and Timothy greet the believers at Colossae, a church Paul has never visited, thank God for what Epaphras has told them, and pray that they grow in knowledge, having been rescued out of darkness into the kingdom of God's Son.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 2:1-12, Gentle as a nurse, firm as a father
usedIn.s: Paul reminds the church how he and his companions came to them after being mistreated in Philippi: no deceit, flattery or greed, gentle among them like a nursing mother, working night and day so as not to burden anyone, and urging each of them like a father.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 12:18-29, Sinai, Zion and the unshakable kingdom
usedIn.s: Believers have not come to the burning, quaking mountain of Sinai but to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, with myriads of angels, the assembly of the firstborn enrolled in heaven, God the judge, the spirits of the righteous, and Jesus, whose blood speaks better than Abel's. Since God will shake heaven and earth once more, they are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken.

usedIn.n: Revelation 11:15-19, the seventh trumpet and the ark
usedIn.s: At the seventh trumpet heaven announces that rule over the world now belongs to God and his Messiah for ever. The elders worship, the angry nations meet God's judgment, and the heavenly temple opens to reveal the ark of the covenant.

entries.title: Elijah expected
entries.summary: Malachi promised Elijah would come back before the great day of the Lord. By Jesus' time many were waiting for him, and the Gospels keep raising his name.
entries.plain: **When the advance team shows up, you know the main event is close.** Elijah was a prophet who did not die; he was taken up into heaven. The last book of the prophets said God would send him back before the great day. So people kept asking about new prophets: is this Elijah?
entries.then: Many looked for Elijah to come back and ready things for the end (Malachi 4:5-6). Sirach (48:10) also predicts his return, and it is common in later Jewish writing. Elijah was taken to heaven alive (2 Kings 2:11). Wright says that because he had not really died, it seemed fitting that he might come back. Keener's notes on John 1:21 name Elijah and the prophet like Moses as two separate figures expected before the Messiah. Later rabbis pictured the returning Elijah as a master of the law who would settle legal disputes. John's leather belt recalls Elijah's in 2 Kings 1:8, and his camel hair was the clothing of mourning. Other rabbinic traditions pictured Elijah acting like an angel who helped rabbis in need, which helps explain the bystanders at the cross. The ESV Study Bible calls the hope widespread in Judaism. It notes that Jesus speaks of John as coming with Elijah's spirit and power. Some elites held that prophecy had ceased after Malachi. Only a few holy men were thought able to bring rain by prayer, and Honi the Circle-drawer, Josephus' Onias, was chief among them. Elijah was their great model, and James 5:17-18 makes him a model for every believer instead. A probable Jewish tradition held that Elijah's drought lasted three and a half years, the span of the two witnesses of Revelation 11. Hippolytus, Tertullian and Jerome expected Enoch and Elijah, who had never died, to return as those witnesses.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a herald walking ahead of a royal procession. When you see him turn the corner, you stop looking at him and start looking past him for the king.
entries.changes: When a prophet appears, people ask whether this is Elijah, as they do of Jesus in Mark 6:15. Jesus calls John the Elijah who was to come in Matthew 11:14. Luke 1:17 says John would go in the spirit and power of Elijah.
entries.not: **Not a herald anyone could fill.** The hope was for one particular prophet, taken up alive, to come back himself. When Jesus calls John the Elijah who was to come, Keener reads it as figurative, and the ESV Study Bible says Elijah on the mountain is no reincarnation.

xref.s: The transfiguration, six days later, on a high mountain.

usedIn.n: Matthew 3:1-12, John at the Jordan
usedIn.s: John preaches repentance in the Judean wilderness because the kingdom of heaven has come near. He calls Pharisees and Sadducees a brood of vipers and warns of the winnowing fork.

usedIn.n: Matthew 11:2-30, John's question, children in the square, an easy yoke
usedIn.s: John asks from prison whether Jesus is the one to come. Jesus praises John, compares his generation to sulking children, pronounces woes on the lake towns, and offers rest under his yoke.

usedIn.n: Matthew 27:27-56, Mock king, the cross and the torn curtain
usedIn.s: Soldiers dress Jesus as a mock king. He is crucified as king of the Jews between two rebels, cries out in the words of Psalm 22 and dies; the curtain tears, the earth shakes, and women watch from a distance.

usedIn.n: Mark 1:1-13, John in the wilderness
usedIn.s: John preaches and baptizes at the Jordan, dressed like Elijah. Jesus is baptized, hears the voice from heaven and is driven into the wilderness for forty days.

usedIn.n: Mark 6:14-29, Herod's banquet and John's death
usedIn.s: Herod hears of Jesus and thinks John has risen. Mark then tells how Herod, at his birthday banquet, had John beheaded.

usedIn.n: Mark 8:27-9:1, Peter's answer at Caesarea Philippi
usedIn.s: Asked who he is, Peter says the Messiah. Jesus says the Son of Man must suffer, rebukes Peter, and calls followers to take up the cross.

usedIn.n: Mark 9:2-13, The transfiguration
usedIn.s: On a high mountain Jesus is changed before three disciples, Elijah and Moses appear, and a voice says to listen to him. Coming down, they ask about Elijah.

usedIn.n: Mark 15:21-41, The cross
usedIn.s: Jesus is crucified as king of the Jews between two bandits, mocked by passers-by, and dies with a loud cry. The temple curtain tears, and women watch from a distance.

usedIn.n: Luke 1:5-25, A priest's turn at the incense altar
usedIn.s: An elderly village priest, picked by lot to offer incense in the sanctuary, learns from the angel Gabriel that his childless wife will have a son who will prepare Israel for God with an Elijah-like power.

usedIn.n: Luke 7:11-17, A widow's only son on the bier
usedIn.s: At the gate of Nain Jesus meets a funeral for a widow's only son. He touches the bier, raises the young man and gives him back to his mother, and the crowd says a great prophet has arisen.

usedIn.n: Luke 9:51-62, A Samaritan refusal and three would-be followers
usedIn.s: Setting out for Jerusalem, Jesus is turned away by a Samaritan village and rebukes James and John for wanting to call down fire. On the road he tells three would-be followers what following him will cost.

usedIn.n: John 1:19-34, Not the Messiah, not Elijah, not the Prophet
usedIn.s: Priests and Levites from Jerusalem ask John who he is. He denies being the Messiah, Elijah or the Prophet, calls himself the voice in the wilderness, and points to Jesus as the Lamb of God.

usedIn.n: James 5:13-20, Elders, oil and Elijah's prayer
usedIn.s: The suffering should pray and the cheerful sing; the sick should call the church's elders to pray over them and anoint them with oil. The prayer of a righteous person is powerful, as Elijah's was, and whoever turns a sinner back covers a multitude of sins.

usedIn.n: Revelation 11:1-14, the measured temple and the two witnesses
usedIn.s: John is told to measure God's temple and its worshipers but to leave out the outer court, given to the nations to trample for forty-two months. Two witnesses in sackcloth prophesy with the powers of Elijah and Moses, are killed by the beast from the Abyss and left unburied in the great city, then raised and taken up to heaven.

entries.title: The Messiah, son of David
entries.summary: The anointed king most Jews expected from David's line, who would free Israel from its enemies. Nobody expected him to be killed.
aliases: denies that Jesus is the Christ
Lion of the tribe of Judah
King of kings and Lord of lords
entries.plain: **Everyone was waiting for the rightful heir to come home and drive out the invaders.** Messiah means anointed one, and kings were anointed with oil. Most Jews hoped for a king from David's family who would rescue Israel from Rome and put things right.
entries.then: Jewish people held a range of views about the Messiah. Most expected a coming king from David's house (Isaiah 9:6-7; 11:1-5; Psalms of Solomon 17:21) who would need military power to overthrow Rome. A Messiah who would be killed was not part of the usual hope at the time. A suffering Messiah, Messiah ben Joseph, appears perhaps from the second century, and there is no evidence for it earlier (Keener). Wright's glossary agrees there was no single template. Hopes often centered on defeating Israel's enemies and rebuilding or cleansing the temple, and the Dead Sea Scrolls speak of two Messiahs, a priest and a king. Son of God was already a messianic title in the Dead Sea Scrolls. Son of David implies the messianic king. For Romans, king of the Jews meant treason, since only the emperor could grant the title. Most hopes pictured the Messiah as a ruler or a warrior rather than a healer, though David was the only exorcist reported in the Old Testament. In the letters of John the confession that Jesus is the Christ becomes a test. Keener and his notes suggest that Jewish believers might deny it to remain in the synagogues. Wright and Bird note that in the teaching of Cerinthus the Christ had come to mean a divine self, a word moving away from its Jewish messianic meaning.
entries.bridge: An analogy: the heir of a deposed royal family, toasted in secret by loyalists. When he finally comes home, they expect a march on the capital, not a funeral.
entries.changes: Hopes for a warrior king from David's line explain why Jesus' messiahship was misunderstood, as when Peter rebukes him in Mark 8:32. Son of David on the lips of the sick and the crowds, as in Matthew 9:27, is a royal title. On the cross, king of the Jews becomes the charge.
entries.not: **Not one known heir waiting in exile.** Jewish hopes had no single template. Most looked for a king from David's line, but the Dead Sea Scrolls expect two Messiahs, a priest and a king, and many hopes centered on the temple. Son of God was a royal title for the Messiah, not yet a claim to divinity.

usedIn.n: Matthew 1:1-17, The family tree
usedIn.s: Matthew opens with Jesus' ancestry from Abraham through David and the exile, in three sets of fourteen generations, and names four women along the way.

usedIn.n: Matthew 1:18-25, Joseph and the betrothal
usedIn.s: Mary is found pregnant while betrothed to Joseph. He plans a quiet divorce until an angel in a dream tells him to take her as his wife and name the child Jesus.

usedIn.n: Matthew 2:1-12, Magi at Herod's court
usedIn.s: Magi from the east arrive in Jerusalem asking for the newborn king of the Jews. Herod consults his scholars, sends the visitors to Bethlehem, and they go home another way.

usedIn.n: Matthew 3:13-4:11, Baptism and the test in the desert
usedIn.s: Jesus is baptized and hears the voice from heaven, then is led into the wilderness for forty days, where the devil tests him three times.

usedIn.n: Matthew 9:18-34, A ruler's daughter, a bleeding woman, the blind and the mute
usedIn.s: A synagogue ruler asks Jesus to raise his daughter; on the way a woman touches the fringe of his cloak. Then two blind men call him Son of David, and a mute man speaks.

usedIn.n: Matthew 12:22-50, Beelzebul, the strong man, Jonah and his true family
usedIn.s: When Jesus heals a blind and mute man, the crowds wonder if he is the Son of David and the Pharisees say he works by Beelzebul. Jesus answers with the strong man, refuses a sign except Jonah's, and names his true family.

usedIn.n: Matthew 15:21-28, A Canaanite mother and the dogs
usedIn.s: In the region of Tyre and Sidon a Canaanite woman begs the Son of David to free her daughter. Jesus is silent, then speaks of bread and dogs, and her answer wins him over.

usedIn.n: Matthew 16:13-28, The rock, the keys and the cross
usedIn.s: At Caesarea Philippi Peter confesses Jesus as the Messiah, the Son of the living God, and is called the rock and given the keys. When Jesus speaks of his death, Peter rebukes him and is called Satan.

usedIn.n: Matthew 21:1-11, A donkey, a colt and the Hallel
usedIn.s: Jesus sends for a donkey and her colt, rides into Jerusalem as Zechariah foretold, and the pilgrim crowds spread cloaks and branches, crying Hosanna to the Son of David.

usedIn.n: Mark 8:27-9:1, Peter's answer at Caesarea Philippi
usedIn.s: Asked who he is, Peter says the Messiah. Jesus says the Son of Man must suffer, rebukes Peter, and calls followers to take up the cross.

usedIn.n: Mark 11:1-11, The ride into Jerusalem
usedIn.s: Jesus sends for a colt no one has ridden and rides into Jerusalem over cloaks and branches while the crowd shouts Hosanna.

usedIn.n: Mark 12:13-17, The coin with Caesar's face
usedIn.s: Pharisees and Herodians ask whether it is right to pay tax to Caesar. Jesus asks for a coin and asks whose image is on it.

usedIn.n: Mark 14:53-72, At the high priest's house
usedIn.s: The council tries Jesus at night. He says he is the Messiah and quotes the Son of Man coming with the clouds, and is condemned for blasphemy while Peter denies him in the courtyard.

usedIn.n: Mark 15:1-20, Before Pilate
usedIn.s: The chief priests hand Jesus to Pilate as king of the Jews. Pilate releases Barabbas to the crowd, has Jesus flogged, and the soldiers mock him as a king.

usedIn.n: Luke 1:26-56, A village girl, a greeting and a song of reversal
usedIn.s: Gabriel greets Mary, a betrothed girl in Nazareth, with news that she will bear the son of David. She goes to Elizabeth in the hill country and sings of God bringing down rulers and lifting up the humble.

usedIn.n: Luke 2:8-20, Shepherds hear of a savior
usedIn.s: Angels announce to shepherds in the fields near Bethlehem the birth of a savior who is Christ the Lord, and the shepherds find the child lying in a manger as they were told.

usedIn.n: Luke 2:21-40, Two birds, Simeon and Anna
usedIn.s: Jesus is circumcised and named on the eighth day. At the temple his parents make the offering the law allowed the poor, and two old people waiting for God's comfort, Simeon and the widow Anna, speak about the child.

usedIn.n: Luke 18:35-19:10, A blind beggar and Zacchaeus at Jericho
usedIn.s: Near Jericho a blind beggar calls Jesus Son of David and receives his sight. In the town Jesus invites himself to the house of Zacchaeus, a rich chief tax collector, who promises to give half his goods to the poor and repay fourfold.

usedIn.n: Luke 23:1-25, Before Pilate, before Antipas, and Barabbas
usedIn.s: The council brings Jesus to Pilate charged with forbidding tribute and claiming to be a king. Pilate sends him to Herod Antipas, who mocks him, and in the end Pilate gives in to the crowd and releases Barabbas.

usedIn.n: Luke 24:13-35, A stranger on the Emmaus road
usedIn.s: Two disciples walking home to Emmaus are joined by a stranger who explains the Scriptures to them. They press him to stay, and they recognize him when he breaks the bread.

usedIn.n: John 1:35-51, Come and see
usedIn.s: Two of John's disciples follow Jesus and spend the day with him. Andrew brings his brother Simon, Philip brings Nathanael, and Jesus promises they will see heaven opened and angels going up and down on the Son of Man.

usedIn.n: John 2:13-25, Tables overturned at Passover
usedIn.s: At Passover Jesus drives the animal sellers and money changers out of the temple courts. Asked for a sign, he tells them to destroy this temple and he will raise it in three days, and John explains that he meant his body.

usedIn.n: John 7:1-36, Up to the Festival of Tabernacles
usedIn.s: Jesus stays in Galilee while the Judeans look for a chance to kill him, then goes up to Tabernacles privately and teaches in the temple. The crowds argue over whether he is a deceiver or the Messiah, and the chief priests send guards to arrest him.

usedIn.n: John 7:37-52, Rivers of living water on the last day
usedIn.s: On the great last day of the feast Jesus cries out that the thirsty should come to him and drink. The crowd divides over whether he is the Prophet or the Messiah, and the Pharisees scorn a prophet from Galilee.

usedIn.n: John 10:1-21, The good shepherd and the hired hand
usedIn.s: Jesus contrasts the shepherd who enters by the gate, calls his sheep by name and lays down his life for them with thieves who climb in another way and a hired hand who runs from the wolf.

usedIn.n: John 10:22-42, In Solomon's Porch at the Festival of Dedication
usedIn.s: In winter, at the Festival of Dedication, the Judeans press Jesus to say plainly whether he is the Messiah. He says he and the Father are one, they pick up stones, and he answers from Psalm 82.

usedIn.n: John 12:12-19, Palm branches and a donkey's colt
usedIn.s: The festival crowd goes out with palm branches, shouting Hosanna and hailing Jesus as King of Israel, and he rides in on a young donkey, as Zechariah had said Zion's king would come.

usedIn.n: John 19:16-30, The cross, the notice in three languages, and his mother
usedIn.s: Jesus carries his own cross to Golgotha. Pilate's notice, King of the Jews, is written in Aramaic, Latin and Greek; soldiers cast lots for his seamless tunic; he gives his mother to the beloved disciple, takes the sour wine and says it is finished.

usedIn.n: Acts 2:14-41, Peter's sermon: the Spirit poured out
usedIn.s: Peter explains the scene from Joel: God has poured out his Spirit, the crucified Jesus is raised and exalted as Lord and Messiah, and three thousand are baptized in his name.

usedIn.n: Acts 11:19-30, Antioch, and the name Christian
usedIn.s: Scattered believers bring the message to Gentiles in Antioch, where the disciples are first called Christians. When a prophet foretells famine, the church sends relief to the elders in Judea.

usedIn.n: Acts 13:13-52, The synagogue at Pisidian Antioch
usedIn.s: Invited to speak after the synagogue readings in a Roman colony, Paul tells Israel's story from the exodus to Jesus. Gentiles welcome the message, and the city's leading men and women drive the apostles out.

usedIn.n: Romans 1:1-7, A slave of the Messiah writes to Rome
usedIn.s: Paul opens with his name and titles, a short summary of the good news about God's Son, and a greeting of grace and peace to believers in Rome he has never met.

usedIn.n: Romans 9:1-5, Israel's privileges
usedIn.s: Paul grieves for his own people and lists what belongs to Israel: the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the law, the worship, the promises, the patriarchs and the Messiah.

usedIn.n: Colossians 1:15-20, Firstborn over creation, over thrones and powers
usedIn.s: Paul describes the Son as the image of the unseen God and firstborn over all creation, through whom and for whom everything was made, thrones and powers included, and through whose cross God makes peace with all things.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 2:1-13, Soldier, athlete and farmer, and a prisoner in chains
usedIn.s: Timothy is to pass on what he heard to reliable people who will teach others, and to endure hardship like a soldier, compete by the rules like an athlete and work like a farmer, remembering Jesus Christ, raised from the dead and descended from David, for whom Paul is chained like a criminal.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 1:1-14, The Son above the angels
usedIn.s: God, who spoke in many ways through the prophets, has now spoken through a Son, heir of all things, who made purification for sins and sat down at the right hand of the Majesty. A chain of Scripture quotations sets the Son above the angels, who worship him and are sent to serve those who will inherit salvation.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 4:14-5:10, A high priest who can sympathize
usedIn.s: Jesus is a great high priest who has passed through the heavens and was tested in every way, yet without sin, so his people can approach the throne of grace with confidence. Like every high priest he was appointed by God, not self-chosen, and God named him a priest for ever in the order of Melchizedek.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 7:11-28, A priest from Judah, by oath, for ever
usedIn.s: If the Levitical priesthood had brought perfection, no other priest would have been promised. Jesus comes from Judah, a priest by the power of an indestructible life and by God's oath, the guarantee of a better covenant; Levitical priests died and offered daily for their own sins, but he lives for ever and offered himself once for all.

usedIn.n: 1 John 2:18-27, The last hour and many antichrists
usedIn.s: It is the last hour: the readers heard that antichrist is coming, and many antichrists have already come. They went out from the community, which shows they never belonged; whoever denies that Jesus is the Christ is the liar and the antichrist. The readers have an anointing from the Holy One and need no one else to teach them.

usedIn.n: Revelation 2:18-29, Thyatira, the guilds and Jezebel
usedIn.s: To Thyatira the Son of God, with eyes like fire and feet like bronze, praises a growing church but rebukes it for tolerating Jezebel, a self-styled prophetess who leads his servants into immorality and idol food. Those who hold fast are promised authority over the nations and the morning star.

usedIn.n: Revelation 5:1-14, the sealed scroll and the Lamb
usedIn.s: In God's right hand is a scroll written on both sides and sealed with seven seals, and no one is worthy to open it until the Lion of Judah, the Root of David, appears as a Lamb that looks slain. The living creatures, the elders, countless angels and all creation worship him.

usedIn.n: Revelation 11:15-19, the seventh trumpet and the ark
usedIn.s: At the seventh trumpet heaven announces that rule over the world now belongs to God and his Messiah for ever. The elders worship, the angry nations meet God's judgment, and the heavenly temple opens to reveal the ark of the covenant.

usedIn.n: Revelation 12:1-6, the woman, the child and the dragon
usedIn.s: A radiant woman, crowned with twelve stars and standing on the moon, labors to give birth while a great red dragon waits to devour her child. The child, destined to rule the nations, is caught up to God's throne, and the woman escapes to the wilderness, where she is kept safe for 1,260 days.

usedIn.n: Revelation 19:11-21, the rider on the white horse
usedIn.s: Heaven opens and a rider on a white horse, named Faithful and True and the Word of God, leads heaven's armies, his robe stained with blood and a sword coming from his mouth, his title King of kings. Birds are summoned to feast on the fallen, the beast and the false prophet are seized and cast into the fiery lake, and their armies fall to the rider's sword.

usedIn.n: Revelation 22:6-21, I am coming soon
usedIn.s: The angel confirms that the words are trustworthy, and Jesus says he is coming soon. John is told not to seal up the prophecy, since the time is near; those who wash their robes may enter the city while dogs, sorcerers and liars stay outside. The book closes with the Spirit and the bride saying come, a warning against adding to or taking from it, and the prayer, come, Lord Jesus.

entries.title: The Son of Man
entries.summary: Plain Aramaic for a human being, and also the figure in Daniel 7 who comes on the clouds and receives a kingdom. It is Jesus' favorite way of speaking about himself in the Gospels.
aliases: one like a son of man
standing at the right hand of God
one like a son of man among the lampstands
one like a son of man on a white cloud
entries.plain: **A guy like me doesn't get invited to these things.** Son of man could simply mean a person, or a modest way of saying I. But Jews also knew a vision in the book of Daniel where one like a son of man comes on the clouds to God and is given everlasting rule. Jesus used the phrase so that both meanings stayed in the air.
entries.then: In Hebrew or Aramaic the phrase simply means a mortal or a human being, and in later Judaism it could mean I or someone like me. In Daniel 7:13 a human figure is brought to the Ancient of Days on the clouds, vindicated after suffering and given kingly power. Daniel itself explains the figure as the holy people of the Most High. Even so, some Jews of the first century took it as a promise of the Messiah (Wright). At Mark 2:28 hearers could take the phrase as human being, so that human need comes before the Sabbath, though the context points to a larger claim (Keener). Mark 2:10 echoes Daniel 7:13-14. The Son of Man was expected to reign, but in Mark 10:45 he comes to serve and give his life, as in Isaiah 53. The ESV Study Bible calls it Jesus' favorite self-designation in Mark, its full meaning revealed only gradually. A Son of Man who commands angels, as in Matthew 13:41, is no ordinary human. Paul draws on the same picture. The Lord coming with the clouds in 1 Thessalonians 4:17 recalls Jesus' teaching about his coming, which alludes to Daniel 7:13. Wright reads it as Daniel's vindication of the suffering people of God. In Hebrews 2:6, quoting Psalm 8, the phrase seems to mean simply a human being, though Wright allows the Messiah's sense as well.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a modest nickname, like the new guy, that can just mean me, but in one company's history is also what everyone called the founder. Each time it is used, the room has to decide which is meant.
entries.changes: The phrase moves between an ordinary human being and Daniel's exalted figure, so each use, as in Mark 2:10 or Matthew 13:41, has to be read for which it carries. A Son of Man who sends angels to gather the wicked is doing what no ordinary man could. Stephen sees him standing at God's right hand in Acts 7:56.
entries.not: **Not a nickname from a company's past.** The second meaning came from Scripture, Daniel's vision of a human figure given everlasting rule, and Daniel itself reads that figure as the people of the saints. The phrase is neither a statement that Jesus was only human nor, in the sources here, a plain title of divinity.
entries.dissent: What the coming on the clouds means. Keener lists three views. Some scholars tie it strictly to Jesus' exaltation. Others tie it to the judgment of AD 70, and more of them to his return at the end. Wright argues that in Daniel 7 the son of man comes to God, not back to earth. The line is then about vindication after suffering and judgment on the system that opposed him. The ESV Study Bible reads the title as pointing to his humanity and his deity together.

xref.s: Thrones are set in place, plural, the court sits, and one like a son of man comes on the clouds.

ddd.s: A human-looking figure in Daniel's vision who arrives on the clouds and is handed authority over everything.

usedIn.n: Matthew 13:24-52, Darnel, mustard, yeast, treasure and a net
usedIn.s: More parables of the kingdom: weeds sown among wheat, a mustard seed, yeast in flour, treasure in a field, a pearl, and a dragnet, with the weeds and the net explained as the judgment at the end of the age.

usedIn.n: Matthew 24:29-51, The Son of Man on the clouds and the slave in charge
usedIn.s: After the distress, sun, moon and stars fail and the Son of Man comes on the clouds to gather his chosen. No one knows the day, so the household must stay ready, like a slave left in charge.

usedIn.n: Matthew 25:31-46, Sheep, goats and the least of these
usedIn.s: The Son of Man comes in glory with his angels, gathers the nations, and separates them as a shepherd separates sheep from goats, judging them by how they treated the least of his brothers and sisters.

usedIn.n: Matthew 28:16-20, Make disciples of all nations
usedIn.s: On a mountain in Galilee the risen Jesus claims all authority in heaven and on earth and sends the eleven to make disciples of all nations, baptizing and teaching them.

usedIn.n: Mark 2:23-3:6, Grain and a withered hand on the Sabbath
usedIn.s: Jesus defends his disciples for picking grain on the Sabbath, heals a man's hand in the synagogue, and the Pharisees start plotting with the Herodians.

usedIn.n: Mark 8:27-9:1, Peter's answer at Caesarea Philippi
usedIn.s: Asked who he is, Peter says the Messiah. Jesus says the Son of Man must suffer, rebukes Peter, and calls followers to take up the cross.

usedIn.n: Mark 9:2-13, The transfiguration
usedIn.s: On a high mountain Jesus is changed before three disciples, Elijah and Moses appear, and a voice says to listen to him. Coming down, they ask about Elijah.

usedIn.n: Mark 10:32-45, James and John ask for the best seats
usedIn.s: On the road to Jerusalem Jesus predicts his death a third time. James and John ask to sit at his right and left, and he tells them the first must be slave of all.

usedIn.n: Mark 13:1-37, The temple's fall and the Son of Man
usedIn.s: Leaving the temple, Jesus says not one stone will be left on another. On the Mount of Olives he warns of what is coming and of the Son of Man on the clouds.

usedIn.n: Mark 14:53-72, At the high priest's house
usedIn.s: The council tries Jesus at night. He says he is the Messiah and quotes the Son of Man coming with the clouds, and is condemned for blasphemy while Peter denies him in the courtyard.

usedIn.n: Luke 12:35-48, Slaves waiting up for the master
usedIn.s: Jesus tells his followers to be dressed for action with lamps lit, like slaves waiting for their master to come home from a wedding, and asks what a slave left in charge will do if the master is delayed.

usedIn.n: Luke 21:5-38, The temple's stones and Jerusalem surrounded
usedIn.s: When people admire the temple's stones, Jesus says not one will be left on another. He warns of false claimants, arrests in synagogues, Jerusalem surrounded by armies, and signs in the sky before the Son of Man comes.

usedIn.n: John 1:35-51, Come and see
usedIn.s: Two of John's disciples follow Jesus and spend the day with him. Andrew brings his brother Simon, Philip brings Nathanael, and Jesus promises they will see heaven opened and angels going up and down on the Son of Man.

usedIn.n: John 5:19-47, The Son sent by the Father, and his witnesses
usedIn.s: Jesus answers the charge of making himself equal with God: the Son does what he sees the Father doing, gives life and judges, and has witnesses in John, in his works, in the Father and in the Scriptures.

usedIn.n: John 12:20-50, Greeks at the feast, and the ruler of this world cast out
usedIn.s: Some Greeks who came up to worship ask to see Jesus. He says his hour has come, that the ruler of this world will be driven out, and that when he is lifted up he will draw everyone to himself; many leaders believe but stay silent.

usedIn.n: Acts 1:1-11, The kingdom question and the cloud
usedIn.s: Luke's second volume opens with the risen Jesus speaking about God's kingdom for forty days. Asked whether he will now restore the kingdom to Israel, he promises the Spirit, sends the apostles as witnesses to the end of the earth, and is taken up in a cloud.

usedIn.n: Acts 7:54-8:3, The stoning of Stephen
usedIn.s: Stephen sees the Son of Man standing at God's right hand, and his hearers drag him out and stone him while a young man named Saul looks after their coats. Persecution scatters the church.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18, Grief with hope, and the welcoming party
usedIn.s: Paul tells a grieving church that believers who have died are not lost: when the Lord comes down from heaven with a shout, the archangel's voice and God's trumpet, the dead in Christ will rise first, and the living will be caught up with them to meet the Lord in the air.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 2:5-18, The world to come is not for angels
usedIn.s: God did not put the world to come under angels. Psalm 8 promised rule to human beings; it is not yet seen, but Jesus, made a little lower than the angels for a while, is crowned with glory, and he shared flesh and blood to break the devil's power and become a merciful and faithful high priest.

usedIn.n: Revelation 1:1-8, a revelation sent as a letter
usedIn.s: The book opens as a revelation God gave Jesus, sent by his angel to his servant John, with a blessing on the one who reads it aloud and on those who hear. It then greets seven churches in Asia like a letter, from the one who is, was and is to come, and from Jesus, ruler of the kings of the earth, who is coming with the clouds.

usedIn.n: Revelation 1:9-20, Patmos, the Lord's day, lampstands and stars
usedIn.s: On the island of Patmos, in the Spirit on the Lord's day, John hears a voice like a trumpet telling him to write to seven churches. He turns and sees one like a son of man among seven golden lampstands, holding seven stars, who holds the keys of death and Hades and explains what the stars and lampstands mean.

usedIn.n: Revelation 14:6-20, Babylon fallen, the harvest and the winepress
usedIn.s: Three angels announce an eternal gospel, the fall of Babylon and the undiluted cup of God's wrath for those who worship the beast, and a voice blesses those who die in the Lord. Then one like a son of man reaps the earth's grain with a sickle, and an angel gathers its grapes into the great winepress, from which blood flows as high as the horses' bridles.

entries.title: Shepherd and sheep
entries.summary: Scripture pictured Israel without a leader as sheep without a shepherd, and promised that God himself would come to shepherd them.
aliases: the Lamb will be their shepherd
follow the Lamb wherever he goes
entries.plain: **The team had no coach, and it showed.** In the Bible a shepherd often meant a king or a leader. Sheep without a shepherd meant a people with no one to lead or protect them, scattered and hungry.
entries.then: Scripture spoke of a leaderless people of God as sheep with no shepherd (Numbers 27:17; 1 Kings 22:17; Zechariah 10:2). God himself might then step in as their shepherd (Ezekiel 34:8-16). Wright calls it a regular biblical way of describing Israel with no leader and no king. He reads it against Herod, off in his palace beheading prophets, while the people go leaderless. The question in the background is whether Jesus is the king in waiting. The ESV Study Bible links Mark 6:34 to Ezekiel 34, where God promises to shepherd the people directly because their leaders failed. It links the seating on the green grass to Psalm 23:2. At 14:27 Jesus quotes Zechariah 13:7, strike the shepherd and the sheep will scatter, a line tied back to 6:34. The shepherd of Ezekiel 34 feeds, heals and brings back the lost. Calling the crowds shepherdless implies that Israel's leaders were failing. Real shepherds stood low on the social ladder. Most people of status saw them as lowly and sometimes as rough, unclean or dangerous, and flocks kept out at night point to a warmer season. Bailey adds that shepherds were poor, and that three of the five rabbinic lists of banned trades include them, lists later than the New Testament. Describing the village shepherding he knew, Bailey says sheep follow the shepherd's voice and a few favorites have names. In a wilderness enclosure the shepherd sleeps across the opening. The Greek of Isaiah 63:11 says God brought up from the sea the shepherd of the sheep, Moses. That is the line behind the great shepherd brought back from the dead in Hebrews 13:20.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a flock whose owner has died, with hired hands who ran off. Everyone in sheep country knows what happens next unless someone steps in.
entries.changes: Sheep without a shepherd describes a people whose leaders have failed, as in Mark 6:34, and leaves room for God's promised shepherd. Sending disciples to the lost sheep of Israel, in Matthew 10:6, uses the same picture. In John 10:11 Jesus calls himself the good shepherd.
entries.not: **Not a farming problem waiting for a new hand.** In Scripture shepherd was king language, so a shepherdless flock meant a nation whose rulers had failed. The answer promised in Ezekiel 34 was God himself coming to shepherd his people, not another hired man.
entries.dissent: How low shepherds stood. On Luke 2:8, Keener says many religious people despised shepherds, whose work kept them from the community's religious life. He also writes that the Pharisees counted herding an unclean trade. Bailey calls shepherds close to the bottom of the social scale. The CSB Study Bible calls their position lowly but notes that the Bible often views the role positively. It also says the temple's sacrificial sheep were kept in the fields outside Bethlehem, which Keener reports only as a suggestion of some scholars. Levine rejects the whole picture of despised shepherds. The usual proofs, Philo, the Mishnah (Qiddushin 4.14) and a late midrash on the Psalms, do not show what is claimed, and Jewish tradition used the shepherd as a positive image. The newer sources split the same way. The cultural backgrounds article Caesar and Christ calls shepherds lowly and often despised. Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary, agrees they were lower class. But he notes that the picture of dishonest shepherds comes from later rabbinic writings, and that the Bible's portrait is almost always positive.

usedIn.n: Matthew 9:35-10:15, The Twelve sent with nothing
usedIn.s: Seeing the crowds as sheep without a shepherd, Jesus sends twelve apostles to the lost sheep of Israel, with no money, bag or staff, to stay with whoever will have them.

usedIn.n: Matthew 14:13-36, Bread in a deserted place, a walk on the sea
usedIn.s: Jesus feeds five thousand men, besides women and children, in a deserted place, then comes to the disciples walking on the lake, and Peter tries to walk to him.

usedIn.n: Matthew 18:1-14, Little ones, a millstone and their angels
usedIn.s: Asked who is greatest in the kingdom, Jesus stands a child among the disciples. He warns against causing little ones to stumble, speaks of their angels, and tells of a shepherd who leaves ninety-nine sheep.

usedIn.n: Matthew 25:31-46, Sheep, goats and the least of these
usedIn.s: The Son of Man comes in glory with his angels, gathers the nations, and separates them as a shepherd separates sheep from goats, judging them by how they treated the least of his brothers and sisters.

usedIn.n: Mark 6:30-52, Bread in a deserted place, a walk on the sea
usedIn.s: Jesus feeds five thousand men from five loaves and two fish, then comes to his disciples walking on the lake at night.

usedIn.n: Mark 14:12-31, The Passover meal
usedIn.s: Jesus eats the Passover with the Twelve, names a betrayer at the table, gives the bread and the cup new meaning, and warns that all will scatter.

usedIn.n: Luke 2:8-20, Shepherds hear of a savior
usedIn.s: Angels announce to shepherds in the fields near Bethlehem the birth of a savior who is Christ the Lord, and the shepherds find the child lying in a manger as they were told.

usedIn.n: Luke 15:1-10, A lost sheep and a lost coin
usedIn.s: Pharisees and teachers grumble that Jesus welcomes sinners and eats with them. He answers with a shepherd who searches for one lost sheep and a woman who sweeps the house for one lost coin.

usedIn.n: John 10:1-21, The good shepherd and the hired hand
usedIn.s: Jesus contrasts the shepherd who enters by the gate, calls his sheep by name and lays down his life for them with thieves who climb in another way and a hired hand who runs from the wolf.

usedIn.n: John 16:16-33, A woman in labor
usedIn.s: Jesus tells the puzzled disciples that in a little while they will not see him and then will see him again, and that their grief will turn to joy like a mother's after childbirth. He warns that they will be scattered.

usedIn.n: John 21:15-25, Feed my sheep, and stretch out your hands
usedIn.s: Three times Jesus asks Peter whether he loves him and three times tells him to tend his sheep. He foretells Peter's death and answers his question about the beloved disciple, whose testimony closes the book.

usedIn.n: Acts 20:17-38, Farewell to the Ephesian elders
usedIn.s: Hurrying to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost, Paul calls the elders of Ephesus to Miletus. He reminds them how he lived among them, warns of wolves who will attack the flock, charges them as overseers to shepherd God's church, and leaves them in tears.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 4:1-16, The conqueror goes up and gives gifts
usedIn.s: Paul urges unity, one body and one Spirit, then reads Psalm 68 as Christ ascending in victory and handing out gifts: apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers, to equip the church to grow up into him.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 13:18-25, Timothy released, greetings from Italy
usedIn.s: The writer asks for prayer so that he may be restored to his readers soon, blesses them in the name of the God of peace who brought back from the dead the great shepherd of the sheep, calls the letter a brief word of exhortation, and reports that Timothy has been released. Those from Italy send greetings.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 2:18-25, Household slaves and a harsh master
usedIn.s: Peter tells household slaves to submit to their masters, the harsh as well as the kind, because suffering unjustly while doing good is commendable before God. Christ suffered for them, leaving an example: insulted, he did not insult in return, and by his wounds they have been healed.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 5:1-14, Elders, the roaring lion, and greetings from Babylon
usedIn.s: As a fellow elder Peter urges the elders to shepherd God's flock willingly, not for gain, until the Chief Shepherd gives them an unfading crown. All must be humble, for their adversary the devil prowls like a roaring lion. Peter writes through Silvanus and sends greetings from she who is in Babylon and from his son Mark.

usedIn.n: Revelation 7:1-17, the sealing of the 144,000 and the crowd in white
usedIn.s: Four angels hold back the winds until God's servants are sealed on their foreheads, 144,000 from the tribes of Israel. Then John sees a crowd no one can count, from every nation, in white robes with palm branches, who have come out of the great tribulation and whom the Lamb will shepherd.

usedIn.n: Revelation 14:1-5, the Lamb and the 144,000 on Mount Zion
usedIn.s: The Lamb stands on Mount Zion with 144,000 who bear his name and his Father's on their foreheads, singing a new song only they can learn. They have kept themselves pure, follow the Lamb wherever he goes, and are offered as firstfruits to God and the Lamb.

entries.title: Gehenna
entries.summary: The valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, a place with a dark history, whose name had become the word for the fiery place of the wicked after death.
aliases: fire prepared for the devil and his angels
entries.plain: **Everybody in town knew the name of the valley, and nobody wanted their name connected with it.** Gehenna is the Greek form of a Hebrew place name, the valley of Hinnom, just outside Jerusalem. Kings of Judah had burned children there to a foreign god. By Jesus' day the name had become the usual word for the place where the wicked are punished after death.
entries.then: Gehenna is the Greek form of Gehinnom, which in Judaism had come to mean the abode of the wicked dead in torment. Jewish teachers disagreed about it. In some views the wicked were burned up, in others tormented without end, and some sources had the wicked detained or even released. Heiser traces the name to the valley where Ahaz and Manasseh burned their sons to Molech. He writes that by New Testament times "gehenna had become a designation for the fiery realm of the dead." Wright's glossary places the valley on Jerusalem's south-west slopes and writes, "From ancient times it was used as a garbage dump," smoldering with a continual fire. By Jesus' time some Jews used the name for punishment after death. Other Jewish texts set the damned in outer darkness (1 Enoch 10:4-6) or a furnace. Matthew 25:41 speaks of fire made ready for the devil and his angels. Heiser notes that the Old Testament has no such idea and traces it to 1 Enoch's account of the Watchers' punishment. Keener adds that the Qumran War Scroll has Belial created for the pit, and that Jesus here sides with the teachers who held the punishment to be eternal. Jewish pictures of Gehenna typically included flame, so a tongue set on fire by it shows where its fire leads. Revelation's lake of fire is a striking picture, since lakes hold water. Daniel 7:10 has a river of fire before God's throne, Greeks pictured one in the underworld, and 1 Enoch 90 sends fallen angels and the wicked into an abyss of fire.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a town whose old execution ground has given its name to every curse and nightmare. Say the name and nobody thinks of geography.
entries.changes: Gehenna names the end of the road in the strongest warnings, as in Matthew 5:22 and Mark 9:43. Its pictures, fire, furnace and outer darkness, were familiar from other Jewish texts. The same word stands behind warnings about the tongue in James 3:6.
entries.not: **Not a curse word for a place in the past.** The valley's dark history was child sacrifice, not executions, and by Jesus' day its name meant a real place of punishment after death. Jewish teachers argued over whether the wicked there burned up or suffered without end, a debate no swear word carries.
entries.dissent: Three disagreements. First, why the valley meant fire. Heiser points to its history of child sacrifice. Wright's glossary describes a smoldering garbage dump. Wilkins, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary, says the valley was later used to burn Jerusalem's refuse, so its constant burning suited fires of punishment. The Zondervan dictionary also says a fire was kept burning there to consume the city's refuse, and no source read here denies the dump. Second, what Jesus' warnings mainly concern. Wright reads many of them as judgment coming on Jerusalem in his own generation, blended with final judgment. Keener's glossary and notes read them as individual judgment after death. Third, how long punishment lasts: Jewish sources differed, as Keener notes.

ddd.s: The god associated with child sacrifice in a valley outside Jerusalem that gave us the word Gehenna.
Angels who, in 1 Enoch, come down to earth, marry women, and teach humanity things it should not know.
The Greek word for slanderer, used interchangeably with Satan.

usedIn.n: Matthew 3:1-12, John at the Jordan
usedIn.s: John preaches repentance in the Judean wilderness because the kingdom of heaven has come near. He calls Pharisees and Sadducees a brood of vipers and warns of the winnowing fork.

usedIn.n: Matthew 5:21-32, Anger, lust and divorce
usedIn.s: Jesus takes the commands against murder and adultery to the heart, warns of the fire of Gehenna, and speaks against divorce except for sexual immorality.

usedIn.n: Matthew 10:16-42, Wolves, floggings, a sword and a cup of water
usedIn.s: Jesus warns the Twelve of councils, floggings in synagogues and trials before governors and kings, of family turned against family, and promises that whoever receives them receives him.

usedIn.n: Matthew 13:24-52, Darnel, mustard, yeast, treasure and a net
usedIn.s: More parables of the kingdom: weeds sown among wheat, a mustard seed, yeast in flour, treasure in a field, a pearl, and a dragnet, with the weeds and the net explained as the judgment at the end of the age.

usedIn.n: Matthew 25:31-46, Sheep, goats and the least of these
usedIn.s: The Son of Man comes in glory with his angels, gathers the nations, and separates them as a shepherd separates sheep from goats, judging them by how they treated the least of his brothers and sisters.

usedIn.n: James 3:1-4:10, The tongue on fire, zeal and wars
usedIn.s: James warns would-be teachers that the tongue is a small fire set alight by hell, contrasts bitter envy and selfish ambition with the peaceable wisdom from above, traces fights and quarrels to desires at war within, calls friendship with the world enmity with God, and tells his readers to resist the devil.

usedIn.n: 2 Peter 2:1-10, Angels in Tartarus, Noah, Sodom and Lot
usedIn.s: As there were false prophets in Israel, so false teachers will come, greedy and denying the Master who bought them. God punished the angels who sinned, keeping them bound in darkness in Tartarus for judgment; he swept away the ancient world but kept Noah; he burned Sodom and Gomorrah but rescued righteous Lot. So the Lord knows how to rescue the godly and keep the unrighteous for judgment.

usedIn.n: Revelation 20:7-15, Gog and Magog and the great white throne
usedIn.s: Released at the end of the thousand years, Satan gathers Gog and Magog, the nations from the four corners of the earth, around the camp of God's people, but fire from heaven consumes them and the devil is thrown into the lake of fire. Before a great white throne the dead, given up by the sea, death and Hades, are judged from the books, and anyone not found in the book of life is thrown into the lake of fire, the second death.

entries.title: Hades and Abraham's side
entries.summary: Jews spoke of the dead going down to Hades, and of the righteous resting at Abraham's side or in paradise. The pictures were traditional, varied, and could be borrowed by a story.
entries.plain: **Grandma is with Grandpa now, my aunt said, and nobody at the funeral asked where exactly.** Jews in Jesus' day had several ways of talking about what happens at death. Hades, the Greek name for the Old Testament's Sheol, was simply the place of the dead. The righteous were pictured resting at Abraham's side, close to him the way an honored guest lay close to the host at a feast, or in paradise, the garden of Eden. The wicked were pictured in torment. The pictures were familiar, and they did not all fit together.
entries.then: Blomberg calls Abraham's bosom and Hades "two traditional Jewish names for the places of the righteous and wicked dead." The picture of Abraham's side comes from the banquet, where the most honored guest reclined nearest the host, his head close to the host's chest. True Israelites, martyrs above all, hoped for a place beside Abraham in the age to come. Many believed that descent from Abraham secured a seat at the feast with the patriarchs. Hades by itself names the realm of the dead, the Greek equivalent of Sheol. Where torment and fire are added, it is what Jewish tradition called Gehinnom, or something like it, and Jewish literature often pictured hell as burning. In Jewish stories and art, angels carried the righteous off to paradise, and demons sometimes hauled the wicked away; Blomberg points especially to the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs. Paradise, the garden of Eden, was set over against Gehenna. Jewish texts disputed where it lay, in the third heaven or at the edge of the earth, but often made it the home of the righteous after death or after the resurrection. The Talmud uses both paradise and Abraham's side for the place of blessedness. A folk tale in which a rich man and a poor man trade places after death, Egyptian in origin, was retold in Jewish circles (Blomberg). Keener calls the rabbinic form of it a story of uncertain date.
entries.bridge: An analogy: people today say a loved one is in a better place, or looking down on us, without drawing a map. Everyone knows the phrases, they comfort and they warn, and nobody takes them for a floor plan.
entries.changes: The poor man at Abraham's side and the rich man in Hades, in Luke 16:22-23, are placed with names every hearer knew, and then the expected places are reversed. Paradise named the home of the righteous, and Paul uses the word in 2 Corinthians 12:4 for the place he was caught up to. In Revelation 20:13-14 death and Hades give up their dead and are themselves thrown into the lake of fire.
entries.not: **Not vague comfort words.** The Jewish pictures were concrete: a banquet beside Abraham, angels carrying the righteous to paradise, fire and torment for the wicked. They carried claims too, since many believed descent from Abraham secured a place at the feast. They were still not a map; Jewish texts did not agree even on where paradise lay.
entries.dissent: How much Luke 16 teaches about the afterlife. Keener says some of its details are standard Jewish tradition and some only make the story work. The ESV Study Bible grants that the details should not be pressed but holds that the story seems clearly to teach awareness at once after death. Blomberg suggests that Abraham's side may be better defined as a relationship with God than as a place.

ddd.s: Death and the grave, treated in Revelation as figures who ride and get thrown into fire.

usedIn.n: Luke 16:19-31, The rich man and Lazarus
usedIn.s: A rich man feasts every day while a beggar named Lazarus lies at his gate. Both die; Lazarus is carried to Abraham's side, and the rich man finds himself in torment in Hades.

usedIn.n: Luke 23:26-49, The road to the cross, paradise, and the ninth hour
usedIn.s: Simon of Cyrene carries the cross, the women of Jerusalem mourn, and Jesus warns them of days to come. Crucified between two criminals, he promises one of them paradise and dies at the ninth hour.

entries.title: Prophets rejected and killed
entries.summary: Israel's memory of prophets mocked, beaten and killed by their own people. By Jesus' day tradition had lengthened the list of martyred prophets.
aliases: the world was not worthy of them
the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord
entries.plain: **The whistle-blower was the last person his own town wanted to hear from.** Israel's Scriptures tell of prophets who were ignored, jailed or killed for bringing God's word. Jewish tradition remembered even more of them. So to be rejected for speaking God's word put you in old company.
entries.then: Many Old Testament prophets suffered for bringing God's word to Israel (Jeremiah 26:11), and Jewish tradition increased the number of prophetic martyrs and made it a major theme. The burden of proof lay on the prophet who said what people wanted to hear. Rejection at home was an old pattern: Jeremiah was threatened by the men of his own town, Anathoth. Most Jews did not think prophets in the Old Testament sense still existed. Comparing disciples to the prophets therefore gave them an extraordinary role. Judaism honored martyrs for God's law, but Keener notes that no other rabbi called disciples to die for his own name. Wright reads Jesus' expectation of his own death in this prophetic mould, with Jerusalem as the city that kills the prophets. Tradition added to the list. Some Jewish traditions held that Jeremiah was stoned, and that Isaiah, hiding in a tree, was sawn in two under Manasseh. Prophets driven out of society wore skins and lived in the wilderness and in caves.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a long honor roll of reporters jailed for telling the truth. Each new name added to it is shamed by those who jailed him and honored by those who read the list.
entries.changes: Persecution puts the followers in line with the prophets, as in Matthew 5:11-12. A prophet's rejection by his own town was expected, which is the proverb at Mark 6:4. Stephen turns the tradition on his hearers in Acts 7:52.
entries.not: **Not a list of strangers.** The honor roll picture breaks because Israel's prophets were rejected by their own people, the very nation they spoke for, and the sources describe an honored tradition about faithfulness under pressure, not a wish to suffer.

usedIn.n: Matthew 5:1-12, The Beatitudes
usedIn.s: Jesus sits on a mountain to teach and pronounces God's blessing on the poor in spirit, the mourners, the meek, the merciful, the peacemakers and the persecuted.

usedIn.n: Matthew 7:13-29, Two ways, false prophets, two builders
usedIn.s: Jesus ends his sermon with the narrow gate, a warning about false prophets known by their fruit, and two houses built on rock and on sand. The crowd is struck by his authority.

usedIn.n: Matthew 13:53-58, No honor in Nazareth
usedIn.s: Teaching in his hometown synagogue, Jesus is dismissed as the carpenter's son whose family everyone knows, and he says a prophet is not without honor except at home.

usedIn.n: Matthew 21:23-46, By what authority, two sons and the tenants
usedIn.s: The chief priests and elders demand to know Jesus' authority. He answers with a question about John, then with two parables: a son who says no and goes, and tenants who kill the owner's son.

usedIn.n: Luke 4:16-30, The year of the Lord's favor in Nazareth
usedIn.s: In the Nazareth synagogue Jesus reads Isaiah's promise of good news for the poor and release for captives and says it is fulfilled today. When he points to Elijah and Elisha helping foreigners, the town tries to throw him off a cliff.

usedIn.n: Luke 6:20-36, Blessings, woes and lending with nothing back
usedIn.s: Jesus blesses the poor, the hungry, the weeping and the hated, pronounces woes on the rich and the well fed, and tells his hearers to love enemies, turn the other cheek and lend without expecting anything back.

usedIn.n: Luke 11:37-54, Woes at a Pharisee's table
usedIn.s: At a Pharisee's meal Jesus does not wash before eating, and when his host is surprised he pronounces woes on Pharisees and lawyers: clean cups and greedy hearts, tithed herbs, the best seats, unmarked graves and the tombs of the prophets.

usedIn.n: Luke 13:22-35, The narrow door, the feast, the fox and the hen
usedIn.s: On the way to Jerusalem Jesus warns that many will find the door shut while people from east and west recline at the feast in God's kingdom. Warned that Herod wants to kill him, he calls Herod a fox and grieves over Jerusalem.

usedIn.n: Luke 20:9-19, The tenants who killed the heir
usedIn.s: Jesus tells of a vineyard owner whose tenants beat his servants and kill his beloved son to take the inheritance. The leaders realize he has told it against them.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 11:32-40, Sawn in two, dressed in skins
usedIn.s: Time fails to tell of the judges, David, Samuel and the prophets, who conquered kingdoms and escaped the sword. Others were tortured and refused release to gain a better resurrection; they were mocked, flogged, chained, stoned, sawn in two, and wandered in skins and caves, people the world was not worthy of.

usedIn.n: James 5:7-12, Early and late rains, Job, and no oaths
usedIn.s: James tells the oppressed to be patient until the Lord comes, as a farmer waits for the autumn and spring rains, to stop grumbling, to remember the prophets and Job, and above all not to swear.

entries.title: The satan, the tempter
entries.summary: The accuser, tempter and deceiver of Jewish belief, seen as the power behind human and political evil. In the Gospels he tests Jesus and is the strong man Jesus binds, and John calls him the ruler of this world.
aliases: prince of the power of the air
ruler of the kingdom of the air
ruler of the realm of the air
spirit at work in the disobedient
the one who is in the world
the whole world under the evil one
the evil one cannot harm them
disputing about the body of Moses
entries.plain: **The prosecutor who has spent years building a case against you shows up in person with an offer.** Satan is Hebrew for accuser. In the Old Testament the satan appears in God's court bringing charges. By Jesus' day many Jews saw him as the great tempter and deceiver, the power behind evil in people and in nations. The Gospels show him facing Jesus directly.
entries.then: The Hebrew word means the accuser. At times he is a member of God's heavenly council acting as prosecutor (Job 1-2; Zechariah 3). Later he was identified with the serpent in Eden, and many Jews saw him as the source behind both human wickedness and large-scale injustice. He is accuser, tempter and deceiver, and the word devil means slanderer. What would surprise most Jewish readers in Matthew 4, Keener notes, is the devil tempting in person. Heiser reads the testing against Deuteronomy 32:8-9, where the nations were handed to lesser gods at Babel. He writes, "Satan offered Jesus the nations that had been disinherited by Yahweh at Babel." Nearly all Jewish texts make God ruler of the world. Yet they speak of fallen angels ruling much of it under his decree, with their prince ruling most of the world except Israel. Judaism expected their defeat only when the kingdom came. Jewish texts recognized Satan's dominion over the world. Of the title prince of this world, though, the cultural backgrounds notes say "there is no record of them using this title for him." Keener reads the binding of the strong man as a sign that Jesus has already defeated Satan. Many Jewish sources say Satan or demons were bound after God subdued them. The prince of demons had many names. Beelzebul is related to Baal-zebub of 2 Kings 1:2, and Heiser traces it to a Ugaritic title of Baal, prince, lord of the underworld. The rabbis called him Sammael, Jubilees Beliar or Mastema, and the Dead Sea Scrolls Belial, from a Hebrew word for worthlessness. Judaism held that Satan deceived and came in disguises.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a rebel warlord who controls provinces he was never given and offers to share them with the rightful heir if he will just bow once. The offer is real enough to tempt, and accepting it would concede the warlord's claim.
entries.changes: The satan stands behind the testing in the wilderness, as in Matthew 4:1-11, where the offer of the kingdoms is the center. In the Beelzebul dispute of Mark 3:23-27 Jesus pictures his exorcisms as robbing a strong man's house. In Luke 10:18 Satan falls like lightning as the mission goes out.
entries.not: **Not a rival with power of his own.** A warlord holds what he seized by his own strength. In these sources the satan is a created being, and Jewish texts had the fallen angels ruling only under God's decree, with their defeat already promised.
entries.dissent: Whether the kingdoms were his to give. Keener says the devil held them only as a usurper, and the CSB Study Bible says they belong to God. Heiser holds that the offer was real, since Satan was presumed lord over the rebel gods of the nations. Second, what Jesus saw in Luke 10:18. Keener and the ESV Study Bible read Satan's power broken. Wright hears the prophets on the ancient enemy's downfall. Heiser reads Satan's expulsion from God's council, his work as accuser finished. Third, who the ruler of this world is. The ESV and CSB Study Bibles say Satan, defeated at the cross. Wright reads two levels: Caesar, and "the dark power that stands behind even Caesar." Fourth, the god of this age in 2 Corinthians 4:4. Heiser grants, "Nearly all scholars identify this figure as Satan," but notes that the name is not in the verse and the phrase may mean God himself (Isaiah 6:9-10). Fifth, when Satan is thrown down in Revelation 12. Keener and Beale place it at Christ's death and exaltation, Heiser at the kingdom's start. Arnold calls it "an event that is yet future", and the CSB Study Bible agrees.
