xref.s: The Most High divided the nations, and the number He divided them by is where the whole argument turns.
The sons of God present themselves and the satan comes among them.
The nachash in the garden, and the sentence passed on it.
Seventy sent out, and Satan falling like lightning when they return.

ddd.s: The name the New Testament gives the chief adversary, a role that had become a name.
The Greek word for slanderer, used interchangeably with Satan.
The accuser in Job, a job title in God's court rather than a personal name.
The name Jesus's opponents used for the ruler of demons when they accused him.
A Philistine god whose name Israel deliberately misspelled into lord of the flies.
John's title for Satan, conceding real authority and announcing its end.
A Hebrew word for worthlessness that hardened into a name for the enemy of God.
Paul calls the blinder of unbelievers a god, and translators have to decide what case to use.
The talking serpent of Eden, which the New Testament identifies with Satan though Genesis never does.

ddd.n: The prince of the power of the air
ddd.s: Paul's title for the ruling evil power, with the air meaning contested territory overhead.
The beast of Revelation, identified there as the serpent, the devil and Satan all at once.

usedIn.n: Matthew 3:13-4:11, Baptism and the test in the desert
usedIn.s: Jesus is baptized and hears the voice from heaven, then is led into the wilderness for forty days, where the devil tests him three times.

usedIn.n: Matthew 12:22-50, Beelzebul, the strong man, Jonah and his true family
usedIn.s: When Jesus heals a blind and mute man, the crowds wonder if he is the Son of David and the Pharisees say he works by Beelzebul. Jesus answers with the strong man, refuses a sign except Jonah's, and names his true family.

usedIn.n: Luke 4:1-13, The devil offers the kingdoms
usedIn.s: Full of the Spirit, Jesus is led through the wilderness for forty days, where the devil tests him with bread, with all the kingdoms of the world, and with a leap from the temple.

usedIn.n: Luke 10:1-24, Seventy sent out, and Satan falling
usedIn.s: Jesus sends seventy others, or seventy-two, ahead of him in pairs, with no purse, bag or sandals, to towns that will welcome or refuse them. They come back rejoicing that even the demons obey, and Jesus says he saw Satan fall like lightning.

usedIn.n: Luke 11:14-26, By Beelzebul, or by the finger of God?
usedIn.s: When Jesus drives out a demon that kept a man from speaking, some say he does it by Beelzebul, the ruler of demons. He answers that a divided kingdom falls, and that if he drives out demons by the finger of God, God's kingdom has come.

usedIn.n: Luke 13:10-21, A bent woman freed on the Sabbath; mustard and leaven
usedIn.s: Teaching in a synagogue on the Sabbath, Jesus frees a woman bent double for eighteen years. The synagogue ruler objects, and Jesus answers with an ox untied for water, then compares God's kingdom to a mustard seed and to leaven.

usedIn.n: Luke 22:24-38, Benefactors, thrones, sifting and two swords
usedIn.s: At the last supper the disciples argue over who is greatest. Jesus contrasts kings who are called benefactors with himself as one who serves, promises them thrones, warns Peter that Satan has asked to sift them, and speaks of swords.

usedIn.n: John 8:31-59, Abraham's children, and before Abraham, I am
usedIn.s: Jesus tells Judeans who had believed him that the truth will make them free. They answer that they are Abraham's children and were never slaves, and the argument ends with Jesus saying before Abraham was, I am, and stones in their hands.

usedIn.n: John 12:20-50, Greeks at the feast, and the ruler of this world cast out
usedIn.s: Some Greeks who came up to worship ask to see Jesus. He says his hour has come, that the ruler of this world will be driven out, and that when he is lifted up he will draw everyone to himself; many leaders believe but stay silent.

usedIn.n: John 14:1-31, Rooms in the Father's house, and another Advocate
usedIn.s: Jesus tells his troubled disciples that he is going to prepare a place for them in his Father's house, that he is the way, and that the Father will send another Advocate, the Spirit of truth. He leaves them his peace.

usedIn.n: John 15:18-16:15, Hated by the world and put out of the synagogue
usedIn.s: Jesus warns that the world will hate his followers as it hated him, that they will be put out of the synagogues and even killed by people who think they are serving God, and that the Advocate will prove the world wrong.

usedIn.n: Acts 4:32-5:11, Barnabas, Ananias and Sapphira
usedIn.s: The believers share everything, and Barnabas sells a field for the common fund. Ananias and Sapphira sell land too but lie about the price, and both fall dead.

usedIn.n: Romans 16:17-27, Tertius, Gaius and Erastus
usedIn.s: Paul warns against those who cause divisions, promises that God will soon crush Satan under the believers' feet, and passes on greetings from Corinth, including his scribe Tertius, his host Gaius and Erastus the city treasurer.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 5:1-13, A man and his father's wife
usedIn.s: A church member is living with his stepmother and the church is proud of itself. Paul tells them to hand the man over to Satan, clear out the old leaven as a household does before Passover, and not eat with a so-called brother who lives that way.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 2:5-13, Forgive the offender; no rest at Troas
usedIn.s: The man who caused the grief has been punished enough by the majority, so Paul urges the church to forgive him lest Satan outwit them, then tells how he left an open door at Troas because Titus had not come.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 4:1-6, The god of this age
usedIn.s: Paul renounces cunning and tampering with God's word; if his gospel is veiled, it is veiled to the perishing, whose minds the god of this age has blinded, while God has made his light shine in believers' hearts.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 6:14-7:1, Unequal yoke, Belial and the temple of God
usedIn.s: Paul tells the Corinthians not to be yoked with unbelievers, for light has no fellowship with darkness nor Christ with Belial, and calls them the temple of the living God, who must come out and be separate.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 11:1-15, The betrothed virgin, the free gospel and the angel of light
usedIn.s: Jealous as a father who has promised his daughter to one husband, Paul fears the Corinthians will be led astray as Eve was; he defends preaching to them free of charge and calls his rivals false apostles disguised as Satan disguises himself as an angel of light.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 12:1-10, Caught up to the third heaven; the thorn
usedIn.s: Paul tells of a man caught up to the third heaven and into paradise who heard things no one may utter, then of the thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan, which God would not remove because his power is made perfect in weakness.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 2:1-10, The ruler of the kingdom of the air
usedIn.s: Paul reminds his readers that they were once dead in sins, following the ruler of the kingdom of the air, until God in his mercy made them alive and seated them with Christ in the heavenly realms, saved by grace.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 4:17-32, No longer as the Gentiles live
usedIn.s: Paul tells Gentile believers to stop living as the Gentiles do, to put off the old self and put on the new, to give the devil no foothold, to work with their hands and share, and not to grieve the Spirit who sealed them.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 6:10-17, The armor of God
usedIn.s: Paul calls the believers to stand firm in God's armor, because their struggle is not against flesh and blood but against rulers, authorities and spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 2:17-3:13, Orphaned, blocked by Satan, crowned
usedIn.s: Torn away from the church, Paul tells how he longed to come back but Satan blocked the way, how he sent Timothy from Athens, how Timothy's good news has revived him, and prays that the Lord will make them blameless at his coming with all his holy ones.

usedIn.n: 2 Thessalonians 2:1-12, The man of lawlessness and the restrainer
usedIn.s: Paul tells a church unsettled by claims that the day of the Lord has already come that the rebellion must come first and the man of lawlessness be revealed, who sets himself up in God's temple claiming to be God; something holds him back for now, and the Lord Jesus will destroy him by the breath of his mouth.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 1:12-20, A blasphemer shown mercy, and two men handed over to Satan
usedIn.s: Paul thanks Christ for taking a former blasphemer and persecutor into his service as an example of mercy, then charges Timothy to fight the battle well, as the prophecies about him foretold, unlike Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom Paul has handed over to Satan.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 2:14-26, Gangrene, a resurrection already past, and vessels in a great house
usedIn.s: Timothy is to warn the church against quarreling about words and to handle the word of truth correctly; the teaching of Hymenaeus and Philetus, who say the resurrection has already happened, spreads like gangrene, but God's foundation stands sealed, and in a great house some vessels are for honor and some for dishonor.

usedIn.n: James 1:1-18, To the twelve tribes scattered
usedIn.s: James greets the twelve tribes scattered among the nations, tells them to count their trials as joy and to ask God for wisdom, warns that the rich will wither like a wildflower, and insists that God tempts no one but gives every good gift from above, as the Father of lights.

usedIn.n: James 3:1-4:10, The tongue on fire, zeal and wars
usedIn.s: James warns would-be teachers that the tongue is a small fire set alight by hell, contrasts bitter envy and selfish ambition with the peaceable wisdom from above, traces fights and quarrels to desires at war within, calls friendship with the world enmity with God, and tells his readers to resist the devil.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 5:1-14, Elders, the roaring lion, and greetings from Babylon
usedIn.s: As a fellow elder Peter urges the elders to shepherd God's flock willingly, not for gain, until the Chief Shepherd gives them an unfading crown. All must be humble, for their adversary the devil prowls like a roaring lion. Peter writes through Silvanus and sends greetings from she who is in Babylon and from his son Mark.

usedIn.n: 1 John 2:28-3:24, Children of God, Cain, and love in deed
usedIn.s: Those who do right are born of God, whose love makes them his children, and when he appears they will be like him. Whoever keeps on sinning belongs to the devil, who has sinned from the beginning, and the Son came to undo his work. The readers are not to be like Cain, who murdered his brother, but to love in deed and in truth, as Christ laid down his life.

usedIn.n: 1 John 4:1-6, Test the spirits
usedIn.s: The readers must test every spirit instead of trusting each one, since many false prophets are now abroad. A spirit that confesses Jesus Christ as truly come in the flesh is from God, and one that refuses is the spirit of the antichrist. God in them is greater than the power in the world, and this is how the Spirit of truth is told from the spirit of error.

usedIn.n: 1 John 5:13-21, The sin that leads to death, the evil one and idols
usedIn.s: John writes so that believers may know they have eternal life, and that God hears them. They are to pray for a brother or sister whose sin does not lead to death, though there is a sin that does. Those born of God are kept from the evil one, while the whole world lies under his power; the letter ends with a warning to keep away from idols.

usedIn.n: Jude 8-13, Michael and the body of Moses, and hidden reefs at the love feasts
usedIn.s: The intruders claim dream visions, defile the body, despise authority and slander the glorious ones, though the archangel Michael, disputing with the devil over the body of Moses, did not dare to slander him but left the rebuke to the Lord. They have taken the way of Cain, Balaam and Korah; they are hidden reefs at the love feasts, waterless clouds, wild waves and wandering stars.

usedIn.n: Revelation 2:8-11, Smyrna, poor and slandered
usedIn.s: To Smyrna the risen Jesus says he sees their hardship and poverty and the abuse they suffer from local opponents claiming to be the true Jews, whom he condemns in harsh terms. Some will be jailed for a short time; if they stay loyal even to death he will reward them with life.

usedIn.n: Revelation 12:1-6, the woman, the child and the dragon
usedIn.s: A radiant woman, crowned with twelve stars and standing on the moon, labors to give birth while a great red dragon waits to devour her child. The child, destined to rule the nations, is caught up to God's throne, and the woman escapes to the wilderness, where she is kept safe for 1,260 days.

usedIn.n: Revelation 12:7-17, war in heaven and the accuser thrown down
usedIn.s: Michael and his angels fight the dragon and throw him out of heaven, and a voice celebrates the fall of the accuser of the brothers, defeated by the Lamb's blood and the witnesses' testimony. On earth the dragon chases the woman, who is given eagle's wings, and when the earth swallows the river he spews after her, he turns to make war on her other children.

entries.title: Parables and riddles
entries.summary: Short stories that compared one thing to another. Jewish teachers used them to make a point plain, and without the point stated they worked as riddles.
entries.plain: **The teacher told a story about a farmer, and only the ones who stayed after class found out what it meant.** A parable is a comparison told as a story. Jewish teachers used them all the time. Jesus' parables come from farm and village life. Some hearers got the point; for others the story stayed a puzzle.
entries.then: Jewish sages used parables to illustrate a point. If the point was not stated, the parable amounted to a story or a riddle, and rabbis kept some teaching for close disciples. Openings such as to what may this be compared, or the kingdom is like a man who, meant that the whole story explained the subject, not the next word. Wright argues that "the parables followed well-known Jewish lines." He points to Old Testament models such as Nathan's story to David and the vineyard, and to visions explained afterward, as in Daniel 7. Jesus' parables stay with farmers and villages, while later rabbinic parables favor royal courts. Blomberg argues for limited allegory: a few main characters, each carrying a point. The Hebrew mashal, often rendered parabole in the Greek Old Testament, covered proverb, riddle and comparison, and the word appears nine times in Sirach. Most of Jesus' parables tell a story. The cultural backgrounds article calls that a Jewish form, nearer to the story parables of the rabbis than to Greek fables. Jewish parables often came with interpretations attached, and in the article's judgment the ones without them are what look odd in antiquity.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a political cartoon. Readers who know the situation get it at once and laugh or wince. Readers who do not see only a funny drawing of animals.
entries.changes: A parable compares the kingdom to a whole scene, so in Matthew 13:24 the kingdom is like the story, not like the man. Without its explanation a parable could hide its point, which is why the disciples ask in private, as in Mark 4:10. Luke 15 answers critics with three in a row.
entries.not: **Not something every insider got at once.** A cartoon is drawn to be understood on sight by anyone who knows the news. A parable whose point went unstated worked more like a riddle, and rabbis kept some teaching for close disciples, so even an informed hearer might need it explained.
entries.dissent: How far rabbinic parables can be used as background. Keener writes as if rabbis commonly taught in parables. Blomberg counts 325 early rabbinic parables and says almost none can be dated to the first half of the first century: "The examples surveyed are largely second- or third-century compositions." The sources also differ on whether the allegorical explanations in the Gospels go back to Jesus; Blomberg defends a limited allegory, and the cultural backgrounds article answers the doubters that other Jewish parables also carried interpretations with several points of contact.

usedIn.n: Matthew 7:13-29, Two ways, false prophets, two builders
usedIn.s: Jesus ends his sermon with the narrow gate, a warning about false prophets known by their fruit, and two houses built on rock and on sand. The crowd is struck by his authority.

usedIn.n: Matthew 11:2-30, John's question, children in the square, an easy yoke
usedIn.s: John asks from prison whether Jesus is the one to come. Jesus praises John, compares his generation to sulking children, pronounces woes on the lake towns, and offers rest under his yoke.

usedIn.n: Matthew 13:1-23, The sower
usedIn.s: From a boat Jesus tells the parable of the sower to the crowd on the shore, explains why he speaks in parables, and interprets the story for his disciples.

usedIn.n: Matthew 13:24-52, Darnel, mustard, yeast, treasure and a net
usedIn.s: More parables of the kingdom: weeds sown among wheat, a mustard seed, yeast in flour, treasure in a field, a pearl, and a dragnet, with the weeds and the net explained as the judgment at the end of the age.

usedIn.n: Matthew 18:21-35, Ten thousand talents and a hundred denarii
usedIn.s: Peter asks whether forgiving seven times is enough. Jesus tells of a king who cancels an impossible debt, and of the forgiven servant who then chokes a colleague over a small one.

usedIn.n: Matthew 20:1-16, A day's wage for an hour's work
usedIn.s: A landowner hires laborers for his vineyard at dawn and again through the day, then pays everyone a full denarius, starting with the last. Those hired first complain.

usedIn.n: Matthew 21:23-46, By what authority, two sons and the tenants
usedIn.s: The chief priests and elders demand to know Jesus' authority. He answers with a question about John, then with two parables: a son who says no and goes, and tenants who kill the owner's son.

usedIn.n: Matthew 25:1-13, Ten young women and the bridegroom
usedIn.s: Ten young women wait with their lights for a bridegroom who comes late at night. Five brought extra oil and go in to the feast; five go to buy oil and find the door shut.

usedIn.n: Matthew 25:14-30, Five, two and one talent
usedIn.s: A man going abroad entrusts his property to three slaves. Two double what they were given and are rewarded; the third buries his talent and is thrown out.

usedIn.n: Luke 12:13-21, Bigger barns
usedIn.s: A man asks Jesus to make his brother divide the inheritance. Jesus refuses, warns against greed, and tells of a rich farmer who plans bigger barns for his surplus and dies that night.

usedIn.n: Luke 12:35-48, Slaves waiting up for the master
usedIn.s: Jesus tells his followers to be dressed for action with lamps lit, like slaves waiting for their master to come home from a wedding, and asks what a slave left in charge will do if the master is delayed.

usedIn.n: Luke 14:15-24, The great banquet and the excuses
usedIn.s: A guest blesses whoever will eat bread in God's kingdom. Jesus tells of a man whose invited guests all excuse themselves when the feast is ready, so he fills his house with the poor and with people from the roads.

usedIn.n: Luke 18:1-8, The widow and the judge
usedIn.s: Jesus tells of a judge who neither feared God nor respected people and a widow who kept coming to him for justice until he gave in. How much more, he says, will God see justice done for his chosen ones.

entries.title: Angels
entries.summary: God's messengers and his heavenly army. Jews of Jesus' day spoke of guardian angels, of the greatest angels standing before God's face, and of angels coming with God at the judgment.
aliases: let all God's angels worship him
seven angels who stand before God
entries.plain: **The king's couriers carried his word, and his protection, wherever they went.** In the Bible angels are God's messengers and the soldiers of his heavenly army. By Jesus' day many Jews believed that each of God's people had an angel watching over them, that the greatest angels stood before God's throne, and that angels would come with God when he judged the world. Seeing one was terrifying.
entries.then: Many Jews believed in guardian angels (Tobit 5:22 among other texts), and Keener says the usual view gave every Jewish person one. Angels took their orders from God's throne, and only the highest angels regularly saw God's glory. It was widely agreed that angels had no children, since in most traditions they did not die, and that they did not usually eat or drink. Heiser reads Jesus' words about the resurrection closely: the text says angels do not marry, not that they cannot. Ancient Judaism typically thought angels were made of fire. God's heavenly armies were invincible (2 Kings 6:17), and a legion was about six thousand soldiers. The angel of the Lord announced special births in the Old Testament (Genesis 16:11; Judges 13:3). Fear met by do not be afraid is the old pattern. Scripture names only Gabriel and Michael (Daniel 8:16; 10:13), though Jewish tradition named many more. Gabriel stood among the archangels before God's throne. Going beyond the Hebrew text, Jewish tradition said the law came through angels. Heiser traces the idea to the Greek text of Deuteronomy 33:2, where angels stand at God's right hand at Sinai. The holy ones who come with God in Zechariah 14:5 were sometimes taken as angels. In the Dead Sea Scrolls, clouds stand for the hosts of angels at God's coming. Many Jewish traditions held demons to be fallen angels. Heiser traces the fire prepared for the devil and his angels to 1 Enoch's account of the Watchers, since the Old Testament says nothing of the kind.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a sovereign's household guard and couriers, who stand in the throne room and are sent out with orders. To meet one is to meet the authority behind him.
entries.changes: Angels act as God's messengers and army, so a Son of Man who sends out his own angels, as in Matthew 24:31, does what belonged to God. Talk of a child's angel who sees God's face assumes the belief in guardian angels. Gabriel standing in God's presence and sent with news of a birth, in Luke 1:19, follows the pattern of the angel of the Lord in the Old Testament. Hebrews 1:14 calls angels ministering spirits sent out to serve.
entries.not: **Not mere staff.** A sovereign's guards are ordinary men in his pay. These sources make angels fiery beings who do not die, and Jewish tradition counted some of them fallen and turned against God. Nor do people become angels when they die.
entries.dissent: Whether Matthew 18:10 means one angel for each person. Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes point to the common Jewish belief that every Jew had a guardian angel. The ESV Study Bible says the phrase does not imply an assigned guardian for each disciple. The CSB Study Bible compares the angels of nations in Daniel 10 and reads angels representing believers before God. Second, who the mediator of Galatians 3:19 is. Keener and the ESV Study Bible name Moses, and Wright agrees that "the mediator is clearly Moses." The CSB Study Bible makes an angel the mediator. Heiser holds that "The intermediary is Yahweh in human form." Third, what the worship of angels in Colossians 2:18 was. Keener thinks some Jews abroad prayed to angels and invoked them, and Arnold writes, "It is quite possible Paul was denouncing a magical invocation of angels." The ESV Study Bible takes it as calling on angels for protection. Others read worship with the angels, joining heaven's praise as some Dead Sea Scrolls describe. Wright and Bird point to the Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice. The CSB Study Bible allows either sense, and Keener doubts Paul would attack that idea.

usedIn.n: Matthew 18:1-14, Little ones, a millstone and their angels
usedIn.s: Asked who is greatest in the kingdom, Jesus stands a child among the disciples. He warns against causing little ones to stumble, speaks of their angels, and tells of a shepherd who leaves ninety-nine sheep.

usedIn.n: Matthew 22:23-33, Seven brothers and one bride
usedIn.s: Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, pose a riddle about a woman married in turn to seven brothers. Jesus answers that the raised do not marry, and that God is the God of the living.

usedIn.n: Matthew 24:29-51, The Son of Man on the clouds and the slave in charge
usedIn.s: After the distress, sun, moon and stars fail and the Son of Man comes on the clouds to gather his chosen. No one knows the day, so the household must stay ready, like a slave left in charge.

usedIn.n: Matthew 25:31-46, Sheep, goats and the least of these
usedIn.s: The Son of Man comes in glory with his angels, gathers the nations, and separates them as a shepherd separates sheep from goats, judging them by how they treated the least of his brothers and sisters.

usedIn.n: Matthew 26:47-75, Arrest, twelve legions, the council and the rooster
usedIn.s: Judas comes with an armed crowd and a kiss. Jesus refuses the sword and the twelve legions of angels, is tried at night before Caiaphas, and is condemned for blasphemy while Peter swears he never knew him.

usedIn.n: Matthew 28:1-15, Women at dawn and a bribed guard
usedIn.s: At dawn after the Sabbath an angel rolls back the stone and tells two women that Jesus is risen. They meet him on the road, while the chief priests pay the guards to say the disciples stole the body.

usedIn.n: Luke 1:5-25, A priest's turn at the incense altar
usedIn.s: An elderly village priest, picked by lot to offer incense in the sanctuary, learns from the angel Gabriel that his childless wife will have a son who will prepare Israel for God with an Elijah-like power.

usedIn.n: Luke 1:26-56, A village girl, a greeting and a song of reversal
usedIn.s: Gabriel greets Mary, a betrothed girl in Nazareth, with news that she will bear the son of David. She goes to Elizabeth in the hill country and sings of God bringing down rulers and lifting up the humble.

usedIn.n: Luke 2:8-20, Shepherds hear of a savior
usedIn.s: Angels announce to shepherds in the fields near Bethlehem the birth of a savior who is Christ the Lord, and the shepherds find the child lying in a manger as they were told.

usedIn.n: Luke 15:1-10, A lost sheep and a lost coin
usedIn.s: Pharisees and teachers grumble that Jesus welcomes sinners and eats with them. He answers with a shepherd who searches for one lost sheep and a woman who sweeps the house for one lost coin.

usedIn.n: Luke 16:19-31, The rich man and Lazarus
usedIn.s: A rich man feasts every day while a beggar named Lazarus lies at his gate. Both die; Lazarus is carried to Abraham's side, and the rich man finds himself in torment in Hades.

usedIn.n: Luke 20:27-40, The Sadducees and the woman with seven husbands
usedIn.s: Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, ask whose wife a woman married to seven brothers will be. Jesus answers that the risen do not marry and are like the angels, and argues from the burning bush.

usedIn.n: Luke 24:36-53, Not a ghost; hands lifted in blessing
usedIn.s: Jesus stands among the disciples, who think they are seeing a ghost. He shows his hands and feet and eats fish, opens the Scriptures to them, and leads them out to Bethany, where he lifts his hands and blesses them.

usedIn.n: Acts 5:12-42, Peter's shadow, the prison and Gamaliel
usedIn.s: Crowds bring the sick for Peter's shadow to fall on them. The apostles are jailed, freed by an angel, and brought before the council, where Gamaliel compares the movement to the failed causes of Theudas and Judas the Galilean.

usedIn.n: Acts 6:8-7:53, Stephen's charge and speech
usedIn.s: Men from the Diaspora synagogues accuse Stephen of speaking against the temple and the law. He answers with Israel's story, from Abraham to the temple, and turns the charge back on his judges.

usedIn.n: Acts 12:1-25, Herod Agrippa, the prison and the king struck down
usedIn.s: King Herod Agrippa kills James and jails Peter at Passover, but an angel leads Peter out. Later, in Caesarea, the king accepts the crowd's cry that he speaks with a god's voice and is struck down.

usedIn.n: Acts 22:30-23:11, Paul before the council
usedIn.s: The tribune brings Paul before the chief priests and the council. Struck on the high priest's order, Paul calls him a whitewashed wall, then declares himself a Pharisee on trial for the hope of the resurrection, and the council splits.

usedIn.n: Romans 8:31-39, Angels, rulers and powers
usedIn.s: With God on the believers' side, Paul asks who could oppose them, then names hardships and powers, from the sword to angels, rulers, height and depth, and none of them can cut believers off from God's love in Christ.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 11:2-16, Heads covered and uncovered
usedIn.s: Paul tells men who pray or prophesy to keep their heads uncovered and women who do so to cover theirs, arguing from headship, creation, the angels, nature and the custom of the churches.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 13:1-13, Noisy bronze and a dim mirror
usedIn.s: Paul says that tongues, prophecy, knowledge, faith and even martyrdom are nothing without love, describes what love is, and sets today's partial knowledge, like a dim reflection in a mirror, against seeing face to face.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 15:35-58, Seeds, stars and the last trumpet
usedIn.s: Asked what kind of body the dead will have, Paul answers with the seed that dies and rises as a plant and with the differing glories of sun, moon and stars, sets the first Adam beside the last, and ends with the trumpet and death swallowed up.

usedIn.n: Galatians 3:15-22, A will no one can change, and a law given through angels
usedIn.s: Paul argues from the way a ratified will cannot be altered that the law, coming 430 years after the promise to Abraham and his seed, cannot cancel it, and says the law was added because of transgressions, put in place through angels by a mediator.

usedIn.n: Colossians 1:15-20, Firstborn over creation, over thrones and powers
usedIn.s: Paul describes the Son as the image of the unseen God and firstborn over all creation, through whom and for whom everything was made, thrones and powers included, and through whose cross God makes peace with all things.

usedIn.n: Colossians 2:16-23, Food, new moons, Sabbaths and the worship of angels
usedIn.s: Paul tells the believers not to let anyone judge them over food, drink, festivals, new moons or Sabbaths, or disqualify them with self-denial, the worship of angels and visions, and calls rules about what not to touch or taste human commands with no power over the flesh.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18, Grief with hope, and the welcoming party
usedIn.s: Paul tells a grieving church that believers who have died are not lost: when the Lord comes down from heaven with a shout, the archangel's voice and God's trumpet, the dead in Christ will rise first, and the living will be caught up with them to meet the Lord in the air.

usedIn.n: 2 Thessalonians 1:3-12, Suffering now, and the Lord revealed in blazing fire
usedIn.s: Paul thanks God for a church whose faith and love keep growing under persecution, and promises that God will repay their persecutors and give them relief when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his powerful angels in blazing fire.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 3:14-16, God's household and the hymn
usedIn.s: Paul writes so that, if he is delayed, Timothy will know how people ought to behave in God's household, the church of the living God, and quotes what seems to be a hymn about Christ.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 5:17-25, Double honor, two witnesses, the elect angels and a little wine
usedIn.s: Elders who lead well deserve double honor and pay; charges against them need two or three witnesses; Paul charges Timothy before God, Christ and the elect angels to act without favoritism, to lay hands on no one hastily, and to take a little wine.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 1:1-14, The Son above the angels
usedIn.s: God, who spoke in many ways through the prophets, has now spoken through a Son, heir of all things, who made purification for sins and sat down at the right hand of the Majesty. A chain of Scripture quotations sets the Son above the angels, who worship him and are sent to serve those who will inherit salvation.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 2:1-4, The message spoken through angels
usedIn.s: The readers must hold to what they have heard, or drift away. If the message spoken through angels was binding and every breach was punished, there is no escape for those who neglect the greater salvation announced by the Lord and confirmed by God with signs.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 2:5-18, The world to come is not for angels
usedIn.s: God did not put the world to come under angels. Psalm 8 promised rule to human beings; it is not yet seen, but Jesus, made a little lower than the angels for a while, is crowned with glory, and he shared flesh and blood to break the devil's power and become a merciful and faithful high priest.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 12:18-29, Sinai, Zion and the unshakable kingdom
usedIn.s: Believers have not come to the burning, quaking mountain of Sinai but to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, with myriads of angels, the assembly of the firstborn enrolled in heaven, God the judge, the spirits of the righteous, and Jesus, whose blood speaks better than Abel's. Since God will shake heaven and earth once more, they are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 13:1-6, Strangers, angels, prisoners
usedIn.s: The writer turns to everyday duties: brotherly love, hospitality to strangers, since some have entertained angels without knowing it, care for prisoners as if in prison with them, honor for marriage, and freedom from the love of money.

usedIn.n: James 2:14-26, Faith that shudders, Abraham and Rahab
usedIn.s: Faith without deeds is dead, James argues. Wishing a hungry brother well helps no one, the demons believe that God is one and shudder, and Abraham and Rahab were counted righteous by what they did.

usedIn.n: Jude 8-13, Michael and the body of Moses, and hidden reefs at the love feasts
usedIn.s: The intruders claim dream visions, defile the body, despise authority and slander the glorious ones, though the archangel Michael, disputing with the devil over the body of Moses, did not dare to slander him but left the rebuke to the Lord. They have taken the way of Cain, Balaam and Korah; they are hidden reefs at the love feasts, waterless clouds, wild waves and wandering stars.

usedIn.n: Jude 14-25, Enoch's prophecy, scoffers, and a closing doxology
usedIn.s: Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied about such people that the Lord comes with his countless holy ones to judge all and convict the ungodly. The apostles foretold scoffers in the last times; the readers are to build themselves up, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep themselves in God's love and show mercy, snatching some from the fire. Jude closes with praise to the one able to keep them from stumbling.

usedIn.n: Revelation 8:1-13, silence, incense and the first four trumpets
usedIn.s: The seventh seal brings half an hour of silence in heaven. Seven angels receive trumpets, an angel offers incense with the prayers of God's people at the golden altar and hurls fire to the earth, and the first four trumpets bring hail and fire, a burning mountain into the sea, the star Wormwood and a darkening of sun, moon and stars.

usedIn.n: Revelation 10:1-11, the mighty angel and the little scroll
usedIn.s: A mighty angel robed in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, plants one foot on the sea and one on the land, swears by the one who lives for ever that there will be no more delay, and gives John a little scroll to eat, sweet in his mouth and bitter in his stomach.

usedIn.n: Revelation 12:7-17, war in heaven and the accuser thrown down
usedIn.s: Michael and his angels fight the dragon and throw him out of heaven, and a voice celebrates the fall of the accuser of the brothers, defeated by the Lamb's blood and the witnesses' testimony. On earth the dragon chases the woman, who is given eagle's wings, and when the earth swallows the river he spews after her, he turns to make war on her other children.

usedIn.n: Revelation 15:1-16:11, the song of Moses and the first bowls
usedIn.s: Those who have overcome the beast stand beside a sea of glass mixed with fire and sing the song of Moses and of the Lamb. Seven angels dressed like priests come out of the heavenly temple with seven golden bowls of God's wrath, and the first five bring sores, seas and rivers turned to blood, scorching sun and darkness on the beast's throne.

usedIn.n: Revelation 19:1-10, the marriage supper of the Lamb
usedIn.s: A vast heavenly crowd shouts hallelujah because God has judged the great prostitute, and again because the Lamb's wedding day has arrived and his bride stands ready in fine linen. The angel declares those invited to the wedding feast blessed, and when John bows to him, tells him to worship God alone.

entries.title: The resurrection of the dead
entries.summary: Most Jews, with the Pharisees, expected God to raise the dead to bodily life at the end of the age. The Sadducees denied it. Nobody expected one man to rise ahead of everyone else.
aliases: the life of the age to come
resurrection of the just and the unjust
to depart and be with Christ
the resurrection has already taken place
the sea gave up its dead
death and Hades gave up their dead
entries.plain: **The family gathered Grandpa's bones into a box and said they would see him again on the last day.** Most Jews in Jesus' time believed that God would one day raise the dead to new bodily life, when he set the world right. The Sadducees, the party of the leading priests, said there was no resurrection at all. Those who believed in it expected the dead to rise together at the end, not one person first.
entries.then: Most Jews of Jesus' day held the Pharisees' view: God would raise them to new life when he brought in the new age. Eternal life was the life of the coming age (Daniel 12:2), promised to the righteous after the resurrection. The Sadducees were notorious for denying it. Rabbis who saw themselves as heirs of the Pharisees counted them heretics for it, and the Pharisees held that the Sadducees would be shut out of the world to come. Josephus says they "take away the belief of the immortal duration of the soul, and the punishments and rewards in Hades." The CSB Study Bible says they believed a person ceased to exist at death. Pharisees argued for the resurrection from the books of Moses, which the Sadducees accepted. Some traditions held that the dead would rise in the form in which they died before being made whole. Martyrs expected to get back limbs lost in God's service (2 Maccabees 7:11). Keener ties the custom of gathering bones into a box a year after burial to the hope of a bodily resurrection. He also explains why some who saw the risen Jesus doubted: they expected everyone to rise at once at the end, so a Messiah raised first did not fit. Martha's belief in the resurrection at the last day was that of the Pharisees and of most Jews. Wright reads Lazarus, who came back to ordinary life still bound in grave clothes, as a signpost only. Greeks had no final judgment and no bodily resurrection. They pictured a shadowy underworld or the soul's flight upward, and educated Romans thought the idea barbarian.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a promise that a demolished family home will be rebuilt on the same plot, with the same family moving back in. It is not a move to another country, and nobody expects one room to be finished years ahead of the rest.
entries.changes: Resurrection was a disputed hope, so the Sadducees' riddle in Matthew 22:23-28 tests a known position, and Paul can split a council over it in Acts 23:6-8. Because the dead were expected to rise together at the end, one man raised ahead of the rest, the firstfruits of 1 Corinthians 15:20, was new.
entries.not: **Not the whole story once Easter came.** The analogy fits the Jewish hope that everyone would be raised together at the end. The Gospels report the Messiah raised ahead of everyone else, which is why some who saw him doubted. Nor is the hope the survival of the soul alone.
entries.dissent: Why the Sadducees rejected it. The ESV Study Bible points to their canon: they drew mainly or only on the five books of Moses, where the theme is less developed. Wright gives a political reason: they knew it was a revolutionary doctrine and, as the people in power, wanted to stop it.

usedIn.n: Matthew 22:23-33, Seven brothers and one bride
usedIn.s: Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, pose a riddle about a woman married in turn to seven brothers. Jesus answers that the raised do not marry, and that God is the God of the living.

usedIn.n: Matthew 28:1-15, Women at dawn and a bribed guard
usedIn.s: At dawn after the Sabbath an angel rolls back the stone and tells two women that Jesus is risen. They meet him on the road, while the chief priests pay the guards to say the disciples stole the body.

usedIn.n: Luke 14:1-14, Dropsy at a Pharisee's table, and guests who cannot repay
usedIn.s: On a Sabbath at the house of a leading Pharisee, Jesus heals a man with dropsy, tells the guests not to grab the best places, and tells the host to invite people who cannot invite him back.

usedIn.n: Luke 20:27-40, The Sadducees and the woman with seven husbands
usedIn.s: Sadducees, who deny the resurrection, ask whose wife a woman married to seven brothers will be. Jesus answers that the risen do not marry and are like the angels, and argues from the burning bush.

usedIn.n: Luke 24:36-53, Not a ghost; hands lifted in blessing
usedIn.s: Jesus stands among the disciples, who think they are seeing a ghost. He shows his hands and feet and eats fish, opens the Scriptures to them, and leads them out to Bethany, where he lifts his hands and blesses them.

usedIn.n: John 5:19-47, The Son sent by the Father, and his witnesses
usedIn.s: Jesus answers the charge of making himself equal with God: the Son does what he sees the Father doing, gives life and judges, and has witnesses in John, in his works, in the Father and in the Scriptures.

usedIn.n: John 11:1-44, Lazarus four days in the tomb
usedIn.s: Jesus waits two days after hearing that his friend Lazarus is ill, reaches Bethany to find him four days buried, weeps with the mourners, and calls him out of the tomb still bound in his grave clothes.

usedIn.n: John 16:16-33, A woman in labor
usedIn.s: Jesus tells the puzzled disciples that in a little while they will not see him and then will see him again, and that their grief will turn to joy like a mother's after childbirth. He warns that they will be scattered.

usedIn.n: John 20:1-18, The empty tomb and the gardener
usedIn.s: Mary Magdalene finds the stone moved and runs to Peter and the beloved disciple, who see the linen cloths lying in the empty tomb. Weeping outside, she takes the risen Jesus for the gardener until he says her name, and he sends her to tell the others.

usedIn.n: John 20:19-31, Locked doors, and my Lord and my God
usedIn.s: On the evening of the first day Jesus stands among the disciples behind locked doors, shows his hands and side, sends them as the Father sent him and breathes the Spirit on them. A week later Thomas sees the wounds and confesses him as Lord and God.

usedIn.n: Acts 4:1-31, Before the temple rulers
usedIn.s: The temple authorities arrest Peter and John for proclaiming the resurrection in Jesus. Before the council the unschooled fishermen speak boldly, are warned and released, and pray with the believers in the words of Psalm 2.

usedIn.n: Acts 17:16-21, Athens: idols, the marketplace and the philosophers
usedIn.s: Waiting in Athens, Paul is distressed at a city full of idols. He argues in the synagogue and the marketplace, and Epicurean and Stoic philosophers take him for a preacher of foreign gods and bring him to the Areopagus.

usedIn.n: Acts 17:22-34, Paul before the Areopagus
usedIn.s: Before the Areopagus, Paul starts from an altar to an unknown god and from the Athenians' own poets, speaks of the one Creator who made every nation from one man, and ends with a coming judgment and a man raised from the dead. Some mock; a few believe.

usedIn.n: Acts 22:30-23:11, Paul before the council
usedIn.s: The tribune brings Paul before the chief priests and the council. Struck on the high priest's order, Paul calls him a whitewashed wall, then declares himself a Pharisee on trial for the hope of the resurrection, and the council splits.

usedIn.n: Acts 24:1-27, The hearing before Felix
usedIn.s: The high priest's orator Tertullus charges Paul before Felix with stirring up riots and trying to profane the temple. Paul answers point by point; Felix puts off a decision and keeps him in custody for two years, hoping for a bribe.

usedIn.n: Acts 25:13-26:32, Agrippa and Bernice hear Paul
usedIn.s: King Agrippa II and his sister Bernice visit Festus, who asks them to hear Paul so that he will have something to write to the emperor. Paul tells his story; Festus calls him mad, Agrippa turns the question aside, and all agree he could have been set free had he not appealed to Caesar.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 6:12-20, The body and the prostitute
usedIn.s: Answering slogans such as everything is permissible and food is for the stomach, Paul argues that the body belongs to the Lord, will be raised, and must not be joined to a prostitute, for believers were bought at a price.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 15:1-11, What I received
usedIn.s: Paul reminds the Corinthians of the good news he handed on to them as he had received it: that Christ died for sins, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to Cephas, the Twelve, more than five hundred, James, all the apostles and last of all to Paul.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 15:12-34, If the dead are not raised
usedIn.s: Against some who say there is no resurrection of the dead, Paul argues that then Christ was not raised either, calls Christ the firstfruits, and asks why anyone is baptized for the dead or why he fights wild beasts if the dead are not raised.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 15:35-58, Seeds, stars and the last trumpet
usedIn.s: Asked what kind of body the dead will have, Paul answers with the seed that dies and rises as a plant and with the differing glories of sun, moon and stars, sets the first Adam beside the last, and ends with the trumpet and death swallowed up.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 4:7-18, Treasure in clay jars
usedIn.s: Paul carries God's treasure in a clay jar, hard pressed but not crushed, carrying Jesus' dying in his body so that Jesus' life may show, while the outer self wastes away and the inner self is renewed day by day.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 5:1-10, The tent and the judgment seat
usedIn.s: Paul sets the earthly tent of the body against a building from God, longs to be clothed rather than found naked, names the Spirit as a down payment, and says that all must appear before the judgment seat of Christ.

usedIn.n: Philippians 1:12-26, Chains known to the whole palace guard
usedIn.s: Paul tells how his imprisonment has carried the gospel through the palace guard and made other preachers bolder, some from rivalry, then weighs living against dying and expects to stay on for their sake.

usedIn.n: Philippians 3:12-4:1, The race, citizens of heaven, and a Savior from there
usedIn.s: Paul pictures himself as a runner straining toward the prize, warns against those whose god is their stomach, and reminds a Roman colony that its citizenship is in heaven, from where it awaits a Savior who will transform its lowly bodies.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 1:1-10, Turned to God from idols
usedIn.s: Paul, Silas and Timothy thank God for a young church that received the message in the middle of suffering, whose story is now told everywhere: they turned to God from idols to serve him and to wait for his Son from heaven.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18, Grief with hope, and the welcoming party
usedIn.s: Paul tells a grieving church that believers who have died are not lost: when the Lord comes down from heaven with a shout, the archangel's voice and God's trumpet, the dead in Christ will rise first, and the living will be caught up with them to meet the Lord in the air.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 2:14-26, Gangrene, a resurrection already past, and vessels in a great house
usedIn.s: Timothy is to warn the church against quarreling about words and to handle the word of truth correctly; the teaching of Hymenaeus and Philetus, who say the resurrection has already happened, spreads like gangrene, but God's foundation stands sealed, and in a great house some vessels are for honor and some for dishonor.

usedIn.n: Revelation 20:1-6, Satan bound and the thousand years
usedIn.s: An angel with the key to the Abyss and a great chain seizes the dragon, binds him for a thousand years and seals him in the Abyss so that he cannot deceive the nations. Those beheaded for their witness, who refused the beast and its mark, come to life and reign with Christ for the thousand years, the first resurrection, over which the second death has no power.

usedIn.n: Revelation 20:7-15, Gog and Magog and the great white throne

entries.title: The day of the Lord
entries.summary: The prophets spoke of a coming day when God would judge the world and rescue his people. Paul calls it the day of Christ, giving Jesus the place the prophets gave to God.
aliases: day of our Lord Jesus Christ
the day of the Lord has already come
where is the promise of his coming
a day is like a thousand years
confident and unashamed at his coming
confidence on the day of judgment
entries.plain: **A court date set years ahead hangs over everything the defendant does until it arrives.** The prophets of Israel warned of the day of the Lord, a coming day when God would step in to judge the world and set his people free. Paul uses the same picture but calls it the day of Christ, the day Jesus returns. For believers it is a day to look toward with hope, and also the day when their lives and work will be weighed.
entries.then: The phrase comes from the prophets' day of the Lord (for example Joel 1:15 and Isaiah 13:6). Paul applies this language to the return of Jesus, and in doing so recognizes his deity. Day of Christ Jesus adapts the Old Testament phrase, so it assumes that Christ is divine (Philippians 1:6; 2:16; 1 Corinthians 1:8). The day of the Lord was the time when God would judge the world and vindicate his people, and the day of redemption in Ephesians 4:30 belongs with it. Jewish hope expected God to destroy his people's oppressors in the end time and to save his people (Isaiah 66:14-16). The ESV Study Bible reads the day of Jesus Christ as the day he returns (1 Thessalonians 5:2-11; 2 Peter 3:10-13). It notes that Paul does not say when it will come. In the Greek world even Jews often neglected God's future promises, and the Corinthians may have needed correcting on this point. Bailey ties Paul's hope to boast that he did not run or labor in vain to the same day: "For Paul this positive type of boasting has to do with the Day of Judgment". Nearer judgments sometimes prefigured the day. Jewish apocalyptic spoke of an unexpected end that signs nonetheless preceded. The thief in the night was a saying of Jesus (Matthew 24:43) that other early Christian writers took up. Jewish tradition held that the world's next destruction would come by fire, the background to 2 Peter 3:6-7.
entries.bridge: An analogy: an audit date announced well in advance, when every account will be opened. Honest bookkeepers look forward to it, and everyone else dreads it.
entries.changes: Because the prophets' day of the Lord was God's own day of judgment and rescue, the day of Christ Jesus in Philippians 1:6 gives Jesus God's role. 1 Corinthians 1:8 speaks of being blameless on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ, and 1 Thessalonians 5:2 says the day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night.
entries.not: **Not a date anyone can circle.** An audit is announced with its date, so everyone can prepare on schedule. The day was announced without one: Paul does not say when it will come, and the thief in the night saying stresses surprise.
entries.dissent: Two questions. What the Lord is near means in Philippians 4:5. Keener leans toward God's nearness to his people, who hears them when they cry out (Deuteronomy 4:7; Psalm 145:18), though it could refer to his coming. The ESV Study Bible reads it of his return as judge. The cultural backgrounds notes and the CSB Study Bible allow both. Second, whether the day names only the end of history. The CSB Study Bible links the day of the Lord in 1 Thessalonians 5:2 with the great tribulation of the end. The prophets used such language for disasters that struck Jerusalem within history. Wright reads it as giving events their meaning before God, so Paul can see near events through the lens of the final judgment. Wright and Bird draw the same conclusion from 2 Thessalonians 2:2: since some believed the day had already come, it cannot have meant the end of the world. The ESV Study Bible treats the day and the second coming as one event, and the Zondervan dictionary has the day begin at the second coming and run through the final judgment.

usedIn.s: Paul, Silas and Timothy thank God for a young church that received the message in the middle of suffering, whose story is now told everywhere: they turned to God from idols to serve him and to wait for his Son from heaven.

usedIn.s: Paul reminds the church that the day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night: while people say peace and security, sudden destruction comes like labor pains, but they are children of the day who keep awake and sober, armed with faith, love and hope.

usedIn.s: Paul thanks God for a church whose faith and love keep growing under persecution, and promises that God will repay their persecutors and give them relief when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his powerful angels in blazing fire.

usedIn.n: 2 Thessalonians 2:1-12, The man of lawlessness and the restrainer
usedIn.s: Paul tells a church unsettled by claims that the day of the Lord has already come that the rebellion must come first and the man of lawlessness be revealed, who sets himself up in God's temple claiming to be God; something holds him back for now, and the Lord Jesus will destroy him by the breath of his mouth.

usedIn.n: 2 Peter 3:1-18, Scoffers, the flood and the day of fire
usedIn.s: Scoffers will ask where the promised coming is, since everything goes on as it has since creation. Peter answers that the world once made by God's word was destroyed by water and is now kept for fire on the day of judgment; the Lord does not count time as people do, and he delays out of patience. The day will come like a thief, and the readers wait for new heavens and a new earth, as Paul too wrote in letters some twist like the other Scriptures.

usedIn.s: Those who do right are born of God, whose love makes them his children, and when he appears they will be like him. Whoever keeps on sinning belongs to the devil, who has sinned from the beginning, and the Son came to undo his work. The readers are not to be like Cain, who murdered his brother, but to love in deed and in truth, as Christ laid down his life.

usedIn.s: At the fifth seal the souls of those killed for God's word cry out from under the altar, how long, and are given white robes and told to wait. At the sixth a great earthquake shakes the world, the sky rolls up like a scroll, and kings and slaves alike hide in the caves from the wrath of the Lamb.

entries.title: Antichrist and the lawless one
entries.summary: Daniel's king who exalts himself above every god and defiles the sanctuary became a pattern Jews saw again in Antiochus, Pompey and Caligula. Paul's man of lawlessness, who sets himself up in God's temple claiming to be God, belongs to that line.
aliases: the one who now holds it back
terrible times in the last days
the beast that was and is not
entries.plain: **Every generation has a tyrant who seems to fit the old description a little too well.** The book of Daniel describes a king who exalts himself above every god, speaks against the Most High and defiles the sanctuary. Jews saw that picture come true in Antiochus Epiphanes, who desecrated the temple, and saw it again in the Roman general Pompey, who walked into the Holy of Holies, and in the emperor Caligula, who ordered his own statue set up in the temple. Paul tells the Thessalonians that before the day of the Lord a man of lawlessness will set himself up in God's temple and claim to be God, and that something, or someone, is holding him back for now. Paul does not say who the restrainer is, and scholars have never agreed.
entries.then: A general future antichrist appears mainly in later Jewish texts. Writers of the time described past and present rulers in such terms, among them Daniel's evil kings. The pagan king who makes himself a god is an old theme (Isaiah 14:13-14; Ezekiel 28:2). The Dead Sea Scrolls speak of a man of lies, and Roman emperors lent themselves to the part. Paul's picture comes especially from Jesus' saying about the abomination (Matthew 24:15), which draws on Daniel (11:36-37). Wright and Bird name Antiochus Epiphanes, Daniel's boastful horn, and Pompey, who entered the Holy of Holies. Wilkins adds Pilate bringing the emperor's images into Jerusalem in AD 26. Caligula, Josephus writes, "asserted his own divinity, and insisted on greater honors to be paid him by his subjects than are due to mankind". He ordered the governor Petronius to set up his statue in the temple, by consent or by war. Only his murder in AD 41 prevented disaster, Wright notes. In AD 70 the Romans carried their standards into the temple court, Josephus says, "and there did they offer sacrifices to them". Heiser adds that many read Gog of Ezekiel 38-39 as a template. In his account, Second Temple writers saw "Sennacherib of Assyria or Antiochus or a Roman emperor" as prototypes of the enemy. Nero became the next model. After his death in AD 68 rumor said he was alive or would return, and impostors appeared. Jewish oracles and later Christian writers cast him as the antichrist. Many Jewish thinkers also expected widespread apostasy just before the end.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a wanted poster sketched from witnesses to several past crimes. Each new suspect who matches the sketch is measured against it, though the sketch was never a photograph of one man.
entries.changes: Because Daniel's self-exalting king had been seen again in Antiochus, Pompey and Caligula, the abomination Jesus warns of in Matthew 24:15 and the man of lawlessness of 2 Thessalonians 2:3-4 would sound to first hearers like a known pattern rather than a riddle. 1 John 2:18 speaks of many antichrists already come.
entries.not: **Not a hunt for one suspect to arrest.** A wanted poster exists to catch a single man. Paul gives no name and says the Thessalonians already knew what held the lawless one back, and Christian interpreters have read the fulfillment in at least four different ways.
entries.dissent: Who or what restrains him, a thing in verse 6 and a person in verse 7. Keener lists the gospel preached to all nations, God's own restraint, Michael, the Jerusalem believers and the emperor. Many church fathers said the Roman Empire. Keener rejects the church as restrainer, while the CSB Study Bible prefers the Holy Spirit, perhaps working through the church. Wright and Bird report Augustine's confession that he did not know. Second, which temple. The ESV Study Bible lists the church, the heavenly temple, the Jerusalem temple or a figure modeled on Antiochus. The CSB Study Bible suggests a future rebuilt temple, Keener and Wright the Jerusalem temple Caligula threatened. Third, how it is fulfilled. Keener lists a tribulation still future, the war of AD 66-70, the whole course of history, or language reused in several true ways. Wilkins and the Zondervan dictionary read a person still to come. Fourth, whether Nero stands behind the beast of Revelation 13 and 17. Keener says most commentators think so. Carson, Moo and Morris find the legend a poor fit, and Heiser doubts Nero for 666, since the count needs juggled spellings.

entries.title: The book of life
entries.summary: An old picture of God keeping a register of the names of those who belong to him. Jewish writers developed it, and the New Testament uses it from Luke to Revelation.
aliases: names in the book of life
entries.plain: **A town keeps a roll of its citizens, and having your name on it settles whether you belong.** The Old Testament speaks of a book in which God writes the names of his people, and of names being blotted out of it. Jewish writers after the Old Testament made much of this picture. To have your name in the book of life meant that you belonged to God and would share in the life he promised.
entries.then: Keener calls the book of life an Old Testament image that ancient Judaism developed further. He points to Exodus 32:32-33, Daniel 12:1 and Malachi 3:16, to the Essene Damascus Document 20:19 and to Jubilees 36:10. Jewish tradition often emphasized the picture. On Luke 10:20 Keener notes that a heavenly book listing the names of the righteous turns up often in Jewish writings such as Jubilees and 1 Enoch. Old Testament precedent also includes Isaiah 4:3 and perhaps Psalms 56:8 and 139:16. The ESV Study Bible calls it God's record of those who belong to him, with roots in Exodus 32:33 and Psalm 69:28. It appears several times in Revelation, from 3:5 to 21:27. The CSB Study Bible notes that the New Testament mentions it rarely, and that it refers to those listed among the saved. Hebrews 12:23 speaks of the firstborn whose names are enrolled in heaven. That recalls the citizen registers of Greek cities as well as the book of life. Greek and Roman cities kept official rolls of citizens, adding new citizens and removing those expelled. In some cities an offender's name was struck off just before execution. So the promise in Revelation 3:5 never to blot out a name from the book of life also spoke in civic terms, and Sardis was known for its royal archives. Jubilees, the books of Enoch and the Testament of Abraham speak of heavenly tablets of deeds, with angels recording sins. Beale cites 3 Enoch, where Satan and the angel princes of Rome and Persia write Israel's sins on tablets for God.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a city's register of citizens, where a name entered brings rights and a name struck out means exile. Once the roll is read, no one argues with the clerk.
entries.changes: Because the book recorded those who belonged to God, Paul's remark in Philippians 4:3 that his quarreling coworkers' names are in the book of life sets their quarrel inside a shared belonging. In Luke 10:20 Jesus tells his messengers to rejoice that their names are written in heaven, and Revelation 20:12 pictures the books opened at the judgment.
entries.not: **Not a roll kept by human clerks.** A city register records the decisions of officials, and it records only names. The book in these sources is God's own record in heaven, and Jewish texts set beside it tablets of deeds kept by angels.

entries.title: This age and the age to come
entries.summary: Jews divided history into the present age, under the rule of evil nations, and the age to come, when God would rule unchallenged. The sufferings expected before the change were called birth pangs.
aliases: this age and the one to come
when the times reach their fulfillment
what is lacking in Christ's afflictions
the end of all things is near
new heavens and a new earth
life of the age to come
the true light is already shining
first heaven and first earth passed away
entries.plain: **The labor pains are terrible, but everyone in the room knows they mean a birth is coming.** Jews of Jesus' time saw history in two parts: this age, with God's people under foreign power, and the age to come, when God would rule and set things right. Many expected a time of terrible suffering just before the change, and compared it to a woman's labor.
entries.then: Keener says nearly all Jews of the time split history into two ages. In this one, evil nations held power; in the one to come, God would rule with no rival. Many Jewish writers listed sufferings that would come just before the end: wars, famine, apostasy, persecution and strange portents. Some called these the birth pains that would bring the Messiah, or the new world, into being (4 Ezra, 2 Baruch, the Sibylline Oracles and the Qumran Hymns; compare Isaiah 13:8). The prophets used labor pains both for terrible suffering in general and for what Israel would endure before its deliverance. Daniel 12:1 promised a final distress worse than any before it, and Josephus judged the sufferings of 66 to 70 the worst in history. Some teachers tried to calculate the date of the end, while others held that it depended on Israel's repentance. The word for the renewal in Matthew 19:28 was a Stoic term for the fiery destruction and rebirth of the world. In a Jewish setting it meant the promised new creation. Wright reads the chapter on the temple's fall through the same picture: the present age would come to its convulsive end and the new age would be born. Women often died in childbirth. In some prophetic texts the pains announced the birth of a messianic era (Isaiah 66:7-10; Micah 5:1-4). Early Judaism applied them to the last suffering before the resurrection of the dead. Isaiah 26:17-20 sets childbirth, a little while and the raising of the dead side by side.
entries.bridge: An analogy: the last hard winter before a long-promised spring, when every storm is read as a sign of how close the thaw is. The storms are real, but they are not yet the spring.
entries.changes: The two ages explain why the end of this age and the age to come appear side by side in the Gospels, and why disasters could be read as birth pangs, the beginning and not the end, as in Matthew 24:8. Paul pictures creation groaning in labor in Romans 8:22, and Galatians 1:4 speaks of rescue from the present evil age.
entries.not: **Not a season that comes round on schedule.** Spring follows winter by the calendar, and everyone knows roughly when. Jewish teachers disagreed whether the end could be dated at all, some held that it waited on Israel's repentance, and in the Gospels the wars and famines are only the beginning.
entries.dissent: What the birth pangs of Matthew 24 lead to. Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes read them as the ordinary troubles of this age, with the one real sign coming at Jesus' return. Wright reads them as the run-up to the temple's fall, when the old order would give way to the new, and reads the Son of Man's coming on the clouds as his vindication. Second, whether the new heavens and earth of Revelation 21:1 replace this world or renew it. Keener thinks Revelation pictures replacement and the ESV Study Bible weighs both; Beale reads new as new in kind, Wright stresses heaven and earth joined, and the Zondervan dictionary writes that "the old universe will be marvelously regenerated".
