usedIn.s: As the disciples admire the temple, Jesus says not one stone will be left on another. On the Mount of Olives he warns of false messiahs, wars and persecution, the beginning of the birth pangs.

usedIn.n: Matthew 24:15-28, The desolating sacrilege and the flight
usedIn.s: When the desolating sacrilege spoken of by Daniel stands in the holy place, those in Judea must flee to the mountains at once. False messiahs will say he is in the wilderness, but his coming will be like lightning.

usedIn.n: Matthew 24:29-51, The Son of Man on the clouds and the slave in charge
usedIn.s: After the distress, sun, moon and stars fail and the Son of Man comes on the clouds to gather his chosen. No one knows the day, so the household must stay ready, like a slave left in charge.

usedIn.n: Luke 18:18-30, A rich ruler and the needle's eye
usedIn.s: A ruler asks what he must do to inherit eternal life; told to sell everything and follow, he goes away sad, and Jesus says it is easier for a camel to go through a needle's eye than for a rich man to enter God's kingdom.

usedIn.n: John 16:16-33, A woman in labor
usedIn.s: Jesus tells the puzzled disciples that in a little while they will not see him and then will see him again, and that their grief will turn to joy like a mother's after childbirth. He warns that they will be scattered.

usedIn.n: Acts 14:21-28, Elders appointed, and home to Antioch
usedIn.s: Paul and Barnabas retrace their route, warning that the kingdom comes through hardships and appointing elders in each church, then report to Antioch that God has opened a door of faith to the Gentiles.

usedIn.n: Romans 8:18-30, Groaning and firstfruits
usedIn.s: Creation groans as in labor, waiting to be freed from decay, and believers who have the firstfruits of the Spirit groan too as they wait for their adoption and the redemption of their bodies.

usedIn.n: Romans 11:25-36, The full number of the nations
usedIn.s: Paul reveals a mystery: a partial hardening has come on Israel until the full number of the Gentiles comes in, and so all Israel will be saved. He ends in praise of God's wisdom.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 2:6-16, The rulers of this age
usedIn.s: Paul speaks of a hidden wisdom of God, planned before time began, which the rulers of this age failed to grasp, or they would never have put Jesus to death.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 7:25-40, The present distress
usedIn.s: Because of the present distress and the shortness of the time, Paul advises the unmarried to stay as they are, though marrying is no sin, and tells a widow she is free to remarry, only in the Lord.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 5:11-6:13, New creation, Christ's ambassadors and a list of hardships
usedIn.s: Because one died for all, anyone in Christ is a new creation; Paul, God's ambassador, appeals to the Corinthians to be reconciled to God and commends his ministry with a long list of hardships and paradoxes.

usedIn.n: Galatians 1:1-10, A letter with no thanksgiving, and a curse
usedIn.s: Paul opens by insisting that his commission came from God and not from people, skips the thanksgiving his letters usually give, and pronounces a curse on anyone, even an angel, who preaches a different gospel.

usedIn.n: Galatians 4:21-5:1, Hagar, Sarah and Sinai in Arabia
usedIn.s: Paul reads the story of Abraham's two sons as a figure of two covenants: Hagar the slave stands for Sinai and the present Jerusalem, Sarah the free woman for the Jerusalem above, and he calls the Galatians to stand firm in freedom.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 1:1-14, A circular letter opens with praise, a seal and a down payment
usedIn.s: Paul greets God's holy people and launches one long blessing of God for choosing, adopting, redeeming and sealing a mixed people, with the Spirit as the down payment of their inheritance.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 1:15-23, Far above every name that is invoked
usedIn.s: Paul prays that the believers will know the hope, the inheritance and the power God showed when he raised Christ and seated him above every ruler, authority, power and name, in this age and the next.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 2:1-10, The ruler of the kingdom of the air
usedIn.s: Paul reminds his readers that they were once dead in sins, following the ruler of the kingdom of the air, until God in his mercy made them alive and seated them with Christ in the heavenly realms, saved by grace.

usedIn.n: Colossians 1:24-2:5, Sufferings for the body, and a steward of the mystery
usedIn.s: Paul rejoices to suffer for the church, fills up what is lacking in Christ's afflictions, calls himself the servant entrusted with God's long hidden mystery, and tells churches he has never met how hard he struggles for them.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 2:17-3:13, Orphaned, blocked by Satan, crowned
usedIn.s: Torn away from the church, Paul tells how he longed to come back but Satan blocked the way, how he sent Timothy from Athens, how Timothy's good news has revived him, and prays that the Lord will make them blameless at his coming with all his holy ones.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 5:1-11, A thief in the night, and peace and security
usedIn.s: Paul reminds the church that the day of the Lord comes like a thief in the night: while people say peace and security, sudden destruction comes like labor pains, but they are children of the day who keep awake and sober, armed with faith, love and hope.

usedIn.n: 2 Thessalonians 1:3-12, Suffering now, and the Lord revealed in blazing fire
usedIn.s: Paul thanks God for a church whose faith and love keep growing under persecution, and promises that God will repay their persecutors and give them relief when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with his powerful angels in blazing fire.

usedIn.n: Titus 2:11-3:8, Grace has appeared, be subject to rulers, and the washing of rebirth
usedIn.s: God's grace has appeared, training believers to live with self-control now while they wait for Christ's glorious appearing; they are to respect rulers and be gentle to all, because God saved them by his mercy, giving them new birth and new life by the Holy Spirit.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 2:5-18, The world to come is not for angels
usedIn.s: God did not put the world to come under angels. Psalm 8 promised rule to human beings; it is not yet seen, but Jesus, made a little lower than the angels for a while, is crowned with glory, and he shared flesh and blood to break the devil's power and become a merciful and faithful high priest.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 3:1-4:13, Moses the servant, and the rest still open
usedIn.s: Moses was faithful in God's house as a servant; Jesus is faithful over it as the Son. Psalm 95's warning not to harden hearts as in the wilderness still speaks today, because the rest God promised was never reached under Joshua and remains open for God's people.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 9:23-10:18, Once for all, and a seated priest
usedIn.s: Christ entered heaven itself, not a copy, and offered himself once at the climax of the ages; as people die once and then face judgment, he will appear a second time to save. The yearly sacrifices only reminded people of sin, but his body offered once has made his people holy, and he has sat down, his offering finished.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 1:1-12, To the exiles of the dispersion
usedIn.s: Peter writes to God's chosen exiles scattered through five provinces of Asia Minor, blesses God for a new birth into a living hope and an inheritance kept in heaven, and tells them their trials test their faith as fire tests gold. The prophets searched for this salvation, and angels long to look into it.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 4:12-19, The fiery ordeal and the name Christian
usedIn.s: The readers should not be surprised at the fiery ordeal, but rejoice to share Christ's sufferings. No one should suffer as a murderer, a thief or a meddler, but anyone who suffers as a Christian should not be ashamed; judgment begins with God's household, so those who suffer should commit themselves to their faithful Creator.

usedIn.n: 2 Peter 3:1-18, Scoffers, the flood and the day of fire
usedIn.s: Scoffers will ask where the promised coming is, since everything goes on as it has since creation. Peter answers that the world once made by God's word was destroyed by water and is now kept for fire on the day of judgment; the Lord does not count time as people do, and he delays out of patience. The day will come like a thief, and the readers wait for new heavens and a new earth, as Paul too wrote in letters some twist like the other Scriptures.

usedIn.n: 1 John 1:1-4, What our hands have touched
usedIn.s: The letter opens with the Word of life, which was from the beginning and which the writer and those with him heard, saw and touched. They announce the eternal life that was with the Father and appeared to them, so that the readers may share their fellowship with the Father and the Son.

usedIn.n: 1 John 2:18-27, The last hour and many antichrists
usedIn.s: It is the last hour: the readers heard that antichrist is coming, and many antichrists have already come. They went out from the community, which shows they never belonged; whoever denies that Jesus is the Christ is the liar and the antichrist. The readers have an anointing from the Holy One and need no one else to teach them.

usedIn.n: Revelation 21:1-8, new heaven, new earth, no more sea
usedIn.s: John sees a new heaven and a new earth, with no more sea, and the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down from God like a bride dressed for her husband. A voice announces that God's dwelling is now with people, that he will wipe away every tear, and that he makes all things new; the thirsty will drink freely, while the cowardly, the faithless, murderers, sorcerers, idolaters and liars have their place in the lake of fire.

entries.title: The Spirit of prophecy
entries.summary: Jews of Jesus' day linked God's Spirit above all with prophecy. Many believed the prophets had fallen silent long ago, and they looked for the day God would pour out his Spirit again.
aliases: carried along by the Holy Spirit
entries.plain: **The phone had not rung in four hundred years, and then it rang three times in one family.** In the Old Testament, when God's Spirit came on someone, they often spoke for God. By Jesus' day many Jews believed real prophecy had stopped after the last prophets and would return only when God restored Israel. Others thought the Spirit rested only on the holiest people. So when ordinary people in Luke start speaking by the Spirit, readers would notice.
entries.then: The Old Testament often joins the Spirit to prophecy (Numbers 11:25-26; 1 Samuel 10:6, 10; Joel 2:28-29). Early Jewish circles stressed that role even more consistently, though often about the prophets of the past; the Essene writings are the main exception. Many Palestinian Jews believed prophets in the Old Testament sense had ceased. The ESV Study Bible says most Jews believed the Spirit had not been active in Israel for more than four hundred years, since Malachi. Most people believed the Spirit had departed, rested on a few of the holiest people, or belonged to the community, as the Dead Sea Scrolls held. The prophets had promised a future pouring out of the Spirit (Isaiah 44:3; Ezekiel 39:29; Joel 2:28-29). In Scripture only God pours out God's Spirit. In the Old Testament the Spirit came on a few selected people. Prophetesses appear in the Old Testament, but in the Jewish tradition of this period they were much less prominent than male prophets. Few if any movements had many prophets at once, though Josephus says many Essenes could prophesy. Most Jewish teachers held that the Spirit came only on the most pious or belonged to the age to come. So its coming on uncircumcised Gentiles showed that God accepted them (Acts 10:45-47). Heiser reads the wind and fire of Pentecost as the imagery of a divine council commissioning. Keener calls claims of prophecy rare and sometimes marginal in Judaism but apparently common in early Christianity. His notes know of no other ancient group in which prophecy was so widespread.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a nation whose last great statesman died generations ago, where the old speeches are still read aloud but nobody expects a new one. Then someone stands up and speaks in that voice again.
entries.changes: Because the Spirit meant prophecy, people filled with the Spirit in Luke's opening chapters, as at Luke 1:67, speak for God, a sign that the long silence is ending. Acts 2:17 quotes Joel to say the promised outpouring has come on all God's people, and 1 Corinthians 14:1 tells a whole church to seek to prophesy.
entries.not: **Not one new voice.** The analogy pictures a single successor taking up an old style. In Acts the Spirit comes on whole communities, Gentiles included, and the sources know of no other ancient group where prophecy was so widespread. The voice was also taken to be God's own.
entries.dissent: How silent the Spirit was thought to be. The ESV Study Bible says most Jews believed the Spirit had been inactive for over four hundred years. Keener's background commentary gives a range of views: some believed the Spirit had departed, some that it rested on a few of the holiest, and the Dead Sea community that it belonged to them; his notes add that Essene writings did not tie the Spirit so narrowly to prophecy.

usedIn.n: Luke 2:21-40, Two birds, Simeon and Anna
usedIn.s: Jesus is circumcised and named on the eighth day. At the temple his parents make the offering the law allowed the poor, and two old people waiting for God's comfort, Simeon and the widow Anna, speak about the child.

usedIn.n: Luke 4:16-30, The year of the Lord's favor in Nazareth
usedIn.s: In the Nazareth synagogue Jesus reads Isaiah's promise of good news for the poor and release for captives and says it is fulfilled today. When he points to Elijah and Elisha helping foreigners, the town tries to throw him off a cliff.

usedIn.n: John 15:18-16:15, Hated by the world and put out of the synagogue
usedIn.s: Jesus warns that the world will hate his followers as it hated him, that they will be put out of the synagogues and even killed by people who think they are serving God, and that the Advocate will prove the world wrong.

usedIn.n: John 20:19-31, Locked doors, and my Lord and my God
usedIn.s: On the evening of the first day Jesus stands among the disciples behind locked doors, shows his hands and side, sends them as the Father sent him and breathes the Spirit on them. A week later Thomas sees the wounds and confesses him as Lord and God.

usedIn.n: Acts 1:1-11, The kingdom question and the cloud
usedIn.s: Luke's second volume opens with the risen Jesus speaking about God's kingdom for forty days. Asked whether he will now restore the kingdom to Israel, he promises the Spirit, sends the apostles as witnesses to the end of the earth, and is taken up in a cloud.

usedIn.n: Acts 2:1-13, Pentecost and the nations
usedIn.s: On the day of Pentecost wind and fire come on the gathered believers, and Jewish pilgrims from every nation hear them speaking in their own languages.

usedIn.n: Acts 2:14-41, Peter's sermon: the Spirit poured out
usedIn.s: Peter explains the scene from Joel: God has poured out his Spirit, the crucified Jesus is raised and exalted as Lord and Messiah, and three thousand are baptized in his name.

usedIn.n: Acts 8:4-25, Samaria and Simon the magician
usedIn.s: Philip preaches the Messiah in Samaria, and even the famous magician Simon is baptized. When Peter and John lay hands on the Samaritans and they receive the Spirit, Simon offers money for the power.

usedIn.n: Acts 10:24-11:18, Peter in Cornelius's house
usedIn.s: Peter enters a Gentile home, preaches Jesus, and sees the Spirit fall on the uncircumcised listeners. In Jerusalem he is criticized for eating with Gentiles, and his account silences the critics.

usedIn.n: Acts 11:19-30, Antioch, and the name Christian
usedIn.s: Scattered believers bring the message to Gentiles in Antioch, where the disciples are first called Christians. When a prophet foretells famine, the church sends relief to the elders in Judea.

usedIn.n: Acts 15:22-35, The letter to the Gentile churches
usedIn.s: The council sends Judas and Silas with Paul and Barnabas to carry a letter to the Gentile believers of Antioch, Syria and Cilicia. It is read to the church at Antioch, who rejoice at its encouragement.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 12:1-31, Mute idols and one body
usedIn.s: Paul reminds the Corinthians that as pagans they were led astray to mute idols, describes the many gifts of the one Spirit, and pictures the church as one body whose weaker and less honored members are indispensable.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 14:26-40, Order when the church meets
usedIn.s: Paul regulates a meeting where everyone brings a hymn, a teaching, a revelation or a tongue: speakers take turns, prophets weigh one another's words, women are to be silent and ask at home, and everything is to be done decently and in order.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 12:19-13:14, Two or three witnesses
usedIn.s: Paul warns that on his third visit every charge will be established by two or three witnesses and that he will not spare the unrepentant, then closes with a call to restoration, the holy kiss and a threefold blessing.

usedIn.n: Galatians 3:1-14, Who bewitched you? Abraham's blessing and the law's curse
usedIn.s: Paul asks the Galatians who has bewitched them, since they received the Spirit by believing, then argues from Abraham that those who believe share his blessing, while Christ took the law's curse by being hung on a tree.

usedIn.n: 1 Thessalonians 5:12-28, Leaders, prophets, a holy kiss and a letter read to all
usedIn.s: Paul asks the church to honor those who work hard over them, to warn the idle and help the weak, to rejoice, pray and give thanks, not to quench the Spirit or despise prophecy but test everything, and to have the letter read to all.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 1:12-20, A blasphemer shown mercy, and two men handed over to Satan
usedIn.s: Paul thanks Christ for taking a former blasphemer and persecutor into his service as an example of mercy, then charges Timothy to fight the battle well, as the prophecies about him foretold, unlike Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom Paul has handed over to Satan.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 4:1-5, Deceiving spirits, no marriage, no foods
usedIn.s: The Spirit warns that later on some will desert the faith for deceiving spirits and demonic teaching, banning marriage and certain foods, though God made food to be eaten with thanks.

usedIn.n: 2 Timothy 3:10-17, Antioch, Iconium and Lystra, and the sacred writings
usedIn.s: Timothy has followed Paul's teaching, life and sufferings, as in Antioch, Iconium and Lystra; he is to continue in what he learned, knowing from whom he learned it and how from infancy he has known the sacred writings, for all Scripture is God-breathed.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 1:1-12, To the exiles of the dispersion
usedIn.s: Peter writes to God's chosen exiles scattered through five provinces of Asia Minor, blesses God for a new birth into a living hope and an inheritance kept in heaven, and tells them their trials test their faith as fire tests gold. The prophets searched for this salvation, and angels long to look into it.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 4:1-11, The neighbors' parties and their abuse
usedIn.s: Armed with Christ's attitude, the readers have done with the life of the Gentiles, its debauchery, drinking parties and idolatry, and their old companions are surprised and heap abuse on them; they will give account to God. The end of all things is near, so they must be sober, love one another, be hospitable without grumbling, and use their gifts as stewards of God's grace.

usedIn.n: 2 Peter 1:1-21, A reminder before the tent is folded
usedIn.s: Simeon Peter writes to those who share a faith as precious as his, through whom they may share in the divine nature, and urges them to add virtue to virtue. Knowing his death is near, he means to remind them, for he was an eyewitness of Christ's majesty on the holy mountain, and the prophetic word is a lamp in a dark place until the morning star rises.

usedIn.n: 1 John 4:1-6, Test the spirits
usedIn.s: The readers must test every spirit instead of trusting each one, since many false prophets are now abroad. A spirit that confesses Jesus Christ as truly come in the flesh is from God, and one that refuses is the spirit of the antichrist. God in them is greater than the power in the world, and this is how the Spirit of truth is told from the spirit of error.

usedIn.n: 2 John 7-13, Deceivers at the door, paper and ink
usedIn.s: Many deceivers who refuse to confess that Jesus Christ came in the flesh are abroad in the world; such a one is the deceiver and the antichrist. Whoever runs ahead and does not keep to Christ's teaching does not have God, and the readers are not to take such a person into the house or greet him. The elder would rather not use paper and ink, and hopes to talk face to face.

usedIn.n: Jude 14-25, Enoch's prophecy, scoffers, and a closing doxology
usedIn.s: Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied about such people that the Lord comes with his countless holy ones to judge all and convict the ungodly. The apostles foretold scoffers in the last times; the readers are to build themselves up, pray in the Holy Spirit, keep themselves in God's love and show mercy, snatching some from the fire. Jude closes with praise to the one able to keep them from stumbling.

usedIn.n: Revelation 2:18-29, Thyatira, the guilds and Jezebel
usedIn.s: To Thyatira the Son of God, with eyes like fire and feet like bronze, praises a growing church but rebukes it for tolerating Jezebel, a self-styled prophetess who leads his servants into immorality and idol food. Those who hold fast are promised authority over the nations and the morning star.

usedIn.n: Revelation 10:1-11, the mighty angel and the little scroll
usedIn.s: A mighty angel robed in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, plants one foot on the sea and one on the land, swears by the one who lives for ever that there will be no more delay, and gives John a little scroll to eat, sweet in his mouth and bitter in his stomach.

entries.title: Babel and the seventy nations
entries.summary: Genesis 10 lists the nations of the world, seventy in the Hebrew text and seventy-two in the Greek. Jewish tradition counted the nations that way, and Deuteronomy 32 tells how God divided them and kept Israel as his own. Luke's list of nations at Pentecost recalls them.
entries.plain: **The map in the old book had exactly seventy countries on it, and everyone knew the number.** Genesis 10 lists the families of Noah's sons as the nations of the earth. Jewish tradition counted them as seventy, or seventy-two in the Greek version of the Old Testament. Deuteronomy 32 adds that when God divided the nations, he kept Israel as his own portion. Some readers, Heiser among them, see the other nations placed under lesser heavenly powers at Babel. A number like seventy could call all of that to mind.
entries.then: Jews reckoned seventy, or sometimes seventy-two, nations. If the twelve stood for Israel's tribes, Keener suggests, the larger group of Luke 10:1 may stand for the nations and point ahead to the Gentile mission. Heiser explains the split. The Greek Old Testament has seventy-two nations in Genesis 10 and the traditional Hebrew text seventy, so either number points back to the nations divided at Babel. He prefers seventy, which matches the number of El's sons in the Ugaritic council. Heiser reads Deuteronomy 32:8-9 as God dispersing the nations at Babel and fixing their borders by the number of the sons of God. God took Jacob as his own portion, so the nations were in effect disinherited and left under lesser gods. On Luke 10 he writes, "Seventy is the number of nations listed in Genesis 10," the nations dispossessed at Babel. Keener also names a second background: the seventy elders of Moses who prophesied, plus Eldad and Medad, who made seventy-two (Numbers 11:24-26). Keener suggests that the list of nations at Pentecost updates the names of Genesis 10. In his reading God there reverses Babel's judgment. Wright writes that "with the day of Pentecost this curse is itself overturned." Heiser notes that the words for the divided tongues and the crowd's confusion in Acts 2 are the words the Greek Old Testament uses at Deuteronomy 32:8 and Genesis 11:7. He writes that "Babel’s disinheritance was going to be rectified by the message of Jesus." Heiser carries the picture to Paul's plan to reach Spain, where Tarshish, the most westerly nation of the list, had been.
entries.bridge: An analogy: an old empire's map of its provinces, each under a governor. When a new king sends envoys to every province on the map, everyone who knows the map understands what he is claiming.
entries.changes: Seventy or seventy-two messengers sent ahead of Jesus, as in Luke 10:1, can echo the nations of the world, a first hint of a mission beyond Israel. Pilgrims from every nation hearing the apostles in their own languages, in Acts 2:5-11, reads as Babel's scattering undone. Paul tells the Athenians in Acts 17:26 that God made every nation and fixed the boundaries of where they live.
entries.not: **Not a map every hearer carried.** The analogy assumes everyone knew the provinces and their governors. Luke never says why he gives the number, and the sources offer more than one background for it. The link to Genesis 10 and the gods of the nations is a reading of the text, not a statement in it.
entries.dissent: What the number in Luke 10:1 recalls. Keener's two works give both the nations of Jewish reckoning and Moses' seventy elders with Eldad and Medad. The ESV Study Bible and Heiser point to the nations of Genesis 10, and Heiser sees in the mission the start of the defeat of Satan and the nations' gods. On seventy against seventy-two, the ESV Study Bible says the manuscripts are hard to decide between and most modern translations choose seventy-two, while Heiser judges seventy best on external grounds. What Pentecost reverses. Heiser reads the nations of Acts 2 as peoples once handed over to other gods and now being reclaimed. Keener and Wright speak of Babel's judgment on language reversed and Abraham's blessing reaching the nations, without the divine council frame. Strauss, in the Zondervan backgrounds commentary, explains the variant: the Hebrew text of Genesis 10 lists seventy nations and the Greek seventy-two, so Luke may have written seventy-two and later scribes matched the Hebrew.

xref.s: Seventy sent out, and Satan falling like lightning when they return.
The Most High divided the nations, and the number He divided them by is where the whole argument turns.
Babel, the scattering, and the moment the nations are set aside.
God stands in the divine assembly and passes sentence on the elohim He put in charge.
Paul tells the Areopagus that God fixed the times and the boundaries of the nations.

ddd.s: Sons of God: a group of lesser divine beings who show up at God's throne.
A psalm where God stands up in a room full of gods and sentences them to death.

ddd.n: The princes of Persia and Greece
ddd.s: Spirit figures in Daniel who rule nations and can hold up a messenger from God for weeks.

usedIn.n: Luke 10:1-24, Seventy sent out, and Satan falling
usedIn.s: Jesus sends seventy others, or seventy-two, ahead of him in pairs, with no purse, bag or sandals, to towns that will welcome or refuse them. They come back rejoicing that even the demons obey, and Jesus says he saw Satan fall like lightning.

usedIn.n: Acts 1:1-11, The kingdom question and the cloud
usedIn.s: Luke's second volume opens with the risen Jesus speaking about God's kingdom for forty days. Asked whether he will now restore the kingdom to Israel, he promises the Spirit, sends the apostles as witnesses to the end of the earth, and is taken up in a cloud.

usedIn.n: Acts 2:1-13, Pentecost and the nations
usedIn.s: On the day of Pentecost wind and fire come on the gathered believers, and Jewish pilgrims from every nation hear them speaking in their own languages.

usedIn.n: Acts 8:26-40, The Ethiopian official
usedIn.s: On the desert road to Gaza, Philip meets a eunuch who serves the queen of the Ethiopians, reading Isaiah in his chariot on the way home from worship in Jerusalem, and baptizes him.

usedIn.n: Acts 17:22-34, Paul before the Areopagus
usedIn.s: Before the Areopagus, Paul starts from an altar to an unknown god and from the Athenians' own poets, speaks of the one Creator who made every nation from one man, and ends with a coming judgment and a man raised from the dead. Some mock; a few believe.

usedIn.n: Romans 11:25-36, The full number of the nations
usedIn.s: Paul reveals a mystery: a partial hardening has come on Israel until the full number of the Gentiles comes in, and so all Israel will be saved. He ends in praise of God's wisdom.

usedIn.n: Romans 15:14-24, To Spain by way of Rome
usedIn.s: Paul describes his priestly work of offering the Gentiles to God, from Jerusalem round to Illyricum, and his plan to visit Rome on his way to Spain and be helped on his journey there.

usedIn.n: Revelation 18:1-8, come out of her, my people
usedIn.s: A shining angel announces that Babylon the great has fallen and become a haunt of demons and unclean birds, because the nations drank her wine and the merchants grew rich on her luxury. A voice calls God's people to come out of her, and to pay her back double, since she boasts that she sits as a queen and will never be a widow.

usedIn.n: Revelation 22:1-5, river and tree of life
usedIn.s: The angel shows John a clear, life-giving river running from God's throne through the middle of the city, with the tree of life on both banks, fruiting every month and healing the nations with its leaves. Nothing cursed remains; God's servants will see him face to face, carry his name and reign for ever in his light.

entries.title: The Word and Wisdom
entries.summary: Greek thinkers spoke of the logos, the reason that ordered the world, and Jewish teachers spoke of God's Word and Wisdom, through whom he made everything. John opens his Gospel with that language and then says the Word became flesh.
aliases: through him all things were made
in him all things hold together
entries.plain: **Everyone in the room knew the word, and each of them heard something different in it.** In John's day the Greek word logos meant more than a word on a page. Philosophers used it for the reason that holds the universe together. Jews spoke of God's word, which made the world and came to the prophets, and of God's Wisdom, pictured as a person at his side when he made everything. John takes up this language, and then says something none of them had said: the Word became a human being.
entries.then: Many philosophers used the Greek term for word to mean reason, the force that structured the universe. Philo, a Jewish philosopher, combined this with Jewish ideas of God's word. The Old Testament personified Wisdom (Proverbs 8), and ancient Judaism came to identify Wisdom, Word and Law. The standard Jewish view, Keener says, made this Wisdom older than the rest of creation, yet still a created thing. God spoke the world into being. Jewish teachers said he created through his Wisdom joined with his word (Psalm 33:6; Wisdom of Solomon 9:1-3), and the rabbis counted ten commands in Genesis 1. Jews thought of Wisdom or Word as divine yet distinct from the Father, the closest term John had (Keener). Heiser points to another layer. In the Old Testament the word of Yahweh is sometimes seen as well as heard, coming to Abram in a vision and bringing him outside (Genesis 15:1-6). He writes, "These appearances of the Word of Yahweh are the conceptual backdrop" to John's language. The ESV Study Bible also stresses the Old Testament background (Genesis 1:3; Psalm 33:6; Isaiah 55:10-11) and contrasts the Greek idea of an impersonal principle. Wright sums up John's answer to the philosophers: "the Word isn't an abstract principle, it's a person." The next step was new. Keener writes, "Neither Greek philosophers nor Jewish teachers could conceive of the Word becoming flesh." Paul uses the same language of Christ. Colossians 1:15 describes him in the terms Judaism kept for divine Wisdom, God's archetypal image through which he made the world. Philo calls the Logos God's image and firstborn son, and the beginning was a title for God, Wisdom and the Logos.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a speaker who takes a word everyone already uses, from the lecture hall and from the family Bible, and then points to a man and says, this is what it meant. Each listener hears an echo first, and then a surprise.
entries.changes: The Word through whom everything was made, as in John 1:1-3, draws on Jewish talk of God creating by his Word and Wisdom. Paul uses the same pattern when he says all things come through one Lord in 1 Corinthians 8:6, and Colossians 1:16 says all things were created in him.
entries.not: **Not a speaker redefining a term.** Anyone with a lectern can give an old word a new sense. John claims the Word was with God in the beginning and became flesh, which neither Greek philosophers nor Jewish teachers could conceive; the philosophers' logos was an impersonal principle.
entries.dissent: Where the language comes from. Keener and his cultural backgrounds notes trace it to Jewish Wisdom, Word and Torah, with Philo joining that to the philosophers' logos. Wright reads the opening against both Genesis and the pagan philosophers' principle of rationality. Heiser finds the backdrop in Old Testament appearances of the visible word of Yahweh, as in Genesis 15:1-6 and 1 Samuel 3. The ESV Study Bible stresses the Old Testament background and sets John's Word against the Greek concept. A second question is what fullness in Colossians 1:19 and 2:9 draws on. Keener and his notes give two options: the Old Testament picture of God's glory or wisdom spreading through the world, or the sum of the powers by which God rules, as in Philo. The ESV Study Bible hears God's glory filling the temple.

usedIn.s: Paul describes the Son as the image of the unseen God and firstborn over all creation, through whom and for whom everything was made, thrones and powers included, and through whose cross God makes peace with all things.

entries.title: The prophet like Moses
entries.summary: Moses promised that God would raise up a prophet like him. In Jesus' day people asked whether a new preacher was the Prophet, and some expected the manna and the wonders of the exodus to return with him.
aliases: the prophet who is to come
entries.plain: **The founder said someone like him would come after him, and the members keep checking every new face.** In Deuteronomy Moses tells Israel that God will raise up a prophet like him and that they must listen to him. By Jesus' day that promise had become a hope. People asked whether this or that preacher was the Prophet. Some expected him to bring back the bread from heaven that fed Israel in the desert, and some were ready to follow anyone who promised signs like the ones Moses did.
entries.then: The Prophet in John's Gospel is the prophet like Moses promised in Deuteronomy 18:15-18. Some first-century Jews held the Prophet and the Messiah to be different persons, and Keener's notes have the Prophet and Elijah coming before the Messiah. Samaritans looked for the Taheb, a restorer who was a prophet like Moses, not a son of David. Moses' day was remembered for bread from heaven, so many Jews expected the manna to be restored in the world to come. Some writers, Philo and the rabbis among them, viewed Moses as a king. In this period several prophets promised signs like those of Moses or Joshua and drew thousands. Most of these movements ended with Romans killing the followers. Josephus tells of Theudas, who led a crowd to the Jordan, for "he told them he was a prophet, and that he would, by his own command, divide the river". The governor Fadus sent cavalry, killed many and had Theudas beheaded. Under Pilate a Samaritan gathered people at Mount Gerizim, promising to show them sacred vessels Moses had buried there. Pilate's horsemen and foot soldiers fell on them. Wright counts such leaders among the popular prophets who copied Moses or Joshua and tried to lead a movement of liberation. Hebrews 3:2-6 sets Jesus beside Moses through Numbers 12:7, where God calls Moses faithful in all his house. Many Jewish traditions ranked Moses above everyone else in history, or below Abraham alone.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a movement that keeps an empty chair for its founder's true successor. Every time a strong new leader appears, someone asks whether he is the one for the chair.
entries.changes: When people ask a preacher whether he is the Prophet, as in John 1:21, they mean the one Moses promised. A sign that repeats the exodus, such as bread in the wilderness in John 6:14, raises the same hope. In Acts 3:22 Peter applies Moses' promise to Jesus.
entries.not: **Not a seat the movement fills by its own choice.** A movement picks its founder's successor. The Prophet was promised by God through Moses, and the crowds who decided for themselves that a leader was the one, as with Theudas, mostly ended under Roman swords.
entries.dissent: Whether the Prophet and the Messiah were one figure. The ESV Study Bible says some held them to be different persons, and Keener's notes have the Prophet with Elijah coming before the Messiah. In John 6:14-15 the crowd moves straight from calling Jesus the Prophet to making him king, which Keener explains from traditions of Moses as a king and Wright describes as a jump from prophet to Messiah. The ESV Study Bible adds that Jesus' kingship at his first coming was spiritual.

usedIn.s: Near Passover Jesus feeds five thousand men from five barley loaves and two fish. The crowd hails him as the Prophet and wants to make him king, and that night he comes to his disciples walking on the sea.

usedIn.s: In the synagogue at Capernaum the crowd asks for a sign like the manna. Jesus answers that he is the bread of life come down from heaven, and his hard words about eating his flesh drive many disciples away.

usedIn.n: John 7:37-52, Rivers of living water on the last day
usedIn.s: On the great last day of the feast Jesus cries out that the thirsty should come to him and drink. The crowd divides over whether he is the Prophet or the Messiah, and the Pharisees scorn a prophet from Galilee.

usedIn.n: Acts 3:1-26, The lame man at the Beautiful Gate
usedIn.s: At the afternoon hour of prayer Peter heals a man lame from birth who begged at the temple gate, then tells the gathering crowd that Jesus is the prophet Moses promised.

entries.title: God's council and throne room
entries.summary: Israel's Scriptures picture God presiding over an assembly of heavenly beings, the sons of God, and Psalm 82 calls its members gods. Who those gods are is one of the hardest questions behind John 10.
aliases: let all God's angels worship him
entries.plain: **A king does not rule alone. He sits with a council, and the council answers to him.** Several Old Testament passages picture God the same way, seated among heavenly beings who serve him. Psalm 82 opens with God standing in that assembly and judging its members, whom it calls gods and sons of the Most High, and it ends with them sentenced to die like men. Jesus quotes this psalm in John 10. Who the psalm's gods are is debated, and the answer changes how his argument works.
entries.then: Heiser reads Psalm 82:1 as God standing in a council of elohim, divine beings. He argues that Psalm 89:5-7, which places an assembly of holy ones in the heavens, cannot describe human beings. On John 10 he writes that Jesus' quotation recalls that "the Jewish Scriptures bore witness to nonhuman sons of God." The quotation sits between Jesus' claims to be one with the Father (10:30) and that the Father is in him (10:38). For Heiser, it sets Jesus above all the divine sons of God. Keener's background commentary reads the psalm as aimed at the kings of the earth, viewed as God's council, who thought themselves divine but would die like mortals. His notes say it probably mocks Near Eastern rulers who saw themselves as gods, which fits a festival that remembered Antiochus. Jewish tradition sometimes applied the verse to Israel receiving the law at Sinai, the reading Wright follows. The ESV and CSB Study Bibles read the gods as human judges, called gods as God's representatives. Jesus argues in a standard Jewish how-much-more form. Heiser also finds the council behind Hebrews 1-2: at 1:6 the angels worship the Son, in a line of Deuteronomy 32:43 whose Dead Sea Scrolls text reads sons of God. Hebrews 2:5 puts the world to come under God's human family, not his divine one. He writes that "the divine council was there at Sinai witnessing the delivering of the law." The picture of ranked gods is older. Podany dates the start of kingship to around 2900 BC. About a thousand years later, the belief that the gods too had a king and a hierarchy was written down. She also describes Babylon's New Year festival of the sixth century BC. There the gods of many cities conferred, and Marduk, king of the gods, declared the fates. The comparison with Psalm 82 is drawn here, not by Podany.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a royal court where the king sits among the governors who rule his provinces in his name. Calling them lords honors their office, and the king can still strip them of it.
entries.changes: The council picture lies behind Jesus' quotation of Psalm 82 in John 10:34-36, whose force depends on who the gods are. In Heiser's reading it also lies behind Paul's remark in 1 Corinthians 6:3 that believers will judge angels, and behind the command in Hebrews 1:6 that the angels, sons of God in one ancient text of the verse, worship the Son.
entries.not: **Not a court of human officials.** A king's governors are men he appointed and can replace with other men. In Heiser's reading the council members are divine beings, and in Psalm 82 God sentences them to die like mortals. Other sources here read them as human rulers or judges.
entries.dissent: Who the gods of Psalm 82 are. Heiser: divine beings of God's council, so the quotation sets Jesus above all divine sons of God. Keener's background commentary: earthly kings viewed as God's council, who thought themselves divine. Keener's notes: Near Eastern rulers who saw themselves as divine, though some Jewish interpreters applied the verse to Israel at Sinai, and Jesus may be using his hearers' reading or leaving a riddle. Wright: Israel at Sinai, exalted by receiving the law. The ESV and CSB Study Bibles: human judges, called gods as God's representatives.

usedIn.s: At the seventh trumpet heaven announces that rule over the world now belongs to God and his Messiah for ever. The elders worship, the angry nations meet God's judgment, and the heavenly temple opens to reveal the ark of the covenant.

entries.title: God's name and I am
entries.summary: God gave his name to Moses at the burning bush as I AM, and in Isaiah he says I am he. To make God's name known was to show who he is, and when Jesus uses those words in certain settings, his hearers can take them as God's own name.
aliases: for the sake of the Name
entries.plain: **Some words are ordinary until the wrong person says them.** I am is about the plainest phrase there is. But Israel's God gave his name to Moses as I AM, and in Isaiah he says I am he. So when Jesus says I am in certain places in John, above all before Abraham was, I am, his hearers can take it as a claim to God's own name, and they pick up stones.
entries.then: I am was a title for God (Exodus 3:14), and in the Greek Septuagint of Isaiah 43:10 God declares, I am. Bailey notes that Jesus' words to the Samaritan woman in 4:26 are the Greek Old Testament's exact phrase for God at the burning bush. On the lake in 6:20, it is I is literally I am. Keener calls that a legitimate translation but finds the nuance of deity probably present, since in the Old Testament only God walked on the water (Job 9:8). At 8:58 Jesus does not say before Abraham was, I was. The ESV Study Bible hears the Greek of Exodus 3:14, a claim to be the God of the burning bush. Wright calls I Am a central meaning of YHWH, God's holy name. He says Jesus is so one with the Father that he can use the Name of himself. Heiser reads 8:56-58 against Genesis 12 and 15, where the word of Yahweh appeared to Abraham. The hearers reach for stones, the penalty for blasphemy. A mere claim to be the Messiah was not counted blasphemy, Keener notes, so they understood him to claim deity. Revealing God's name meant revealing his character (Exodus 33:19; 34:5). Many Jews prayed for the day God would show his name holy in all the world. Heiser says Jesus' making the name known in John 17 meant "showing them who God was and what he was like." He recalls that Yahweh's name dwelt in his Angel (Exodus 23:20-23). A tradition attributed to Artapanus said Pharaoh fell when Moses spoke God's name.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a soldier who answers the sentry's challenge with the general's own password. The words are ordinary, but everyone on the wall knows whose they are.
entries.changes: When Jesus speaks the words I am in a setting that recalls God naming himself, as at John 8:58 or on the water in Mark 6:50, the hearer is meant to catch an echo of the divine name. The same words can also simply mean it is I, so the setting decides.
entries.not: **Not a borrowed password.** A soldier who gives the general's password claims only to serve him. In these readings Jesus uses the Name of himself, and his hearers took it as a claim to deity and reached for stones. Most I am sayings are ordinary speech; the setting carries the echo.
entries.dissent: How much to hear in the words. On John 6:20 Keener allows that it is I is the right everyday sense and sees a probable nuance of deity, and his notes say the context supports an allusion to deity. On 8:58 the ESV Study Bible hears the formula of Exodus 3:14, Wright hears Jesus using the Name in union with the Father, and Heiser hears the Word of Yahweh who appeared to Abraham. Keener adds that a later tradition of priests reciting Isaiah's I am he at Tabernacles may not be early enough to explain the verse.

entries.title: Children of Abraham
entries.summary: Jews called Abraham our father, and many believed that being his descendants all but guaranteed a place among God's saved people. The Gospels and Paul argue over who his true children are.
entries.plain: **Our family has been in this church for six generations, so of course we belong.** Every Jew traced his people back to Abraham, the man God called and made promises to. Being his children meant being God's chosen people, and in popular belief it nearly guaranteed a share in the world to come. Calling someone a father could also mean the person whose ways you follow. So an argument about who your father is could turn into an argument about how you live.
entries.then: In popular Jewish belief, Keener notes, being born of Abraham's line all but assured a person of salvation, unless he was among the very wicked, since Israel was chosen in Abraham. Abraham was also the model convert. He was a Gentile until his circumcision and was said to have destroyed idols, and traditions held that his merit sustained Israel in later generations. Father could mean ancestor. It could also mean the one whose ways a person imitated, often a teacher, or whose character a person showed. In Jewish literature children of Abraham was equal to children of God, because God had adopted Abraham's descendants (Exodus 4:22). To suggest that someone had one father by law and another by nature was to accuse his mother of adultery. Tradition said God showed Abraham, the model of hospitality in Genesis 18, the kingdoms that would oppress Israel and the messianic age beyond them. Samaritans claimed descent from Jacob too, which Jews denied. Wright says the argument in John 8 turns on confusing two family memberships, children of Abraham and children of God. John the Baptist, Jesus and writers like John and Paul insisted they were not the same. The ESV Study Bible reads John 8:39-40 with Romans 2:28-29 and 9:6-8: Abraham's true children are those who believe, as he believed God (Galatians 3:6; James 2:23). Jews called themselves Abraham's offspring and heirs of his covenant. They applied the title occasionally to the outstandingly righteous but never to Gentiles. When later rabbis applied Abraham's seed to one person, they meant Isaac. Jews of Paul's day saw the Nabatean Arabs as Ishmaelites, Hagar's descendants.
entries.bridge: An analogy: an old family firm where the founder's name on the door is supposed to guarantee the work. A grandson who cheats the customers can still claim the name, but people start asking whether he is really a son of the house.
entries.changes: When people say Abraham is their father, as in John 8:39, they are claiming a place among God's people, and a reply about deeds turns descent into likeness. John the Baptist's warning in Matthew 3:9 makes the same move, and Paul argues in Romans 9:6-8 that not all who descend from Abraham are his children.
entries.not: **Not a bloodline closed to outsiders.** A family firm passes only to the founder's own descendants. Reading Paul, the ESV Study Bible counts as Abraham's true children those who believe as he did, so the house takes in Gentiles, a use of the title Jewish writers of the day never allowed.

usedIn.n: Romans 9:1-5, Israel's privileges
usedIn.s: Paul grieves for his own people and lists what belongs to Israel: the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the law, the worship, the promises, the patriarchs and the Messiah.

usedIn.n: Romans 11:11-24, The olive tree
usedIn.s: Israel's stumbling has brought salvation to the Gentiles. Paul pictures Gentile believers as wild olive shoots grafted into Israel's tree and warns them not to boast over the natural branches.

usedIn.n: Romans 11:25-36, The full number of the nations
usedIn.s: Paul reveals a mystery: a partial hardening has come on Israel until the full number of the Gentiles comes in, and so all Israel will be saved. He ends in praise of God's wisdom.

usedIn.n: Galatians 3:1-14, Who bewitched you? Abraham's blessing and the law's curse
usedIn.s: Paul asks the Galatians who has bewitched them, since they received the Spirit by believing, then argues from Abraham that those who believe share his blessing, while Christ took the law's curse by being hung on a tree.

usedIn.n: Galatians 3:15-22, A will no one can change, and a law given through angels
usedIn.s: Paul argues from the way a ratified will cannot be altered that the law, coming 430 years after the promise to Abraham and his seed, cannot cancel it, and says the law was added because of transgressions, put in place through angels by a mediator.

usedIn.n: Galatians 3:23-29, The law as a guardian until faith came
usedIn.s: Before faith came, Paul says, we were held in custody under the law, which served as a guardian until Christ; now all who have been baptized into Christ are God's children, one in him, Abraham's seed and heirs.

usedIn.n: Galatians 4:21-5:1, Hagar, Sarah and Sinai in Arabia
usedIn.s: Paul reads the story of Abraham's two sons as a figure of two covenants: Hagar the slave stands for Sinai and the present Jerusalem, Sarah the free woman for the Jerusalem above, and he calls the Galatians to stand firm in freedom.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 11:8-16, Strangers looking for a city
usedIn.s: By faith Abraham left home without knowing where he was going and lived in tents in the promised land as a foreigner, waiting for a city with lasting foundations that God himself designed and built. He and Sarah and their family died still waiting, admitting they were strangers on earth and longing for a better, heavenly country.

usedIn.n: James 2:14-26, Faith that shudders, Abraham and Rahab
usedIn.s: Faith without deeds is dead, James argues. Wishing a hungry brother well helps no one, the demons believe that God is one and shudder, and Abraham and Rahab were counted righteous by what they did.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 3:1-7, A wife who does not share her husband's gods
usedIn.s: Wives are to submit to their husbands so that husbands who do not believe may be won without a word, by their conduct. Their beauty should be a gentle and quiet spirit rather than braided hair and gold, like Sarah, who obeyed Abraham and called him lord. Husbands must be considerate and honor their wives as co-heirs of the gracious gift of life.

entries.title: Rulers and powers over the nations
entries.summary: Many Jews believed each nation had a spiritual ruler set over it, often hostile to God's people. Paul's rulers, authorities, powers and thrones belong to that picture.
aliases: rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms
in heaven and on earth and under the earth
the world to come not subject to angels
under the control of the evil one
entries.plain: **The map showed each country under its own flag, but the real question was who stood behind each flag.** The book of Daniel speaks of a prince of Persia and a prince of Greece, heavenly rulers who fought against the angel sent to Daniel. From texts like these many Jews believed that each nation had a heavenly ruler over it, and that these rulers were often hostile to Israel. Many people also believed the stars and Fate ruled their lives. When Paul lists rulers, authorities and powers, he is using words that carried that meaning.
entries.then: The cultural backgrounds notes take the rulers and powers of Romans 8:38 as the guardian angels thought to rule the nations, often hostile to God's people. The idea appears as early as Daniel 10:13 and 20-21 and in the Greek version of Deuteronomy 32:8. Keener writes that "Many ancient Jewish writers used these terms in this way," for the spiritual forces ruling the nations and opposing God's people. Heiser lists Paul's vocabulary: rulers, principalities, authorities, powers, lords, thrones and world rulers. He argues that these words were used for authority over geographical domains, the worldview of Deuteronomy 32:8-9. Sometimes they mean human rulers, but in places Paul plainly means spiritual beings. The Greek translations of Daniel 10 call Michael and the prince of Persia by the word archon, the word Paul uses for the rulers of this age. Arnold notes that Paul's terms all appear in Jewish writings of the period, such as 1 Enoch 61:10. He adds that later tradition made the rulers of the other nations deceivers: Jubilees 15:31 says God set spirits over them to lead them astray. Almost everyone believed the heavens had several levels, with different spiritual beings in each and God in the highest. So heavenly realms could mean where God is or where the powers live. The air was thought the lowest heaven, inhabited by spirits. Keener reads the rulers of Ephesians 3:10 as the angels of the nations, shown God's wisdom in a church drawn from many peoples. Heiser reads the mission to the Gentiles as the reclaiming of nations disinherited at Babel and left under lesser gods.
entries.bridge: An analogy: an empire whose provinces are run by governors, some of whom have gone rogue and rule for themselves. When the rightful king comes back, every governor's claim is in question.
entries.changes: Because rulers and powers named alongside angels meant the spiritual rulers of the nations, Paul's promise in Romans 8:38 that none of them can separate believers from God's love answers a real fear. Ephesians 6:12 sets the believer's struggle against the same rulers and authorities, and Colossians 2:15 says they were disarmed at the cross.
entries.not: **Not a map of provinces with named governors.** An empire knows which governor holds which province. Paul never names or ranks these powers or ties them to a country, and the sources disagree on how far his terms mean spirits, human rulers or both.
entries.dissent: How specific the terms are. Heiser, Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes read spiritual rulers over the nations, in the line of Daniel 10 and Deuteronomy 32. The ESV Study Bible says only angelic and demonic authorities. Arnold notes: "Paul himself never connected the powers of darkness with any specific country or territory." Second, how the rulers of Ephesians 3:10 receive what the church shows them. The ESV and CSB Study Bibles read angels watching with interest. Wright thinks the rulers are unlikely to welcome the news, and Heiser that the plan was hidden from hostile powers until after the resurrection. Third, where the air of Ephesians 2:2 was. Heiser sets the Israelite picture beside the Greco-Roman one and leaves the choice open. Fourth, whether the four terms of Colossians 1:16 form a ladder of rank. The CSB and ESV Study Bibles see ranks of angels. Heiser finds that no one has traced a coherent order, and Arnold takes every power in Colossians as hostile, since 2:15 defeats them. Fifth, who the rulers of this age are in 1 Corinthians 2:6-8. Heiser and Arnold read spiritual rulers; Keener thinks earthly rulers fit the context better.

A prince of Persia resists for twenty-one days, a prince of Greece is coming, and Michael fights for Israel.

ddd.n: The princes of Persia and Greece
ddd.s: Spirit figures in Daniel who rule nations and can hold up a messenger from God for weeks.
A word that means messenger and describes a job, not a species of being.

usedIn.n: Romans 8:31-39, Angels, rulers and powers
usedIn.s: With God on the believers' side, Paul asks who could oppose them, then names hardships and powers, from the sword to angels, rulers, height and depth, and none of them can cut believers off from God's love in Christ.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 2:6-16, The rulers of this age
usedIn.s: Paul speaks of a hidden wisdom of God, planned before time began, which the rulers of this age failed to grasp, or they would never have put Jesus to death.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 6:1-11, Lawsuits before unbelievers
usedIn.s: Paul is appalled that believers take one another to court before pagan judges, reminds them that God's people will judge the world and even angels, and asks why they would not rather be wronged.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 15:12-34, If the dead are not raised
usedIn.s: Against some who say there is no resurrection of the dead, Paul argues that then Christ was not raised either, calls Christ the firstfruits, and asks why anyone is baptized for the dead or why he fights wild beasts if the dead are not raised.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 4:1-6, The god of this age
usedIn.s: Paul renounces cunning and tampering with God's word; if his gospel is veiled, it is veiled to the perishing, whose minds the god of this age has blinded, while God has made his light shine in believers' hearts.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 1:15-23, Far above every name that is invoked
usedIn.s: Paul prays that the believers will know the hope, the inheritance and the power God showed when he raised Christ and seated him above every ruler, authority, power and name, in this age and the next.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 2:1-10, The ruler of the kingdom of the air
usedIn.s: Paul reminds his readers that they were once dead in sins, following the ruler of the kingdom of the air, until God in his mercy made them alive and seated them with Christ in the heavenly realms, saved by grace.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 3:1-13, The prisoner, the steward and the mystery shown to the powers
usedIn.s: Paul, a prisoner for the sake of the Gentiles, breaks off to explain the stewardship of grace given him: the mystery, now revealed, that Gentiles are co-heirs, made known through the church even to the rulers in the heavenly realms.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 3:14-21, Kneeling before the Father of every family
usedIn.s: Paul kneels in prayer before the Father of every family, heavenly and earthly, and asks that they be strengthened by the Spirit and grasp the vast dimensions of Christ's love, closing with praise.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 4:1-16, The conqueror goes up and gives gifts
usedIn.s: Paul urges unity, one body and one Spirit, then reads Psalm 68 as Christ ascending in victory and handing out gifts: apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers, to equip the church to grow up into him.

usedIn.n: Ephesians 6:10-17, The armor of God
usedIn.s: Paul calls the believers to stand firm in God's armor, because their struggle is not against flesh and blood but against rulers, authorities and spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms.

usedIn.n: Philippians 2:1-11, The form of a slave, a cross, and every knee
usedIn.s: Paul urges humility and concern for others, then sets out Christ, who did not exploit his equality with God but took the form of a slave and died on a cross, and whom God exalted so that every knee will bow.

usedIn.n: Colossians 1:15-20, Firstborn over creation, over thrones and powers
usedIn.s: Paul describes the Son as the image of the unseen God and firstborn over all creation, through whom and for whom everything was made, thrones and powers included, and through whose cross God makes peace with all things.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 2:5-18, The world to come is not for angels
usedIn.s: God did not put the world to come under angels. Psalm 8 promised rule to human beings; it is not yet seen, but Jesus, made a little lower than the angels for a while, is crowned with glory, and he shared flesh and blood to break the devil's power and become a merciful and faithful high priest.

usedIn.n: 1 Peter 3:8-22, A defense, and the spirits in prison
usedIn.s: Peter calls for harmony and for blessing in return for insult, and tells his readers to be ready to make a defense of their hope. Christ suffered once for sins, was put to death in the body and made alive in the Spirit, and went and made proclamation to the spirits in prison who disobeyed in Noah's day; the flood that saved eight people prefigures baptism, and Christ has gone into heaven, where every angelic authority and power is subject to him.

usedIn.n: 1 John 5:13-21, The sin that leads to death, the evil one and idols
usedIn.s: John writes so that believers may know they have eternal life, and that God hears them. They are to pray for a brother or sister whose sin does not lead to death, though there is a sin that does. Those born of God are kept from the evil one, while the whole world lies under his power; the letter ends with a warning to keep away from idols.

usedIn.n: Revelation 1:9-20, Patmos, the Lord's day, lampstands and stars
usedIn.s: On the island of Patmos, in the Spirit on the Lord's day, John hears a voice like a trumpet telling him to write to seven churches. He turns and sees one like a son of man among seven golden lampstands, holding seven stars, who holds the keys of death and Hades and explains what the stars and lampstands mean.

usedIn.n: Revelation 12:7-17, war in heaven and the accuser thrown down
usedIn.s: Michael and his angels fight the dragon and throw him out of heaven, and a voice celebrates the fall of the accuser of the brothers, defeated by the Lamb's blood and the witnesses' testimony. On earth the dragon chases the woman, who is given eagle's wings, and when the earth swallows the river he spews after her, he turns to make war on her other children.

entries.title: Adam in Jewish tradition
entries.summary: The Old Testament says little about Adam outside Genesis, but by Paul's day Jewish writers spoke often of his lost glory and of the sin and death he brought into the world. Each person, they added, became his own Adam.
entries.plain: **Every family has a founder, and the stories about him explain why things are the way they are.** In Genesis Adam disobeys God and is driven out of the garden. The rest of the Old Testament hardly mentions him. By the first century, though, Jewish teachers said a great deal about him: how glorious he had been, how that glory was lost, and how his sin let death into the world. They also held that each of his children chose sin for themselves. Many hoped that the glory Adam lost would be given back to the righteous in the age to come.
entries.then: Adam is hardly mentioned in the Old Testament outside Genesis, Keener notes, but Jewish traditions had made him far more prominent. They dwelt on the glory Adam had and lost when he fell. In their view his sin opened the door to sin and death, and every one of his descendants bore his guilt; some traditions stressed this biblical idea. Yet 4 Ezra 7:118 and 2 Baruch 54:15 also say that each descendant chose to follow Adam, and 2 Baruch 54:19 calls each person "our own Adam." Falling short of God's glory in Romans 3:23 may allude to the idea that humanity lost God's glory when Adam sinned. The hope ran the other way too. Most Jewish interpreters expected the righteous to get Adam's glory back in the coming world. Israel would reign in that world as Adam and Eve reigned before the fall. Wright and Bird set Israel in Canaan in the place Adam held in Eden. They add that the sectarians at Qumran looked for a day when the sons of light would recapture "the glory of Adam." Ancient Israelite thought could picture one person standing for or affecting many, which the cultural backgrounds notes call corporate identity. Jewish texts often described Adam, or people as a whole, as bearing God's image. The old self of Romans 6:6 could be translated old humanity, humanity in Adam. Later Jewish stories made Eve's guilt or deception larger than Genesis does. Some argued from it that women were less able to reason, and parts of Judaism tied the curse on Eve to death in childbirth.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a family that tells the story of the ancestor who lost the estate. Every generation knows the story, every generation repeats some of his mistakes, and every generation hopes someone will win the estate back.
entries.changes: Because Jewish tradition made Adam the door through which sin and death came in, Paul can set Adam and Christ side by side in Romans 5:12-21 and expect his Jewish hearers to follow. The same pairing returns in 1 Corinthians 15:22, where all die in Adam and all are made alive in Christ. 1 Timothy 2:13-14 argues from the order of creation and from Eve's deception, a story Jewish tradition had already enlarged.
entries.not: **Not a family memory.** In a family the ancestor's loss is a story, and each heir's mistakes are his own. Many Jewish traditions blamed Adam's sin for the sin and death of everyone after him, and Israelite thought could picture one person standing for many.
entries.dissent: Whether Jews thought Adam's guilt passed to his descendants. Keener writes that Jewish traditions held that all Adam's descendants shared his guilt, and the cultural backgrounds notes say some traditions stressed it; the cultural backgrounds article Adam in Jewish Tradition says "Jewish tradition did not normally speak as if people genetically inherited Adam's sin" or his guilt, but held that Adam brought sin and death in and that his descendants then sinned as he did. Both agree that Jewish tradition counted everyone a sinner.

usedIn.n: Romans 5:1-21, Peace with God, and Adam
usedIn.s: Justified by faith, believers have peace with God and are reconciled to him by the death of his Son. As sin and death came through Adam, grace and life come through Christ.

usedIn.n: Romans 6:1-23, Slaves of a new master
usedIn.s: Baptized into Christ's death, believers are dead to sin. Once slaves of sin, they have been set free to become slaves of God, whose gift is eternal life.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 15:12-34, If the dead are not raised
usedIn.s: Against some who say there is no resurrection of the dead, Paul argues that then Christ was not raised either, calls Christ the firstfruits, and asks why anyone is baptized for the dead or why he fights wild beasts if the dead are not raised.

usedIn.n: 1 Corinthians 15:35-58, Seeds, stars and the last trumpet

usedIn.n: Colossians 3:1-17, Things above, and no Greek, Jew, barbarian or Scythian
usedIn.s: Raised with Christ, the believers are to set their minds on things above, put to death the old ways, take off the old self and put on the new, in which there is no Greek or Jew, barbarian, Scythian, slave or free, and above all put on love.

usedIn.n: 1 Timothy 2:8-15, Lifted hands, braided hair, women learning, Eve and childbearing
usedIn.s: Paul wants men to pray without anger or arguing and women to dress modestly; women are to learn quietly, and he does not permit a woman to teach or have authority over a man, arguing from Adam and Eve, before a hard saying about being saved through childbearing.

entries.title: The new covenant
entries.summary: Jeremiah and Ezekiel promised a day when God would write his law on hearts instead of stone and put his own Spirit within his people. Some Jews of Paul's day believed the promise belonged to their own group.
entries.plain: **The old rules were carved on the wall; the new ones are written into the people who keep them.** At Sinai God gave the law on stone tablets, and Moses came down the mountain with his face shining so brightly that he covered it with a veil. Centuries later, facing exile, the prophets promised a new covenant. God would forgive his people, give them new hearts, write his law inside them and put his own Spirit in them. Jews in Paul's day knew these promises, and some groups believed they were already coming true among them.
entries.then: The first law was written by God's finger on tablets of stone (Exodus 31:18). The prophets promised a new giving of the law (Isaiah 2:3), this time written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:31-34). Keener notes that the heart was the law's intended home from the start (Deuteronomy 30:6, 11-14). Ezekiel promised that God would replace hearts of stone with hearts of flesh and put his Spirit within his people (Ezekiel 11:19-20; 36:26-27). Many Jews of the time expected this new or renewed covenant. The sect behind the Dead Sea Scrolls applied it to their own group in the Damascus Document, and they kept the law of Moses more strictly still. The blood of the first covenant was itself sometimes called the eternal covenant (Psalms of Solomon 10:4). Wright reads Jeremiah's promise as a new marriage of God and his people. It had to deal with their sins and set the relationship on a new footing, with the gift of God's own Spirit at its center. The future coming of the Spirit was a common Jewish hope. Moses' shining face (Exodus 34:29-35) had been expanded at length in Jewish tradition. Many in the empire saw Moses as a divine man, one of the ancient heroes with special powers from God. The law was read aloud regularly in synagogues. Comparisons argued from the lesser to the greater, the Jewish principle qal vahomer, how much more, were common among Jewish teachers and others. Wright and Bird sum up Paul's contrast in 2 Corinthians 3 as a ministry of the Spirit, of life and of lasting glory, set against a ministry of death whose glory faded.
entries.bridge: An analogy: the difference between a safety manual pinned to the workshop wall and a master craftsman who has the rules in his hands. The rules have not changed; where they live has.
entries.changes: Because the prophets promised a covenant written on hearts by the Spirit, the contrast in 2 Corinthians 3:3-6 between stone and hearts, letter and Spirit, claims that the promise has arrived. Luke 22:20 speaks of the new covenant in Jesus' blood, and Hebrews 8:8-12 quotes Jeremiah's promise in full.
entries.not: **Not a skill learned at the bench.** A craftsman gets the rules into his hands by years of practice. In the prophets God himself writes the law on the heart and puts his own Spirit within his people, so the change is his gift, not the worker's achievement.
entries.dissent: Why Moses veiled his face. The cultural backgrounds notes say the people could not bear the glory, which could harm them, and that it also faded over time. The CSB Study Bible says the veil's main purpose was to keep Israel from seeing the old covenant's glory fade, a law designed to become obsolete. Keener stresses that the glory had to be covered, unlike Paul's open speech, and would always fade.

usedIn.n: 2 Corinthians 3:1-18, Letters of recommendation and Moses' veil
usedIn.s: Paul needs no letters of recommendation, since the Corinthians are his letter, written by the Spirit on hearts; he sets the fading glory on Moses' veiled face against the greater glory of the new covenant.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 8:1-13, Copy and shadow, and a new covenant
usedIn.s: The high priest believers have is seated in heaven and serves in the true tabernacle set up by the Lord. The earthly sanctuary was a copy and shadow built to the pattern shown to Moses, and Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant shows that the first was growing old and ready to disappear.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 9:11-22, Blood, ashes and a will
usedIn.s: Christ entered the greater tent once for all with his own blood, not the blood of goats and calves. If the ashes of a heifer could make the unclean outwardly clean, how much more will his blood cleanse the conscience; and as a will takes effect only at a death, the new covenant was put in force by his.

entries.title: Caught up to heaven
entries.summary: Jewish visionaries told of being caught up through the heavens to see God's throne and paradise, and writers numbered the heavens differently. Paul's third heaven speaks that language, though he refuses to make it his credential.
aliases: in the body or out of the body
set your minds on things above
entries.plain: **He would only say it happened to a man he knew, and then he changed the subject.** Some Jews in Paul's day told stories of holy men taken up into heaven, through layer after layer of sky, to see God's throne and the garden of paradise. Writers disagreed about how many heavens there were; three and seven were the favorite numbers. Some people tried to prepare for such experiences by fasting and prayer. Paul says a man was caught up to the third heaven and into paradise, tells it as if about someone else, and will not repeat what he heard.
entries.then: Jewish visionaries sometimes described their experiences of heaven as being caught up. The experience could be so vivid that the whole person seemed taken up, as in Ezekiel, and some texts, such as 1 Enoch, explicitly included the body. Greek writers also spoke of ascents of the soul, especially after death. Many Greek readers thought the pure soul rose to the highest heaven when it died. Texts varied in the number of heavens they pictured, from three to 365. Keener notes that "three and seven were the most common numbers", with paradise, the new Eden, kept in the heavens until the world to come. The ESV Study Bible explains three heavens: the air where birds fly, the higher sky of sun, moon and stars, and the unseen realm where God dwells. The CSB Study Bible gives the same three. Paradise, a Persian loanword, names the garden of Eden in the Greek Old Testament. Wright remarks that "Since heaven was often subdivided into seven," a third heaven might have seemed a letdown. Some Jewish writers cultivated visions with fasting and sleep deprivation. Wright writes that prayer, fasting and strict keeping of the Torah could create the conditions for being caught up. These practices are known mostly from later traditions, but he finds signs that they existed in Saul's day. Revelations in the Greek mystery cults were likewise said to be unutterable, and Josephus and Philo used the idea of God's highest wisdom or his name. Heiser describes Eden as God's home on earth, where his council met. Linking that picture to Paul's paradise is an inference drawn here, not by the sources.
entries.bridge: An analogy: an astronaut who, asked to prove his worth, mentions his walk in space in one sentence, says he cannot describe it, and spends the rest of the talk on the injury that still slows him down. The audience knows what the trip means, which is why his refusal to dwell on it stands out.
entries.changes: Because stories of ascent were a known way to claim heavenly knowledge, the third heaven of 2 Corinthians 12:2-4 matches anything a rival could boast of, and is turned to weakness. Revelation 4:1-2 opens a door in heaven and calls the seer up, and Luke 23:43 promises paradise.
entries.not: **Not a trip he planned or trained for.** An astronaut earns his walk in space by years of preparation and knows exactly where he was. Paul tells it as something done to him, and he does not know whether he was in the body or out of it.
entries.dissent: How much is known about Jewish ascent practice in Paul's day. Keener cautions that, except for Philo, all the Jewish ascent stories are pseudonymous or later than Paul, so the practice of his time is hard to reconstruct. Wright grants that the evidence comes mostly from later traditions but finds indications that such ways of prayer were already known in Saul's day. A second question is what lies behind the visions of Colossians 2:18. Keener and his notes point to Jewish mystics who fasted and sought visions of God's throne, Wright to Jewish traditions of meditation that hoped for a sight of the heavenly realm, and Wright and Bird to the angels' worship in the Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice from Qumran. The ESV Study Bible reads the rare verb for entering from inscriptions near Ephesus, where "It denoted the higher stage of mystery cult initiation", and so finds a pagan rite behind the teacher's claims.
