entries.title: The elements of the world
entries.summary: Paul twice says that people were enslaved under the stoicheia, the elements of the world. The word could mean basic rules, the stuff the world is made of, or the powers people worshiped in nature and the stars, and scholars still disagree which he meant.
aliases: elemental spiritual forces of this world
entries.plain: **She says she does not believe in horoscopes, but she will not book the wedding on an unlucky day.** The Greek word stoicheia meant things set in a row: the letters of the alphabet, the first lessons of a subject, or the four elements the world was thought to be made of, earth, water, air and fire. Many of Paul's Gentile neighbors worshiped those elements, and the sun, moon and stars, as gods, and feared that Fate ruled their lives through the stars and through lucky and unlucky days. Paul says that before Christ both Jews and Gentiles were slaves under the elements of the world. Scholars do not agree whether he meant religious rules, the forces of nature, or spiritual powers standing behind them.
entries.then: The root meaning is a row or line of elements. That could be the sounds of a language, the earth, air, water and fire of physics, or the principles of a teaching. Wright reports that recent research finds the physical sense the most common. The word could also mean anything rudimentary, such as the alphabet. Many Gentiles revered the elements of the universe, such as wind, fire, stars and sea, as deities. Keener writes that "Judaism had long since demythologized them as angels who ruled over nature" (compare Psalm 148:2-4). Most people of the time feared personified Fate, thought to work its will through the astral spirits that ruled the stars. Some pagan thinkers after Euhemerus counted the sun, moon, planets and stars as gods by nature, unlike gods invented by people. Gentiles kept festivals for their gods and counted some days lucky or unlucky. Judaism had its own calendar of holy days, new moons and sabbatical years. The cultural backgrounds notes call a return to "a ceremonial, calendrical religion regulated by heavenly bodies they once regarded as gods" a return to pagan bondage. Wright points to Wisdom of Solomon 7:17-19, which joins the activity of the elements to solstices, seasons, the cycles of the year and the constellations. He also cites Philo on people who revere the elements under the names Hephaestus, Hera, Poseidon and Demeter. Phrygia's native cults, such as that of the mother goddess, were closely tied to nature. Arnold notes that pagans and Jews alike used words such as powers and world rulers for the spirits of the stars. He adds that Paul uses stoicheia only in letters to churches in Asia Minor.
entries.bridge: An analogy: someone who gives up reading the horoscope page but keeps a private list of lucky and unlucky days. The rules have changed, and the fear underneath has not.
entries.changes: Because the word could mean basic rules, the stuff of the world or the powers worshiped in the sky, Galatians 4:3-10 can set the old life of Jews and of Gentiles side by side as two kinds of slavery. Colossians 2:8 warns against philosophy that follows the elements of the world rather than Christ, and 2 Peter 3:10 uses the word for the elements of the physical world.
entries.not: **Not a pagan habit carried over.** The analogy pictures one superstition kept under new rules. Paul sets the Jewish calendar of the law, which God gave, beside the Galatians' old pagan days, and several sources read the elements of Galatians 4:3 as the law itself.
entries.dissent: What the elements are in Galatians. The cultural backgrounds notes give two options: rudimentary principles kept by Jews and Gentiles, or, as many scholars hold, elements of the universe treated as gods. Keener reads the nature spirits the Galatians once worshiped, chief among them astral spirits tied to special days. The ESV Study Bible reads elementary principles, the law for Jews and pagan religion for Gentiles. Wright once read the guardian deities of the nations, but now writes "not the tutelary deities of the nations, as I have previously supposed", taking them as astral bodies or idols. Heiser splits Paul's usage: the law in 4:3, "divine beings, probably astral deities" in 4:9. Arnold reads personal spirits in both verses, calling that "the most compelling view", though his evidence comes mostly from the second and third centuries. The same split runs through Colossians 2:8 and 2:20. Keener writes that "here it may refer, as usually, to elementary principles". The ESV Study Bible writes, "Paul is likely using it here to refer to demonic spirits", and Arnold reads spirits that "inspire this teaching". Carson, Moo and Morris allow either sense.

entries.title: Curse and blessing
entries.summary: God's covenant set blessings for keeping it against curses for breaking it, and Deuteronomy spelled both out. Curses were also a familiar part of ancient religion, magic and everyday life.
entries.plain: **The contract had two lists at the back: what you get if you keep your side, and what happens if you break it.** In the Bible God's covenant came with blessings and curses. Genesis promises a blessing on those who bless Abraham and a curse on those who curse him, and Deuteronomy ends with long lists of blessings for keeping the law and curses for breaking it, the last of them being driven out of the land. People in the Greek and Roman world used curses too, often as secret spells against a rival. When Paul calls down a curse, or says that Christ became a curse, his readers heard all of that. Scholars disagree about what the law's curse meant for Paul.
entries.then: Genesis 12:3 and Deuteronomy 28 set curses on those who oppose Abraham or break the covenant against blessings on those who keep it. Reasoning by opposites was normal Jewish reading, and Deuteronomy 27:26 summed up the curses. Jewish teaching held that human obedience was always imperfect, so God could not demand perfect obedience as a condition of salvation. Yet Paul, like a good rabbi, presses Deuteronomy 27:26 for all it can give (Keener). Wright reads the curse as an event in history. In Deuteronomy it is exile from the land, while blessing was "the original purpose of the covenant" and curse its opposite. Written curses are very old. Podany describes the succession treaty the Assyrian king Esarhaddon imposed on his vassals in 672 BC. It carried about a hundred lines of curses on anyone who damaged the tablet and more than 150 fiercer lines on anyone who broke the oath. The likeness to Deuteronomy's covenant curses is drawn here, not by Podany. Oaths and curses were familiar in religion, magic and everyday life. People cursed rivals in sport and romance, usually in secret magic rather than in public letters. The word for curse in Galatians 1:8-9 is the one the Greek Old Testament uses in Deuteronomy 13 for Israelites who followed false gods. Deuteronomy 21:23 curses anyone hung on a tree. Israelites hung only the dead, and the CSB Study Bible takes the tree in Galatians to be the cross. By Paul's day the blessing of Abraham included the whole world to come. Curse invocations were the opposite of blessings, and the synagogue prayer "Peace be on Israel" answers the curse on the law's distorters.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a lease with a schedule of penalties at the back. Most tenants never read it until the landlord starts quoting it clause by clause.
entries.changes: Because the covenant joined blessing and curse, Paul can say in Galatians 3:13 that Christ took the law's curse by being hung on a tree, so that Abraham's blessing could reach the nations. Curse and blessing remain opposites in 1 Corinthians 16:22, where Paul curses anyone who does not love the Lord.
entries.not: **Not a contract between strangers.** A lease binds parties who owe each other nothing beyond its terms. Deuteronomy's curses sit inside a covenant whose first purpose was blessing, and Wright reads the curse as a judgment in history, exile from the land, not a fine.
entries.dissent: What the curse of Galatians 3:10 is. The ESV and CSB Study Bibles read it as falling on everyone, since no one keeps everything the law commands. Wright answers that "the curse in question wasn't a kind of other-worldly curse"; in Deuteronomy it is exile, a judgment in history on Israel, and Jesus bore it on a Roman cross. Keener notes that Jewish teaching did not require perfect obedience, and reads Paul as pressing Deuteronomy 27:26 to its limit.

entries.title: Deliberate sin and falling away
entries.summary: The law set sins done in ignorance apart from sins done in defiance, and sacrifice covered only the first. Many Jews held that someone who knowingly threw off God's law could not be restored, though teachers argued over who had gone that far.
aliases: no sacrifice for sins is left
impossible to be brought back to repentance
sin that does not lead to death
entries.plain: **A firm forgives the clerk who made an honest mistake; it does not rehire the one who walked out and set fire to the office.** The law of Moses separated sins done unknowingly from sins done openly and on purpose (Numbers 15:27-31). Sacrifices covered the first kind. For the second the law offered none, and the sinner was to be cut off from the people. By the first century many Jews believed that someone who knew God's law and deliberately rejected it could reach a point where there was no way back, though teachers argued about how far a person had to go.
entries.then: Judaism had long distinguished intentional from unintentional sin (Numbers 15:29-31; Leviticus 4:2). One who knew better was punished more strictly than one who did not. Sacrifices atoned for sins of ignorance. Jewish tradition taught that no sacrifice availed for a person who knowingly rejected the authority of God's law. Many teachers held that such a person needed repentance, the Day of Atonement and death. They warned that those who sinned expecting to be forgiven automatically had not truly repented. Early Judaism debated which kinds of sin the Day of Atonement covered. In common Jewish thought an Israelite who willfully rejected the law was shut out of the world to come, and some teachers called that sin unpardonable. Saying in effect I reject parts of God's word was counted as rejecting the whole law. The Dead Sea Scrolls set temporary penance for slight transgressions but expelled the deliberate rebel. A member of ten years' standing who then turned away was never allowed back. The rabbis disagreed among themselves. One tradition has Rabbi Meir holding that even Elisha ben Abuya, the famous apostate, could still repent. Most seem to have thought some people, King Manasseh among them, had gone past return. In many Jewish groups the apostate, or at any rate the worst kind, was thought beyond forgiveness. Judaism treated apostates as spiritually dead, as did Pythagoreans and some other groups. Some Jewish texts, the Dead Sea Scrolls and Jubilees among them, called a capital offense "a matter of death". It was normally enforced by expulsion from the community rather than by execution.
entries.bridge: An analogy: the difference in law between a driver who causes a crash and one who drives into a crowd on purpose. The first can make amends; the second has put himself outside the arrangements made for mistakes.
entries.changes: The line between ignorance and defiance stands behind the warning of Hebrews 10:26 that no sacrifice for sins is left for one who deliberately turns from the truth. 1 John 5:16 also separates sin that leads to death from sin that does not, and Mark 3:29 names a blasphemy that is never forgiven.
entries.not: **Not a single act judged once.** A driver's guilt rests on one moment at the wheel. The sources speak of knowing rejection of God's law as a settled turning away, and teachers argued over whether such a person could still repent; a court's verdict leaves no such question open.
entries.dissent: Who is in view in Hebrews 6:4-6. Keener argues that the language of being enlightened, tasting the heavenly gift and sharing in the Spirit means people genuinely converted, and the cultural backgrounds notes speak of believers deliberately turning from the truth. Wright and Bird lean toward people on the fringe of the community who had never fully come to faith. The CSB Study Bible sets out four readings: genuine Christians reverting to Judaism, hearers who understood but never believed, a warning about sanctification rather than justification, and a possibility the writer raises rather than a reality.

entries.title: The heavenly Jerusalem
entries.summary: Jews looked for a Jerusalem built by God for the age to come, and some spoke of it as already waiting in heaven. Exiles and resident aliens knew what it was to look for a city that would be home.
aliases: the city that is to come
pillar in the temple of my God
entries.plain: **Families driven from home keep the key to the old house and talk about the day they will go back.** Many Jews in the first century lived far from the land, counted as resident aliens in Greek cities. The prophets had promised a renewed Jerusalem and a Zion from which God's law would go out to the nations. Some Jews spoke of a new Jerusalem that God would build for the age to come; others, like Philo, made heaven itself the true home city of the righteous. Either way, the city that mattered most was one God would build.
entries.then: Abraham called himself a foreigner and stranger in Canaan (Genesis 23:4), and the law reminded Israel that the land was God's (Leviticus 25:23). Diaspora Jews were often counted as resident aliens in the cities where they lived, and they saw themselves as sojourners among the nations. Diaspora Judaism often called God the architect and builder of the world. Philo, like philosophers who compared the cosmos to a city, called heaven the mother city that God designed and built. For him the heavenly Jerusalem was not to be looked for on earth. More often Judeans and some Diaspora Jews looked for a new Jerusalem as the city of God in the age to come, as the Dead Sea Scrolls did. Zion rather than Sinai was to be the place of the new giving of the law in the end time (Isaiah 2:1-4). Everyone in antiquity counted a heavenly place of revelation above an earthly one. The Old Testament already pictures a heavenly Zion (Psalm 2:6; Isaiah 62:6-12). Wright and Bird read the final contrast of Hebrews as Sinai against the heavenly Jerusalem, a city in which believers are already citizens. Wright adds that, as in Galatians 4, the present Jerusalem stands under judgment and believers belong to the Jerusalem still to come. Keener holds that Christian hope stays tied to Israel's own history (Psalm 137:5-6). Jewish writers also described the coming city in detail: Tobit 13, a Qumran blueprint and the Temple Scroll's twelve gates. Heiser reads Eden, Sinai and Zion alike as God's mountain and temple. Beale notes that 1 Enoch sets God's throne and the tree of life on a high mountain.
entries.bridge: An analogy: an emigrant who already holds citizen's papers for a city he has never seen and is waiting for its gates to open. Where he lives now, he lives as a guest.
entries.changes: The hope of a city God builds explains why Hebrews 11:10 has Abraham live in tents while looking for a city with foundations. Paul sets the present Jerusalem against the Jerusalem above in Galatians 4:26, and Revelation 21:2 sees the new Jerusalem coming down from God.
entries.not: **Not a move to a city that already stands.** An emigrant leaves for a country that exists now. In most of these sources the city comes with the age to come and is tied to Jerusalem and Israel's promises; Philo's heavenly home for the soul is the view they set against it.
entries.dissent: Whether John's city is meant literally. Keener, Beale, Wright and Heiser's podcast read its size as symbolic, and the cultural backgrounds article Dimensions of the New Jerusalem sets it against Babylon's walls, nine miles around. The ESV Study Bible allows literal dimensions, and the Zondervan dictionary reports two views: a symbol of the ideal church, since John is promised the bride and shown the city, or a literal eternal home, which premillennialists have God create at the start of the millennium and keep above earthly Jerusalem until the eternal state. The sources also give different figures for its side: about 1,400 miles (the article) or 1,500 (Keener; the dictionary).

usedIn.n: Hebrews 11:8-16, Strangers looking for a city
usedIn.s: By faith Abraham left home without knowing where he was going and lived in tents in the promised land as a foreigner, waiting for a city with lasting foundations that God himself designed and built. usedIn.s: Believers have not come to the burning, quaking mountain of Sinai but to Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem, with myriads of angels, the assembly of the firstborn enrolled in heaven, God the judge, the spirits of the righteous, and Jesus, whose blood speaks better than Abel's. Since God will shake heaven and earth once more, they are receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken.

usedIn.n: Hebrews 13:7-17, Foods, an altar and outside the camp
usedIn.s: Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and for ever, so the readers must not be carried away by strange teachings about foods. Believers have an altar the tabernacle priests may not eat from; as the bodies of the sin offerings were burned outside the camp, Jesus suffered outside the gate, and they must go out to him, bearing his disgrace, seeking the city to come.

usedIn.n: Revelation 2:1-7, Ephesus and the Nicolaitans
usedIn.s: To Ephesus the one who holds the seven stars praises a church that tested false apostles and hates the works of the Nicolaitans, but warns that it has abandoned its first love and may lose its lampstand. The one who conquers will eat from the tree of life in God's paradise.

usedIn.n: Revelation 3:7-13, Philadelphia and the key of David
usedIn.s: To Philadelphia the one who holds the key of David sets before a weak but faithful church an open door no one can shut. Those of the synagogue of Satan will bow at their feet, and the one who conquers will be a pillar in God's temple, bearing the name of the new Jerusalem.

usedIn.n: Revelation 14:1-5, the Lamb and the 144,000 on Mount Zion
usedIn.s: The Lamb stands on Mount Zion with 144,000 who bear his name and his Father's on their foreheads, singing a new song only they can learn. They have kept themselves pure, follow the Lamb wherever he goes, and are offered as firstfruits to God and the Lamb.

usedIn.n: Revelation 16:12-21, the Euphrates dried and Armageddon
usedIn.s: The sixth bowl dries up the Euphrates to make way for the kings from the east, and three frog-like spirits from the dragon, the beast and the false prophet gather the kings of the world to battle at the place called Armageddon. The seventh bowl brings a voice saying it is done, the greatest earthquake ever, the splitting of the great city and hundred-pound hailstones.

usedIn.n: Revelation 21:1-8, new heaven, new earth, no more sea
usedIn.s: John sees a new heaven and a new earth, with no more sea, and the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down from God like a bride dressed for her husband. A voice announces that God's dwelling is now with people, that he will wipe away every tear, and that he makes all things new; the thirsty will drink freely, while the cowardly, the faithless, murderers, sorcerers, idolaters and liars have their place in the lake of fire.

usedIn.n: Revelation 21:9-27, the city of gold and twelve stones
usedIn.s: An angel carries John to a high mountain to show him the bride, the holy city Jerusalem, shining with God's glory, with twelve gates named for Israel's tribes and twelve foundations named for the Lamb's apostles. The city is a cube of pure gold, its foundations set with twelve precious stones and its gates each a single pearl; it has no temple, since God and the Lamb are its temple, and its gates never shut as the nations bring their glory into it.

usedIn.n: Revelation 22:1-5, river and tree of life
usedIn.s: The angel shows John a clear, life-giving river running from God's throne through the middle of the city, with the tree of life on both banks, fruiting every month and healing the nations with its leaves. Nothing cursed remains; God's servants will see him face to face, carry his name and reign for ever in his light.

entries.title: The Watchers, the flood and the bound angels
entries.summary: Most Jews of the period read the sons of God of Genesis 6:1-4 as angels who took human wives before the flood. Their books, above all 1 Enoch, had the guilty angels bound under the earth in darkness until the judgment, and 1 Peter, 2 Peter and Jude speak of that prison.
aliases: angels who did not keep their positions
did not keep their positions of authority
four angels bound at the Euphrates
entries.plain: **A story everyone in the room already knows, so the speaker only has to name it.** Genesis 6 says that the sons of God took human wives and that giants were born, just before the flood. Most Jews in the first century read those sons of God as angels who rebelled. Their books, above all 1 Enoch, told how God had the guilty angels bound and shut up under the earth in darkness until the last judgment, and how Enoch was sent to tell them their plea had been refused. The flood belonged to the same story, and Noah and the few saved with him became a picture of the people God rescues. 2 Peter and Jude speak of angels who sinned and are kept in chains of darkness, and many readers hear the same story behind the spirits in prison of 1 Peter, though not all agree.
entries.then: Most later rabbis aside, almost every ancient Jewish reader took Genesis 6:1-3 to mean that angels lusted after women and fell in Noah's day. After the flood these angels were said to be imprisoned, below the earth or in the air. Charles's 1 Enoch tells it at length. Two hundred angels led by Semjaza swear an oath and descend on Mount Hermon (6:1-6). Raphael binds Azazel hand and foot and casts him into darkness until the day of judgment (10:4-6). Michael binds Semjaza and his fellows in the earth for seventy generations, after which they go to the abyss of fire (10:11-13). An angel tells Enoch, "This place is the prison of the angels, and here they will be imprisoned for ever" (21:10). When the Watchers ask Enoch to plead for them, he must answer, "from henceforth you shall not ascend into heaven unto all eternity" (14:5). Josephus has angels of God who "accompanied with women, and begat sons that proved unjust", and Noah urging that generation to change (Antiquities 1.3.1). Jewish teachers held the flood generation especially wicked. They used the flood as a pattern of the coming judgment and told of Noah as a preacher of repentance. In Greek myth Tartarus held the worst offenders, the Titans above all. The verb of 2 Peter 2:4 is "the typical word used for the punishment of the Titans" (Dictionary of Deities and Demons), and Jewish writers borrowed the name for the angels' prison. Heiser argues that the angels' punishment comes from 1 Enoch rather than Genesis. He adds that the angelic reading held until it fell from favor in the late fourth century, especially with Augustine.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a famous trial whose verdict everyone in the country remembers. A speaker need only say that the convicts are still behind bars for the audience to supply the rest of the story.
entries.changes: Because the story of the bound angels was widely known, 2 Peter 2:4 can mention angels held in Tartarus in chains of darkness without explaining who they were, and Jude 6 can do the same. Readers who knew that Enoch had been sent to the imprisoned Watchers would hear an echo when 1 Peter 3:19 has Christ make a proclamation to spirits in prison, whoever those spirits are taken to be.
entries.not: **Not a sentence already served.** Convicts behind bars have had their trial and their verdict. In these texts the prison is a holding place where the angels wait for a judgment still to come. Heiser stresses that Tartarus was part of the underworld, the realm of the dead, which is not the same thing as hell.
entries.dissent: First, who the sons of God of Genesis 6 were. The ESV Study Bible sets out three views without choosing: fallen angels, tyrannical human rulers, or godly descendants of Seth. Keener notes that most later rabbis rejected the angelic reading. Heiser argues that no other angelic sin in the Old Testament fits what 2 Peter and Jude describe. The Zondervan dictionary instead reads 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 6 as a fall of angels before Adam's, with no tie to Genesis 6. Second, who the imprisoned spirits of 1 Peter 3:19 are. Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes call the fallen-angel reading the view of most scholars today, and Wright and Bird call it the most likely. Heiser notes that neither the New Testament nor 1 Enoch puts disobedient human souls in a prison. Others read Christ preaching through Noah to the people of his day, which the CSB Study Bible calls plausible and the ESV Study Bible counts among the two best fits. Many church fathers had Christ preach to the dead in Hades between his death and resurrection. Arnold has Christ proclaim his victory to the fallen angels on a descent before the ascension.

entries.title: Babylon as a name for Rome
entries.summary: Babylon burned Jerusalem's first temple and carried Judah into exile. By the first century Jews were calling Rome by its name, and Christians did the same for the city that ruled and scattered them.
entries.plain: **Calling a new enemy by the name of an old one says what you think of it without a speech.** Babylon was the empire that burned Jerusalem's first temple and took Judah into exile. By the first century the old city was a ruin, but its name had become a byword for the power that oppresses God's people. Jewish writers used it for Rome, and when 1 Peter sends greetings from she who is in Babylon, the sources read here take the city to be Rome.
entries.then: Jews of this period saw Rome as the fourth of the four kingdoms of Daniel 7, the successor of Babylon. "Babylon" thus became "a fairly common cryptogram for Rome", even more so after the temple fell in AD 70 (the cultural backgrounds notes). Rome, like Babylon, destroyed the temple and enslaved God's people, though Rome does not exhaust what Babylon means. The old city was still inhabited but had sunk further under the Parthians. The name carried a long memory. Podany dates Nebuchadnezzar II's capture of Jerusalem to March 597 BC and the burning of the temple to 587 BC. She judges his Babylon, so far as the evidence goes, the biggest city on earth in its day. Some Jews had transferred the prophecies of Babylon's fall to the new empire, though later rabbis preferred the name Edom. In the Old Testament Babylon stands for earthly power opposed to God (Isaiah 13-14; Jeremiah 50-51). The CSB Study Bible says the name was used for a place of exile, specifically Rome. The Sibylline Oracles, in Charles's edition, foretell that "Then shall flee from Babylon a king fearful and shameless", meaning Nero. Charles notes, "Babylon probably means Rome"; later lines burn Babylon and Italy, for whose sake many faithful Hebrews perished. Wright and Bird list 4 Ezra, 2 Baruch, the Sibylline Oracles and Revelation as using the name. They note that the Qumran writers could already call Rome the Kittim of Asshur, Assyria, before AD 70. Revelation draws Babylon as a woman. Gentiles pictured their cities as women, and coins showed the goddess Roma seated on Rome's seven hills. The prophets called Tyre and Nineveh harlots for their trade and their sorcery.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a family that calls a ruthless new landlord by the name of the one who evicted their grandparents. Everyone at the table knows what the name means, and the landlord does not need to.
entries.changes: Because Babylon had become a name for the city that ruled and scattered God's people, greetings from she who is in Babylon, in 1 Peter 5:13, place the church in the capital of its exile. Revelation 17:5 names the great city Babylon the great, and Revelation 18:2 announces its fall in words the prophets had spoken against the old Babylon.
entries.not: **Not a private family code.** The family's nickname works because the landlord never hears it. Babylon for Rome was widely understood, and Wright and Bird, following Doering, read it as an open verdict on Rome, the power behind the persecution and scattering of God's people. Nor is it the ruined city on the Euphrates, which the Jews had left well before Peter's day.
entries.dissent: Whether the name points to a date after AD 70. The cultural backgrounds notes say Babylon became a common name for Rome, even more so after the temple's destruction, and Wright and Bird report that some scholars take the usage to require a date after 70. Wright and Bird answer that Qumran writers already equated Rome with the Kittim of Asshur before 70, so the name need not mean Rome as destroyer of the temple. Beale notes that the only early metaphorical uses, in 4 Ezra, 2 Baruch and the Sibylline Oracles, come after 70, and reports J. Christian Wilson's argument that before 70 the name meant exile rather than destruction, which Beale calls plausible but partly an argument from silence. Wright, in his commentary on 1 Peter, questions the identification itself: we cannot be absolutely sure that Babylon there is code for Rome.

entries.title: Sodom and Gomorrah
entries.summary: The cities of the plain that God destroyed with fire in Lot's day. The prophets and later Jewish teachers made Sodom the byword for wickedness and sudden judgment, and its burned ruins by the Dead Sea were still pointed out in the first century.
entries.plain: **A town whose name has become shorthand for disaster.** Genesis 19 tells how God rained fire on Sodom and Gomorrah and rescued Lot and his daughters. The later prophets used Sodom as the name for a people gone completely wrong, and Jewish teachers paired it with the generation of the flood as the two great examples of wickedness and judgment. In the first century people could still look at the scorched land by the Dead Sea. What exactly Sodom's sin had been, the ancient writers did not all say in the same way.
entries.then: Sodom was the epitome of sin in the prophets, who often applied the image to their own people (Deuteronomy 32:32; Isaiah 1:9-10; Ezekiel 16:46-49). Jewish teachers often paired it with the flood generation as the great examples of wickedness. 3 Maccabees 2:5 does so, and the rabbis often do. Sirach 16:7-8 has God not sparing the giants of Noah's day and then Sodom, the same order as 2 Peter 2:4-6. Keener observes that Philo is the exception: hardly any other ancient Jewish writer made the Sodomites' homosexual acts the main charge. Most pointed instead to their inhospitality, their arrogance or sexual immorality in general. Josephus says the Sodomites "grew proud, on account of their riches", were unjust to men and impious toward God. They "hated strangers, and abused themselves with Sodomitical practices" (Antiquities 1.11.1). By the Dead Sea, he writes, "the traces [or shadows] of the five cities are still to be seen", with fruit that turns to smoke and ashes in the hand (War 4.8.4). According to Philo and Wisdom of Solomon 10:7, smoke still rose from the site, and it was taken as a sign of eternal judgment. Jewish tradition was divided over whether Lot was righteous. Most rabbis said he was not, though Genesis shows him personally righteous, and Wisdom of Solomon 10:6 has Wisdom rescue him as the righteous one. Heiser notes that 2 Peter and Jude place the angels' sin before the flood in the same category as Sodom's.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a place name that has become a byword for catastrophe. A speaker need only say it for the whole audience to remember what happened there, and why.
entries.changes: Because Sodom was the standard example of a city judged by God, 2 Peter 2:6 can set it beside the fallen angels and the flood as proof that God judges and rescues, and Jude 7 can call it an example of eternal fire. When Jesus warns in Matthew 10:15 that a town refusing his messengers will fare worse than Sodom, he uses the same byword for a place that rejected God's messengers.
entries.not: **Not a byword everyone read the same way.** A modern byword carries one agreed story of what happened and why. Ancient writers named Sodom's sins differently, pride, contempt for strangers and sexual sin among them, and the New Testament uses the city first as an example of judgment.
entries.dissent: What Jude 7 means by going after strange or other flesh. Wright and Bird read it as the Sodomites' lust for the unnatural flesh of the angelic visitors, and Keener allows that reading, since in the same way as the angels of Jude 6 may imply angels and people having intercourse. Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes also point out that Jewish tradition would not call angels flesh and that the Sodomites did not know their visitors were angels, so that attempted homosexual acts may be in view; the ESV Study Bible takes the phrase as the homosexual activity of Sodom, citing Josephus and Philo.

entries.title: Balaam, the prophet for hire
entries.summary: The seer from beyond the Euphrates whom Moab's king hired to curse Israel, who could only bless, and who then, Numbers says, showed Midian how to lead Israel into sin. Jewish tradition remembered him as the greatest prophet of the Gentiles and a byword for greed.
entries.plain: **The expert who sells his gift to whoever pays.** In Numbers 22 to 24 the king of Moab hires Balaam to curse Israel, and on the way his donkey sees God's angel before the prophet does. Balaam ends up blessing Israel instead. But Numbers 31 says that he later advised the Midianites, and Israel fell into sexual sin and the worship of other gods. Jewish readers remembered him as a powerful prophet who used his gift for money and for harm.
entries.then: In Jewish tradition, and in the likeliest reading of the Old Testament, Balaam was dishonorable. Keener explains that he took money to lure Israel into sacred prostitution with Midian, which brought judgment on Israel and death on himself (Numbers 31:8, 16; Joshua 13:22). Jewish literature counted him the greatest prophet of the Gentiles, sometimes their philosopher. It judged his scheme worse than any enemy's attack because it brought God's judgment on Israel. Inspired, he knew God blessed those who blessed Israel, yet for wealth he showed Israel's enemies how to strip away God's protection. Josephus has Balaam tell the Midianites to "set out the handsomest of such of your daughters as are most eminent for beauty". The aim was to draw the young Hebrews away from their laws to the gods of Midian, and the Midianites do so (Antiquities 4.6.6-7). Philo made Balaam a figure for fools, the rabbis said that those who walk in his paths inherit hell, and tradition lengthened the donkey's rebuke. The CSB Study Bible notes that the donkey showed more moral sense than its rider. The ESV Study Bible stresses his greed, a life of gain at others' expense. Jewish tradition made Cain and Balaam symbols of leaders in wickedness, and Korah, who rebelled against Moses (Numbers 16), the standard rebel against the law. The ESV Study Bible says all three were discontent with the place God gave them. In Revelation 2:14 Balaam is probably a nickname for a local teacher who claimed to speak for God, as Jezebel is at Thyatira. Beale notes that rabbis explained the name Balaam much as Nicolaitan can be explained: he overcomes the people.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a celebrated consultant who, denied one fee, quietly sells the other side a better plan. People remember the talent, and they remember the betrayal more.
entries.changes: Because Balaam was remembered as a gifted prophet who sold his gift and led Israel into sin, false teachers who follow the way of Balaam in 2 Peter 2:15 stand accused of greed and of leading others into immorality. Jude 11 sets him beside Cain and Korah, and Revelation 2:14 names his teaching at Pergamum, where it means eating food offered to idols and sexual immorality.
entries.not: **Not a free agent selling his own ideas.** A consultant owns his expertise. Balaam's gift was prophecy from God: in Numbers he speaks true oracles and blesses Israel, and the tradition faults him for selling advice that stripped away the very protection he had announced.

entries.title: Light and darkness
entries.summary: Jewish writers, the Dead Sea Scrolls above all, divided people into children of light and children of darkness, and pictured the present age as darkness that the coming age of light would end. John, Paul and Jesus use the same contrast.
entries.plain: **We say someone was kept in the dark, or that the truth came to light.** In the Bible light goes with God, knowledge and goodness, and darkness with ignorance and wrong. In Jesus' day some Jewish groups pushed the picture further. The people behind the Dead Sea Scrolls called themselves the children of light and everyone outside the children of darkness, and they expected a last battle in which light would win. They also spoke of a spirit of truth and a spirit of error at work in people. John uses much of the same language, and the sources are careful about how far he shares the Scrolls' outlook.
entries.then: Jewish texts, especially the Dead Sea Scrolls, used light and darkness to set the followers of righteousness against those of sin. From Scripture they held that God is wholly righteous (Psalm 92:15). The Scrolls named the two camps children of light and children of darkness, and sometimes called the faithful the children of God's truth. Wright and Bird describe the War Scroll as a liturgy of "an end-time battle between the sons of light and the sons of darkness". After Pompey took Jerusalem, they add, some Jews cast Rome as "the power of darkness ranged against the children of light". Many Jewish traditions pictured the present age as ruled mostly by darkness and the age to come as light's triumph. In the Scrolls light was predestined to win. The Scrolls went further and made every act the work of a spirit of truth or a spirit of error. Outside them the rabbis taught a similar doctrine of two impulses. Keener calls the Testament of Judah 20 the closest parallel to two spirits, but it is often suspected of Christian additions, so the question is not settled. In the Old Testament light stands for both knowledge and purity, and walking in darkness meant the danger of stumbling. Paul pairs day with light and night with darkness as common images for good and evil, and children of meant people marked by something. Wright and Bird read John's contrast as an overlap of light and darkness in a world where the age to come has begun while the old age goes on. They find the labels apocalyptic and dualism too many-sided to help.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a film that lights its heroes and leaves its villains in shadow. The audience can tell who stands on which side from the lighting alone, before anyone speaks a line.
entries.changes: Because light and darkness already named the two sides of good and evil, Jesus can urge his hearers to become children of light in John 12:36 without explaining the phrase, and Paul can tell the Thessalonians that they are children of the day in 1 Thessalonians 5:5. 1 John 1:5 builds its first test on the claim that God is light, with no darkness in him at all.
entries.not: **Not a matter of fixed casting.** In a film the lighting is set before the scene and never changes. John calls his hearers to walk in the light and become children of light. Keener and the cultural backgrounds notes stress that he stops short of the Scrolls' view that every act is fixed by one spirit or the other.

entries.title: The book of Enoch
entries.summary: A collection of Jewish writings in the name of Enoch, who walked with God and was taken, composed over the last centuries before Christ and widely read in the first. It tells of the fallen Watchers and the coming judgment, and Jude quotes it by name.
aliases: ten thousands of his holy ones
entries.plain: **A well-loved old book everyone in a community has read, even though it never made it into the official collection.** Genesis says only that Enoch walked with God and then was gone, because God took him. Centuries later Jewish writers composed several books in his name, telling of his journeys through the heavens, the angels called Watchers who sinned and were bound, and the judgment to come. In the first century these writings were widely read, and Jude quotes them as Enoch's prophecy. Whether Jude counted the book as Scripture, as a true report on one point, or as an illustration his readers would know, is read in more than one way.
entries.then: The work Jude quotes "is not genuinely by Enoch but was widely circulated", the cultural backgrounds notes say, and it is normally dated to the second century BC. Keener writes that Jude cites a popular story still extant, and that the passage reflects themes running through that whole section of the book. Its makeup is described in different ways. Wright and Bird call it "a composite document made up of five major books" compiled from roughly 200 BC to AD 300, with the date of the Parables (chapters 37-71) disputed. Heiser reports the current consensus that it is "a composite of seven separate composed works". In his account these date from at least the second century BC and were complete by the end of the first century AD. Its first part, the Book of the Watchers (chapters 1-36), tells of the angels who sinned before the flood. Heiser writes, "That book informed the thinking of Peter and Jude". In Charles's translation of 1 Enoch 1:9 the Lord comes with his holy ones in their tens of thousands "To execute judgement upon all", the words of Jude 14-15. Second Temple readers took Enoch for God's spokesman, Heiser explains, because he carried God's verdict to the fallen sons of God (1 Enoch 13-16). Some early Christians gave the book high standing. The Dictionary of Deities and Demons notes that the Enochic literature "is treated as prophecy in Jude 14". It adds that the Epistle of Barnabas and Tertullian supported its authority. Heiser quotes Tertullian's argument that "Enoch possesses a testimony in the Apostle Jude". He reports that Origen cited it as Scripture while admitting that not all the churches accepted it. Wright and Bird add that the Ethiopian Orthodox Church still counts it in its canon.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a preacher quoting a line from a classic novel the whole congregation has read. Everyone recognizes it at once, and the quotation carries weight, whatever status the novel itself is given.
entries.changes: Because the book of Enoch was widely read, Jude can quote its opening prophecy by name in Jude 14-15 and expect his readers to know it. Its story of the bound Watchers lies behind the angels held in chains of darkness in 2 Peter 2:4, and many readers hear it behind the spirits in prison of 1 Peter 3:19.
entries.not: **Not a novel everyone knew to be fiction.** A classic novel is read as a story by author and audience alike. 1 Enoch was written in Enoch's name, and some early Christians treated it as prophecy, even Scripture, while the synagogue and most churches did not; only the Ethiopian church gave it full canonical standing.
entries.dissent: What Jude's quotation says about the book's standing. The ESV Study Bible says Jude cites its content as true and prophetic in this instance, but that using a nonbiblical source does not put the book in the same category as Scripture; the CSB Study Bible writes that "this does not mean that Jude viewed these noncanonical books as authoritative Scripture", only that he used them as illustrations. The cultural backgrounds notes say the message of the lines quoted "may be prophetic". Wright and Bird list three possibilities, that Jude thought the texts true as history, true as principles, or merely illustrative, and add that with no fixed canon yet "Jude may well have regarded these texts as on par with scripture!" Heiser stresses that the book shaped Peter's and Jude's thinking and traces early writers who treated it as Scripture. Carson, Moo and Morris record the reverse effect: "some in the early church were sure that no canonical writer would do this", and doubted Jude for a time.

entries.title: Apocalypses, visions and numbers that mean something
entries.summary: Jewish books of visions, usually written in the name of a hero from long ago, in which a heavenly guide shows a seer what heaven sees in the present trouble and how God will end it. They spoke in pictures and in numbers that carried meaning, and Revelation is the one that calls itself an apocalypse.
aliases: time, times and half a time
entries.plain: **Nobody thinks the fat cat in a political cartoon is a real animal, but everyone gets the point.** An apocalypse was a kind of Jewish book in which a seer is shown hidden things, often by an angel who explains them: what heaven sees in the present trouble, and how God will put things right. Most were written under the name of a hero from long ago, such as Enoch, Moses or Ezra. They spoke in pictures, and in numbers that carried meaning, seven above all. Revelation borrows the form but names its own author and writes to real churches. How far its pictures and numbers stand for literal events is read in more than one way.
entries.then: Revelation calls itself a revelation, apokalypsis, an unveiling. It also calls itself a prophecy, and it is framed as a letter. Jewish apocalypses were usually written in the name of a figure from the distant past: Enoch, Abraham, Moses, Baruch or Ezra. That borrowed ancient authority and presented recent events as prophecy fulfilled (Wright and Bird). John writes in his own name, which the cultural backgrounds notes tie to the early Christian belief that prophecy was still alive. Revelations often came through angels and guides. Wright and Bird cite a standard definition. An apocalypse is a revelation passed by an otherworldly being to a human, disclosing a reality both future and heavenly, meant to shape how readers see the present. Most of Revelation's images have roots in Isaiah, Ezekiel, Daniel and Zechariah. The dominant ones, though, are those popular in 1 Enoch, 4 Ezra and 2 Baruch. Keener calls much of John's symbolic language "evocative imagery", meant to stir a response more than to draw a literal picture. John sometimes explains a symbol himself (1:20). Numbers worked the same way: symbolic numbers "were standard fare in Jewish views of the future" (Keener). Beale reports general agreement among commentators that three, four, seven and twelve and their multiples carry meanings drawn from the Old Testament, seven above all for completeness. Ten thousand was the largest single number in Greek, so myriads of myriads meant beyond counting. Daniel's 1,260 days, forty-two months and three and a half years are one span on a 360-day year. Works that could be read as foretelling Rome's fall were politically dangerous, and the circles that wrote them were quickly repressed.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a newspaper under occupation that reports the news as fables. Its readers know who the wolf is and take heart, the censor may not, and nobody reads the fable as a lesson about animals.
entries.changes: Because apocalypses spoke in pictures and in numbers that carried meaning, John can explain in Revelation 1:20 that his seven lampstands are churches, and a reader has to ask of each later picture and number what it stands for. The ESV Study Bible sets Jesus' words about the darkened sun and falling stars in Mark 13:24-25 and Paul's man of lawlessness in 2 Thessalonians 2:3 in the same apocalyptic wing of prophecy.
entries.not: **Not a disguise for the present alone.** An occupied newspaper's fables are all about today's news. Ancient apocalypses often did speak of the future, sometimes in detail, and first readers would have heard at least Revelation's closing visions as still to come. Many seers probably had real visionary experiences, so the form was not always only a literary device.
entries.dissent: What kind of literature this is. The ESV Study Bible describes Jewish apocalyptic as pessimistic, splitting humanity into two fixed camps, and sets Revelation apart from it. Wright and Bird trace the charge of dualism to a fear among some nineteenth-century scholars and say such books share the scriptural belief that heaven and earth overlap. Whether Revelation is one. Carson, Moo and Morris are reluctant to call it an apocalypse, since John writes in his own name and grounds hope in the slain Lamb. They call it "a prophecy cast in an apocalyptic mold and written down in a letter form". The Zondervan dictionary files it with apocalyptic literature. How to read the numbers. Beale takes them as symbolic for the same reason the pictures are, while noting that literal interpreters argue for a consistently literal reading. Keener says the 144,000 must be read either consistently literally or consistently symbolically, and the CSB Study Bible calls the most literal reading of that number "highly plausible". The cultural backgrounds notes and Keener set out the main ways of reading the book: idealist, historicist, preterist, futurist and blends of them.

entries.title: The plagues of Egypt
entries.summary: The blows God struck on Egypt before the exodus, from water turned to blood to the death of the firstborn, while Israel was spared. Revelation's trumpets and bowls replay them on the whole world.
entries.plain: **A remake can shuffle the scenes of a film everyone has seen, and the audience still knows the story.** Before Israel left Egypt, God struck the land with plagues: water turned to blood, hail, locusts, darkness and at last the death of the firstborn, while Israel was spared. Every Jewish reader knew that story by heart. Revelation's trumpets, and later its bowls, retell those plagues on a world scale, in a new order and in sets of seven. Whether these plagues mainly warn people to turn back or mainly judge those already hardened is read in more than one way.
entries.then: Keener writes that the trumpet and bowl judgments draw chiefly on the ten plagues of Egypt, reworked into sevens. Other Jewish retellings, such as Pseudo-Philo and Artapanus, also treated the number and order of the plagues freely. Beale sets out the pattern. The first trumpet matches the hail of Exodus 9, and the second and third the water turned to blood of Exodus 7. The fourth matches the darkness of Exodus 10 and the fifth its locusts, though the order differs. Wright and the cultural backgrounds notes read the trumpets the same way. Beale adds that each Egyptian plague was suited to a particular Egyptian god and so was a judgment on that god. The cultural backgrounds notes link the darkness with Egypt's sun god (Exodus 12:12). God had protected his people in Goshen during the plagues, and the seal on the foreheads of God's servants in Revelation 7 plays the same part. The blood of the Passover lamb delivered Israel from the last plague, so the slain Lamb of Revelation 5 is the one whose blood shields his people. Pharaoh's refusal set the pattern for a world that will not turn. Jewish people counted unrepentance in the face of plain judgments as folly. Jewish thinkers, with many Gentiles, held that God sends such judgments in mercy, to invite repentance. The cultural backgrounds notes add that John is doing more than retelling the exodus: he describes judgments on the whole world in the language of the familiar biblical story.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a protest song set to a hymn tune everyone knows. The words are about today, but the tune tells the listeners which old story they are standing in.
entries.changes: Because every Jewish reader knew the plagues on Egypt, the hail, bloodied waters, darkness and locusts that follow the trumpets from Revelation 8:7 onward announce a new exodus, with God's sealed people spared as Israel was in Goshen. Paul quotes God's word to Pharaoh from the plague story in Romans 9:17, and Stephen recalls the wonders done in Egypt in Acts 7:36.
entries.not: **Not the old tune left untouched.** A protest song keeps the hymn's melody note for note. John reorders the plagues and fits them into sevens, and the target is now the whole world rather than one nation; the old story supplies the pattern, not a script.
entries.dissent: What the plagues are for. Beale argues that, as in Exodus, where God had already hardened Pharaoh's heart, the trumpet plagues are best seen less as warnings meant to bring the majority to repentance than as judgments on those already hardened, though they carry a warning too. The cultural backgrounds notes and Keener stress that God sends such judgments mercifully, to invite repentance, and the cultural backgrounds notes add that striking only a third or a tenth leaves the majority a chance to turn.

entries.title: Daniel's four beasts and the fourth kingdom
entries.summary: Daniel 7 pictured four empires as four beasts rising from the sea, the last with ten horns, judged before one like a son of man receives the kingdom. In the first century many Jews read the fourth beast as Rome.
entries.plain: **Political cartoons have long drawn nations as animals, a bear for one and an eagle for another, and readers know at once who is meant.** In Daniel 7 a prophet sees four beasts climb out of the sea: a lion, a bear, a leopard and a fourth beast with iron teeth and ten horns. They stand for empires that rule one after another until God judges them and gives the kingdom to one like a son of man. By the first century many Jews read the fourth beast as Rome, so when Revelation's beast comes out of the sea with parts of all four, hearers who knew Daniel knew what kind of power they were looking at. Which empire Daniel himself meant, and how far the picture reaches beyond Rome, are read in more than one way.
entries.then: Daniel's four beasts stood for four successive empires. Keener notes that Daniel's fourth meant Alexander's Greek empire, while readers in John's time commonly took it as Rome. Jewish tradition in this period understood the fourth beast as Rome, which most Jews took to be the fourth world empire to subdue Israel. Wright calls Daniel 7 a chapter "hugely popular in the first century". Many believed it foretold the overthrow of pagan empire and the rise of God's people. So it was studied for clues, and fresh expositions such as 4 Ezra were written. 4 Ezra also has Rome, as an eagle, rise from the sea, and Beale notes that the later Midrash on Psalms names Rome as Daniel's fourth kingdom. Revelation's beast takes the leopard, the bear's feet, the lion's mouth and the ten horns into one body, a composite of all four. The cultural backgrounds notes and Keener take its ten horns as the client kings Rome allowed to rule, whose number varied. The Greek word for beast, therion, meant a wild animal. In mythic imagery it could name a griffin, a hydra or a dragon, and Daniel 7 sets the pattern for most of its uses in Revelation.
entries.bridge: An analogy: a villain's part handed from actor to actor in a long-running series. Viewers know the part the moment it appears, whoever is wearing the costume this time.
entries.changes: Because Daniel's beasts were read as empires and the fourth as Rome, a beast rising from the sea in Revelation 13:1 names a kind of power, which in their day was Rome. The ESV Study Bible notes that some identify that beast with the man of lawlessness of 2 Thessalonians 2:3-12, while the Daniel 7 imagery shows it stands for present world powers as well as any future figure.
entries.not: **Not a part that exists apart from the players.** In a series the role is written before anyone plays it. In Daniel and Revelation the beast is the empire itself, judged for what it does, and the sources disagree over whether John meant Rome alone or every empire that demands absolute allegiance.
entries.dissent: Which empire the beast stands for. Keener says Daniel's fourth beast was the Greek empire of Alexander, reread as Rome in John's day, and Wright puts it bluntly: "The monster is Rome." The ESV Study Bible reads Revelation's composite beast as every human empire that demands absolute allegiance, from Egypt and Assyria to Rome and its successors, and notes that some identify it with a future Antichrist. Beale reads it as oppressive world government through the ages, whose first-century form was Rome.

entries.title: The thousand years
entries.summary: Several Jewish apocalypses expected an in-between kingdom, a reign of the Messiah or an age of peace between the present age and the final judgment, of varying length. Revelation 20 gives it a thousand years, and Christians have read that span in three main ways ever since.
entries.plain: **A long holiday weekend sits between the working week and the next one, and families argue about whether it has started yet.** Several Jewish books from this period expected a stretch of time between the present troubled age and God's final judgment, sometimes a reign of the Messiah, sometimes a last time of trouble, and they gave it different lengths. In Revelation 20 Satan is bound, the martyrs come to life and reign with the Messiah for a thousand years, and only then come the last battle and the judgment. Christians have read that thousand years as a future reign after Jesus returns, as a golden age before he returns, or as a picture of the present age, and the sources set out each view without settling it.
entries.then: Keener writes that "Many Jewish texts pictured an intermediate kingdom between the present and future eternal reign". In some it was an age of messianic peace, in others the last tribulation, later called the messianic travail. Its length varied: forty years, three generations, four hundred years and other figures. A few writers divided history into seven periods of a thousand years, with the last one a time of peace. Keener suggests that Psalm 90:4, a thousand years as a day, applied to the days of Genesis 1, explains the number. The cultural backgrounds article The Millennium adds a Gentile prophecy of Rome falling after 6,000 years, "followed by a 1,000-year period of peace". Some Jews pictured a final thousand years as a Sabbath. Wright and Bird list interim messianic reigns in 1 Enoch 91 and 93, 4 Ezra 7 and 12, 2 Baruch 29-30, 40 and 72-74 and the Sibylline Oracles. Revelation 20 to 22 follows the order of Ezekiel 37 to 48: the dry bones raised, the war with Gog and then the new temple and city. Binding an evil power for a set time was also familiar. Beale points to Jubilees, where the chief evil spirit is bound so that he cannot accuse Israel. He also points to Isaiah 24:21-22, where the host of heaven is shut in a pit and punished after many days. Many early church fathers, Papias, Melito, Justin, Irenaeus and Tertullian among them, expected a literal reign, and amillennialism grew popular only after Constantine (Wright and Bird). Other fathers found the doctrine abhorrent for its supposed Jewish roots and materialism (Carson, Moo and Morris). By Eusebius's day its holders were "apparently an easily dissuaded minority" (the article).
entries.bridge: An analogy: the interval in a long play. Everyone agrees there is one in the script, but some think it comes after the final act, some think the play is in it now, and some think it is still to come.
entries.changes: Because Jewish hearers knew of an in-between kingdom before the end, the thousand-year reign of Revelation 20:4-6 would sound like a known hope given a Christian shape, not an invention. Wright and Bird take the martyrs' reign as Revelation's picture of what Ephesians 2:6 and Colossians 3:1 say of all believers, seated with Christ in heaven.
entries.not: **Not a break of fixed length.** A play's interval is a set pause that everyone sits through. Jewish writers gave the interim kingdom many lengths and meanings, and Wright, among others, reads Revelation's thousand years as a symbol rather than a measured span.
entries.dissent: How to read the thousand years. The ESV Study Bible sets out three main views. Premillennialists expect a future, usually literal, reign after Christ returns. Postmillennialists expect the gospel to transform societies for a long age of peace before he returns. Amillennialists take the thousand years as the present church age. Keener names Augustine, Calvin and Luther among the amillennialists, Irenaeus and Justin among the premillennialists, and Edwards among the postmillennialists. He says the narrative most naturally reads as a future period, though his commentary takes no side. Wright reads the number as symbolic, the martyrs sharing the Messiah's rule now. Beale reads Satan's binding as Christ's restraint of his power to deceive the nations through the church age, begun at the cross. The cultural backgrounds article gives the strongest case each way. For a future reign it cites the logic of the narrative, with Satan plainly unbound in chapters 12-13. For the present age it cites the absence of an interim kingdom elsewhere in the New Testament and Revelation's habit of retelling its judgments in cycles. Heiser's podcast reads the binding as the church age while expecting a literal, unending kingdom on a renewed earth, and refuses both labels.
